en: Vyāsa said: Those who have beheld with their very eyes Someśa—the ancient Puruṣa who is praised everywhere and who is joined by the gods—on the surface of the earth, having crossed over the vast expanse of the fear of worldly existence (bhava), become adorned with prosperity and proceed to heaven by means of excellent celestial vehicles, just as performers of sacrifice go there through their meritorious rites.
Salutations to the one whose form is pure consciousness alone, whose body consists of the thirty-six principles, whose nature is composed of pure nectar, and in whom the *bindu* and *nāda* expand.
All the gods die even while nectar remains within their bellies; may he who lives even with poison situated in his throat protect you.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the great ṛṣis of Naimiṣa questioned the sinless Sūta Romaharṣaṇa regarding the meritorious Purāṇasaṃhitā.
O Sūta of great intelligence, you have properly served the Blessed One Vyāsa, the best among the knowers of Brahman, regarding the meaning of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Because all his body hairs were made to bristle with joy by your words, he became known as Romaharṣaṇa (the Hair-raiser) through the power of Dvaipāyana.
The Lord Vyāsa himself first addressed you alone to speak the Puranic narrative, the compendium of the sages.

For you, O Hari, the Supreme Person, were born by means of a portion of yourself at the Svāyambhuva sacrifice on the day of the Soma-pressing, when the ritual was spread out, in order to proclaim the Saṃhitā.
Therefore, we ask you concerning the Purāṇa glorified by Skanda: regarding the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, the Brāhmī pilgrimage was heard of in the past.
O master proficient in the meaning of the Purāṇas, you ought now to describe to us the Vaiṣṇava and Raudra pilgrimages, which are endowed with all benefits.
Having heard the words of the sages, Sūta, the best of those versed in the Purāṇas, bowed his head and spoke to Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.

Romaharṣaṇa said: [I bow] to the one marked with the Śrīvatsa, the source of the universe, Hari, whose form is the syllable Om, the immeasurable Guru, the God who is stainless and the refuge of the stainless. (12)
The swan dwelling in purity, pervading the sky, the bestower of all, auspicious, indifferent, effortless, free from conceptual proliferation, and stainless. (13)
One should meditate upon that which is empty, whose nature is the bindu, and which is beyond meditation; that which they call "it exists" and "it does not exist," and which is both far away and near.
The supreme abode, graspable by the mind, called the Puruṣa, consisting of the universe, seated within the lotus of the heart, whose form is splendor, and who is beyond the senses. || 15 ||
Having thus paid homage to the Supreme Self, the Lord, I shall relate the two-fold narrative, which likewise possesses two bodies.
Endowed with the divine language, joined with the foundation of the Vedas, possessed of the five junctures, and adorned with the six ornaments. || 17 ||
Endowed with the seven means of accomplishment, colored by the eight qualities of aesthetic flavor (rasa), filled with the nine virtues, and free from the ten defects. || 18 ||
Likewise, it is adorned with the Vibhāṣā, captivating as it rests solely upon [the Buddha], endowed with five causes, and esteemed for its fourfold efficacy. || 19 ||
Furthermore, listen to that meritorious and sin-destroying [account], which likewise bestows a multitude of knowledges, spoken by Vyāsa and consisting of two parts. || 20 ||
Having heard which, even one who has committed evil deeds shall indeed go to the supreme goal—liberated from the threefold suffering and freed from all afflictions. (21)
One should never speak this meritorious discourse to an atheist; it should be recited for a twice-born who is faithful and tranquil.

He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending with the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras is eligible for this scripture; it should be known that no one else is so eligible. (23)
Purity belongs to the Brahmin who is bright on all four sides; one of virtuous conduct has the right to this scripture which is in accord with the Vedas. (24)
Just as Maheśvara is the supreme god among the gods, as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes; || 25 ||

Just as the syllable *oṃ* is the foremost among all letters, just as the mother is the most venerable among those worthy of honor, and just as the father is the foremost among gurus, even so, the *Skandapurāṇa* is proclaimed to be the preeminent among all scriptures. (26)
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, in the presence of Brahmā and the other gods, the Skanda Purāṇa was narrated by the wielder of the Pināka bow before Pārvatī.
By Pārvatī it was told before the six-faced one (Kārttikeya); by him to the attendant Nandin; by Nandin to Kumāra; and by him to the wise Vyāsa.
It was related to me by Vyāsa; I shall proclaim it to you.
Since you are all great sages endowed with true being, I have the confidence to speak the Skanda-saṃhitā to you.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Chapter on Questions," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: Tell us the definition of a narrative (kathā), along with its qualities and defects in detail; and the examination of the characteristics of poetry composed by seers and that composed by humans. O one of great intelligence, how is this to be known? We wish to hear it.
Sūta said: Now, I shall briefly describe the sequence of the Purāṇas, as well as their characteristics, their number, and likewise their stated divisions.
In ancient times, the Grandfather of the immortals performed severe penance; from that, the Vedas appeared along with their six auxiliary limbs, word-for-word analyses, and step-by-step recitations.

Then [he spoke] the entire ancient Purāṇa, which consists of all the scriptures, is eternal and fixed, composed of the word that is perpetual, meritorious, and extends for hundreds of millions of verses.
The Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, the Bhāgavata, the Bhaviṣya, and the Nāradīyaka emerged from the mouth of Brahmā.
Then the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, and the Brahmavaivarta; likewise the Laiṅga, the Vārāha, the Skānda, and the Vāmana.
The Kaurmya, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and immediately after that the Vāyavīya; the eighteenth is thus designated, which destroys all sins.
Indeed, in the beginning there was only one cosmic egg, which [later] became divided into a hundred crores.
Then, having divided [the Veda] into eighteen parts in age after age, Vedavyāsa, who is born as a direct portion of Nārāyaṇa, makes it renowned in this world.
Other Upapurāṇas have indeed been narrated by the Sage; I shall recount them to you in brief, so let them be understood. (10)
The first is that spoken by Sanatkumāra; after that is the Nārasiṃha; the third is designated as the Skānda, which was related by Kumāra.
The fourth is called the Śivadharmākhya, spoken directly by Nandīśa; after that is the wonderful one spoken by Durvāsas, and beyond that is the one spoken by Nārada.
The Kāpila, the Mānava, and likewise that which was proclaimed by Uśanas; the Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and another called the Kālikā.
Likewise, the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, the Saura which contains the collection of all goals, the supreme Parāśarokta, the Mārīca, and that called Bhārgava. || 14 ||
These Upapurāṇas have been recounted, O best of the twice-born. || 15 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, you who know everything without exception, tell us in detail and in due order the number of Purāṇas, as well as the dharma of giving, according to the proper sequence.
Sūta said: Listen now to that which the Ancient Person, the Soul of the Universe, spoke in this Purāṇa to Manu in the past. || 17 ||
Among all the scriptures, the Purāṇa known as the Brahmāṇḍa is remembered as the first; immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths. (18)

In that previous kalpa, there was only one Purāṇa, which was meritorious, the means for achieving the three aims of life (trivarga), and extended to a vast extent of one hundred crores [of verses]. (19)

When the worlds had been utterly consumed by Kṛṣṇa, who possesses infinite forms, [he retrieved] the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, as well as the Purāṇas and the extensive treatises on Nyāya.
Having taken hold of the Mīmāṃsā and the Dharmaśāstra, he made them his own; and again, at the beginning of the Kalpa, in the form of a fish, [he recovered them] from the ocean of water.
It was told in its entirety to Brahmā, who possesses divine vision; and Brahmā, whose perception knows the three periods of time, spoke it to the sages.
From that, the manifestation of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa occurred.
Then, in the course of time, that Hari, assuming the form of Vyāsa, will condense the eighteen Purāṇas in age after age.
In every Dvāpara age, it always consists of four hundred thousand verses; then, O Kṛṣṇa, it is proclaimed in eighteen divisions here in this world of Bhūrloka.
Even today, that [work] exists in the world of the gods with an extent of one hundred crores; its meaning has been set down here in a concise form of four hundred thousand [verses].
Eighteen Purāṇas exist; they shall now be mentioned here. O best of sages, I will state them by name and their number. (27)
That which was previously declared by Brahmā to Marīci, consisting of ten thousand verses, is here called the Brāhma Purāṇa.
And whoever, having written this, should give it along with a water-cow on the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
When this very world became a lotus made of gold, that [Purāṇa] which contains the account of its origin is called the Pādma by the wise.

That Padma Purāṇa is recited here as consisting of fifty-five thousand [verses]. He who gives that Purāṇa, accompanied by a golden lotus and sesame seeds in the month of Jyeṣṭha, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. || 31 ||
That wherein the Supreme Being, higher than the highest, speaks all dharmas concerning the events of the Vārāha-kalpa, that they know as the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
They know that Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, which is adorned with the deeds of Viṣṇu, to consist of twenty-three thousand verses; thus it is proclaimed. (33)
Furthermore, he who gives [this] in the month of Āṣāḍha, accompanied by a ghee-cow, on the pure full-moon day, attains the state of Viṣṇu.
Then, in the course of the discussion on the Śrutakalpa, Anvayu spoke of the Dharma; therein was that which pertained to Vāyu, joined with the majesty of Rudra.
It consists of twenty-four thousand verses, contains various narratives, and is endowed with the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the conduct of the virtuous. (36)

On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that man who gives to a Brahmin with a family a cow made of jaggery combined with curd, shall become a purified soul and dwell in the world of Śiva for one kalpa.

Again, that mortal is born as a Brāhmaṇa, the most excellent among those who know the Vedas; he is a knower of the true meaning of Vedic knowledge and sciences, and the most excellent among those who understand the reality of the meaning of the commentaries. || 38 ||
That work in which the expansion of dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī, and which includes the slaying of the asura Vṛtra, is called the Bhāgavata. (39)
Whatever men and gods there may be during the Kalpa of Sārasvata, [this work contains] the merit arising from their history, together with the account of their meritorious marriages.
And whoever, having written this, should give it away together with a golden lion on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, goes to the supreme goal.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of eighteen thousand verses. || 42 ||
In this [Purāṇa], Nārada proclaimed the dharmas based on the Bṛhatkalpa; consisting of twenty-five thousand verses, it is called the Nāradīya.

He who gives [this gift] together with a cow on the fifteenth day of that month attains the highest perfection in this world and in the next; he obtains all his desires—there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
That Purāṇa which, concerning the birds, deals with the investigation of dharma and adharma, consists of nine thousand verses and is called the Mārkaṇḍeya. (45)
And he who, having drawn [the image], should give it along with a golden elephant on the full moon day of Kārttika, shall partake in the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice. (46)
That which was spoken by Agni to Vasiṣṭha concerning the events of the Īśāna Kalpa is proclaimed as the Āgneya Purāṇa.

Having written this and given it away, accompanied by a golden lotus, according to the prescribed rite in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise joined with a cow made of sesame seeds—that work, consisting of sixteen thousand verses, bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. (48)

In this [work], the four-faced Lord of the World, having taken as his subject the majesty of the Sun, recounted in the context of the events of the Aghora Kalpa the characteristics of the multitude of living beings to Manu.
Fourteen thousand and five hundred [verses] are spoken here as the Bhaviṣya, which consists primarily of accounts of future events.
He who, free from envy, gives this on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, accompanied by a jar of molasses, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Based on the account of the Rathantara Kalpa, the deeds of Brahmavarāha—endowed with the majesty of Kṛṣṇa—as they were told by Sāvarṇi to Nārada, are here described.

That *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* is said to consist of eighteen thousand verses. Whoever gives this *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* to an excellent Brāhmaṇa on the full moon day of the month of Māgha is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
There, situated in the midst of the emblem of fire (agniliṅga), the Lord Maheśvara spoke concerning the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, with reference to the Āgneya [Purāṇa].
That Purāṇa was called the Laiṅga by Brahmā himself in the past.
He who bestows that eleven-thousand [verse collection] on the full moon day of Phālguna, together with a sesame-cow, attains identity with Śiva.
Furthermore, concerning the majesty of Mahāvarāha, that which was spoken by Viṣṇu to the Earth is here called the Vārāha [Purāṇa]. (57)
O best of sages, on account of its connection with Mānava, that Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses.
Having fashioned a golden Garuḍa together with a sesame-cow, one should give it on the full-moon day to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family; by the grace of Vārāha, he attains the station of Viṣṇu.
In which, concerning the dharmas of Maheśvara and regarding the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), it is augmented by the deeds that occurred during the Tatpuruṣa Kalpa.
The Purāṇa named Skānda is said to consist of eighty-one thousand verses; thus it is recited among mortals. (61)
And he who, having drawn a picture, should give it along with a golden trident, attains the state of Śiva when the sun enters Capricorn.
The Four-faced One (Brahmā), concerning the majesty of Trivikrama, expounded upon the three goals of life; that [work] is celebrated as the Vāmana Purāṇa.
The auspicious Purāṇa consisting of ten thousand verses, which follows the Kaurma Kalpa.
He who gives [this] at the autumnal equinox, accompanied by gold and cloth, covered with linen, and joined with a cow, goes indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu.
And Janārdana, in the form of a tortoise, recounted the majesty of dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation within the netherworld (rasātala).
In connection with Indradyumna, in the presence of Śakra, seventeen thousand sages [recited] the Lakṣmī-kalpa as an incidental discourse.
The man who gives a tortoise made of gold, complete with a tortoise-vehicle, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Wherein Janārdana, in the form of a fish at the beginning of the kalpa, [bestowed] the Narasiṃha description upon Manu for the sake of setting the Vedas in motion. (69)
O you who observe the vows of sages, know that it was concerning these fourteen thousand verses that he spoke of the events of seven kalpas; that is known as the Mātsya Purāṇa.
At the equinox, he who gives a golden fish together with a cow and a pair of linen garments, by him the entire earth is given.
Or when, in the Garuḍa-kalpa, Garuḍa emerged from the cosmic egg (Viśvāṇḍa), Kṛṣṇa spoke with reference to that; therefore, it is here called the Gāruḍa.

Then, eighteen thousand and one [verses] are recited here; he who gives [this manuscript] adorned with golden swans during the latter solstice (ayana) attains preeminent perfection and a permanent residence in the world of Śiva. || 73 ||
Brahmā spoke again concerning the majesty of the Brahmāṇḍa; that Brahmāṇḍa consists of twelve thousand verses and two hundred more.
That Purāṇa, in which the detailed account of future kalpas is heard, is the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as proclaimed by Brahmā. (79)
The man who gives a pair of woolen garments during the Vyatīpāta yoga obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
That [gift] of ten thousand golden cows bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā; this [work], consisting of four hundred thousand [verses], was proclaimed by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds. (77)
O twice-born ones, this was condensed for the benefit of the world during the Dvāpara age.
Even today, this [work] exists among the gods with an extent of one hundred crores; I shall now declare its subdivisions as they are established in the world. (79)
That description of Narasiṃha which was proclaimed in the Padma Purāṇa, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is here called the Nārasiṃha [Purāṇa]. (80)
O best of the twice-born, where the greatness of Nandin was described by Kārttikeya, this is indeed known in the world as the Nandipurāṇa.
O you who observe the vows of sages, that narrative which shall take place with Sāmba placed at its forefront is called "The Sāmba" alone in the world.

In that very place, the one known as the Āditya-purāṇa is also recited. Furthermore, whatever Purāṇa is seen to exist separately from the eighteen, know, O best of the twice-born, that it has emerged from among these.

The Purāṇa has five constituent parts; the narrative is considered the other [part]. Primary creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), genealogy (vaṃśa), the periods of the Manus (manvantara), and the history of the lineage and its descendants (vaṃśānuvaṃśacarita) constitute the Purāṇa with its five characteristics.
The majesty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra, as well as that of the universe and its dissolution, are clearly seen in the Purāṇa characterized by five marks.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are proclaimed in all the Purāṇas, as well as whatever fruit is rooted therein. (86)
In the Sāttvika Kalpas, the majesty of Hari is supreme; in the Rājasa Kalpas, they know the majesty of Brahmā to be supreme.
In the same way, the majesty of Śiva is proclaimed among the tāmasa [beings], that of Sarasvatī among the mixed [beings], and that of the ancestors (pitṛs) as well. 88.
Lord Viṣṇu appears in four [Purāṇas], Brahmā likewise in two, and the Sun in two; in the remaining eighteen Purāṇas, Lord Śiva is present. (89)
O best of the twice-born, I consider the Purāṇa to be as immovable as the Vedas; all the Vedas are established within the Purāṇa, of this there is no doubt. (90)
The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "This man will cause me to waver"; however, in ancient times, this [Veda] was rendered stable by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
O twice-born ones, that which is not seen in the Vedas and is not seen in the Smṛtis, yet is seen in both, is proclaimed in the Purāṇas.
That twice-born who knows the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and Upaniṣads, yet does not know the Purāṇa, cannot be considered truly wise.
Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī (Vyāsa) composed the narrative known as the Bhārata, which is augmented by the meanings of the Vedas.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, that was proclaimed by the high-souled Vālmīki in one hundred thousand verses, as was the supreme narrative concerning Rāma.
That which was ordained by Brahmā and extends to one billion verses, he [Viṣṇu] spoke to Nārada, and he in turn to Vālmīki. || 96 ||
And by Vālmīki, it was established in the world as the means for accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha. || 97 ||
Thus, these five hundred thousand [verses], together with the additional quarter-lakhs, are proclaimed as meritorious; so the wise know in the Purāṇa of the ancient Kalpa.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas differ according to the weight of time; such is the case with the Skānda, the Brahmāṇḍa, and the Laiṅga Purāṇas as well. (99)
O best of Brahmins, in the Vārāha Kalpa, their division proceeds in eighteen ways; indeed, the Brahmāṇḍa is divided accordingly.
By him the eighteen Purāṇas were produced on the surface of the earth; the auspicious Laiṅga was divided into eleven types during the Dvāpara age.
The Skanda Purāṇa was divided into seven parts by the wise Vyāsa; its total number is eighty-one thousand and one hundred verses.
Its first division is known as the Māheśvara, endowed with the greatness of Skanda; the second is remembered as the Vaiṣṇava. (103)
The third is declared to be indicative of the summary of creation; the fourth is recited as being joined with the majesty of Kāśī.

The fifth part [of this work] is proclaimed as that concerning the Revā together with Ujjayinī; the sixth section is the Nāgara-kalpa, which indicates the greatness of the sacred fords (tīrtha-māhātmya). 105.
O twice-born ones, this seventh division is known as the Prābhāsika; all these divisions are proclaimed to consist of twelve thousand verses each.
In this [chapter], the entire extent of the Prābhāsika field is described, as well as the majesty of the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the majesty of Śaṅkara.
And the greatness of other deities as well is proclaimed; thus, O twice-born ones, the distinction between the Purāṇas has been briefly described. (108)
He who recites this sequence of the eighteen Purāṇas during offerings to the gods and ancestors goes to the abode of Hari.
For this is a purifier and a treasury of glory; it is beloved even by the ancestors. It is eternally the source of immortality among the gods, and it removes the great sins of men.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Giving Manuscripts of the Purāṇas, Preceded by the Description of the Number of the Eighteen Great Purāṇas and Upapurāṇas," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: You have described the primary creation as well as the secondary creation, the history of the dynasties and their branches, and the sequence of the Purāṇas.

The duration of a Manvantara, the expansion of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), and the true nature of the stellar sphere have been described by you exactly as they are; now we wish to hear from you the detailed account of the sacred fords (Tīrthas). || 2 ||
O son of Sūta, you ought to describe in their entirety and according to the truth all those holy fords on earth which destroy sin and are auspicious.
Sūta said: This was asked of old by the Goddess on the excellent peak of Kailāsa, whose body is variegated with various minerals and endowed with diverse jewels.
It was crowded with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers, filled with yakṣas and vidyādharas, and frequented by hosts of apsarases.
Therein were Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Skanda, Nandin, and Gaṇeśvara; the Moon and Sun together with the planets, and the circle of the constellations and the Pole Star.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, as well as Kubera the giver of wealth, Īśāna, Agni, Indra, Yama, and Nirṛti as well. || 7 ||
All the rivers, oceans, mountains, and serpents, as well as the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī and the sages whose wealth is austerity; || 8 ||
The sacred fords, holy sites, and shrines were present in embodied form, as were the Dānavas, Asuras, Daityas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Rākṣasas.
There, a divine lion-throne extends for a hundred yojanas.
It was surrounded by hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Rudras; in its center was the Sarvatobhadra [palace], adorned with lion-gates and beautiful archways.
Resembling clear pearls, it was surrounded by the tops of its ramparts and encircled by the hosts of gatekeepers Nandīśvara and Mahākāla.
It was adorned with banners resonant with networks of tiny bells, and with fragments of canopies and umbrellas from which strings of pearls were suspended.
It was adorned with mirrors beautified by bells and chowries, and with water-pots placed at the doors and joined with jewels and sprouts.
It was decorated by experts in the science of painting with brilliant gem-dust, using svastikas, scrollwork (patravallī), and motifs such as the liṅgodbhava and creepers. || 16 ||
It was strewn with hundreds of lion-thrones and adorned with altars, and it was filled with throngs of Rudras seated there along with multitudes of Rudra-maidens.
It was adorned with white lotuses rich with a hundred thousand petals, crowded with celestial nymphs (apsarases), and strewn with profuse heaps of flowers.
It was perfumed with incense sticks, sprinkled with saffron water, and accompanied by flutes, lutes, mṛdaṅga drums, gomukhas, and wind instruments.
With the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, the resonance of dundubhi drums, and with the hosts of gaṇas roaring with sounds like the thundering of clouds.
It was graced by the sound of hymns from the assemblies, by the resonance of the Sāmaveda, by magnificent spectacles, and by loud shouts beautified by the chanting of *huṃ* syllables.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the sound of the trumpeting of bulls, the neighing of elephants and horses, and the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets.

The glorious temple of Śaṅkara alone brings about all prosperity; it resounded here and there with the sounds of flutes, lutes, and drums. And the Ṛgveda itself was present there in embodied form, possessing a splendor like that of a sapphire.
With his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments, he stood to the east of him, blazing with his own splendor.
To the north is the Yajurveda, resembling pure crystal; he wears divine earrings, possesses a massive body, and has mighty arms. || 25 ||
The eternal Sāmaveda stands in the western quarter, wearing red garments, glorious, and possessing a luster like that of a ruby. || 26 ||
Wearing a garland of flowers, variegated, and adorned with ornaments of song, or else dark as collyrium, he stands likewise on the right side. (27)
Tawny-eyed, with a red neck, golden hair, and a massive body; [he knows] the Itihāsas, the six Vedāṅgas, and all the Purāṇas. (28)
The Vedas, the Upaniṣads, the Chandas, the Mīmāṃsā, the Āraṇyakas, as well as the utterances of Svāhā and Vaṣaṭ, and likewise the secret doctrines (Rahasyas). || 29 ||
And there Brahmā himself remained, accompanied by these mantras which assume the form of Śaktis and are endowed with yogic powers and lordly sovereignty.
[He was] marked with thousand-petaled lotuses, worshipped by the gods, honored by the Gaṇas and Rudras, and saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra. || 31 ||
Fanned on all sides by the waving of yak-tail whisks and fans, he is ever resplendent and glorious, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.

His soul was perfectly satiated with the nectar of knowledge; he was the bestower of the sovereign power of yoga, a royal swan in the lotus-pond of the minds of the lords of yogis, and the most excellent of the twice-born.
There resides Candraśekhara, the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, adorned with the thirty-six principles, and the bestower of all happiness.
Seated upon his lap was the Goddess, radiant as molten gold, worshipped by hosts of Yoginīs, by practitioners, and by gods and Kinnaras.
Perfectly endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament, she eternally bestows the perfection of yoga and grants both liberation and worldly prosperity. (36)
And Pārvatī, the beautiful-eyed goddess, having beheld the face of the Lord—the root-seed of the plantain tree of good fortune—was filled with wonder.
Perceiving his state of bliss and seeing his eyes moist with tears of joy, the virtuous goddess, with her palms joined in reverence, spoke sweetly.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the World, throughout thousands of crores of births and hundreds of crores of births, you have been purified by me through the constant thought of my life-breath. (39)
Or even by being stationed in half of my body through the desire to meditate upon your face—nevertheless, O Maheśvara, Lord of the World, no end to you has been found.
O God of gods, salutations be to you who are formless; salutations to the secret of the Vedas, and salutations to him who is praised by the Vedas. || 41 ||
Homage to the one who eternally delights in the cremation ground, to the wanderer of the sky, to the secret essence of the Jyeṣṭha Sāman, and to the beloved of the hundred Rudras.
Salutations to the one marked by the bull, the bearer of the Yajurveda, who wears a garland composed of millions of cosmic eggs, and whose self is the sky.
Salutations to the one whose navel is adorned with jewels, the accomplisher of all aims; salutations to the one whose nature is the Vedas, O twice-born, and who is dear to the Siddhas. 44.
Salutations to the one whose form consists of transformations of male and female, who bears the crescent moon; salutations to Agni together with Umā, and to Āditya and Varuṇa.
To the Earth and the Atmosphere, to Vāyu and to the consecrated one; to conjunction and disjunction, to the Ordainer, the Maker, and the Depriver. || 46 ||
Salutation to him who holds a blazing trident in his hand and wields the staff of Brahmā; salutation to the Lord of lords, salutation to the Lord of the great.
Salutation to Kālāgnirudra, who dwells within the seven worlds; you are the refuge of all beings; salutation to the Lord of beings. 48.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Rudra; salutations to you, O Blessed Śiva. Salutations to you, the most excellent beyond the beyond; salutations to you, the highest beyond the high.
O Lord, you have been troubled by me through the fickleness of my tongue; therefore, O Great Lord, this must be forgiven. Salutations to you, whose knowledge is divine! 50.
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, why do you sit upon my lap with eyes clouded by tears? Is there still something unfulfilled for you? I shall accomplish all of that."
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you—for this hymn of praise, O lady of virtuous vows; I shall grant it to you without a doubt. Cast away your grief, O Great Goddess. (52)
O Goddess, whether partless or with parts, gross or subtle, moving or unmoving—O Mistress of Gods, I do not perceive anything that could exist devoid of you.
O Gaurī, I am established in your heart and you are established in my heart; I am your brother, your son, your kinsman, and likewise your husband.
But you are my sister, my wife, my daughter, my kinswoman, and my daughter-in-law; I am the sacrificer and the performer of the rite, and you are Faith accompanied by the sacrificial fee.
I am the syllable Oṃ, I am the Vaṣaṭ-call, I am the Sāman, as well as the Ṛk and the Yajus; I am the sacrificial fire, the priest, and likewise the sacrificer.
I am the Adhvaryu, I am the Udgātṛ, and likewise I am the Brahmā who knows the Veda; but you, O Goddess, are proclaimed to be the Arani and the wife.
O fair-hipped one, Svāhā and Svadhā—everything is established in you. I am the desired great sacrifice; you are said to be the primordial sacrifice.
O lady of excellent hips, I am called Puruṣa, and you are declared to be Prakṛti; I am Viṣṇu of great prowess, and you are Lakṣmī, the source of the worlds.
I am Indra, possessed of great splendor, and you are the Supreme Goddess, the East; through the form of the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), I abide as everything.
Those who are their leaders, you abide as them through various forms; O Great Goddess, I am said to be the day and you are the night.
I am the *nimeṣa* (twinkling of an eye) and the *muhūrta*; you are the *kalā* and indeed *siddhi*. I am the sun of exceeding splendor, while you are proclaimed as the *saṃdhyā* (twilight).
I am the supreme bearer of the seed, O lovely-faced one, while you are the field. I am the Plakṣa tree, the lord of the forest; you are called the mistress of the forest.
O eternal one, you bear the form of Śeṣa, adorned with the jewels upon your hoods; O large-eyed Revatī, your eyes are tremulous with passion.
I am liberation from all sufferings, O Goddess, while you are the supreme goal; I am the lord of the waters, O auspicious one, while you are the best of rivers, O Goddess.
O blessed lady, I am the submarine fire (Vaḍavāgni) and you are proclaimed as its radiance; I am Prajāpati, the creator, and you are the progeny as well as primordial nature (Prakṛti). || 66 ||
"I am the lord of the nāgas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla; you are a nāgī, and I am a king of nāgas adorned with a thousand hoods. (67)
I am the most excellent moon, and you are the supreme night-maker; I am desire, O Goddess, the bestower of desires, while you are Rati and indeed Smṛti.

O auspicious lady, I am Durvāsas and you are Kṣamā (Forgiveness) who acts with equanimity; I am greed, delusion, and austerity, while you are known as Tṛṣṇā (Thirst) characterized by darkness. || 69 ||
I am the humped bull and the ascetic mother of Yoga; I am also the unmanifest wind, and you are the goal that destroys the mind.
I am the liberator from greed, while you, O illustrious one, are freedom from possessiveness; I am policy in all undertakings, while you, O lotus-eyed one, are statesmanship.
I am the food and the eater; you are declared to be the medicinal herbs. I am the fire and the smoke; you are the heat and the flame itself.
I am the cloud at the end of the eon, and you are indeed the manifold showers; I exist in the form of sages, and you are proclaimed as their wives.
I am indeed the creator of saṃsāra, while you, O fair-faced one, are the creation itself; I am the semen, bones, and hair, while you are the marrow and strength.
O illustrious one, I am Parjanya, and you, O Supreme Goddess, are the rain; O Goddess, I am proclaimed to be the year, and you are the season.
O Goddess, I am the Kṛta Yuga, while you are called Tretā; O Supreme Sovereign, I am the glorious Dvāpara Yuga, and you are Kali.
O blessed lady, I am the ether and you are said here to be the earth; I am of invisible form and you are said to be of visible form.
O lady of beautiful hips, I am the giver of boons, and you are said to be the mantra; I am the seer and the hearer, while you are the object seen and the very act of hearing.
I am the speaker and the delighter, while you, O Supreme Goddess, are the object of speech; I am the listener and the singer, and you are the song as well as that which is sung.
I am the protector and the fragrance, while you are merely the sense of smell; I am the toucher and the agent, while you are the object of touch and that which is created.
"I am all this that has come into being, and you, O Goddess, are likewise—of this there is no doubt. I am your creator, O Queen of the Gods, while you create the entire universe. (81)
O Goddess of gods, this entire world is woven warp and woof by you and me—whether as one, or as ten, or likewise as a hundred thousandfold.
Endowed with sovereignty and established within all living beings, O large-eyed one, both you and I are perpetually situated therein.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I sport with you in play; you are certainly steadfastness, the sustainer, fortune, my beloved, and my very nature.
Rati, Smṛti, and Kāmacārī dwell within my body; O Goddess, what need is there for much speaking? She is dearer to me than even my own life-breaths. (85)
"Choose a boon, O Goddess, whatever resides in your mind; being pleased, I shall grant it to you, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (86)
The Goddess said: "I am blessed; I have performed meritorious deeds and well-practiced penance, since I, O Lord of the World, have been beheld by you with a joyful gaze. (87)
"If you are pleased with me, O God, and if you wish to grant me a boon, then tell me now, O Lord of Gods, the full extent of the sacred fords."
O Lord of Gods, you ought to describe in their entirety and according to truth all those sacred fords on earth that destroy sin and bestow auspiciousness. (89)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of the holy ford (tīrtha), which removes all sins of men, is meritorious, and is honored by gods and sages. 90.
O Goddess of the gods, the sight of sacred fords (tīrthas) and bathing therein are supreme; the best of sages always praise even the mere hearing of them. (91)
Naimiṣa on earth, Puṣkara in the intermediate space, as well as Kedāra, Prayāga, Vipāśā, and likewise Ūrmilā; || 92 ||
The Karṇaveṇā, the great goddess Caṇḍrabhāgā, the Sarasvatī, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and likewise the auspicious Vārāṇasī.
Arghatīrtha is fully proclaimed, as well as Gaṅgādvāra; the great pilgrimage site Himasthāna, and likewise the auspicious Māyāpurī. (94)
The highly fortunate Śatabhadrā and the great river Sindhu, as well as the Airāvatī, the Kapilā, and the great river Śoṇa. || 95 ||
Likewise the ocean, the Kauśikī, and the auspicious Godāvarī; Devakhāta, Gayā, and the auspicious Dvārāvatī. || 96 ||
And Prabhāsa is a great sacred ford that destroys all sins. || 97 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, having beheld whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) such as these exist upon the surface of the earth, one does not undergo rebirth again. || 98 ||
Three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) have arisen here on the surface of the earth; they are pure and destroyers of all sins. (99)

O Great Goddess, one should go to those places for the increase of one's own dharma; however, O Sovereign of the Gods, it is impossible to go to all those auspicious sites. Therefore, with a concentrated mind, one should visit them all even mentally. (100)
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, all living beings are beset by every kind of affliction; they are short-lived and perpetually bound by the delusions arising from their own minds. (101)

"In the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, and indeed in the terrible Kali age, what can be done? Therefore, for the sake of their welfare, proclaim that sacred ford (tīrtha) by the sight of which the fruit of all sacred fords is obtained. (102)
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord, the Master, smiled and spoke with supreme affection in sweet words.
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, you alone are indeed the moving breath and the source of the entire world; deprived of you, O Goddess, I cannot endure even for a moment."
O Pārvatī, there is likewise no difference between Śiva and Śakti; O Great Goddess, O beautiful one, there is nothing that you do not know. (105)
Without you I am nowhere, and you, O Goddess, are not without me; for it is just as the moon cannot exist without its light, or fire without its heat.
O Goddess, O beloved, there is no difference here between you and me; O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall tell you everything exactly as it is.
This secret of secrets must be guarded with great effort; it should not be given to an atheist, nor to one who is devoted to sin. 108.
It should be given to one's own disciple or son who is endowed with devotion; O beloved, I have previously declared this to you as the most essential of essentials.
O Goddess, the Tīrthopaniṣads, as well as the Liṅgopaniṣads and the Yogopaniṣads, have indeed been previously recounted to you.
Pārvatī said: Even with a mere fraction [of effort], those who desire the supreme state do not attain perfection; men of atheistic conduct are seen wandering through various wombs. (111)
They practice the vows of sacred fords, yet no conviction arises; O Śaṅkara, the world was previously deluded by false knowledge. (112)
O best of gods, what fruit have you gained by causing delusion in the world? (113)
"O Lord, tell me that which is the most essential of all essentials, for it is dearer to you than life itself; O Lord of Gods, O Master, if I am dear to you. (114)
Thus addressed by that goddess, the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the leader of the gods, smiled and spoke these words of profound meaning.
Īśvara said: Listen with focused attention; that which has now been asked by you, I shall explain—the fruitless [worldly pursuit] and the reality of things as they truly exist. 116.
O beautiful goddess, those sacred fords (tīrthas) previously mentioned by you—which number three and a half crores within the moving and unmoving universe—[have been described]. (117)
And their sacred bathing-place, Prabhāsa, was likewise concealed, O lady of virtuous vows.
Thus it was said, O Great Goddess, regarding Prabhāsa, the supreme sacred field: those deluded by sin in the Kali age will see it as devoid of sanctifying rites. || 119 ||
Those who are characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), whose minds are afflicted by sin—men who delight in the wives of others, the wealth of others, and the harming of others. (120)

Those fools, deluded by false knowledge and self-conceited, experience extreme agitation and burn with distress here and there; those base ones who perform at a sacred ford (tīrtha) acts contrary to the rules of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama).
O lady of excellent complexion, those men who undertake pilgrimages with hypocrisy and deceit do not attain perfection even when they die at a sacred site.

For this purpose, O Goddess, O lady of beautiful hips, I have diligently concealed various sacred fords (tīrthas) and lingas; yet, O Queen of the Gods, they do not bestow success upon those who commit sins in the Kali age.
Those men who have conquered anger, conquered greed, and conquered their senses—whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who are free from deceit and envy; (124)
O Goddess of noble vows, those of excellent conduct who, imbued with my nature, frequent this sacred ford—for their benefit alone, O illustrious one, I shall now speak. (125)
There is a sacred field renowned as Prabhāsa, worshipped by the three worlds; those who are deluded by my māyā do not recognize that field at all.
But those who have worshipped me with single-minded devotion throughout many births—they know that supreme field, Prabhāsa, which destroys all sins. (127)
O Goddess, those who are permeated by my nature and who observe my vows—for them, Prabhāsika-kṣetra is known; of this there is no doubt. (128)

For those who are endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) and are devoid of egoism, I shall speak upon your most difficult question; this ancient account of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra has been told by me.
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall speak; lend me your ear, O fair-faced one. Among all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth, O beautiful goddess, [I shall describe the most excellent]. (130)

Among them, one is my favorite, the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa. In that great field, I was honored by Soma with various boons; having granted those boons to him, I remained there forever in solitude.
O Goddess, that secret place which was established by him has been revealed to you; there, for me who was engaged in yoga, a divine liṅga indeed came into being.
Endowed with divine splendor, adorned with a girdle of fire, and standing at a distance of a hundred thousand [yojanas], it was peaceful yet difficult for humans to behold. || 133 ||
And those three powers known as will, knowledge, and action, which have arisen from that Liṅga for the sake of being the cause of the agency of the universe. (134)
In that Liṅga, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings goes to dissolution; then, by that very same [Liṅga], the world of moving and non-moving beings is seen to be produced once again.
That which has arisen as a secret is not known by anyone else beyond it; that sign is recognized on earth by men through the practice of birth. (136)
The field is said to be luminous, and I am the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), of this there is no doubt; therein, O fair-faced one, I am named Someśa in this field.
And those who are born from my own portion, having arisen in this field—for them, the Bhairava-liṅga was known in the previous kalpa.
O Goddess, this Liṅga is very difficult to attain even in other ages; it is especially difficult to attain in the terrible and sinful Kali Yuga. (139)
O Pārvatī, I shall explain another illustration regarding that matter.
In the most terrible Kali age, men who delight in speculative reasoning, great sinners all established in heresy, will speak thus. (141)
All this has been falsely done and proclaimed even by fools; where is the sacred field, where is the power, and where indeed are the deities? (142)
And all that has been proclaimed by the deluded is likewise false. || 143 ||
Thus the fools will speak, and others will mock—the hell-dwellers, the nihilists, and those whose minds are afflicted by sin—who shall not attain perfection when the Kali age has arrived. (144)
Furthermore, those who die at a sacred ford (tīrtha) while being devoted to reviling Śiva are seen to be born among animals and in all manner of wombs.
For this reason, O Goddess, at the very sacred ford, people are seen to be deeply afflicted by suffering due to the greatness of the age, being devoid of truth and purity. (146)
This indeed has been declared as the reason for the protection of the sacred fields; all this has been told to you, by which success is very difficult to attain. (147)
O Goddess of the Suras, holy places are celebrated in every age; yet among them, O Goddess, the sacred field of Prabhāsa alone is my favorite.
Thus, O Goddess, has this secret that destroys sin been told; it is the seed of the sacred field, O Great Goddess. What else do you wish to ask? 149.
Those who indeed hear of this great power of the sacred field, which destroys even the most heinous sins, shall, by my power, go to Triviṣṭapa, the abode of meritorious beings. (150)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Question," in the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the seventh section (*Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: When the power [of the Liṅga] had been thus described by Śaṃkara, O lords of sages, that virtuous goddess, with her hands joined in reverence, questioned him again. || 1 ||
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, O Master consisting of sacred fields and holy fords, tell me in detail the majesty of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

How do you find satisfaction in that field of mortals who lack discernment? Why is it that what is chanted, given, offered in sacrifice, worshipped, and whatever austerity is performed at Prabhāsa, that great field, becomes inexhaustible there? (3)
O Śaṅkara, tell me how that sin accumulated in the past over thousands of different births comes to an end.
If Prabhāsa is considered the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas), what need is there for many other extensive sacred fords there? (5)
If there were but one sacred ford, the mind would undoubtedly become steady; but when there are many sacred fords, the minds of men waver.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, having completely set aside the entire extensive network of other sacred fords, please recount the majesty of Prabhāsa alone.
O Lord, you ought to tell me all of this—the measurement of the field, its boundaries, and indeed its essential nature—for my curiosity is great. (8)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most excellent of sacred fields; among all sacred fields, the field of Prabhāsa is indeed dear to me. 9.
In Prabhāsa, however, there is supreme accomplishment; in Prabhāsa, there is the supreme goal, where I am eternally and continuously present, O auspicious lady.
I shall declare its measurement, including all its boundaries; the field is said to be of three kinds, and I shall describe them to you in due order.

The sacred field (kṣetra), the seat (pīṭha), and the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) are proclaimed as belonging to Prabhāsa; the fruit thereof is traditionally held to increase progressively by ten million times ten millionfold.
The field (kṣetra) is said to be the first, and it measures twelve yojanas; the seat of the field (kṣetrapīṭha) is proclaimed to be five yojanas in extent.
The inner sanctum is one *gavyūti*, and that pericarp is dear to me; O Goddess, listen as I describe the boundaries of the sacred field in due order.
It is established according to its length and breadth at the beginning, middle, and end; Svāmī is remembered as being in the east, and Mādhava in the west. || 15 ||
Likewise, there is an ocean to the south, and the Bhadrā river is considered to be to the north; thus, the field, bounded by these limits, measures twelve yojanas.
This Prābhāsika field is the destroyer of all sins; in its center is said to be a pedestal extending five yojanas in width.
Nyaṅku is located by another [mountain] alone to the east of Vajriṇī, while Māheśvarī is to the south and Samudra is likewise to the north.
This pedestal is declared to be five yojanas in both length and breadth; now hear concerning the inner sanctum.

From the southern and northern oceans as far as Kauraveśvarī, and from east to west as far as Gomukha and Aśvamedhika—this is declared to be my womb-chamber (garbhagṛha), beloved of me, [located] at Kailāsa.
In the meantime, O Goddess of the gods, whatever holy places exist upon the earth—whether ponds, wells, tanks, or temples of the deities—[all came there].
Lakes, rivers, ponds, and pools—all of these are pure and destroyers of all sins. (22)
Having bathed anywhere there, a man is glorified in the heavenly world; the first portion of the sacred field is remembered as the pure domain of Maheśvara. || 23 ||
The second part belongs to Viṣṇu, and the third part belongs to Brahmā; indeed, ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) are established within the portion belonging to Brahmā.
O lady of excellent complexion, there is one crore of holy places in the Vaiṣṇava portion, while it is declared that there are one and a half crores in the central Rudra portion.
Thus, O Goddess, has that field of the three deities been fully described; it is a field more secret than the secret, and most dear to me, O auspicious one. (26)
It is declared that there are three and a half crores [of villages] in the field according to their divisions; know that the pilgrimage is of three kinds—listen to it, O fair-faced one. (27)
The first expedition is indeed Raudrī, the second is Vaiṣṇavī, and the third is reckoned as Brāhmī; it is the destroyer of all sins. (28)

O fair-faced one, the power of will (icchā-śakti) is proclaimed to reside in the portion belonging to Brahmā, while the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is celebrated in the second portion, that of Viṣṇu.
In the third division of Raudra, O fair-faced one, resides the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti); whether a man be sinful, deceitful, or even treacherous, [he attains success there]. (30)
He who dwells in the middle region, having abandoned the Himavat and the Gandhamādana mountain, shall be liberated from all sins.
Kailāsa and Niṣadha, the immensely radiant summit of Meru, the beautiful Triśikhara, and the great mountain Mānasa.
Having abandoned all those delightful celestial gardens, including the Nandana grove, as well as the charming regions of heaven, sacred fords, and shrines, my delight is indeed in Prabhāsa.
O Goddess, he who dwells there with a restrained mind and concentrated soul becomes equal to one who subsists on air alone, even if he eats three times a day. || 34 ||
He who does not abandon Prabhāsa even when being agitated by obstacles abandons old age, death, and the eternal cycle of birth. || 35 ||
O Goddess, yoga may perhaps be attained after hundreds of other births, but liberation is not attained even in a thousand births.
O Great Goddess, for those who remain at Prabhāsa with firm resolve, liberation is attained in a single birth; of this there is no doubt.
Those Brāhmaṇas of firm vows who indeed reside at Prabhāsa recite the Śatarudriya conjoined with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. || 38 ||
Residing in the southern direction in the presence of Kālāgnirudra, knowledge arises there within six months.
The Veda is indeed declared to be Śiva by means of synonymous names; and its essential nature is proclaimed to be the Śatarudrīya. (40)
O Goddess, it is traditionally held that throughout the kalpas the Vedas recur again and again, as do the mantras—with the exception of the Śatarudriya.
Furthermore, those who, having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, worship me alone with the mantra "īḍya," are liberated; of this there is no doubt. (42)
Whether accompanied by mantras or even without mantras, whatever man dwells there attains that goal which cannot be achieved through sacrifices or gifts.
In this field, the Self-Existent One, Maheśvara himself, is present; and ten million Rudras are likewise established in Prabhāsa.
Meditating thus upon the syllable Om, they remained to the south of Someśa.
O lady of virtuous vows, whatever holy places exist within the interior of the cosmic egg shall all go to Someśvara on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, as well as desire, anger, and others—these constantly protect Someśa, the destroyer of sins. (47)
That destination which is ordained for men who dwell in the sacred field of Prabhāsa is not attained at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Tripuṣkara. 48.
Even those beings belonging to the animal realm who have made their abode in Prabhāsa, upon meeting their death in due time, attain the supreme goal. (49)
That is the secret of the God of gods; it is that sacred ford (tīrtha) and that grove of asceticism (tapovana). There, the gods headed by Brahmā and preceded by Nārāyaṇa [reside]. (50)
Likewise, O Blessed One, the yogins and the Sāṃkhyas worship the eternal Prabhāsa; my devotees, who are devoted to me alone, also do so.
For ascetics of restrained self, the monastic residence (vihāra) should last for eight months; some, however, must dwell in one place for four or eight months as a fixed rule.
For those who have entered Prabhāsa, however, no [ordinary] monastery exists; here, yoga and liberation—which are difficult for men to attain—are obtained. (53)
Therefore, having abandoned Prabhāsa, one should not go to any other penance grove; those fools who do not resort to Prabhāsa are enveloped by darkness.
They are born again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen; [therein arise] desire, anger, greed, hypocrisy, arrogance, and envy. (55)
Sleep, lethargy, laziness, and backbiting—these ten constantly guard Someśa, the leader of the holy sites.
No sinner who dies at Prabhāsa goes to hell, provided that he dwells there with firm resolve for as long as he lives. (57)

By means of the Agnihotra sacrifices, by renunciations, and by well-maintained stages of life (āśramas), as well as by those who carry the triple staff (tridaṇḍins) or the single staff (ekadaṇḍins), and even by the Śaivas and Pāśupatas; || 58 ||
O Goddess, whatever auspicious fruit is obtained by these and other ascetics, all of that is attained through the pilgrimage to Śrī Someśvara. (59)
For one person indeed worships the Liṅga, while another practices austerities; between those two, however, he who worships Someśa is the superior.
That which is to be known through Yoga, Sāṃkhya, the Siddhānta, the Pañcarātra, and other scriptures, is fully established at Prabhāsa.
This entire universe, both moving and unmoving, is situated within the Liṅga; therefore, the Lord should always be worshipped in the Liṅga with great effort.
That supreme form of mine alone exists under the name of Śrī Someśa; therefore, being intent upon worship, I [worship] myself by means of that very self. 63.
Wandering through thousands of various births over many lifetimes, who indeed can attain that liberation without the worship of Someśa? (64)
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by means of human intellect, all of that goes to dissolution through the worship of Śrī Someśvara. 65.
Whatever sin has been committed by living beings over many tens of millions of births, all of that comes to destruction through the worship of Śrī Someśvara. (66)
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) in this world are resorted to by those seeking liberation from sin, they all indeed enter into Prabhāsa for the sake of purification. || 67 ||
He who is called Kālāgnirudra by the exponents of the Vedas, he is established here at Prabhāsa under the name Bhairava.
O Goddess of the Gods, stationed in the midst of the sacred field, I assume a terrifying form and destroy all the evil deeds of people. 69.
Having traversed the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, I remain there; therefore, I am known by the name Bhairava, established in Prabhāsa.
Where it was heated by fire for a cycle of four divine ages, during the Meghavāhana Kalpa, a Liṅga indeed came into existence there.
O beautiful lady of the gods, his power is proclaimed by the Veda in the hymn beginning with "Agnim īḷe," and he is called Kālāgnirudra by all the deities. (72)

"O Goddess of gods, the triad of names beginning with Agnīśāna is thus declared. However, O fair-faced one, it is impossible for even Brahmā to recount these names in every single Kalpa, because the Kalpas are innumerable. (73)
And thus, O fair-faced one, this secret which is to be strictly guarded has been proclaimed by me to you out of great affection and devotion. (74)

On the one hand, the entire world is established in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), [consisting] of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, oblations, Vedic studies, and libations to the ancestors.
By means of fasts, complete vows, hundreds of cāndrāyaṇas, as well as six-night and three-night observances, and by supreme pilgrimages to sacred sites and the like; || 76 ||
It was filled with hermitages of various forms, and with ascetics, celibate students, forest-dwellers, and householders, all devoted to the rituals of the Vedas.
O Goddess, that supreme state cannot be perceived anywhere even by others who abide on the worldly path through various auspicious forms.
O Goddess, as long as one does not worship Someśa, the presiding Lord of the Liṅga, even in play, that supreme state is difficult for them to behold.
Those by whom Bhairava Someśa, the Lord of the World, has been worshipped—even those who have entered the womb of animals, such as beasts, birds, and ants—[attain liberation]. (80)

Those worms, insects, and moths dwelling within the water; other beings, both stationary and moving; humans, animals, and women; children, the elderly, and likewise eunuchs; dogs, donkeys, and crows; Caṇḍālas, Puṣkasas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and others born of inferior wombs—[all these attain liberation].
But fools, as well as scholars and others who are despised on earth—all of them attain liberation if they die at the auspicious Prabhāsa.
O auspicious lady, all those living beings who have died at Prabhāsa are consumed by the fire of Rudra as the fire of cosmic destruction and by the fire of Kālarāja.
O Goddess, praised by the world, my sacred field of Prabhāsa is difficult for sinners to attain; a person of sinful soul does not meet death there. (85)
By me, Vighneśa has been installed on the southern side, and Daṇḍapāṇi on the north; he protects this sacred field.
Likewise, O Goddess of gods, all the other Gaṇapas, who remain subject to my command, protect the sacred field; hear their names from me. || 87 ||
Mahābala, Caṇḍīśa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Gomukha, Vināyaka, Mahānāda, Kākavaktra, Śubhekṣaṇa, Ekākṣa, Dundubhi, Caṇḍa, and likewise Tālajaṅgha. || 88 ||
Bhūmidamḍa, Caṇḍa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vaidhṛti, Tālacaṇḍa, Mahātejas, Vikaṭāsya, and Hayānana. || 989 ||
Hastivaktra, Śvānavaktra, and likewise Biḍālavadana; others with the faces of lions and tigers, as well as Vīrabhadra and the rest. (90)
Placing Vināyaka at their head, they approached the god of gods, Kapardin; there were eleven crores and thirteen million [of them]. 91.
Resorting to Arbuda, Gaṇānāṃ, and the sacred field of Prabhāsa, those fierce ones stand at every door, holding tridents and mallets in their hands.
They protect Prabhāsa-kṣetra, the abode of the God of gods; it is the established rule that no one with an evil intent shall enter.
Surrounded by hosts numbering one hundred crores at the eastern gate, the group named Aṭṭahāsa protects Prabhāsa there.
Kālākṣa, Bhīṣaṇa, and Caṇḍa, surrounded by eighteen crores, along with the Gaṇa named Ghaṇṭākarṇa, have taken their place at the southern gate.
The Gaṇa Viṣṭara stood taking recourse to the western gate, and Daṇḍapāṇi stood there to the north of the God of gods.
Constantly providing security and prosperity to those of purified soul at Prabhāsa, Bhīṣaṇākṣa is likewise in the northeast, while Chāgavaktraka is in the southeast.
In the southwest is Caṇḍanāda, and in the northwest is Bhairavānana; likewise, Nandin, Mahākāla, Daṇḍapāṇi, and Vināyaka.
These guardians of the quarters, surrounded in the center by hosts numbering hundreds of millions—indeed, many such lords of the Gaṇas, beyond counting—protect [the world] in this manner. (99)
And for those whose intellects are impaired by the arising of the defilements of the Kali age, that abode of the one who wears the crescent moon on his crest will not be accessible.
Having worshipped Someśa, the lord of gods and destroyer of sins, with Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Apsarases, as well as Uragas and Siddhas, [they departed]. (101)

Those who have attained invisibility constantly resort to Prabhāsa; those who are the perfected ones (siddhas) dwelling in the seven worlds and in the nether regions (pātāla) perform circumambulation of Someśa Kālabhairava.
Whatever holy fords and sacred shrines exist upon the earth—Lākulin, Bhārabhūti, Āṣāḍhin, and Daṇḍa as well—[are all here]. (103)
Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and likewise Amareśa; Bhairava, Madhyama, Kāla, Kedāra, and Kaṇavīraka. (104)
Haricandra, Śaileśa, as well as Vastrāntikeśvara, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, Śrīśaila, and likewise Gayā. || 105 ||
All these sacred fords perform circumambulation of the Lord, the divine Someśvara, and they offer hymns of praise to the Liṅga there.
Brahmā, Janārdana, and the other gods who dwell in the world, standing near the Agnilinga, offer praise at the time of twilight.
Sixty-six thousand million and sixty-six hundred million [beings] all go to Someśvara on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
And at that time, whoever should offer a "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala) to Someśa, [attains great merit].
Having combined ghee, juice, sesame seeds, milk, and water infused with camphor together with saffron—this is known as the "Ghee-Blanket" (ghṛtakambala). || 110 ||
This must be performed on Śivarātri; it is a secret dear to me. When this is done, the merit that arises cannot be described.
There, on the southern side, O Goddess, one who desires success for oneself should first worship the self-manifested Bhūtavināyaka.

Of all saline lands, Prabhāsa-kṣetra is the saline land; of all sacred seats (pīṭhas), it is the seat, and of all fields (kṣetras), it is the supreme field. Of all places of doubt, this is the highest place of doubt. (113)
Whatever yogins there may be, even those numbering in the hundreds of millions, their delight is in the field of Prabhāsa alone, and nowhere else.
O beautiful goddess, she is situated in the northeastern quarter of the Liṅga.
O Goddess, that auspicious digit named Umā whom I have described to you is called Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa in ancient times.
Due to Dakṣa’s wrath, that supreme digit, having abandoned her body, was born in the house of Himavat and became renowned by the name Umā. (117)
Therefore, O Goddess, while staying there together with you, the bestowers of boons were remembered; for nine crores of Cāmuṇḍās are themselves stationed in that sacred field.
If one should worship you there on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, poverty shall not befall that person for twenty-one births.
If the new moon (amā) is ever found conjoined with Monday (soma), one who beholds Someśvara on that day shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
This field is a great secret that destroys all sins; it is here that eleven crores of Rudras reside.
Here, twelve suns and eight Vasus have assembled; there are also Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, as well as innumerable lords of the Gaṇas.
Umā also was there, standing by his side, praised by all the gods; as was Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas, who belongs to the trident-bearing God of Gods.
And those other leaders of the Gaṇas who are the attendants of Mahākāla, as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the goddess Sarasvatī. || 124 ||
And there were other sacred rivers, as well as streams, lakes, oceans, mountains, wells, and even lordly trees. 125.
Both the immobile and the mobile [beings] have gathered at Prabhāsa, as well as other hosts who are established there in Prabhāsa. || 126 ||

I have not described them all in detail here and there; rather, O Goddess of the gods, one endowed with supreme devotion should worship Vināyaka as the third deity there, if one desires the fruit of the sacred field.
O beautiful lady, twelve, eight, and forty crores of rivers stand thus at the gateway of Agnitīrtha.
If any transgression regarding the discarded flower offerings (nirmālya) has been committed through ignorance or otherwise, all of that is dissolved by the mere sight of Agnitīrtha.
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? This field possesses such great splendor that it cannot be fully described by you even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.

Those [shrines] which are in the atmosphere, those on earth, and those deities which are in the various quarters—of all these, O Goddess, Prabhāsa is indeed the most excellent field, and likewise Someśvara is the most preeminent.

O Goddess, whatever living beings—whether born from eggs, born from sprouts, born from sweat, or born from a womb—lose their lives at Prabhāsa, they attain supreme liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus has been narrated to you, O Goddess, this wondrous and inconceivable deed of Śaṅkara, the God of gods; by reading, hearing, or constantly praising it in this manner, even every person in the world shall attain the destruction of the impurities of the Kali age.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Measurement of the Sacred Field," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, when this had been spoken by the high-souled Śaṅkara, that goddess, her mind filled with joy, questioned him again.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, for the benefit of all living beings, O Lord, tell me in detail the majesty of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
The Lord said: O illustrious one, I shall tell you another illustration by which, O Great Goddess, this field dear to me was created.
Whatever goal belongs to those yogis who are constantly meditating and free from attachment, that same supreme goal is attained by those who give up their lives at Prabhāsa.
And Mārkaṇḍeya, of great ascetic power, who remains for many kalpas—he too always worships the god Virūpākṣa at Prabhāsa.

Having wandered through all the holy fords (tīrthas), Durvāsas, possessed of great splendor and intent upon the worship of the Liṅga, did not leave Prabhāsa; O Goddess, he did not depart from that sacred field of the Moon-crested Lord for even a moment.
Bharadvāja, Marīci, and the sage Uddālaka, as well as Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Bhṛgu. || 7 ||
Dakṣa, Sāvarṇi, Yama, Aṅgiras, Śuka, Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Gobhila; || 8 ||
Gautama, Ṛcīka, Agastya, the great Śaunaka, Nārada, Jamadagni, Viśvāmitra, and Lomaśa; || 9 ||
Furthermore, other sages as well as divine celestial rishis do not leave this great sacred field, being intent upon the propitiation of the Liṅga.
I remain right there, intent upon the worship of the Liṅga; I do not leave this great sacred field, truly, truly, O fair-faced one. (11)
O Goddess of gods, all the sacred fords on the surface of the earth have been seen by me, but a holy field equal to Prabhāsa has never been seen at any time.
O Goddess, sixty thousand [sages], with Yājñavalkya at their head, are established on the Candrabhāgā river and perform the recitation of the Rudra hymns.
Forty thousand sages of perpetual celibacy, having taken refuge on the banks of the Devikā, recite the Śatarudriya.
And fifty crores of sages with sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), having approached the Lord of Umā, remained right there at that very liṅga. || 15 ||
In the past, they performed the recitation of ten million Rudra-mantras right there; ten million attained perfection at that very liṅga, without a doubt. (16)
And hundreds of thousands of great Siddhas, who dwell in my sacred field, worship the Lord of Gods, whose ornament is the moon.
Whatever fruit has been proclaimed by the great sages in the Vedāntas, all that fruit is obtained there from the sight of the Moon-Adorned One (Śiva).
O auspicious one, more than ten million sages reside at Agnitīrtha; likewise, one hundred thousand are recorded at Rudreśvara and at Kaṃpardeśa.
At Ratneśvara, there are a thousand sages of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), while at the highly meritorious and auspicious Arkasthala, more than ten million reside.
Sixty thousand [siddhas] reside there at Siddheśvara, and seven thousand reside at Mārkaṇḍeya.
At the Brahmakuṇḍa on the Sarasvatī, innumerable sages are recorded; specifically, three hundred million and ten thousand times ten million.
The sages dwell there where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows, and where the sin of killing a Brahmin vanished from Śaṅkara at that very moment.
The body attained a golden hue and the skull fell from his hand; having realized this, he who was previously filled with apprehension performed great penance there.
The Lord Śrī Śaṅkara was pleased by that excellent abode of the Liṅga; the fruit of ten million sacrifices is obtained by bathing and by worshipping the Liṅga in the eastern direction. (25)

An offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) at Gayā is a hundred times more meritorious on a day joined with the new moon; one who offers a piṇḍa there on the fourteenth day (bhūtā) shall deliver ten million members of his lineage.
And those men who shall plunge here for the destruction of their impurities, they too shall obtain the merit born of giving ten cows in gift.

Even for those men who, while playing with their feet, desire water [at this place], the fruit of the śrāddha will accrue to them according to the prescribed rite. There, the Liṅgas beginning with Śūlabheda are to be worshipped.

Having thus described the lingas that yield the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), [it is said that] by the mere sight of all of them there is merit, while by touching them the fruit is indeed twofold.
Thus pleased, the Lord of the World remained permanently in the forest of Prācī; what then need be said of those who will apply even their minds to bathing and giving gifts there? (3)
Śaṅkara, the blue-and-red Lord of the World, was pleased with them; there, thirty crores of his attendants protect the eastern quarter on all sides.

Even one who practices great sins, the most wicked, or is exceedingly sinful, shall go to Śiva after casting off his life-breaths in the east, like the accidental formation of a syllable by a woodworm.
In that place, a gift of a white bull with a dewlap should be given to an excellent brahmin; it is declared to be the certain pacifier of sins, the most essential of all essentials. (33)
Now I shall fully describe the great glory of Hiraṇyā; there, Durvāsas performed penance, and the Sun was installed.
Right there, however, was a single group of sages who had sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), possessing power and form that surpassed even the twenty-four principles (tattvas). || 35 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, the fruit that one obtains elsewhere by [worshipping] ten million Brāhmaṇas is obtained where Bhṛgu resides accompanied by ten million [others]. || 36 ||

The same fruit is obtained by feeding even a single person at the station of Brahmā; knowing this, O Great Goddess, I remain there in contentment, surrounded by millions of divine sages and gods. Indeed, in the Kali age, all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside there in a hidden state.
In that most delightful field where Someśvara is situated, O Goddess, I have two attendants, Vibhrama and Saṃbhrama, who are supreme.
And there, they always engage the minds of those dwelling in that field with delusions and distractions, making them crowded with manifold conceptual constructions.
The Vināyakas, the Upasargas, and likewise the ten other defects—these protect the sacred field from sinners of wicked intent. (41)
But those best of men who behold Daṇḍapāṇi here with devotion, no obstacle shall arise for them while they dwell in that sacred field.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes—whoever dies at the auspicious Prabhāsa, whether against their will or with desire—[attain the highest state].
All those men who are born there in my divine city of Śiva have the crescent moon as their crest-jewel, an eye on their forehead, and the bull as their emblem.
The brahmin who dwells there, self-restrained and composed in mind, even if eating three times a day, becomes equal to one who subsists on air alone. || 45 ||
O beloved, it is possible to describe the qualities of Meru, as well as the qualities of the continents; likewise, it is possible to describe the qualities of all the oceans.
O Goddess of gods, the qualities of the primordial god Maheśa, the great lord, cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Multitudes of Sages and Deities Residing in the Sacred Field," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, you have narrated to me a most wonderful majesty; O Lord of the gods, it is unprecedented, never before heard by me. (1)
Regarding those Lingas in the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) that have been described by you to me, tell me how it is that Someśa possesses such superior power among them? || 2 ||
O Mahādeva, O Lord of the Gods, what is the power of this sacred field? Tell me that, O Lord of the Suras, exactly as it is, in my presence. (3)
Īśvara said: Hereafter, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall proclaim to you the supreme secret, the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra and of Someśa. 4.
The supreme among holy places, the supreme among vows, the supreme among prayers to be recited, and the highest among meditations. || 5 ||
The supreme yoga among all yogas, the greatest and most profound secret—that I shall fully declare to you; listen with a single-minded heart, O beloved.
Someśa is the supreme abode, endowed with five faces; I do not abandon this Liṅga—this is the truth, the truth that I have spoken.
And that which is supreme, O Goddess—constant, imperishable, and immutable—know that to be Someśa; do not let your mind be filled with doubt.
Fearless, stainless, eternal, independent, without support, untainted, beyond phenomenal expansion, unattached, and free from affliction.
Know that the talliṅga is established in Prabhāsa; it is liberation, inconceivable, delightful to the mind, and free from ailment.
And [he praised] the eternal cause, the god who destroys the sacrifices, whose face is turned in every direction, Śiva, the soul of all, the subtle, the beginningless, and that which is the deity.
It is to be known through the perception of the Self, devoid of mental reflection, liberated from coming and going, and absolute both externally and internally.
The object of self-perception, beyond the sphere of praise, partless, pure in nature, manifest, and the lamp of knowledge. (13)
Know this, O beautiful goddess, to be the Talliṅga at Prabhāsa; it is a sound devoid of any intervening space, yet it is within the range of perception of sound.
The partless, stainless God, the God of gods, whose nature is that of the deities; who is devoid of cause and means of proof, and free from the absence of conceptual construction. || 15 ||
Know that the Praṇava, which is the object of the observation of the mind and is situated both externally and internally, is the radiant one in the form of a Liṅga.
The Great-Souled One is motionless, his vision devoid of worldly joy; he stands upon the path of beholding the worlds, possessed of pure and absolute knowledge.

Abiding on the path of the distinction of knowledge, designated by many forms, it is to be grasped through the cultivation of its own nature; it transcends all existence and is devoid of defining characteristics. || 18 ||

Śiva is devoid of the elaboration of speech and the like, consisting of the non-conceptual (niṣprapañca), abiding in the vision of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, and free from fallacious reasons.

Know that Someśvara at Prabhāsa exists in the form of a *liṅga*, consisting of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), residing within sound, and arising from the collection of sound and the other [objects of the senses]. (20)
It is situated within the Śabdabrahman, tranquil, the abode that reaches the end of sound; its object transcends all else, and it is established upon the plane of all meditation. || 21 ||
Beginningless, undecaying, divine, beyond all measure, and beyond the reach of the senses; it extends eternally below and above, known as the *jīva*, residing within the body. (22)

[He meditated upon] that which resides from the heart to the dvādaśānta, which arises and sets with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, which is ungraspable, whose nature is beyond the senses, stainless, and all-pervading.
Beyond vowels and consonants, devoid of phonemes and the like, it is the object that cannot be expressed by words, possessing a form that is half of the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra).
Inconceivable, inexpressible, devoid of mental construction and time, soundless, motionless, serene, transcending the body, and higher than the highest. (25)
Free from the obstruction of the elements, devoid of existence and non-existence, unknowable, supreme, subtle, and arising from the five-fifths and so forth. || 26 ||
Immeasurable, called infinite, inexhaustible, and able to assume any form at will; the source of all beings, arising like a sprout from a seed. || 27 ||

It is all-pervading, known as the fulfillment of all desires, imperishable, supreme, and great; it abides within the divisions of the gross and the subtle, manifest and unmanifest, and is eternal. (28)
