Devoid of beginning or end, existing through kalpa after kalpa, he is the Great One, the Great Being, the Great Body, Śiva, Nirvāṇa, and Bhairava.
In this way, know Sadāśiva at Prabhāsa to be in the form of a linga—liberated from yoga and ritual action, the conqueror of death, and without beginning.
It is free from all calamities, all-pervading, auspicious, unmanifest, supreme, eternal, absolute, and devoid of duality. || 31 ||
Hara, who dwells in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, is not overcome by the splendor of others; he is renowned for his abundant self-luminosity and surpasses all other radiant beings.
To the Lord who is the refuge, the Sovereign, the syllable Om, whose form is Śiva; the God of gods, Mahādeva, the five-faced one who has the bull as his banner.
Stainless, beyond the reach of the mind, graspable through meditative state, incomparable, eternally peaceful, three-eyed, holding a trident in his hand, and wearing matted locks.
Know that Sadāśiva, who resides in the center of the lotus-casket of the heart, whose form is emptiness and is stainless, exists in the form of a *liṅga* within the Prabhāsa [tīrtha]. (35)
O Goddess of excellent vows, that very deity who is higher than the highest, proclaimed by the name Haṃsa and known as Nāda, resides here in this place himself.
O Goddess, this primordial nature and so forth has been realized by me through the power of yoga; thus have I, the divine Self, spoken of myself by means of my own self. (37)

Established in the Ṛgveda during the forenoon, situated in the Yajurveda at midday, established in the Sāmaveda during the afternoon, and indeed established in the Atharvaveda at the onset of night—38.
I know this Great Person, resplendent as the sun, beyond the darkness. Only by knowing Him does one escape death; indeed, there is no other path for men. (39)
Thus has been narrated to you a single portion of the great power of the Someśa Liṅga; it cannot be fully described by anyone, even with thousands of mouths over many years.
If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should recite this, he shall be liberated from all sins and attain all his desires. || 41 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrī Someśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having thus heard that supreme majesty there at that time, the Goddess, with a voice trembling with joy, questioned Śaṅkara once again.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of grace upon your devotees, endowed with all knowledge; salutations be unto you, O Maheśvara! (2)

Salutations indeed to the Great-Souled One, the destroyer of Tripura and the subduer of Tāraka; salutations to You, who bestowed the Ocean of Milk upon the child of the Lord of Sages while he was absorbed in meditation.
Homage be to you, the ordainer of the entire world, the universal self, the creator of all; homage be to Bhava, homage to Abhava, and homage be to you who are eternally omnipresent. 4.
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, what do you ask even now? Everything has been told to you by me. O beautiful lady, if there is anything remaining in doubt, ask again."
The Goddess said: At what time did that name "Someśvara" come into being? What was the name of the Liṅga formerly, and what will its name be now? (6)
"O Lord, thus the power of others—of the various holy sites and deities—has indeed been described by you, yet such [power] as that of Śrī Someśa has not been told by you before. (7)
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, previously I alone existed in the form of the Sparśaliṅga; yet no person here on earth knew me in reality."
O Goddess, when a great aeon has arisen and the dissolution of Brahmā occurs, the name and form of the Liṅga shall become something else again and again.
Six cycles of Brahmās have passed; this is the seventh Prajāpati, O Goddess, who is currently known as Śatānanda. || 1 ||
O Goddess of the gods, when this Brahmā had indeed reached his eighth year, from that time onwards he became renowned as Someśa.
And regarding the past, O Goddess of gods, listen now, O Pārvatī, to those names that arose following the dissolution in the sleep of Brahmā.
When the Grandfather Brahmā was first known by the name Virañci, the name of Somanātha was proclaimed as Mṛtyuñjaya.
O auspicious Ambikā, when the second Brahmā became renowned as Padmabhū, then the name Kālāgnirudra was proclaimed.
When the third Brahmā appeared, renowned as Svayambhū, then the name of the Lord was proclaimed as Amṛteśa. || 15 ||
The fourth was like Brahmā, renowned as Parameṣṭhin; at that time, O auspicious lady, the name of the god was remembered as Anāmaya.
O Ambikā, when Brahmā became the fifth, known as Surajyeṣṭha, then the name Kṛttivāsas was proclaimed for the Lord.
And when the sixth Brahmā, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, came into being, then the name of the Lord was proclaimed as Bhairavanātha.
This Brahmā who currently exists is known as Śatānanda; at present, the name of the Lord is Somanātha.
Henceforth, when he who shall become the four-faced Brahmā appears, the name of the Lord will then be "Prāṇanātha."

Those who were creators in the past and those who will be so now—so long as another [creation] lasts for eight years, they exist under the names Viṣṇu, Ananta, and Sanātana, distinguished by the divisions of the Sandhyā and Sandhyāṃśa periods.
Thus, the names of the Lord have been proclaimed by me in brief; they cannot be told in detail because of the vastness of time.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the gods, O Master, it is a marvel that you have spoken thus; for why do I not remember the names previously mentioned? (23)
O Lord of the World, for the sake of the welfare of all beings and out of a desire to favor me, please explain this in detail and its underlying cause.
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, because you take incarnation in every kalpa, you have no recollection of it due to the power of Prakṛti, my dear.
Within the veil of reality (tattvāvaraṇa), you are established there as the primordial one; O fair-faced one, having descended into the midst of the cosmic egg, you are together with me.
For the sake of favoring the worlds, she has manifested again and again; in the first kalpa she was the Mother of the World, and in the second, the Source of the World.
In the third [kalpa] she is named Śāmbhavī, in the fourth Viśvarūpiṇī; in the fifth she is named Nandinī, and in the sixth Gaṇāmbikā.
In the seventh kalpa she was Vibhūti, and in the eighth she was Subhūti; then in the ninth kalpa she was Ānandā, and in the tenth she was Vāmalocanā.
In the eleventh [kalpa] she was Varārohā, in the twelfth Sumaṅgalā, and in the thirteenth kalpa she is indeed proclaimed as Mahāmāyā.
Then, in the fourteenth kalpa, she was celebrated by the name Anantā; in the fifteenth she was Bhūtamātā, and in the sixteenth she is remembered as Uttamā.
Then, in the seventeenth kalpa, known as the Pitṛkalpa, she was born as the daughter of Dakṣa, highly renowned and possessed of great splendor, by the name of Satī.
Due to the insult from Dakṣa, she again abandoned her own body; having formerly filled a digit of the moon, Umā remains established there.
Then, O beautiful goddess, when the Vārāha Kalpa had commenced, you were once again propitiated by Himavat and thus made his daughter.
Then, O Goddess, having performed a most difficult and extraordinary penance, you shall regain me as your husband and be called Pārvatī. (35)
O fair-faced one, O Goddess of gods, I, whose abode is Kailāsa, shall sport with you until the end of the kalpa.
Having attained these four qualities in the Dvāpara age along with Viṣṇu, she was born as Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā for the purpose of slaying Mahiṣa.
Under various synonymous names such as Kātyāyanī and Durgā, you have appeared upon the surface of the earth in nine crores of different forms.
O beautiful one, those mental constructions which were previously mentioned by you have been recounted to me as occurring thirteen aeons ago.
O beautiful one, O beloved, all things—past, future, and present—should be known in this manner, up until the end of the Brahma-kalpa.
The Goddess said: "O Destroyer of Tripura, how can that name 'Somanātha' which was previously uttered by you be considered an immutable name? (41)
And because of the innumerability of moons, due to the distinctions of their births and names, when a Manvantara has occurred, consisting of seventy-one Yugas. (42)
The gods, beginning with the Moon and the Sun, are withdrawn again and again; so too are the Seven Sages, the deities, Śakra, Manu, and his sons, the kings. (43)
They are created and withdrawn at one and the same time, as before. O Lord, you ought to explain this doubt of mine to me correctly. (44)
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, you have asked well regarding this secret that destroys sin; I shall tell it to you in its entirety, which has not been told to anyone else."
This Brahmā who exists now is known as Śatānanda; and in his eighth year, he who will be the first Manu shall appear.
O Goddess, in that Manvantara, he who was the Lord of Rohiṇī at the beginning was born from the womb of the ocean, together with Lakṣmī, the Kaustubha gem, and other [attendants].
And by him, through great austerity in the past, during fourteen yugas, the Liṅga named Kālabhairava was propitiated.
O beautiful one, having seen his wonderful asceticism, I was pleased with him; and I said to that maker of night, "Choose a boon."
Then, O auspicious goddess, having praised me with devotion, he spoke thus.
Candra said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, or if I am worthy of a boon, O Lord, let my name be 'Somanātha' until the end of Brahmā's life."
"O Lord of Gods, may this deity become the family deity for all others who shall exist in the future and who consider themselves to be cool-rayed ones."
O All-pervading Lord, may they all, remaining in this field, worship you according to the measure of their own lifespans until after the dissolution of Brahmā.
O Lord of Gods, may your name "Somanātha" attain renown throughout the Brahmāṇḍa, including all things mobile and immobile; O Tejo-liṅga, salutations be unto you! 54.
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, "So be it," I again entered into dissolution within the Liṅga. O Goddess, this entire cause has been told to you in its entirety, without omission.

Since you previously asked for a concise account free from doubt, I have provided only a brief outline regarding the qualities of Śrī Someśa; for its full extent is as inconceivable as that of the jewels within the ocean. (56)
It is delusive to those who are not my devotees, but it increases the intelligence of my devotees; those fools, being deluded, do not perceive my true nature at all.
The Goddess said: O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the Gods, where in that sacred field does that Liṅga of Splendor (Tejoliṅga) stand, whose majesty is such as this?
Īśvara said: Listen with diligence, O Goddess, and having heard, take it to heart; this supreme Prabhāsa, O Goddess, is a sacred field (kṣetra) dear to me. 59.
The abode of the gods is twelve yojanas in extent, and the pedestal there is proclaimed to be five yojanas in measure.
In the midst of that, O Goddess, is my abode, which extends for a distance of one gavyūti; it is situated on the northern shore of the ocean, O Goddess, and is known as Devikāmukha.
From the east of Vajriṇī as far as the river Nyaṅkumatī, it is four [yojanas] in width and five yojanas in length.

This is declared to be the *kṣetrapīṭha*; now hear concerning the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). From the ocean to Kauravī, measured from south to north, it should be known to extend from Gomukha to Aśvamedhaka from east to west. (63)
O Goddess, this is my abode; I never abandon it. The Linga situated in its center is that which has been proclaimed to you. (64)
Having taken recourse to the western direction and being in the vicinity of the ocean, at a distance of three hundred dhanvantaras to the west of Kṛtasmara.
The self-manifested Liṅga of great power is established there; the god Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, is present in that place.
In the meantime, O Goddess, at a distance of two hundred bows from Someśa, in the fourteenth division, there is [a place]. (67)
That pericarp, circular in shape on all sides, is dear to me; O Pārvatī, whatever living beings die there in due course of time, [they attain my state].
Worms, insects, moths, and other such beings—whether superior or middling—all go to my world as well, once they have shaken off their impurities.
One need not consider whether it is the northern or the southern solstice; for all those who have died within the sacred field, every time is auspicious.

O Great Goddess, for the benefit of all living beings, the Primordial Lord Śarva brought forth the primordial principles and illuminated this field of great splendor, wherein human beings attain perfection.
O Goddess of gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, that wise man who has made his vow shall remain even if he is struck by hundreds of obstacles for as long as he lives.
He shall go to the supreme abode, reaching which he no longer grieves, by virtue of the majesty of that sacred field and of Sthāṇu, whose deeds are wondrous.
Having committed thousands of sins, one indeed later experiences remorse; however, at Prabhāsa, one shall be liberated and shall not go to the city of the Lord of Death.
Having recognized the terrible Kali age, which is senseless and filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!", the Lord of Obstacles was appointed there for the sake of protection, O Goddess.
But those who hate Brāhmaṇas, those who engage in caviling against devotion to Śiva, those who are slayers of Brāhmaṇas, those who are ungrateful, and likewise those who are deceitful; || 76 ||

Those hated by the world, those who hate their gurus, thorns in the side of sacred fords and shrines, those devoted to every kind of sin, and whoever else is likewise contemptible—[these are the ones he should avoid]. (77)
Indeed, for the sake of their protection, a leader of obstacles was appointed at the side of Kālāgnirudra, possessing prowess equal to that of Rudra. (78)
O Goddess of gods, this field protects and restrains even the most sinful; even if Brahmin-killers and men who have committed great crimes should die there, [they are saved]. (79)
O lady of excellent hips, O goddess with lotus-like eyes, hear now of their destination in this field: for ten thousand divine years. (80)
And they are born as the sons of slave-girls; at the end of that time, they become Brahmarākṣasas. Then, O Goddess, when their sin has been exhausted, they again enter into a state of low birth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not commit sin there; for sin committed elsewhere is destroyed in this sacred field.
Furthermore, a sin committed against him leads to rebirth as a Piśāca or in hell; yet the Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, extends his grace even to those born in the animal kingdom.
O beloved, he grants the supreme abode, but not to those who hate Brahman; rather, to those who, having attained meditative absorption, are self-disciplined and composed in mind.
O Goddess, those who, having restrained the collection of their senses, recite the Śatarudriya while stationed at Prabhāsa, have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt. (85)
If any man should go to Prabhāsa, the supreme sacred field, he should employ such means that he may never return again.
This must be kept secret, O lady of beautiful hips; it should not be given to just anyone. This scripture must be guarded like one's own life-breaths, my dear. (87)
He by whom this scripture, which illuminates the field of Prabhāsa, was composed—he should be known as Śiva himself, abiding in human form. (88)
O Pārvatī, I always abide within his physical form; when he is saluted, worshipped, or meditated upon, it is as if I myself have been so honored—of this there is no doubt. (89)

O Goddess, in the Kali age, the supreme Prabhāsa-kṣetra is difficult to attain; yet now, out of affection for you, I shall indeed describe its special excellence. Truly, truly, again truly—truly three times, O beautiful lady of the gods. (90)
O Goddess, among all those lingas of Someśa that exist in the world of Bhūrloka, I am most fond of this linga; for whatever qualities it possesses, O Goddess, they are known to me.
I alone understand; no one else knows in any way. Among all other lingas, I am the one to be worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
Furthermore, O Goddess, we ourselves shall worship this very liṅga. || 93 ||
O illustrious one, at that time when there was indeed no Brahmā, no earth, and no sun, [there remained] the entire world, O Lord of the World. 94.
At that time, during the dissolution of Brahmā, this Liṅga, adopting its future mode of existence, protects this very place.
O fair-faced one, ten crores of lingas from Gaṅgādvāra come here at midday and merge into this linga.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth and those that reside in the sky, they all come at all times for the purpose of bathing this Liṅga.
Blessed indeed are those mortals established at Prabhāsa who shall behold Someśvara, the liberator from the fear of saṃsāra. || 98 ||
O Goddess, for those who, with purified minds, remember the Someśvara Liṅga, there will be the destruction of all their sins; of this there is no doubt.

O Goddess, this sacred field, which is always delightful to hosts of sages and perfected beings, is known to me as my most beloved; even one who has died after exhausting all his life-force, O Goddess, attains a state higher than heaven when he dies here—of this there is no doubt. (100)
That which the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, do not understand—neither through Sāṃkhya, nor through Yoga, nor even through Pāśupata. || 101 ||

O illustrious lady, that which is the partless state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) is indeed obtained in this liṅga; yet gods and others continue to wander in saṃsāra as long as they remain [elsewhere].
"As long as they do not find the three-eyed god Someśvara, this field is called Prabhāsa; I am the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), of this there is no doubt. (103)
Indeed, this great majesty of Someśvara himself has been told to you for the sake of awakening; those men who shall read this constantly will go to that very abode of the Moon-crested Lord.
Those humans who, full of devotion, have sought refuge in Someśvara, the best of gods, do not wander again in the terrible and fearsome wheel of saṃsāra. (105)
Those twice-born who, having resorted to the southern form, constantly recite the Śatarudriya, do not undergo rebirth in this world; they have indeed reached the supreme further shore of saṃsāra.
I have related to you this mere outline, a single portion of the glorious Somanātha; it could not be told by a single mouth even in many years or many yugas. (107)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Śrī Somanātha," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, O benefactor of the world, speak again of the majesty of the illustrious Lord Someśvara, which destroys all sins. Furthermore, tell me of the triad of deities here—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa. || 1 ||
Īśvara said: Listen with a focused mind to my ancient secret, and to that most wonderful and great event which occurred at that liṅga.
Sixty thousand crores of sages with upward-directed vital energy entered that liṅga, like offerings of ghee into a fire.
Success, growth, contentment, prosperity, and nourishment as the fifth—fame, peace, and likewise fortune—arose from that liṅga. || 4 ||
There is the origin of seventy million mantras and supernatural powers (siddhis), as well as other divine yogic elixirs and divine medicinal rasāyanas.
The Gāruḍa, the Bhūtatantra, the Khecarīs, and likewise the Vyaṃtarīs—all of them emerged from that Liṅga together with Yoga.
Furthermore, whatever other eight siddhis have been proclaimed, they all emerged from that place together with the Liṅga.
O Goddess, I shall speak of another matter: those who have attained perfection here, born from a portion of myself, have reached dissolution in this liṅga.
And I shall describe all their heroic exploits in due order: the Purākramas, the Grahas, the Muṇḍas, and the Guḍakas, along with their causes.
Vimala and Daṇḍika—these seven are remembered as the Kutsikas; they attained perfection in this Liṅga in ancient times through my Pāśupata Yoga.
Rudra, Vipra, Dāna, Candra, Mantha, Avalokaka, and Sūryāvaloka—these seven are proclaimed as the descendants of Garga. (11)
And those Siddhas, O fair-complexioned lady, are at Someśvara and Prabhāsa: Mūka, another Śiva, Prakāśa, and likewise Kapila.
Satkula and Karṇikāra were proclaimed as men who attained perfection in ancient times at Someśvara, in the sin-destroying Prabhāsa.
In age after age, O my beloved, these and other Brahmins who have been perfected in the past, as well as those who will exist in the Kali Yuga, [have attained perfection] in that Linga of mine.
There they shall attain a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain. All this has been told to you regarding that supreme liṅga which bestows success. (19)
That which is established at Prabhāsa is difficult for all mortals to attain; yet no one recognizes it, being shrouded by inauspicious karmas.

Whatever defects caused by planets there may be, as well as other defects caused by spirits (bhūtas), including ḍākinīs, pretas, vetālas, rākṣasas, grahas, and pūtanās—[all these are destroyed]. || 17 ||
Piśācas, yātudhānas, mātṛs who carry off newborns, child-seizing spirits, and likewise other such grahas as well as those grahas who are Buddhas. || 18 ||
Fever, spirits, and other seizing demons; diarrhea, fistula-in-ano; urinary stones, dysuria, and thousands of other diseases. (19)

Likewise, those with foul names (leprosy), as well as others, and other diseases of leprosy; likewise other diseases of consumption, and similarly wind-tumors (vātagulma); and whatever other diseases have been proclaimed—[all these are destroyed]. || 20 ||
Having approached Someśvara, by the sight of that Liṅga, all [sins] are utterly destroyed, like fuel cast into a fire. || 21 ||
And other calamities, such as serpents, crocodiles, and scorpions—all these perish there upon the sight of Śrī Someśvara. (22)
He who is known by the name Someśvara is remembered as the western Bhairava; he is celebrated under synonymous names such as Kālāgnirudranātha.
O Goddess of gods, I abide there as the bestower of grace upon my devotees; I consume all the evil deeds of men, without a doubt. (24)
That vital breath which resides in the bodies of embodied beings and moves through their forms; within whose interior this entire cosmic egg exists, who is both one and manifold.
All the Vedas and the great sages praise that God, through whose gateway the form of the Supreme Brahman is attained. (26)
O Goddess, this very Mahādeva is established at Prabhāsa; just as no man finds a jewel hidden within a house, [so too is he not perceived]. || 27 ||
That very Liṅga, which in a former Kalpa split open the seven netherworlds (pātālas), remains likewise in my house like a precious jewel at Prabhāsa.
It was described as being like ten million suns, resembling the fire of universal dissolution; therefore, Someśvara was formerly called Kālāgnirudra.
Thus, O Goddess Pārvatī, the majesty of Someśvara, which destroys all sins, has been told to you in brief. (30)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sovereignty of Śrī Someśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: I bow to that divine splendor which was seen by me in ancient times, situated between Kālāgnirudra at Prabhāsa, born from Śaṅkara.

I go for refuge to that God of gods, Someśvara, the cause of the destruction of sins, who was worshipped in ancient times by the ṛṣis of the Vedic collections and also through the yogas declared in the Vedas. || 2 ||
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of grace upon devotees! There is a certain doubt in my heart; you ought to sever it.
Īśvara said: O illustrious goddess, what doubt has arisen within you? Tell me that, O auspicious one, and I shall explain it all to you.
The Goddess said: "If you are indeed Mahādeva, how was this garland of skulls made? You are the Creator, without beginning or end, the agent of creation and destruction."
Then, smiling, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods, spoke these words: "This garland of mine, which shines resplendent with many millions of skulls," || 6 ||
Then, with the skull-caps of thousands of Nārāyaṇas and ten thousand Brahmās, she was fashioned as one who is without beginning or end.
One becomes Viṣṇu and another indeed becomes Brahmā; in every kalpa, I create Viṣṇu as the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) within that kalpa.
O Goddess, I am such as this, stationed in the Prābhāsika field at the base of the Kālāgni-liṅga, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a rosary, peaceful, and devoid of beginning, middle, or end; seated in the lotus posture, bestowing boons, he resembles the snow, the kunda flower, and the moon. || 10 ||
Viṣṇu stands on my left and Pitāmaha on my right; the four Vedas are in my belly, and the eternal Brahman is in my heart.
Agni, Soma, and Sūrya are established within the eyes.
O Great Goddess, such a one is established in Prabhāsa; since he has been brought here through the attainment of the essential reality, let there be no doubt in you regarding this at all. (13)
Having been addressed thus, the goddess, filled with supreme devotion, then praised the Lord of the gods of gods with a voice faltering with joy.
The Goddess said: Victory to you, O God, Mahādeva, the Lord who brings all things into being! Salutations be to you, the Lord of the gods; salutations indeed to the Supreme Lord. || 15 ||

Salutations to the creator of the beginningless creation, and salutations to the all-pervading one; salutations to you who abide in all things, and let there be salutations to you, the abode of all abodes. (16)
Salutations to you who have six ends; salutations to you who have twelve ends. Salutations to you, O Hamsabheda; and salutations to you, the bestower of liberation.
Thus praised by the Goddess at that time, the Lord whose crest is the trembling moon was pleased and spoke these words.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise lady! I am pleased; let a boon be chosen."
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased with me, or if I am indeed worthy of a boon, then speak once more in detail regarding the majesty of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra. (20)
O Lord of Beings, why has the Blessed Viṣṇu, the foremost leader in the destruction of the Daityas, abandoned Dvārakā and taken refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa? (21)
How did Hari disregard the sixty thousand holy fords and the sixty billion [others] situated within Dvārakā? (22)
Having thus abandoned that holy Dvārakā, which is surrounded by the immortals and frequented by those who have performed meritorious deeds, how did you come to Prabhāsa?
Hari, the leader of gods and men and the source of heaven and earth—for what reason did he abandon Dvārakā and meet his end at Prabhāsa? (24)
How did he, the foremost of wheel-bearers, who alone sets in motion the mind-made wheel among men, pass away at Prabhāsa? (25)
How is it that the Lord Viṣṇu, who provides protection for the entire world throughout all its realms, has taken refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa?
At the time of dissolution, having drunk the water and made his body composed of water, he turned the world into a single ocean by means of his vision and his perceived self.
O Lord of Pārvatī, how did he meet his death at Prabhāsa—he who was formerly the Ancient One himself, assuming the form of a boar in the Purāṇa? (28)
He lifted up the entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves; how then did he cast off his body at Prabhāsa, the destroyer of sins?
How is it that he, by whom Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain after assuming the form of a lion, has taken refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, O Lord of the God of Gods? (30)
The Vedas indeed describe that God, who has a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand heads, and great splendor, in age after age.
How did that god abandon his own body at Prabhāsa, from which arose his ancestral abode in the Nābhyaraṇya? 32.
When the world had become a single ocean, that lotus was not born of mud; by whom was it raised up in a mere moment—is he not Hari residing at Prabhāsa?

How did that Supreme Lord, the slayer of enemy heroes, who lies upon the northern shore of the ocean—the Ocean of Milk, the sea of nectar—having resorted to eternal yoga, abandon his body at Prabhāsa?
He made the gods consumers of *havya* offerings and the ancestors consumers of *kavya* offerings; how then has he, the Lord of the Gods of gods, resorted to the sacred field of Prabhāsa? (35)
How can that God, who for the welfare of the world assumes a form appropriate to the age and thereby upholds the Dharma, have taken refuge in a mere field? (36)

The three castes, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three reciters, the three times, the three types of action, the three gods, and the three qualities—how is it that the Lord by whom these were created in the past has now resorted to a field? (37)
He is the destination for those endowed with righteousness and the non-destination for evildoers; he is the source of the fourfold social order and the protector of the fourfold social order.
Why did he who was the knower of the four Vedas and established in the system of the four stages of life pass away at Prabhāsa, having abandoned Dvārakā? (39)
The quarters of space, the sky, the earth, water, wind, and fire; the two luminaries, the moon and sun; the Lord of the Yugas, whose body is the night. (40)
He who is heard of as the supreme light, he who is heard of as the supreme austerity; he who is declared to be beyond the beyond, he who possesses the supreme Self.
How did he who is the divine one beginning with Āditya, the all-pervading destroyer of the Daityas, become the son of Devakī and attain perfection at Prabhāsa?

He who is the Ender at the end of the age, and he who is the Ender of the Ender of the worlds; he who is the bridge for the existence of the worlds, and he who is the pure one among those of pure deeds.

He who is the knower among those learned in the Vedas, the lord of those who possess sovereign power, who has become the moon for all beings, and who has become the fire for those on the path of fire; 44.
He is the mind of men, the asceticism of ascetics, the discipline of those who possess statesmanship, and the splendor even of the splendid. (45)
He who is the embodiment of all forms and the ultimate goal of all that moves—how is it that he has left Dvārakā and taken refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa? (46)

Wind originates from space; fire has wind as its life-force; the gods have fire as their life-force; and Madhusūdana is the life-force of fire. How then is he, who is the life-force of the Lotus-born, established in the sacred field of Prabhāsa?
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by the Goddess at that time, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, spoke these words to Pārvatī while smiling.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the detailed account of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra; it is a secret that destroys all sins and is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (49)
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, there are many sacred fields on earth; the number of holy fords (tīrthas) is in the tens of millions, and your power is equal in measure to theirs.
Indeed, the radiance of immeasurable power has been fully proclaimed; likewise, the reality of Brahmā, the reality of Viṣṇu, and the reality of Rudra.
Furthermore, O Pārvatī, such a conjunction is difficult to find elsewhere; at Prabhāsa, O Goddess of the lords of gods, the triad of principles (tattvas) is established.
And Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, together with the twenty-four principles (tattvas), remained there in that place himself in the form of a child, under various names.
The sovereign of the twenty-five principles, the foremost of deities, the manifest destroyer of the Daityas, resides in that auspicious place.
O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, I dwell together with you at Prabhāsa, the destroyer of sins, endowed with the thirty-six principles.
Know that this auspicious Prabhāsa alone is the field consisting of reality and comprising all sacred fords; do not entertain any doubt whatsoever.
Even those insects and moths that die there, as well as human beings, go to the supreme abode; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Goddess, women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, beasts, birds, and wild animals who die at Prabhāsa go to the world of Śiva.
Those who are bound by lust and anger, and brought under the sway of greed; those overcome by the darkness of ignorance, and established in the principle of illusion (māyātattva). || 59 ||
Those who are bound by the noose of Time, deluded by the net of craving, those who are devoted to unrighteousness, and those who remain as evildoers—[these are they]. (60)

Even those who have killed a Brahmin, those who are ungrateful, others who have violated the teacher’s bed, and even those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka)—they all go to the supreme goal.
Even those men who are killers of their mother and likewise killers of their father—all of them attain liberation; how much more so, then, those who perform auspicious deeds?

Knowing this, O Great Goddess, Hari, the destroyer of the Daityas, reached the holy site of Prabhāsa and cast off his own body. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Question Regarding the Abiding of Śrī Hari at Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first section (Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Furthermore, O beautiful lady, I shall tell you another secret; that which has not been told to anyone, I shall speak to you, O fair-faced one. (1)
Brahmā is situated in the portion of earth, Janārdana in the portion of water; Rudra is situated in the portion of fire, and likewise Īśvara in the portion of air.
Established in the spatial division of the sky, Sadāśiva himself is present there.
Whichever portion belongs to whichever deity, whatever sacred sites (tīrthas) are located therein, there is no doubt that he alone is remembered as the lord of each.

Chāgalaṇḍa, Dugaṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kāliñjara, Vana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthaleśvara, the renowned Śūleśvara situated in the *pṛthvītattva*, Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpeśa, and Unnāntikeśvara. (5–6) *Note on "Mahābhūtopari": This refers to the location above the great elements.*
Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava—O fair-faced one, these indeed constitute the eight purifiers situated in the water.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara; Āṣāḍhi, Daṇḍi, Bhārabhūti, and Lāṅgala.
Indeed, this primary group of eight secrets is established in the principle of fire (tejas-tattva); likewise, Gayā, Kurukṣetra, and the sacred site of Kanakhala.
Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Māhendra, and the one known as Bhīma—this Vāyvaṣṭaka, which is more secret than the secret, has indeed been proclaimed to you.
Vastrāpatha, Rudrakoṭi, Jyeṣṭheśvara, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Rudrakarṇa, the one named Varṇa, and the one known as Sthāpa; || 11 ||
O fair-faced one, this indeed is the group of eight purifiers situated in the sky; all these sacred fords of reality (tattvatīrtha) have truly been described.
Whichever deity resides within a particular principle (tattva), that deity indicates its greatness; and the great principle of water, O beloved, is exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu.

Therefore, the Śruti declares that Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the one who reclines upon the waters; and as for the principle of water, those which are called sacred fords (tīrthas) have been described by me to you.
O Goddess of gods, those [elements] are indeed certainly dear to Nārāyaṇa; and that which is the watery principle (tattva) is remembered as being within the Prābhāsika. || 15 ||
Therein the Lord undergoes dissolution, and Hari does so birth after birth; he is Vāsudeva, the subtle Self, abiding in that which is higher than the highest.
That Śiva is the supreme ether, the all-pervading one without beginning or end; there is nothing higher than him in any of the scriptures or traditional teachings.
O illustrious lady, there is no difference between them and me regarding the Siddhānta, Āgama, Vedānta, and the philosophical systems (darśanas). || 18 ||
In that place, Hari is personally and perceptibly present; though endowed with four lingas, he is not recognized by anyone.
Whatever fruit is obtained by those of the various castes who are committed to lifelong vows for the sake of liberation, that same fruit one attains simply by beholding the Bhalluka-tīrtha.
That site is the size of a cow-hide, circular on all sides; indeed, O beautiful lady, no one knows it except through the scripture.
O Pārvatī, even today the equinox flows there for men; and right there are five liṅgas, some of which have five faces.
Some were as large as hen's eggs; they were entirely encircled by serpents and marked with tridents. (23)
By the mere sight of them, one obtains the fruit of worshipping ten million liṅgas; therefore, this great sacred field (mahākṣetra) is constantly frequented by Brahmā and the other gods.

And by the foremost of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, by those perfected ones, and by ascetics, [this should be done] every month on the eighth day and likewise every month on the fourteenth day.
O fair-faced one, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, the liṅgas situated at Prabhāsa are worshipped.
At Saṃnihatyā in Kurukṣetra, together with all the tens of thousands of holy fords—namely Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, Prayāga, and Pṛthūdaka—[he performed his ablutions].
Sixty thousand and sixty billion holy fords (tīrthas) will assemble at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean on every Māghī day.
O lady of excellent vows, by remembering that sacred ford or even by chanting its name, one shall cast off the sins arising at the time of death.
Ānarttasāra, Saumya, as well as Bhuvanabhūṣaṇa, the divine Pāñcanada, Puṇya, Ādiguhya, and Mahodaya.
The ocean-enclosure named Siddharatnākara, as well as Dharmākāra, Kalādhāra, and Śivagarbhagṛha. || 31 ||
It is the abode of all the gods and the destroyer of all sins; O beloved, the names of this sacred field differ in every Kalpa.
O beautiful goddess, know the secret measurements and so forth; O Goddess, in the first aeon of old, it was known as Pramodana.
Surrounding that [lake] is Nandana, and beyond that is Śiva; beyond Śiva is Ugra, and further beyond that is Bhadrika.
After that is the Samindhana [Kalpa], and after that the Kāmada; then also the Siddhida, the Dharmajña, the Vaiśvarūpa, and the Muktida. (35)
Likewise, [he saw] the illustrious Padmanābha and the greatly radiant Śrīvatsa; and likewise Pāpasaṃhāra, who bestows all desires.
O Varārohe, likewise, O Goddess, there is Sudarśana, which contains the essence of dharma among all dharmas, is radiant, and destroys evil; beyond this, there are here the Utpalāvartikas.
O Goddess, that which is known as my inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) in the center of the field—its names have been told to you, O Goddess, in due order. (38)
Having heard all these names as well as the majesty of the sacred field, their desired success shall undoubtedly come to pass. (39)
For one who recites this at the three periods of the day, which brings great prosperity, the sin committed during the intervals between the twilight prayers perishes within a single day and night.
Even those who are hypocritical, of small intellect, deluded, and living as mere beggars—such Brahmins, upon death, go to heaven.
O Goddess of gods, within the center of this field, at the middle of the sun’s yojana, there are thousands of other secondary fields (upakṣetras).
Some are in the form of lotuses, some have the shape of barley grains; some are hexagonal, some triangular, and some are shaped like staffs.
O Goddess, the deities beginning with Brahmā, distinguished by the divisions of the lunar disc and the square, are situated within the center of the field.
Some are half a yojana in size, some are half of that [quarter], and some are measured by the standard of a nivarttana or by the measure of a daṇḍa.
In Prabhāsa, there are tens of millions of sites, some the size of a cow's hide, some the distance of a bowshot, and others merely the size of a sacred thread.
O lotus-eyed one, even an eighth part of a finger’s breadth of space exists where there are no sacred fords or divine realms in the expanse of the sky. (47)
Having reached the field of Prabhāsa, they remain there until the dissolution; likewise, O Goddess, that which is the Liṅga at Kedāra and that which is at Mahālaya.
And [he saw] Madhyameśvara, likewise Pāśupateśvara, Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, and also Bhadreśvara. || 49 ||
Some [worship] Śvaramathaikāgra, Kāleśvara, Ajeśvara, Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, and likewise Kāyāvarohaṇa. || 50 ||
The meritorious Cāpaṭeśvaraka, as well as Badarikāśrama, Rudrakoṭi, Mahākoṭi, and the auspicious Śrīparvata. || 51 ||

And Kapālī, the Lord of Gods, as well as Karavīra again; O Goddess, the supremely meritorious Oṃkāra and Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage, where ten million Rudras capable of assuming forms at will are said to reside.
And whatever other meritorious places there are on my earth, they all dwell at Prabhāsa, having placed Prayāga before them.
The daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) is in the north, while the ocean is remembered as being in the south; this is proclaimed to be the measurement from south to north of this sacred field.
To the east of Rukmiṇī and to the west of Taptatoyā—this is proclaimed as the measurement from east to west of Prabhāsa. || 55 ||
O beautiful goddess, having reached this interval, those sacred fords (tīrthas) indeed reside there, extending from Pātāla down to the outer shell of the universe.
Knowing this, O Great Goddess, Hari—who is composed of all the gods—reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa and cast off his own body.

Those who shall hear this divine and indeed formidable account of mine, whether on the sacred festival days or at any time, they too, by my grace, shall go to Triviṣṭapa, the abode of the meritorious.

Thus, O Goddess, this wondrous and meritorious life-story of yours has been told in its entirety; now tell me something else that is exceedingly dear to you, which brings great exaltation to the sages.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Prabhāsa-kṣetra as the Supreme among All Kṣetras by Means of the Majesty of the Tīrthas and Kṣetras Situated within Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, having been addressed thus, the goddess, her eyes wide with wonder and her fair-browed form covered in horripilation, questioned him once again.
The Goddess said: "I am blessed, I have performed meritorious deeds, and I have well-practiced austerity, since this greatness of the sacred field has been heard by me from Mahādeva. (2)
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence! O Hara, you have explained everything that was previously asked by me.
Furthermore, O Lord of the gods of gods, though delighted by the nectar of your words, I do not attain satiety, O Maheśvara, God of gods. (4)
I am desirous of asking something regarding the extent of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra; therefore, O Lord of Desire, O Sovereign of the World, show me compassion and tell it to me. (5)

Īśvara said: O beautiful one, that which is situated in the central womb of the earth is known as Jambūdvīpa; and it is indeed divided into nine parts according to the distinction of its regions (varṣas).
Of that [Jambudvīpa], the first is Bhāratavarṣa, which is also recorded as being divided into nine parts; it measures nine thousand yojanas from south to north.
It is recorded as being eighty thousand [yojanas] in length from east to west; the Himavat mountain is situated to the north, and the Kṣīroda ocean is recorded to be to the south.
In the meantime, O Goddess, the supreme field of Bhārata underwent the four ages: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Tiṣya.

In this very [Kṛta Yuga], there is this state of the ages (yugāvasthā) and the people consisting of the four castes; [their lifespans] are four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, and likewise one hundred years.
O Goddess, men live here in the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages in succession; this four-petalled earthly lotus which has been described by me— 11.
The regions of Bhārata and others are its petals in the four directions: Bhārata, Ketumāla, Kuru, and Bhadrāśva. (12)

That region called Bhārata which I have described as being in the south, has the great ocean to its south and west, and to its east; and to its north lies the Himavat mountain, like the string of a bow. (13)
This very land of Bhārata, O fair-faced one, contains all seeds; it is the field of action, for nowhere else is there the attainment of the fruits of merit and sin.
O Goddess of the gods, this is the constant desire even of the gods: "May we indeed attain human birth upon the land of Bhārata. (15)
In Bhadrāśva Viṣṇu is Aśvaśiras; in Bhārata he is established as Kūrma; in Ketumāla he is Varāha; and likewise in the North (Uttara), he is Matsya.
O Great Goddess, through the arrangement of the constellations within those [regions], the territories are established; in all four [directions], O Great Goddess, the body consists of nine parts.
O Great Goddess, he who is Bhārata, established in the form of a tortoise—I shall now describe to you the arrangement of the constellations and planets upon his body. (18)
The Blessed Lord, in the form of a tortoise, stands facing the east, having stepped upon this land of Bhārata with its nine divisions, O beloved.
Learn from me the constellations belonging to this [constellation] which is situated in nine parts: Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and the third, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), are located on the back of the tortoise.
Furthermore, O Dear One, the three constellations Raudra, Punarvasu, and Puṣya are at the mouth; likewise, the one called Āśleṣā, Paitra, and the first Phālgunī.
Three constellations are situated in the southeastern quarter; Phālgunī, Uttarā, Hasta, and Citrā are known as this triad of stars.
In the right flank of the tortoise, the other quarter of the asterisms is likewise situated; Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā (Maitra) are recorded as the triad in the southwest (Nairṛta).
The root [constellation] is Ārdrā, and likewise three are recorded as being in the back: Āṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, and Dhaniṣṭhā are declared to be here.
O illustrious lady, there are three constellations in the northwest quarter: the constellation Vāruṇa and likewise the two Proṣṭhapadas.

O Dear One, three [asterisms] are situated in the left flank of the Tortoise: Revatī, the asterism presided over by the Aśvins, and the southern asterism (Bharaṇī)—this is the triad. It is declared to be at the foot of Īśa; hear now its auspicious and inauspicious results. (26)
O Great Goddess, whatever planet is the lord of a particular asterism, from that [planet] comes danger for that region; likewise, when it is in its exaltation, there is the arrival of auspiciousness.
This tortoise has been described by me here in the Bhārata as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, whose nature is inconceivable, in whom everything is established. (28)
Aries and Taurus are in the center of the heart and the mouth; Gemini and the following signs are in the front and right foot; likewise, Cancer and Leo are situated in the [left] foot.
Leo, Virgo, and Libra are known as the three zodiac signs in the belly; Libra and Scorpio are both in the south-western foot.
In the tail, however, Scorpio (Vṛścika) and Sagittarius (Dhanus) are situated; and in the northwest, on the left foot, are the triad beginning with the Archer (Dhanurgrāha).
Likewise, O Great Goddess, Aquarius and Pisces are situated upon his northern flank; and Pisces and Aries are located at his northeastern foot.

Likewise, O beloved, the regions of the tortoise and the constellations are situated within these regions; the zodiac signs are within the constellations, and the planets are established within the zodiac signs.

Therefore, when there is affliction from planets or constellations, one should predict affliction for the country; in such cases, people perform ritual bathing, as well as giving gifts, fire-offerings (homa), and other rites.
O Goddess, this very Vaiṣṇava foot is that which is the central planet of this [system]; it is known as Nārāyaṇa, the inconceivable self, the cause and the Lord of the universe. (35)
Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, and Mars; Jupiter, Saturn, and Rāhu are the lords of the signs beginning with Aries. (36)
O Great Goddess, Janārdana exists in such a form as the Tortoise; on his southwestern foot, there is the land renowned as Saurāṣṭra.
And thus, O beautiful one, it is divided into nine parts according to the divisions of the city; its ninth part is situated near the ocean.
O Goddess, the place known as Prabhāsa is always dear to me; it is twelve yojanas in extent and circumference.
The pedestal of this [mountain] is said to be five yojanas in extent; in its center, O Goddess, my abode stands near the ocean.
In its center, O Great Goddess, I dwell in the form of a liṅga.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of beautiful countenance, I dwell there together with you, three hundred bow-lengths to the west of Kṛtasmara.
O Great Goddess, that place of mine is dearer even than Kailāsa; it is only the size of a cowhide, O fair-faced one, and is to be kept strictly secret. (43)
O Goddess of the gods, that which was unspeakable has been revealed out of affection for you; this Prābhāsika field is illuminated by my own radiance. 44.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, it was called Prabhāsa in the first kalpa; but in the second, radiance (prabhā) was obtained by all the gods, including Indra.
O Goddess of gods, because of my radiance (*prabhā*), it is remembered as Prābhāsika; O Goddess of gods, it is where the great Asuras possess power (*prabhāva*). (46)

Alternatively, it is celebrated as Prabhāsa because of its radiance in the worlds. O Goddess, since it first shines forth among all splendors on earth, that Prabhāsa is renowned as the primordial shrine (āditīrtha) of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 47 ||
Alternatively, it is called Prābhāsika because the sun was highly polished there by Viśvakarman, whereby a direct descent of light occurred. 48.

Alternatively, O Goddess, because the Moon had been cursed by Dakṣa and was devoid of luster, he regained his radiance there; therefore it is remembered as Prābhāsika. Indeed, the goddess Bhāratī brought forth the Aurva fire, the submarine fire. (49)

Alternatively, O Goddess of the Gods, it is celebrated as Prabhāsa because the sublime speech of Brahmā (Bhāratī), spoken by the Brahmins, is heard there on the path; since this is always so, O Great Goddess, it is therefore called Prabhāsa.
O beloved, that ocean always shines with surging waves; therefore, it is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Prabhāsa.
O beautiful lady, because the sun always remains there visibly present, it became famous on earth by the name Prabhāsa.
I grant there every supreme desire for those who are destined to attain it; therefore, that sacred site (tīrtha) is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Prabhāsa.

O beautiful goddess, in the same way, names differ according to the divisions of the Kalpas; they are distinguished in many ways through etymological variations and specific causes, O beloved. That name which is to be given as "Prabhāsa" is remembered as being eternal.
"O Goddess, it is established in the element of air within the primordial body of Viṣṇu. Thus, O Goddess, I have told you in brief the cause of the sacred field."
O fair-faced one, I shall tell you again today that which you ask; speak quickly, O auspicious lady, whatever dwells in your mind. (56)
The Goddess said: O Hara, tell me in detail how this Prābhāsika Kṣetra came into being in this Kalpa, as well as its origin and its cause.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the cause of the sacred field (kṣetra) exactly as it is; by hearing which, a human being through devotion is liberated from all sins. (58)
O beautiful lady, O noble one, out of affection for you, I shall describe the greatness and the secret of the primordial field, which destroys all sins. (59)
But in this kalpa, O goddess of beautiful countenance, at the very beginning during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, long ago while Brahmā was engaged in creation—
O beloved, he was first born from the right eye as Sūrya; thereafter, in the course of time, he came to have two wives.
Of those two, the queen is to be known as Dyau (the Sky) and Nikṣubhā is remembered as Pṛthivī (the Earth). On the seventh day of the month of Saumya, Dyau is joined with the Sun.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, the Sun shall be in conjunction with the Earth; then the Earth and the divine Āditya go into union.
There, the Earth, having bathed at the proper season, conceives a fetus from the Sun; and here on this terrestrial plane, the Sky gives birth to water as its fetus during these rainy seasons.

Thereupon, for the sake of the sustenance of the three worlds, the earth produces crops; and through the consumption of those crops, the twice-born, being delighted, offer oblations with sacrificial offerings.
The ancestors and deities are worshipped with the utterances of Svāhā and Svadhā; for she makes them free from hunger by means of embryos, medicinal herbs, nectar, and ambrosia. (66)
Because it sustains mortals, ancestors, and gods, the earth is known as Bhūḥ; and just as she became a queen, so too is this daughter considered hers.
And I shall describe without omission those who are her offspring: Marīci was the son of Brahmā, and his son is known as Kaśyapa, the descendant of Marīci. (68)
From him was born Hiraṇyakaśipu, and his son was Prahlāda; Prahlāda’s son is known by the name Virocana. (69)
She who was Saṃjñā, the sister of Virocana, was the mother; she is remembered as the granddaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the daughter of Diti. (70)
She is the wife of Viśvakarman and is called Prāhlādī by the wise.
Now, the daughter of Marīci named Atirūpā was auspicious; she was indeed the wife of Aṅgiras and the mother of Bṛhaspati.
The sister of Bṛhaspati was renowned as a teacher of Brahman; she became the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
She gave birth to Viśvakarman, the best among all masters of crafts; he is indeed known by the name Tvaṣṭṛ, the carpenter of the gods.
This daughter of that preceptor of the gods, Viśvakarman, is known as Sureṇu, a beautiful woman renowned throughout the three worlds. (75)
She who was called the daughter of Prahrāda is remembered as the wife of Vaṣṭu; upon her he begot those daughters who are the mothers of the world.
The queen Saṃjñā, daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, is perceived as Dyaus and Prabhā; her shadow, Valayā, is known as the great Nikṣubhā.
That illustrious lady was the wife of the high-souled Mārtaṇḍa; she was a virtuous goddess, devoted to her husband, and endowed with beauty and youth.
But formerly he did not enjoy her as his wife in human form; rather, he dwelt here in the state of being heated by the great heat of his own splendor as the Sun. (79)

On her unattractive limbs, it was as if a month had passed; moreover, when Saṃjñā looked at the Sun, she would close her eyes. Consequently, the Sun, filled with wrath, spoke these words to Saṃjñā: || 80 ||
The Sun said: "O foolish woman, because you always close your eyes whenever you see me, you shall therefore give birth to Yama, the restrainer of living beings."
Īśvara said: Then that goddess, agitated by fear, cast a fickle glance; seeing her with her eyes rolling, Ravi spoke to her again.
The Sun said: "Since your gaze was cast restlessly upon me as soon as I was seen, therefore you shall give birth to a daughter, a river named Vilolā."

Īśvara said: Then, indeed, by that curse of her husband, there were born to her Yama and this Yamunā, the world-renowned great river; and she gave birth to a third son, the auspicious Manu Śrāddhadeva.
Then Saṃjñā, unable to endure the heat of Ravi’s orb, which was intensely radiant and blazing with great splendor, reflected thus in her mind: || 85 ||
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? And where, having gone, will there be peace for me? How might my husband not bring about his own destruction through anger? (86)
Having reflected thus in many ways, the daughter of Prajāpati, the highly fortunate one, then considered taking refuge with her father to be the best course.
Then the illustrious lady, having resolved to go to her father’s house, [beheld] her own shadow-form, as if fashioned limb for limb from her very self.
Beholding that goddess face to face, he spoke these words as if to his own shadow.
Saṃjñā said: "I shall go; may it be well with you—to my own father's abode. O auspicious one, you must remain here without any change of state, according to my command."
"These two children of mine and this maiden of excellent complexion must not be revealed; you must not tell this to the Blessed One. (91)
"Even when asked, you must not speak of this departure of mine; therefore, you are addressed by the name 'Nāmasaṃjñā' (She Who Is Known by Name) for the sake of that very stability."
Chāyā said: "O Goddess, until my hair is seized or until a curse is pronounced, I shall never reveal your secret; you may go wherever you desire. (93)
Īśvara said: Having been addressed thus, the goddess then went to her father’s abode; there she beheld Tvaṣṭṛ, whose impurities had been shaken off by ascetic penance.
And out of great respect, she was honored by Viśvakarman as well; dwelling for a thousand years in her father’s house, that blameless woman remained in her father’s home for some time.
Then her father, having praised his daughter Cārvaṅgī—who had not been away for very long—spoke to her with affection and great respect.
Viśvakarman said: "O child, even though many days pass for one who beholds you alone, they would seem like half a moment; however, dharma is being lost. (97)
For women, a long residence among their kinsmen does not bring glory; the kinsmen’s desire is for the woman to remain in her husband's house. (98)
O daughter, you who are united with your husband Sūrya, the lord of the three worlds, ought not to remain for a long time in your father’s house. 99.
"Go now, my dear, to your husband's house; you have seen me and have been honored by me. O lady of pure smiles, you must come again for a visit. (100)
Īśvara said: Having been addressed thus by her father, "Go, go!", she, assuming the form of a mare, then paid homage to her father once more.
To the north of Meru, O illustrious lady, is that region shaped like a bow, which is renowned in the world as Uttarakuru.
There the virtuous woman, assuming the form of a mare, performed penance without food. In the meantime, O Goddess, the shadow of that Vivasvat—
Then the goddess Saṃjñā, standing nearby and intent on her husband's words, [gave birth]; and upon that second [wife], the Blessed Sun, the Lord of Day, [beheld her].
Thinking, "She is to be known [as my wife]," and infatuated by her physical beauty, he begot upon her two sons and a daughter. (105)
O beautiful goddess, because he was equal to Manu in former times, he became known as Sāvarṇi; he was the first of the two sons born from the Sun.
The second who was another became the planet Śanaiścara; she who was Tapatī became a maiden, and King Saṃvaraṇa chose her as his wife.
And this river named Tāpī, flowing with eternally meritorious waters toward the western ocean, has issued forth from the foot of the Vindhya mountains; it is always auspicious for bathing. (108)
And another daughter of great splendor was likewise born, Bhadrā; however, Chāyā, the earthly Saṃjñā, acted toward her own children as follows. || 109 ||
The virtuous woman did not show such affection toward her elder sisters as she did toward her daily enjoyment of their caresses and other comforts.

O Pārvatī, that future husband of hers who will be patient with her will not treat her as she does toward her own people; for she, O beautiful woman, behaves in one way toward her own kin and in another toward others.
O fair-faced one, he remains on Mount Meru even today performing penance; he forgave everything done by his mother, but Yama did not tolerate that which she had done to him.
Though he entreated him many times, he was exceedingly provoked by the shadow; indeed, out of anger, childishness, and the force of destiny yet to come, [he struck him]. (113)
Then, out of anger, he raised his foot to strike him; however, being full of patience, he did not let it fall upon the body.
With his foot, Yama, the son of Saṃjñā, threatened Chāyā.
Then Chāyā, the daughter of the Earth, being greatly enraged, cursed him; her lips quivered slightly and her sprout-like hands trembled. (116)
Chāyā said: "O transgressor of bounds, since you threaten me, the wife of your father, with your foot, therefore this foot of yours shall fall to the earth this very day. (117)
Īśvara said: But Yama, his mind deeply afflicted by that curse, the righteous-souled one, reported everything to his father along with Manu. || 118 ||
Yama said: "O father, this is a great marvel that has never been seen here by anyone: that a mother, casting aside maternal affection, should bestow a curse upon her son. (119)
Today our mother does not behave toward us with the same affection as before; for, having set aside her elder sons, she desires to show it toward the younger ones. (120)
My foot was raised against her, but it was not actually brought down upon her body; whether out of childishness or through delusion, you ought to forgive that. (121)
"O dear one, O best among speakers, it is clear that I have been cursed by her in anger, saying, 'You are my son'; therefore, she shall not be my mother. (122)
"Even toward sons who are devoid of merit, a mother does not become devoid of affection; how is it that she spoke these words, 'May your foot fall, my son'? (123)
O Blessed One, O Lord of the Cowherds, consider it so that by your grace my foot may not fall today due to my mother’s curse.
Ravi said: "Without doubt, O son, there must be a great cause for this, by which anger has entered you, a high-souled knower of dharma. (126)
A counteraction exists for all curses whatsoever; however, there is never any reversal of a curse pronounced by one's mother.
"It is not right for you to make your mother's word false; however, out of affection for my son, I shall grant you some favor."
"Vermin shall take up the flesh and depart for the surface of the earth; her word shall be made true, and you shall be saved. (128)
Īśvara said: Āditya then spoke to Chāyā: "For what reason do you show greater affection toward one among your sons, even though they are all equal? (129)
Surely you are not their mother; that woman Saṃjñā must have gone elsewhere. For a mother would never utter a curse even toward her children when they are distressed.

"Even if a son were to commit thousands of offenses, even if he were intent on taking one's life, a mother would not commit a sin; therefore, tell me the truth, lest you fall under the power of a curse. (131)
Īśvara said: Seeing the Lord of Day prepared to curse him, the great and virtuous goddess Chāyāsaṃjñā trembled with fear and related everything exactly as it had happened.
And she said: "O Vibhāvasu, I am Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ; I am your wife, O Divākara, duly wedded to you as my husband."
Although Vivasvat questioned her thus many times, she did not speak otherwise with her words; he became enraged and prepared to utter a curse.
Seeing Sūrya with his hand raised to pronounce a curse, Chāyā, the shadow of Vivasvat, related all of Saṃjñā’s secret conduct.
Having heard that, the Blessed Sun went to the abode of Tvaṣṭṛ; there he then worshipped him who is honored by the three worlds.

O Pārvatī, the Creator of the Universe consoled the radiant Sun, who had arrived at his own home with the desire to burn everything down in his wrath; and when the Sun asked, "Where is Saṃjñā?", he spoke to him. (137)
Viśvakarman said: "Indeed, you have already arrived at my abode; listen to my words. This form of yours, though renowned and rich in splendor, is very difficult to endure."
Unable to endure it, Saṃjñā is indeed performing austerities in the forest; you shall see her today, your own wife of auspicious conduct. (139)

"For the sake of beauty, she wanders the forest performing most great penance; this is my opinion based on the word of Brahmā, if it pleases you, O Lord. Today I shall restore your beautiful form, O Lord of Heaven. (140)
Īśvara said: Since the form of the radiant one was indeed originally circular, the Blessed Lord Ravi then said "So be it" to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Permitted by Vivasvat in Śākadvīpa, Viśvakarman placed him upon the earth and proceeded to diminish his splendor.
As the radiant Lord of all beings wandered through the entire world, the oceans, filled with wealth, were agitated on every side.
O Goddess of gods, O illustrious one, as it was indeed wandering, the world—including the moon, planets, and stars—fell into a downward course, becoming cast down and agitated.
All the rivers likewise had their waters agitated, and the mountains were rent asunder, their ridges and foundations shattered.
O lady of excellent complexion, all the celestial abodes, including the Dhruva pole and the entire array of constellations, bound together by revolving rays, descended by the thousands.
The great clouds, resounding with terrible roars, were shattered; the earth, the sky, and the surface of the world were bewildered by the whirling of the sun.

O lady of excellent complexion, at that time the entire world was exceedingly distressed; O Goddess, as all the three worlds were wandering in confusion, the great ṛṣis and the gods, together with Brahmā, offered praises to the Resplendent One.
The gods said: "You are the primordial god of the gods; this entire world was born from you yourself. At the times of creation, preservation, and destruction, you abide in a threefold division. (149)

"May there be well-being for you, O Lord of the World, O maker of heat, rain, and cold! Then Indra, having approached that god while he was being drawn, praised him: "Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World! Victory to you, O God, Master of the World! (15)

Then the seven sages, led by Vasiṣṭha and Atri, praised him with various hymns, uttering "May there be well-being! May there be well-being! And the Vālakhilyas also offered praise with the most excellent declarations of the Vedas.

The Vālakhilyas said: Salutations to you whose nature is the Ṛgveda; salutations to you whose form is the Sāmaveda. Salutations to you whose form is the Yajurveda; salutations to you who are the abode of the Sāmans. || 152 ||

Salutation to Him whose body is the singular form of knowledge, who has shaken off all darkness; salutation to the one whose nature is pure light, who exists as the triple form, and whose essence is stainless.

Salutations to the most excellent, to the one worthy of choice, to the Supreme Self of all; salutations to Him whose form pervades the entire universe and who possesses infinite manifestations. || 154 ||

Salutation to the one who is the cause of all things, the ultimate goal, and the consciousness of all cognitions; salutation to him whose nature is like the sun, whose form is illumination yet remains unperceivable.
Salutations to you, Bhāskara; likewise, salutations to Dinakṛt (the Maker of Day). Salutations to the Cause of all, and to the one who performs the full conjunction of the twilight offerings.

O Blessed One, as you revolve, this entire world revolves with you; the whole universe, the cosmic egg including all that is mobile and immobile, revolves along with it. Indeed, everything here becomes pure when touched by your rays.
The purification of water and other elements is brought about by the touch of your hands. || 158 ||
O Father, until this world is united with your rays, dharma consisting of fire-offerings, gifts, and the like, does not lead to true benefit. 159
For all these Ṛg verses, as well as those Yajus formulas and all the Sāmans, fall forth from your limbs.
O Lord of the World, you consist of the Ṛgveda, and you alone consist of the Yajurveda; since you also consist of the Sāmaveda, therefore, O Lord, you consist of the three Vedas.
You alone are the form of Brahman, both the supreme and the non-supreme; you abide in the form of the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as the subtle and the gross.

Consisting of moments such as *nimeṣa* and *kāṣṭhā*, you are the very essence of time and its instants. Be gracious; by your own will, pacify your own form and splendor. O Lord, for the sake of the worlds, you endure unbearable suffering. (163)

O Lord, you are the liberation of those seeking liberation; you are the supreme object of meditation for those who meditate; you are the refuge of all beings who have turned away from the ritualistic path of action. 164.
May there be welfare for all creatures, O Lord of Gods; may there be welfare for us, O Lord of the worlds. (165)

You alone are the Sustainer who emits the universe; you are the Protector engaged in its maintenance; at the end, all this returns to dissolution in you. Indeed, O Sun, there is no other giver than you for all things.

You are Brahmā, you are known as Hari and Hara, you are Indra, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), the Father of the Fathers (Yama), Varuṇa, and Vāyu; you are Soma, Agni, the sky, the great earth, and all other forms—what is there that you do not grant to every desire? 167.

Devoted to their own duties, the twice-born worship you daily with sacrifices, praising you with various words; while mortals established in yoga, meditating upon you with humble minds, attain the supreme state.

In the form of Fire (Tapaḥ), you cook the universe; as the Sun, you protect it and reduce it to ashes, manifesting yourself with rays filled with light that gladden all beings. As the Lotus-born (Brahmā), you create; as the one named Acyuta (Viṣṇu), you preserve; and at the end of the age, in the form of Rudra, you destroy—you alone are all this.
Ishvara said: Then, as Viśvakarman Prajāpati was drawing the sun, his hair standing on end with joy, he composed this hymn of praise to Vivasvat.

To Vivasvat, who is compassionate toward those who bow before him, the great-souled one, the possessor of seven horses of equal speed, the radiant one, the kinsman of the lotus-clusters and their bees, and the eternal renter of the veil of the mass of darkness.

Salutation to the one whose eye is the supreme purifier of all, who bestows the objects of manifold desires, who is garlanded with radiant and stainless rays of light, and who acts for the welfare of all beings. 172.

Homage to the unborn one, the creator of the three worlds, the self of all beings, the lord of rays, the bull; homage to the supreme among the greatly compassionate, to Sūrya, the source, the origin, and the abode of all things.

Salutations to Vivasvat, the inner self who bears knowledge, the foundation of the world, the seeker of the world's welfare, the self-existent one, the stainless eye of the world, the supreme among gods, possessed of immeasurable splendor. 174.

For a moment, you were like the rising sun upon the peak of the Eastern Mountain, your song being the most excellent among the hymns sung by the hosts of gods; furthermore, you are like the thousand-rayed sun that causes the lotuses in the world to blossom. 175.
From the intoxication of drinking the wine of darkness, your form becomes intensely red; yet, through the radiance of the sun, you remain solely intent upon illuminating the three worlds.

O Blessed One, having mounted a chariot with perfectly symmetrical parts and splendid, unimpeded divine horses, you constantly move through the enemy forces, your passion fixed upon the welfare of the world.
O destroyer of the hosts of enemies, you satisfy even the gods and the ancestors with a nectar-like essence; therefore, having approached you in prostration, I shall paint your form.

O Sun, composed of pure and radiant light, made holy by the dust of your feet, you who are compassionate toward those who bow to you and the purifier of the three worlds—protect me as I prostrate before you. 179.

Thus, I bow down to the God of gods, the foremost of the thirty, who is the source of the entire world, the single cause of the light that sustains the three worlds, and the sun that serves as the lamp for the whole universe. 180.
Īśvara said: Hāhā, Hūhū, and the Gandharva Nārada, as well as Tumburu—all skilled in the Gandharva arts—began to sing praises to Ravi.

Expert in the three scales (*grāma*) of Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Gāndhāra, they provide happiness through the excellent application of melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) and musical ornaments (*tāna*). || 182 ||
It is produced from the seven notes, adorned with three pauses, endowed with the seven musical scales, consisting of six melodic types, and resting upon the three qualities.
It is endowed with four songs, arisen from the four castes, the remedy for the four castes, and adorned with the seven ornaments. || 184 ||
Pure in its three stages, possessing the three dissolutions, correctly established in time, it is joined with dissolution in every thought, in dance, and in the aesthetic sentiments.
And the singers sang a song endowed with twenty-four qualities; Viśvārcī, Ghṛtācī, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā [also performed]. (186)
Menakā, Sahajanyā, and Rambhā, the best among the Apsarases, [performed] the fourfold rhythmic measure (pada-tāla), the three types of tempo (laya), and the three-fold timing. || 187 ||
While the Fire-god was being drawn, the three types of ascetics, as well as musical instruments and the fourfold dance, danced before the Lord of the worlds. (188)
Then, hundreds and thousands of divine drums and conchs, which produce many effects according to the prescribed rites, were sounded by those skilled in the manifestation of phenomena. (189)
O Great Goddess, unstruck sounds resonated like the rumbling of clouds, accompanied by Gandharvas singing and throngs of Apsaras dancing.
Then, there they were sounded: flutes, lutes, and jharjharas; as well as paṇavas, puṣkaras, mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and ānakas. || 191 ||
The entire place was filled with a tumultuous din from the sounds of musical instruments; then, with palms joined in reverence, their bodies bowed low in devotion, [they spoke]. (192)
Then, amidst that clamor at the assembly of all the gods, Viśvakarman [prepared] for the sun who had been wandering for a year.
While being praised by the deities, the architect reduced the brilliance of the divine image; having placed the deity upon it, he caused it to be whirled around.
Like a potter touching a lump of clay with a razor-sharp blade, Viśvakarman composed a hymn of praise for the Lord of Heaven.
He held the sixteenth part of that splendor situated within the mandala; O fair-faced one, his brilliance was diminished down to his feet.
O beloved, that splendor of his which consisted of the Ṛgveda fell upon Prabhāsa; O Goddess of gods, the sky was permeated by the majesty of that Great Lord consisting of the Yajurveda.
He established heaven, consisting of the Sāman, as well as the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar; then, by means of those portions of splendor, ten and five respectively.
By him indeed were created the discus of Viṣṇu and the trident of Hara, as well as the highly radiant and massive palanquin of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
The staff of the Lord of the Dead (Yama) and the spear of the Commander of the Divine Army (Kārttikeya), as well as whatever other weapons are indeed mentioned for the other gods; || 200 ||

The Creator of All fashioned those [discs] for the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas; thereafter, the Blessed Lord Ravi bears the sixteenth part. And that portion of Ravi’s splendor, O beloved, moves about situated in the sky.
Thus, having had his brilliance blunted by his father-in-law, that Mārtaṇḍa assumed an exceedingly beautiful form, as enchanting as a flower-arrowed god.
Then Bhānu, assuming a beautiful form, went to the northern Kurus; there he beheld Saṃjñā, who had taken the form of a mare.
Free from sin toward all beings through her asceticism and self-restraint, she, seeing him approaching with the suspicion that he was another man, went out to meet him as he bore the form of a horse.
Then, as they were joined there at the nose, two sons, the Aśvins known as Nāsatya and Dasra, emerged with the faces of horses.
And at the end of the emission, Revanta—armed with a sword, bearing a parasol, and clad in armor—took his father’s excellent horse and fled as soon as he was born.
Having once mounted him, he did not let go of that horse at all. Then Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala were commanded by Arka.
"Bring back my horse; do not let it escape through a gap by force. Stand at its side, watching for any opening in the horse. (208)
Even now, those two find no opening against that Great-Souled One; while Revanta goes in front, Daṇḍa and Piṅgala follow behind.
Departing from the Northern Kurus, those two, possessing great speed, reached the southern land of Bhārata, where the sacred field of Prabhāsa is located.
Both of them were exceedingly exhausted by the speed, and Revantaka as well; with perspiring limbs and heavy breathing, Revanta remained stationed there.
In a mere moment, O Goddess, the circle of a hundred thousand yojanas was traversed from north to south by the high-souled Revata.
Then, O Goddess, with his limbs perspiring, he stationed himself at Prabhāsa; accompanied by Daṇḍa and Piṅgalaka, he remained there mounted upon a horse.
O Goddess, the son of the queen is stationed not far from Sāvitrī in the south-western quarter; where the queen’s son is, there the venerable king is.
He attained renown in the world as Rājabhaṭṭārikā, and Revanta was appointed to the status of Guhyabhaṭṭāraka. || 215 ||
Having approached him in this manner, the Blessed One, the scorcher of the worlds, then said: "O child, you too shall become worthy of worship by the entire world."
And those mortals who shall remember you in the forest, in the great wilderness, or amidst the perils of enemies and robbers, shall be liberated from great calamity. (217)
Being highly pleased and honored by men, you shall bestow security, prosperity, happiness, sovereignty, health, fame, and advancement. (218)
The two Aśvins were made physicians by their high-souled father; and Yama, whose vision is fixed on dharma, is impartial toward friend and foe alike. (219)
