Then Timirāpaha performed that service for him, and he made the river Yamunā flow through the interior of Mount Kalinda.
And Chāyāsaṃjñā’s son, the highly illustrious Sāvarṇi, shall be the eighth Manu, Sāvarṇika, in a future time.
"O beloved, that lord still performs severe penance even today on the summit of Mount Meru; and his brother Śanaiścara has certainly become a planet."
Having thus granted boons to them, the Lord Bhāskara further performed the etymological derivation of Revanta’s name.
Since this son bestows peace upon perception (saṃjñā), he thus goes [to his destination]; moreover, he was appointed by Bhānu to the sovereignty over horses.
O lady of excellent complexion, he who worships [the deity] on the road travels his path in safety; such a one is always easy for mortals to propitiate and brings them happiness. (225)

Īśvara said: She who is known as Saṃjñā is remembered as Rājñī; she who is Chāyā is Nikṣubhā. The verbal root *rājṛ* is recorded in the sense of "shining," and he who always shines is called a *rājā*. || 1 ||
Because he is superior to all beings, he is called "rājā"; and because she is the wife of the rājā, she is proclaimed as "rājñī. || 2 ||

The verbal root *kṣubh* means "to tremble" or "to move"; therefore, she is *nikṣubhā* because she is immovable. Alternatively, she is so called because her own limbs are free from hunger (*kṣud*). || 3 ||
The divine shadow entered her; therefore she is remembered as Nikṣubhā. O high-minded one, he who currently exists in the world as Manu [is his son].
Born in his lineage was one who bore the conch, discus, and mace; yet, cursed by his mother, Yama became footless upon the surface of the earth.
Having reached Prabhāsa-kṣetra, O beloved, he performed extensive penance for more than ten thousand years and worshipped the Liṅga.

Being pleased by that, I then granted him a hundred boons. Even today, O Goddess of Devas, it is known there as Yameśvara; having seen it on the second day of the lunar fortnight (Yamadvitīyā), one does not behold the realm of Yama.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Yameśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, when the Sun-god was standing upon the lathe, he was shaved with a razor-edge by his father-in-law, the son-in-law, out of affection. (1)
O Lord, tell me what became of that abundant splendor which was severed and fell at Prabhāsa; please explain that to me.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of the Sun; having heard this with devotion, a human being is liberated from all sins. (3)
O illustrious goddess, I shall relate to you the ancient narrative concerning the descent of the Lord of Arkasthala at Prabhāsa.
O Great Goddess, in Śākadvīpa, while the sun was situated on its orbit and the fire was being whetted for over a hundred years, [the following occurred].
O beloved, that splendor born of the portion which fell today at Prabhāsa, having fallen there, took on a solid form.
O Goddess, that [image] formerly existed on earth made of Jāmbūnada gold; now, through the power of the Tiṣya age, it has become made of stone.
And there, having assumed a form consisting of light, the divine Sun was born upon the surface of the earth for the welfare of all living beings.
In the Kṛta age he is celebrated by the name Hiraṇyagarbha, in the Tretā he is called Sūrya, in the Dvāpara his name is remembered as Savitṛ, and in the Kali age he is known as Bhāskara.
And in the Kali age, O Goddess, this place named Arkasthala, which is celebrated throughout the three worlds, has descended here of its own accord and is firmly established.
O Goddess, when Svārociṣa was the second Manu in ancient times, at that time this god Divākara descended there.
O Goddess, you are the bestower of devotion and liberation, and the destroyer of disease and suffering; five yojanas around are pervaded by the dust particles arising from his splendor.
O Goddess, it extends from south to north, and from east to west as far as the river Māheśvarī to the north of the ocean.
And to the west of the Nyaṅkumatī, as far as Kṛtasmara, this entire region, O Great Goddess, is pervaded by those auspicious particles of splendor.
O Great Goddess, that subtle radiance which issued forth from the primordial light pervaded an area extending for twelve yojanas.
To the north is the son of the Sun (Yama), and to the south is the lord of rivers (the Ocean). To the east and west, O Goddess, the pair of Rukmiṇīs is traditionally remembered.
In the meantime, O Goddess, the solar splendor spread forth; by it, the sacred field extending twelve yojanas was rendered pure. || 17 ||
O beautiful one, that which is the center of that center is my abode; O Maheśvarī, my place is situated in the midst of the circle of splendor.
Just as, O Goddess, there is the pupil in the middle of the circle of the eye, so from east to west, O Goddess, [the distance] from Gomukha to Aśvamedhika is [one hundred and fifty yojanas].
O Goddess, from the ocean to the north and south lies the land of the Kaurava sovereigns; within this intermediate field, O lady of beautiful countenance, I am the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña).
"O beloved, because that house of mine was illuminated by the splendors of the sun, it became renowned in this kalpa by the name Prabhāsa."
There, that best of men who beholds the Sun in the form of Arka, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun. || 22 ||
He has bathed in all sacred fords, he has performed great sacrifices, he has given all gifts, and he has gratified his ancestors.
Since the Sun was born there on the surface of the earth in the form of Arka, therefore the Arka plant must always be avoided in food; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful lady, that mortal who, having seen Arkasthala, eats from arka leaves, has effectively committed the act of eating cow's flesh.
If the sun-leaf is eaten by him, that man is born with leprosy; therefore, one should avoid the leaves of the Arka tree with every possible effort.
O Goddess, he by whom the Sun, the maker of light, is first seen during the pilgrimage—having seen him, one should give a buffalo to a wise Brāhmaṇa.
The Sun is pleased by one who is copper-colored and wears red garments; he is situated in the southeast corner, in close proximity to him.
Not far from here, O illustrious lady, is the one known as Siddheśvara; it is a Liṅga that bestows all perfections, O Goddess, and is worshipped by the three worlds. (29)
O beloved, that which was formerly known as Jaigīṣavyeśvara in the Kṛta Yuga became famous as Siddheśvara in the Kali age.
O Goddess, having seen that, a person shall obtain all perfections; O Sovereign of the Gods, it is situated not far from that very place.
O Dear One, to the south and southwest of the Sun is the subterranean opening (pātālavivara), where the Maṃdeha Rākṣasas and the Śālakaṭaṃkaṭas dwell.
In former times, those scorched by the splendor of the sun went to Pātāla; but in the Kali age, O beloved, that very gateway remains closed, and there is no access to Pātāla.

The Yoginīs as well as the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, protect that place. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should worship the hosts of Mothers at night with offerings of oblations and flowers; thereafter, success (siddhi) will be attained.

Thus, indeed, having heard of the scraping of the body of the Sun—who is the cause of the existence of all dharmas and who is praised by Hara, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—one goes to the world of the Sun at the end of one's life.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Arkasthala and the Naming of Prabhāsapavitra," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: "O God of gods, O Lord of the world, tell me in detail that majesty of the Sun-god which has been described by you."
How did Arkasthala come to be the ornament of the Prabhāsa field, and how is Mahādeva there to be worshipped by those desiring the full fruit of a pilgrimage? (2)
What are the mantras, what is the ritual procedure, and on which festival days should one worship? How did Jaigīṣavyeśvara become Siddheśvara? O Lord of Gods, tell me all of that in full detail.
There is a fissure there in Pātāla; what happened there in ancient times? Likewise, how did the assembly of Mothers come to be there in the past? (4)
O Lord of the World, O Virūpākṣa, having shown compassion, tell me all of this in its entirety, O Hara, if I am dear to you.
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, you have asked well; I shall tell you in brief how Jaigīṣavyeśvara Hara indeed became Siddheśvara."
Having expanded upon the ritual procedure for worship, listen as I declare it to you; O Goddess, in this Kṛta age there was one who was proficient in all forms of knowledge.
The son of Śatakalāka, known as Jaigīṣavya, having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, performed austerities difficult to practice.
It is said that he stood for a hundred years subsisting on air alone; for a thousand years he subsisted on water, and likewise for ten thousand years he fed on leaves.
He performed a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances and again the Sāṃtapana; having withered his body through a restricted diet, he became clothed only by the directions (naked).
It is heard that in a former kalpa, one named Mahodaya appeared spontaneously; he installed the linga of the God of gods and worshipped it.

Lying upon ashes and smeared with ashes, he delighted [the deity] with dances and songs; purified and sanctified by austerity, he pleased him through recitation, the sounds of the bull, and his devotion.
To him who was thus pleasing [the Lord] and endowed with supreme devotion, the Blessed One approached and spoke these words: || 13 ||
"O Jaigīṣavya of great intelligence, behold me with your divine eye! I am pleased and I am a granter of boons; tell me what is in your heart. (14)
Having been addressed thus by the god, he beheld the three-eyed deity, bowed his head at his feet, and spoke these words: || 15 ||
Jaigīṣavya said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, O Master, if you are pleased with me, then grant me that yoga of knowledge which cuts asunder the cycle of worldly existence."
O Blessed One, I desire no benefit other than yoga; may I have constant devotion toward you, and toward the Goddess, Skanda, and Gaṇeśvara. (17)
There shall be no fear of disease, nor any loss of luster or humiliation; likewise, there shall be freedom from pride, as well as forbearance, self-control, and tranquility.
O Mahādeva, O Three-eyed One, I desire these boons from you.
Īśvara said: He is undecaying and immortal, entirely free from all sorrow; he is a great yogin of great heroism, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga. || 20 ||
And by the power of this secret field of mine, which is eternal, you shall attain the supreme and great sovereignty consisting of the eightfold qualities of yoga.
O best of sages, you shall become a highly renowned teacher of yoga.
Whoever shall worship this liṅga made by you according to the prescribed rule, being liberated from all sins, shall attain divine yoga. || 23 ||
And whoever, having reached this cave of Jaigīṣavya, practices yoga with a disciplined mind, shall cross over the cycle of worldly existence within seven nights.

Within a month, he will know his former birth and the life passed before; after one night, his body becomes pure; after two nights, he delivers his ancestors; and when three nights have elapsed, he shall deliver seven others.
Furthermore, O brahmin-sage, you shall possess invincibility against yogis, and my very sight shall be granted to you whenever you desire it.
Having thus granted the boons, the Lord vanished on that very spot. O Goddess, this account of what occurred in the Kṛta Yuga has been narrated to you.
O Great Goddess, it was likewise in the Tretā Yuga and in the Dvāpara as well; but at the onset of the Kali Yuga, the great sages known as the Vālakhilyas [appeared].
In this Prābhāsika field, near Sūryasthala, they were worshipping the Lord of Gods who dwells within the cave.
Eighty-eight thousand sages with upward-directed vital energy, having performed austerity for ten thousand years, then attained perfection consisting of that very [state].

Then, O fair-faced one, there is the Siddheśvara Liṅga, renowned in the Kali age; when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Śiva is joined with the moon, even then, O Goddess, the vision of that deity is difficult to obtain.
O Goddess, by worshipping the Siddhaliṅga, one obtains that merit which arises from giving away the entire universe as a gift.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Siddheśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess of gods, to the southeast of that [place], at a distance of three bows from the Siddhaliṅga, there is one established by Aruṇa. || 1 ||
O Goddess, a Liṅga was installed there by Sūryasārathi; it is named Pāpahara in the Kali age, and it destroys sins through its mere sight.

O lady of excellent complexion, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, one who worships according to the rules with devotion shall obtain the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Pāpanāśana," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, listen now to the majesty of the Pātālavivara, which was previously asked about by Brahmā and Viśvakarman.
When the state of darkness arose, Rākṣasas were born right there; they were all haters of the sun, innumerable, and possessed of great strength. || 2 ||
But seeing the high-souled one rising like the sun, all those led by Dhūmra laughed at Sūrya outright.
"Who is this doer of evil deeds who stands as our end?"—thus they spoke various words while standing before the Sun at that time.
Having heard this, the god Divākara, his lips quivering with anger at the words of the Rākṣasas while being devoured, [spoke]. || 5 ||
Then, with eyes overcome by wrath, he gazed; he who was the lion to the elephant of darkness, the destroyer of cruel Rākṣasas.
The great-rayed Sun, the bird-like lord of the day, contemplated his destruction; yet the lord of the heavens did not perceive the vulnerability of the Rākṣasas.
Seeing those whose minds were afflicted by evil and who had fallen away from the Dharma, the Blessed One, the Maker of Light, reflected thus and entered into meditative absorption.
Unaware that the three worlds were seized by the power of the night-stalkers, they were then beheld by the Sun with eyes swollen with rage.
Falling from the sky like planets whose merit has been exhausted, Dhūmra, surrounded by Rākṣasas, shone as he descended from the heavens.
Like half-ripened palmyra fruits surrounded by monkeys, those stones released from the machine fell down by chance.

Then, driven by the power of the wind, they fell and pierced through the earth to the subterranean realm (rasātala); having reached that region, O woman of excellent complexion, they arrived at Prabhāsa.
And where the god Arkasthala, the bestower of all perfections, resides, there, O Goddess, is situated a great opening leading to Pātāla.
O beautiful lady, there are millions of others that have been lost, from the time of Kṛtasmara until the sun reached Arkasthala.
Having obtained the boon from the mother of the gods, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) became established there. In the meantime, O Goddess, that place was proclaimed as Sūryakṣetra.
O Goddess, that middle region of the sun's splendor is indeed so described; it is entirely made of gold, O Goddess, and one who lacks merit does not behold it there.
There are one hundred and one openings and indeed crores of touch-points there, O Great Goddess; Siddheśa protects them all.
O Great Goddess, this field is always dear to the Sun; O Beloved, when the solar festival arrives, it is even more dear than Kurukṣetra.
The Brāhmī, the Hiraṇyā, and the confluence with the great ocean—this triple confluence, O Goddess, bestows the fruit of Koṭitīrtha.
Devamātā is also right there, and Maṅkīśa resides there as well; the abode of the Nāgas and the abode of the mountain are likewise declared to be in that very place. (1) 20.
Thus has been briefly described the great glory of Arkasthala, and how the opening came to be through the falling upon it of the Rākṣasas.
O Goddess of gods, other cavities there have indeed disappeared; yet, O beautiful lady, it is seen even today as manifest in that place.
O beloved, that gate named Śrīmukha is guarded by the Mothers; he who worships there with self-restraint on the fourteenth day for one year [attains the fruit]. || 23 ||

There, O Goddess, by means of the groups of Mothers beginning with Sunandā according to the prescribed rite, through offerings of animals and flowers, as well as excellent incense and lamps, and by providing meals for Brahmins, O Goddess, his success shall be achieved.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship all the Mothers there in the vicinity of Arkasthala, if one desires success for oneself. (25)
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, these Mothers, known by the names of the Sunandas, attain renown in this sacred field of Prabhāsa.
This has been declared in brief from the middle of the *Pātālottara*. Having heard this, O Goddess, the best of men is liberated from all calamities. (27)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Group of Mothers beginning with Pātālavivara and Sunandā," within the "Glorification of Arkasthala" in the first section, the "Glorification of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 16 ||
Īśvara said: Now, O illustrious lady, I shall describe to you the procedure for the worship of the god Arkasthala, as he is to be worshipped by the best of men. || 1 ||
The Āditya is said to be the beginning of all the gods; because he is the primordial creator, he is therefore called Āditya.
Without the sun, there would be no night, no day, and no libations; indeed, there would be neither dharma nor adharma, and the world of moving and non-moving beings would not endure.
The Sun protects everything; the Sun always creates; the Sun withdraws everything; therefore, he consists of the three Vedas.

O Great Goddess, I shall describe the method for propitiating that high-souled Bhāskara through the extensive mantras declared in the Vedas. Listen to it, O lady of excellent limbs; it is the destroyer of all sins. || 5 ||
O Maheśvarī, I shall explain to you in its entirety the procedure by which the twelve-fold Sun is worshipped when established in an image.
Having first performed the purification of the mouth, and having especially performed a bath, and having accomplished the purification of the garments and the body, one should then touch the sun.

I shall first describe to you the rules for the tooth-stick: by using one from the *madhūka* tree, there will be the gain of a son; by one from the *arka* tree, there is happiness for the eyes, O beloved.
By means of the Badarī and the Bṛhatī tree, one may indeed conquer people through eloquence; and there is no doubt that sovereignty shall be attained through the Bilva and the Khadira.

The destruction of disease occurs with the *kadamba* tree, while the acquisition of wealth occurs with the *atimuktaka*; [the attainment] of the Maruts occurs everywhere through those produced from the *āṭarūṣaka*.
The aśvattha tree bestows fame by granting preeminence in one's lineage; through the service of the śirīṣa tree, one attains complete prosperity.
For one who resorts to the priyaṅgu tree, supreme good fortune shall arise; through the constant service of the plakṣa tree, there shall be the accomplishment of all desired aims.
One should not consume a tooth-stick that is split, nor one that has a wound, nor one that is dried at the top, nor one that is crooked, nor indeed one that is devoid of bark. (13)
One should eat only as much as fits within the span of a span (vitasti), avoiding both what is too long and what is too short; facing north or east, sitting comfortably, and remaining silent. (14)
Having formed the desire as he wishes in his heart and having consecrated it with this mantra, the wise man should eat the tooth-stick. 15.
O Lord of the Forest, having granted this boon, you understand my desire; O tooth-stick, grant me constant success—salutations unto you! (16)
Having recited [the mantra] three times in this manner, one should chew the tooth-stick; afterwards, having washed that wood, one should cast it away in a clean place.
O Goddess of gods, one should not wipe the tongue with the tooth-stick; rather, those two acts should be performed separately if one desires extensive fame. (18)
Using a finger to clean the teeth, using a tooth-stick, and consuming salt directly—these, as well as eating clay, are equal to the eating of cow-flesh. (19)
If the mouth remains stale, a twice-born man is perpetually impure; therefore, he should chew a tooth-stick, whether dry or moist.
On the day [of the fast] that has been avoided, one should perform sixteen gargles with water scented with various lotuses, or otherwise effect the purification of the mouth.
That twice-born man who touches the sun without having purified his mouth shall be born as a leper for three thousand years.
Having thus purified his garments and other items, he should then perform his bath; having taken up earth with the Astra-mantra in a clean and pleasant place.
The letter *ha* joined with the vowel *u* and the anusvāra, followed by *phaṭ*—having seized [the space] with this weapon-mantra, one should perform the ritual bath there.
The three parts [of the ground] should be thoroughly purified and cleared of grass and stones; one part should be consecrated with the Astra-mantra, and likewise the other with the Bhāskara-mantra.

Having consecrated the water three times with the limb-mantras, reciting them once each, and having chanted the Astra-mantra, one should scatter it in all directions; thus the water shall become free from obstacles.
Having smeared himself with clay at Sūryatīrtha a second time and at [the third] a single time each, a person should then bathe at Ravitīrtha.

Having meditated upon the Sun-god with the sounding of musical instruments and conchs, and having bathed with royal honors, one should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with diligence. || 28 ||

Then, O Goddess, having performed the bath accompanied by the king of mantras—consisting of *ha*, *ra*, *pha*, the nasal dot (*bindu*), and *lakṣmī* (the vowel *i*), as well as another [syllable] together with the long [vowel]. (29)
The letter *ha* joined with the vowel *mātrā* (a) and the letter *repha* (*ra*), together with the *bindu*; and the letter *sa* with the *visarga*—this is called the King of Mantras.

Then, one should satisfy all those mantras with water from the tips of the fingers; the gods by raising [the hand] upward, the sages likewise with the left hand turned downward, and the ancestors with the hand turned downward using the heart-seed syllable (hṛdbīja). || 31 ||
That which is sung as the preeminent among syllables in the world by the wise is proclaimed to be the nineteenth syllable of the *mātrā*.

Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rule, he should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) according to the rite; thereafter, the wise man should offer a handful of water (añjali) to the Sun.
And one should recite the three-syllabled mantra and that of the Six-faced One at will; this king of mantras, O beloved, which was previously described by me to you— (34)

Then, having withdrawn the mantras by means of the western tīrtha, one should place them in the heart; having unified oneself with the mantras in one place, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented.
Having bathed with pure red sandalwood scents upon the surface of the earth, he drew a circular mandala and remained there with a one-pointed mind.
Having taken karavīra flowers and placed them in a copper vessel, together with sesame seeds and rice, along with kuśa grass and scented water.
Having prepared the vessel with red sandalwood incense and the offered water (arghya), he placed that vessel upon his head and knelt upon the ground.
One should offer the arghya to the Sun conjoined with the root mantra; indeed, he who makes this offering is liberated from all sins. (39)

Whatever fruit is obtained at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara by a thousand *yugādi* days, a hundred *vyatīpāta* conjunctions, and a thousand solstices (*ayana*), that same fruit one attains by offering an *arghya* oblation to the Sun.
O Goddess, even one devoid of initiation and mantras obtains the fruit through devotion in a year by means of the arghya offering; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, that learned man who, having been initiated, offers the arghya according to the prescribed rite, is not reborn on earth; he goes to dissolution in the Sun.
In this very life, O Goddess, he who is accompanied by his wife shall soon obtain good fortune, long life, the wealth of health, and become a vessel of happiness. (43)
Thus has the solar rite of bathing been declared to you in brief; it is for the benefit of the lords of men and is the destroyer of all sins. (44)
Alternatively, the best of the twice-born may perform the bath according to the Vedic path, provided he is unable to elaborate upon the mantras due to a lack of initiation.
Īśvara said: Now, O illustrious lady, I shall describe to you the procedure for worship according to the divine Vedic path, for the benefit of the Brāhmaṇas. 46.
Having thus gathered the necessary materials and prepared the flowers and other offerings, one should then invoke the Sun and establish him upon the pericarp.
O lady of excellent vows, having performed the service with this mantra, the mantra "udutyaṃ jātavedasam" is fully proclaimed. (48)
O beautiful lady, having invoked Agni with this mantra, "agnim dūtam," one should worship him with this mantra, "ākṛṣṇena rajasā."
One should worship with this mantra, "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," and one should worship the Sun, O Goddess, with the mantra beginning with "apatyetā. (50)
O Goddess, one should worship the Sun with this [mantra]: "We have seen his splendor"; and one should constantly perform recitation with this: "The sun, the all-seeing. (51)
The wondrous splendor of the gods rises; one should always worship the auspicious god. One should constantly worship the manifestation with that purifying vision. 52.
O lady of excellent vows, one should always worship Vimalā and Amoghā daily with this mantra: "vidyāmepirajaspṛthvi. (53)
One should worship the god with the mantra "sapta tvā haritaḥ" for the attainment of success in all rites; and one should worship the god with lightning with the mantra "sapta tvā haritena."
O Goddess, one should constantly worship the ninth goddess, who faces in all directions, with this mantra: "udvayantam" (RV 10.89.4), indeed, O Goddess.
"Rising today, O you of Mitra-like luster, one should mutter the first syllable; O Goddess, one should worship the second with the mantra 'śukeṣu me harimāṇam'. (56)
"Ud agād ayam ādityaḥ" is indeed the third; "tat savitur vareṇyam" is proclaimed as the fourth. (57)
"Mahāhiva mahāya" is proclaimed as the fifth; "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata" is proclaimed as the sixth seed-syllable. || 58 ||
O fair-complexioned one, Savitṛ is in the west, and Savitṛ is the seventh; having thus deposited the seed-syllables, O auspicious lady, one should establish the Sun-god.
Having established Āditya, one should subsequently assign the ancillary limbs (aṅgas).
Having placed the heart-mantra in the southeast, one should place the head-mantra in the northeast; the crest-mantra in the southwest, and the armor-mantra in the northwest.
Having placed the weapon-mantra in the directions, one should worship the pericarp with its own seed-syllable; then, with the mantra "amosi prāṇitena," one should worship the heart.
O Goddess, one should worship the head with the mantra "āyuṣyaṃ varcase"; then, having worshipped the crest-lock (śikhā) with the Gāyatrī, it is situated in the southwest (nairṛtya).
One should worship each individual armor as if it were that of Jīmūta; with the mantra "dhanvannāgā dhanvanā," one should always worship the weapon.
O Goddess, one should worship the Eye with the mantra "aśvinā tejasā," and likewise, Soma to the east and Budha to the south.
Having placed Guru in the west and Bhārgava in the north, one should place Maṅgala in the southeast and Śanaiścara in the southwest.
One should place Rāhu in the northwest and Ketu in the domain of Īśāna; O Goddess, one should always worship Soma with the mantra "āpyāyasva. (67)
"Awake, O Great Goddess! One should always worship the wise one there; with the mantra 'O Bṛhaspati,' one should constantly honor the Guru. (68)
O Goddess, one should worship Bhārgava with the mantra "śukraḥ śuśukvān," and one should always worship Maṅgala with the mantra "agnirmūrddhā. (69)
One should worship the son of the Sun (Saturn) with the mantra "śamagniḥ," and, O Goddess, one should always worship Rāhu with the mantra "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat."
"One should make Ketu the banner; indeed, a wise man should constantly worship him. Outside, to the east, one should worship Śukra, and likewise Yama to the south. (71)
One should know Īśvara to be in the northeast; Agni is said to be in the southeast; Virūpākṣa in the southwest; and Pavana in the region of the wind (the northwest).
One should indeed worship Indra with the hymn "tamuṣṭavāma," and one should always worship Vaivasvata with the hymn "udīratām avare. (73)
O Goddess, one should worship Varuṇa with the mantra "tattvāyāmi," and one should sacrifice to Dhanada with the mantra "indrāsomāvata."
O Goddess, one should worship Pāvaka with the mantra "agnim īḷe purohitam"; one should always worship Virūpākṣa with the mantra "rakṣohaṇaṃ vājinam. (75)
O Goddess, one should always worship Vāyu with the mantra "vāyavāyāhi. O Goddess, a wise person should indeed worship all these [deities] in their proper sequence. (76)
Outside, O Goddess, on the east and all around [the seats] of Indra and the others, [he is] red in color, of great splendor, and seated upon a white lotus. || 77 ||
Endowed with all the major marks, adorned with all ornaments, having two arms and one face, and holding five gentle objects in his hands. (78)

One should meditate upon and constantly worship this form of Āditya, which is circular, a mass of radiance, situated in the center, and clothed in red garments; it is honored in all the worlds. One should worship it daily upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) based on a mandala.
The Goddess said: O best of gods, you have described that ritual procedure by which the Sun, stationed within the mandala, is worshipped with devotion by human beings. (80)
O Śaṅkara, tell me that ritual by which one should worship the Sun, who is born from the lotus—the omnipresent God residing within the physical form.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! Well asked by you, O noble lady. Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess, to how one should worship the Mūrti."
One should always worship the head with the mantra "iṣe tvā," and one should worship the right hand with the mantra "agnim īḷe."
One should worship the feet of the God with the mantra "agna āyāhi," and one should worship [the deity] with a garland of flowers using the mantra "ājighra."
One should cast a handful of loose flowers with the mantra "yoge yoge"; with this [mantra] that is declared as "samudrāgaccha," one should bathe the Sun.
O beautiful lady, one should also wash the Sun according to the prescribed rite with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge" as well as the mantra "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ. (86)
One should bathe [the image] with water from a conch shell while reciting the mantra "sinīvālī," and one should protect it with decoctions while reciting the mantra "yajñaṃ yajña. (87)
O Goddess, one should bathe [the Sun] with milk while reciting the mantra "Āpyāyasva"; likewise, one should duly bathe the Sun with curd while reciting the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo. (88)
O beautiful lady, it is traditionally taught that bathing with medicinal herbs is performed with this mantra: "imaṃ me gaṅge" as well as "samudrajyeṣṭhā. (89)
Then, O fair-faced one, one should rub the body with the *Dvipadā* verses; one should perform the bath simultaneously with the mantra beginning "mā nas toke. (90)
One should bathe [the deity] with scented water while reciting the *viṣṇorarāṭam* mantra; one should present the *arghya* and *pādya* offerings while reciting the *sauvarṇa* mantra.

One should cause the water offering (arghya) to be presented with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," and one should cause the sacred thread (upavīta) to be presented with the mantra "vedo'si. || 92 ||
With the mantra beginning "bṛhaspate," one should offer garments to the Sun; then, while manifesting prosperity, one should worship him with a garland of flowers.
One should offer incense containing guggulu with the mantra "dhūrasi," and one should cause collyrium to be offered with the "samiddhoṃjana" mantra.
With the mantra "yuñjāna," one should touch the radiant sun; furthermore, one should perform the waving of lights (ārārtika) for the sake of long life. (95)
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; one should worship the Sun upon his head. With the mantra "Śambhavāya," one should touch the eyes of the Sun.
With the mantra "viśvataścakṣuḥ," one should touch the body of the Sun; with "śrīśca te lakṣmīśca," one should worship Ravi on all his limbs.
The Lord said:
Now, O Great Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe to you in brief the ritual procedure for worship and the mantras of Meru, which has eight peaks.
O Great Goddess, one should worship the Eight-Peaked Mountain according to this rite; O lady of excellent vows, one should first worship it in the center with this mantra: ||| 99 ||
One should always worship the eastern peak with clusters of various flowers while reciting the mantra "mahāhivo mahāya" and the "trātāram indra" mantra.
O beautiful goddess, one should worship with the mantra "tamuṣṭavāma"; one should worship the southeastern horn with "agnimīḷe purohitam. || 101 ||
One should worship with the Āgneyī Gāyatrī or else with this [mantra]: "To Yama thee, to Makha thee"—thus one should worship the southern horn.
Or else, one should worship with the mantra "udīratām avare"; and with the mantra "āyaṃ gauḥ," one should worship the southwestern horn.
One should worship either Rakṣohaṇa Vājina, who is near to the Asuras, or one should worship with the mantra "indrāsomā" (Indra and Soma). || 104 ||
One should worship the Lord with the mantra "Abhi tvā sūra nonumaḥ," or with "Iśānam śṛṅgam arcayet," or with "Yenedam bhūtam," or otherwise with this [mantra]. || 105 ||
One should always worship Merupīṭha with the mantra "namostu sarpebhyaḥ," and one should further always worship it in the center with the mantra "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata."
One should worship Savitṛ from behind with a garland of flowers; O Goddess, one should worship him at the three times of day and respectfully offer the arghya water.
One should worship her in the forenoon as the mother of the Rudras and the daughter of the Vasus; at midday, O Goddess, one should worship that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 108.

Or, in the afternoon, one should always worship with the mantra "The swan dwelling in purity" (haṃsaḥ śuciṣat). In this manner, O woman of excellent complexion, one should worship the Sun together with the planets.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, please graciously tell me which flowers are always recommended for the worship of the Sun. (110)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed meditation on Puṣpa, by which the Lord, when worshipped at Arkasthala, O Goddess, is quickly pleased. (111)
Worship with *mālatī* flowers brings about divine presence; and by means of *mallikā* flowers, a man becomes a possessor of enjoyments. (112)
Through white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), there arises good fortune and eternal wealth; through kadamba flowers, O Goddess of Gods, one enjoys supreme sovereignty.
Food becomes inexhaustible when the Sun is worshipped with Bakula flowers; worship with Madāra blossoms destroys all forms of leprosy.
With the leaves and flowers of the *bilva*, one attains great prosperity; with a garland of *arka* flowers, one gains wealth that grants the fruit of all desires. (115)
If one gives away a beautiful maiden while being honored with a garland of *bakula* flowers, and is worshipped with *kiṃśuka* blossoms, O Goddess, the sun does not cause affliction. (116)
Likewise, one bestows favor with *agasti* flowers; and with *karavīra* flowers, O Goddess of Gods, one becomes an attendant of the Sun. (117)
O Goddess, by means of a garland of lotuses, one shall attain the same world as the Sun; O Great Goddess, by means of *baka* flowers, poverty never arises.
Having worshipped the Sun with the fragrance of ṛtukusuma flowers, he enjoys this earth bounded by the four oceans.
Whoever, out of devotion, should smear the abode of the Sun with red ochre, shall attain great fortune and be liberated from diseases as well. (120)
The eighteen types of leprosy and whatever other diseases afflict men—all these go to their destruction if one should smear [the body] with clay.
Among all ointments, saffron and red sandalwood are the best; among flowers, oleanders are highly praised, O lady of beautiful countenance. (122)
There is nothing superior to this for bringing satisfaction to the Radiant One (the Sun), such as saffron, jasmine, the hundred-petaled lotus, and likewise agallochum. || 123 ||
What would not belong to that person in this world who would worship the Sun with these [offerings], and who, having smeared the temple, should create an auspicious maṇḍala? (124)
By one [repetition] he attains his purpose; by two, he enjoys good health; by three, he becomes possessed of all sciences; and by four, he becomes a possessor of enjoyments.
With five [lines], one obtains abundant grain; with six, longevity, strength, and fame; and with seven, a man shall become a conqueror of circles and a sovereign of the realm.
By the gift of a ghee lamp, a man becomes possessed of keen vision; by a lamp of pungent oil, a man conquers his own enemy. || 127 ||
By the offering of a lamp with oil, one is glorified in the world of the Sun; by a lamp with madhūka oil, one shall obtain supreme good fortune.
Among flowers, the Jātī is the most excellent; among incenses, Vijaya is supreme; among fragrances, saffron is the best; and among ointments, red sandalwood is preeminent. || 129 ||
Ghee is the best for the offering of lamps, and the *modaka* sweet is supreme for the food offering (*naivedya*). By these, the Lord of Gods is pleased and attains his presence.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites and performed the circumambulation of the ancestors, one should bow with the head to the God there at Arkasthala, O beloved.
Then, seated comfortably and facing the sun, he should take a single white mustard seed in his hand along with water. (132)
Having formed the desired object in one's heart as one wishes, O Goddess, one should drink pure water near Arkasthala, provided it has not been touched by the teeth even once. 133.
By acting thus, O Goddess, a man shall obtain the fruit of ten million pilgrimages; [he becomes] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, Agni, and likewise Kubera. (134)
Relying upon Bhānu, they all rejoice in heaven, O lady of excellent vows; therefore, I do not see any deity whatsoever who is equal to Bhānu.
Having done this, O Great Goddess, one should again perform circumambulation of the sun seven times with the mantra, O Queen of Gods, O fair-faced one. (136)
"tam u ṣṭavāma" is proclaimed as the first ṛc; "etonvindraṃ stavāma" is proclaimed as the second. || 137 ||
"O Indra, come to us pure"—this is proclaimed as the third [verse]. "For Indra, pure, [grant] wealth to us"—this is proclaimed as the fourth. || 138 ||
The fifth [verse] is proclaimed as "asya vāmasya" for the auspicious occasion; and the sixth is indeed proclaimed as "tribhis tvam deva. || 139 ||
One should cause the seventh [vow] to be performed with those ten Sāman chants which are indeed celebrated as preeminent by the wise and are constantly sung by the Sāmavedins.
O beautiful lady, I shall now tell you those ten Sāmans: the *huṃkāra*, the *praṇava*, the *udgītha*, and the *prastāva*—these constitute the first four. (141)
The fifth is Prahara, where likewise is the sixth, Māraṇyaka; Nidhana is the seventh of the Sāmans, remembered as the "Seven Siddhis. || 142 ||
It is declared that there are five types [of mantras] by means of the syllable *hrīṃ* and the *praṇava*; likewise, the eighth is the *sādhya* and the ninth is the *vāmadeva*.
The tenth Sāman, the eldest and most excellent, is dear to Vedhas; O Goddess, the recitation of these Sāmans must indeed be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Now listen as I speak of the second, which is indeed the supreme Jyeṣṭhasāman; however, this second one must not be recited aloud, but should be muttered by one desiring liberation. (145)

That is declared by the Lord Bhānu himself to be the supreme recitation (jāpya). Learn from me the application and the characteristics of this recitation: it is known by the wise as having the essence of *stobha*, being absorbed in the breath, and beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*. (146)
Ūrbbhānu likewise, Dharma, Satya, and Ṛta; those who were righteous in accordance with Dharma, and who indeed found their end in Dharma. || 147 ||
That which is to be recited by the twice-born Sāmavedins using these words as prescribed has been declared as the supreme mantra by the Lord Bhānu himself. (148)
Indeed, by reciting this, one does not return again; freed from all diseases, one is liberated even from the sin of killing a Brahmin. 149.
"Ājyadoha" and so forth, as well as "adodohe," are also characteristics of the Jyeṣṭhasāman. || 150 ||
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then perform a supreme hymn of praise with five Rig-verses; listen to them with a focused mind. (151)
The first [verse] is proclaimed as "ukṣāṇaṃ pṛśnim"; the second is proclaimed as "catvāri vāk". || 152 ||
The third ṛc is proclaimed as "indraṃ mitram," and likewise, the fourth is proclaimed as "kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam. (153)
The fifth [verse] is proclaimed as "dvādaśaprathama"; with this [verse], one should join the crown of the Sun [image] using the [mantra] beginning with "yo ratnavāhī". || 154 ||
With this [verse] beginning "gate hanām," one should place the unimpaired Sun; O Goddess, by this procedure one should worship the Sun according to the rules. (155)
Thus, this procedure for the worship of an image has been declared to you by me. || 156 ||
Whoever constantly worships the Sun according to this rite attains abundant desires both in this world and in the hereafter. || 157 ||
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth; one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter; and one desiring knowledge becomes a knower of the Vedas. || 158 ||
He who worships without desire certainly attains liberation, indeed, through the majesty of this sacred field and by the power of Arka-sūrya. (159)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by [feeding] ten million Brahmins elsewhere, that same fruit is obtained by feeding a single person at Arkasthala. 160.
Whatever bathing, giving, recitation, or fire-offering is performed on the occasion of the solar festival, all that is multiplied ten millionfold by the power of ten million suns. || 161 ||
O Great Goddess, that man who, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha falling on a Sunday, performs a vigil with faith near Arkasthala, attains the supreme goal. (162)
Whatever fruit is obtained from giving a hundred cows at Kurukṣetra, that same fruit one attains there by beholding Arkasthala.
Arkasthala is to be worshipped in that place by the residents, especially by those who are sick, with hibiscus flowers and arka flowers.
The Sun-god is not to be worshipped with cloth-silk flowers, nor with those produced from the *unmatta* plant, nor with flowers born of the *āmrātaka* tree. || 165 ||
The flower of the *āmrātaka* tree appears like a discarded offering (*nirmālya*); because it is not fresh on the outside, one should therefore avoid it. (166)
One who desires prosperity should not offer a garland that is unknown [to the recipient], nor one that is withered, nor one that is defiled, nor one that has been stale for a long time. (167)
If one should pluck a flower from the deity out of a desire for its blossoms—whether they be fragrant flowers or others belonging to the Bhojaka—[he incurs sin]. (168)
The host, deluded by greed, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin; having reached the Mahāraurava hell, he is cooked there for eternal years. || 169 ||
Come now, I shall proclaim to you the supreme rite for offering incense; by which incense, through its offering to the God of gods, one obtains that fruit.
Through incense used in daily worship, the Sun-god grants his proximity; he bestows every desire whatsoever that a human being may wish for.
In the same way, one should grant any desired treasure by means of aguru incense; one who desires health and one who desires wealth should constantly burn guggulu.
The Sun is always pleased by the offering of rice-balls and incense; he himself bestows health, and supreme happiness shall prevail. (173)
Through the incense of śrīvāsaka, one obtains all forms of trade; likewise, by burning resin and sarjarasa, there shall be an influx of wealth. (174)
For one burning devadāru wood, there arises inexhaustible food; anointing with saffron yields the fruit of all desires. (175)
Having become happy in this world, one shall attain imperishable heaven; by anointing oneself with sandalwood paste, one finds prosperity and long life. (176)
By applying an ointment of red sandalwood, the Sun-god bestows everything; even one seized by hundreds of diseases shall attain well-being and health. (177)
A man obtains a pervasive fragrance and supreme good fortune; by rubbing with musk, he shall attain incomparable sovereignty.
By means of perfumes blended with camphor, one becomes a sovereign over the lords of the earth; by means of the "four-ingredient" perfume (catuḥsama), one shall obtain all desires.
This supreme majesty of the Sun has been told to you, O Goddess; it has been explained by me in full detail. What else do you wish to ask?
The Goddess said: "If this is so, O Lord, and the Sun is the foremost of all luminous beings, how is it, O God, that he is swallowed by Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā?"
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which destroys all sins, which is the cause of [the cessation of] eclipses, and which brings about the severance of delusion. 182.
O beautiful lady, Rāhu stands beneath the solar disc, seated in his celestial chariot, seeking the nectar as long as it flows.
O Goddess, when the sun is obscured by Bimba, that is indeed a solar eclipse; no one is able to devour the sun, for the sun surely burns [the devourer]. 184.
Brahmā and the others worship Him; He is the primordial source of all the inhabitants of heaven.
All those born from the body of Āditya, as well as other gods and dānavas. || 185 ||
Because he is himself the original creator, he is called Āditya; the Lord, who destroys all sins, is established at Prabhāsa.

The Lord bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and effects the destruction of diseases and evil deeds. There, O Goddess, in ancient times, the world-protectors and great sages attained perfection.
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and likewise the Munis; Dhanada as well as Bhīṣma, Yayāti, and Gālava—[all these were there]. || 188 ||
And likewise, O Goddess, Sāmba has attained supreme perfection from this; this, O Queen of the Gods, is the secret and most excellent majesty of the Sun. (189)
It should not be given to those of wicked intellect, nor especially to sinners; it must never, under any circumstances, be given to an atheist, one lacking faith, or to a cruel person.
One should recount this narrative likewise to one who is not envious, O Auspicious One; [but] to a son, a disciple, or one who is righteous and walks the path of justice. (191)
O Great Brahmā of virtuous vows, you must relate this supreme majesty of the deity Arkasthala to one who is devoted to the Sun.
O Goddess, for that man who causes the Brāhmaṇas of strict vows to hear this during a Śrāddha ceremony, whatever gift he gives shall indeed become infinite, O Goddess. (193)
Wherever this meritorious [account] is recited, there indeed prosperity always abides.
The Yātudhānas, overwhelmed by fear, do not harm that śrāddha.
Even those who are defilers of the assembly attain the status of purifiers of the assembly; he shall possess sons and progeny, and be delightful through the fulfillment of all desires. (195)
A man shall always be reunited with his kinsmen living abroad; he shall be reunited with lost wealth and with other things he has long desired. (196)

He is protected by the yoginīs and is never separated from his beloved ones. Having sipped water and become pure, a brāhmaṇa should always listen [to this]; he obtains all desires—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (197)

O fair-faced one, by the recitation of this account of the Sun’s birth, a Vaiśya shall attain incomparable prosperity, a Kṣatriya shall become a lord of the earth, and merchants shall obtain unimpeded trade a hundredfold. (198)
O beautiful lady, even Śūdras shall obtain their desired objects; they shall be freed from the terrible fear of untimely death and even the great fear of death itself. (199)
Whatever has been committed at the royal gate perishes; of this there is no doubt. With his soul enriched by the fulfillment of all desires, he is glorified in the world of the Sun. || 200 ||
Thus, O Goddess, has this majesty of the Sun-deity been recounted in connection with Arkasthala; what else do you wish to hear? 201.

May the orb of the sun protect you—the eternal abode of splendors, the refuge of the waters, the inexhaustible lamp of the quarters, the gate to perfection that pierces through darkness, the common eye of the worlds, the golden lotus of the celestial lake, the radiant earring of heaven, and the unimpaired measure of time and its dissolution. 202.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Arkasthala and the Ritual for the Worship of Arkasthala," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, when the illustrious goddess had been addressed in this manner by Śaṅkara, she again asked for a detailed account of the greatness of the sacred field (Kṣetramāhātmya). || 1 ||
The Goddess said: "O Lord, today my birth has become fruitful and my ascetic penance as well; O Śaṅkara, by your grace, divinity has been attained by me this very day."

Today I have become one who has accomplished auspiciousness; today my vision of knowledge has been established by you. Today my ears have been adorned with the ornament of the majesty of this sacred field.
Today the mass of my splendor has been born; today knowledge is established in my heart; today my noble lineage and character [are realized]; today my beauty and auspicious marks [are perfected].
Today my delusion, born from wandering among sacred fords, has been severed; O best of the proud, my mind has become steadfast at Prabhāsa.
"I have propitiated him in the past, and today the Lord of the Gods is pleased with me; I stood for a long time encircled by fire, standing on one foot. (6)
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, that penance of mine has today become fruitful; the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra has been revealed to me today.
I ask again, O Lord of Gods; tell me the truth, O Master.
Even now, O Lord, there remains a doubt concerning the greatness of the holy ford; O God Maheśvara, tell me of another marvel.
"O Lord, this moon that exists and rests upon your head—whose is it, how was it produced, and at what time? Tell me, O Master. (10)
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, at this time, during the second half of the life-span of Brahmā known as the Vārāha-kalpa, while it is currently proceeding— || 11 ||

At the beginning of the second month, the first lunar day (pratipad) is proclaimed; on that day, O beloved, the Earth was lifted up by Vārāha at the very outset. Therefore, the name "Vārāha-kalpa" arose upon the surface of the earth.
In that kalpa, O Great Goddess, when the period of twilight had passed, O beloved, at the beginning of the first Manu, Svāyambhuva, indeed, O Goddess.
While the Ocean of Milk was being churned by both the gods and the demons, fourteen jewels were indeed produced there.
Among them, O Goddess, the Moon of great splendor, born of the ultimate reality (tattva), is this very one whom I still bear upon my head today, my beloved.
O Great Goddess, when poison was drunk by me while I was always stationed at Prabhāsa, the moon was formerly made into my ornament by the gods for the sake of my liberation.
Because I am adorned by the moon, I am known as Śaśibhūṣaṇa; even today, the Self-Existent One remains in that place in the form of a Liṅga.
O beloved goddess, he is the bestower of all accomplishments and shall remain for the duration of the eon; this much has been told, O Goddess—what else do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Moon’s Origin as the Ornament of Śiva’s Head," in the first section on the Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 18 ||
The Goddess said: "If it is so, O Lord, why was the full moon not retained by you? Tell me the reason for that, given that its digits were within [your body]."
Īśvara said: O Goddess, the Great Kalā, known as Amā, is said to have sixteen divisions; she is the supreme Māyā, residing within the bodies of embodied beings as their sustainer.
Those very digits of the moon, beginning with the new moon (Amā) and ending with the full moon (Paurṇamāsī), are declared to be the lunar days (Tithis); they are proclaimed to be exactly sixteen.
The subtle, supreme power is Amā; you, O Goddess, are proclaimed as that. Abiding through the union of dissolution and origination, you manifest according to the sequence of time.
O Dear One, those sixteen vowels which begin with 'A' and end with 'Au' are to be known as the limbs of Time by those who understand Time.
The truṭi, lava, nimeṣa, kalā, kāṣṭhā, and muhūrta; as well as the night, day, fortnight, month, solstice, year, and yuga. || 6 ||
Likewise, she exists for a Manvantara, a Kalpa, and sixteen Mahākalpas; she who is the Visarjanī digit abides having taken refuge in the individual soul (jīva).

She creates the entire universe, joined with the two equinoxes; likewise, O beloved Maheśvarī, she who is Saṃvaraṇī withdraws the universe. A fourth part of the closing of an eye is declared to be the duration of a *truṭi*; know that a *nimiṣa* is twice that, O Great Goddess.
Thirty *nimiṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*; twenty of those make a *kalā*; a *muhūrta* consists of twenty *kalās*, and fifteen of those [muhūrtas] make a day.
The day-measure is known as the night; from the two [day and night] comes an ahorātra (a full day). Fifteen of those constitute a pakṣa (fortnight), and two pakṣas are called a māsa (month).
Six months constitute an *ayana*, and two *ayanas* make a year. [The duration of a day for the gods is] forty lakhs and three lakhs [of years]. (12)
Twenty thousand [years] are to be known as one solar cycle of four yugas; seventy-one such cycles of four yugas are declared to be a manvantara.
This lifespan of Indra is thus proclaimed, including its final summary; when fourteen Indras have passed away, a Kalpa, which is a day of Brahmā, occurs.
And the night is of the same duration; thus, consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas, he lives for a hundred years by this measure of a day, O beloved. (15)
In half a moment of my own time, fourteen thousand [ages] perish; thereafter, even the countless Grandfathers (Brahmās) of Viṣṇu pass away.
Thus, O Goddess of gods, this infinite world has arisen in succession, possessing a variegated form through the division of the moon and the sun.
O Goddess, when that which is without beginning or end, unborn and immutable, is present as the *kalā*, the Moon is joined with it and remains situated within it with its face turned downwards.
Thus, the process of dissolution and emergence, established by the moon and the sun, should be known. I have declared the sequence of creation; now hear about the withdrawal [of the universe].
A great kalpa (mahākalpa) is destroyed by [lesser] kalpas; a kalpa is destroyed by manvantaras; having made a month destroyed by fortnights, that too is divided into days and nights.
A day and night [is divided] by a muhūrta; a muhūrta, however, is struck by a kalā; having made a kalā struck by a kāṣṭhā, one should divide a kāṣṭhā by a nimiṣa. || 21 ||
Having divided a *nimiṣa* by *lavas*, and having divided a *lava* by *truṭis*, that which has passed away is tranquil, changeless, and without defining characteristics.

And this supreme illusion (māyā) of his, consisting of a digit (kalā), is borne upon his head; it is the power (śakti) of the God of gods, whose form is the universe, and which is supreme, O beloved. Having deluded the lineage [of beings], it causes them to wander in saṃsāra, O Pārvatī.
Thus it is, O Goddess: this world is characterized by its arising and its subsistence; wherever it arises in its entirety, there indeed it is dissolved again.
This power, consisting of illusion (māyā), whose nature is both pure and impure, exists in the form of the moon; O Goddess, she shall manifest herself to you.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, O Master of the Universe, that penance of mine, performed for many tens of millions of years while scorched by five fires, has today become fruitful. (26)
O Maheśvara, the yoga of creation and the yoga of dissolution have been understood by me, as well as the nature of the moon's origin and likewise the measurement of its phases.
Now, O Lord of Gods, a doubt resides within my heart; O God, O Maheśvara, tell me of this great curiosity.
Born from nectar itself, the moon brings delight to all; O Lord of Gods, the moon is dear to you and likewise beloved. (29)
Regarding the word "candra," this verbal root *cad* is accepted in the sense of "to delight"; however, by me, it is understood in the senses of "whiteness" and "the state of being water. (3)
The moon is the lord of all medicinal herbs, the supreme gratifier of the ancestors, and its very refuge; it is devoted to you and intent upon your service. (31)
Nevertheless, though he is stained with blemish, he arouses my curiosity, O Goddess, for his crest is adorned with a garland of joined cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
O Lord, if even the moon, which rests upon your head, suffers such distress, then indeed those who partake in suffering within this worldly existence are not to be pitied.
There is nothing in the three worlds, nor will there ever be, by which you are able to bring about the complete destruction of this suffering. (34)
O Maheśvara, a doubt exists in all of us just as it does in me: what is the cause that has arisen by which the moon bears a mark?
O Lord Maheśvara, tell me what is the cause of this: how can there be a mark upon him whose very origin is in the nectar of immortality?
O Lord of Gods, you are dear to me and your mark also remains [upon me]; O God, my curiosity is great, so you ought to tell me the truth of this.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, being supremely delighted, spoke with love to the daughter of the mountain.

Īśvara said: O Goddess of excellent complexion, what great anxiety has arisen within you today? You must not harbor it toward me; be free from distress, my beloved. It was through the power of your father that the mark appeared upon the moon.
"O Goddess, because of the ripening of karma and due to Dakṣa’s transgression of my command, behave equally toward all your wives"—thus was the Moon addressed.
O beloved, he then altered those words; thus was the Moon cursed. O Goddess, as for this cause of the mark which you have asked about—
In age after age, O beautiful lady, there exists a distinct state [of being] due to various causes; and because it is innumerable, O beloved, it is simply not possible for me to describe it.
O Goddess of the Gods, innumerable moons arise again and again, and they all perish at the end of every manvantara.
Innumerable are those called Kalpas, innumerable are the Pitāmahas, and innumerable are the Haris; yet Maheśvara is indeed one alone. (44)
O my beloved, O Goddess, tens of millions of billions of cosmic eggs have arisen here through my play, like bubbles upon the water. (45)
In each of those places, four-faced Brahmās, Haras, and Bhavas were then created by Pradhāna; thus, the presence of Śambhu was attained.
He brings about dissolution as well as mutual merging, and he effects the beginning and the end; the Lord Maheśvara is the creator of creation, destruction, and maintenance.
In creation, I am joined with *rajas*; in preservation, I abide in *sattva*; and in dissolution, I am united with *tamas*. Thus, O Goddess, I exist in three ways. (48)
Therefore, Brahmā is a devotee of Maheśvara, and Śiva is the Lord of Brahmā; Viṣṇu becomes Sadāśiva, for Brahmā is thus the soul of all.
That very Lord Rudra is Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the entire universe; within this egg are these worlds, and within them is this whole world.
O wise goddess, the moons, suns, and planets within this universe—those that have passed away and those that will come to be—cannot possibly be numbered. (51)
O wise lady, while this present Vārāha-kalpa is occurring, O great goddess, six lords of Rohiṇī have already passed away in the past.
"O Great Goddess, this seventh [son], born of nectar, is now seen to have been diminished by Dakṣa’s curse. (53)
Then, when the second half-cycle of Brahmā had arrived, during his thirtieth kalpa, which is renowned as the Pitṛ-kalpa.
O Great Goddess, when the Svāyambhuva Manvantara had arrived, at its very beginning, you were indeed Satī; at that time, he who was your father was Dakṣa.
The birth of that Prajāpati Dakṣa from Prāṇa has been proclaimed; O Goddess, in this Manvantara, Dakṣa was the son of the Pracetasas.
"O beloved, Dakṣa shall now arise from my right thumb; in every age, all these twice-born ones, beginning with Dakṣa, will come into being. (57)
Furthermore, they perish once again; the wise man is not deluded by this. O Goddess, it was indeed because of that contempt that you abandoned your body in the past.
O Goddess, I was separated from you and became liberated for as long as the interval of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara within the Varāha Kalpa, O beloved. (59)
This is the twenty-first Manu in the aeon known as Vārāha; O Great Goddess, in every aeon you shall have a different name.
In this Vārāha Kalpa, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had passed and the Himavat mountain had been won through penance, the goddess Pārvatī was born.
One day of Brahmā is indeed the limit for you, consisting of six months; O beautiful lady, you were separated from me due to the wrath of Dakṣa.
O Goddess, those sages who were formerly cursed by me through your anger have also been born together with you in this Vaivasvata interval.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these eight are the sons of Brahmā.
O Goddess, having been cursed previously at the sacrifice of Dakṣa during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, you were indeed born again once this Cākṣuṣa Kalpa had passed.
In the sacrifice of the Great God, while bearing a body of Varuṇa and offering his own pure essence into the fire, Brahmā formerly performed this out of a desire for progeny.

O beloved, those sages of former times, possessing a radiance equal to the orb of the sun, were previously sent by me to your father’s presence for the purpose of choosing you; you know this truth, O lady of excellent vows. (67)
Now, what is the use of much speaking? I shall tell you the most excellent answer to your question: regarding this second half of the aeon (parārdha) currently existing for the Creator (Brahmā).
O fair-faced one, listen to those moons that have passed away, beginning from the Śveta Kalpa up to the period of the Varāha [Avatāra]. (69)
O Goddess of gods, four hundred and twenty-six [moons] have passed; O beloved, the twenty-seventh is now present.
When the Vaivasvata interval arrived, he who exists now in the tenth Tretā Yuga was preceded by Dattātreya.
O beloved, regarding that Lord of Rohiṇī who has now been born, [I shall tell you] by way of his origin, [the story] of Viṣṇu’s incarnation as a human being.
O beloved, I shall describe the incarnations of the body starting from the first; that fifth one indeed appeared in the fifteenth [tithi] during the Tretā age.
In his status as a universal monarch (cakravartin), Māndhātṛ, preceded by Utathya, became the destroyer of all kṣatriyas during the nineteenth Tretā age.
Likewise, the sixth was Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, preceded by Viśvāmitra; in the twenty-fourth yuga, he was accompanied by Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest.
In the seventh [Dvāpara], the son of Daśaratha was born for the sake of Rāvaṇa; in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara, Viṣṇu [was born] from Parāśara in the eighth [period].
From him was born Vedavyāsa, preceded by Jātūkarṇya; and right there, the ninth Viṣṇu was born as the son of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Preceded by Brahmagarga, when the portion of this twenty-first Dvāpara age had diminished and dharma had perished, Viṣṇu himself was born from Vasudeva in Devakī within the Vṛṣṇi clan.
In order to establish the order of dharma and to destroy the asuras, that powerful Viṣṇu was, in a previous birth, named Pramati.
In the lineage of Candramas, during the period of the mixed twilight (saṃdhyāmiśra), there will arise one named Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas, possessing the prowess of Vyāsa.
The tenth was Bhāvyasaṃbhūta, who, preceded by Yājñavalkya, drew along the army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, with hundreds of thousands of Brahmins firmly grasping their weapons, he will leave those Śūdra kings utterly destroyed.
He [subdued] thousands of heretics, Mleccha tribes, and bandits, as well as those who were not particularly righteous and who were anywhere haters of the Veda and Brahmanas.
With his wheel set in motion, powerful and the mighty ender of heroes, he will wander the earth invisible to all beings.

He, as a portion of the divine Manu, shall indeed be the lord upon earth; having destroyed all those who are impelled by destiny, he will reach his final end in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, accompanied by his followers.
Then, when Kalki had passed away along with his ministers and his army, and when the kings had also perished, the subjects were left defenseless at that time.
When their protection had ceased and they were slaying one another in battle, they, struck down by each other, were left without a protector and deeply distressed.
When this Kali Yuga, lasting ten thousand years, has come to an end, and when its transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśa) is entirely exhausted, the Kṛta Yuga shall indeed be established.
And when the Moon, the Sun, as well as Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati, shall come together in a single zodiacal sign, then the Kṛta age will commence.
The lunar mansion was named Abhijit, the night was named Jayantī, and the auspicious hour was named Vijaya, at which time Janārdana was born.

The Goddess said: "The entire account of the workings of Bhṛgu’s curse has not been told exactly as it happened. O Maheśvara, tell me of my previous incarnations, which have not been mentioned before. (91)
Īśvara said: When the earth was pervaded by exceedingly powerful Dānavas, from that time forth, indeed, due to the curse occasioned by Bhṛgu. 92.
Viṣṇu was born again and again to establish the order of dharma; from dharma, Nārāyaṇa, who is to be realized, was manifested during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
And he inaugurated a sacrifice during the Vaivasvata Manvantara; at that time of his manifestation, Brahmā was the officiating priest.
But during the fourth age, known as the Yuga, when the gods here had fallen into distress, he was born from the ocean for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu.
In the seventh yuga of the Tretā age, when the worlds were under the dominion of Bali, there appeared a second Narasiṃha, with Rudra as his precursor.
When the three worlds were assailed by the Daityas, he became a third dwarf; contracting his body into its limbs, he was preceded by Bṛhaspati.

In the tenth Tretā Yuga, when a fourth part of Dharma had perished, Dattātreya appeared, preceded by Mārkaṇḍeya; these indeed are declared to be the divine incarnations in the human world from of old. (98)
Īśvara said: Now, the sequence of the incarnations of the Daityas is told once more. King Hiraṇyakaśipu shone for a hundred million years (arbudam).
Likewise, for seventy-two hundred thousand years and eighty thousand years, he was the lord of the three worlds. || 2 ||
On the day of the Sautya sacrifice of the Atirātra, at the Aśvamedha of Kaśyapa.
That golden seat which had been prepared for the sake of the Hotṛ priest became here the pit where Hiraṇyakaśipu sat; therefore, it was called Hiraṇyakaśipu.
In former times, he performed extremely difficult austerities for a hundred thousand years; meanwhile, he remained within the womb of Diti for ten thousand years.
An ancient verse was sung by the Daityas concerning Hiraṇyakaśipu: "Whichever direction King Hiraṇyakaśipu gazes upon," (6)
In each and every direction, the gods, together with the sages, paid homage to him.
Furthermore, in another succession of births, Bali became king for ten million years.
For sixty thousand and thirty million years, he indeed held the authority of sovereignty over the army.
For that duration, Prahlāda was likewise held captive by the gods.
Those renowned ones, Indra and the others, slew the Asuras by their might.
It is said that all this was occupied by the Daityas for ten yugas; thereafter, it remained entirely without a rival for eighteen yugas.
This entire triple world was protected by Mahendra without agitation; however, in the tenth Tretā Yuga, there arose the exceedingly powerful Kārtavīrya.
For eighty-five thousand years, that lord of men became a sovereign emperor, a universal monarch (cakravartin) possessed of the seven jewels.
Indeed, on those seven islands, that king—armed with a sword, shield, and bow, and mounted on a chariot along with his followers—beheld the thieves through the power of yoga.
By remembering him, the loss of wealth shall not occur for men; this was said when the four ages had passed and the eleventh Manu was the sovereign lord.
When that Dvāpara age had proceeded for half its duration, there was indeed a son of Mānava Nariṣyanta named Mada.
His ninth descendant was known as Tṛṇabindu; he became king at the beginning of the third age, the Tretā Yuga.
His daughter, Ilavilā, was peerless in beauty; that royal sage bestowed that maiden upon Pulastya.
In her was born the sage Viśravas, the son of Ilavila; she had three wives who were the ornaments of the Paulastya lineage.
The auspicious daughter of Bṛhaspati was named Vedavarṇinī; both Puṣpotkaṭā and Vīkā were the daughters of Mālyavat.
Kekasī was the daughter of Mālin; O Goddess, hear now of the offspring she bore. That woman of excellent complexion gave birth to his eldest son, Vaiśravaṇa. (20)
He had eight teeth, a greenish beard, spike-like ears, and was deep red; he had dog-like feet, short arms, tawny eyes, and was adorned with pure ornaments.
Seeing his son thus deformed in appearance—having three feet, a massive body, a thick head, and large jaws—at that time, [he was struck with wonder].
Seeing him then, Kubera himself said, "This is 'Kubera' (the Wretched). The word 'ku' denotes contempt, and 'vera' refers to the body. (23)
Because of his deformed body, he was named Kubera and marked by that name; his wife was Vṛddhi, and his son was Nalakūbara.
Kaikasī gave birth to a son, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas—Śaṅkukarṇa, the ten-necked one, tawny, with red hair. || 25 ||
He has eight feet and twenty arms, a massive body, and great strength; he resembles black collyrium, possesses fangs, and has blood-red eyes.
Endowed with the vigor of a Rākṣasa, as well as with beauty and strength, he was naturally fierce and cruel; thus he is known as Rāvaṇa, the "Terrifier. (27)
In a previous birth, that king was Hiraṇyakaśipu; as a Rākṣasa, he remained king for fourteen yugas. || 28 ||
O beloved, those who are skilled in calculation have declared that the number [of years] is five crores and sixty-one lakhs. (29)
Indeed, for sixty thousand years, that Rāvaṇa kept the deities and the sages awake with his terrifying conduct.
In the twenty-fourth Tretā Yuga, Rāvaṇa, due to the exhaustion of his ascetic merit, met his destruction along with his hosts upon encountering Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
O Goddess, he who was born as the ten-necked one, the crusher of enemies, was the son of the royal sage Damaghoṣa, renowned for his prowess.
And from Śrutaśravā was born Śiśupāla, the king of Cedi; likewise [from Kaikasī were born] Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and the daughter Śūrpaṇakhā.
And Kaikasī gave birth to four sons: Vibhīṣaṇa, Manohara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, and Khara.

Puṣpotkaṭā’s sons were [Kumbhakarṇa, Atikāya, and Mahodara], and her daughter was Kumbhīnasī; Triśiras, Dūṣaṇa, and the Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva were also born to her. It is recorded that the offspring of Vīkā was a single daughter named Śyāmikā.
Thus, these nine Rākṣasas of the lineage of Pulastya were performers of cruel deeds; the tenth is proclaimed to be Vibhīṣaṇa, whose soul was pure.
The sons of Pulaha were all deer, as well as fanged beasts of prey; likewise, spirits, piśācas, serpents, boars, and elephants. (37)
In this Vaivasvata Manvantara, Kratu is remembered as being childless; Atri had ten wives who were beautiful and devoted to their husbands.
From Bhadrāśva were born ten Apsarases, ending with Ghṛtācī.
Bhadrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Naladā, and likewise Jaladā; Urṇā, Pūrṇā, O Goddess of Gods, and that which is known as Gopucchalā. (40)
Likewise, the tenth is named Tāmarasā, who has ten million red [beings] as her followers; O Great Goddess, Prabhākara is known as the husband of these.
When Sūrya was struck by Svarbhānu and he fell from heaven to the earth, and when this world was overwhelmed by darkness, it was by him that light was set in motion. || 42 ||
And as the Sun was falling here, he cried out, "May it be well with you! Because of those words of that Brahmarṣi, the Lord did not fall.
Then, having been addressed as "Prabhākara" by the great sages, the Lord begot upon Bhadrā a glorious son named Soma.
The radiant son of Dharma, that excellent god Soma, the night-walker with cool rays, was born under the Kṛttikās. 45.
O Goddess, the venerable sage Atri was indeed born as the father of Soma; there, Atri remained with his own eyes fixed upon the Lord of all the worlds.
Performing only auspicious deeds through action, mind, and speech, he stood with arms raised, as radiant as a great light, like a piece of wood, a wall, or a stone.
O beautiful goddess, in former times he performed a great penance called Sudustara for three thousand divine years.
O auspicious lady, as that great-minded one remained there with his vital energy drawn upward and without blinking, his body indeed attained the state of Soma.
As he, whose self was honored by Soma, ascended upwards, Soma flowed from his two eyes, illuminating the ten directions.
Having seen that embryo according to the prescribed rite, they then placed it in the ten directions; having come together, they sought to sustain it, yet they were unable to hold it.
Then, from those very directions, the eternal embryo—the cool-rayed moon who brings all things into being—suddenly descended here, nourishing the worlds. || 52 ||
When those women were no longer able to bear that embryo, he, the cool-rayed one, then descended from them onto the earth.
Beholding Soma fallen, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O Goddess, O beautiful lady of the gods, at that very moment, he who was true to his promise was yoked by me for the sake of dharma with a thousand white horses.
O Goddess, when that supreme soul had descended into the womb of Aditi, the seven sons of Brahmā who are known as the mind-born (Mānasa) offered praise.
In the same way, all the descendants of Aṅgiras and likewise the sons of Bhṛgu [praised him] with Ṛks, Sāmans, and also with the hymns of Aṅgiras.
As he was being thus praised, the increasing splendor of that radiant Soma illuminated all three worlds in every direction.
With that preeminent chariot, he of exceeding fame circumambulated the earth, bounded by the oceans, twenty-one times.
And that energy of his which fell upon the earth, from it the herbs were produced, which blazed forth again with his splendor.
By means of these, he nourishes this world and the fourfold classes of living beings. Plants that end with the ripening of their fruit are known as the seventeen grains.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame seeds; || 62 ||
Priyaṅgu, kovidāra, koradūṣa, satīnaka, māṣa, mudga, masūra, niṣpāva, and kulattha. (63)
Āḍhakīs, caṇakas, and kaṇas are recorded as seventeen; these are remembered as the varieties of cultivated plants. || 64 ||
The fourteen sacrificial plants, both cultivated and wild, are as follows: rice, barley, wheat, beans, and sesame seeds; || 65 ||
Priyaṅgu is the sixth; these [six], together with kulattha as the seventh, are [the grains]. Then there are śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, and gavedhuka. (66)
The ūruvinda, the markaṭaka, and those which are veṇuyava—these are the fourteen medicinal plants, both cultivated and wild. || 67 ||
Grasses, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, vines, clusters, and so forth—by the tens of millions; the Moon is the lord of these and sustains the entire world. (68)
Out of a desire for the welfare of the world, the blessed Soma [shone] with his moonbeams; then Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed the kingdom upon him.
O fair-faced one, that highly resplendent King Niśākara was consecrated in his kingdom as the lord of seeds, medicinal herbs, brahmins, and mantras. (70)
