The best of luminaries caused the three worlds to shine with his own radiance; Sinī, Kuhū, Dyuti, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, and Vasu [were his wives].
Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī—these nine goddesses waited upon him; and the twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, observers of great vows, were the wives of the Moon.
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave her [the stars] which they know as the constellations; having obtained that great sovereignty, Soma, the best among those who possess the Soma, [reigned].
He performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, for which a hundred thousand were given as sacrificial fees; Hiraṇyagarbha was the Udgātṛ priest, and Brahmā assumed the office of the Brahman priest.
The Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign, was his member of the assembly, surrounded by the primordial Brahman-sages headed by Sanatkumāra.
O fair-faced one, Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to those foremost Brahman-sages and to the members of the assembly, O auspicious lady. (76)
Having completed the final ablution (avabhṛtha) without agitation, honored by all the gods and sages, that lord of kings shines exceedingly, illuminating the ten directions.
By that [means], he attained that sovereignty so difficult to be reached by those who have not disciplined themselves; thus does he abide, renowned as Candra Ātreya. (78)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Moon," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: "I have heard in its entirety the cause of the Moon's birth; now proclaim how his mark came to be."
Īśvara said: O Goddess, in ancient times there was a son of Brahmā named Dakṣa; formerly, Dakṣa was commanded by the Self-born One (Svayaṃbhū) to create progeny. || 2 ||
The patriarch Dakṣa begot sixty daughters by Vairiṇī; he gave ten of them to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Twenty-seven [sacrifices] were for Soma, four for Ariṣṭanemi, two for the son of Bhṛgu, and two for the wise Kṛśāśva.
And likewise two for Āṅgiras; O Goddess, hear from me now the names of these mothers in detail, and the expansion of their progeny from the beginning.
Marutvatī, Vasu, Jāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Arundhatī, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā, O beautiful lady. || 6 ||
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave these as his lawful wives: Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, and Surasā.
Surabhi, Vinatā, Krodhavaśā, Ilā by name, Kadrū, Tviṣā, and likewise Vasu; I shall indeed tell you of their sons.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; from Marutvatī came the Marutvats, and likewise the Vasus from Vasu.
From Bhānu came the Bhānus; from Muhūrtā came the Muhūrtakas; from Lambā came those named Ghoṣas; and Nāgavīthī was born of Jāmī.
From Saṃkalpa, however, came Saṃkalpa; these are remembered as the ten sons of Dharma: Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anala, and Anila. || 11 ||
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus; the sons of Āpa are Vaidhaṇḍya, Śrama, Śānta, and Dhvani.
The lord Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, was the son of Dhruva; and the lord Śarva and Dhruva were the sons of Soma, who awakens the household.
Hutahavyavāha was known as the wealth of Dharma, while Manojava, whose course was likewise unknown, became the wealth of Anila. || 14 ||
The venerable Devala was a yogi; at dawn, his sons were born. Bṛhaspati’s sister was Bhuvanā, a teacher of the Veda.
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus; his son was Viśvakarman, the Prajāpati who is the creator of all crafts.
I shall now tell you the names of those who are to be perfected among the Tuṣitas: Mano’numantṛ, Prāṇa, Nara, and the powerful Apāna. (17)
Bhakti, Bhaya, Anagha, Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa, Vibhu, and Prabhu—these are proclaimed as the twelve Sādhyas. || 18 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall proclaim the lineage of Kaśyapa: Aṃśa, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. (19)
Vivasvān, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumān, and Viṣṇu—these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas, each possessing a thousand rays. || 20 ||
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata; Hara, Bahurūpa, and Tryambaka, the lord of the gods. || 21 ||
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the lords of the hosts. || 22 ||
Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa who were proud of their strength: the eldest, Hiraṇyakaśipu, and likewise his younger brother, Hiraṇyākṣa.
An ancient verse was sung by the Daityas concerning Hiraṇyakaśipu: || 24 ||
Whichever direction King Hiraṇyakaśipu looked toward, in that very direction the gods, together with the great sages, paid him homage. Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of exceedingly great strength.
Prahlāda was the eldest of them, followed by Anuhrāda; Hrāda and Hrada were also their sons—these are the ones proclaimed.
Both Sunda and Upasunda were the sons of Hrāda; however, Hrāda had one other son who was well-known as Mūka. || 27 ||
Mārīca, the son of Sunda, was born of Tāḍakā; he was slain in Daṇḍaka by the powerful Rāghava.
Mūka was also slain by Savyasācin during the Kairāta encounter; furthermore, the Nivātakavacas were destroyed in the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhrāda.
Three crores of renowned beings were slain by Savyasācin—namely Gaveṣṭhī, Kālanemi, Jambha, and Valkala.
Jṛmbha was remembered as their sixth younger brother; these were known as the sons of Prahrāda. Śumbha and Niśumbha are recorded as the two sons of Gaveṣṭhin.
Dhanuka and Asiloma are proclaimed as the two sons of Śumbha; and the son of Virocana was the powerful Bali alone. (32)
The five sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were valiant and possessed of great strength: Andhaka, Śakuni, and likewise Kālanābha. (33)
And Mahānābha, Vikrānta, and Bhūtasaṃtāpana—hundreds of hundreds of thousands of them were slain in the Tārakāmaya war.
Thus has the lineage of Kaśyapa’s progeny been briefly described, by which the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is pervaded. (35)
Now, O Great Goddess, among those twenty-seven maidens who were given to Indra, Rohiṇī was his beloved.
Then, among them, the goddess Rohiṇī became the most beloved of the Lord of the Stars (the Moon), even dearer than his own life.
Having completely abandoned all of them, his soul overwhelmed by passion, he took delight in secret with Rohiṇī in forests and groves, in delightful regions, and in caves and mountain recesses.
Then, O illustrious lady, those remaining wives, overwhelmed by suffering, sought refuge with Dakṣa and spoke these words: (39)
Soma, having surpassed all others, rejoices with Rohiṇī for a thousand years, sporting according to his pleasure.
But the remaining twenty-six [nakṣatras] were soiled and bereft of splendor; for ever since the taking of her hand, the Moon has been with Rohiṇī alone.
He perceives a thousand years as but a single night; yet we, O dear one, have been abandoned by the Moon, though we are free from fault.
He took delight with Rohiṇī, bringing us misery; for us, who are consumed by grief, death would therefore be better. (43)

Having heard those words of theirs who were afflicted by grief, Prajāpati—endowed with Brahmanic splendor yet drawn by affection for his daughters—went to where the Lord of the Bears was and spoke these words.
"O Maker of Night, behave with equality toward my daughters; otherwise, you will undoubtedly become a partaker in the fault. (45)
Having heard those words of his, the lord of the bears stood with his head bowed in shame and said "So be it" in the presence of Dakṣa.
"From this day forward, O brahmin-sage, I shall treat your daughters with equality; I swear this truly by your oath. (47)
When the Lord of the Night was thus joined with his vow, O Mother, all his daughters, endowed with beauty, were presented to him.
Having gone to his own abode, Dakṣa attained supreme bliss; and Candra, O Goddess, as before, became devoted to Rohiṇī.
Having completely abandoned all of them, his mind afflicted by desire, he then spoke these words once more to all of them: || 50 ||
They were all soiled, emaciated in limb, wretched, and deprived of their senses; then, seeing them in such a state, Dakṣa fell into a swoon.

Having regained consciousness, his hair standing on end from rising anger, he spoke to all his daughters: "Why are you thus dressed in soiled garments? Why are you all devoid of luster? Tell me, O sinless ones, what is this? (52)
"O daughters, today I shall undoubtedly strike down with a curse the Asuras along with their followers, as well as those others who are the best among the gods."
Thus addressed by Dakṣa, they all raised their voices together.
O Lord, Master of the Night, not even for a single season do you grant us [a boon]; therefore, we have come into your presence. (55)
But disregarding your words, he, his soul overwhelmed by passion, took delight in secret with Rohiṇī, increasing our grief. (56)
Having heard those words of theirs, O Great Goddess, Dakṣa became enraged; he went to Candra and cursed him as he stood before him.

"Since you have disregarded my word and, out of passion for Rohiṇī, have abandoned our other daughters—who are otherwise free from fault—therefore consumption shall devour your body; of this there is no doubt. (58)
At that very time, O daughter of the mountain, Yakṣman, commanded by Dakṣa, entered his body.
With his body seized by consumption, he goes to ruin day by day.
Thus cursed by Dakṣa, O Goddess, Soma lost his luster and fell to the earth, motionless, accompanied by Rohiṇī.
Having regained consciousness after a moment, he spoke these words to Rohiṇī: || 62 ||
"O Goddess, what must be done now? For I have been cursed by your father; afflicted with wasting consumption, O beloved, what shall I do now? (63)
Thus addressed, Rohiṇī, her eyes clouded with tears, beholding Soma afflicted by Dakṣa’s curse, spoke these words: || 64 ||
Go for refuge to him alone by whom that curse was given to you; he will surely provide for your welfare when you are overcome by that curse.
By his grace, you shall regain that auspicious splendor which was formerly yours.
Having heard Rohiṇī’s words, Candra went into the presence of Dakṣa and spoke with humility, his eyes agitated by tears.
O Dakṣa, show favor with a gracious inner self; O great sage, abandon your anger and have compassion for me.
Whether there was a cause or no cause for it, you were overcome by anger; yet, having shown compassion toward me, you have performed the release from the curse. (69)
But it is known to you, O illustrious one, by what deed I have been cursed; O Dakṣa, show favor to me, who am wretched and entreat you.
While the high-souled Soma was thus lamenting, [the Lord], having resolved to show him favor, spoke these words: || 71 ||
Dakṣa said: "O Soma, struck down by my curse, you cannot be saved even by the gods. Whatever I say, O Soma, shall be exactly so; of this there is no doubt. (72)
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these indeed arise exactly as they were ordained in previous creations. (73)
The Asuras, the Suras, and whoever else there are—the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas—all of them are incapable of protecting [him], with the sole exception of Maheśvara.

"This curse has been pronounced upon them by me; Śaṅkara will show them favor. No one else will be able to save them except Bhava, the Lord of Creatures. Therefore, go very quickly and propitiate Śaṅkara. (75)
No other moon is capable of making you pure again, except for Mahādeva, the blue-throated lord of Umā.
Having heard the words of Dakṣa, Soma stood with his palms joined in reverence and replied then with a joyful heart.
"O Blessed One, O observer of noble vows, if you are pleased with me, your devotee, and have set your mind upon showing me favor, then tell me: whence comes Śiva?"
"O skillful one, in what place am I to behold that Maheśvara? Tell me of those places where he dwells, so that I may travel to them. (79)
Dakṣa said: Listen with diligence, O Soma, and having heard, take it to heart; having taken refuge in the western quarter, near the coastal marshlands of the ocean. (80)
Three hundred *dhanus* to the west of Kṛtasmara, there stands a self-manifested Liṅga of great power.
Resembling the orb of the sun, adorned with a girdle of serpents, and measuring the size of a hen’s egg, it is situated in the midst of the earth.
Know that indeed to be the *sparśaliṅga*; through devotion to it, you shall come to know it. Therein is present the god Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord.
Go, and propitiate the Lord of the Gods through fierce asceticism.
Having praised the Lord of the gods, make yourself pure; by his swift granting of a boon, you shall obtain an excellent form. (85)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction for the Worship of Śiva by Dakṣa for the Cure of the Consumption and Leprosy of Candra, who was afflicted by the disease of consumption resulting from his own curse," occurring in the context of the Origin of Someśvara, within the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Lord said: Having been thus permitted by Dakṣa, he then, grieving over his own deed and with his soul overwhelmed by pain and sorrow, arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Having gone to the southern shore near the ocean, he saw there a mountain known as Kṛtasmara.
It was crowded with yakṣas and vidyādharas, adorned by kinnaras, and filled with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, aśoka trees, and auspicious tilaka trees.
With blossoming and fruit-bearing *kalhāra* and *śatapatra* lotuses, and with auspicious mangoes, rose-apples, wood-apples, pomegranates, and jackfruit trees; (4)
It was adorned with nimba, jambīra, and nāga trees, as well as groves of plantains, betel-nut trees, nāgavallī and other creepers, along with śāla, tāla, and tamālaka trees.
With citron and dates, with grapes and sweet pāṭala flowers, with bilva, campaka, tinduka, and the like, as well as kadamba and kakubha; || 6 ||
It was adorned with various trees such as the dhava, aśoka, and śirīṣa, and with auspicious trees that fulfilled desires, both in bloom and laden with fruit.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by *cakravāka* birds, and resounded with the songs of various birds such as cuckoos and parrots.
The birds, possessing the memory of their past births, spoke in human speech; and [the place was filled] with pairs of Gandharvas and Kinnaras, along with Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
That best of mountains was adorned by various divine beings sporting there, and it resounded with the dances of gods and gandharvas and the music of flutes and lutes.

It was completely filled with the sound of Vedic chanting and the smoke arising from sacrifices, burnt offerings, and the Agnihotra fire, all rising up and permeated with the fragrance of clarified butter.
It was graced by divine sages and the best of the twice-born who were masters of the four Vedas: Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Manu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Viṣṇu, Śātātapa, and Parāśara; || 13 ||
Āpastamba, then Saṃvarta, Kātya, the sage Kātyāyana, Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, as well as the sage Vācaspati; || 14 ||
Jāmadagnya, Yājñavalkya, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka, Gārgya, Śaunaka, Dālbhya, Vyāsa, Uddālaka, and Śuka. || 15 ||
Nārada and Parvata, Durvāsas of fierce asceticism, Śākalya and Gālava, as well as Jābāli and Mudgala; || 16 ||
Viśvāmitra, Kauśika, Jahnu, Viśvāvasu, as well as Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Vaiśampāyana, and Jiṣṇu. (17)
Śākaṭāyana, Vārddhikya, Agnika, Bādarāyaṇa, the high-souled Vālakhilyas, and those who dwell upon the circle of the earth. || 18 ||
O beloved, all those sons of Brahmā, radiant and righteous sages, remain there on that mountain which preserves its sacred memory.
All were blazing with ascetic fervor like smokeless fires; some observed month-long fasts, while others observed fortnightly fasts.

Some were observers of the three-night penance, others were performing the *sāṃtapana* austerity, and still others remained without food; some subsisted on flowers and fruits, while others ate only withered leaves.
Some subsist on cow dung, while others take only water as their food; they are highly learned observers of the agnihotra sacrifice, contemplating the path to liberation.
Thus spoke these and many others, headed by Mārkaṇḍeya, who were experts in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Śrutis, and Smṛtis. (23)

Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he remained on Mount Kṛta; thus Kṛtasmara stayed there, honored by all the gods, O Goddess, he who was consumed by the submarine fire during this Manvantara.

Having seen that beautiful mountain and having beheld the great ocean, the maker of night then performed a circumambulation seven times; having completed the circumambulation of the mountain, he went to where Maheśvara was.
Near the ocean, however, assuming the form of a Sparśaliṅga, he propitiated the Lord with a tranquil inner soul.
Reflecting upon death or taking refuge in Maheśvara, I would prefer death at the hands of Śaṅkara rather than the blow of his curse.
Having thus resolved his mind, Soma propitiated Śiva through austerity, subsisting on fruits and roots for a full thousand years.
When the fourth thousand years were complete, O lady of excellent complexion, the Blessed Lord Rudra was pleased and spoke these words.
"I am well-pleased with you, O Moon, O observer of noble vows; choose a boon. What desire of yours shall I fulfill today? Speak, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (30)
Having thus seen the bull-bannered god manifest before his very eyes, Niśākara bowed to him with devotion and offered him praise.
Candra said: Om, salutations to the God of gods, to Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose nature is immeasurable, and who possesses both manifest and unmanifest forms. (32)
You are the Lord of yogis, O Sovereign; everything is established in you. You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are Prajāpati. || 33 ||
Above that world-system of two hundred and twenty-four worlds, your supreme light alone shines eternally.
Salutations to you, the fiery Liṅga who have become the supporting pillar for the maintenance of the cosmic egg released by Ādivarāha at the end of the kalpa.
Salutations to you whose name is "The One Without Disease," salutations to you who are clothed in an animal hide; salutations to Bhairavanātha, and salutations to you, Someśvara.
Thus, by these praiseworthy names, O Lord of the Immortals, you are praised by the best of gods—by those of the past, the present, and the future.
The first was Brahmā, named Viriñci, the grandfather of the worlds; at that time, O Lord of Pārvatī, your name became Mṛtyuñjaya.
When the second Brahmā became renowned as Padmabhū, at that time your name was proclaimed as Kālāgnirudra.
When the third Brahmā appeared, renowned as Svayambhū, your name was proclaimed as Amṛteśa, which increases one's fame.
When the fourth Brahmā became renowned as Parameṣṭhin, O Lord of Gods, your name was then remembered as Anāmaya.
When Brahmā became the fifth [Prajāpati], renowned as Surajyeṣṭha, your name, O Destroyer of Tripura, became Kṛttivāsas.
And when the sixth Brahmā appeared, who is remembered as Hiraṇyagarbha, at that time your name was proclaimed as Bhairavanātha.
Now he who is known as Śatānanda exists; and he who was born from the left eye of Ādisoma—by you two [he was brought forth]. (44)
For the purpose of consecrating the Liṅga, he who was eight years old was brought there in the form of a child; therefore, it was celebrated as Somanātha.
From that time onwards, two hundred thousand lunar months have passed.
And indeed two thousand, one hundred, and six more. || 46 ||

"O Mahādeva, I am the seventh [son], renowned as Ātreya; having been cursed by Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, I have come to you for refuge. O Lord of the gods, protect me, who am wasting away, afflicted with a sinful disease. (47)
As Candraka was thus offering praise, the Lord Rudra, the mine of compassion, was pleased and spoke these words.
"I am well-pleased with you, O Moon, observer of noble vows; choose a boon. What desire of yours shall I fulfill today? Speak, even if it be something very difficult to obtain. (49)
Those men who shall recite my secret names, which are most dear to me, I will grant them whatever is in their hearts.
This Liṅga is to be worshipped by all those moons that have passed, those that will come, and those of the present, until another moon reaches its eighth year.
Furthermore, when the four-faced Brahmā comes into being, the name of the Lord shall then be "Prāṇanātha" (Lord of Life).
The vital breaths are said to be the winds; that [practice] is called their propitiation. What was previously called "Prāṇanātha" will now become mine.
Therefore, immediately after the name Agnīśa, the name Kālarudra shall follow; thereafter, the name Tāraka will indeed be proclaimed.
Immediately after that, the god shall be known as Mṛtyuñjaya; then as Tryambakeśa, then as Īśa, and thereafter as Bhuvaneśa.
"Bhūtanātha," "Ghora," "Brahmeśa"—these are the names; then "Pṛthivīśa" will be the future one, followed by "Ādinātha. (56)
"O Lord of the Kalpa! Immediately after 'Candranātha,' that name which is destined to belong to the god shall now be revealed to you. (57)
Thus, these and other names, numbering sixteen, have passed away and will come to be, due to the infinite nature of time. (58)
Each individual name persists until the dissolution of Brahmā; thereafter, another name is born, corresponding exactly to its form.

Now, what is the use of much speaking? The secret has been revealed to you. O child, tell me in its entirety the reason for which you have performed all this penance here; being pleased with you, I shall grant you a boon.
Candra said: "I have been cursed by Dakṣa for a certain reason and have been brought to exhaustion by consumption; therefore, you ought to protect me."
Śambhu said: "Now, O sir, look equally upon all those daughters of Dakṣa; there shall be waning for you for one fortnight, and waxing shall occur for the next fortnight."
O Soma, by my grace you shall regain the splendor you formerly possessed, once the sins of Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, have been destroyed through his ascetic penance.
It is not possible for even other gods to make his word otherwise; for if Brahmins are angered, they can destroy and reduce everything to ashes by their own splendor.
They could turn gods into non-gods and destroy this world; for both Brāhmaṇas and gods are a single energy divided into two.
The Brāhmaṇas are the gods manifest before our eyes; the deities in heaven are beyond our sight. There are no gods without the Brāhmaṇas, nor are there Brāhmaṇas without the gods.

In one place reside the mantras, and in another resides splendor; the Brahmins are the deities in this world, and the Brahmins are the deities in heaven. In the three worlds, the Brahmins are supreme; the Brahmins alone are the cause.

Appointed by their father, they become the ancestors (pitṛs) in ancestral rites; in divine rites, they become the gods (devas). When the best of the twice-born have water poured into their hands, they become gods in that very body.

For those Brahmins who are constantly devoted to the six duties, who take delight in the meaning of the Vedas, the terrible and great fear of existence as a ghost never enters them through their devotion. (69)

Whatever the Brahmins declare to be most worthy of praise, that the deities practice through their actions; when those whose gods are perceptible are satisfied, the gods whose gods are imperceptible are likewise constantly satisfied. (70)
Just as the Rudras, the gods, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins, as well as Brahmā, Soma, and Sūrya, so too are the best of the twice-born in this world. (71)
All subjects are dependent on the gods, and the gods are dependent on sacrifice; those sacrifices are dependent on the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, the twice-born are the best of the gods.
One should constantly honor the Brāhmaṇas and always satisfy the Brāhmaṇas; the Brāhmaṇas are the saviors in this world, and through the Brāhmaṇas one attains heaven.

They preserve the ancient ordinance, which is indivisible, uncuttable, beginningless, and inexhaustible; having honored those twice-born ones with great intelligence, one shall become invincible in heaven like the king of the gods.
Indeed, armor can be pierced by an iron arrow or even by a shaft; yet the blessing of a Brahmin is exceedingly difficult to breach, even by a thousand thunderbolts.
Sin is pacified by burnt offerings; the burnt offering is pacified by food; food [is pacified] by the gift of gold; and gold [is pacified] by the benediction of Brahmins.
He who, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen, desires to go to hell, should commit an offense against the gods, the Brahmins, and the cows.
If one, out of delusion, hates Brahmins, the gods, cows, or sacrifices, for that evil-minded person there is neither the next world nor this world.
Brahmins, cows, gold, water, women, and the earth—these six are beyond reproach; he who censures them is a sinner. (79)
Kings are the summit of dharma; Brahmins are the root of dharma. Therefore, one must not harm the root, for the summit is established upon the root. 80.
Kings are the fruit of Dharma; Brāhmaṇas are the flower of Dharma. Therefore, one should not harm the flower, for from the flower the fruit is produced.

The king is the tree; the Brahmins are its root, the citizens its leaves, and the ministers its branches. Therefore, the Brahmins must be protected by the king; when the root is guarded, there is no destruction of the tree. (82)
For fire burns when near, but a Brahmin burns from afar; what is scorched by fire grows back, but that which is consumed by a Brahmin does not grow.
By the curse of the Brahmins, the consumer of oblations (Agni) became a devourer of all things, the ocean became undrinkable, and Purandara became fruitless.
You are the moon afflicted by consumption and the saline wastes upon the earth; you are the falling away of the sun and the moon, and their subsequent restoration. (85)

The resin of the forest trees, the defeat of the Dānavas, the subjugation of the Nāgas, as well as the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, the reversal of the origin of the gods, and the upheaval of the worlds. || 86 ||
Such are the splendors of the high-souled Brāhmaṇas; therefore, a king should always bow down before the twice-born.
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke brahmins; for if they are angered, they can instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts.
Just as fire is a great deity whether it is consecrated or unconsecrated, so too a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity whether he is learned or unlearned.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled; when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if he is engaged in all kinds of undesirable occupations, the Brāhmaṇa is to be honored by all as the supreme and great deity.

When the Kṣatriya power becomes excessively overgrown, it is through the influence of the Brāhmaṇas that it is restrained; for the Brāhmaṇical power is supreme and worthy of worship, and the Kṣatriya power indeed has its origin in the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone; the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
Upon whom the worlds of the gods always depend for their existence, and whose word is indeed the Veda—who, desiring to live, would harm them? (94)
Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a Brāhmaṇa; nor should a Brāhmaṇa living within his realm perish from hunger.
In whose kingdom a Brahmin perishes from hunger, his realm will soon perish in a hundredfold manner.
Whatever sin the king commits through negligence or through delusion, the Brahmins dwelling in the kingdom who are learned in the Vedas pacify that.
That king, along with his kingdom, prospers through the spiritual luster of Brahman when the rites for him are performed by the twice-born during the first and last watches of the night.
A ruler of the earth should always worship the Brāhmaṇas after rising in the morning; by the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, the gods shine in heaven. (99)

Now, what is the use of much speaking? O Brāhmaṇas, my own body is that very form of Śiva, the God of gods and the Supreme Self, which is celebrated among all the twice-born on this earth extending to the edge of the ocean. (100)
Those fools who hate these Brahmins of firm vows certainly hate me; indeed, by honoring them, they honor me. (101)
Therefore, a wise person should not harbor malice toward Brahmins; for through malice, men struck by the curse of a Brahmin are swiftly destroyed. 102.
Thus, O Candra, has the ocean of virtues of the Brāhmaṇas been described; now perform the task that I myself shall tell you. 103.
O Maker of Night, I have granted you this favor regarding the curse; yet it is not possible for me to make the word of those twice-born ones otherwise.
Therefore, O Moon, you who are wise, you should not feel any grief, even though all the gods, including Indra, are capable of both inflicting curses and bestowing favors.
Your waning shall occur for one fortnight, and your waxing shall occur for the next; furthermore, O Moon, hear another word regarding how you must act. (106)
This supreme Liṅga which stands on the shore of the ocean is situated within the earth, yet it is within the range of vision for the gods.
Resembling a hen’s egg and adorned with a serpent-girdle, this is my supreme primordial splendor; no one else knows it.
From here, three hundred bow-lengths out into the middle of the ocean, there stands a well-guarded liṅga endowed with auspicious characteristics.
"In the first kalpa, my linga fell into the middle of the ocean due to the curse of the great sages; bring that true object here quickly. (110)
"Install my linga, known as Sparśa, in that place; having installed it with great effort, together with Viśvakarman. (111)
Then, having summoned Brahmā together with the lords of sages, he said: "O Lord, perform the consecration after sacrificing there with great sacrifices."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there; then, O lady of excellent countenance, the Lord of Night regained his luster once more.
From that time forward, that sacred field became renowned as Prabhāsa; because light was bestowed upon Niṣprabha, it is called Prabhāsa.

Dakṣa’s curse was not rendered in vain, for it became a mark [upon Soma]; yet Soma shines through the worlds, having obtained a boon from Maheśvara. That Lord of Gods manifested himself specifically for the sake of the high-souled Soma. || 115 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowing of Boons by Soma," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 22 ||
The Lord said: Then, having become tranquil in mind and filled with wonder, the Moon, his soul pervaded by devotion to Śambhu, established himself at the sacred site of Prabhāsa.
The omnipresent Lord did exactly as he had been told by the God; having gone into the midst of the ocean, he took up that supreme linga.
Having summoned Viśvakarman along with his attendants, Soma himself commanded Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine architect.
Candra said: "O Viśvakarman, this liṅga has been given to me by Śambhu; take it, O mighty-armed one, and install it in a suitable place. (4)
"O Lord, protect [this place] for now; I shall go to my own abode to bring back the sacrificial implements for the sake of the sacrifice."
Īśvara said: Having spoken thus, Candra then departed for the world of Candra. O Great Goddess, having gone there to the world of Candra, which is of great splendor— || 6 ||
Extending for ten million yojanas, auspicious and consisting of eternal nectar; having summoned the wise gatekeeper there, O Great Goddess, [he spoke].
Taking the minister, whose limbs were filled with gold and who was equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, they quickly gathered all the requisites and materials for the sacrifice.
"Let them go to Prabhāsa-kṣetra, devoted to my command; let them go to that supreme field together with Brāhmaṇas who maintain the sacred fires."
"Let everything be prepared quickly so that the sacrifice for all these brahmins, who dwell in the world of the Moon, may proceed. (10)
To each of them, a separate celestial mansion and great wealth should be given, as well as ten lakhs of milch cows with their calves.
And there were one hundred and twenty-five thousand horses with black ears, adorned with loads of gold and possessing a luster like that of the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu.
Ten thousand elephants, adorned with ornaments of bells, as well as four thousand chariots possessing the speed of the wind.
There were one hundred thousand camels adorned with jewels and rubies, and ten million troops consisting of the fourfold army.
Garments purified by fire for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas, as well as auspicious and divine ornaments for the sake of the officiating priests. || 15 ||
There were various kinds of foods to be eaten, diverse drinks, a hundred thousand laborers, and exactly a hundred thousand female slaves.
"Whatever property, up to wood and bamboo, has been declared [as belonging to me] by my command, and whatever else the Brahmins may say, let all that be brought there. (17)
Of the gods, the dānavas, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas; of the lords of the earth with its seven continents, and of those dwelling in the seven netherworlds. || 18 ||
Let a proclamation be made repeatedly among thousands of various kings; a proclamation must be issued to all regarding the journey to Prabhāsa.
Having spoken thus to the minister there, Candramas, filled with haste, went to the world of Brahmā into the presence of Brahmā for the sake of the sacrifice.
And that minister of the Moon, Hemagarbha, possessed of great luster, having received the command of Soma upon his head, gathered the materials for the sacrifice.
Having arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he became intent on performing a sacrifice; likewise, he summoned the inhabitants of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar.
Having heard the proclamation, everyone quickly assembled there, having surveyed that entire field extending for twelve yojanas.

Having summoned the Brahmins, he said to them: "O twice-born ones, all the components of the sacrifice have been brought by me at the command of Soma; now, let that which is to be done by you be performed."
Thus addressed, all those brahmins, whose sins had been shaken off by austerity, beheld there the divine architect Tvaṣṭṛ.
Having seen that, all the twice-born, upon seeing the Liṅga nearby, said, "How is this? O Viśvakarman, tell us! Why indeed are you stationed here, accompanied by ten million artisans? (26)
Viśvakarman said: "O twice-born ones, I have been appointed by Soma and am engaged in the protection of the Liṅga; therefore, I exert myself in the fulfillment of that command. (27)
Īśvara said: Having heard this, O brahmins, and having understood the entire cause, they performed the rites for the sake of the sacrifice and then commenced the undertaking. || 28 ||
There, within an extent of one yojana, was the auspicious sacrificial ground of the gods; having prepared that *devayajana*, they constructed the *patnīśālā* (the chamber for the wives).
They established the Havirdhāna, the Sadas, the Uttaravedi, the seat of the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra; such were the places they constructed.
There, Viśvakarman quickly fashioned sacrificial posts and pavilions extending for a yojana, as well as various types of sacrificial pits.
There, up to the pavilion, were a thousand sacrificial pits; all those brahmins there were experts in the ritual of installation.
Adorned with various ornaments and jewels, all the Brahmins, having consulted the scriptures again and again, performed everything according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, [he gathered] trees, divine herbs, sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth; all materials for the fire-oblation (homa), clarified butter (ājya) in abundance, and fresh milk.
Likewise, whatever other sacrificial implements are prescribed, such as the *vardhanī* vessel, the *kalaśa*, and so forth—all should be made of auspicious gold.

With great devotion, they performed everything according to the prescribed rules for the consecration sacrifice; there, the assembly of Brahmins was delighted, being gratified with various kinds of food and edibles.
Resounding with the thunderous sounds of the Vedas, touching both heaven and earth, that pavilion shone brilliantly there, adorned with banners.
He was seated upon a divine throne, adorned with strings of pearls, and graced by divine sandalwood garlands and archways of kalpa-tree foliage.
With divine fragrances, sweet scents, and the like, it became like a celestial realm; there, the fourteen classes of living beings assembled. (39)
The immobile, the serpent species, and likewise the bird species; the fourth is known as the wild animal (mṛga), and the fifth is recorded as the domestic animal (paśu). || 40 ||
The sixth is declared to be human, the seventh is remembered as Paiśāca; the eighth is declared to be Rākṣasa, and the ninth is indeed Yajña.
The Gāndharva, Śākra, Saumya, Prājāpatya, and likewise the Brāhma; thus is the group declared to be of fourteen kinds.
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus; the eight guardians of the world (Lokapālas), and the lunar mansions (Nakṣatras) together with the planets (Grahas). || 43 ||
All those deities who reside within the cosmic egg arrived there at the sacred field of Prabhāsa, filled with joy, once the sacrificial rites had commenced.
Rivers flow with ghee and milk, with mud made of curds and milk-rice; there are heaps of cooked foods and fruits as vast as mountains. (45)
Various forms were seen at that great festival of sacrifice; there the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The gods, the sages, and the fourteen classes of beings were satisfied with various kinds of food and edibles, as well as with drinks that fulfill all desires.

Having thus prepared all the components of the sacrifice along with the necessary materials, the minister left guards right there and went to the world of Brahmā for the purpose of summoning Soma. || 48 ||
Īśvara said: Having seen Soma standing by the side of Brahmā, possessing great luster, he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before both Soma and Brahmā.
With palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed, Hemagarbha spoke. Hemagarbha said: "O Blessed One, by your command, every single component of the sacrifice has indeed been prepared."
There, in the Prābhāsika field, I have made you proficient; there all the Brahman-sages as well as other royal sages [reside]. (51)
All those who gaze upon your path remain agitated; therefore, you ought to perform whatever task must be done next.
Ishvara said: Thus addressed then by the son of the ocean, Candra, laughing, spoke to Brahma, the witness of the world.
O Blessed One, Lord of all gods, out of a desire to show me favor, O Lord, grant hospitality to me who am desirous of performing the sacrifice of consecration.
Today my birth has become fruitful, O Lord, and my ascetic penance as well; today, O Brahman, through your grace, I shall attain the status of a god.
And by means of fierce austerity, this Liṅga of Umāpati was obtained by me; you should perform the entire ritual for its installation. (56)
Brahmā said: "I shall certainly effect for you an installation of the nature of Śaṅkara, especially within the Someśa Liṅga which is the object of your worship."
Whoever shall be, or whoever were, the moons of the past—for all of them belonging to the lunar lineage, he is the primordial deity.
That Lord Someśvara, who at the beginning bore the name Bhairava, I have established again and again as each manvantara has passed. (59)
When I was eight years old, I went to the Prabhāsika field; I had been previously summoned by Indra at the time of Bhairava’s consecration.
From that time onwards, my name has been proclaimed as Bālarūpī; in all other holy places, I dwell in the form of an old man.
Furthermore, O Candra, he dwelt at Prabhāsa from his childhood; and whatever holy places exist in the universe, and whatever Brāhmaṇas are remembered as residing in them—[he dwelt there as well].
Of them, the first is Niśānātha; I am established at Prabhāsa. In every kalpa, O Niśānātha, there shall be another name for me.
In the first [kalpa] he is named Svayambhū; in the second he is remembered as Padmabhū; in the third as Viśvakartṛ; and in the fourth he is Bālarūpī.
For me, as I remain established in Prabhāsa until the end of two parārdhas, there will be a repeated succession of these very names.
There, indeed, by Ādīsoma—who was born from the eye of Śambhu—Lord Īśvara was made manifest after he had performed austerities at Prabhāsa.
Then, being pleased, the wielder of the trident granted a boon to Pūrvacandra: "O Soma, since I have been worshipped by you for a long time with devotion," (67)
Therefore, the name Someśa shall belong to this liṅga for as long as Brahmā Śatānanda is not dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti). || 68 ||
Whosoever shall indeed become lords of the night and makers of the night, they shall perform my worship here again and again.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu vanished right there. At that time, O Soma, the primordial Liṅga was installed by me.
From that time onwards, two hundred thousand, two thousand, one hundred and six lakṣas of Somas have passed away. (71)
"O mighty-armed Soma, you are now in your seventh [manifestation]; these many forms of mine have been established. (72)
This very person is now that same "I," the fruit born of his propitiation; I shall be the one to install [the deity], may you be blessed, O Soma, for that task is indeed mine.

Īśvara said: Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā—endowed with Vedic knowledge, consisting of all the gods, accompanied by the deities, and joined by the sacred fords (tīrthas)—[departed]. || 74 ||
Together with Sanatkumāra and other eminent sages who were lords of yogis, he summoned Bṛhaspati and placed that priest at his head.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of the World, having mounted his swan-vehicle together with ten million Brahmanical sages, arrived along with King Soma.
At the great sacred ford called Prābhāsika, where the Dāruvana grove is remembered to be, and where the river Ṛṣitoyā flows, which destroys even the greatest sins.
In this holy place of Prabhāsa, that is called the portion belonging to Brahmā; O beloved, I have thus described to you this sacred field of the three deities.
Having arrived there at the exceedingly pure Brahma-quarter, the four-faced one summoned the sages who dwell in the elevated region.
Seeing the Creator approaching, accompanied by celestial sages and preceptors, they all honored him with hymns of praise consistent with the Vedas.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke to all the twice-born: "After worshipping Someśa, the destroyer of sins, for a long time with Soma... (81)
When he was propitiated, Soma obtained an unsurpassed liṅga; then the best of the twice-born arrived for the purpose of installing the deity. 82.
"Just as the installation of the nature of Śaṅkara must always be performed by me, so too must it be carried out by you, who rely upon my portion. (83)
Since your linga has fallen to the earth out of anger, its re-installation must indeed be performed by you; of this there is no doubt.
Īśvara said: Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, having taken all the sages with him, was brought by Soma, the king, at which time Brahmā, the lord of the universe, arrived.
At the great sacred ford of Prabhāsika, the Lord, accompanied by Sāvitrī, caused hundreds upon hundreds of sacrificial pits and pavilions to be constructed.
In each pavilion there, seventeen officiating priests (ṛtvij) were appointed; Brahmā was directed there by the Guru, together with the priest of the gods.
Then Brahmā, standing at his side, initiated the powerful Soma, who was accompanied by Rohiṇī, with the rites prescribed in the Vedas. 88.
And having made Rohiṇī, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, his wife—the goddess wearing a deer-skin and veiled in silken garments—[he should worship her]. (89)
Led by the officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas, Candramā was brought into the wife’s chamber; endowed with the consecration of initiation, he was praised by sages and Gandharvas.
Encased in a staff of udumbara wood and covered with a deer skin, he, endowed with exceeding splendor, shone brilliantly as he stood in the assembly.
Then, O Great Goddess, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, performed the selection of the officiating priests according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
The preceptor Vasiṣṭha was chosen there as the Hotṛ priest, and he likewise served as the Adhvaryu; Marīci was the Udgātṛ, and Nārada was appointed to the office of Brahman.
The members of the assembly there were indeed associated with Sanatkumāra; they were adorned with garments, ornaments, crowns, and finger-rings.

At that sacrifice, those sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij), who were experts in their respective duties, were adorned with a multitude of ornaments; thus there were four for each of the four [priestly roles]. || 95 ||
Kaśyapa was the Prastotṛ there, while Gālava was the Pratihartṛ; likewise, Garga was the Subrahmaṇya, and Pulaha was appointed as the Sadasya.
The Hotṛ was known as Śukra, and the Neṣṭṛ was declared to be Kratha; the Maitrāvaruṇa was Durvāsas, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin was Kauśika. || 97 ||
And Śākalya was the Acchāvāka priest, Kratu was the Grāvastut, and Śālaṅkāyana was the Pratiprasthātṛ. || 98 ||
Agnīdhra was made the Manu there, and Tvaṅgirā was made the Unnetṛ; having thus appointed these and others as officiating priests (ṛtvij) in the pavilions, the Lord [proceeded]. || 99 ||
In each of the other pavilions, individual officiating priests were appointed; having prepared sacrificial pits in hundreds of those very pavilions, he established them.
Each pavilion there shall measure twenty cubits; having purified the ground with the Astra-mantra and sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [one should proceed].

O Pārvatī, having covered it with leather and drawn [the design] with the Astra-mantra, having scraped [the ground], performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and dug a pit according to the rule; || 102 ||

O beloved, having consecrated eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as well as one in a single pavilion, and having performed the smearing of the pavilion and the ritual of laying the foundation stone (vajrākaraṇa), [one should proceed].
Having diligently constructed squares, bow-shaped figures, circles, and lotus-forms, beginning from the eastern direction. (104)
Having established a square pit in the east, one should likewise place a vulva-shaped pit in the southeast and an arrow-shaped pit in the south. (105)
In the southwest there is indeed a triangle, while in the west it is circular; in the northwest there is a hexagon, and likewise in the north it is in the shape of a lotus.
Having fashioned an eight-cornered pavilion in the northeast and another single one in the center, each pavilion should be auspiciously white and provided with sixteen pillars.
Brahmā constructed [the pavilion] according to the prescribed rules, provided with banners and archways; having placed a banyan tree to the east, he likewise placed an udumbara tree to the south.
Having erected banners there according to the measurement of an arm-span, one should place an Aśvattha tree to the west and a Palāśa tree to the north in due order.
In the directions beginning with the east (Aindrī), flags of yellow and other colors were envisioned; then Brahmā indeed began the installation of the fire in the sacrificial pit.
He appointed the Brāhmaṇas to their respective places for the recitation of prayers, specifically the Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamāna hymns, and always the Vājin hymns.
Likewise, the Bahvṛcas recited the Vṛṣākapi and the Indra hymns from the east, as well as the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Krokādhyāya, and the Vaikriya.

Those who follow the Yama [tradition] should recite the Brāhmaṇa, the Paitrya, and the Aindra [hymns], as well as the Yajus formulas; and [those following other traditions] should chant the Devavrata, the Vāmadevya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and the Rathantara.
The Chhandoga recited the Bheruṇḍa Sāmans in the west; the Atharvan [recited] the Atharvaśiras, the Skambha-stambha, and the Atharvaṇa.
Atharvan then recited the Nīlarudra Atharva-veda to the North; thereafter, the omnipresent Lord performed for Agni all the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna).
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he likewise commenced the rite of bathing, using earth combined with the five sprouts (pañcapallava).
Then he began the ritual bath with decoctions, the five products of the cow, the five nectars, and fruits, combined with water from sacred fords and accompanied by mantras.

Having opened the eyes of the Lord and performed the rite of applying the sectarian mark (tilaka), [he invoked] all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist upon the earth and especially those in the netherworld (pātāla).
And whatever [objects] were there in the heavenly world, those they brought at that time; meanwhile, while the gods were looking on, Brahmā then [appeared]. 119.
Then, having split the earth, he entered it and beheld there a linga known as Sparśa, which was concealed by honey and the roots of darbha grass.
There, having placed the Brahma-stone, the self-possessed one established a highly radiant Liṅga upon it, making it immovable.

Having established himself in the supreme reality, he then performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). Having thus installed the Liṅga there, Brahmā, the preceptor of the world, worshipped it according to the prescribed rites with extensive mantras declared in the Vedas.

When the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) had been performed there by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, the assembly of Brahmins there became joyful with auspicious sounds such as shouts of "Victory! The fire became smokeless and possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The celestial drums resounded and the lords of the quarters became serene; a shower of flowers fell profusely during that great festival of sacrifice.
Then, having installed the Liṅga of Śrī Someśa, the Grandfather (Brahmā) caused abundant sacrificial fees to be given to the Brahmins. || 125 ||
In ancient times, Soma, surrounded by the primordial Brahman-sages headed by Sanatkumāra, gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmā.
To those foremost Brahmanical sages and likewise to the members of the assembly, he gave gold, jewels, and abundant sacrificial fees by the tens of millions.
Then, consecrated by all the brahman-sages, that one of great splendor, the best among those who shine, caused the three worlds to flourish with his own radiance.
Sinī, Kuhū, Dyuti, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Vasu, Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī—these nine goddesses attended upon him.
Having performed the Māheśvara sacrifice and completed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) without agitation, the Lord of Night became one who had achieved his purpose and was fully fulfilled.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, bestowed upon him a vast kingdom over seeds, medicinal herbs, Brahmins, and grains, O fair-faced one.
Whatever lords of the earth gathered at that sacrifice, to them he gave their kingdoms, wealth, enjoyments, and likewise imperishable heaven.
The Lord of Herbs himself fed the Brahmins and then gave everything to those residents of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
When he gave the sixteen great gifts, beginning with gold, whatever any person—whether common or ordinary—sought therein, that very thing they received in accordance with their own past actions.
When the sacrifice had been thus completed, all the gods, together with Indra, installed their respective lingas and departed as they had come.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the all-pervading Moon, together with Brahmā, worshipped the Liṅga at Prabhāsa, the destroyer of sins.
O Goddess of gods, he worshipped him three times a day with incense, garlands, and ointments; and having prostrated before him, the Lord of Night constantly offered praise.
The Goddess said: O Lord of the World, at what time was that Liṅga installed there? How did the husband of Rohiṇī perform its worship and attain his goal?
Īśvara said: O beloved, in the tenth Tretā Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manvantara, Rohiṇī’s husband was indeed born accompanied by Durvāsas.
At that time, when a thousand years had passed, he performed penance there and thus brought Śaṅkara into his direct vision.
He installed the Liṅga by means of Brahmā, the creator of the worlds; furthermore, he worshipped Śaṅkara for another thousand years.
Then, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, the Lord of the Night, who had beheld Śaṅkara face-to-face, offered a hymn of praise.
Candra said: There is no god equal to Śarva; there is no goal equal to Śarva. There is no god equal to Śarva; there is no goal equal to Śarva. (6)
Salutation to that Self who is the object of knowledge, whom the Sāṃkhyas always recite and the Yogins contemplate as the Supreme Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, whom the wise know to be the cause of the birth and destruction of gods, asuras, and humans. (8)
Salutation to that Yogic Self, the supreme Brahman, which is imperishable, without beginning or end, eternal, everlasting, constant, and partless.
Salutation to Him, the soul of all sacred fords (tīrtha), the primordial God Maheśvara, who is the purifier among all purifiers and who sanctifies by his mere sight alone.
Salutation to that Soul of All, from whom everything proceeds, in whom everything dissolves, and who protects the entire world. || 11 ||
Salutations to that Soul of Sacrifice, whom the twice-born worship with sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, accompanied by complete sacrificial fees.
Ishvara said: While he was thus being praised day and night, the blessed Lord Shankara, the maker of the night, spoke with pleasure as if smiling.
Śaṅkara said: "I am well-pleased with you, my child, by this hymn of praise, O Moon; choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever further desire is in your heart."
Candra said: "O Lord, if a boon is to be granted to us, and if you are pleased with me, O Master of Gods, O All-pervading One, then grant your constant presence in this Liṅga. (15)
O Lord of the Gods, those who behold you while you are situated here, endowed with supreme devotion, shall attain the highest perfection through your grace.
Śambhu said: "O great lord Moon, my presence shall reside here in this liṅga from now on, especially due to your constant devotion. (17)
"From this day forward, you must remain in this field together with Umā; since you have obtained radiance (prabhā) in this field through my grace, therefore its name shall become 'Prabhāsa'. (18)
"O Soma, because this auspicious linga has been established by you for me, my name shall therefore attain renown as 'Somanātha'. (19)
That name of mine which was previously known as Brahmāvasānika shall again circulate as Somanātha. Indeed, those men who, devoted to me, behold me stationed here [shall attain their goal].
Listen, O child Niśākara, to the fruit that shall accrue to them: by my power, O Candra, neither disease, nor poverty, nor misfortune, nor separation from what is dear shall befall them. (21)
For those who perform a pilgrimage with devotion, desiring a vision of me, the fruit is declared to be equal to that of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
O Maker of the Night, what is the use of performing many sacrifices or fasts? Those who behold me here even once have all obtained the fruit [of their merit]. (23)
But he who, intent on devotion, performs a month-long fast, beholds me alone here for as long as a thousand years.
The fruit from both is equal; there is no doubt whatsoever.
O Maker of Night, one should remain a celibate student for as long as life lasts; he who beholds me here even once is said to obtain a fruit equal to that of those two [paths]. (26)
One person bestows all kinds of gifts upon the twice-born; another beholds me here. It is taught that the fruit for both of them is equal.
O Moon, one person performs all the vows, while another merely beholds me here; it is taught that the fruit for both of them is equal.
One person visits sacred fords and performs numerous recitations and prayers; another beholds me here—the fruit for both of them is declared to be equal. (29)
One person certainly becomes a seeker of liberation through the yoga of knowledge and other means; another perceives Me here [in this world]. The fruit for both of them is declared to be equal.
O Moon, one goes to death by leaping from a cliff, while another beholds me here; the fruit for both of them is remembered as equal.
One excellent man always bathes at Prayāga during the month of Māgha; another beholds me here—the fruit for both of them is declared to be equal.
One person should perform the offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at the sacred site of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), while another observes me here; the fruit for both of them is declared to be equal.
"One who gives a thousand cows to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, and one who beholds me here—the fruit of these two is remembered as equal. (34)
One person may practice the five-fire penance during the most terrible summer season; another may behold me here—the fruit of these two is considered equal. (35)
He who, having bathed with devotion on the occasion of a lunar eclipse, or on a Monday, beholds me, obtains the fruit of all these acts.
The Sarasvatī, the ocean, Soma, the Soma-vessel, and the sight of Somanātha—these five things beginning with the letter 'sa' are difficult to obtain. (37)
Whoever worships according to the prescribed rite without interruption for six months obtains that same merit made fruitful through worship on the equinox.

This very [act] should be understood as being [efficacious] during an eclipse, during the northern solstice, on the days of the sun's transition (saṃkrānti), at the intercalary periods, and at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti.

The merit that one obtains by worshipping Śaṅkara according to the prescribed rites for four months, that same merit is said to be obtained on the full moon day of Kārttika; on the full moon day of Caitra, it is twice that amount. This same merit is also obtained on the full moon days of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha.
One person might give a hundred thousand milch cows to a master of the Vedas; another might worship my Liṅga—the merit of the latter is greater than that. (41)
O Goddess of the Gods, whether one should eat once every month for as long as one lives, or whether one should worship the Liṅga even once, these two are equal; of this there is no doubt.

The fruit that is obtained by giving ten million gold pieces to a worthy recipient (pātra) endowed with the virtues of austerity and moral conduct, and who has mastered the Vedas, is attained by means of this flower alone.
Even by offering a single Arka flower to Śiva, one obtains that same fruit which is gained by giving ten pieces of gold.
The karavīra flower is superior to a thousand arka flowers; the droṇa flower is superior to a thousand karavīra flowers. || 45 ||
Indeed, the apāmārga is superior to thousands of droṇa flowers; the kuśa flower is superior to thousands of apāmārga flowers; and the śamī flower is superior to thousands of kuśa flowers. || 46 ||
The flower of the śamī tree and the blossom of the bṛhatī are said to be equal [in value]. The jātī, vijayā, and pāṭalā flowers are to be known as equal to the karavīra. (47)
The white mandāra flower is like a white lotus; it is said that the flowers of the nāga, campaka, punnāga, and dhattūra are also [to be used]. (48)
One should avoid the flowers of the ketakī, jāti, mukta, kanda, yūthī, madantikā, śirīṣa, sarja, and jambūka.
One should avoid the flower of the *ākulī*, the leaf produced from the *karañja* tree, the fruits of the *bibhītaka*, and its flowers. (50)

Kanaka and kadamba flowers should be offered to Śaṅkara at night; the remains of offerings to other deities [should be offered] during the day, and mallikā flowers may be offered both by day and by night.

The Mallikā flower remains fresh for a watch (three hours), while the Karavīra remains so day and night; however, flowers that are infested with insects or have hair upon them, as well as those that have been kept overnight, [are not fit]. || 52 ||
One should discard flowers that have fallen on their own as well as those that are defiled; likewise, one should avoid *tulasī*, the *śatapatra*, *gandhārī*, and *damanaka*.
Among all species of leaves, the marubaka is remembered as the best; with these specific flowers, Someśvara should always be worshipped.
One obtains the fruit of the pilgrimage and is glorified in the heavenly world; having spoken these words, he vanished right there.
Freed from consumption, the Moon became established in his own place. Having summoned Viśvakarman, he had him construct a palace that resembled pure crystal and was radiant, white as cow’s milk. (56)
There is a palace named Meru, with golden walls and archways; fourteen other palaces are arranged around it. I shall state their names one by one; listen to them from me. (57)
Kesarī, Sarvatobhadra, Nadana, Nandiśālaka, Nandīśa, Mandara, Śrīvṛkṣa, and indeed Amṛtodbhava. || 58 ||
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Kailāsa, Pṛthivījaya, Indranīla, Mahānīla, Bhūdharas, and Ratnakūṭaka. || 59 ||
Vaiḍūrya, Padmarāga, Vajraka, and Mukutojjvala; likewise Airāvata, Rājahaṃsa, Garuḍa, and Vṛṣabha. (60)
Meru is the king of palaces, for it is indeed the abode of the gods; it should be known as having five domes (aṇḍakas) at the beginning, situated by the name Kesarin. (61)
And its increase by one-fourth part continues until it is proclaimed as Mount Meru. || 62 ||
Having thus caused fourteen palaces to be constructed separately for the deities beginning with Brahmā who dwell in the vicinity, || 63 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, he first made Kapardin the foremost and then constructed ten other temples, beginning with Bhūdhara and ending with Vṛṣabha.
Indeed, that Meru, the king of palaces, was constructed at Someśvara during the tenth Tretā Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manu.
Having caused pavilions to be constructed and having installed them according to the prescribed rites, he constructed a hundred rivers, as well as a thousand ponds and wells.
Having caused thousands of houses to be built according to the prescribed rites as shelters for the poor and the helpless, he bestowed them individually upon the Brahmins.
Having established a city in the vicinity of the illustrious Someśvara, Soma then requested the twice-born for the purpose of propagating his own religious rites.
"I am Soma, your king, by the grace of the Supreme Lord; nevertheless, out of humility and devotion, I address you. (69)
Wealth such as gold and gems, grain such as rice and barley, cattle such as cows and buffaloes, and various kinds of garments. (70)
Plantations of plantains and coconuts, lined with rows of betel vines and areca palms, stood on all sides, their beauty captivating the mind.
All the lords of Jambūdvīpa who dwell here will carry out your command, placing it beautifully upon their heads.
Your houses have become filled with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood brought from other continents, as well as various other substances. (73)
Merchants desiring profit, who observe the conventions of trade regarding hundreds of commodities, carry out transactions that result in a surplus of Brahman.
Behaving toward you with the disposition of servants and desiring your welfare, they and the other citizens likewise never fall into despair.
Thus, with your full resources, for my spiritual welfare, let sacrificial rites be performed according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
May all [deities] beginning with Brahmā remain active day and night; may the suffering of the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others be destroyed.
And let hospitality be offered with propriety to these high-souled ones who have arrived in the course of their pilgrimage. (78)
"O you of firm vows, let shelter always be given to the brahmin-sages in their hermitages; for I have established this Liṅga here for all time. (79)
Let the best of the twice-born worship with pure offerings; let eight authoritative men from among the citizens be overseers of the affairs.
"O best of the twice-born, you who are experts in the sacred law and traditional conduct, attend to legal proceedings and establish this ordinance made by me here. (81)
May the great-souled ones uphold this place, just as the elephants of the quarters support the earth; thus, having established their sovereignty in this auspicious location.
"O twice-born ones, practice the duties declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas,"—having heard these humble words of Soma, those twice-born ones [acted accordingly]. (83)
Among them, the twice-born Kauśika, the foremost of their lineages, said: "That which has been well-advised for us by the king of the twice-born is entirely correct. (84)
"We shall do all of this; however, listen to one thing: [the fate] of those who, by command, consume the remains of Śiva's offerings (śivanirmālya)."
"An infamy, censured by the Śruti and Smṛti, will befall us; for the Śruti and Smṛti are indeed the two great commands of Rudra. (86)
What fool would transgress that, even at the cost of his life-breaths reaching his throat? || 87 ||
Furthermore, by performing sacrifices within the fire—the mouth of the god who is one of the eight forms of Śiva—in accordance with the path of the Vedas, we gratify the entire world.
This world is the manifest form of the Blessed One, the enemy of Tripura; though it appears mutually distinct, it is nevertheless non-different from the Lord.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
For those who are devoted to the constant study of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other sacred texts, and whose every action is undertaken for the sake of merit toward those respective goals; 91.
Even our opportunity for the worship of the Liṅga is rare; we worship the Lord in this manner through the recitation of the Rudra-hymns and great sacrifices. (92)

"O Great-minded One, we shall worship this Liṅga according to the proper occasion and at the appropriate time. Furthermore, O Soma, as for that worship of Śrī Someśvara which is dear to you, we shall perform it with special distinction. (93)
Listen to that means by which your desire may be fulfilled, having heard the dialogue between Gaurī and Śaṅkara from the mouth of the Blessed One.

Nārada previously told us; we shall relate that very thing to you. Formerly, hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas who were hostile to Brahmā and the gods sought refuge with Śaṅkara through various kinds of fierce austerities. (95)
The Lord, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, bestowed his grace upon them, whose minds were unattached to anything else and who were engaged in most intense austerity.
For he, the Lord of the three worlds, the God of gods, Maheśvara, requires nothing but unwavering devotion to grant a boon.
Being satisfied by their devotion alone, even though they were haters of the gods and Brahmins, he granted them desired boons consisting primarily of sovereignty over the worlds.
Who indeed can know the intention of that Lord, whose power is inconceivable and whose end cannot be found even by Brahmā or Viṣṇu? (99)
To the Supreme Lord, who had granted boons even to the Daityas of wicked conduct through his ascetic penances, Pārvatī, with a pure heart, addressed him.
Pārvatī said: "O Blessed One, having obtained your grace, they have become arrogant toward the three worlds; they harass the gods headed by Indra and cause them great agitation. (101)
Why do you grant boons to such evil-minded ones, whose actions do not contribute even slightly to the welfare of the world? (102)
Disregarding these divine beings who enjoy various pleasures and have been granted boons by you, how can Viṣṇu slay them while setting aside your own sovereignty? || 103 ||
Furthermore, O Lord, tell me: what would be the destiny of those who have been slain? (104)
Īśvara said: "The worlds are indeed of three kinds—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. Among them, these [present] ones consist mostly of darkness and are difficult to approach."
Competing even with the gods through their tamasic austerities, they repeatedly worship me out of delusion, intent upon the destruction of the world.
I grant them a boon, and devotion toward that [deity] is the cause; for I am easily won over by devotion—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (107)
O Goddess, understand from me why those evildoers, having obtained boons consistent with their asceticism, were slain by Viṣṇu. (108)
That I and Hari are distinct is due to a portion of the qualities (guṇas) acting as the cause; yet in the ultimate sense we are non-different, for this is the supreme secret.
The distinction between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator exists only in a general sense for us both; for instance, I [regard] this Gaṅgā as having issued from the tip of Viṣṇu’s foot.
"Even though I am apprehensive regarding your gaze, I carry [this] upon my head with devotion; for even Viṣṇu, by his established order, carries the three worlds to protect them. (111)
Having worshipped me for a long time, he obtained the discus that destroys the wicked; and from you, he obtained Mahāmāyā, belonging to Hari, whose nature is immeasurable.
With devotion to Him, I propitiate the cause of the birth of the three worlds; likewise, Hari places another [form] upon my head, which is His very power (śakti).
Although unborn, he indeed assumes births to protect the world; and he assumed the form of Narasiṃha to slay Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Desirous of destroying the world, he was quelled by me in the form of a Śarabha; and as for me, while I was raising my trident to protect Bāṇa, [he was struck down]. || 115 ||

Even during his descent into human form, that Hari, having effortlessly subdued both [Bali and Virocana], increased my power and majesty; indeed, as the all-pervading Inner Self, he constantly worships me.
Then, I constantly meditate upon this Supreme Self, which is devoid of beginning and end, through the yoga of meditation and in deep absorption.
Thus, there exists no ultimate difference between us; only the deluded project distinctions and degrees of superiority. (119)
Assuming the form of Viṣṇu, I slay those of wicked conduct; now, O Maheśvarī, behold their destiny. (119)
However, at the conclusion of their devotion toward me, through the vision of Hari, they do not attain liberation because they were overcome by anger and pride.
But by our power, they have once again had their impurities washed away and have attained birth in a family of Brahman-sages as a cause for liberation. (121)
Having observed the vow of celibacy and thereafter resorted to the Pāśupata yoga, they—due to the impressions of their past actions—again worship me.
And having undertaken the Pāśupata and other such vows through the yoga of devotion, some dwell in cremation grounds naked, while others wear but a single garment. (123)
Those who subsist on alms, who wear ashes, and who worship my emblems, likewise possess minds one-pointedly focused on me and are firm in their vow of constant meditation upon me.
To those who bow down even to you, the sovereign lady of the worlds and of myself, I grant liberation at the time of the body's end.

Since this Pāśupata yoga does not lead to liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti) for those whose minds are absorbed in me—liberation that consists of similarity of form (sārūpya) or residence in the same world (sālokya)—it has been censured by the virtuous sages according to their tradition and conduct. 126.
The twice-born said: "On the occasion of our pilgrimage, we shall bring those twice-born men who have arrived here—whose minds are won over by devotion—under our own authority."
Honored with pure alms-food, loincloths, water-pots, and other requisites, these ascetics, having no other duties, constantly come here. (128)
Unwearied by the various offerings bestowed by you, those who have realized the true nature of reality through the enumeration of the principles are solely intent upon the dharma of Śiva.
Having worshipped Śrī Someśvara, those who increase your welfare will, at the end, attain the liberation of the Lord, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (130)
After them others, and after them yet others, and after them still others rich in asceticism—these we have examined, O Lord of the Night; they shall be your future subjects.
The twice-born said: Thus spoke the three-eyed Lord when questioned by the Goddess; and there, Nārada [recounted] the entire dialogue uttered by Śiva and his consort.
Having heard it, he related this story to us when we questioned him in our assemblies; and now all of this has been recounted by us to you.
Thus addressed by them, Soma went to his own abode pleased; and by his command, they too performed everything exactly as it had been told.
The Goddess said: "Such is the power of Someśa, the Lord of Gods and destroyer of sins; by what means, by what vow, or by what observance will he be pleased? (135)
Īśvara said: I shall clearly declare the dharma for the benefit of human beings; listen, O beautiful goddess, to that by which the Lord is pleased. 136.
Constant fasts, night-vows, and various other observances; all gifts given at sacred fords, and everything bestowed upon worthy recipients without exception. (137)
By him alone was austerity performed; by him alone was one bathed at Puṣkara; and having gone to Kedāra, water was certainly drunk by him. 138.
O lady of excellent hips, he beheld a jyotirliṅga of great luster, by whom the divine vow of Monday (Somavāra) was observed with devotion. || 139 ||
O beautiful one, what is the use of giving many other gifts to worthy recipients? (140)

O Goddess, by whatever disposition one honors [the deity] on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight falling on a Monday, everything has been accomplished by that person, and the great vow has been observed therein.
O beloved, O Great Goddess, I shall first relate to you this ancient history concerning the Somavāra vow, exactly as it occurred.
Īśvara said: O Maheśānī, situated to the north of Kailāsa and above Niṣadha, there is an extensive city named Svayaṃprabhā. 143.
Richly adorned with various jewels, filled with diverse gandharvas, and complete in all its parts, it was like Amarāvatī, the city of Śakra.
And the Gandharva named Ghanavāhana resides there; he enjoys there great pleasures that are very difficult even for the gods to obtain. (145)
His wife was endowed with fresh youth, captivating, mature in speech, virtuous, and possessed full, elevated breasts. (146)
Together with her, the leader of the Gandharvas enjoyed pleasures; in time, a daughter was born to him, following upon his eight sons.
Endowed with all limbs and cognizant of all forms of knowledge, she was renowned by the name Gandharvasenā, O Supreme Goddess. (148)
Among thousands of maidens, she was preeminent and endowed with beauty; out of curiosity, her father said to her, "Play, O beautiful lady! (149).
In this delightful garden, crowded with various trees and creepers, filled with many kinds of trees and endowed with fruits and flowers. (150)
Thus she always took her delight, constantly surrounded by young maidens; seeing her thus playing, the mother spoke to her husband. (151)
"O Lord, my life, along with that of my kinsmen, is fruitless, since such a daughter remains in the house, deprived of a husband. (152)
Thus addressed, that Gandharva spoke these words to his wife: "O daughter, I shall search for a charming husband for your sake."
Having spoken thus, Ghanavāhana summoned his daughter; being called by her father and mother, O beautiful one, she arrived in haste. (154)
In due order, the auspicious woman fell at the feet of them all and said, "O father, give me your command; what must I do now? (155)
Then Ghanavāha, filled with joy, spoke these words: "O daughter, whatever bridegroom is now pleasing to you, I shall behold that crown-jewel of the Gandharvas, who is divine and your equal. (156)

Thus addressed, her eyes copper-red with anger, she spoke these words to her father: "Is there anyone in the three worlds who possesses even a ten-millionth part of my beauty? Hearing those wonderful words, both the father and the mother were bewildered.
"All the kinsmen and other people fell into despair, saying, 'This speech uttered by the maiden is inauspicious. Having said this, all the mother, the people, and the kinsmen departed. (158)
In that very great garden, the beautiful woman took delight together with her friends, having mounted a swing during the month of spring.
Meanwhile, Śikhaṇḍī, the leader of the Gaṇas, while traveling through the sky seated in a divine celestial chariot, beheld a maiden endowed with exquisite beauty and nobility.
Delighting in song, instrumental music, dance, and the sounds of kettledrums, he descended from his celestial chariot at the time of the midday twilight.
Then, while sporting with the Apsarases, he remained in that garden and heard the words of a maiden, the daughter of a Gandharva.
No one at all is seen in this world who is my equal in beauty; whether a god or even a demon, none possesses even a ten-millionth part of my form. (163)
Having heard these words, the lord of the Gaṇas, filled with wrath, cursed that woman of beautiful limbs who was full of pride.
The Gaṇa said: "O large-eyed one, seeing me, you who are proud of your beauty and good fortune, being yourself arrogant, you insult the Gandharvas, the gods, and others. (165)
"Therefore, leprosy shall appear upon the bodies of those joined with pride. Having heard this curse, the ascetic maiden was then struck with fear.

Then, prostrating with all eight limbs, she entreated him for the sake of his grace: "O Blessed One, O Lord, grant me, who am wretched, relief from this curse; O highly fortunate one, never again shall I act in such a manner. (167)
Thus addressed, Śikhaṇḍī, the leader of the Gaṇas, out of compassion, then bestowed his grace upon that daughter of the Gandharva.

Śikhaṇḍin said: "Any living being who is puffed up with pride because of his birth, his appearance, his learning, or his sense of self-importance, perishes as soon as he encounters that very thing. (169)
Therefore, pride must never be indulged in; this is remembered as the fruit of pride. Listen to this favor, O girl, and having heard it, take it to heart. (170)
"O beloved, having spoken thus, that bull among sages, Gośṛṅga, who dwells in the midst of the Himavat forest, will perform a service; he has departed."
