At that very moment, twilight arrived throughout the world.
Then the daughter of the Gandharva, her enthusiasm shattered and her face downcast, abandoned the beautiful forest and came into the presence of her father. || 173 ||
He related all that was the cause of his leprosy; having heard that, his parents were consumed by grief and their luster departed.
Having reached the Himavat mountain in haste along with their daughter, they beheld the hermitage of the sage Gośṛṅga there.
There, seeing the bull among sages standing in the middle like a cow's horn, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and praised him with many hymns.
Having sat down before him and prostrated again and again, he spoke these words there concerning what had previously occurred.
When the account had been told, he asked again for the cause; and when the cause was questioned there, the Gandharva then spoke.
The Gandharva said: "My daughter's body is afflicted by the disease of leprosy; you ought to perform that which will bring about its alleviation. (179)
O brahmin-sage, show favor now to me, who am wretched, so that my daughter's leprosy may be pacified. (180)
Gośṛṅga said: In Bhārata, near the ocean, there dwells the deity named Someśvara, possessed of great splendor and saluted by all the gods. 181.
Indeed, by observing a fast for a single day and performing worship for a moment, men [attain] the destruction of all diseases and the accomplishment of the purpose of all their undertakings. (182)
"Worship Lord Śaṅkara with the Monday vow (somavāra-vrata). When this is done, the destruction of your daughter's disease will come to pass. (183)
Īśvara said: Having heard these words of that great sage of purified soul, he set his mind on going there for the purpose of worshipping Someśa.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Monday Vow," within the "Description of Śrī Someśvara" in the first section, the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 24 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, that Gandharva, desiring then to propitiate Bhava, questioned the best of sages regarding the vow known as Somavāra-vrata.
The Gandharva said: How is the Soma-vow to be performed? What is its ritual procedure like? At what time should it be observed? Tell me all this in detail.
Gośṛṅga said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! This which benefits all living beings, which has not been told to anyone, I shall now relate to you. (3)
This divine vow called Somavāra-vrata removes all diseases, bestows all spiritual perfections, and grants the fruit of all desires.
It is to be accepted at all times, bringing auspiciousness to the social orders; women should always act upon it, whether they see its immediate result or not.
This great vow was performed by the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and again by King Soma, who had been struck by Dakṣa’s curse.
Śambhu was propitiated by him who was devoted to the meditation on Śambhu; consequently, Mahādeva was pleased with Somarāja because of his devotion.
He said: "If you are pleased, [then grant that] I may remain perpetually established in the consecration."
"As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the mountains remain, so long may this Liṅga installed by me abide together with Umā."
Having then entreated Maheśvara and established [the image], he inscribed his own name upon it; thereupon, he was liberated from his diseases.
Then, with his body purified, he shines resplendent while stationed in the sky.
From that time forward, whatever men on earth perform [this rite], they too shall attain that state, with limbs as pure as the moon.
Now, what is the use of saying more? I shall proclaim its ritual procedure: on whichever month it may be, during the bright fortnight, on a Monday.
Having first used a tooth-stick during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should perform the ritual bath; then, having performed the duties prescribed by one's own dharma, one should go to a pleasant place.
Having placed a beautifully adorned jar upon a pure, level ground that is well-smeared with sandalwood paste and decorated with mango sprouts; || 15 ||
Having first placed Śiva, together with his support (the fire-pan), into a vessel that is clothed in white garments and adorned with all ornaments; || 16 ||
One should worship the eightfold group of the eight forms in the cardinal directions, and there, one should worship Somanātha together with his Śakti and accompanied by Umā, using white flowers.
One should likewise offer various kinds of food and drink, as well as the bījapūra fruit; indeed, one should perform everything there with this very mantra.
Oṃ, salutations to the five-faced one, who has ten arms and three eyes; he is mounted upon a white bull and adorned with white ornaments. 19.
"Obeisance to you who are joined with half of Umā’s body; obeisance to you whose form is everything. With this very mantra, one should perform the worship and the fire-oblation (homa). || 20 ||
Having done this during the day, a man should likewise look upon [the deity] at night and sleep while reclining on a bed of darbha grass, meditating upon Hara, the Lord of Soma.
When this is done, there shall be the destruction of the eighteen types of leprosy. On the second Monday, however, one should use the karañja tree for brushing the teeth.
One should worship the subtle deity endowed with the power of Jyeṣṭhā; having worshipped him with lotuses of a hundred petals, one should consume honey according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered an orange there, one should perform the remainder as before; when this is done on the second day, one obtains the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows. || 24 ||
On the third Monday, having used a tooth-stick and other items produced from the *apāmārga* plant, one should worship the Three-eyed Lord.
One should offer a pomegranate fruit and worship with jasmine flowers; having consumed a sprout of turmeric at night, one should worship while endowed with spiritual success.
On the fourth Monday, however, a staff made of udumbara wood is prescribed; there one should worship Gaurīśa together with Sūkṣmā.
One should offer a coconut fruit and worship with damana grass; one should consume sugar at night and likewise observe a vigil. || 28 ||
On the fifth Monday, one should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas; one should worship the God, accompanied by Vibhūti, with Kunda flowers.
One should cause [the practitioner] to consume an *aśvattha* tooth-stick, as well as *arghya* with grapes and a *moca* fruit at night; he shall obtain the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice. (30)
On the sixth lunar day, during the day of the Moon, one should worship the deity named Surūpa; there, endowed with supreme devotion, one should consume camphor.
On the seventh Monday, however, one should use a tooth-stick of Mallikā; there, one should worship Sarvajña together with Dīptā.
One should offer a jambīra fruit and worship with jātī flowers; one should consume cloves there, and for that person, the fruit shall be infinite.

On the eighth Monday, one should worship the Lord Amoghāyuta with a plantain leaf as the offering vessel and with marubaka flowers; by consuming milk at night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

Whatever fruit is traditionally said to result from properly bathing in the Gaṅgā ten million times, that same fruit is obtained at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse for the gift of ten thousand gold pieces.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, that merit is multiplied ten millionfold when this vow is performed.
When a vow is observed on a Monday, the fruit obtained from giving a hundred elephants, a hundred thousand chariots, and horses is multiplied ten millionfold.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by performing the incense offering of guggulu a billion times, that same merit shall belong to him when the Monday vow has been observed.
Endowed with all sovereign powers and possessing prowess equal to Śiva, he shall dwell in the world of Rudra until the dissolution of Brahmā.
When the ninth cycle has arrived, one should perform the auspicious concluding rite (udyāpana); O Gandharva, I shall now tell you how that is to be done.
Having constructed the mandala, the pavilion, and the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules, one should adorn it with banners and flags and set up four archways.
In the center, a very beautiful square altar (vedi) should be constructed; having prepared a mandala there, one should fashion a lotus in its middle.
Having placed eight jars, each containing gold, in the eight directions, one should then install the Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, in order starting from the east.
In the pericarp of the lotus, however, [one should place] the greatly resplendent Śrī Someśa, endowed with the form of an image, made of gold, and joined with his Śakti.
Seated upon a couch of gold and accompanied by Manonmanī, [he is worshipped] with honey poured into vessels such as golden cups. (45)
One should worship him who is situated there upon a bed covered with gold; one should worship him in sequence with the names beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
And with perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings; as well as garments, ornaments, betel, umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors. (47)
A lamp-stand, a canopy, and a couch with a cushioned cover should be given to a teacher learned in the Purāṇas, dedicated to Someśvara.
Having thus adorned the preceptor, one should have the fire-oblation (homa) performed right there; and at the conclusion of the bali-rite, one should remain awake there throughout the night.

Then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should meditate on Someśvara in the heart; then, having bathed at dawn, one should likewise meditate upon him according to the prescribed rite.
Then, O Gandharva, with devotion he should feed the Brāhmaṇas with various kinds of foods and edibles, prepared with milk, sugar-candy, and other ingredients.
Then, having given a pair of garments and having given a cow, he should bid them farewell. || 52 ||
Having thus duly observed the vow, he obtains imperishable merit; his self becomes enriched with wealth and grain, and he is endowed with sons and a wife.
In his family, no one shall be born poor or even miserable; the childless shall obtain sons, and the barren woman shall become possessed of children.
This rite should be performed especially by those women who are barren, those whose children have died, those who are unfortunate, and those who give birth only to daughters.

When this rite has been performed, upon the falling away of the body, one shall go to Śiva; for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas, he enjoys vast pleasures until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus I have related to you in due order everything concerning the Monday vow (Somavāravratam). Go quickly, O highly fortunate one, to where Someśvara resides.
Īśvara said: Thus addressed, O lady of excellent countenance, that Gandharva, accompanied by his daughter and provided with all ritual offerings, took refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Having beheld Someśvara there, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, he worshipped him according to the sequence of the pilgrimage and duly performed the Soma-vow.

The illustrious Maheśvara, being pleased with him along with his daughter, granted him the kingdom of the Gandharvas—which destroys all diseases and fulfills all desires—as well as devotion unto himself. (69)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Gandharva Maiden," within the description of the majesty of Someśvara, in the first section on the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, in the seventh part (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 25 ||

Īśvara said: Then, having obtained the boon, fulfilled in purpose, and endowed with devotion, that Gandharva Ghanavāhana installed a Liṅga named Gandharveśvara, which bestows the fruits of the Gandharva arts, in the northern part of Someśa, near Daṇḍapāṇi. || 2 ||

Situated five bow-lengths away in the north-western quarter, a man who worships [the deity] on the fifth lunar day shall never again be born into suffering. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gandharveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Then, O Goddess of the gods, right there a Liṅga was installed by Gandharvasenā, the daughter of Ghanavāha, in the vicinity of Gaurī. || 1 ||
Situated there at a distance of three *dhanus* from the eastern section is the one named Vimaleśvara, who destroys all diseases.
Having worshipped on the third lunar day, a woman is released from misfortunes; she attains all her desires and becomes firmly established with sons and grandsons.
Thus, O Great Goddess, when the transitional period of the Tretā age had passed, this vow was proclaimed to the Gandharva; it has been heard to be the destroyer of sins.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gandharvaseneśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, I have heard from you all this wonder—the greatness and the origin of Maheśa in detail. Now, you ought to speak truly concerning Somanātha."
By what rite is he to be seen, and how should the pilgrimage be performed by men? At what time, O Mahādeva, and of what nature are the observances? (2)

Īśvara said: O beautiful lady, whether it be in the winter, the cool season, or even the spring; whenever the mind is inclined, or when wealth is available, or on a sacred festival day (parvan). || 3 ||

At that very time, the journey must be undertaken; the internal disposition is the sole cause for it. However, O lady of excellent complexion, one should first observe some form of restraint while at home.
Having mentally bowed to Rudra and performed the Śrāddha according to the prescribed rule, he circumambulated the sacred site, remaining silent and well-composed.
Restrained and moderate in diet, he should proceed on the path, having abandoned desire and anger, as well as greed and delusion.
Therefore, men should undertake a pilgrimage only after abandoning envy, stinginess, and greed; for the meritorious journey to sacred sites is superior even to sacrifices.
By performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees, one obtains that very fruit which is acquired by visiting sacred fords.

Having reached this most terrible Kali age, which is filled with sin, dharma and heaven cannot be attained by any other means in this world than by the pilgrimage to Someśa, O Great Goddess; of this there is no doubt. (9)
Those men who undertake the pilgrimage in this Kali age, endowed with purity and faith, have achieved their life's purpose; others, however, are devoid of meaning.
Just as there is no other reservoir of water equal to the great ocean, so too there exists no sacred site (tīrtha) equal to the Prābhāsika field. 11.
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords, and without giving gold and cows, one is born as a pauper.
Sacred fords that are inaccessible, difficult to reach, and rugged should be visited mentally by one who desires to go to all sacred fords.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who is self-restrained, moderate in diet, devoted to bathing and the chanting of prayers, and intent upon vows and fasting, attains the fruit of the sacred fords.
O Goddess of gods, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, firm in his vows, and who regards all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
A Brahmin should visit those sacred fords such as Kurukṣetra that are accessible by chariot; indeed, there is no fault in giving gifts at them.
Those virtuous ones who possess wealth and are devoted to the remembrance of sacred fords (tīrthas) obtain even greater fruit through giving at those fords and through yoga.
Those who are poor and destitute of wealth, yet devoted to visiting sacred fords (tīrthas), obtain the fruit of sacrifice even without the accumulation of riches.
For all castes indeed, and for those dwelling in all stages of life, a sacred ford (tīrtha) should be known as bestowing fruit; no deliberation is required in this matter. (20)
He who, having gone for another purpose, performs a bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha), does not obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage; for him, there shall be only the fruit of the bath.
Wandering to sacred fords on foot is said here to be the highest form of austerity; by traveling there by vehicle, one obtains only the fruit of bathing.
O Goddess, if another person performs a pilgrimage to sacred sites on one's behalf according to their ability, using their own wealth and vehicle, the merit for that person is fourfold.
O Great Goddess, those who have visited sacred fords (tīrthas), subsisting on alms and having their senses subdued, obtain tenfold the fruit at a sacred ford.
Deprived of an umbrella and shoes, subsisting on alms, and with his senses subdued, a Brahmin is liberated from the terrible sins born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka).

One should not accept alms that are another's cooked food, nor should one accept alms as a gift; for alms-gathering is equal to drinking the Soma juice, therefore one should practice the life of a mendicant.

In this world, there are two kinds of sacred fords (tīrthas): those created by independent beings, as well as those that are self-existent, such as Prabhāsa and others, which were fashioned by the gods. || 27 ||
In that self-existent great sacred ford, which is the most exalted of all natures, all acts of acceptance have been performed by accepting within that very ford.
For one who has desisted from accepting gifts, the fruit is ten times that of mere subsistence; by him, gifts have been bestowed and the gods have been thoroughly gratified through sacrifices.
By whom, having reached the sacred field, supreme liberation was achieved; whereas he who, out of greed for material things, likewise has a desire for receiving gifts at that very field— (30)

Neither this world nor the next belongs to that evil-minded man; however, if a Brāhmaṇa who is weak for want of livelihood accepts [the gift], one should give him a tenth part of what was earned—thus, in that matter, no harm is incurred.
Having assumed the guise of a Brahmin and become a Śūdra, if he accepts a gift—even one as insignificant as grass or wood—he falls downward.
Thus, O fair-faced one, in the millions of great hells beginning with Kumbhīpāka, [one remains] for as long as fourteen thousand Indras [reign].
Therefore, nothing at all should be accepted even from other Brahmins, whether the sacred ford (tīrtha) has been prepared in two ways—either made or unmade.
One who is joined with his own true disposition enjoys the full fruit; however, he who goes [to the pilgrimage] on another's food obtains only a sixteenth part.
A vehicle is prescribed for one who is powerless, blind, lame, or a wandering mendicant; how could such a thing be permitted for a Brahmin who is free from defects? 36.
By providing bathing, food, and drink to those who carry [the pilgrim's belongings], one who serves a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) obtains the entire fruit arising from that sacred site.
If he does not bestow with effort even a sixteenth part of the wealth obtained, he should instead give a fifth part to the twice-born there.
One who bestows merit upon the deities, the gurus, and one's mother and father out of devotion, obtains that very same fruit multiplied eightfold. (39)
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities—merit should be bestowed everywhere, but demerit is never given at any time. (40)
One who immerses oneself in a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) while intending for one's father, mother, brother, friend, or teacher, shall obtain a twelfth part of the merit for that person.

Having fashioned an image out of *kuśa* grass, one should immerse it in the waters of sacred fords; O Great Goddess, whoever is the object of this dedication shall receive an eighth part of the merit.
Those Brahmins who, weak in knowledge, accept great gifts, are born as Brahma-rākṣasas in the form of trees.
One should not become fond of receiving gifts by relying on the power of the Vedas; for it is through ignorance or negligence that one burns away [the merit of] action, and not otherwise.
Having touched wood from a funeral pyre, as well as a sacrificial post, or having touched a seller of the Vedas, bathing alone is prescribed. (45)
He who recites the instruction and he who imparts the instruction—both of these are doers of evil deeds and shall dwell in the depths of the netherworld.

He who recites the *ādeśa* with a desire to receive a gift, especially at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), is indeed a slayer of Brahmins and none other; standing at the gate of a king, he should not engage in the sale of the Vedas. (47)

A base twice-born man might rather kill cows and eat their excellent meat; he might rather live together with fish than engage in the sale of the Vedas. A sin equal to the murder of a Brahmin has never existed, nor will it ever exist. (48)
One may even perform a sacrifice for a boon, O Goddess, but one should never sell the Vedas, especially at a sacred ford or in a great field of pilgrimage. 49.
But he who, while visiting a sacred ford, renounces a gift that is being offered, makes the sacred ford itself a sacred ford and purifies his ancestors.
A sin committed elsewhere becomes diminished at a sacred site (tīrtha), but that which is performed at a sacred site is never dispelled anywhere else.
The Brahmin who visits sacred fords and guards himself like a vessel of oil, being self-restrained, obtains the full fruit of the ford without any loss.
Whatever cooked food a pilgrim eats, whether it be little or much, half of that he bestows upon the one who has bathed.
That brahmin who, though not afflicted by passion, begs as a mendicant, speaks the truth, and abides in meditative concentration—he is a benefactor of the sacred ford.
In the Kṛta Yuga, Puṣkara is the foremost; likewise, Naimiṣa in the Tretā; Kurukṣetra in the Dvāpara; and Prābhāsika in the Kali Yuga.
If a man were to stand on one foot for a thousand yugas, it may or may not be equal to performing the Prabhāsa pilgrimage alone.
O fair-faced one, having arrived at this sacred field, men should abandon their vehicles in the central area and proceed on foot.

Having rolled there upon the rolling-stone where the deities have rolled, one should then become like a wandering mendicant, dancing, laughing, and singing; having first seen Kapardin, one should go to the god Someśvara.
Seeing such a person standing with his face directed toward Someśvara, the ancestors are eternally satisfied and the great-grandfathers roar with joy.
"O Goddess, a descendant of our lineage has set out for the sake of our deliverance; having gone to Someśvara, O Goddess, he should first perform the rite of shaving. (60)
Listen to me as I explain how the fast at a sacred ford (tīrtha) should be properly observed: there is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, and there is no destination equal to that of sacrifice.
There is no prayer equal to the Gāyatrī, no oblation equal to that performed with the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise, there is nothing within the water that destroys sin like the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
There is no merit equal to non-violence; there is no greater accumulation [of merit] than through giving; there is no austerity superior to fasting, nor likewise any from visiting sacred fords.
O Goddess of gods, there is nothing whatsoever superior to fasting at a sacred ford; it pacifies sins and fulfills the desires of the virtuous. (64)
Fasting is prescribed specifically for one who has taken refuge in a deity; however, for a Brahmin, abstaining from food is said here to be the supreme austerity.
Eating only at the sixth meal-time is declared by the wise to be the supreme austerity for a Śūdra; for those born of the intermixture of castes, it is prescribed for a single day.
If a Śūdra should ever perform penance after the sixth mealtime, it should be known that then there will be the ruin of the kingdom and great calamity for the king. (67)
A Śūdra, however, should eat at the sixth meal-time and perform penance according to his ability; he should not pluck Darbha grass, nor should he drink the milk of a brown cow.
O beautiful lady, one should not eat from the middle leaf of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree; one should not utter the Praṇava mantra, nor should one consume the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
He should not wear a topknot nor a sacred thread, nor should he utter refined speech; he should not recite Vedic words, nor indeed should he observe the three-night vow.
Through the practice of *namaskāra*, the success of a Śūdra’s rites will certainly be achieved; however, by performing prohibited acts, he sinks into hell along with his ancestors.
That man by whom the eleven sense organs have indeed been restrained obtains the fruit of the sacred ford; any other man shall be a partaker of suffering.
And whoever performs the ancestral śrāddha rite at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and carries out the ritual bath there, being a benefactor to all beings, shall enjoy the fruit born of that sacred ford.
That man who, though always greedy and devoted to the wives of others, makes a pilgrimage to sacred fords, shall indeed become a sinner. (74)

Having understood this, O Great Goddess, one should perform the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rules; first, having observed a fast at the sacred site, one should be endowed with faith and firm in one's vows. (75)
If he desires his own welfare, he should not eat at all; on that day, a Brahmin should never consume the food of others under any circumstances.
One may accept all things such as elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, land, cattle, gold, and so forth, but one should not partake of food [from them]. || 77 ||

The merit of one who eats or even gives at [this place] is a hundred times greater than that of [ordinary] raw food; therefore, O fair-faced one, one should observe a fast at that sacred ford (tīrtha). 78.
O Goddess, for one who observes vows, a pilgrim, and especially a widow, eating the food of another results in the fruit belonging to that person whose food it is. (79)
I shall now describe the procedure for the livelihood of a woman who is a widow: saffron, sandalwood paste, betel leaf, and likewise garlands. (80)
All red garments, beds, and coverlets; conversing with the undisciplined, as well as eating twice a day; 81.
One should avoid showing oneself to men, laughter, and walking in the dark; likewise, one should avoid shoes that make a sound, dancing, and [excessive] walking. || 82 ||
One should renounce the grooming of hair, the application of collyrium and ointments, association with unchaste women, and the pursuit of mere scholarship. (83)
One should perform a daily bath and wear white garments; this is especially true for ascetics, celibate students, and widows. (84)
They know betel, honey, and meat to be equal to the drinking of liquor; by avoiding these, O Goddess, one obtains the full fruit of the pilgrimage. 95.
The Goddess said: "What austerities are prescribed for men in the Prabhāsika field? What gifts are to be given, and at which sacred sites (tīrthas), and in what manner? (86)
Īśvara said: "In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is desired; in the Dvāpara age, sacrifice is meritorious; and in the Kali age, charity alone [is supreme]. (87)
In the Kṛta Yuga, sages and other people go to the Prābhāsika field and perform austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. || 88 ||
If gifts are bestowed according to the prescribed rule upon Brāhmaṇas after reaching the sacred field of Prabhāsa, the fruit of ascetic penances is obtained. || 89 ||
The tulāpuruṣa, the brahmāṇḍa, the earth, and the kalpapādapa; likewise the golden kāmadhenu, as well as elephants, horses, and chariots. || 90 ||
The Ratnadhenu, Hiraṇya, Aśva, Saptasāgara, Mahābhūtaghaṭa, Viśvacakra, and the one named Kalpalatā. || 91 ||
At Prabhāsa, the king should bestow the sixteen great gifts: grain, jewels, molasses, gold, sesame seeds, cotton, and sugar.

These ten mountains are traditionally known as Ghee, Salt, Silver, and so forth; and these ten cows are considered to be Molasses, Clarified Butter, Curd, Honey, Water, Salt-water, Milk, and Sugar, while those called Jewels are regarded as being according to their own forms.
One of these gifts should be given separately at each sacred ford (tīrtha), or else all should be given at once at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean.
In the *Priyamelaka*, one should give one's entire property, or a house along with its furnishings—whether much or little—to the most learned Brahmins.
At whatever sacred ford one obtains a liṅga and a holy site with pure water, having first performed the fire-rite there, a distinguished gift is prescribed.

The libation for the ancestors and gods, the śrāddha rite, and the giving of gifts accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as the gift of a cow at every sacred ford—this is the established rule prescribed for those who are self-restrained.
The gift of a bull is prescribed at these distinguished and renowned lingas; one should perform the bathing, anointing, and worship of the deities. (98)
One should worship the Jagatī with devotion and likewise smear it [with cow dung]; one should cause a white temple or mansion to be built and restore what is dilapidated. (99)

The observer of the vow should cause a flower garden and a pure bathing well to be constructed, and he should give abundant gifts to the Brāhmaṇas and to those who perform the worship of the deity. (100)
This rule applies everywhere during a festival for the gods: one should restore a dilapidated sacred site (tīrtha), clean it, and proclaim its merit.

At a famous site, a great gift is required; at a middling site, a middling one. The gift of a cow is prescribed for all sacred fords, as is the payment of gold. Indeed, the gift of gold is the ultimate atonement for all other gifts.

By acting thus with devotion, a person obtains the fruit of their birth. I shall now describe the gifts to be given at sacred fords (tīrthas), specifying those which are to be given at particular places and on specific lunar days.
At Prabhāsa, on the first lunar day (pratipad), auspicious gold should be given as a gift; likewise, on the second day, clothing, and on the third day, land.
On the fourth day, one should cause grain to be given; likewise on the fifth, a tawny cow; on the sixth, a horse; and on the seventh, one should cause a buffalo to be given there.
On the eighth day, having given a blue bull endowed with auspicious marks, one should on the ninth day give a house, as well as a discus, a conch, and a mace.
On the tenth day, all types of fragrances; on the eleventh, pearls; and on the twelfth, one who observes good vows should likewise duly offer food and coral.
Women should be given away on the thirteenth lunar day; on that day, one becomes a giver of knowledge. Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should cause all kinds of gifts to be bestowed.
Having thus bestowed this gift, one shall obtain the fruit tenfold. || 109 ||
The Goddess said: "Tell me, what is the fruit for those who have come to the sacred field of Prabhāsa devoid of devotion and charity, and lacking both ritual bathing and mantras?"
Ishvara said: Whether they possess wealth or are destitute, whether they are accompanied by mantras or devoid of mantras, all who meet their death at Prabhasa go to the abode of Shiva.
O beloved, to those men who have died devoid of mantras and devoid of dharma, I grant a single, most magnificent celestial chariot.
According to the merit of their bathing and giving, men attain the supreme state—some through the power of bathing and others through the power of giving. (113)
Some by prostrating before the liṅga, some by worshipping the liṅga, some by the power of meditation, and some by the power of yoga. || 114 ||
Some [attain it] by the recitation of this mantra, O auspicious lady, some through austerity, some by renunciation at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and some in accordance with their devotion. || 115 ||
These and many others—superior, inferior, and middling—all go to the city of Śiva in celestial chariots resembling the sun.
With hands marked by tridents and all having the bull as their vehicle, they sport by my power, surrounded by hosts of divine apsarases.
Thus, in accordance with one's devotion, I grant an imperishable fruit; it is stainless and radiant, for one is not tainted by merit or demerit.
Whether they practice righteousness or unrighteousness, they go to Śiva; of this there is no doubt. || 119 ||
O Goddess, even that man who has been deprived of his eyes from birth, if he dies in my sacred field, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O Goddess, he who from birth has been deprived of hearing, yet meets his death at Prabhāsa, shall become my own possession. || 121 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for touching sacred bathing places (tīrthas); when consecrated with a mantra, the tīrtha likewise becomes present there.
First, one should touch the sacred water with the *praṇava* to make it pure; then, having entered the water, one should bathe through the application of spiritual mantras.
Oṃ, salutation to the God of gods, to the blue-throated one, to the wielder of the staff; salutation to Rudra, to the one with the left hand raised, to the wielder of the discus, to the Creator. 124.
O Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Mother of the Vedas, Radiant One, O destroyer of sins, be present here at this sacred ford! This mantra is declared for all sacred fords alike. (125)
Having recited this and paid homage, one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules; thereafter, O lady of excellent vows, one should observe a fast on that day.
That lunar day (tithi) should be observed with fasting for one year by those intent on devotion.
The Goddess said: O Great Goddess, tell me in detail: at which sacred bathing place (tīrtha) should men who have previously arrived at the holy site of Prabhāsa perform their ritual ablution? 128.
Īśvara said: "Behold, I shall fully describe to you that primordial sacred site of great splendor; listen to me as I tell of where bathing was formerly performed by men."

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Procedure for the Pilgrimage," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: From there, one should go to Agnitīrtha on the auspicious shore of the ocean, where that Vāḍava fire was released by Sarasvatī, O fair-faced one.
To the south of Somanātha is a holy site that destroys all sins, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name of Padmaka.

One hundred *dhanus* from Someśa, situated in the midst of the water, is said to be a sin-destroying pool measuring one hundred cubits (*hasta*) in extent; there, having plunged into that treasure of waters, one should perform ablution. (3)

Having first performed the shaving of the hair near the Śoṇa river while meditating upon Śaṅkara in one's mind, one should discard the hair there; then, having removed the hair, one should perform the bath once again.
O Daughter of the Mountain, whatever sin a man oppressed by the need for a livelihood commits, all of that remains caught in his hair.
Therefore, with every effort one should cast one's hair there; by doing so before Somanātha, the fruit indeed becomes twofold.
That which is situated near the Agnitīrtha and located within the Kaparddin gate should be known as having double the merit; elsewhere, it is traditionally held to have single merit.
O lady of beautiful countenance, the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma) is not prescribed for women who have husbands; listen now from me to the specific rule regarding them.
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths; thereafter, one should gratify the gods and the ancestral deities according to the prescribed ritual.
Shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule at all sacred fords.

Shaving of the head is prescribed in seven instances: at the Gaṅgā, in the region of Bhāskara, upon the death of one's mother, father, or guru, at the time of the *ādhāna* rite, and during the drinking of the Soma juice.
Even one who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which is gained from the act of sowing [the seeds].
O Goddess, he who performs a bath there without the mantra may occasionally attain some merit, with the single exception of the day of a festival.

O Goddess of the Gods, the great ocean must not be touched even by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, except by men who have performed the ritual shaving without mantras, on a sacred festival day, or without other people present.
Having thus bathed according to the prescribed rite and offered the arghya water to the great ocean, he should worship it with flowers, perfumes, garments, and sacred unguents.
One should place a golden bracelet there according to one's ability.
Having performed the ritual procedure in this manner, O Goddess of the Gods, one should touch the salt ocean with this mantra; then it will attain presence.
Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇugupta; salutations to you who are the very form of Viṣṇu. O Lord of Gods, be present here in this salt-water ocean.
"Agni is the seed and Mṛḍayā is the body; Viṣṇu, the placer of the seed, is the navel of immortality. O Pārvatī, speaking this truthful word, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers.
"O beautiful lady, with this mantra, 'Oṃ, homage to Ratnagarbha,' one should cast a bracelet there; thereafter, one may bathe as one pleases. (20)
Then, endowed with perfect faith, he should offer libations to the gods, human beings, and ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds. (21)
Whatever sin a man commits throughout hundreds of thousands of births, he may cast it off by bathing but once in the salt waters of the ocean.
When the rite of shaving has commenced, a bull should be given there, as well as a gift corresponding to one's own nature and likewise a yellow garment.
One should perform the ritual bath there according to this procedure; otherwise, one might touch the submarine fire and become a partaker of fault.
This boon and this curse were granted to him in former times by the twice-born, just as they had been.
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, at which various places does one become purified by bathing in water? For what reason is there a fault in the ocean? This is a great curiosity. (26)
Where all rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, have found their rest; where Viṣṇu himself lies down, and where Lakṣmī herself resides.
For what reason was that boon and curse given to him by the twice-born in the past? Tell me everything in detail, for I have a great doubt in this matter. (28)

Īśvara said: O Goddess, in ancient times, a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) was commenced by the best of the gods after they had reached the holy site of Prabhāsa, being fully endowed with perfect faith.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrificial session, having bestowed gifts of many kinds and his entire wealth upon the eminent Brahmins residing in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, [he departed]. (30)
Meanwhile, other twice-born ones arrived there for the sake of sacrificial fees—both those from the region and local residents by the hundreds and thousands.
Then the gods, including Indra, fearing the failure of their prayers, fled; and seeing those deities gone, the Brahmins followed after them.

O Goddess, in former times there was a great power of moving through the air (khecaratva) belonging to those born first; by means of that, they all go swiftly wherever the abodes of the gods are located. || 33 ||
Thus, observing their all-pervading power, the inhabitants of heaven entered the ocean in fear and spoke these words to him once again: ||| 34 ||
"We have come to you for refuge, having fallen into fear of the Brahmins; we possess no wealth for the purpose of giving. Therefore, protect us, O Great Ocean! (35)

On one side are all the sacrifices completed with the bestowal of excellent sacrificial fees; on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being terrified by fear. Especially for the gods, such protection yields great merit.
The Ocean said: "O best of gods, you should not fear the Brahmins in any way; I shall protect you. Enter into my belly."
Then all those gods, delighted by his words and free from fear, entered the deep cavity of his very belly.
The ocean also, having assumed his own vast form in many ways and taking up multitudes of aquatic creatures, drew near to the shore. (39)
Then he devised a stratagem for the destruction of the brahmins; having cooked the meat of fish, it was concealed within a great quantity of food.
Then, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he said to all the twice-born: "O Brahmins, please grant me your favor for a moment now."

"Simply because you have accepted this hospitality, and since you are both distressed and prostrate before me, I have prepared this meal for your sake with great care. Please eat; thereafter, you must follow after the gods."
Then those brahmins, perceiving that the ocean was filled with faith, said "So be it" to him and ate from golden vessels.
Afflicted by hunger, they did not realize that the meat was concealed and delicious.
Then those brahmins, having been satisfied and freed from hunger, all those brahmins of praised vows bestowed their blessings. (45)

The end of Brahmins is at their meal; the end of those born as Kṣatriyas is at the loss of life; the anger of venomous serpents should be known to last until death. He then urged the gods, saying to them, "You must go."
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, traveling swiftly through the sky, were seen by the brahmins there as they proceeded, and were saluted by them.
They rose up from behind, intent on seizing the sacrificial fee for the sake of the gods.
Then those twice-born ones suddenly fell again to the ground; indeed, those brahmins had fallen due to eating what is unfit for consumption—namely, the eating of meat.
Having understood that means of atonement for the ocean, O Great Goddess, they, filled with wrath and assuming fierce forms, uttered a terrible curse.
Since meat is indeed remembered as the supreme forbidden food for Brahmins, yet you have offered it to us, well-concealed and mixed with edible substances. (51)
On one side are all kinds of meat, and on the other side is the flesh of fish; on one side are all sins, and on the other side is another's wife. (52)
Even though we understand this as a condemnation of meat, we have all been deceived by acting without due investigation. (53)
"O evil-minded one, since we have indeed been deceived by you through this cruel act of consuming meat, therefore you shall become undrinkable. (54)
"You shall be untouchable on earth for the foremost of the twice-born and for other men as well; those mortals of wicked intellect who perform [rites] with your water," || 55 ||
Those who bathe there will undoubtedly go to a terrible hell—the worlds reserved for the ungrateful and the worlds reserved for evildoers. (56)
Through the contact with the water of those [tīrthas], men on earth shall obtain [their desires]. || 57 ||
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent complexion, having been thus cursed by those brāhmaṇas, the ocean then became untouchable for a thousand years.
Then, becoming agitated with fear, he said this to them all: "O brahmins, this task of the gods was performed by me, who am lacking in wisdom. (59)
By one desiring to practice the supreme dharma arising from providing refuge, whoever should abandon one who has sought refuge out of desire, anger, fear, or greed— [is a sinner]. (60)
Or rather, he should be known as a perpetrator of a great sin from the truth that the inhabitants of heaven have come to me for refuge out of fear of you. (61)
"They have been properly protected by me according to my ability and through skillful means; yet, because I have been cursed out of anger, I shall wither away my own self."
"I cannot bear to remain here deprived of the touch of people. Having spoken thus, O Goddess, the ocean, the lord of rivers, remained there in great sorrow and caused himself to dry up.
Then all the hosts of gods, filled with great fear, gradually beheld the great ocean appearing like dry land.
Having gone to the Lord of the World, the God of gods, the Grandfather, they said: "On our account, Sāgara has been cursed by the twice-born, the most excellent of Brāhmaṇas. (65)
Afflicted by great suffering, he withers away his own body; yet the clouds, having taken water from the ocean, pour it down as rain. (66)
From that, grain is produced; from grain, sacrifices arise; and through sacrifices, the satisfaction of all the inhabitants of heaven is brought about. (67)
"In this way, by its destruction, our own destruction will come to pass. Therefore, go and protect it so that it does not wither away. (68)
Let policy be enacted in such a way that those Brahmins may be satisfied.
At the word of the gods, Brahmā went to the vicinity of the ocean and, for the sake of the sea, entreated those Brāhmaṇas residing in the sacred field.
Brahmā said: "O best of the twice-born, let favor be shown to this ocean; act according to my word so that it may attain purity."
He will bestow upon you various kinds of jewels.
"By my word, you shall truly become 'Earth-gods' (Bhūmidevas) on this earth by name; this which I have spoken is certainly the truth. (73)
The Brahmins said: "O Lord of the World, we do not wish to act otherwise than according to your word; nor is our own speech false, for you indeed are the authority in this matter. (74)

Therefore, O best of gods, whether by our word it be beneficial or even harmful, act so that there may be the highest welfare for the worlds and for all the inhabitants of heaven; do so, O Lord of the World, for the sake of our benefit. (76)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke to the lord of rivers: "Do not wither yourself; listen to my beneficial words."
Indeed, that word of the twice-born cannot be made otherwise; for if the Brahmins were to become angry, they would surely reduce everything to ashes by their own splendor.
They could turn gods into non-gods; therefore, one should never provoke them. For this reason, your touch shall become pure in three ways.
And when the time of a festival has arrived, at the confluence of rivers, at Setubandha, at the Indus, and likewise joined with other sacred fords (tīrthas). || 79 ||

Among all such [acts], and not elsewhere than in this ritual, whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices—that fruit shall come to you simply from the touch of your water. (80)
Whatever merit is gained from performing a śrāddha at Gayā or by dying in the protection of cows, that fruit shall be yours simply by the touch of this water. || 81 ||
Likewise, you shall become undrinkable by mere taste alone; yet even a mouthful of water drunk from you shall be the destroyer of inauspiciousness.

In the world of men, there shall be an increase in your happiness for him who performs the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors with your water according to the previously mentioned rite; hear now the fruit of his merit. || 93 ||
"As long as you remain in the world, and as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist, so long shall your ancestors remain satisfied by the nectar of your water. (84)
And for one who bathes continuously in the month of Māgha with a purified mind, the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice shall accrue to him day after day.

Whether on a pilgrimage, elsewhere, during a festival, or at the time of a lunar eclipse, that person who properly bathes here in the salt-water ocean shall obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Those men who die in the interval between Śrīsomeśa and the ocean, even if they are sinners, shall go to heaven with their impurities shaken off.
"O Lord, it shall always be so according to my word; grant various kinds of jewels to the best of the twice-born. (88)
Being pleased by that, they will grant you yet another boon as you desire. || 89 ||
The Lord said: Having heard the words of the Grandfather, the Ocean replied, "So be it," and, filled with faith, gave excellent jewels to the Brahmins.
The Brahmins carried out the word of Brahmā in its entirety; having likewise performed the rite of shaving, they all performed their ritual ablutions.
Thus having attained purity, the salt ocean became a sacred ford (tīrtha). In its midst, O Great Goddess, there are fifty million liṅgas.
O Goddess, in this Manvantara, they were rendered invisible within the ocean; and right there, there was a fire-pit as well as another lotus-lake.
But in this Manvantara, O beloved, everything is covered in the middle; that which lies between Mount Cakra and Mount Maināka is called the southern direction.
In a pitcher made of gold, ten thousand bows in width, situated in the center of that pitcher is the one known as the Vaḍavānala fire.
Having a needle-like mouth and a massive body, he drinks water constantly; having reached this interval, it is proclaimed as Agnitīrtha.
In its center is the great essence, the Vāḍava fire, where indeed is its mouth; it extends from Śrī Someśa for a hundred *dhanus* to the south, and from Mānasa to the north as far as Kṛtasmara.
This must be kept secret, O lady of beautiful hips; it should not be given to just anyone. Even a slayer of a Brahmin would be purified by hearing this—of this there is no doubt. (98)
Thus I have related everything regarding how the curse and the boon were granted to the ocean by the twice-born, first when they were enraged and later when they were pleased. 99.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Reason for the Sea’s Undrinkability," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The Goddess said: "O Lord of the Gods, having bathed there in the Agni-tīrthas, which deity should one worship first so that the pilgrimage of men may become free from obstacles? You ought to explain that procedure for the pilgrimage to me exactly as it is."

Īśvara said: Having thus bathed according to the prescribed rite and having offered the *arghya* oblation into the great ocean, one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, garments, and floral unguents.
One should cast a golden bangle there according to one's ability; then, having offered libations to the ancestors, one should go to the Lord Kapardin.
Having worshipped with devotion using flowers, incense, perfumes, and garments, one should offer him the *arghya* water with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
Furthermore, O Goddess of gods, for Śūdras, the mantra is remembered as the eight-syllabled one (aṣṭākṣara). There, one should go to the god Someśvara, the supreme remover of sins.
Having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should recite the Śatarudriya, as well as the Rudra-mantras with their five ancillaries (pañcāṅga), and other Rudra-saṃhitās.
One should bathe [the deity] with milk, as well as with curd mixed with ghee, and with honey and sugarcane juice; one should then anoint [the deity] with saffron.
Then, one should worship the object of worship with fragrant sandalwood mixed with camphor, ushira root, and musk.
Having fumigated the deity with various kinds of incense according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter wrap [the image] in garments and offer excellent food oblations (naivedya).

Then, having performed the ārārtika rite, one should perform a dance according to one's desire; thereafter, having prostrated with the eight limbs, one should likewise engage in song, instrumental music, and so forth.

O Lord, one should have a dramatic performance presented that is connected with the hearing of the Dharma; thereafter, one should give gifts to the twice-born and to ascetics according to one's ability.

One should give gifts to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and to pilgrims; in that place, a bull should be given when cruel rites are performed. Then, O beautiful lady, one should observe a fast on that day.
On whichever day a man beholds the god Someśvara, that lunar day (tithi) should be observed as a fast for one year by those intent on devotion.
By acting thus with devotion, a person obtains the fruit of his birth, and likewise, he attains the entire fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 14 ||
O beautiful lady, one shall uplift the host of ancestors and the host of maternal kin; whatever sin was committed in childhood, in old age, or even in youth.
Having beheld Someśvara, a man should wash away all that [impurity]; he shall never be born miserable, poor, or unfortunate. || 16 ||
Within seven births, upon seeing the omnipresent Lord Someśvara, one is born into a prosperous family endowed with wealth and grain.
Furthermore, devotion toward the Lord Somanātha arises; first there is bathing with milk, and thereafter that which originates from the stream.

Those men who behold the Great Bath of the God of gods during the first watch, and thereafter at midday, as well as the evening twilight and the waving of lamps, are not born again as human beings. (19)
O fair-faced one, considering the Kali age to be fierce and full of many sins, a man cannot cross over that difficult passage or his miserable state by any other action.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Worship of Someśvara," within the "Greatness of Someśvara" section of the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||
The Goddess said: O Śaṅkara, regarding those five *sakāra*s that were mentioned by you to me—how did they come to be here? This is a great doubt of mine.
How did Sarasvatī come here from wherever she came? How was that Vāḍava fire born, at what time, and how did it come to be? You ought to relate all this in detail and exactly as it happened.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to how Sarasvatī was born in that sacred field, and from where that destroyer of all sins originated. (3)
Hiraṇyā, Vajriṇī, Nyaṅku, Kapilā, and Sarasvatī. || 4 ||
Listen now to how she was summoned here by the five sages as in the past, and how she was joined with the Vāḍava fire when she was born.
Formerly, when the war between the gods and the asuras had ceased on account of Soma, Candra delivered Tārā to him at the command of the Grandfather.
Then the gods, having departed for heaven while looking down upon the earth, beheld there another heaven, as it were, upon the ground.

He reached the world-renowned hermitage of Dadhīci, the foremost of sages, which was endowed with flowers of every season, adorned with trees, and filled with the fragrance arising from ketaka, kuṭaja, and bakula blossoms.
Having reached that venerable hermitage of such a kind, all the gods began to look upon it with curiosity, for it was truly enchanting.
Having left their vehicles at that hermitage of the holy ford, they proceeded with self-restraint to see that sage, like ordinary men.
All the gods beheld him as if he were another Grandfather (Brahmā); then they were all honored by the sage with water for the feet, guest-offerings, and other rites.
As has been described, all the gods, including Indra, took their seats; then, rising from among them, Śakra spoke to that sage.
"Having set aside your weapons first, please indeed accept these. Hearing those words, Dadhīci spoke to Pākaśāsana (Indra).
"Cast off your weapons and go from my presence to heaven. Śakra said to them: "Indeed, these [weapons] are for when the time for action has arrived."
"Furthermore, these must be given to you so that we may conquer our enemies in battle. Having thus instructed the best of sages again and again, Śakra [departed].
"O Sage, these must be given by you to us alone and not to anyone else. When this was said, Śakra replied, "So be it," and the best of sages spoke.

"I shall give them all to you, especially at the time of battle. Thinking, "May his word not prove false," the Lord of Śacī then released those weapons in his presence and returned once more to heaven.

The king on earth who, being self-restrained and pure-minded, listens with diligent effort to this *astrārpaṇa*, shall indeed attain supreme victory in battle and obtain sons who delight in virtue, wealth, and fame. (18)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of Their Own Respective Weapons by All the Gods to the Great Sage Dadhīci," within the account of the Origin of the Vaḍavānala Fire, in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 31 ||
Ishvara said: Then, after those gods of gods had departed, that twice-born sage remained there for a hundred years and set out to perform penance.
Then, from that northern hermitage, toward the divine northern quarter, his highly fortunate attendant Subhadrā also [departed].
Unable to take up the weapons, that beautiful woman said to the sage: "I am not capable of taking the weapons with my hand."
Then that sage drank that semen together with water; having caused all his divine weapons to reside within himself, that muni, a treasure-house of austerities, departed for the northern quarter.
He beheld Himavat, who bore the Gaṅgā, whose body was white, whose form was covered with serpents, and who, like Śiva, bestows happiness upon men.
Likewise, he beheld a lofty hermitage protected by Aśvattha trees, situated on the banks of the Candrabhāgā river, and provided with sacrificial fuel, flowers, and Kuśa grass.
That tiger among sages dwelt there together with the other sages and joined by Subhadrā, just as the moon is accompanied by its moonlight.
Once, while he was living there, his maidservant Subhadrā, having become menstruating on the fourth day, set out to go for her bath.
As she was walking away, she saw that the loincloth covering had been discarded; realizing this through the turn of fate, she took it up.
Having put on her loincloth again, which was stained with semen, she began to bathe at her ease near the water in a secluded spot.
Then the queen, languid from the heavy burden of her womb, suddenly beheld as she desired the embryo that had arisen within her own belly.
Having tormented myself by my own self, I have come here without a womb; by whom, then, has such a defilement been inflicted upon me, so unfortunate? (12)
Overcome by shame, she entered a grove of *aśvattha* trees there and gave birth to that fetus, not knowing from where it had come.
Having bathed once again, and remaining unaware of her own misdeed, she began to utter an unbearable curse upon the one who had caused her pregnancy.
Whether through knowledge or through ignorance, he by whom this censure was made shall meet his death this very day, provided that I am a devoted wife.
"If even in my mind I desire no other husband, by this word of truth, let my paramour go to his own destruction. (16)
Having thus cursed him, the goddess, unaware of who had caused her pregnancy, began once more to return to the abode of Dadhīci.
Then, having cast off the fetus which resembled the sun, she reached the delightful penance grove where that bull among sages resided.
In the meantime, all the gods and the world-protectors of great strength arrived at the hermitage of the sage for the purpose of obtaining weapons.
Śakra said to that sage: "O observer of noble vows, the deposit of weapons which was given to you by us—return those to us quickly. (20)
The sage said: "O Vāsava, those [seeds] which were formerly placed in my hermitage remain in that very place; they have not been brought here."
O Vasava, O destroyer of enemies, whatever strength and vigor they possessed in battle, all of that has been drunk up by me along with the water.
This being the case, O sinless one, if weapons are to be given to you by me, then I shall give you bones that possess their very forms, O observer of noble vows. (23)
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed one said to that best of sages: "That fierce power which is established within them does not exist in others."
Because Rudra, the auspicious one, having deposited a thousandth part of his own splendors within them, bestowed them upon us for the protection of the worlds.
Having taken all of those, we remained established for the sake of protecting the world; therefore, by that [act], we are known as the Lokapās (World-Protectors).
Among all these weapons, the thunderbolt (vajra) is considered the most excellent; for it is by wielding it that our status as the king of gods is desired.
The discus, which is superior even to the thunderbolt and was acquired by Viṣṇu, became the means by which victory over the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas was achieved.
Therefore, O best of sages, O foremost among those who know what must be done, reflect and act in such a way that we may obtain them. (29)
When this had been said, the Sage spoke to Śakra, who stood before him: "I shall tell you another means for the sake of attaining that."
"Take these bones of mine; with them all, you must fashion weapons that exactly replicate their forms in every respect. (31)
These beings, arisen from him, shall possess even greater strength than they; they will accomplish for you in battle that which I have intended.
Then Śakra spoke to Dadhīci, that treasury of asceticism: "I am not able to bring about the taking of your life, whomsoever you desire."
Moreover, we do not have the power to take hold of your bones, which are immortal; therefore, having considered everything, let that which ought to be done be declared. (34)
Thus addressed, the sage said: "O Lord, for the sake of accomplishing this purpose, I myself shall abandon this very body. (35)
When this body is unstable, the locus of all sufferings, and utterly loathsome, then it is indeed appropriate to renounce it immediately. (36)
By the renunciation of this [body], the suffering arising from saṃsāra does not arise for me; for one who is born in another life may indeed die yet again. (37)

Through the application of the fruits of one's own karma, she is born as a wife, a sister, or a daughter; by that very process, she becomes an object of loathing in this worldly existence for the sake of sexual pleasure. (38)
And since he will certainly abandon this body of his own accord, it is better that its abandonment be carried out by him himself before long. (39)
Having thus proclaimed this in the presence of Purandara, that great sage Dadhīci then quickly brought about the end of his own life.
Having thus recognized him as lifeless, the gods reflected upon what should be done with his body, which was now devoid of blood and me. (41)
Then, for the sake of purifying that bone, the Lord of the Gods spoke these words: "The tongues of the Gaurīs are rough; let them extract this. (42)
Then, when Nandā was meditated upon by those gods while she was established in the worlds, she arrived there, surrounded by her companions.
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā—these five mothers of the cows arrived from Goloka. (44)
They said to all those gods: "Whatever purpose must be accomplished by us, we shall perform it; let it be told after due deliberation. (45)
The gods said: "Let this skeletal frame, which was cast off by the sage himself, be cleared of its flesh and other [tissues]. (46)
Having performed that censurable and most dreadful deed by the command of the gods, those best of deities went again to see the Grandfather.
Then they reported to the Grandfather (Brahmā) everything regarding that terrible deed which had been performed by them, exactly as it had happened.
Having heard that, the Grandfather summoned all the gods and, desiring purification, touched Surabhi on all her limbs.
Touched by those gods, they became perfectly pure and remained so; however, it is traditionally held that their single mouth alone was not touched and is considered impure.
The mouth of one among them would be impure and loathsome, while the rest of the bodies of all were made excellent by the gods. (51)
But Sarasvatī declared that they were slayers of Brahmins; otherwise, for what reason would their faces not have been touched by the immortals?
Then Sarasvatī, the goddess, was addressed there by them: "It is not proper for you to speak such words from this mouth."
Our very hearts have been consumed by these words of yours; therefore, you shall soon meet with burning yourself.
Having then pronounced that curse upon Sarasvatī, those Surabhis, who are worshipped by the gods, departed for Goloka.
Having summoned Viśvakarman the carpenter, the best of the gods said to him, "Fashion weapons for us for the sake of war. (56)
Having heard these words, he had those weapons fashioned from the heaps of Dardhoca’s bones, which were pure, new, and firm.
In that battle, he fashioned those [weapons] for the gods so that they were endowed with the forms of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and were invincible. || 58 ||
He properly fashioned the thunderbolt for Indra, the spear for Agni, the staff for Yama, the sword for Nirṛti, and the noose for Varuṇa.
Viśvakarman fashioned for Vāyu a banner, and for Kubera a heavy mace; likewise, he fashioned a trident for Īśāna.
Having taken up these weapons and that power of missiles, the gods then set out to conquer the Daityas and the Dānavas.
In the meantime, Subhadrā, having performed the funeral rites for Dadhīci along with those sages, went to search for her son.
And in the Aśvattha grove he saw that charming one; seeing him alive, she wept for a long time, shedding tears as she released her grief. (63)
Addressing her as "O Mother," he said: "Do not weep, O illustrious lady; for this is the fruit of past deeds, belonging both to you and to me."
Whatever action has been performed here by whomsoever, in whatever manner, and in whatever place, throughout other births—that must necessarily be experienced; therefore, abandon all grief.
"And you, O beautiful one, should feel no shame here regarding the abandonment of me; for this is the fruit of my past deeds, which must indeed be experienced by me as well. (66)
O illustrious mother, bestow upon me the affection due to a son; for by abandoning an infant, a mother is stained with fault. (57)
Addressed thus by the boy, she meditated upon the god Janārdana and, with palms joined in reverence, said this: "Let that which is well-determined be told to me. (68)
I do not truly understand whose this manifestation of valor is; therefore, O Lord of Gods, speak to me your certain word. (69)
Then Janārdana Kṛṣṇa spoke to his mother Subhadrā: "This son of Dadhīci is born from the field of your husband."
Having thus understood the cause of his birth, Subhadrā, her mind filled with joy, placed the child upon her lap and wept with a voice full of distress.
He said, "O child, you have been born; tell me the cause of your grief. Then he was asked, "How was your life sustained when you were deprived of breast milk? (72)
For it is traditionally taught that the fourfold creation of living beings was fashioned by Brahmā: namely, the viviparous, the oviparous, the soil-born, and the sweat-born.
The species born from the womb—known as male, female, and neuter—and likewise quadrupeds, both domestic and wild animals; || 74 ||
All birds born from eggs, fish, tortoises, and reptiles; those born from sweat, such as bugs, lice, gadflies, and mosquitoes. || 75 ||
Immobile beings are said to be those born from sprouts, such as grasses, shrubs, and creepers; thousands of others are likewise included therein according to their respective categories. (76)
On this earth, egg-born creatures sustain their young by fanning them with wings; all sweat-born creatures do so by means of heat, and those born from sprouts indeed by means of water.
Through the combination of the five elements on earth, there arise beings born from sprouts and those born from a womb, who are unable to live without breast milk. (78)
"O son, how were your life-breaths sustained without him? To his mother, who was thus speaking with eyes clouded by tears, he replied: (79)
"By drinking the resin extracted from the fruit of the *aśvattha* tree, my life was sustained by me; therefore, she figuratively designated him as 'Pippalāda'. (80)
Thus, the name of that great-souled one became eternally renowned in this world; and there, all the sages residing in that place performed [the rites] for him in due order.

The ritual procedures (*saṃskāra*) of Pippalāda were proclaimed by those who had mastered the Vedas; the Vedas, together with their six limbs and sub-limbs, were recovered by him and bestowed in full abundance upon the sages dwelling in that hermitage.
Remaining there once more, he saw the young sons of sages seated upon his father's lap and spoke to his mother, who possessed a pure smile.
"Where is my father? May you be blessed, Subhadrā; tell me clearly so that, standing in solitude, I may play with the children. (84)
When her ascetic mother was thus questioned by him, she began to weep and did not give any answer at all. || 85 ||
Seeing her weeping, that son of a sage became angry and said: "Who is this despicable person because of whom you do not tell me? (86)
When this was said, the son spoke thus: "The father has been slain by the gods; abandon your anger—blessings be upon you—he whom I have described as Dadhīci. (87)
His soul inflamed by the fire of anger, he spoke again to his mother: "Tell me, what wrong has my father done to the gods?"
Subhadra said: "O observer of noble vows, that bull among sages was slain by fools because of his weapons; even though he offered other objects of that same appearance."
Having heard these words, that sage of fierce austerities then created a very powerful Kṛtyā against those gods by whom my father had been slain.
Having raised him up, I shall strike the life-taking weapon upon his head; were it not that I must spare my grandfather, I would have slain him. (91)

I shall crush all others who have gathered with the weapon of the *kṛtyā*; even if the gods, distressed by fear of me, should seek refuge, I will nevertheless strike them down along with him [Indra] as they stand united.
Perceiving the sage to be thus enraged, all those best of gods, afflicted by great fear, sought refuge with Brahmā. (93)
Knowing that they had sought refuge with him, the compassionate Lord Janārdana went there quickly and spoke to the gods.
I have now devised a means for your protection; by that, I shall delude the Kṛtyā who has arrived to kill you. (95)
In the meantime, Pippalāda, recollecting his enmity toward his father, resolved to slay the gods and entered the Himālaya mountain.
Having heard those unpleasant words issuing from his mother’s mouth, Pippalāda departed once more from that place for the Himalayas.
He reached that snowy mountain, which was like a staircase to heaven for men, like the sky become solid ground, and resembling the expanded body of Śeṣa.
He made a vow, remaining there as immovable as a pillar: "I shall slay those who killed my father, even if they flee. (99)
Seated there in the assembly of Śiva’s abode, he became enraged at all those who were arrogant because of their immortality, using the weapon of his *kṛtyā*.
Staying here, I shall accomplish that *kṛtyā*, contemplating it in my heart; either I will master the *kṛtyā*, or I shall go to the abode of Yama.
Becoming free from dualities and fearless, remaining without food day and night, I then rubbed my left thigh with my left hand.
"Therefore, I shall bring forth the Mahākṛtyā," he resolved; and when a year had passed for him, she emerged from his thigh.
Then, afflicted by the heavy burden and accompanied by Vāḍava, that mare emerged from his thigh and gave birth to one of great strength.
The mare, having released from her womb that fetus which was filled with garlands of flames and intensely radiant, placed it before that sage.
Then she went away somewhere and was not perceived by the sage; at that time, a man emerged from her womb like the submarine fire (vaḍavānala). || 106 ||
Seeing him standing before them, resembling the end of an eon for all beings, possessing a brilliance like the fire of time, and appearing like a mass of lightning; || 107 ||
And he too was greatly astonished, wondering, "What is this? Then, by that Vāḍava fire standing before him—
"The seer Pippalāda has been propitiated by you through your power; now I must perform for you that task which has been resolved. (109)

I shall accomplish all of that here, even that which is impossible to achieve; for by him who was born from the churning of my own thigh, I—though now deprived of that thigh—shall fulfill your desire within a year.
Having heard those words of his, the sage, filled with anger, said to all the gods: "Eat yourselves those who have been given by me!"

Perceiving that he was intent on vengeance due to the slaughter of his father—a wrath so exceedingly fierce and terrible—the gods, together with their wives, all assembled and suddenly sought refuge with the Ancient Puruṣa.
Having comforted those gods, he went there joyfully toward that most excellent fire of wrath; and beholding it, which resembled a mass of suns, Viṣṇu spoke these most excellent words: || 113 ||

O Lord of the Gods, I have been sent to your very side by the gods who have become afraid; listen to my words, for they are beneficial, being wholesome for the celestial bards as well as for you. (114)

Your power is known by the gods to be inconceivable, and it is certain that you will destroy those who possess self-control. This being the case, follow the words of the gods: eat each one of them individually every day.
There are thirty million principal gods endowed with great strength; how indeed will you devour them all simultaneously? (116)
Therefore, you must consume them one by one; it is not possible for you alone to perform the act of eating them all at once.
Furthermore, in former times, the Fire-god himself contracted jaundice due to overeating; therefore, excessive consumption is not proper—heed my words.
And so, when they have been devoured simultaneously, you must again devise a means for their consumption every day due to your hunger. (119)
Your promise shall indeed be fruitful; the word spoken by the sage is not false. Even when you have acted thus, everything you desire will come to pass.
"I shall do all that," said Janārdana; "that Vāḍava fire will devour the gods one by one."
Then the gods, having bowed to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods and possessor of immeasurable splendor, said what was appropriate: "A most excellent deed has been performed by you."
Furthermore, today you alone are capable of performing the remedy to pacify this very fault; there is no other protector of the denizens of heaven.
Then Mādhava, wearing yellow garments and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, said to the gods, "I shall remove your fear. (124)
Having heard this, all the gods, their eyes wide with joy, were filled with delight.
Then, seeing those gods, that Vāḍava spoke: "Tell me now, what must be done by me for you? Let that indeed be told. (126)

In the meantime, the one of universal form and great power, seeking to delude that fire by his own intelligence, spoke as the high-souled one: "Consume those waters which were created in the beginning."
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this resolve of Viṣṇu shall be freed from the fear of transgression and shall attain both knowledge and liberation.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Deception of the Vaḍavānala Fire," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The Goddess said: Whatever deeds were performed in the past by the great sage—the son of Dadhīci and subduer of the gods—who was filled with intense fury born from the indignation over his father’s slaughter, all of that has indeed been heard by me through meditative concentration.
Furthermore, whatever significant events occurred repeatedly among the gods, I desire to know all those deeds in their proper sequence out of curiosity. (2)

Īśvara said: When he was thus addressed by all the gods, "In former times you drank the waters upon the earth; for the waters were born first among the immortals, being the first-born before all the gods and asuras. (3)
Thus addressed by that high-souled one, he then said: "Show me those [liquors] where they are located; having drunk all the liquor, I shall first perform the act of devouring the gods."

If you are able to lead me even there, where the masses of water are gathered together, then I am not a speaker of falsehood; otherwise, once my life has departed, I shall be a follower of the sage’s word.
"O lotus-eyed one, when shall I bring you to the Aurva Vāḍava fire? By what vehicle, O Vāḍava, shall I convey you to where the waters are? (6)
Vāḍava said: "I do not venture to go there by means of vehicles such as horses; for my mind is resolved upon nothing other than contact with the hand of the maiden."
Viṣṇu said: "This vehicle of yours is easily obtained; I shall bring that maiden who will be capable of leading you to the abode of the waters with absolute certainty."
Īśvara said: Sarasvatī, tormented by the curse of Surabhī and experiencing the fruit of her previously acquired state, was transformed into a mare by Viṣṇu.

Then the Lord spoke to Gaṅgā, who stood by his side: "O highly fortunate one, carry this fire with speed to the great ocean; O purifier of the world, no one else besides you is capable of bringing it there."
Gaṅgā said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, I have no power to carry the Aurva fire; for this great fire, possessing a fierce form, burns most intensely. (11)
Then, the noble-minded one spoke to the Yamunā, and immediately after her, to the Sindhu and various other rivers, each individually.
Being asked by the best of the gods, they were unable to bring her back. Then Janārdana, the God of gods, spoke to Sarasvatī: "O auspicious one, you yourself go to the western salt ocean."
When this is done, all the gods will be freed from fear; otherwise, they will be consumed by the submarine fire through its own radiance.
