Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, protect the gods from that tumultuous fear; be like a mother, bestowing fearlessness upon the deities.
Thus addressed by that powerful Viṣṇu, she said: "I am not independent; my father has been long away. (16)
I am her constant servant, a maiden firm in my vows; it is heard by the wise that a daughter is never independent, even throughout the three periods of time. (17)
"Without my father's command, I will not go even a single step anywhere; therefore, O Hari, let some other means be devised. (18)
Having thus understood his true nature and approached the Grandfather, Vāsudeva said to him, "Perform this task for the sake of the gods."
Otherwise, it is impossible to lead away the immensely powerful Vāḍava fire, unless you release this maiden, your daughter, who is free from any perceived fault.
Having heard what was spoken by Viṣṇu, the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) then placed his granddaughter, Kumārī, upon his head and spoke to her with affection.

"O Goddess, you who protect all the gods when fear has come upon them, take this Vāḍava fire and cast it into the salt waters. Having heard her father's words, she, whose very nature is the Vedas, replied:
Sarasvatī said: "O dear one, at your word I am setting out without a doubt; this fierce Vāḍava fire will consume my body. (23)
"The terrible Kali age has now arrived upon the surface of the earth; O Lord, people of sinful conduct will touch me. (24)
What could be more painful than this: association with evildoers? (25)
Brahmā said: "If you do not desire the surface of the earth crowded with sinful people, then, remaining in the subterranean realm (Pātāla), carry the fire into the great ocean."
O daughter, whenever you are excessively consumed by fire due to the exhaustion of your labors, then, having split open the earth, become visible before my eyes.
"O large-eyed one, O slender-waisted lady of beautiful smiles, turn your face toward the east; then the holy places shall go to you when you have grown weary. (28)
And all those thirty-three crores, O fair-faced one, shall come at my command and provide you with assistance. (29)
"Go, daughter; you must not feel any grief whatsoever. Travel on a path free from misfortune; let there be no adversaries to oppose you. (30)
Ishvara said: Having been addressed thus by Brahmā at that time, Sarasvatī cast off her fear and, with a joyful heart, prepared to depart. 31.
At the time of her departure, the world was filled with the auspicious sounds of conchs and dundubhi drums, and with the resonant cries of other auspicious instruments.
The goddess wears white garments, is smeared with white sandalwood paste, resembles an autumnal cloud, and is adorned with necklaces of pearls.
With a face like the full moon and eyes as long as lotus petals, she filled the ten directions with her fame, just like that of Mahendra.
"Illuminating everything with her own splendor and causing the entire world to shine, Gaṅgā indeed followed her as she was addressed by her, O lady of excellent complexion. (35)
"O friend, where indeed shall I see you dwelling again? Thus addressed by her, Gaṅgā replied with affectionate words:
O lady of excellent vows, at the very moment you behold the eastern direction, you shall find me there, surrounded by all the gods.
"I shall grant you my vision; cast off your grief, O lady of pure smiles! Having taken leave of Gaṅgā, may there be a meeting with you again. (38)
"Go to your own abode, O blessed one; I am to be remembered by you, O sinless one. Yamunā likewise, as well as the most beautiful Gāyatrī, [shall do so]. (39)
Then all her friends, accompanied by Sāvitrī, were sent away; thereafter, having dismissed them, that goddess became the river Sarasvatī.
Having reached the Himavat mountain, she emerged there from the Plakṣa tree and descended upon the surface of the earth, teeming with fish and tortoises.
Filled with the drum-like roar of crocodiles and joined by swarms of whales and sea-monsters, the Great Goddess laughs in every direction with her masses of foam.
Praised by the twice-born on account of her merit, the goddess, taking up the Vāḍava fire, emerged with the speed of a horse.

Having pierced the surface of the earth with great force, she then entered the depths of the world; whenever she became exhausted or was scorched by the submarine fire (Vāḍava-agni), at those very times the river would manifest herself visibly in the mortal world.
Thereupon the eastern direction becomes scorched by the Vāḍava fire; from there indeed proceed those sacred fords (tīrthas) which have been celebrated by the ancients.

O beautiful lady, the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial [deities] came into her presence; then, consoled by them, that river Sarasvatī reached the depths of Pātāla and went to the abode of the sea-monsters.
Having reached the Khadirāmoda forest and beheld the ocean there, that beautiful celestial woman set out to go toward that fire, O lady of the gods.
Having reflected that her burden was now laid down by the command of the gods, she became joyful and cheerful of mind, and from there she set out facing the south.
At that very time, O Great Goddess, four sages who had mastered the Vedas took refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Furthermore, Hariṇa, Vajra, Nyaṅku, and Kapila, staying there with their minds intent on the study of the Vedas, perform penance.
The Sarasvatī was summoned separately by each of them for the purpose of bathing; suddenly, the Ocean appeared before her face-to-face.
Then she reflected, "How might this turn out well for me? And that virtuous woman, fearing the curse, then became the river Pañcasrotas.
O woman of excellent complexion, she gratified each of those sages one by one; consequently, five names arose for her upon the surface of the earth.
The Hariṇī, Vajriṇī, Nyaṅku, Kapilā, and Sarasvatī—through drinking from and bathing in these, the five-streamed Sarasvatī [bestows her grace] upon men.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife, and that fifth which arises from the combination of these among men—these indeed [are the great sins]. (55)
This river, existing in five ways, together with her five companions, destroys the terrible sin of men who are likewise fivefold.
The Sarasvatī flows in reverse and destroys even the most terrible sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa; indeed, through drinking her water or bathing in her, she removes every single sin of men.
For the sake of removing that [sin] from those whose souls are afflicted by the fault of drinking liquor through negligence, the river Kapilā flows for the twice-born.
Through fasting, recitation, burnt offerings, bathing, and drinking [the water] from twice-born men, one shall destroy sin within seven days with a mind focused on each respective [deity].
Even they themselves become purified by performing the prescribed rites, having reached the Nyaṅku river after committing great sins.
By bathing in, worshipping, and drinking from [the water of] Vajriṇī, one destroys all the extremely terrifying sins of men, including the sin of violating the teacher’s bed.
She is remembered as Hariṇī because she removes the sins born of association; by bathing in this river filled with meritorious water for seven days, [one is purified]. 62.
In this way, O beautiful goddess, the river Sarasvatī, with her five streams, truly destroys all these sins.
Then that goddess again beheld on the path a beautiful mountain situated at the edge of the ocean, standing as if to block the way.
"This best of mountains stands before me like a measuring-stick for the universe; it has positioned itself as an obstacle to me as I proceed on a mission for the gods. (65)
Then Sarasvatī, beholding the great mountain rising higher still, was struck with wonder as her current was blocked by the mountain.
While he was thus reflecting upon that great wonder with his mind, he was awakened by auspicious sounds and restored to mindfulness.
She saw a man moving between two mountain peaks; that mountain spoke to the goddess: "O lady of virtuous vows, there is no path here."
"Go elsewhere, O auspicious one, wherever you desire. When he had spoken thus, that goddess spoke to the man standing on the mountain peak.
"Having arrived by the command of the gods, you must not be obstructed by you, O Mountain. When this was said, the Mountain spoke to that most beautiful goddess.
"O blessed lady, why was I, Parvata, who am devoted to you, not recognized by you? There is no fault in touching you, O sinless one, since you are still a maiden. (71)
Therefore, O Goddess of noble vows, I choose you; become my wife.
Sarasvatī said: "Since my father still lives, I cannot choose a husband for myself; I shall become your wife. Grant me passage now. (73)
Thus addressed, the mountain said to her who was unwilling: "O blessed lady, I shall marry you by force; who now is your protector? (74)
Perceiving with her divine eye that he was overcome by the god of love, she said: "I have no protector; I have come to you alone for refuge. (75)
"O you of great strength, if I must certainly be wedded by you, then do not marry me while I am unwashed, O Lord; grant me leave to perform my bath. (76)
Then the mountain, possessing pride in his own opulence, said to her: "O fortunate one, behold in me my complete majesty, which bestows happiness. (77)
There, the Kinnaras sing enchanting duets, and the beautiful sound of other stringed instruments is heard. (78)
There, palmyra trees, tamāla trees, pippala trees, and likewise jackfruit trees—always laden with flowers and fruit—are seen, most delightful to the mind. (79)
With *kuṭaja*, *kovidāra*, *kadaṃba*, and *kurabaka* trees, all resounding with the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees, the mountain shines on every side. (80)
In some places it shines like the body-unguent of Śiva due to the *kuṭaja* buds; in other places, through the *karṇikāra* flowers, it possesses a luster equal to the garment of Viṣṇu.
In some places, covered by tamāla leaves, the mountain possesses the splendor of Yama; in other places, with its body smeared with minerals, it has the form of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
In some places, this mountain shines like the four-faced Brahmā with a body of yellow orpiment; in other places, it gleams with the form of Viṣṇu through its saptacchada trees.
In some places it resembles Kātyāyanī, being densely covered with priyaṅgu plants; in other places, joined with kesara trees, it shines like fire.
In some places, it shines with *bilva* fruits that are covered in downy fuzz, smooth, and like the breasts of women—difficult for those of little merit to obtain. (85)
In various places, it shines with lions, tigers, deer, elephants, boars, and monkeys, all following one another in mutual pursuit.
As they spoke thus, making the sky seem as if it were pierced by pikes, Śāradā replied to that best of mountains.
"If you would marry me while I am thus weeping all alone, then take this Vāḍava fire in your hand while I perform my ablutions."
When this was said, the lord of serpents seized that discarded [garland]; having remembered [the curse], by its touch he was instantly reduced to ashes.
From that time forward, those stones of his attained softness; they were taken by artisans for the purpose of building houses and temples.
Having burned Kṛtasmara and having taken up the Vāḍava fire once more, the goddess stood near the ocean with her hair standing on end in joy.
Remaining there, that great goddess said to Vaḍavānala: "O Vāḍava, behold the roaring ocean standing before you. (92)
Seeing him roaring and surging forward with his waves, he said to her: "O blessed lady, what is this? The salt ocean is afraid of me."
Laughing, that young woman said: "O Anala, who is not afraid of you? O one of great strength, for you have been ordained as food by the gods. (94)
Having heard those words of hers, the Fire-god was greatly delighted and said: "O blessed lady, I shall grant you a boon; ask of us whatever you desire. (95)
Thus addressed by that Vāḍava fire, the goddess then remembered Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one, who is the self of all causes.
That Lord Janārdana, the supreme lord of the three worlds, was seen by her situated within her own heart as soon as he was remembered by Sarasvatī.
Beholding Acyuta, who was situated within him, with her mind's eye, she said to him: "The submarine fire offers a boon; what shall I request from him? (98)
Then the goddess Sarasvatī was addressed by him who resided within her heart: "O auspicious lady, you should respectfully request a boon—the state of having a needle-like face."
Then he was addressed by the goddess: "O mighty one, if you are the granter of boons to me, then become needle-mouthed and drink the water."
When he had spoken thus, the truth pierced him like the prick of a needle; he drank up the water from his mouth just as one fills a water-clock.
Thus that Vāḍava fire, intent on devouring the gods, having been deceived by Viṣṇu, departed after diligently applying his intelligence.
The man who hears this meritorious account of creation being recited attains the world of Viṣṇu and rejoices there together with him.
Īśvara said: Having obtained that most excellent boon from the Vaḍavānala fire, the high-minded Sarasvatī prepared once more to cast it back into the ocean.
Then, by the command of the gods, she stood before Prabhāsa, desiring to offer the Vāḍava fire to the ocean after having summoned it.
"You are the origin of all the gods; you are always the vital breath of living beings. O Ocean, come and receive the Vāḍava fire by the command of the gods."
When the Lord of Waters had been thus meditated upon by the Goddess, he of great splendor emerged from the water and arrived there.
Seeing him, who was like another divine Viṣṇu, dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, and exceedingly beautiful, the goddess was struck with wonder. || 5 ||
Adorned with various garlands and ornaments, and anointed with colorful garments and unguents, it was surrounded by river-like women who possessed beautiful forms.
Having observed such a state, that goddess Sarasvatī, the daughter of Brahmā, spoke these words to the ocean with a pure smile.
You are the first-born of all beings who arise from existence; you are the life of men who possess birth. Therefore, accomplish the desired task of the gods; accept the fire brought here to you.

In the meantime, he too reflected upon all the tasks with his own intellect, considering what was appropriate here: "By my taking up the fire, this task shall be accomplished for the sake of the gods."
As he was reflecting thus, the proposal for the marriage became pleasing to him, since it was for the sake of the submarine fire and the ocean when they were causing affliction to the gods.
Then, standing before him, he spoke earnestly to that goddess: "O Sarasvatī, bestow this enemy of the gods upon Vāḍava."
Then, with her limbs beautifully adorned, she quickly bowed down to the Cāraṇas standing in the sky before the Grandfather (Brahmā), while Sarasvatī was also present.
Furthermore, that Vāḍava fire, held in her hand, was addressed by her: "Consume the waters," to which he replied, "These [waters] were so commanded by the gods."
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly powerful Vāḍava fire was then delivered by Sarasvatī to the ocean at the command of the gods.
Having surrendered him there, the goddess Sarasvatī became a river and entered the ocean by way of Nāradeśvara.
Having offered the *arghya* in the salt water in the presence of Daityasūdana, he installed Arghyeśvara to the west of Daityasūdana. (16)
Then that great river, consisting of five streams, entered the ocean; by its very nature, that meritorious river became even more meritorious.

Due to contact with the sacred field of Prabhāsa and its confluence with the ocean, even Sāgara, having reached the Vāḍava fire of the Sarasvatī, felt like a pauper who has suddenly acquired wealth and thought, "Where shall I deposit this? (18)
With that very blazing fire held in his hand, Sāgara shone like another Mount Meru with its peak ablaze. || 19 ||
Seeing it in such a state, the hosts of aquatic creatures dwelling there let out a great roar, terrified by the burning heat.
Hearing that terrifying sound, the slayer of demons arrived and said to all the hosts of aquatic creatures, "Do not fear, O you of great strength!"
Since only the first water is to be consumed by him, and not that which contains living beings, you must not fear it, by my command.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, the aquatic creatures became silent.
When all the water-born beings had become silent, Acyuta said to the Lord of Waters: "Cast the Vāḍava fire into the midst of the waters."
Therefore, that submarine fire was cast by Varuṇa into the unfathomable waters; there, possessing great strength, it remains drinking that water.
Shaken by the wind of his exhalations, that water from the ocean runs hither and thither beyond its bounds like a young woman who has cast off all restraint.
Then, O Goddess, as time passed, the water gradually began to dry up; perceiving that those waters were wasting away, the ocean then [acted].
He said this to the lotus-eyed one: "Make these waters inexhaustible; otherwise, O Janārdana, this Vāḍava fire will consume me right here in front of you with the destruction of all the waters. (28)
Having heard those terrifying words of the ocean, he made that water inexhaustible, thereby destroying his own fear.

Having understood all this activity—the binding of this fire-creature (Kṛtyānala) as well as the enemy's stratagem preceded by the water— the gods worshipped Keśava, who moves within them, while leading with water as a lure.
Thus, O Great Goddess, Sarasvatī, the destroyer of all sins, arrived at the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa from the world of Brahmā.
To the south-east of Someśa, in the vicinity of the ocean, the Great Goddess is established, bearing the submarine fire (vaḍavānala).
Having first bathed at Agnitīrtha, a man should worship her according to the prescribed rite; there, he should provide a meal for a married couple and offer them clothing along with a bodice.
Having given [these], one should then worship Mahādeva Kapardin; thus, O Goddess, occurred this event in former times during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.
O Great Goddess, when this Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived once again, the high-souled Vāḍava born of the lineage of Dadhīci was reborn as the great twice-born Aurva in the Bhārgava clan. (35)
This highly resplendent one was condensed by Sarasvatī, the mother of the gods; he shall remain within the womb of the waters for the duration of a manvantara.
Thus, O Goddess, I have narrated to you the origin of Sarasvatī; when heard, it removes the sins of men, bestows fame, and increases merit. (37)
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, tell me, O Lord, of the birth of that Aurva who was mentioned by you as being in the lineage of Bhṛgu during this Vaivasvata Manvantara.
Īśvara said: Those Brāhmaṇas who were slain by Kṣatriyas for the sake of wealth have all been brought to destruction, along with their sons and even those still in the womb. || 2 ||
While everyone else was dying, one woman remained; she protected the fetus by placing it within the region of her thighs.
And by those lowest of Kṣatriyas, O beautiful lady, the fetuses of all other women as well were caused to be aborted for the sake of wealth.
Then, after some time, having burst through the land of the Kurus, he emerged with great radiance, his head held high and his flaming mouth most terrifying.
Bearing that enmity in his heart, he produced through his ascetic power the fierce Aurva fire that consumes the waters, and thereby scorched the surface of the earth.
O woman of excellent complexion, Indra flooded him with torrents of rain; when he was unable to carry him away, he then stood there with his speech restrained.
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, went to Brahmā for refuge; terrified by fear, they all stood with their palms joined in reverence.

The gods said: "O Blessed One, someone of great luster was born in the lineage of Bhṛgu; in the form of fire, he has consumed the entire surface of the earth. O best of beings, we previously made an effort to destroy him, but he increases through water, and from that, fear has come upon us."
O Lord, when the surface of the earth has perished, rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others will be cut off; consequently, our own destruction will surely follow.
Therefore, O Lord, exert yourself out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds.
Then Brahmā, together with the gods and the great seers of the Bhṛgu lineage, arrived and said to Aurva: "For what purpose are you burning the earth?"
O best of the twice-born, let a cessation be made immediately for my sake.
Aurva said: "O best of beings, it is by your word that I have desisted; O Lord, this fire was released by me only at your command. (15)
Let policy be so ordained that it may lead us to the very end of the ocean.

Then the Lotus-born one, having summoned his own daughter, the goddess, said: "O daughter, go, taking the fire to the great ocean. My word must not be made otherwise; go quickly, O lady of great splendor! (17)
Sarasvatī said: "O Lord, here I am, setting out at your command without doubt. When she had spoken thus, Brahmā proclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! to her who was virtuous. (18)
Then, having cast the consecrated fire into a golden pitcher, Brahmā, the Grandfather himself, gave it to Sarasvatī; and after bestowing various blessings, he spoke this again and again: || 19 ||
"Go, daughter; you must not feel any grief whatsoever. Travel your path safely; let there be no adversaries on your way. (20)
Īśvara said: Thus addressed then by Brahmā, Sarasvatī departed from the hermitage of Pippalāda and reached the Himavat mountain.
Then that goddess emerged from beneath the foot of the tree, having entered the tip of the cottage-like hollow of that tree for the sake of the twice-born who had entered therein. 22.
The resonant sounds of the Vedas are heard there by those whose hearts are deeply impassioned; there dwells the god Viṣṇu, the preeminent deity and the teacher of the gods. (23)
From that place, the goddess went facing westward; by means of her power of invisibility, she reached Kedāra situated in the midst of the snows.
Having flooded that mountain peak, Sarasvatī stood before Kedāra; she was being scorched by that fire held in his hand.
Splitting the earth, she entered beneath it with the gait of an elephant; by way of that subterranean path, she proceeded facing the west.
Having transcended the land of evil and pierced through the earth, she went forth; there a well came into being, known by the name Gandharva. (27)
From that well, that great river became visible once again; she was Mati, Smṛti, Prajñā, Medhā, Buddhi, and Girādhārā. (28)
Then these six female attendants of Sarasvatī set out; from that very source, she began to flow once again, facing toward the west.
She arrived at Bhūtīśvara, where the great sage Siddha resided; she reached that beautiful place situated near Bhūtīśvara. || 30 ||
She went to the famous region of Śrīkaṇṭha, situated in the southern direction, characterized by ten million Rudras and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
From that most meritorious region of Śrīkaṇṭha, that wise Sarasvatī reached Kurukṣetra together with the Fire-god.
Again, from that Kurukṣetra, she emerged near the city of Virāṭa; having been hidden, that beautiful river rose up once more at the mountain Gopāyana.
Where those sons of Pāṇḍu were protected by Keśava while performing their own duties, they were not observed by anyone.
The goddess who destroys great sins resides in that pool; furthermore, due to her protection, she reached this most beautiful sacred field.
Having entered a grove of date palms there, she was known by the name Nandā; then, from that grove called Kharjūra, Sarasvatī [emerged] once more.
Having reached the foot of Meru, she arrived at the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍa, where the Mārkaṇḍaka Tīrtha is situated at the base of Meru.
Sarasvatī, moreover, departed from that Arbuda forest and went to the beautiful Vaṭavana from the auspicious hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya.

From that holy banyan grove, where Vasiṣṭha had formerly performed his austerities, she went to the Udumbara forest; and right there at the foot of Mount Meru is the place where Taṇḍi performed penance.
From that forest of Udumbara trees, the goddess Sarasvatī, the great river, once again reached another peak by means of her disappearance.
The Merupāda mountain is indeed very great and frequented by gods and siddhas; having the appearance of a heap of crushed collyrium, it is known as Golāṅgūla.
From that delightful place, that slender-waisted woman emerged; issuing from the bamboo stalk, she proceeded toward the south.
There, the well named after her is situated; from that time forth, that goddess has remained manifest with great splendor.
Having abandoned her power of invisibility out of compassion for living beings, there are millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) upon her delightful banks.
Among all those sacred fords (tīrthas), Sarasvatī is the cause of dharma; on this path of Rudra’s incarnation, she is remembered as the foremost and first.
There is the highly radiant Kākatīrtha, rich with the name of the Taratara waves; and there is yet another holy site there, known as Dhāreśvara Tīrtha.

Furthermore, beyond Dhāreśvara is that which is known as Gaṅgodbheda; likewise, there is Sārasvata where the waters of the Sarasvatī and the Gaṅgā are situated as one. Beyond that is another supreme holy site, and after that is Puṇḍarīka.
The Mātṛtīrtha is supremely meritorious and the supreme remover of all afflictions; it is situated not far from that very Mātṛtīrtha.
There is a sacred ford named Anaraka, which removes the fear of the agony of hell; beyond that Anaraka, another sacred ford is situated.
Renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Saṅgameśvara, there is another holy site (tīrtha) following that, called Koṭīśvara.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, that is remembered as Śambhukuṇḍeśvara; and at that sacred site on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Siddheśvara is remembered.
Flowing once more from that Siddheśvara, facing westward to reach the western ocean, she wept while remembering her friend.
Standing there facing the east, the goddess said: "Alas, O Gaṅgā! Without you, where shall I, unfortunate and friendless, go all alone? (53)
Then, perceiving her weeping and emaciated by grief, Gaṅgā quickly descended from heaven accompanied by ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, having abandoned her sorrow, the Prācī Sarasvatī, endowed with all divine qualities, remained there in that manner. || 55 ||
There, the sacred ford named Siddhavaṭa is remembered as belonging to the Grandfather (Brahmā); situated in front of Vaṭeśvara, it causes the destruction of all sins.
That place where Rudra arrives and remains established during the three periods of the day is called Mahālaya, the abode of that Great-Souled One.
This supreme ancient pilgrimage site called Piṇḍatāraka, situated on Mount Kumbhakukṣi, bestows success in rites performed for the ancestors.
Situated directly in front of the deity Prācīneśvara, where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows—what more could one seek beyond that? (59)
When the Bhārata war had concluded, at that sacred site, the wearer of the diadem (Arjuna), impelled by Viṣṇu himself, formerly performed a penance.
Because he was liberated from that previously accumulated sin by means of it, that place thereafter became renowned as Naratīrtha, which removes the fear of evil.
O beloved, another sacred ford besides Naratīrtha is known as Puṇḍarīka; it is there that Hari, having arrived with Arjuna, performed his ablutions.
Beyond Prācīneśa is the great Vālakhilyeśvara Tīrtha; from that great Tīrtha, there is another Tīrtha of great grace.
There was another highly auspicious sacred ford named Gaṅgāsamāgama; having seen the Goddess there once again with a dejected face and a distressed mind, [he approached her].

Brahmā created for her a female companion, Kapilā, who had large eyes; Hari likewise quickly gave him Hariṇī, and the king of the gods, Indra, gave Vajriṇī; and Hara gave Nyaṅku to Sarasvatī for the sake of diversion.
Then, at the command of the God, that goddess Sarasvatī, the destroyer of sins, being greatly delighted, began to flow eastward from that place.

Īśvara said: Then, having taken her stand in the southern direction and facing westward, the great goddess Sarasvatī, who bears the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), [established herself]. On the northern bank of that [river] is the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Ekadvāra.
Because the army attained heaven through that single gate by virtue of that boon, there is another sacred site (tīrtha) beyond that, where Guheśvara resides.
Where the god Maheśvara was formerly established by Guha, not far from Guheśvara, there is the place remembered as Vaṭeśvara.
On the bank of the Sarasvatī is the divine [tirtha] formerly propitiated by Vyāsa, where the river Āmarddakī attains oneness with the Sarasvatī.
He reached that great tirtha which bestows fruit upon all embodied beings—that confluence of the Āmardakī; no one lacking merit knows it. There, the linga named Saṃgameśvara is established.
Thus it became renowned on earth as Muṇḍīśvara; likewise, Mahodaya is situated near Muṇḍīśvara on the Sarasvatī river.
There is a holy site (tīrtha) situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī which faces the east by name; indeed, it is there that the Lord is established under the name Māṇḍavyeśvara.
Furthermore, there is another great sacred site known as Pīlukarṇika, situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī and frequented by sages.
Therefore, another sacred ford on the Sarasvatī is remembered as Dvāravatī; it is the most excellent of all holy sites, O Goddess, where Hari is ever present. (75)
Then there is the holy ford named Govatsa situated near it, where the Lord of Ambikā descended in the form of a calf.
The treasure-house of splendors stands there in the form of a self-manifested *liṅga*; to the southwest of Govatsa, an iron pillar is seen.
Rudra himself is stationed there in the form of a self-manifested liṅga; the fruit that is obtained through twenty-one recitations with devotion is the same as that of the piṇḍa offering.
Whatever merit is obtained by men there at the Gaṅgā by means of a single Śrāddha, that same merit is obtained from that great Tīrtha [at Bālāka] as if by play. 79.
Accompanied by her friends, she played there according to her desire, both in the regular and reverse order, moving from right to left and from left to right.
Having reached Rulla, the beautiful goddess was born again; there the city named Rulla was created by Lord Śambhu. (81)
Together with the gods, Pārvatī, and those who employed water-dripping machines, Śambhu sported there for one thousand years.
There, on the Sarasvatī, is the highly auspicious pool named Rulla; there Mahādeva himself resides, known by the name Ānandeśvara.
Situated there to the west of the abode of Śambhu, that nail is proclaimed to be on the southern foot of Meru. (84)
Those men who behold it with right vision, even if they are free from sin, will certainly obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 85 ||
Beyond that is the great hermitage of the sage Kūṣmāṇḍa; there is indeed the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Kūṣmāṇḍeśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds.
The goddess Kollādevī resides there, removing the fear of all sins; that great river reached Kollā by means of her power of invisibility.
Then, having vanished from there as well, she reached the delightful peak known as Madana, a sacred field frequented by the Siddhas.
Then, having vanished from there as well, she reached again the Himalaya mountain named Khādirāmodana, which was radiant with flowers of all seasons.
Having ascended there and looked out, he then beheld the exceedingly beautiful western ocean, situated in the western quarter, rising high like a mass of clouds.
And beholding him there in such a state, she of great splendor, out of joy becoming like a lioness, prepared herself for the sake of the gods' mission.
The Hariṇī, Vajriṇī, Nyaṅku, Kapilā, and Sarasvatī—these five streams are situated there; thus was the Sarasvatī described by the Sage.

O fair-faced one, that place where [the goddess] resides, dispelling the fatigue of sages, is called a *tattatpādaka*—a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for men seeking a ford—and it is the purifier of all sins. (93)
O beautiful goddess, having reached the Khādirāmoḍa forest and beheld the ocean situated there, she set out to go toward that fire, taking it with her.
Having burnt Kṛtasmara and having taken back the Vāḍava fire, the goddess stood near the ocean with her hair standing on end in joy.
Then that goddess entered the fathomless salt waters; taking the Vāḍava fire with her, she cast it into the midst of the water.
Then, seeing that difficult feat of hers, the Fire-god himself was again pleased and spoke these words: || 97 ||
"I am well-pleased with you, O blessed one; choose a boon, O lady of virtuous vows. Being gratified, I shall grant it to you, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (98)
Īśvara said: Taking the bracelet from his hand, he spoke these words: "O Agni, this bracelet of mine must always be worn by you upon your mouth. (99)
"By this means, you may draw up as much water as you can; however, you must not dry up this ocean, the lord of rivers. (100)

Having said, "So be it," she entered the treasure-house of the waters. Thus, O Great Goddess, this Sarasvatī at Prabhāsa, having taken up the Vāḍava fire, arrived for the satisfaction of the wise. (101)
That beautiful goddess rested at Kurukṣetra and Bhadrāvarta; she is Puṣkarā at Puṣkara, Śrīkalā, and the Mahānadī at Prabhāsa.
Known as Devamātā, she was established there in the salt ocean, O Goddess, at the beginning of this Manvantara, long ago in the Tretā Yuga.
Such was the event that occurred between Sarasvatī and the Vāḍava fire; when this Manvantara has passed, there shall be another Vāḍava fire.
She shall indeed become known by the name Jvālāmukhī from the wrath of Rudra; likewise, the name of Sarasvatī shall attain renown as Brāhmī.
At present, she is known in the world by the name Sarasvatī; however, her past names were Kamaṇḍalubhavā and, truly, Ratnākarā was her other former name as the ocean.
In this Manvantara, O Goddess, it is celebrated as Sāgara; however, O Goddess, its future name shall be proclaimed as Kṣāroda.
Whoever knows this obtains the fruit of the sacred ford; for at Prabhāsa, the Sarasvatī has become a ladder to heaven. 108.
This great river, the divine Prācī Sarasvatī, cannot be reached by men who lack merit; she is difficult to find everywhere, and especially so at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and Puṣkara. (109)
Such is the power of that goddess who sustains the submarine fire; the goddess Sarasvatī remains stationed near Agnitīrtha.
He who worships her first attains the fruit of the sacred ford; for that holy site is the ocean itself, which destroys sin and increases merit.

Merely by seeing him, one obtains the fruit of a great sacrifice; he is like one who has maintained the sacred fires, a tawny cow, a performer of long sacrificial sessions, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean. 112.

These [deities] purify merely by being seen; therefore, one who is purified in mind should indeed behold them. Having bathed at the Agni-tīrtha, a man should then cast a bhāra-weight of guggulu resin into the fire; he is glorified in the world of Agni.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the great glory of Agnitīrtha, as well as the majesty of the Sarasvatī, which destroys all sins. (114)
Having bathed at Agnitīrtha according to the prescribed rites, one should then cast a golden bracelet there, O Great Goddess, in accordance with one's wealth.
Then, having worshipped Sarasvatī, one should worship Kapardin.
Then [he visited] the one named Kedāra, after that Bhīmeśvara, and the one named Bhairaveśvara, after that Caṇḍīśvara. (117)
Then a person should worship the god Someśvara according to the prescribed rite, having likewise worshipped the lords of the nine planets and the eleven Rudras.
Then one should worship the god Brahmā in the form of a child; thus is described the Raudrī festival, which destroys all sins.
That best of men who knows her entire majesty, while dwelling in the midst of the sacred field, enjoys the fruit of the holy ford.
Having done this, one should then go to the great goddess Sarasvatī.

Whence can there be virtues equal to those of Sarasvatī? Whence can there be delight equal to that of dwelling by Sarasvatī? Having reached Sarasvatī and gone to heaven, men will remember the river Sarasvatī once again. (122)

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Agnitīrtha at the Confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Ocean," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
The Goddess said: "That which has been stated by you—that the Prācī [river] is difficult to find everywhere, and especially so at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Puṣkara—[is true]. (1)

O Maheśāna, O Lord, if I am dear to you, tell me how this sin-destroying [river] came to be established after reaching Prabhāsa, and describe her entire majesty which annihilates the sins of those from the East.
Īśvara said: "Well spoken by you, O blessed lady; the Prācī is difficult to find everywhere. It is more excellent at Kurukṣetra and Puṣkara than it is at Prābhāsika."
At Prabhāsa, however, O Goddess of the gods, no one lacking merit knows the Great Goddess Prācī, the destroyer of sins, who is capable of uprooting all karma.
Those men who drink from the meritorious and divine Sarasvatī of the East are not to be known as mere mortals; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O lady of excellent countenance.
Blessed are those sages, they are meritorious, and they are true ascetics, who always drink the waters of the Sarasvatī day after day.
Those who drink from the three rivers—the Candrabhāgā, the Gaṅgā, and likewise the divine Sarasvatī—are gods, not men.
Whether having eaten or not having eaten, whether by day or by night—there is no restriction of time where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows.
Even those deer who constantly drink from the eastern Sarasvatī shall go to heaven, just like the best of the twice-born through sacrifices.
For the sake of fulfilling all desires of men, that field is supreme; there the goddess Prācī Sarasvatī resides, equal to the Cintāmaṇi jewel.
Just as cows that yield all desires bestow the fruits of every wish, so too is the goddess Sarasvatī the eastern quarter for both heaven and liberation. 11.
Eighty-eight thousand sages of sublimated vital energy reside there; what is considered more meritorious than renunciation (saṃnyāsa) than that? (12)
Where Maṅkaṇaka, self-controlled, attained perfection in the east; where, O fair-faced one, the vow for the expiation of Brahmin-slaughter was performed by me.

At the highly meritorious Vṛṣatīrtha, situated on the eastern bank, after the Bhārata war had concluded, the diadem-wearing Arjuna—his soul impelled by Viṣṇu—formerly performed a penance at that sacred site.
Among all sacred fords in the three worlds, that ford is remembered as the most excellent; it destroys the sins of living beings, generates merit, and bestows holy fame.

Sūta said: When this had been spoken, that goddess said to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world: "O Lord, how did Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, obtain expiation? How was the sin arising from the destruction of his kinsmen brought to an end?"
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Universe, Nīlalohita, spoke again regarding the cause for the atonement as it truly stood.
Īśvara said: Listen attentively, O blessed lady, to this story that destroys all sins; by hearing it with devotion, a human being becomes pure in soul. (18)
O Goddess, he who has been described as the one wearing a crown and having white horses, having conquered all the Kauravas and slaughtered their horses and elephants, (will depart). || 19 ||
Afterwards, having slain Suyodhana through Bhīma, that Nara, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, departed from the battlefield for his home.
Having seen the son of Dharma, he stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing down; and he, perceiving that both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were approaching, [acted accordingly].
King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to the doorkeepers stationed at the gate: "These two who are approaching must be stopped by you as they stand at the entrance."
"Nara and Nārāyaṇa are cruel and smeared with the mire of sin"—when they were addressed thus, the two then arrived at the gate.
"The king does not wish to see you two, who have acted with such misconduct. Standing there, the man himself questioned the doorkeeper once more. (24)
"For what reason does the king not look upon us two, who remain under his command? Then the king, bowing down, spoke to the gatekeeper standing before him.

Because he killed Nara, who was accompanied by Nārāyaṇa and was fearless of hell, along with his kinsmen and Duryodhana, and because he slew kings who were like fathers to him, he has indeed become a vessel for sin.
When this had been said by him, he then looked at the face of Hari; and he spoke these truthful words: "That which was spoken by the king is indeed so. (27)
When this was said, the man spoke again to Janārdana: "O Kṛṣṇa, tell us how we may be purified from sin. (28)
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me clearly how my purification may be achieved through bathing at sacred fords (tīrthas), and which of those, such as the Gaṅgā and others, is the destroyer of this sin.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O son of Kuntī, do not go to Gayā, nor to the Gaṅgā, nor to Puṣkara; go instead, O best of the Kurus, to where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows. (30)
Those who have killed a Brahmin, those who drink liquor, and whatever others are evildoers—they are liberated by bathing there where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows.
Addressed by Nārāyaṇa, that man, acting swiftly upon his word, arrived together with him at the supreme eastern holy site (tīrtha).
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, with his self restrained at the three times of day, he is thereby liberated from that previously accumulated sin.
Having learned that he was pure, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, quickly arrived together with his brothers to see that bull among men.
Then, seeing him standing before him bowed down, the son of Dharma, with a joyful heart, embraced him and inquired after his well-being.
Then, surrounded by his brothers Bhīma and the others, as well as by hosts of elders, he was embraced by those who were delighted, like a man endowed with a multitude of virtues.
For this is that great sacred ford (tīrtha), known as Prācīna; by the mere act of bathing, it purifies mortals and others alike.
Even one who has killed a Brahmin, having fasted for three nights and bathed in this sacred ford, is liberated from that sin and rejoices in heaven like Rudra.
O Goddess, I dwell eternally in Prācīna together with you; however, O beautiful lady, I reside there especially in the great sacred field of Prabhāsa.
O lady of excellent hips, he who casts off his body on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī at Prācīna shall not return here again.
Having bathed there, he will obtain the full fruit of a horse sacrifice; let him emaciate his own body through restraints and fasts.
There were ascetics who subsisted on water, those who fed on air, and those who fed on leaves; some always remained on the bare ground, and others observed various distinct vows.
Thus, for those who dwelt in Maṅkya’s hermitage when death arrived, they were not humans but gods; I tell you this as the truth. (43)
But whoever should give even a mere trifle of gold with faith to an eminent brahmin at this sacred ford shall obtain a fruit equal to Mount Meru.
Furthermore, those men who perform a śrāddha at this sacred ford shall certainly go to heaven, accompanied by twenty-one generations of their lineage.
Satisfied by a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) at this holy ford beloved by the ancestors, they shall go to the world of Brahmā, just like those who perform the śrāddha at Gayā.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, bathing is always prescribed. Whoever offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) there, even with oil-cakes or inguda-water, provides inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors; he goes to the world of the ancestors. || 47 ||
Furthermore, they provide food and proceed upon the path to liberation.
Whoever gives delightful curd to a Brāhmaṇa there, having reached the world of Agni, enjoys most splendid pleasures. (49)
Even he who, out of devotion, gives a woolen shawl to an excellent brahmin, attains supreme perfection, which is very difficult for other mortals to obtain. (50)
And those men who enter the water here for the destruction of their impurities, one should declare that they will easily obtain a fruit equal to the gift of a cow.
Any man who performs a ritual bath there with true devotion, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 52 ||
Through libations and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), even those ancestors residing in the hells go to heaven, for they are truly delivered by a virtuous son.
Having reached the eastern Sarasvatī, he goes to the Himālaya pilgrimage site; it is as if he were casting away what is in his hand and attempting to lick it with his elbow.
Whatever desire one contemplates while giving up one's life-breaths at that place, one attains all of it through the power of the greatness of the sacred site (tīrtha). || 55 ||
O Goddess, something else was sung by Gāṅgeya to Yudhiṣṭhira in the past: "Indeed, O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is the truth that we were born in the Gaṅgā."
Of whatever rivers there are in the world, the Sarasvatī is the most meritorious among them.

Sarasvatī is the most meritorious among all rivers; Sarasvatī always brings happiness to the world. Having reached Sarasvatī, even men who are deeply afflicted with suffering never grieve, neither in this world nor in the next. (58)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Prācīsarasvatī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 36 ||
The Goddess said: O Lord, for what purpose is the bracelet cast into the salt waters? You ought to explain its merit properly, as was previously mentioned. || 1 ||
What are the mantras and what is the procedure for that which yields great fruit at what time? O Blessed One, what was that ancient account concerning the bracelet?
Īśvara said: In ancient times, there was a protector of the earth known as Bṛhadratha; he had a virtuous and beloved wife named Indumatī. (3)
Neither among the goddesses, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor the Kinnaras, O Great Goddess, is there one of such form as that slender-waisted woman.
Endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities, she was always devoted to her husband; possessed of all the virtues of women, she was indeed like the virtuous Arundhatī.
Proud with the intoxication of her great good fortune, the king did not take pleasure even for a moment without her.
Once, while she was seated upon half the throne of that royal sage, a great ascetic named Kaṇva—possessed of immense luster and a master of the Vedas—approached the lord of kings.
Then, seeing him arrived, the king rose up suddenly, performed worship according to the rules, and offered him the most excellent *arghya*.
Then, perceiving that the bull among sages was seated comfortably and rested, the king inquired after his welfare, and the sage approved of everything.
Then that sage delivered a discourse on the Dharma in the presence of the king.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, that virtuous wife of the king spoke these nectar-like words with her palms joined in reverence: || 11 ||
Indumatī said: "O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, you know everything—past and future. I ask you out of curiosity; therefore, you should forgive me. (12)
Proclaim to me all the karma that produced this other body, by which I have obtained such good fortune as to have a husband who resembles the son of a god.
"Is this good fortune, devotion to her husband, and conduct renowned throughout the three worlds—the power of this vow, or perhaps of the fast? (14)
Or rather, O best of sages, it is due to my supreme merit from giving that the mighty-armed king is always under my control and follows my word. (15)
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of hers and having meditated for a very long time, the sage Kaṇva, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, spoke these words with a smile. (17)
Kaṇva said: Listen, O Queen, I shall tell you of what arose in another body; neither anger nor shame should be felt by you, O slender-waisted one. (18)
In another body, you were indeed an Ābhīrī woman with five husbands; being destitute in the region of Saurāṣṭra, you went to the god Someśvara.
Then, having entered the salt-water ocean to bathe, she was struck by a succession of waves and fell into a state of distress.
The golden bracelet that fell from your hand was lost in the waters of the ocean, and now remorse has taken hold of you.
Then, after a long time, you passed away and were subsequently born, O beautiful one, in the house of the lord of Daśārṇa.
O auspicious one, you were wedded by Bṛhadratha through the power of a bracelet; previously, no vow, austerity, or gift had been performed by you.
"All this that you asked me has been told to you. Having heard those words, the large-eyed goddess then remained silent with her face cast down in shame, having heard such speech.
Having thus informed the king’s wife, O lady of beautiful countenance, that sage took leave of the lord of the earth and departed for his own abode.
Having understood the fruit of the bracelet through the power of that sage, he went to the god Someśvara and bathed in the salt waters.
O lady of great luster, she cast a bracelet there every year; consequently, O beautiful woman, she attained divinity through its power.
Īśvara said: This very great power of the Kaṅkaṇa has been proclaimed, O Goddess; it bestows all desires and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaṅkaṇa," within the "Majesty of Someśvara" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 37 ||
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, regarding that which was spoken by you—that one should first behold Kapardin—you ought to explain this doubt to me exactly as it is. (1)
O Lord of Gods, O Śambhu, that servant of yours is indeed of great splendor; it is the eternal law that a servant stands immediately after his master.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how he is indeed most worthy of worship; Kapardin, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), is the primordial one among all the gods. || 3 ||
O Great Goddess, that Sadāśiva who is beyond the grasp of the senses, established in the field of Prabhāsa, is Someśvara in the form of a Liṅga.
To his left stood Viṣṇu, who is remembered as Varāha; on his right side stood Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, having assumed the form of Kapardin due to the cause of Sāvitrī’s anger.
In the Kṛta age he is named Heraṃba, in Tretā he is Vighnamardana, in Dvāpara he is Laṃbodara, and in the Kali age he is remembered as Kapardin.
Thus, in age after age, his incarnations arise again and again, each distinct according to the requirements of the task at hand.
O Goddess, when the twenty-eighth cycle of four ages had arrived there, listen to me regarding how Kapardin was born as the causal self (kāraṇātman).
Formerly, at the junction of the Dvāpara age and when the Kali age had arrived, women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, and others who were evildoers, went swiftly to heaven upon beholding the Lord Someśvara.
Neither sacrifice, nor austerity, nor charity, nor study of the Vedas, nor religious vows—O Goddess, even by performing these, all men go to the abode of Śiva. (10)
O Goddess of the Suras, having recognized that power arising from Someśvara, all ritual acts such as the Agniṣṭoma and others became obsolete.
Then, both children and the elderly, sages who have mastered the Vedas, Śūdras, and even women—upon seeing him, they attain the supreme goal.
At that time, when sacrifices and festivals had perished and the surface of the earth was empty, heaven was completely filled with those who stood with their arms raised on high.
Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, filled with distress at being humiliated by humans, went to Śaṅkara for refuge. || 14 ||
With palms joined in reverence, all the foremost of the gods, headed by Indra, said: "O Śaṅkara, by your grace, this heaven has been pervaded by humans. (15)
"O Lord, please assign some place for us to dwell. O God, they wander everywhere at will, conversing with one another, each saying, 'I am the best! Indeed, I am the best! (16)
The King of Dharma, being of virtuous soul, beholds for himself the good and evil deeds they have written down, and remains silent, greatly amazed.

O Lord, seeing those for whom the most dreadful Kumbhīpāka had been prepared, as well as Raurava and Śālmali, standing established in heaven, he was overcome with supreme embarrassment and abandoned his office.
The Blessed Lord said: "O gods, everything has indeed been promised by me, who am pleased by your devotion; my presence shall abide in this sacred field for the sake of Soma."
What has been uttered by oneself cannot be made otherwise; thus indeed shall those go to heaven who behold me there.
Then, agitated by fear upon seeing Pārvatī on all sides, all the gods spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Become our refuge."
Having spoken thus, O best of beings, the gods praised him with this hymn, falling upon their knees on the earth and placing their joined palms upon their heads.

The gods said: Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods; salutations to you, O Sustainer of the universe. Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you, O one of golden luster. (23)
Salutations to you, the destroyer and the creator; salutations to you, O beloved of Śaṅkara! Salutations to you, O Kālarātri; salutations to you, O daughter of the mountain.
O Noble One, O Blessed One, O Large-eyed One, salutations to you, O Beauty of the World! You are Rati, you are Dhṛti, you are Śrī, you are Svāhā, and you are the virtuous Sudhā.
You are Durgā, you are Manī, you are Medhā; you are everything, you are Vasundharā. By you all this triple world, with its moving and non-moving beings, is pervaded.
In rivers, on mountain peaks, in oceans and caves, in forests, at sacred shrines, in battles, and in hermitages—27.
We see that entire triple world where you, O Goddess, are not present; knowing this, O large-eyed one, protect us from this great fear! 28.
Īśvara said: Having been addressed thus by the gods led by Indra, you then, out of compassion, crushed your own body.
Then, as you were massaging [yourself], a great impurity was produced; from that, there was born a charming being with four arms and the face of a lordly elephant.
Then she, whose nature is compassion, said to all the gods: "This very one has been created by me out of a desire for your welfare."
He shall provide all obstacles for living beings. || 32 ||
Possessed by great delusion and with their intellects impaired by lust, those men who do not behold Somanātha shall go to hell.
Having heard these words of his, all those gods, with delighted minds, returned to their own abodes, having abandoned the fear born of humans.
Then Bhavānanda, filled with humility, spoke to you, O Goddess: "What shall I do, O large-eyed one? Let a command be given to me. (35)
The Blessed Goddess said: "Go to the Prābhāsika field where Hara is ever-present; protect it so that it does not come within the range of human sight. (36)
The Linga of the God of gods was installed by Śaśin himself; he who, commanded by you, constantly creates obstacles for men [is that very one].
Seeing a person setting out toward the Lord Somanātha, Kapardin, who is honored by the world, creates a great obstacle for him.
Arising from children, wife, house, fields, wealth, and grain, he generates great delusion; consequently, he does not perceive Hara.
Alternatively, one should abandon diseases such as goiters and swellings; for a person seized by these, through delusion, does not perceive Hara.
Therefore, with every effort and with the desire to attain Someśvara, he should be worshipped constantly and remembered day and night. (41)
O Goddess of the Gods, having propitiated the Lord of the Gaṇas, the protector of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, with this hymn that indeed puts an end to all obstacles; || 42 ||
O Great Goddess, I shall now fully proclaim that hymn which destroys obstacles; listen attentively, O Kapardinī. (43)
Oṃ, salutations to the King of Obstacles; salutations be to you, O Kapardin! Salutations to the one with fierce, great tusks, who dwells in the sacred field of Prabhāsa. 44.
Having paid homage to Kapardin for the sake of ensuring a journey free from obstacles, I shall praise the auspicious Vighnarāja, who is dear to both Siddhi and Buddhi.
To Mahāgaṇapati, the heroic and unconquered increaser of victory; to the one-tusked, the two-tusked, and the four-tusked one with four arms.

He has three eyes, holds a trident in his hand, has red eyes, and bestows boons; he is invincible, has spike-like ears, is fierce, and is the leader of the staff-bearers; he carries an iron staff, has fire for his mouth, and is fond of oblations.
I bow to that leader of the Gaṇas, the son of Umā, who is formidable and fierce, and who creates obstacles for all the undertakings of men when he is not worshipped. 48.
I bow to that Vināyaka, who is intoxicated with passion, who has three eyes, whose splendor is equal to the face of an elephant, who is firm, immovable, and peaceful. 49.
In former times, with your previous form, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, you assumed the form of an elephant and terrified all the Dānavas. || 50 ||
The leadership over both the sages and the deities has been revealed. || 51 ||
Thus praised by the gods at the outset, you are worshipped, O Son of Bhava; having propitiated you, the Lord of the Gaṇas, whose splendor is equal to that of the face of the elephant-faced one.
Steadfast, immovable, and tranquil, he was surrounded by the glory of victory; for the sake of the ritual, [he was honored] with red flowers and water mixed with red sandalwood.
Having dressed in red garments, he who worships on the fourth lunar day—whether once or twice a day—being self-restrained and moderate in diet; || 54 ||
The Lord of all obstacles can bring under his control a king, a prince, a royal minister, or even the entire kingdom along with its realm.
Whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, one obtains that same fruit by remembering the god Vināyaka.
For him there shall be no adversity, nor shall he suffer defeat; no obstacle shall arise for him, and people shall remember their past births.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain a boon within six months; within a year, he attains perfection—of this there is no doubt. (58)

Through his grace, the Lord Someśvara becomes visible to him; since his belly is described as having the form of matted hair (kaparda), therefore know that the name of this great-souled one is Kapardin.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kapardin Vināyaka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Then, having worshipped the God of gods, Kapardin, according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter proceed, O Great Goddess, to the Liṅga situated at Kedāra.
O Great Goddess, situated in the southern portion of that very place near Bhīmeśvara, there is a self-manifested Kalpa-liṅga which is dear to me.
O Goddess, this Vṛddhiliṅga of great luster has been fully worshipped by me; whoever remains there without food and keeps a single vigil, [attains the fruit]. || 3 ||
Especially on the fourteenth day, his eternal worlds are attained; in a former age, the name of that god was Rudreśvara.
Furthermore, when the Tiṣya [age] arrived, Kedāra, distressed by the fear of contact with barbarians, attained dissolution into this Liṅga near the ocean.
Because of that, he became known by the name Kedāra upon the surface of the earth; for in the month of Māgha, having restrained his diet, he bathed in the salt ocean.
In the great Padmaka sacrificial pit, situated ten dhanus to the south of Rudreśa in the midst of this salt-water ocean.
O Goddess, having bathed according to the prescribed rite and worshipped Rudreśa, he shall obtain the full fruit of the Kedāra pilgrimage.
Through worship, there is the great destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; now, [I shall relate] the ancient history of that very deity. (9)
O beloved of the gods, I shall describe to you that which grants all desires to men. O Goddess, in ancient times there was a king renowned as Śaśabindu.
The sovereign ruler of the whole earth, the destroyer of the hosts of his enemies, that lord of the world was born at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages.
He had a virtuous wife, dearer to him than his own life; she was not a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman.
O lady of excellent hips, she was of such a form as his auspicious-eyed wife; he possessed a beautiful golden lotus with a hundred petals.
The aerial vehicle of that great-souled king was swift and constant; O Goddess, he wandered through all the worlds by his own will.
Once, O lady of beautiful countenance, during the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, on the fourteenth day, he arrived at the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then he saw all the sages standing before Śrī Someśa, intent on recitation and fire-offerings for the sake of keeping a night vigil.
Having seen Somanātha, he prostrated according to the prescribed rites and, filled with devotion, worshipped them all as was appropriate for each. || 17 ||
Then, O beloved, having reached Kedāra and having bathed according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the Lord with various garlands of flowers.
Then, with various food offerings, garments, and captivating ornaments, he performed a vigil there with a deeply concentrated mind. (19)
Then all those sages, filled with curiosity—Cyavana, Yājñavalkya, Śāṇḍilya, and Śākaṭāyana—[approached]. || 20 ||
Then Raibhya, Jaimini, Krauñca, Nārada, Parvata, and Śila, placing Mārkaṇḍeya at their head, went into his presence.
They engaged in most diverse conversations and recounted numerous historical legends; remaining there and praising [him], they questioned that best of kings.

The sages said: "O lord of men, why did you abandon the god Someśvara and perform the vigil (jāgara) in front of Kedāra? Tell us that; surely you know the fruit and the great prosperity of this Liṅga. (23)
The king said: "Let all the brahmins listen to my account of a previous birth. Formerly, I was born into the śūdra caste and was a worshiper of brahmins. (24)
In the auspicious region of Saurāṣṭra, which was abundant with wealth and grain, O twice-born ones, there occurred a drought after some time.
Then, overcome by hunger, I took my place at the sacred field of Prabhāsa; there I beheld a bright lake situated at the foot of a *hariṇī* tree.
And having seen that lake named Rāmasaras, adorned with clusters of lotuses and resembling the Ocean of Milk, he, overcome by fatigue, bathed there.
Having satiated the ancestors and the gods and having drunk the clear water, I was then addressed by my wife: "Take these lotuses. (28)
"O Lord, a beautiful and excellent place is seen nearby; let us go there and sell [something] so that we may have food. (29)
Then, O twice-born ones, having descended into the water, I gathered beautiful lotuses and set out toward the city.
Having gone there, O best of sages, they proceeded through the streets, at the crossroads, and at the junctions of three roads, solely to purchase full-blown lotuses.
No one accepted [me], for the sun had set; having reached a certain palace, I fell asleep together with my wife. (32)

Then, as I lay there asleep, my consciousness was awakened upon hearing the sound of singing; it arose especially in me, who was afflicted by hunger, for this must surely be a wakeful gathering in some celestial abode.
Taking these lotuses, I shall go there to the abode of the gods; if someone accepts them, it will serve as sustenance for my life.
Then, O bulls among sages, having risen, I arrived here and beheld this very linga worshipped with auspicious flowers.
This self-manifested ancient Liṅga is named Rudreśvara; it was [worshipped] by a courtesan named Anaṅgavatī, who was devoted to Śivarātri.
Someone before him is keeping watch with songs, dances, festivals, and so forth; therefore, I have seen someone—what is this night vigil? (37)
"Who is this woman seen here, so exceedingly devoted to the festival of song and dance? He replied, "This is Śivarātri, as described in the Śivadharma, which bestows supreme merit. (38)
And this courtesan named Anaṅgavatī, endowed with righteousness, keeps awake for the auspicious Śivarātri vow, which brings about the highest welfare. (39)
Indeed, that man who properly observes this Śivarātri vow does not encounter suffering, nor poverty, nor bondage. (40)
Free from evil planetary configurations or ill omens, and without disease or fear anywhere, such a man is born into a noble family, endowed with happiness and good fortune. (41)
"By his grace one shall become radiant, illustrious, and a vessel for all auspiciousness; thus say the wise. (42)
The king said: "Then my intellect became fixed upon that vow; for this was indeed reflected upon by me in my mind, O best of brahmins. (43)
"Since fasting has come upon me by force due to the lack of food, I shall therefore bathe in the Padmaka Tīrtha and in the salt ocean."
"With these lotuses, I worship the Lord Maheśvara; thus was Rudreśa fully worshipped by me together with my wife. (45)
And with lotuses, especially by his wife, he remained awake before the deity for that night together with his wife, filled with devotion.
Then, at the time of dawn when the solar disc had risen, that courtesan said this to me: "These three palas of silver... (47)
"O best of the twice-born, having adopted a state of pure goodness (sāttvika), I and my wife did not indeed accept the price for those lotuses. (48)
Then, having collected alms, I maintained my life; after a long time, O lords of sages, I met my end. (49)
"This virtuous woman, my beloved, who was dearer to me than my own life, has entered the fire, taking my body with her. (50)
"O best of the twice-born, by its power I was born as a sovereign lord of the earth; together with my wife, I am a rememberer of my former births—this is the truth. (51)
For this reason, my devotion to this Liṅga, along with that of my wife, is constant; I tell you this as the truth. (52)
"O best of beings, this vow was observed by me while I was devoid of ritual action and alienated from devotion; yet, this is its very great fruit. (53)
O lords of sages, I do not know what fruit will accrue to me now through these offerings made with devotion; for this reason, having abandoned Someśa, I am here intent upon devotion to you.
The Lord said: Having heard this, those brahmins, their eyes wide with wonder, praised the king, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! || 55 ||

They worshipped the self-manifested (svayambhu) Liṅga there incessantly. Then, by the grace of this Liṅga, that best of kings attained supreme perfection, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (56)
And by the power of Śivarātri and through the majesty of that Liṅga, that courtesan became an Apsaras named Rambhā.
Therefore, a wise person who desires dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa—the bestower of everything—should worship that liṅga with every effort.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Kedāreśvara Liṅga," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga of great power established by Śvetaketu, which was formerly propitiated by Bhīma.

Situated not far from the presence of Kedāreśvara, one who desires the fruit of the pilgrimage for the sake of attaining heaven after death should worship [the deity] according to the prescribed rites, beginning with the ritual bathing with milk and so forth, in due order.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, regarding that Linga which was described by you to me as belonging to Śvetaketu—how did it come to have the name Bhīmeśvara, O God? (3)
How was it previously emanated, and what is the fruit when that [emanation] is seen? (4)
Īśvara said: Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, there was a royal sage (rājarṣi) renowned as Śvetaketu, who was a performer of very great austerities. || 5 ||
Having arrived at Prabhāsa and installed Maheśvara, he performed very extensive penance on the auspicious shore of the ocean.
The practitioner of the five fires in summer, likewise one who dwells in the open air during the rains, and one who stays in the midst of water during the winter—for nine years and five [months].
Then, O Goddess, at the fourteenth [year], being pleased by her asceticism and self-restraint, I said to her: "O Goddess of noble vows, choose a boon. (8)
Then Śvetaketu said: "O Lord, grant me unwavering devotion; O Master, if you are pleased with me, let you remain in this place."
Having said, "So be it," I then vanished from his sight. Then, after some time had passed, Śvetaketu, who was of great splendor, [appeared].
Having propitiated this Liṅga, he attained a place of great prosperity; consequently, his name became renowned as Śvetaketvīśvara.
At the highly meritorious Agnitīrtha, which destroys all sins, he then arrived accompanied by his brothers once the Kali Yuga had set in.
When the mighty-armed Bhimasena, the son of Vāyu and my own partial incarnation, arrived at Prabhāsa in the course of his pilgrimage to sacred fords; || 13 ||
Having established his own Jāgeśvara [liṅga], he worshipped that tall liṅga, considering the place near the ocean to be a highly meritorious holy site (tīrtha). || 14 ||
From that time forward, O beautiful lady, Bhīmeśa’s name became auspicious once again, simply by the sight of that single Liṅga.
Even very many sins committed in other births, as well as those pertaining to the next world, all go to destruction. (16)

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhīmeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: To the east of that very place, established on the banks of the Sarasvati, is a Linga of great power located to the southeast of Somesha.
The submarine fire, in the form of Bhairaveśvara, was situated within a jar where it had been brought by the Goddess to the vicinity of the ocean.

Having set aside the linga for the goddess for a moment for the sake of rest, and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, he took the submarine fire and cast it into the middle of the ocean out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
Then the gods, exceedingly joyful, filled the sky with the sounds of conchs and drums and praised the Goddess with showers of flowers.
Then the gods, having performed a formidable task that was impossible for both gods and dānavas to achieve, gave her the name Devamātā.
And because you have established here this Liṅga of great prosperity—you, the best of all rivers and the destroyer of all sins—therefore this Liṅga shall attain fame by the name Bhairava.
Thus addressed, the goddess then stood there in embodied form, the virtuous one, on the delightful shore of the ocean to the southwest of Bhairaveśvara.

One should worship her according to the prescribed rite, and likewise that Lord Bhairava; having diligently performed the ritual bath on Mahānavamī according to the rules and having worshipped Sarasvatī, one is liberated from all defects of speech.
Having bathed her linga separately with milk and worshipped it according to the rules with the Aghora mantra alone, one shall duly obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhairaveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme deity Caṇḍīśa, situated at a distance of seven dhanus in the northeastern direction from Someśa.
Not very far to the south of Daṇḍapāṇi’s residence is the shrine formerly established by Caṇḍī and subsequently propitiated by Caṇḍa.
O Goddess of the Gods, because my Gaṇa performed that difficult penance, the Liṅga known as Caṇḍeśvara became famous upon the surface of the earth.
One should first bathe [the deity] with milk, then with curd mixed with ghee, and likewise with honey and sugarcane juice; one should then smear [the image] with saffron.
Then, one should worship with fragrant sandalwood, flowers, and the essence of musk mixed with camphor and uśīra.
O Goddess, having first burned incense and then agallochum (aguru) before the Lord, one should afterwards worship Him with garments according to the extent of one's own wealth.
Having offered an oblation of milk-rice (paramānna) together with a lamp, one should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born according to one's ability.
O lady of beautiful hips, whatever is given there while facing the southern direction all becomes inexhaustible for Caṇḍīśa.
O beautiful lady, the ancestors of one who performs a śrāddha ceremony there, to the south of Caṇḍīśa, attain satisfaction for the duration of a kalpa.
When the northern solstice has arrived, he who performs the "Ghee-blanket" rite shall not again obtain a terrible birth here in this cycle of existence.

By performing the pilgrimage of the trident-bearing Lord with such devotion, a person is liberated from the sins arising from stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) or consuming them out of ignorance, as well as from other sins born of past actions. || 11 ||

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Caṇḍīśa," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O beautiful lady, one should go to the Liṅga installed by Sūrya, situated seven dhanus to the west of Someśa; it is named Ādityeśvara and is the destroyer of all sins. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, in the Tretā Yuga, the Liṅga was worshipped with jewels for ten thousand years by the high-souled Ocean.
Therefore, it is now renowned on earth by the name Ratneśvara. Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship him with the five jewels (pañcaratna).
Then a person should worship according to the prescribed rites with royal offerings; when this is done, O Great Goddess, one obtains the fruit of the gift of Mount Meru.
And of all sacrifices and gifts, there is no doubt in this matter. || 5 ||
A human being shall also uplift the host of ancestors and the host of maternal relatives through all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth and whatever other meritorious deeds exist there.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in old age, or even in youth—a man shall wash all of that away simply by beholding Ratneśvara.
The great seers praise the gift of a cow at that sacred place; the giver of a cow certainly delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants.
He who, having worshipped the Liṅga according to the rules, recites the Śatarudriya on the southern side of the God, is not born again.
Thus has the great glory of Ādityeśa been briefly proclaimed; having heard and diligently mastered it, one is liberated from the bonds of karma.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ādityeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Having worshipped Ādityeśa, one should then proceed to Someśvara; having honored him according to the prescribed rite, especially with the five-fold limb-offering (pañcāṅga). || 1 ||
Having beheld Someśvara and prostrated with the eight limbs, one should perform circumambulations and other rites, and gaze upon him again and again. || 2 ||
Having performed the circumambulation of the Sun and the Moon three times, being self-restrained and pure, one has thereby performed every rite whose essence consists of Agni and Soma.
Then one should go to Umādevī, near Someśvara; thereafter, one should go to the second [liṅga] in the vicinity of Daityasūdana.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Someśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Aṅgāreśvara, established by the Son of the Earth (Mangala) to the northeast of Someśa.
O fair-faced one, in former times, as I desired to burn down Tripura, tears issued forth from my three eyes out of anger.
Having fallen upon the earth, he then became the son of the Earth; from his childhood onwards, he went to Prabhāsa and [worshipped] Śaṅkara.
O beloved, he propitiated [the Lord] through austerity for many groups of years; Mahādeva, being pleased and with a well-pleased soul, granted him a boon.
He said: "O God, O Bull-bannered One, if you are pleased with me, O Lord of All, grant me the status of a planet; I do not desire any other boon."
Having promised "So be it," he spoke these words again: "Any man who comes here and worships me with devotion... (6)
Indeed, you shall suffer no affliction whatsoever from him; [offer] abundant red flowers smeared with honey and clarified butter.
He who, having diligently worshipped you according to the rite of the five offerings (pañcopacāra), shall with devotion perform one hundred thousand oblations (homa) before you; || 8 ||
From his birth onwards, you shall suffer no affliction; likewise, by the gift of coral, he shall obtain his desired fruit.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there; Bhauma also, situated in the midst of the planets, shone resplendent in his celestial chariot.
