Thus has the supreme majesty of Bhauma been briefly proclaimed; when heard, it removes sins and likewise bestows health. (11)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Aṅgāreśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga of great power situated to the north of that very place, which is known as Budheśvara. || 1 ||
O beautiful lady, at a distance of exactly two bows and not very far away, there stands a Liṅga that removes all sins merely by being seen.
And there, O Goddess of gods, Budha performed great penance and, having propitiated Sadāśiva, installed the stainless Liṅga. || 3 ||
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites for forty thousand years, with an undistracted mind and a tranquil soul, he beheld Bhava face to face.

Then the god, being pleased in mind, granted him the status of a planet. Having worshipped that [deity] installed by the son of Soma according to the prescribed rites, especially on the eighth day of the moon's increase, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 5 ||
By his grace, there shall be no misfortune in his family, nor separation from what is dear; he shall have no fear of enemies.
Thus has the majesty of the deity Budha been briefly proclaimed; having heard it and rejoiced, one who is self-restrained attains the supreme state.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Budheśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity served by the Guru, located in the eastern direction from Umā and in the south-eastern region from Siddheśa.
Having worshipped that great Liṅga, established by the Preceptor of the Gods, with supreme devotion for a thousand years, he remained steadfast.
He gratified Bhava, Śarva, the Lord of Devas and husband of Umā, and obtained all his desires, which are unattainable by those who have not disciplined their souls.
Having attained the state of being worshipful even among the gods, as well as divine knowledge and lordship, and likewise having attained the status of a planet, he now rejoices in heaven.
Having seen it with devotion, that man shall not fall into an evil state; those best of men who behold the Liṅga established by Bṛhaspati [attain the same].
Indeed, no affliction caused by Bṛhaspati arises for them there, O beloved, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight when it falls on a Thursday.
Having duly worshipped the Liṅga with the complete royal offerings, or else with a spirit of devotion, one shall attain the supreme state.
That mortal who, with devotion, performs the ritual bath with a thousand palas of the essence of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) is indeed liberated from the three debts.
O Goddess, one whose self is purified of all sins through [the grace of] the mother, the father, and likewise the guru, being free from the pairs of opposites, shall attain liberation.
Thus has the greatness of the Guru-deity been briefly proclaimed; he who listens to it with devotion, his Guru shall become pleased.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vṛhaspatīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 47 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga installed by Śukra, which removes all sins, O Goddess, located to the west of Vibhūtīśvara.
Not far from there stood that place which had been personally created by Śukra, where he had obtained the Saṃjīvanī lore through the power of Rudra.
Having performed most terrible austerities for a thousand years and having propitiated Virūpākṣa, that wise one attained the status of a planet.
By that Śambhu who was swallowed for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, a most difficult penance was performed while remaining right there within his belly.
For more than ten thousand years, Maheśvara was brought to satisfaction; then, Śambhu quickly expelled him by way of his semen.
Consequently, the name Śukra became that of the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu; he who, having made his mind steady, worships the Liṅga at that time [attains success].
One should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra one hundred thousand times; he shall obtain his desired goal.
O beautiful lady, by seeing or even by touching him, one is liberated from sins beginning with birth and ending with death, through his grace.
He whose devotion is perfectly steady shall attain the sovereign powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, for the purpose of reviving the dead; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed the deity Śukra with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having worshipped him with fragrant flowers, one shall not suffer from afflictions caused by Venus.
Thus, O lady of beautiful hips, the entire majesty of Śukra as a deity has been told to you in brief; when heard, it removes the fear of sin.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śukreśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Therefore, O Goddess, one should proceed from Śukreśvara to the Liṅga of great luster named Śanaiścareśvara, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
To the west of Budheśvara and to the south-east of Ajādevī, situated not very far from her, is [the shrine] with five bows' length.
O Great Goddess, the Kalpaliṅga, worshipped by gods and dānavas, was tormented by Chāyāputra as he performed a most difficult penance.
The god who is without beginning or end, by whom [Śiva] was brought down into this *liṅga*, attained the lordship of the planets through devotion and the grace of Śambhu.
There is no living being whatsoever in this universe, including all things mobile and immobile, whom the great hosts of gods and asuras did not fear when he looked upon them.
Whether a god or even a dānava, there is no one who is not afflicted by Saturn, provided they worship Śiva as Saurīśvara with devotion on a Saturday.
O Great Goddess, having gratified [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with śamī leaves, sesame, mung beans, jaggery, and boiled rice, one should present a black bull to a brahmin.
Having praised him with various hymns originating from the Purāṇas and the Śrutis, or else the Lord of Gods was fully gratified by a single hymn.
When King Daśaratha himself was overcome by a powerful affliction, he praised the divine Lord of the Sun for the pacification of all suffering.
The Goddess said: "How did King Daśaratha perform the hymn of praise to Śanaiścara? And how did the god Śanaiścara attain satisfaction with him? (10)

Īśvara said: In the lineage of Raghu, there was a very famous and powerful king named Daśaratha; he was to be known as a universal monarch (cakravartin), the sovereign of the seven continents in ancient times. 11.
Having placed Saturn at the end of Kṛttikā, he was indeed informed by the astrologers: "Saturn shall now proceed after piercing through Rohiṇī."
The "Breaking of the Cart" (Śakaṭabheda), which causes terror to both gods and asuras, has been described; there will be a most dreadful twelve-year famine.
Having heard these words of the sage, the king, together with his ministers, beheld the world—including the citizens, the people of the countryside, and others—to be indeed agitated.
People gathered together constantly spoke thus: "The countries, cities, and villages are overwhelmed on all sides by fear. And the king himself questioned the sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha.
Daśaratha said: "O best of the twice-born, tell me what remedy exists for this."

Vasiṣṭha said: "If even that constellation belonging to Prajāpati has been pierced, from where can progeny arise? Indeed, this situation is impossible to remedy even by the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Indra."
Then, having reflected in his mind upon a most great and daring deed, he took up his divine bow, equipped with celestial weapons.
Having mounted his chariot, he went with speed to the circle of the stars; it was a divine golden chariot, adorned with jewels and gems.
It was adorned with banners, chowries, umbrellas, and small bells; it was yoked to swan-colored horses and equipped with a great standard.
Blazing with great jewels and radiant with his crown and tiara, he then shone in the sky like a second sun.
Drawing his bow back to his ear and fixing the weapon of destruction (saṃhārāstra), he, having ascertained that Saturn was at the end of Kṛttikā, entered Rohiṇī.
Seeing this, Daśaratha stood before him with a frowning face; Śani, for his part, beheld the weapon of destruction that crushes both gods and demons.
Having laughed, Sauri then spoke these words out of haste: "O Indra among kings, your prowess is supreme and strikes fear into your enemies."
Gods, asuras, humans, siddhas, vidyādharas, and serpents—all have been beheld by me, and they all quickly fall into fear.
"I am pleased with you, O Indra among kings, by virtue of your austerity and your manly prowess. Choose a boon; I shall grant whatever is desired by your mind. (26)
Daśaratha said: "O Śani, you must not go by piercing through Rohiṇī, as long as there are rivers and oceans, and as long as the moon, the sun, and the earth exist. (27)
"O son of Sūrya, I have requested this of you; I desire no other boon from you. Being addressed thus, Śani granted him that eternal boon.
Having thus obtained the boon, the king then felt his purpose was fulfilled; yet Sauri spoke once more: "O observer of noble vows, choose another boon. (29)
Then, with a joyful heart, he requested this boon from Śani: "O son of the Sun, the cart must not be broken by you."
"A twelve-year famine must never be allowed to occur; this fame of mine shall circulate throughout the three worlds. (31)
The Lord said: Then, having obtained the two boons, that king, his hair standing on end with joy, set aside his bow upon the chariot and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having meditated upon the goddess Sarasvatī and Gaṇanātha Vināyaka, King Daśaratha then composed this hymn of praise to Sauri.
The king said: Salutations to the one with blue rays and to the one resembling a blue lotus; salutations to the one with a fleshless body and to the one with long beard and matted hair. || 34 ||
Homage to the one with wide eyes, who is terrifying with his emaciated belly; homage to the one with coarse limbs and indeed to the one with thick body hair. 35.

Salutations eternally to you who are afflicted by hunger; salutations indeed to you who are ever tormented. Salutations to you whose form is the fire of time; O Kṛtāntaka, let there be salutations to you.
Homage to you who are long and withered; O Kāladṛṣṭi, let there be homage to you! Homage to you whose eyes are like hollows; indeed, homage to you who are difficult to behold! || 37 ||
Homage to the terrible, the fierce, the terrifying, and the one with formidable hands! Homage to you, the devourer of all; O Valīmukha, let there be homage to you! 38.
O son of the Sun, salutations be unto you; O Bhāskara, giver of fear! O downward-looking one, salutations to you; O dark-bodied one, salutations be unto you! (39)
Homage to you, O slow-moving one; repeated salutations to you, the sword-like one. Homage to you of fierce form; salutations to you of terrible splendor. 40.
Salutations to you, whose body is consumed by austerity, who are ever devoted to yoga, whose eye is knowledge, and who are the grandson of Kaśyapa’s son. 41.
When pleased, you indeed grant a kingdom; when enraged, you take it away in an instant. So too do the gods, asuras, and humans, as well as beasts, birds, and reptiles.
O son of Sūrya, when looked upon by you, even Brahmā, Śakra, Yama, and the seven star-like sages quickly fall into a state of wretchedness.
And all those who have been deprived of their kingdoms, as well as countries, cities, villages, islands, and likewise mountains, have been beheld by your gaze. (44)
But those who are looked upon with a fierce gaze perish at that very moment.
"O son of Sura, show me favor; for the sake of a boon, I have taken refuge in you. O son of Sura, forgive my transgression for the welfare of all living beings. (46)
Ishvara said: Thus praised then by King Dasharatha, the great king Shani, the son of the Sun, spoke these words with a joyful mind. (47)
Śani said: "O Indra among kings, O observer of noble vows, I am pleased with this hymn of yours. Choose a boon, O delight of the Raghus, and I shall grant it according to your wish. (48)
Daśaratha said: "From this day forward, O tawny-eyed one, no harm shall be done to anyone—neither among gods, asuras, and humans, nor among beasts, birds, and reptiles. (49)

Śani said: "I am to be known as the most difficult of the planets to propitiate; I inflict affliction upon the planets. O King, whatever is requested that is not to be given, I shall grant it to you if it is appropriate. (50)
"Those men or women who, being oppressed by fear of me, shall recite this hymn of praise spoken by you for me," (51)
Whether they be gods, asuras, humans, siddhas, vidyādharas, or uragas, whether standing at the threshold of death or having reached the end of their birth; || 52 ||
I bestow prosperity upon them once or twice a day; having performed worship, one should recite the hymn with palms joined in reverence. (53)
I would never cause him any suffering here, whether he were situated in the house of birth or even situated in the house of death. (54)
Whether it be at the birth asterism, the ascendant, or during the major and minor planetary periods, I shall constantly protect him from the affliction of other planets.
In this very manner, he shall indeed be liberated from disease; thus has this boon been granted by me, O delighter of the Raghus. (56)
The Lord said: Having obtained the two boons in the past, King Daśaratha, after bowing down to Śanaiścara, considered himself to have achieved his purpose. (57)
Having praised Śani and received his permission, the valiant king mounted his chariot and returned to his own abode, being honored by the inhabitants of heaven.
The man who, having risen early in the morning on a Sunday, recites this, shall experience no suffering arising from any planetary influence upon the earth.
One should daily remember the god Śanaiścara with devotion; having worshipped him, one should recite his hymn of praise, for then the son of the Sun becomes pleased.
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you the majesty of the deity Śani, which pacifies all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. (61)
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga installed by Rāhu; it is situated to the northwest of Śanaiścareśvara, O Goddess. || 1 ||
To the north of the goddess Ajādevī, situated at a distance of seven bows' length, it stands close to Maṅgalā, not very far away.
The Liṅga of great power was installed by Saiṃhikeya; there, the son of Vipracitti performed penance for a thousand years.
That great Asura Svarbhānu, possessed of immense prowess and fighting with his mouth, propitiated the Lord Mahādeva through divine ascetic penance.

He caused Maheśvara, the lamp of the world, to descend into the Liṅga. Whatever man worships him with devotion and beholds him properly, his sin—even that arising from the murder of a Brāhmaṇa—goes to destruction.
By beholding him on this earth, no mortal is ever born blind, deaf, mute, diseased, or destitute.
Then he becomes endowed with happiness and good fortune, possessed of beauty, his soul fulfilled in all desires, and rejoices in heaven like a god.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the majesty of the deity Rāhu; having heard it, a man who has emerged from delusion shall become free from all taint.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Rāhvīśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 50 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Ketuliṅga of great luster, located to the north of Rāhvīśa and to the south of Maṅgalā.
Situated at a distance of one bow's length, not too far away, is indeed a Liṅga of great power that destroys all sins.
Named Ketu, he was fierce and seized by name; he was permeated by the true being of Śiva, circular, exceedingly vast, and most terrifying to the eyes.
Resembling smoke from burning straw and removing the afflictions caused by malevolent planets, he performed severe penance there for a hundred divine years, O beloved.
O beloved, Mahādeva, being pleased with her, granted her the status of a planet and the lordship over eleven hundred planets.
One should worship with devotion that Ketu-linga of great luster situated there, especially when it is seen at the onset of a most terrible comet.
During fierce afflictions caused by the planets, one should worship him according to the prescribed rite with flowers, perfumes, incense, and various auspicious food offerings.
One should propitiate the deity Ketu, the destroyer of impurities, according to the prescribed rites.
Thus has been briefly declared the Ketu-liṅga of great prosperity, which pacifies the afflictions of the planets and destroys all sins. || 9 ||
These nine lingas of the planets have been described to you; for the man who beholds them constantly, whence can there be fear of affliction? (10)
In his family, O Goddess, no one shall be unfortunate, nor shall anyone be diseased or distressed; he shall be born as if possessed of a son, for the great planetary spirits protect him. (11)
Thus, O beloved, I have correctly described to you the fourteen sacred sites, beginning with Vighneśvara and ending with the establishment of Ketu.
By hearing the sin-destroying majesty of the nine lords of the planets, as well as that of the five liṅgas, one is liberated from all sins.
No man devoid of merit can know these five mudrā-liṅgas, beginning with Kapardin and ending with Caṇḍanātha.
Beginning with Sūryeśvara and ending with Ketuliṅga, no one else indeed knows these Liṅgas of the nine planets.
Thus, the association with the sense-bases (āyatana) has been declared to be of fourteen kinds; he who knows this with true devotion attains the fruit of the field (kṣetra).

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ketvīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O illustrious lady, I shall now describe the five Siddha-liṅgas, by the sight of which, O Goddess, the pilgrimage of men becomes perfected.

In the direction from Someśa toward Īśa (the northeast), there is the one remembered as Varārohā; and to her east is the supreme Lord Siddheśvara. By approaching him with devotion, a person shall attain the supernatural powers beginning with aṇimā.
Having seen the Linga installed by the Siddhas with devotion, a human being is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of the Siddhas. || 3 ||
The obstacles of those dwelling in that sacred field go to their destruction: lust, anger, fear, greed, passion, and envy.
Envy, hypocrisy, as well as laziness, sleep, delusion, and egoism—these are forms of obstacles that indeed create hindrances to spiritual accomplishment.
Those [obstacles] meet their destruction there through the worship of Siddheśvara; knowing this, one should diligently perform a pilgrimage there.
Thus, O Goddess, has been described the great glory of Siddheśvara, which grants all desires to men and, when heard, destroys their sins.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Kapileśvara, situated not far away in the eastern direction of that very place. || 1 ||
The Liṅga possesses great power; by its mere sight, sins are destroyed. It is there that the royal sage named Kapila performed intense penance.
Having established Maheśvara within that liṅga, Hari attained supreme perfection; for Īśāna, the presence of the God, is eternally present in that liṅga.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, for the sake of the welfare of all the world, whoever, having become purified, beholds Mahādeva Someśa Kapileśvara seven times, shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a cow.
O beloved, he who, being composed in mind, gives a sesame-cow at that sacred ford, dwells in heaven for as many yugas as there are sesame seeds.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kapileśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 53 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Gandharveśvara, situated nearby to the north of the abode of Daṇḍapāṇi.
There, indeed, was the king of the Gandharvas known as Ghanavāha; his daughter was famous by the name Gandharvasenā and possessed great splendor.
That woman, proud of her beauty, was cursed by the group led by Śikhaṇḍin; thereafter, the sage Gośṛṅga bestowed his grace upon her.
By means of the Monday vow (somavāra-vrata) alone, for the purpose of propitiating Someśa, he then came to the sacred field and performed an extremely difficult penance.
There, the king of the Gandharvas himself installed a Liṅga; likewise, his daughter also installed a Liṅga in that very place.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, right there in the vicinity of Daṇḍapāṇi, one who would diligently worship the Liṅga named Ghanavāheśvara— || 6 ||
Having seen it, being self-restrained and pure, one attains the world of the Gandharvas. Thus, O Goddess, has this supreme Gāndharva Liṅga been described to you.
The third [pilgrimage] is the destroyer of all sins and the increaser of merit; having bathed at Agnitīrtha and worshipped the one honored by the Gandharvas, a man [attains these benefits].
When the northern course [of the sun] has arrived, he attains Nirvāṇa; having heard and rejoiced in this majesty, he is liberated from great fear.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gandharveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 54 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Vimaleśvara, which is situated to the east of that [Liṅga], located near Gaurī to the east, not very far away. || 1 ||
Situated in the southwest direction from the Guru is the destroyer of sins; even after committing a great sin, whether it be a woman or a man, [one is purified].
Or, one whose body is overcome by decay, having worshipped him with devotion, shall reach the end of all suffering and attain the stainless state. || 3 ||
Where the Gandharva army became spotless despite being afflicted by destruction, that Linga indeed became famous on earth by the name Vimaleshvara.
Thus, O Bhavasundarī, I have told you all this fourth majesty concerning Vimaleśvara, which destroys all sins.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vimaleśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now I shall describe to you the fifth, the Siddhaliṅga of great splendor, situated sixteen dhanus to the southwest of Brahmā. || 1 ||
In the vicinity of the Rāhuliṅga is a Liṅga fashioned by Dhanada, where he attained the status of Dhanada after performing great penance.
Having installed and worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites for a thousand years, he became the lord of Alakā there by the grace of Śambhu.
Having remembered his former birth and understood the fruit of the lamp-wick [offering], he returned once more to Prabhāsa, [recognizing] the power of Śivarātri.
Having recognized his extraordinary power, he installed Śaṅkara there, by whose ascetic penance Śaṅkara had been brought into direct perception.
O Great Goddess, he was brought down into that liṅga with great devotion; having seen it, a human being should worship it with devotion according to the prescribed rites.
Through the five types of offerings and with true devotion, using perfumes, incense, and ointments, no one in his lineage shall ever become poor.
And those men who, endowed with devotion, shall worship this Liṅga, they will become invincible to their enemies and destroyers of their pride.
Thus, I have told you everything regarding the great prosperity of the region of Dhanada; by hearing this and approving it with effort, one shall never again be born poor.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Dhanadeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thus, O beloved, these five Siddhaliṅgas have been described to you; he who knows this secret convention is called a resident of the sacred field (kṣetravāsī). || 1 ||
Now I shall speak in detail of those three powers of the Raudrīs; they are proclaimed to be threefold: the powers of will (icchā), action (kriyā), and knowledge (jñāna). || 2 ||
Furthermore, listen to the sequence for their worship in due order; those which were previously mentioned are fourteen as well as five.
Having worshipped four, three, or even one of those lingas according to his ability, he should then worship the three Shaktis after having fully honored them.
That digit of the Moon known as Amā, which is remembered as Varārohā in the direction beginning with Someśa (the northeast), is subsequently proclaimed as Umā.
That power of will (icchā-śakti) should be known as residing in the sacred field of Prabhāsa; there, O Goddess, for the benefit of all living beings on earth.
O fair-faced one, I shall now tell you her entire majesty; formerly, she was abandoned by her wives by Soma.
Having performed austerities for twenty-six years in the auspicious Prabhāsika-kṣetra, Gaurī was then propitiated for many groups of divine years.
Having appeared before their very eyes, the supreme goddess Pārvatī, the bestower of boons, said: "Speak that which resides in your minds."
Then they said, "O Goddess Pārvatī, if you are pleased, grant us abundant good fortune as well as supreme beauty."
"O auspicious goddess, we have all been abandoned by our master despite being faultless; we are consumed by the defect of misfortune and tormented by ill luck. (11)
Gaurī said: "From this day forward, the Lord of Night shall behold all of you equally; by my grace, O fair-limbed ones, this shall not be in vain."
And because I shall grant boons, I will be known by the name Varadā; for whatever auspicious woman comes here and worships me, [she shall receive a boon].
Women in her family shall never encounter misfortune; for she was devoted to fasting on the third day of the month of Māgha.
"Whosoever with beautiful hips shall behold me, she shall become my equal; sixteen couples here shall be provided with garments with great care. (15)
That woman who shall indeed offer fruits, various kinds of food and edibles, and sixteen types of cooked dishes, she shall become Uma herself.
This is known as the Gaurī-vrata; one should perform it on the third lunar day. Any woman who is childless, or any woman who is unfortunate, [should observe this]. (17)
"By acting thus even once, a man shall attain his desired goal. Having spoken thus, that beautiful-eyed goddess remained there. (18)
And the Lord of the Night beheld them all just as he gazes upon Rohiṇī; yet another was consumed by grief and afflicted by misfortune.
She worshipped the goddess Umā and consequently became fortunate; thus has the majesty arising from Śakti been briefly proclaimed.
At Someśvara, it has been told to you that there is one named Varārohā; she effects the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all poverty. (21)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Varārohā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 57 ||
Īśvara said: Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the second Śakti, whose nature is action (kriyātmikā), the great goddess residing at Prabhāsa who bestows delight upon the gods. (1)
O Great Goddess, situated sixty dhanus away from Someśa in the northwestern quarter is a sacred seat (pīṭha) worshipped by the hosts of Yoginīs. || 2 ||
O Goddess, in that place there was a great opening to the netherworld (pātāla); in that spot of great splendor, she remained stationed in the form of a guardian.
One devoted to its worship shall obtain everything situated within the sacred field—the treasures of Pātāla, deposits, divine herbs, and elixirs of rejuvenation. || 4 ||
And the name of that goddess was previously proclaimed as Bhairavī; however, in this twenty-eighth cycle of four yugas, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, there was a king named Ajāpāla.
And having come to this field, O beautiful lady, that man afflicted by disease worshipped the goddess Bhairavī for five hundred years.
Then the goddess, being well-pleased, spoke to that best of kings: "Enough with this distress, O royal sage; I am satisfied with your devotion."
Thus addressed, that wise king, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and spoke to the goddess, his eyes clouded with tears of joy.
O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, or if I am worthy of a boon, let all diseases be cast out from my body and go to their destruction.
Thus addressed, that goddess spoke again to the king: "O Great King, everything shall indeed come to pass exactly as you have said."
When the goddess had spoken thus, the diseases then emerged separately from the body of that king in the form of goats.
"Five thousand and five hundred [years] will certainly pass," thus spoke the Great Goddess again to the lord of men when this had occurred. (12)
"O King, protect these diseases that have the form of old age in their entirety; what shall they do? They will be the executors of your very commands. (13)
"Your name shall become renowned in the world as 'Ajāpāla'; by your name, my name shall likewise be 'Ajāpāleśvarī' upon the surface of the earth for as long as the four ages endure."
Whoever worships me here on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, I, being pleased, shall grant him eightfold sovereignty; of this there is no doubt. (15)

O King, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, having performed three circumambulations and having bathed and worshipped me individually while keeping Someśa in the center, for him there shall be no fear or grief for three years.
But for a woman who is barren, diseased, or unfortunate, this ninth [day] should be observed as prescribed before me, for it increases her satisfaction. (17)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, the Goddess then vanished right there; that king of incomparable valor remained situated within the holy field of Prabhāsa.
The righteous-souled one protected those goats, which were in the form of diseases, by means of various kinds of medicinal herbs that serve as causes for their nourishment.
There, for more than a hundred years, goats were separately nourished by Ajāpāla, who established a great storehouse for them.
Then, by her grace, that king of vast prowess became the sovereign of the seven continents and an ornament of the Solar dynasty.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, this origin of the unborn Goddess is most wonderful; I desire to hear once more of that great marvel concerning the king. (22)
O Lord of Gods, how did that king alone rule over the earth consisting of seven continents? And how were those diseases created by him? (23)
Īśvara said: In ancient times there was a royal sage renowned as Dilīpa; his son was named Dīrgha, and from him Raghu was born.
The son of Aja was Raghu, and from him came one who was exceedingly powerful; having propitiated Bhairavī, he rendered diseases powerless against his hosts of arrows.
He protected [the earth] with great joy, and thus he became Ajāpāla. At that time, Rāvaṇa then became the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Remaining in Laṅkā, he appointed the hosts of gods to their respective duties; he made the moon, with its unbroken orb, his royal parasol.
He made Indra the commander-in-chief, Vāyu the sweeper of dust, Varuṇa the messenger, and Dhanada the protector of wealth. || 28 ||
He appointed Yama to the restraint of his enemies and Manu to counsel; the clouds vomited forth [water] and the trees smeared themselves with flowers, which they scattered.
The seven ṛṣis, devoted to peace, were the praising brahmins; the beloved nāgas were in the inner courtyard, and the gandharvas were intent on singing. || 3 ||
In the act of being beheld, he was surrounded by throngs of Apsarases; in music, by Vidyādharas; in drinking, by the Gaṅgā and other rivers; and in the domestic fire-ritual, by the sacrificial fire.
Viśvakarman was appointed by him to perform the consecration of the body; all the kings stood before him, intent on rendering service.
They were seen stumbling because of their radiant jewels and ornaments; seeing them, Rāvaṇa spoke to his doorkeeper Prahasta.
"Tell me who has arrived here to perform service at my place. Having bowed down before him, the night-stalker Daṇḍapāṇi replied: ||| 34 ||
This descendant of Kakutstha is Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Nala, Arjuna, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Bhīma, this Rāghava, and Vidūratha. (35)
These and many other kings have come here; they stand in your presence as your servants, but Ajāpāla has not come here.
Enraged, Rāvaṇa said, "Quickly dispatch a messenger! Having been told this, the Rākṣasa named Dhūmrākṣa was sent as a messenger.
"O Dhūmrākṣa, go and say to Ajāpāla by my command: 'O King, come to me to perform service, or else pay tribute.'"
"Or else, with the Candrahāsa sword, I shall make you headless like Vikandhara. Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Dhūmrākṣa became like Garuḍa.
Having reached that beautiful city and entered your royal palace, he saw Ajāpāla approaching alone, surrounded by goats.
With disheveled hair and loosened loincloth, wearing a golden blanket, with a staff upon his shoulder, covered in dust, and surrounded by diseases; || 41 ||
Having drawn upon the earth the names [of the Lord], who is like a slaying tiger, the destroyer of all calamities, and the one who strikes down the host of enemies; || 42 ||
Seeing Manu bathed, fed, and having fulfilled his duties in his own place, Dhūmrākṣa, with a joyful mind, spoke the words uttered by Rāvaṇa.
The cowherd, having replied with a retort and a reasoned answer, sent Dhūmrākṣa away and then attended to his own task.
Having caused Jvara to take his form, the lord of the earth spoke these words: "Go to the abode of the Lord of Laṅkā and carry out what has been commanded. (45)
Commissioned by Ajapāla, that fever went to heaven; having gone there, he made Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, tremble.
But Rāvaṇa, perceiving that most terrible fever, said: "Let the king remain; I have no need for him. (47)
Thereupon, that king, the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), became free from fever; such are his deeds, and there are others as well by the millions.

O Goddess of the gods, she belongs to Ajāpāla, who wears a crown with a brilliance like that of the sun; by that wise Ajāpāla, this goddess—who pacifies all diseases and destroys all calamities—was propitiated. (49)
If a person desires worldly enjoyments, he should worship her according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, incense, ornaments, garments, and other offerings with devotion. (50)
Thus has everything been told to you regarding the origin of Ajādevī, which pacifies all suffering and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ajāpāleśvarī," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now I shall describe to you the third power of knowledge, whose essence is Śiva, situated within the sacred field of Prabhāsa, and which destroys the flood of poverty.
One should worship that goddess named Ajaitā, who stands to the south of Rāhvīśa; she indeed emerged from my sixth mouth, which is worshipped by Viṣṇu.

The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, five faces of yours are well known in your majesty. O God, what is the name remembered for that sixth face? And how was she born from it, she who is heard of as the unborn Goddess (Ajādevī)? (3)
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, you have asked well; that which is to be kept secret even from one's own sons, I shall declare to you, as it is proclaimed in an unestablished scripture."
O Goddess of gods, my faces were indeed seven even from the beginning: five starting with Sadyojāta, and the sixth is remembered as Aja.
The seventh is named Picu; thus, these are my seven faces. Among them, the goat was given to Brahmā, while the Picu-faced one was given to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, I have now become five-faced; the unborn Brahmā was born, and Viṣṇu arose as Picu.
O Great Goddess, from the mouth of Aja was born Aja of great splendor, through my wrath in the terrible battle with the demon Andha, O passionate lady.
The goddess, beautiful in form, bearing a sword and shield, and mounted upon a lion, crushes the great daityas while accompanied by ten million goddesses.
Out of fear of her, those Daityas who had fled to the southern ocean were pursued from behind by that goddess, who was mounted upon a lion.
Running hither and thither while being struck by his hosts, they reached the Prabhāsa region and, seeking refuge, fled toward the great ocean.
Some Daityas were slain there, while others fled to Pātāla; seeing them all destroyed without exception, that goddess mounted upon her lion [roared].
Knowing that field to be pure, the auspicious one remained in that place; situated in the northeast corner from Someśa, she was located to the north of Saurīśa.
Whoever, whether woman or man, should behold her stationed there, shall be endowed with goodness and good fortune for seven births.
Whatever man performs singing, instrumental music, and dancing there, by her grace, misfortune shall not befall his lineage. (15)
O Great Goddess, whatever woman offers a lamp there with ghee and a red wick—however many threads are in that wick—for that many future births she shall obtain good fortune.
Whoever should recite this daily, especially on the third lunar day, or whoever should listen to it with devotion, shall obtain all desires. (17)
Thus, the sequence of the three powers of Rudra has been briefly explained. || 18 ||
Having worshipped these Śaktis, one who desires the full fruit of the pilgrimage should then worship Someśa, or else [worship] only one of them, Varadā.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ajādevī," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent complexion, there is a triad of female messengers of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra; now I shall describe them to you, so listen with a single-minded focus, my dear. 1.
The first goddess is Maṅgalā; the second is Viśālākṣī; likewise, the third is proclaimed to be Catvaradevī. || 2 ||
O fair-faced one, those Śaktis are to be worshipped in their proper sequence if a man desires the fruit of a pilgrimage to Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

The Goddess said: O Lord, in what place do those female messengers who protect the sacred field reside? To whom do they belong, how are they to be propitiated, and how are they to be worshipped, O Lord of the Universe? (4)
Īśvara said: Brāhmī is declared to be Maṅgalā, while Viśālākṣī is indeed Vaiṣṇavī; she is celebrated as the power (Śakti) of Rudra, that goddess who is fond of crossroads.
Maṅgalā is to be worshipped first; she is situated to the north of Ajādevī, not very far to the south of Rāhvīśa, O fair-faced one.
When the ritual of sacrifice had commenced after Someśvara was installed, she arrived there out of a desire to behold the gods who were present with Soma.
Since she brought about auspiciousness for Brahmā and the others, O Umā, she is therefore called Maṅgalā, the bestower of all auspiciousness.
But on the third day, whatever woman or man shall worship [it], all their inauspiciousness and miseries shall go to destruction entirely.
There, a meal for a married couple, the offering of fruit along with a bodice, and the consumption of speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) are highly commended and destroy all sins.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the great fortune and the great prosperity [of this], as well as the majesty of Maṅgalā, which destroys all sins. (11)

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Maṅgalā," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Goddess, one should go to the great goddess Kṣetradūtī, who belongs to Viṣṇu and is situated to the east of Śrīdaityasūdana.
Likewise, she is situated at a distance of seven bows to the northeast of Yogeśvarī; for those consumed by great misfortune, she stands in the form of a medicine.
O Goddess, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa, when the Daityas, fierce in their strength, were being struck down by Viṣṇu, they then entered the southern direction.
There, O Queen of the Gods, the Daityas waged a great battle with Viṣṇu for more than a hundred years, using various kinds of divine weapons.
Then, knowing them to be slayable by means of suffering, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu called to mind the power Bhairavī, who is Mahāmāyā and possesses great splendor.
In a mere moment, she was remembered by the powerful Viṣṇu; thereupon the Great Goddess arrived, her eyes sparkling with joy.
When the two eyes of the Goddess were made large by the sight of Viṣṇu, she then became Viśālākṣī (the Large-eyed One), remaining there as the destroyer of the Daityas.
In this kalpa, O fair-faced one, Lalitā Umā has been fully described; thus the two Umās have been declared at Someśa, the slayer of the Daityas.
One should first visit Someśvara and afterwards Śrīdaityasūdana; by worshipping these two Umās, one obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage.
Whoever worships her according to the prescribed rite on the third day of the month of Māgha, that man shall not be deprived of progeny throughout ten million generations of his lineage.
He who constantly beholds [it] there, endowed with supreme devotion, shall remain for a long time possessed of health, happiness, and good fortune.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the majesty arising from Lalitā; when heard, it serves to destroy sins and to increase righteousness.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Lalitā Umā-Viśālākṣī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the third [shrine], Catvarapriyā, situated ten dhanus away in the eastern direction from Lalitā. || 1 ||
I then released from my midst the field-messenger (kṣetradūtī), who is exceedingly fierce, the power (śakti) of Rudra, and possessed of great splendor, for the purpose of guarding that sacred field.
Accompanied by millions of beings, possessing great bodies and great radiance, [they appear] in dilapidated houses, as well as in gardens, palaces, watchtowers, and on the roads.
And at all four crossroads, remaining in the midst of the field, the Goddess wanders about at night surrounded by tens of millions of spirits.
On the Mahānavamī day, whoever there—whether a woman or even a man—should duly worship the Auspicious One with various offerings and services.
That Goddess, being pleased, will grant all his desires; those who desire the fruit of the pilgrimage should provide a meal for a married couple there.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the sin-destroying majesty of the third Kṣetradūtī; when heard, it bestows sovereign power.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Catvaradevī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Bhairaveśvara, situated not far to the south of Yogeśvarī.
It pacifies all sins and bestows divine sovereignty; it was [revealed] in the past when the Goddess made an effort for the sake of destroying the Daityas.
Then, having summoned Bhairava, she appointed him to the office of messenger; she was thereafter known as Śivadūtī and later as Yogeśvarī.
Where Bhairava was indeed appointed by the Goddess to the office of messenger, by him the Liṅga was proclaimed under the name Bhairaveśvara. || 4 ||

Worshipped by the gods and the daityas and installed by Bhairava, that man who worships it with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of Kārttika, or continuously for six months, obtains his desired fruit.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhairaveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Located five bow-lengths to the east of that very place is the one renowned as Lakṣmīśvara, which destroys the flood of poverty. || 1 ||
Where Lakṣmī was brought by the Goddess after she had slain the Daityas, he himself installed the deity named Lakṣmīśvara. || 2 ||
O beloved, he who worships Him with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the auspicious Pañcamī shall not be separated from Lakṣmī for the duration of a Manvantara.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Lakṣmīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga known as Vāḍaveśvara, located to the north of Lakṣmīśa and to the south of Viśālākṣī.
Indeed, it stands possessed of great power, established by Vāḍava; for when Kṛtasmara was consumed, the mountain was burnt by the Vāḍava fire.
Having leveled the entire site, he installed the Liṅga; one should worship that Śaṅkara according to the prescribed rite after bathing it ten times.
And one should indeed give curd there to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he attains the world of Agni and obtains the full fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vāḍaveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, one should go to the great liṅga known as Arghyeśvara, situated to the north of Viśālākṣī, not very far away.
Indeed, that Liṅga of great power is worshipped by gods and Gandharvas; it was when the Goddess arrived there, bearing the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala).
Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa and beheld the great ocean there, she offered an oblation (arghya) to that great ocean according to the prescribed rite.
Having installed the great Liṅga and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, O Goddess of Devas, he then entered the great ocean for the purpose of bathing.
Because he first offered the arghya and afterwards established the directions, that linga became renowned as Arghyeśa, the destroyer of sins.

O Goddess of gods, he who bathes [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and worships it according to the prescribed rite attains knowledge for seven births; he becomes a perfect expounder of the scriptures and the best among those who resolve all doubts.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Arghyeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thence one should go to the great Liṅga known as Kāmeśvara, which was formerly worshipped by Kāma, located to the west of Daityasūdana.
O Goddess, there stands a being of great splendor at a distance of seven bow-lengths; it was when Kāma was utterly consumed by my third fire.
Then, having propitiated Maheśvara for a thousand years, he attained the realm of desire where, it is said, Anaṅga formerly dwelt.
Therefore, O Goddess, that linga on the surface of the earth became renowned by the name Kāmeśvara; it removes all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava, he shall become like Cupid to women.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kāmeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thus, O Goddess, the five face-liṅgas have indeed been described to you. Now I shall fully describe to you the place where Gaurī’s penance-grove is located—a site of great power, frequented by gods and siddhas. || 1 ||
Situated sixty dhanus to the east of Someśa is the place where, in a previous birth, the goddess Satī indeed performed penance.
And having displayed anger toward me out of affection, O fair-faced one, that ascetic woman reached the holy site of Prabhāsa and remained there.
The Goddess said: For what reason did Satī abandon you and remain engaged in ascetic penance? In what place is the Goddess situated? Tell me this in detail.
Icchārūpa said: "O Great Goddess, formerly you were dark-complexioned and high-minded; and while you were staying in seclusion, I spoke the name 'Kālī' for the sake of its meaning. (5)
Hearing those words of wonder, she became intensely overcome with rage; with her face contorted by a frown, she spoke these harsh words.
"O Śambhu, because I have been called 'Kālī' by you due to this great confusion, I shall therefore depart; for I shall become Gaurī wherever I go. (7)

Having spoken thus, the illustrious lady, surrounded by her circle of friends, went to the holy site of Prabhāsa and installed Maheśvara, who became renowned as Gaurīśvara, worshipping him according to the prescribed rites.
Then, standing on one foot near the Liṅga, she remained there and performed very great penance while worshipping the Liṅga.
The goddess who practices the penance of the five fires was devoted to recitation during the summer; she slept in the open air during the rains and remained immersed in water during the winter.
In whatever measure her great splendor increased through her asceticism, in that same measure her body attained a state of whiteness. || 11 ||
After a long time, she then became Gaurī in every limb; thereupon the Moon-crested Lord, smiling, spoke.
"O Gaurī," he said repeatedly, "Arise and go to your home; choose a boon, O auspicious lady, whatever dwells in your heart. (13)
Gaurī said: "Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever shall behold me standing here, may he be endowed with sons and good fortune for seven births. (14)
"Whoever performs singing, instrumental music, and dance before me, may there be no misfortune in his lineage through your grace. (15)
"Having first worshipped me, he who then worships with devotion the linga installed by me shall go to the supreme state. (16)
"O Lord, his name shall become renowned as Gaurīśvara. Having thus made my promise, I remained established in that place.
O Great Goddess, with a joyful inner soul, together with the Goddess, even now, when either the northern or the southern solstice has arrived. (18)
One reaches the abode of Gaurī, endowed with divine qualities; and he who bestows excellent fruits upon the Brahmins there on that day shall have sons. (19)
But that woman who is childless, if she offers a coconut, shall quickly obtain a son who is strong and endowed with auspicious marks.
O Great Goddess, whatever woman offers a lamp there with ghee and a red wick, for as many threads as that wick possesses [she shall obtain her desire].
For that long she shall obtain good fortune even in other births.
She who performs a dance there, endowed with supreme devotion, shall remain for a long time possessed of health, happiness, and good fortune. (23)
At its end is a very great pool, a sacred ford filled with clear water; whoever performs an ablution there is liberated from all sins.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there with devotion, dedicated to the ancestors, that partaker of merit goes to the supreme abode together with his ancestors.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony there; one should keep a vigil at night with songs, instrumental music, dances, and the like.

And there, clothing for a married couple should be given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). O Goddess, whoever recites this daily, and especially on the third lunar day (tṛtīyā) in the presence of Pārvatī, shall attain good fortune.
Or whoever, being fully devoted to devotion, should listen with faith, he too shall obtain good fortune for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt. (28)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaurī’s Penance Grove," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: "Where is that supreme Liṅga known as Gaurīśvara, which was mentioned by you? Where does that Liṅga reside, and what fruit is obtained when it is worshipped? (1)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the greatness of the god Gaurīśvara, who indeed bestows all desires and is the destroyer of sins. 2.
O Goddess, this penance grove, renowned for its great splendor, belongs to Gaurī; it extends for fifty-five bows in circumference all around.
There, in the center, stands the goddess Ekapadā, endowed with ascetic power; to her north, O Goddess, is situated a certain place facing the northeast.

At the four corners of the bow stands a Liṅga that removes the fear of sin. That man who, endowed with devotion, worships that Liṅga with devotion—especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight—shall be liberated from all transgressions.
In this regard, they praise the gift of a cow and gold to the best of the twice-born; however, the gift of food is especially recommended for the pacification of all sins.
Whether one is a killer of a cow, a slayer of a Brahmin, or even a doer of evil deeds, one shall be liberated from all sins by the sight of that Liṅga.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaurīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Varuṇeśvara, situated twenty bow-lengths to the southeast of Gaurī’s penance grove. This Liṅga of great power was indeed installed by Varuṇa. || 1 ||
O Goddess, when the ocean was previously drunk by the pot-born one, Varuṇa, the lord of rivers, was then consumed with anger.
Then, having recognized that the Prābhāsika field was indeed Kāmika, he performed there, O Goddess, a penance that is exceedingly difficult to practice.
Having installed the great liṅga, he worshipped it with devotion for more than ten thousand years; thus was the Bull-bannered Lord worshipped.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, being pleased, he filled that empty ocean, the lord of aquatic creatures, with the waters of his own Gaṅgā.
He entreated that Liṅga with manifold requests for boons; from that very moment, all those oceans became completely filled.
From that time forward, that Liṅga became known by the name Varuṇeśvara.
O beautiful goddess, what indeed is the purpose of seeing many other lingas? By beholding Varunesha alone, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
If one bathes [the deity] with its curd on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, that person becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of beautiful countenance, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, as well as the mute, the blind, the deaf, children, women, and eunuchs [all attained success]. (10)

Having seen it, O Goddess, those devoted to righteousness go to heaven. Whatever bathing, recitation, offering, oblation, worship, hymn, or dance one performs at that place, all of it becomes inexhaustible. || 11 ||
A man who desires the full fruit of a successful pilgrimage, as well as one who seeks heaven, should likewise cause a golden lotus and pearls to be given there.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Varuṇeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga situated right there, located three bow-lengths to the south of Varuṇeśa.
O lady of beautiful countenance, Uṣā, the wife of Varuṇa, being overwhelmed by grief for her husband, performed most severe penance. || 2 ||
That great Liṅga was established, bestowing all spiritual perfections; it is renowned as Uṣeśvara and is worshipped by all who seek perfection.
Whoever worships that sin-destroying Liṅga with devotion, even if burdened by a multitude of great sins, shall attain the supreme goal. || 4 ||
It bestows the fruit of good fortune upon women and destroys suffering and misfortune.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Uṣeśvara," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: One should behold Vighneśa stationed right there, clothed in water, for the destruction of all obstacles and for the successful accomplishment of all undertakings. (1)

O Great Goddess, Varuṇa worshipped him with devotion using water-born flowers so that his ascetic penance would remain free from obstacles; therefore, he is remembered as Jalavāsa (the Water-Dweller).

On the fourth [lunar day], one should offer libations with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and sweetmeats; according to the measure of one's devotion, the Lord of the Gaṇas shall be pleased with that person.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jalavāsa-Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Kumāreśvara, a linga of great power that indeed destroys even the most heinous sins.
O Goddess, it is situated thirty bows' length from Varuṇa in the south-west; O Goddess, it is located to the south of Gaurī’s penance grove.
O Great Goddess, having performed great penance there, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) installed a great liṅga; therefore, it became known as Kumāreśa. || 3 ||
Whoever worships him with devotion continuously for one month acquires that merit which arises from six months of worship. || 4 ||
If one should worship according to the prescribed rite even once, one obtains in a single day all that merit which is gained from the worship of Kumāreśa performed throughout [one's life]. || 5 ||
Having abandoned desire, anger, greed, passion, and envy, and having become a celibate ascetic, one should worship him even once.
O Goddess, when she has been thus worshipped, one obtains the full fruit of a successful pilgrimage.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kumāreśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Śākalyeśvara, situated thirty bow-lengths to the northwest of Daityasūdana.
O Great Goddess, it was worshipped by Śākalya and grants all desires; it is there that the royal sage named Śākalya performed great austerities.
Having propitiated Mahādeva, he brought Bhava into his direct perception; he caused that gracious Maheśvara to descend into the liṅga.
O lady of beautiful hips, when he is seen, the sins committed by men over seven lifetimes perish quickly, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
There, on the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], one should bathe Śiva with milk and worship him according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order.
Gold should be given there by those desiring the full fruit of their pilgrimage; hear from me as I recount its four names. (6)
O Goddess, in the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, Bhairaveśvara was celebrated; thereafter, O beloved, he was perfectly propitiated by Sāvarṇi Manu.
In the Tretā age, it was known by the name Sāvarṇikeśvara; then, O Goddess, in the Dvāpara age, the bull-bannered Lord in the form of a Liṅga was properly propitiated there by the high-souled Gālava.
The third [manifestation] of that deity is known as Gālaveśvara; indeed, when the Kali age had arrived, there was a sage named Śākalya.
Where one attains perfection and the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, that fourth [state] is therefore renowned by the name Śākalyeśvara.
Thus has been glorified the name of that Liṅga as "Cāturyuga," which destroys the sins of men, bestows merit, and grants all desires when it is praised.
O beloved, listen now to the origin of the sacred field of that very God of gods.
O Goddess, it is eighteen dhanus in circumference all around; O Goddess, it removes great sins for those residing in that sacred field.
It grants liberation even to worms, insects, moths, and animals; wherever water from wells and other sources is known as being of the Sarasvatī, [that place is sacred].
Having bathed here or there, a man is glorified in the heavenly world [as if he had performed] a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
One obtains that fruit simply by beholding that Liṅga; this applies to one who, having arrived at the Soma festival, is pure and self-controlled. || 16 ||
O Dear One, one should properly recite the Aghora mantra accompanied by oblations of clarified butter, staying near that linga for the duration of a month.
O lady of excellent complexion, even one joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) or joined with minor sins (upapātaka), attains all supreme perfection. 18.
That Liṅga is remembered as Kāmika, bestowing the fruits of all desires; there resides the great and terrible Aghora face of the God.
Formerly, it was renowned on earth by the name Bhairaveśvara; however, now that this age has arrived, it is known by the name Śākalyeśvara.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga Śākalakaleśvara, situated sixty dhanus to the southwest of Śākalyeśvara.
That [place], enriched by the names of the four yugas, is remembered as the destroyer of sins; formerly it was named Kāmeśvara, and in the Tretā age it was Pulaheśvara.
In the Dvāpara age he is remembered as Siddhinātha, while in the Kali age he is known as Nāradeśa; likewise, his name Kalakaleśa is also proclaimed for that very same [deity].
And at that time, when the highly fortunate Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, arrived at the greatly meritorious ocean—joyful and contented—at the sound of those waters of the high-souled sea, || 4 ||
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, the Rishis, the Siddhas, and the Charanas, raised a tumultuous, hair-raising clamor there. || 5 ||
By that great sound, my form arose; therefore, it is celebrated as the Linga named Kalkaleśvara.

Thus I have related to you the account of the past and the cause of my name; now, however, I shall fully explain to you how Kalakaleshvara was born once again—listen with an attentive mind, O beloved.
Formerly, at the junction of the Dvāpara age when the Kali age had entered, Nārada arrived at the auspicious Prābhāsika field and performed severe penance there in the vicinity of the Liṅga.

Then, when a hundred years had passed, having propitiated the Bull-bannered Lord and attained mastery over the Gandharva art adorned with the seven musical notes, O Goddess of the Gods, [he became a master].
Then, with a joyful mind, he performed near that liṅga the great sacrifice known as the Pauṇḍarīka.
For the sake of pleasing the God of gods, he, whose self was always cultivated, summoned thousands of sages there from the world of Brahmā.
Then, having gathered all the necessary materials and being provided with the implements for sacrifice, he prepared the sacrificial pit and everything else, and subsequently commenced the ritual.
Then, O fair-faced one, when that sacrifice had reached completion, || 13 ||
Then, O Great Goddess, hundreds and thousands of Brahmins residing in that sacred field arrived there from all directions for the sake of receiving sacrificial fees.
Then, filled with curiosity, he indeed scattered jewels and gold upon the ground there for the very purpose of their battle.
Then all those Brahmins, fighting with one another out of a desire for much wealth, raised a great clamor. || 16 ||
O Goddess, some were naked and had discarded their sacred threads; some were seen with disheveled hair, while others were drenched in blood. (17)
Others struck one another with their fists and likewise with their feet; thus was that wealth which had been cast there by Nārada then scattered.
Now, however, in the absence of wealth, those Brahmins who possess nothing at all—though endowed with learning and humility—are worn out by other Brahmins. || 19 ||
Being greatly pacified, they said to him who was smiling again and again: "O Sage, since this gift was given by you for the sake of a quarrel..."
Having abandoned those endowed with knowledge and having discarded the sacrificial ritual, for that reason, O Sage, his name became famous as Kalakaleśvara.
"O best of the twice-born, by that name this Liṅga shall become known; for this reason, O Goddess, it has come to be called Kalakaleśvara. (22)
The man who, having bathed that [liṅga] with devotion, performs three circumambulations, shall undoubtedly go to the world of Rudra through your grace. (23)
He who worships that [liṅga] with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and ointments, and having given gold to the twice-born, shall go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kalakaleśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Near that very God of gods, there shines a pair of highly meritorious liṅgas installed by Lakulīśa.
There is indeed one named Lakuleśvara belonging to that pair of liṅgas; having seen that unsurpassed pair of liṅgas of the God of gods, [one attains liberation]. || 2 ||
One is liberated from all sins committed from birth until the end of death; O beloved, this occurs there on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having become intent on fasting, he who performs a night vigil after fully worshipping the greatly radiant Lakulīśa in his embodied form, [attains the highest state].

Then, having duly worshipped those two lingas separately there according to the prescribed ritual, with the complete performance of worship and hymns and mantras in their proper sequence, he goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara resides.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Two Lakulīśa Liṅgas Situated Near Kalakaleśvara," within the "Greatness of Someśvara" section of the first part, the "Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 76 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Uttaṅkeśvara, situated not very far away on the southern side of that very place, established with devotion by the high-souled Uttaṅka himself.
Having seen that, O Great Goddess, and having touched it with a well-concentrated mind, one who worships according to the rules with devotion is liberated from all sin.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Uttankeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Vaiśvānareśvara, situated five bow-lengths away in the south-eastern corner of that very place.
It destroys the sins of all living beings through both sight and touch. O Goddess, formerly a certain parrot had built a nest there.
Dwelling in the palace together with his wife, he remained there for a very long time; thereafter, that couple performed circumambulations daily.
O Goddess, it was solely due to the power of their nest and not by any means out of devotion; after a long time, those two met their death.
By that power, they were born on earth as those who remembered their former births, and they attained supreme renown by the names Lopāmudrā and Agastya.
Then this verse was sung by the high-souled Agastya, who, remembering his former body, was filled with wonder born of that experience.
He who, having properly performed a circumambulation, gazes upon the Lord of Fire, will surely attain renown, just as I did here in former times.
Thus, O Goddess, the majesty of the deity Agni has been declared to you; when heard, it removes the sins of men and bestows the fruits of all desires. (8)
Having bathed him with ghee according to the prescribed rite, one should indeed worship him; O best of Brahmins, one should also give gold, being fully endowed with perfect faith.
By performing it in this manner according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the full fruit of the pilgrimage; having reached the world of Agni, one rejoices for an imperishable time.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vaiśvānareśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Lakulisha, who possesses great splendor; he is situated at a distance of seven bow-lengths to the west of that place.
The Lord, the destroyer of the sins of all living beings, peaceful and established in a physical form, arrived at that great sacred field (mahākṣetra) from Kāyāvarohaṇa. || 2 ||
Having performed severe penance there and having initiated his own disciples—Kuśaka and the other three—he spoke many scriptures to them.
Having attained supreme perfection through the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and other systems, the man who, having understood this correctly, worships him [properly], [attains the highest goal]. || 4 ||
Especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, or during the northern solstice, one should likewise bestow the gift of knowledge upon a virtuous Brāhmaṇa.
For seven births, he is born into a noble family of a wealthy Brahmin as one who is intelligent, wise, and prosperous—thus again and again.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Lakulīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: To the east of that very place, to the west of Daityasūdana, is a Liṅga that destroys sins, renowned by the name Gautameśvara.
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, that which is situated at Pañcakadhanus grants all desires; it was indeed propitiated by Śalya, the King of Madra.
Then, having propitiated Maheśvara by performing severe penance, any other man who likewise propitiates him [shall obtain the same].
He shall attain supreme perfection, just as the high-minded Śalya did, who bathed [the deity] with milk on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Then one should worship with scented water and the finest flowers; likewise, by worshipping according to the rules with devotion, one shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O Goddess, whatever sin has been committed through speech, mind, or action—all that is destroyed by the sight of that Liṅga.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gautameśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Lord of Gods, the slayer of the Daityas, who destroys the sins of all living beings residing in the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Established since the beginningless age, auspicious and bestowing all desires, it stands like a boat for crossing over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
O Goddess of the gods, all other things perish at the end of a kalpa during the day of Brahmā, with the exception of these and the banyan tree, which lasts for seven kalpas.
The wish-fulfilling tree, likewise the celestial abode, the supreme mountain of lapis lazuli, the divine Śrī Daityasūdana, and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
O beautiful lady, these are inexhaustible and imperishable for seven kalpas. O Goddess, what is the use of speaking much more, or describing it again and again? (5)
O Goddess, there is no other deity on earth besides the illustrious Śrī Daityasūdana; even the mere shape of his [footprint] destroys the sins of the field.
O beautiful lady, I shall describe the boundaries of that sacred field of Viṣṇu, which is frequented by ṛṣis, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and uragas.
To the east lies Yameśvara, and to the west, Śrīsomeśa; Viśālākṣī is to the north, while the Lord of Rivers (the Ocean) is to the south.
This Vaiṣṇava field, shaped like a barley grain, is the destroyer of sins.
But those men who die in this field, even if they are sinners, all certainly go to heaven just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.

O beloved, whatever is given here as a gift, offered in sacrifice, recited as a mantra, performed as austerity, or whatever else is done—all that is declared to be inexhaustible for the duration of seven kalpas.
O Goddess, whoever shall feed even a single Brāhmaṇa there according to the prescribed rite, dedicating it to Viṣṇu, it becomes as if ten million have been fed.

In that place, whatever man performs a fast endowed with devotion, by that single fast he obtains the fruit of ten thousand fasts. Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a man who is self-controlled and observes a fast [attains this merit]. || 13 ||
On the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, one should give gold to Brahmins after worshipping Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rites; thus, one is liberated from all sins.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, why was the name 'Daityasūdana' proclaimed for him? At what time did this occur? Tell me that in detail. (15)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the sin-destroying majesty of the God who slays the Daityas, a great and exalted account of what occurred in the past. 16.
O Goddess, his very names indeed change from kalpa to kalpa; though they are without beginning or end, they arise again and again.
In the first kalpa he was Śriyāvṛtta, in the second Vāmana; in the third he was indeed Vajrāṅga, and in the fourth Kamalāpriya.
In the fifth [kalpa], he is the Remover of Suffering; in the sixth, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama); and in the seventh kalpa, the Lord is remembered as the Slayer of the Daityas (Śrīdaityasūdana).
I shall now relate, according to the truth, the name and the origin of that very [work]. || 20 ||

Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, all the deities, having been utterly defeated by the dānavas—the thorns of the gods—went for refuge to Hari; standing bowed down, they offered praise to the Lord who dwells in the Ocean of Milk.
The gods said: Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World, crusher of Daityas and Asuras! Having assumed the form of a boar, the earth was lifted up by you.
In the form of a fish, the Vedas were recovered from the midst of the ocean; likewise, having assumed the form of a tortoise, he performed the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Having performed this, O Lord of the World, Śrī has been uplifted by you; salutations be to you! You are the Lord of Śrī, the Bearer of Śrī, the God who destroys the suffering of the afflicted. (24)
Bali was bound by you, the enemy of the asuras, in the form of a dwarf; the great daitya Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu were slain.
In the form of Narasiṃha, you sustained the intermediate space; O Great God, the root of the gods, the world was uplifted by you.
Without you, O Lord of the World, the universe has been rendered lusterless, as if the sun had been overcome by the darkness of the Dānavas. (27)
O Goddess, having heard this hymn, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, awakened by the Ocean of Milk, spoke to the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
"O gods, abandon all fear toward the Dānavas; in a very short time, I shall slay the Dānavas. (29)
Having spoken thus, Janārdana then went along with them and struck down the Dānavas one by one with his discus.
Afflicted by fear, all the Dānavas became intent on flight; having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, they turned toward the ocean.
Seeing the Daityas being destroyed, he [Viṣṇu], the destroyer of the Daityas, struck all those Dānavas without exception with his discus.
When all the Daityas had been slain by the gods, brahmins, and ascetics, there was prosperity there; the world was secure and free from agitation.
