From that time on, the name "Daityasūdana" (Slayer of the Daityas) belonged to the Lord. O beautiful one, this incomparable majesty of the god Daityasūdana—his great fortune and his great exaltation—has been recounted to you.
Having seen it, O fair-faced one, for seven births one is born neither dull-witted, nor blind, nor poor, nor suffering; this is the truth, the absolute truth. (35)
Having diligently observed the meritorious Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, the auspicious Aṣṭamī of Rohiṇī, and the festivals of the Lord’s lying down and rising, a man [attains great merit]. || 36 ||
By fasting on each single day, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand fasts in the presence of the Slayer of the Daityas; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Whether he be a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or even one born of an animal womb, upon the relinquishing of his life there, he shall attain the world of Acyuta.
On the full moon day of both Kārttika and Vaiśākha, one should fast for one month, remaining focused on the Slayer of the Daityas (Viṣṇu) and endowed with perfect faith.
By means of each individual fast, one obtains separately the fruit of ten million times ten million; all that fruit is gained through the power of Viṣṇu’s sacred field.
Whoever offers a lamp there for a month or even for a fortnight, by the gift of each single lamp, shall obtain the fruit of ten million lamps. (41)
Having bathed the four-armed God of gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having worshipped him while fasting on the eleventh day, one becomes Acyuta.
Keśava is pleased with him who, according to the prescribed rule and with self-restraint, spends the four months in the presence of the Slayer of the Daityas.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the Cāturmāsya vows millions of times in other sacred fields, all that fruit is obtained simply from the sight of the Slayer of the Daityas.
Whatever merit one might obtain by giving away the entire universe, one acquires all that merit simply from the sight of the Slayer of the Daityas. || 45 ||
But that man who performs a vigil there on the eleventh day with songs, dances, musical instruments, and various such spectacles, goes to the world of Viṣṇu, from which one does not return.
Tens of thousands of murders and countless thefts of gold committed here in the past—all these are destroyed by anyone, O auspicious lady, through keeping vigil at night. (47)

Neither the paths to the city of the departed spirits, nor the messengers, nor that forest with its sword-leaved trees exist for those men who have passed the night in wakefulness; even in their dreams they do not behold them. (48)

One who, with the intent of fulfilling his own duty, gives a thousand maidens adorned with jewels according to the prescribed rites, or a thousand cows in Kurujāṅgala, attains a result superior even to those who keep the vigil for Viṣṇu. (49)
And having observed a fast, he who eats on the twelfth day the food offering mixed with Tulasī destroys ten million sins of killing.
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you this sin-destroying majesty of the God who slays the Daityas; what else do you wish to ask? 51.
One should cause yellow garments, a cow, and gold to be given to the deity; having bathed in the excellent Cakra-tīrtha, one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrī Daityasūdana," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 81 ||
The Goddess said: "O Bull-bannered One, what is this name 'Cakratīrtha' that you have mentioned? Where is that tīrtha situated, and what is its power? Tell me. (1)
Īśvara said: Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, Janārdana, having slain the Daityas, washed his discus there, which was stained with blood.

Having personally brought eighty million excellent holy fords (*tīrtha*) there, Hari established them at that sacred site after performing purification with the Sudarśana [discus]. He even gave the name to the holy ford, which is known as Cakratīrtha.
Eighty-eight thousand and eighty million sacred fords (tīrthas) are present there at Cakratīrtha, O Great Goddess; of this there is no doubt.
The best of men who, with one-pointed mind, performs a bath there, obtains the entire fruit of bathing at all sacred fords.
O fair-faced one, eighty million sacred fords (tīrthas) reside there, especially on the eleventh lunar day as well as during lunar and solar eclipses.
Having bathed there, O Great Goddess, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices. Listen as I tell you its various names. (7)
In the first kalpa it was Koṭitīrtha; in the second, Śrīnidhāna; in the third, Śatadhāra; and in the fourth, Cakratīrtha.
Thus, all those past conceptual names have indeed been told; in this same manner, other [names] should be understood by the wise in their proper sequence.
Therein, the number of gifts that are given is beyond measure; for the sacred field of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be half a krośa in extent.

The murder of a Brahmin shall not approach him; this which I have spoken is the truth. He who fasts for a month in that sacred field, who maintains the sacred fire, and who is firm in his vows—[for him there is no sin]. (11)

He was devoted to Vedic study and performed sacrifices; he practiced austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, offered water with sesame seeds to the ancestors, and performed the Śrāddha rites according to the prescribed rules.
Whether it be a fast for one night or three nights, the *kṛcchra* penance, the *sāṃtapana*, a month-long fast, or any other such meritorious deed; || 13 ||
Whatever a person performs after reaching the sacred field of the Enemy of the Daityas, that merit shall become ten million times greater than at any other field; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires the full fruit of a proper pilgrimage and seeks purification from all sins should cause the gift of a cow to be given there at the excellent Sudarśana Tīrtha.
Whether he be a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or even one born of an animal womb, if he dies at that sacred ford, he shall duly attain the world of Acyuta.
Thus has been briefly declared the majesty arising from Cakratīrtha, which destroys all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. (17)

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin and Greatness of Cakratīrtha in Connection with the Greatness of Daityasūdana," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 82 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the north of that place to Yogeśvarī, the Great Goddess, who bestows the fruit of the perfections of yoga.
I shall proclaim its origin; listen with faith. Of old, there was a tiger among the Dānavas named Mahiṣa, who possessed great strength.
O Goddess, he became the most excellent [of beings], causing fear to all the gods; able to assume any form at will, he made the three worlds subject to his will and lived in happiness.
Then, at a certain time, a captivating maiden was created by Brahmā, the creator of the world, whose beauty was peerless even in heaven.
That beautiful maiden, being virtuous, performed severe penance; she was then seen by Nārada once, O lady of excellent countenance.
Then, O Goddess, he was suddenly struck with the utmost wonder: "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what splendor! Oh, what youth! (6)
Thinking thus, he spoke these words to the woman there: "Grant me your own self; I have no wife. O Goddess, from the mere sight of you, I am tormented by the arrow of desire. (7)
She said, "O best of beings, I have no need for the dharma of desire; having undertaken the vow of maidenhood, I shall accomplish what I desire. (8)
"And you must not entertain any anger whatsoever regarding this matter. O beloved, having heard those words of hers, that sage Nārada—
He went to the divine city protected by Mahiṣa at the edge of the ocean; for that sage was honored by the high-souled Mahiṣa.

Having inquired after her well-being, O Goddess, and having offered the most excellent *arghya*, he, with palms joined in reverence, said: "Tell me the reason for your arrival; whatever you have resolved upon, I shall do it all, O Nārada. (11)
Then the sage spoke there to Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas: "O great Asura, a jewel of a maiden has been born in Jambūdvīpa."
Neither in heaven, nor among mortals, nor in the netherworld have I seen, nor have I ever heard of, such a form as that by which I have been brought under the sway of the arrows of Love. (13)
Having heard those words of his which were supremely provocative of desire, he went to where that virtuous woman was situated in the Prābhāsika field.
Surrounded by a great force, he sought her out and said: "O timid one, become my wife and enjoy delightful pleasures! O illustrious lady, this asceticism is ill-suited to your youth. (15)
Having heard those words of his, the woman of excellent complexion laughed; O Goddess of the Gods, as she was laughing, [tears] flowed by the hundreds and thousands.
From her breath, fearsome women with weapons in their hands suddenly emerged; by them, the army of the wicked-souled Mahiṣa was utterly destroyed. || 17 ||
While that army was being struck down, the best of the Dānavas became enraged and quickly advanced toward her.
For he was repeatedly shaking those two terrifying, sharp-horned [weapons]; and having engaged in a very great battle with her, the great asura—
With her two horns, she seized the goddess, who stood upon him; then, having trampled him with her feet, the preeminent Daitya was slain by the spear.
When his head was severed by the sword, a man of that same form emerged; though he was fierce, that Daitya, struck down by the weapon of the Goddess, went to heaven.
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Mahendra, beholding Mahisha utterly defeated, offered praise to the Goddess with hearts full of satisfaction.

The gods said: "Obeisance to you, O Goddess, highly fortunate one, profound, of terrifying appearance, established in policy, possessing well-established conclusions, three-eyed, and facing in all directions. (23)

O Goddess who art both knowledge and ignorance, the conqueror, the one to be recited, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura; O omnipresent one, sovereign of all sciences, O Goddess whose very nature is the universe! 24.
O Goddess who is free from sorrow, eternal, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, whose nature is pure, established in vows, fierce in form, and radiant! 25.

O Goddess who bestows supernatural powers and accomplishments, O you who dance at the end of time, O you who delight in fortitude; O Śāṅkarī, O Brāhmaṇī, O Brāhmī, you who are saluted by all the gods! || 26 ||
O you who hold a bell in your hand, who hold a trident in your hand, O crusher of the great buffalo! O you of fierce form, O odd-eyed one, O great illusion, O immortal one, O auspicious one!

O omnipresent one, O goddess who dwells in all, O you who arise from the essence of all beings! O mother of the sciences, the Purāṇas, and the piercing arrows [of knowledge], O sustainer of all creatures! || 28 ||
O auspicious Goddess, you alone are the refuge for all the secrets of the gods and for all living beings; you are the knowledge and the ignorance, the fortune and the misfortune.
Thus praised by the gods and likewise by the sages, O Goddess, she bowed down and, smiling, spoke these words: "Choose an excellent boon."
The gods said: O Goddess, may those best of men who praise you here with this hymn be forever filled with all their desires, raining down boons continuously. (31)
"O lady of pure smiles, you must always make your dwelling in this field."
"So be it," said that goddess to the gods, O fair-faced one; and having dismissed the hosts of sages, she remained absorbed right there.

O fair-faced one, he who, intent on fasting, beholds her with devotion on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja—his sin goes to destruction, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (34)
The man who, having risen early in the morning, recites this hymn, shall indeed experience no fear for as long as he lives. (35)

The eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja that is conjoined with the Mūla asterism is called Mahānāmikā; those whose lives depart on that auspicious day [attain the highest state].
Their residence in heaven is certain; those heroes are beloved by the Apsarases. || 37 ||
O Goddess of the gods, this very sequence is proclaimed for all Manvantaras and at the beginnings of Kalpas; now hear the specific detail.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, which destroys all sins, one should worship at night the [deity] adorned with sword-mantras.

There, the twice-born should cause a pavilion to be constructed, measuring nine or seven cubits, on a site sloping toward the east and north, adorned with banners; he should have it made according to the prescribed rite in the presence of Yogīśvarī.
In the southeast, one should cause a very beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made, measuring one cubit, provided with three girdles and a yoni shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).

Then, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered as an oblation according to the scriptures and accompanied by mantras. Thereafter, having bathed the sword with the essence of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), it should be worshipped with various flowers preceded by mantras by the best of the twice-born.

The fearless one, the slaughterer, the sword, the living being, the unassailable, the inaccessible, victory itself, and likewise the support of dharma—these are your eight names spoken by the Creator himself. (43)
The Kṛttikā constellation is yours; the god Maheśvara is your preceptor; gold is your body; and the god Janārdana is your creator. O God, as father and grandfather, protect yourself always.

Thus ends the mantra for the sword. Having thus worshipped that sword according to the prescribed rite with the most excellent Brahmins, one should cause it to be paraded through the city at night, preceded by the sounding of festive drums (nāndī).

Accompanied by his entire army and the foremost of Brahmins, having thus performed the ritual procedure, he should lead her back to Yogīśvarī; having recited the mantra in this manner, he should indeed present the sword to her.
Having adorned it with collyrium and anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should offer a garland made of bilva leaves to that Goddess.
O Durgā, O Goddess who removes the suffering of distress, O destroyer of all misfortunes! Protect me in all difficulties; O Durgā, I have come to you for refuge. (48)
O Goddess of the gods, having thus offered this arghya, one should keep watch over the sword there, worshipping it daily according to the prescribed rite until the eighth day.
Having kept a vigil that night, at dawn, at the rising of the sun, one should place before [the deity] goats and rams with their necks severed.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with jars filled with fermented liquor, according to one's desire, whether by the hundreds, or fifty, or even half of that.
That should be given to the Kāpālikas, as well as to the male and female servants; then, at the time of afternoon on the ninth day, she [should be placed] upon a chariot.

The king himself, accompanied by his own army, should cause the Mistress of Yoga to be paraded through the kingdom, amidst the sounding of conchs and drums and the chanting of young brahmins and bards.
O beautiful lady, one should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits with this mantra, consisting of blood, water, and cooked rice, combined with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Three times, one should scatter the offering with a trident toward the cardinal and intermediate directions: "May these gods—the Ādityas and the Vasus—accept the offering. (55)
May the Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas be gracious; may the spirits and the departed ancestors be satisfied and bringers of happiness. (56)

O Goddess of the gods, by the grace of Yogīśvarī, neither enemies, nor fire, nor thieves, nor Vināyakas shall create obstacles for those Brāhmaṇas residing in the sacred field who undertake their journey in this manner. || 57 ||
Those men who are constant devotees of Yogīśvarī become happy, enjoyers of wealth, and entirely free from all afflictions. (58)
Thus has this great festival of the Mistress of Yoga been fully described to you; it destroys all inauspiciousness for those who read it and those who hear it. (59)

Having worshipped on the ninth day Durgā—who stands upon the broad back of the demon Mahiṣāsura pierced by the tip of her trident, and whose staff-like arms are adorned with beautiful armlets and upraised swords—mortal beings cross over even the most difficult and impenetrable thickets, accompanied by the Five-faced One (Śiva).

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Yogeśvarī," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 83 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Ādinārāyaṇa Hari; situated to the east of that [place], he is the destroyer of all sins.
O Goddess, in the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a Daitya named Meghavāhana, who was endowed with sandals and a throne and was the destroyer of all the Daityas.

Possessing great strength and a massive body extending ten thousand yojanas, he was invincible to all the gods and the destroyer of the three worlds; O fair-faced one, a boon was granted to him by Brahmā when he was pleased.
When Viṣṇu slays you in battle with his wooden sandal, at that very moment your death shall come; there is no other way for your death to occur.
Having thus obtained the boon, that Daitya tormented the earth for ten million eons, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Having tormented [the world] in many ways, O Goddess, Dakṣiṇa arrived at Dadhi; there he indeed laid waste to the hermitages of the sages.
Then all those sages, their hermitage circles laid to waste, sought refuge in Keśava, the God of gods; and recognizing him as invincible, they praised the one who has Garuḍa upon his banner.
The sages said: Salutations to the one who is the source of supreme auspiciousness, to the master of self-yoga, to the divine Janārdana, to Śrīdhara, and to the Creator.
Salutations to Keśava, who wears a golden crown with lotus filaments, who is exceedingly subtle, and who possesses a vast form; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the Great Soul, the most excellent one, whose navel is a lotus; salutations be to Hari, the remover of illusion, the destroyer of sins, and the creator of the world.
Salutations eternally to Acyuta, the soul who is the cause of the world, the embryo within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations again and again to the infinite one.

Salutations to the Great Soul, the sustainer of the world, who is veiled by the veil of illusion; to the one who provides the boat of knowledge for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra; to the Creator of unimpeded intellect, whose actions consist of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Just as sin is destroyed when the name Vāsudeva is uttered, so may this Daitya Meghavāhana meet his dissolution.
Just as Viṣṇu takes upon himself the sin residing within his devotees, so may this Daitya, the performer of evil deeds, meet his destruction.
Just as Viṣṇu, upon being merely remembered, dispels all evil, so may this Daitya Meghavāhana meet his destruction. 15.
May all blessings be upon the entire world, and may all defects perish, when Vāsudeva—the Supreme Lord of lords, the sustainer of the universe—is remembered with indivisible devotion. (16)

May those living beings on earth, in heaven, in the intermediate space, and in the netherworld—whatever creatures there may be—become endowed with perfection, O best of men, when Vāsudeva, the creator of the world, is remembered. (17)
Whatever living beings exist anywhere here within the cosmic egg, or even beyond it, may they attain supreme and irreproachable perfection by praising Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world. (18)
Īśvara said: O Goddess, having been thus praised, Hari, the primordial Nārāyaṇa, perceiving that future task, mounted his sandals.
The destroyer of sins appeared before those sages; he spoke to all of them as they bowed down, "What is the purpose that resides in your hearts? (20)
"Tell me that, and I shall do it, being gratified by your hymn of praise. || 21 ||
Thus addressed, all the sages stood with their palms joined in reverence; with their heads and necks bowed, they all spoke to Hari, the primordial god. (22)

The sages said: "O Lord, you know everything; there is nothing unknown to you. O Mahādeva, destroy this exceedingly powerful Daitya, so that this entire universe may become free from fear, O Lord. (23)
Having been addressed thus by them, Viṣṇu then summoned the Daitya to battle and struck that Daitya in the heart with his sandal, O auspicious lady. (24)

Slain and deprived of life, that Daitya fell into the great ocean; having killed the foremost of Daityas, the Lord remained stationed at that spot, seated upon his sandals even until today, O lady of beautiful countenance.
That best of men who worships him with devotion on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) attains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and rejoices in heaven like a god.
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by giving a hundred thousand cows to a Brāhmaṇa, that same fruit he shall attain by beholding Govinda, the Primordial God, with devotion.
For those in whom the Lord Ādinārāyaṇa resides within their hearts, even the Kali age is the Kṛta Yuga; for them, their afflictions are surpassed by their abundance of happiness.
Having bathed on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) when it falls on a Sunday, while standing in the water, one who worships Ādinārāyaṇa is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this majesty centered on Viṣṇu as the deity; when heard, it removes the sins of men and destroys the flood of poverty.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ādinārāyaṇa," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The Goddess said: O Bull-bannered Lord, regarding that [tirtha] which was mentioned by you as being present there—how did the great river arrive from Kurukṣetra, O God? What is its power said to be, and what is the fruit of bathing and other rites performed therein?
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe that auspicious place where [the goddess] is ever-present; she destroys the sins of all living beings through both sight and touch.
O Goddess, that great goddess, existing in the form of a river and a mighty stream, is situated three dhanus to the west of Ādinārāyaṇa.
I shall relate it briefly; listen to its origin, O beloved. Out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha, O Goddess, Viṣṇu, together with his attendants, [departed].
Having taken all the Yādavas—the children, the elderly, and the merchants—and having rendered Mathurā empty, he arrived at Prabhāsa.
He requested the ocean for a place as a dwelling; at that very time, however, the Sun, the god of gods, [appeared].
"O Goddess, when the time of the lunar conjunction had arrived, he was seized by Rāhu; seeing this, all the Yādavas fell into the deepest despondency."
When they had not yet reached the place of assembly, Janārdana said to them: "O best of the Yadus, do not despair while I am present."
Behold my power today for the sake of dharma on this earth; I shall properly bring here the Puṇya-sāṃnihita lake.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One entered into a state of meditative absorption; and as Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor was thus contemplating, [the following occurred].
Then, a beautiful stream of water appeared before him, piercing the surface of the earth for the purpose of bathing the enemy of the asuras.
Then, O Great Goddess, all those Yādavas, led by Rāma and Sāmba, performed their ablutions when the sun was seized by Rāhu.
Having fully obtained the fruit of the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra, they indeed became possessors of merit arising from the presence [of the deity].

Thus, O Great Goddess, that merit has been fully attained and is present at the lake. By bathing there when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice in its entirety.
Whoever should feed a Brahmin there with food of six flavors according to the prescribed rite, by feeding just one, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Whoever performs a fire sacrifice there in the vicinity of Sannihitī shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices with each single oblation offered. || 16 ||
If one performs the recitation of mantras while stationed in that place, one obtains the fruit of ten million recitations for each single mantra recited. || 17 ||
Those desiring the fruit of that pilgrimage should give gifts of gold; having bathed, they should worship Janārdana, the Primordial God.
Thus has the fruit been correctly described as being present before you; when heard, O beloved, it removes the sins of men who possess perfect faith.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Saṃnihitī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: To the south of that [Liṅga] stands a Liṅga of great splendor, enriched with the name Pāṇḍaveśvara, which was established in succession by the five [Pāṇḍavas]. || 1 ||
When the Pāṇḍavas, dwelling in the forest, had entered into a life of concealment, they arrived at the sacred site of Prabhāsa on the occasion of their pilgrimage to holy places.
At that time, O Great Goddess, when the lunar festival had arrived, they all assembled together on the bank and installed the Liṅga.
Having appointed Mārkaṇḍa and other preeminent Brahmins as officiating priests, they caused the consecration to be performed according to the Vedic injunctions and presented bulls as gifts.
Then, O beloved, O woman of excellent complexion, the sages headed by Mārkaṇḍeya were pleased because the Liṅga had been installed by the Pāṇḍavas.
The sages said: "Those who shall worship this Liṅga, adored by the Pāṇḍavas, will indeed become worthy of worship even by gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas."
By worshipping them with perfect faith, they shall indeed obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt, by the power of our word.
He who bathes in the Sannihita-kuṇḍa and worships Pāṇḍaveśvara throughout the entire month of Māgha becomes Puruṣottama himself.
Even by the mere sight of him, one's sin is destroyed in a thousand ways; for he is declared to be the very form of Viṣṇu—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pāṇḍaveśvara," within the "Majesty of Saṃnihitī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Having thus performed the pilgrimage endowed with perfect faith, O Great Goddess, a person should then proceed to the eleven Rudras in their proper sequence. (1)
From those situated within the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, which destroy even great sins, whatever eleven kinds of distinct evils have been accumulated by men; || 2 ||
It will come to an end through the worship of the eleven Rudras on the occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), a solstice (ayana), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun. || 3 ||
On other auspicious lunar days as well, one who is purified by right devotion should worship the eleven Rudras in their proper sequence.
I shall declare their names which were in the past; listen, O Goddess, to those that belonged to the first Kṛta Yuga according to the truth.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata; Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara; Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and Aparājita. || 6 ||
O Goddess, in the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, as well as in the Tretā and Dvāpara, but when the Kali Yuga arrived, another name arose once again.
I shall now tell you those eleven forms of the Rudras: Bhūteśa, Nīlarudra, Kapālī, and Vṛṣavāhana; || 8 ||
Tryambaka, Ghoranāman, Mahākāla, Bhairava, Mṛtyuñjaya, Kāmeśa, and he who is celebrated as Yogeśa—these eleven Rudras have been declared in due order, O beloved.
O Goddess, you who are without beginning or end, though divided by distinctions, you exist as separate entities through eleven forms and through the differentiation of distinct names.

The Goddess said: O Blessed One, tell me in detail the sequence of the eleven Liṅgas, according to their locations, boundaries, and divisions, along with the reasons for their origin and their greatness.
O Lord, how are they to be worshipped? What are the mantras, and what ritual is prescribed? On which festival or at what time? Tell me everything in detail. (12)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret that destroys all sins, beginning with Somanātha and culminating in Siddhinātha as the ultimate cause. 13.
Having heard which, a living being is liberated from previously accumulated sins; and those eleven Rudras who were indeed mentioned by me to you, O beloved— (14)
Ten winds have been declared by you, and the self is remembered as the eleventh. I shall state their names; hear from me the names of these winds in their proper order. (15)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 16 ||
And the Self—these are to be known as the successive lords of the Rudras. I shall describe their ritual processions in due order for the welfare of all living beings. (17)
O beloved, he who was formerly Someśvara, the primordial god of the Rudras, should indeed be worshipped according to the prescribed rite by the name Bhūteśvara.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) using a mind purified by faith through the application of royal service, one should worship with the Sadyojāta mantra.

Having meditated with devotion upon the god Sadāśiva with beautiful flowers, and having circumambulated him three times, he prostrated himself before him with all eight limbs touching the ground. || 20 ||

One who desires to undertake the pilgrimage of the eleven Rudras should proceed from there for the sake of being free from obstacles; I shall now tell you that which is proclaimed as its name, "Bhūteśvara. (21)
Since he is remembered as the Lord of that multitude of elements—beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific principles (viśeṣa)—numbering twenty-five; || 22 ||
It is said that in ancient times he was given the name Bhūteśvara; indeed, by knowing the twenty-five principles (tattvas), one attains liberation. || 23 ||

Having fully worshipped Bhūteśa Rudra, one shall indeed attain imperishable liberation. Thus has the glorification of Ādirudra been briefly proclaimed; it is worthy of being glorified by the twice-born, and when glorified, it increases merit. (24)

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Bhūteśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 87 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the second Nīlarudra, situated sixteen dhanus to the north of Bhūteśa.
O Great Goddess, having bathed that Mahāliṅga—which is worshipped by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas—one should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rite with the Īśa-mantra.
One who possesses a well-prepared self, having honored [the deity] with an abundance of white and blue lotuses, should worship him by performing a circumambulation and offering salutations.
Having done this, O Goddess, a man shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice; a bull should be donated right there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage.
In ancient times, the Daitya Antaka, who resembled blue collyrium, was slain; because he caused the women to weep, he is therefore remembered as Nīlarudra.
Its greatness, which destroys sins, has been briefly proclaimed; it should be attained by those endowed with perfect faith and heard by those eager for its vision.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nīlarudra," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 88 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, one should go to the supreme Kapālīśvara, the third Rudra, the destroyer of sins, located to the east of Nīlarudra.
O Goddess, situated seven dhanus to the west of Budheśvara is where, in the past, I severed the fifth head of Brahmā.
With that skull-staff held in his hand, he arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa; thereafter, he remained within the center of that field for a thousand years.
He is remembered as Kapāladhārī (the Skull-bearer), Digvāsas (Clothed in the Quarters), and Kapālī (the Skull-holder); O beloved, I worshipped that Liṅga composed of him for ten thousand years.
Having assumed the form of Kapālin, he is therefore remembered as Kapālīśa; he removes all the sins of men through both sight and touch.
O Goddess, thousands of my hosts, spear in hand, have indeed been appointed there by me for the sake of guarding against sinners of wicked intent.
Therefore, with every effort and endowed with perfect faith, one should worship that Mahādeva, the skull-bearing, the stainless one.
Gold should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, after having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Whatever sin has been accumulated by living beings since birth is destroyed upon seeing that Liṅga at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti period.
Thus, O lady of beautiful countenance, the sin-destroying majesty of the third deity, Kapālirudra, has been briefly proclaimed.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kapālīśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, the seventh book of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the fourth and most excellent Rudra, named Vrishabhesvara, a Kalpa-linga beloved by the gods.
O Great Goddess, where Brahmā himself resides in the form of a child, situated three bow-lengths to the north of that very place.
Indeed, a man devoid of merit does not know that primordial [deity] of great power; I shall now tell you its various conceptual names.
O Great Goddess, in a previous kalpa he was known as Brahmeśvara; O beloved, he was formerly propitiated by Brahmā for ten thousand years.
Then, being pleased by the god who desired to create, Maheśvara [granted his wish], and thereafter the Grandfather (Brahmā) brought about the fourfold creation of beings.
Since Hara attained satisfaction by virtue of being the Lord of Brahmā, that liṅga was formerly known by the name Brahmeśvara.
Then, O lady of excellent complexion, when the second kalpa arrived, it became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Raivateśvara.
In this universe of moving and unmoving beings, there was a king named Raivata; by the power of that liṅga, he conquered this world, which is the source of all existence.
By him, that linga of great splendor was named Raivateśvara; then, O lady of excellent complexion, when the third kalpa arrived once more.
O beautiful lady, that Liṅga came to be known by the name Vṛṣabheśvara; for he who is my very own vehicle, Dharma, assumed the form of a bull.
He worshipped that Liṅga for a thousand divine years; then, O Goddess of Devas, being pleased, he led Vṛṣa to the state of union (sāyujya).
Because of that, it became known as Vṛṣabheśa on the surface of the earth; then, when the fourth kalpa named Vārāha had arrived.
Then, at the beginning of the twenty-eighth Tretā Yuga, there was a king named Ikṣvāku, an ornament of the solar dynasty.
Filled with devotion, he worshipped the Liṅga three times a day; subsisting on a single meal, having conquered his appetite, sleeping upon the ground, and with his senses subdued.
When much time had passed in this manner, Maheśvara was pleased and granted him a most exalted kingdom, as well as progeny consisting of sons and grandsons.
There was a lord named Ikṣvākvīśvara; by him this supreme liṅga [was established]. Whoever worships that god who has the bull as his vehicle with devotion, [attains the highest goal]. (16)
One is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this. Its sacred field extends thirty dhanus in each of its four directions.
Whoever performs bathing, recitation, offering of oblations, fire-sacrifice, worship, and the chanting of hymns at that sacred ford, all of that shall become inexhaustible.
The field within the four corners is thus according to the measure of the *mātrā*; having stayed there for one night in the vicinity of that *liṅga*, [one should perform the rites].

Through the practice of celibacy, he remains awake and is completely liberated from sins; he abides in fire-offerings, silent recitation, and meditative concentration, [unperturbed] by dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the like.
Whether he be a cow-slayer or a killer of a Brahmin, that man is released from his evil deeds who gratifies the Brahmins there with various kinds of foods. (21)
When one Brahmin is fed at [these places], it is as if ten million have been fed: at Bhairava, Kedāra, Puṣkara, and Drutijaṅgama. || 22 ||
Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Mahākāla, and Naimiṣa—O Goddess, these eight sacred sites (tīrthas) are established within that liṅga.

He who keeps a vigil there at night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite, shall obtain the fruit of eight holy pilgrimage sites.
Whoever offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) there in the presence of Śiva when the moon has disappeared, his ancestors remain satisfied until the end of the day of Brahmā.
One should worship that liṅga at night with curd, milk, and ghee, as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), water infused with kuśa grass, saffron, agallochum, and camphor.
Having recited the Aghora mantra and meditated upon the god Sadāśiva, by doing this, O Great Goddess, one is liberated from the five great sins.
If one bathes [the deity] with curd on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, that person is born as a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, if one bathes that Lord of Bulls with milk, he obtains the great fruit of seven thousand cows.
O beloved, O beautiful woman, whatever sin was committed in another birth and whatever is committed now—all that goes to destruction by means of a bath with ghee.
O Goddess, he who bathes Vṛṣabheśvara with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) shall burn away all sins and obtain the fruit of all sacrifices. || 31 ||

Having seen that, even a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a thief, one who violates the teacher’s bed, a slayer of those who have sought refuge, and a betrayer of a friend [are purified]. || 32 ||
One who has practiced wicked and sinful conduct, such as a slayer of mother or father, is liberated from all sins by being intent upon the worship of that Liṅga.
He who worships the great Liṅga Brahmeśvara together with Brahmā throughout the entire month of Kārttika shall be liberated from all sins.

By him everything has been given, by him the gurus have been gratified; by him the śrāddha has been performed at the holy site of Gayā, and by him great austerity has been practiced—by whom this Vṛṣabheśvara, the God of gods, has been worshipped.
Thus, O Goddess, O beautiful lady, I have narrated to you the majesty of the god Vṛṣabheśvara, who is worshipped by the gods and is a Kalpa-liṅga.
O Great Goddess, whether he be a fool or a scholar, whoever hears this majesty of the God of gods attains the supreme goal. (37)

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vṛṣavāhaneśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the seventh book of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 90 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the imperishable Tryambakeśvara; that is declared to be the fifth [Liṅga], the primordial deity of the Rudras. || 1 ||
O beloved, Śikhaṇḍīśvara was known in former times during the Tretā Yuga; today I shall describe how it is recognized by men.
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, there exists Sāṃbapura; situated to the north of that very place is the site known as Kāpālika.
And there resides the Lord named Kapāleśvara, who exists in the form of a *liṅga* for the destruction of the sins of men through being seen or touched.
Therefore, at a distance of sixteen bows in the northeastern direction, the Rudra named Tryambakeśvara himself is stationed there.

The benefactor of all and the bestower of the fruits of all desires, O Goddess, it was here in ancient times that the excellent sage named Guru performed a most terrible and difficult penance, one that was unbearable even for gods and demons.
By whom the leader of mantras, Tryambaka, was recited three crores of times according to the divine rite, after worshipping Śaṅkara at the three periods of the day.
Then, having propitiated the Lord of Gods, he attained divine sovereignty; he himself gave that imperishable deity the name Tryambakeśvara.
Because he attained perfection by chanting the Tryambaka mantra and obtained divine sovereignty endowed with eightfold qualities, he is therefore known as Tryambakeśvara.

Destroying all sins even by sight or touch, the brahmin who recites the *tryambaka* mantra in the presence of Tryambakeśvara attains great perfection; he is indeed Rudra manifest before his eyes. (10)

Moreover, by merely seeing him, one's sin is shattered into a thousand pieces. He who worships him with devotion according to the prescribed rite, established in a state of pure intent, shall be liberated from all sins through the Vāmadeva mantra.
Whoever keeps vigil there during the night on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, through worship, hymns of praise, and sacred discourses, shall obtain his desired fruit.
A cow should be given as a gift at that very place by those who desire the full fruit of their pilgrimage. || 13 ||
Thus, O Goddess, I have narrated to you the sin-destroying majesty of Tryambakeśvara Rudra, which bestows the fruit of merit upon men. 14.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Tryambakeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, the seventh book of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the most excellent Aghoreśvara. It is declared to be the sixth Liṅga; it is remembered as that Bhairava face. || 1 ||
Situated five bow-lengths to the northwest of Tryambakeśvara, it is meritorious, bestows all desires, and destroys the impurities of the Kali age.
That man who worships it with devotion through the successive rites of bathing, offering, and so forth, shall obtain the fruit of giving away the entire Mount Meru.
Whatever is given there while standing before Dakṣiṇāmūrti, all that becomes inexhaustible for the Lord Aghoreśvara. || 4 ||
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there, to the south of Aghoreśvara, his ancestors, being thus gratified, shall remain satisfied for an entire kalpa.
O beloved, what is the use of a śrāddha at the sacred site of Gayā, or what is the use of a horse sacrifice? By performing a śrāddha there, one obtains all that fruit and even more besides.
He who gives even a mere fragment of gold on a pilgrimage obtains the entire fruit of a great gift in abundance.

Whoever performs the Brahmakūrca penance according to the rules on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight of Soma, in the presence of Aghoreśvara, after it has been consecrated with the Aghora mantra—for him, the great expiation for six years shall have been accomplished.
Thus has been briefly declared the great glory of Aghoreśa, whose majesty destroys all sins and, when heard, accomplishes all goals.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Aghoreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, one should go to Mahākāleśvara Hara, situated slightly to the northwest of Aghoreśa.
O Goddess, it has been heard that at a distance of thirty bows lies Pātakanāśana; O Goddess, in the former Kṛta Yuga, Citrāṅgadeśvara was remembered there.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, it is celebrated by the name Mahākāleśvara; the Great Rudra, in the form of Time (Kāla), is established within that liṅga.
The direct teacher of all that moves and is stationary, the destroyer of the pride of gods and demons, who, O beloved, swallows everything within the cosmic egg in the form of the sun.

O Goddess, that god of great splendor is established within that liṅga; he who worships with devotion at dawn that liṅga which is dear to me, by means of the six-syllable mantra, conquers death at that very moment. || 5 ||
Especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, whoever burns guggulu resin mixed with ghee according to the prescribed rite there at the onset of night after having performed worship—
Bhairava forgives even a thousand offenses of his; the great seers praise the gift of a cow at that sacred place.
The giver of a cow surely delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants; so too does he who recites the Śatarudriya on the southern side of the Lord.

A person shall uplift the host of their ancestors and the host of their mothers; having beheld Hara, the Lord of Time (Kāleśvara), they shall wash away all the sin committed in childhood, in old age, or even in youth.
When the northern solstice has arrived, he who performs the Ghṛtakambala rite shall not again obtain a dreadful birth in this cycle of existence.
By beholding Mahākāleśa, one is not born miserable, poor, or unfortunate for seven successive lifetimes. (11)
He is born into a prosperous family endowed with wealth and grain; furthermore, he possesses great devotion to the worship of Mahākāleśvara.
Thus, O beloved, Mahākāleśvara has been described in brief; O Goddess, it was formerly propitiated by the Gaṇa Citrāṅgada.
That Mahākāleśvara lasts for a thousand divine years; therefore, it is renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Citrāṅgadeśvara.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Mahākāleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 93 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Bhairaveśvara, situated ten dhanus away in the south-eastern corner of that very place.
O Goddess, it bestows all desires and destroys the flood of poverty; O beloved, it was formerly known by the name Caṇḍeśvara in the Kṛta Yuga.
O Goddess, there was a group named Caṇḍa; it propitiated [the deity] for a thousand divine years in the past, and for that reason it is known as Caṇḍeśvara. (3)
Having seen that Lord of the Gods of gods and having touched him with a well-composed mind, one is liberated from all sins committed from birth until the end of death.

In that regard, O beloved, he who, having become intent on fasting, performs a night vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
Whatever verbal, mental, or physical evil has been accumulated, all of that comes to destruction by the sight of that Liṅga.
Sesame seeds, gold, and garments should be given there to a wise man by one who desires the full fruit of the pilgrimage for the sake of destroying all sins.
O Goddess of the Gods, because he assumes a terrifying form and seizes the entire universe at the end of the aeon, he is therefore remembered as Bhairava.
In this kalpa, O Great Goddess, Rudra became Bhairava, established in the field of Prabhāsa; at the end of the kalpa, he exists in the form of a liṅga.
Thus has the majesty of Bhairaveśvara been briefly proclaimed; by hearing which, a living being is liberated from most terrible sin.
Īśvara said: From there, O lady of excellent hips, one should go to the Mṛtyuñjayeśvara Liṅga; it is situated ten dhanus away from that very spot, located in the south-eastern corner.
In the west, situated four bow-lengths from Sāgarāditya, it destroys the sins of all living beings through mere sight or even touch.
In a former age, it was known by the name Nandīśvara, where a severe penance was performed by my attendant named Nandin.
Having installed the great liṅga, and being constantly intent upon its worship, the great mantra known as Mṛtyuñjaya was recited there. (4)
O Goddess, when ten billion times a hundred thousand had passed, Maheśvara was pleased and granted him the status of Gaṇeśa as well as liberation in the form of proximity (sāmīpya-mukti).
Since Hara was pleased with him by means of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, that Liṅga became renowned on the surface of the earth as Mṛtyuñjayeśa.
Whoever worships him with devotion, or beholds him with a purified mind, shall destroy even the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes.
One should bathe the Liṅga with milk, and with curd mixed with ghee; one should also bathe it with honey and sugarcane juice, and smear it with saffron.
Then one should worship with fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and uśīra, with the essence of musk, and with flowers.
O Goddess, one should first offer incense before the deity, and then agarwood; having worshipped with various garments according to one's own means, || 10 ||
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) of milk-rice (paramānna) together with a lamp, one should then perform the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta) with devotion.
A gift of gold should be bestowed upon a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
In this way, his journey will be as prescribed by the scriptures; of this there is no doubt. By acting thus, O Goddess, a man obtains the fruit of his birth.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the great majesty of Mṛtyuñjaya, which destroys the sins of all living beings and bestows the fruit of all desires. 14.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mṛtyuñjaya," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 95 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Kāmeśvara, situated three bow-lengths to the north of that very spot; it was renowned as Ratīśvara during the Tretā age, O Sovereign of the Gods.
O fair-faced one, when this is seen and worshipped by men, the sins of seven lifetimes are destroyed and there shall be no ruin of their home.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, by whom was this [liṅga] established, and why is it called Ratīśvara? What is the merit gained from beholding it? Tell me everything in detail. (3)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate the story that destroys all sins. There was a virtuous and illustrious woman named Rati, the wife of Kāma. || 4 ||
Formerly, when the mind-born god (Kāma) had been burnt by the Lord, the enemy of Tripura, Rati indeed performed penance in that region for his sake.
O beloved, standing on the tip of her big toe for the duration of four yugas, she propitiated Mahādeva with a tranquil mind.
Then, at a certain time, O beloved, having pierced through the surface of the earth, a Liṅga of Maheśvara rose up before him.
At that very moment, O lady of beautiful countenance, an incorporeal voice suddenly spoke, gladdening her heart.
"Since this Māheśvara Liṅga has suddenly arisen through your devotion, you should worship it, O highly fortunate lady; thereby you shall obtain a beloved husband."
Having heard these words spoken by the divine messenger, that virtuous woman, endowed with supreme devotion, worshipped that liṅga.
Then, O beloved, Kāma arose like one waking from sleep; from that time forth, that liṅga has been known as Kāmeśvara.
Then she, the beloved of Kāma, being delighted by the attainment of her desire, spoke these words in the presence of the flower-bowed god.
And those others who, with concentrated minds, shall worship this linga, they too shall attain their desired success and, furthermore, reach the state of the righteous.
Whatever is desired by the mind, even if it be difficult to attain, they shall obtain it all through the grace of this Liṅga; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Rati, her desires fulfilled, departed for her own abode with Kāma, her inner soul filled with great joy.
Whoever worships him on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra shall possess all desires; this which has been heard bestows good fortune upon men.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kāmeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eleven Rudras" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Yogeśvara, situated at a distance of seven bows to the northwest of Kāmeśa. || 1 ||
Indeed, this Liṅga of great power destroys sins by its mere sight; in a former age, it was reckoned and known as Gaṇeśvara.
O Goddess, in former times my innumerable hosts of great power, having recognized Prabhāsa as the field of Maheśvara, arrived there. || 3 ||
Remaining there, they performed severe penance, relying upon yoga for a thousand divine years; then Maheśvara was pleased.
And by the power of yoga, he granted them liberation in the form of *sālokya*.
Because the Bull-bannered Lord was pleased with them through the sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), for that reason the Liṅga named Yogeśvara bestows the fruit of yoga.
He who worships him with devotion according to the proper ritual of worship attains perfection in yoga and rejoices in heaven like a god.
He who would give away Mount Meru of gold and the entire earth, yet he who worships the Lord of Yoga—he is considered superior to those two.

A bull should be offered there for the sake of obtaining the full fruit. Thus, the eleven Rudras residing in Prābhāsa have been described; they are to be constantly worshipped and saluted by those desiring the fruits of the sacred field.
Whoever should listen to this very Rudraikādaśasaṃhitā, for him all the merit of the sacred field belongs to those who dwell within Prabhāsa.

And he who does not know these Rudras residing in Prabhāsa—even if he stands in the midst of the sacred field—he is considered a bound soul (paśu) who truly does not exist [as a liberated one]. || 10 ||

Having worshipped all these Rudras, or even just one of them, and having worshipped Someśvara, one should indeed recite the Śatarudriya; one obtains the merit of all the Rudras—of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
O beautiful lady, this secret has been recounted to you as your own majesty; it is the pacifier of sins for the Rudras, and when heard, it increases merit.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Yogeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Chandeshvara, situated sixty dhanus to the north-west of Somesha. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, that divine Liṅga is the destroyer of all sins; it was renowned in the former age, during the interval of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
O Goddess, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, it was established upon the earth; O beloved, this Pṛthvīśvara Liṅga existed even in the previous Manvantara.
Furthermore, O beloved, that Liṅga was obtained by Candra and is known as Candreśvara; it destroys sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and increases merit.
O Goddess, upon seeing it, a person is liberated from all impurities accumulated over seven births and becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose. || 5 ||

The Goddess said: "How did that Liṅga, which destroys sins, become renowned as Pṛthvīśvara? And again, O Lord, how was it proclaimed as Candreśvara? Tell me this in detail, for I am eager to hear it with devotion. (6)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a narrative that destroys sin; by hearing which, a living being is liberated from the threefold bonds of karma. (7)
O Great Goddess, in former times the Earth was oppressed by the burden of the Daityas; sinking rapidly downward, she suddenly assumed the form of a cow.
Running here and there, she found no peace anywhere; then, after a full hundred years had passed, she was wandering from place to place.
He reached the great sacred field renowned as Prabhāsa, frequented by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, which destroys all sins.
Having stayed there in that great field and having formed a firm resolve in her mind, she, endowed with supreme devotion, installed a linga.
When she had performed difficult austerities for more than a full hundred years, the blessed Lord Rudra was pleased and spoke these words to the Earth: || 12 ||
O Goddess Viśvambharā, you have performed every austerity well; do not grieve, O auspicious one, for your desire shall be fulfilled.
The Daityas shall meet their destruction, slain by Viṣṇu upon the earth; O Great Goddess, you shall be freed from the burden of the Daityas.
This most beautiful liṅga which has been installed by you shall become famous in the world, renowned by the name Dharitrī.
"Here I, the Great Lord, eternally abide in the form of a *liṅga*; indeed, in age after age, I shall remain as the remover of the sins of men. (16)
Endowed with eight forms, he is eternally established in this linga; he destroys the sins of men accumulated over hundreds of previous births. (17)
Whoever shall worship this on the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada will undoubtedly obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 18 ||
The fruit of bathing at all sacred fords and of all acts of giving shall belong to him through the worship of this very liṅga. || 19 ||
Its field is declared to be sixteen *dhanus* in circumference all around, bestowing liberation upon living beings.
Whatever living beings die there—whether intentionally or unintentionally, or even those as small as worms and insects—they attain the supreme goal.
He who would give away Mount Meru of gold, or even the entire earth, is considered superior to those two who worship the Lord of the Earth.
The Lord said: Having thus granted the boons, the God vanished right there; from that time forth, Śaṅkara became known by the name Pṛthivīśvara.
Furthermore, in this great eon known as Vārāha, at one time the moon became diminished due to the curse of Dakṣa.
O Goddess, afflicted by consumption, the Moon fell to the surface of the earth after reaching the sacred field of Prabhāsa in the vicinity of that great ocean.
Having beheld the world-ruling Liṅga, which possesses great power and immense luster, he remained devoted to its worship for a thousand years.
He performed fierce austerities, subsisting on withered leaves and water, from which the moon was born, who brings delight to all by his brilliance.
By the very majesty of that Liṅga, he then became Caṇḍreśvara; and by the majesty of that Liṅga, the Moon was freed from his stain.
He attained an exceedingly fierce perfection that reveals the *sparśaliṅga*, which they call the renowned Somanātha, existing in the form of a *liṅga*.
Thus has been briefly declared the majesty of the deity Candra; when heard, it removes sins and likewise bestows health. (30)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Pṛthvīśvara," in the Madhyayātrā section of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 98.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to where Cakradhara resides, and where Dandapani, O Queen of the Gods, is situated in that same place. || 1 ||
It is situated in the eastern direction from Candreśa, to the north of Someśa, at a distance of five dhanus from Gandharveśa.
To the southwest of Umā resides the divine sage Brahmā; I shall describe his origin, which destroys all sins. (3)
In former times, there was Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva in Vārāṇasī; he heard the Purāṇa being recited by the twice-born.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, at the end of the Dvāpara age, the mighty-armed Vāsudeva will take his descent into the dwelling of Kṣatriyas.
But he, of deluded mind, thought "I am Viṣṇu," O beloved; and he bore the marks, such as the discus and others, O fair-faced one.
He dispatched the messenger Mahodara to Dvārakā; having arrived there, he said to Viṣṇu, "Renounce indeed the discus and your other weapons."
Thus spoke King Pauṇḍraka, "If you do not [surrender], you shall meet with death. Then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these pleasing words to him: (8)
"O friend, you must say these words of mine to King Pauṇḍraka: 'I have indeed taken up my discus and shall come to your city, Kāśī.'"
"Therefore, I shall undoubtedly relinquish both this discus and this mace; you may take whichever of these you desire, whether it be the discus or something else."
When this had been said and the messenger had departed, Hari, remembering that [the enemy] had arrived, mounted Garuḍa and went swiftly to that city.
Then, out of affection for his friend, the King of Kāśī, accompanied by his followers and surrounded by his entire army, marched toward Pauṇḍra.
Then, with a great force and the army of the King of Kāśī, that Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva marched toward Keśava.
From afar, Hari saw him standing in an irresistible chariot, holding a discus in his hand, equipped with a mace and the Śārṅga bow, and bearing the banner of Garuḍa.
Seeing him, who was profound in his inner disposition yet marked by his own [false] insignia, the one whose banner is Garuḍa laughed and spoke to the foolish Pauṇḍraka.
As for that which was spoken by Pauṇḍraka to me through the mouth of your messenger, saying "Cast off your insignia," I shall indeed cast all of that away.
This discus has been released, and this mace has been hurled; let this Garuḍa go and indeed ascend your banner.
Having uttered this, he was struck down by the released discus; the chariot was shattered by the mace, and the elephants and horses were crushed to pieces.
Then, while the world raised a cry of "Alas!", the mighty lord of Kāśī, pained by the suffering of his friend, fought with Vāsudeva. (19)
Then, having severed his head with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow, he hurled it into the city of Kāśī, causing amazement among the people.
Having slain Pauṇḍraka and the King of Kāśī along with his followers, Śauri returned to Dvāravatī as if he had merely gone out for a hunt.
Then the son of the Lord of Kāśī, distressed by his father’s grief, propitiated Śaṅkara; and he granted him a boon.
He chose [this boon]: "O Blessed One, O Lord of the Gods, by your grace, let a *kṛtyā* arise for the sake of slaying Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of my father. (23)
When it was said, "So shall it be," a great Kṛtyā rose up from the midst of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire and set out toward Dvārakā.
Seeing her, terrible with garlands of flames, all the Yādavas, overwhelmed by fear, approached Janārdana for refuge. || 25 ||
Then the one whose banner is Garuḍa released the Sudarśana [discus] against her; thereupon she was shattered, overwhelmed by the splendor of the discus.
Viṣṇu’s discus, Sudarśana, quickly pursued the Kṛtyā; the Kṛtyā reached Vārāṇasī, while the discus followed closely behind her.
Then, terrified by fear, she went for refuge to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Soma and Lord of the World; for indeed, no one else was capable of protecting her.
Then Śaṅkara struck the discus with excellent arrows; and that [discus], mixed with Śiva’s shafts, reached Dvāravatī.

Seeing that [the weapon] had been struck by arrows marked with the name of Śiva, the Blessed Lord Hari became enraged; then, seizing that discus in his hand, he went to the place where Someśa Kālabhairava resided.
Having gone there, his eyes copper-red with rage, he stood with a discus raised in his hand; he set his mind upon destroying the *kṛtyā* created by Kālabhairava.

Then he was seen by all the gods and by the host of Daṇḍapāṇi. While the gods were looking on there, the great host of Daṇḍapāṇi, seeing Viṣṇu with his hand raised holding the discus, spoke to the lotus-eyed one: || 32 ||
Daṇḍapāṇi said: "O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the World, do not direct your anger toward Kṛtyā."

Your discus is infallible in battle, as is the Kṛtyā of Śaṅkara. O Hari, if such wrath were to be unleashed by you with the discus, there would be great suffering for the worlds or even their total destruction.
Therefore, O Cakra, you must not release it; listen further to our words. O Hari, I was appointed to this place by Śaṅkara in the past.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting the sinful and for the purpose of obstructing those of wicked intent, therefore, O Hari, you remain here in my presence as the wielder of the discus.
Here, human beings shall worship the god Cakradhara with incense, garlands, offerings, and various kinds of food oblations.
Viṣṇu said: "By the goad of your words, I have indeed desisted; here, with my discus raised in hand, I shall remain by your side."
For in this way, O beloved, the god Cakradhara remains there, as does the Lord Daṇḍapāṇi, the lord of the Gaṇas who possesses my own form.
The man who worships those two, Daṇḍapāṇi and Hari, with devotion in due order, shall be freed from the shrouds of sin and go to the city of Śiva.

On the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, and especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, whoever worships Daṇḍanāyaka with perfumes, incense, and offerings, for him no obstacle shall ever arise while he dwells in the sacred field.
He who, having conquered his appetite, worships the wielder of the discus on the eleventh day, is liberated from all sins and attains the same world as Viṣṇu. || 42 ||
Thus has the majesty of Cakrapāṇi been briefly proclaimed; the majesty of the host of Daṇḍapāṇis as well, which destroys the flood of sins, has been heard.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to that which is situated to the north of those two, and likewise in the northwestern direction from Brahmā in his form as a child.
O best of goddesses, that which was established by Sāmba is Sāṃbāditya; indeed, there are three locations of the god Bhāskara on this island.
First is the one named Mitravana, and likewise it is called Muṇḍīra; situated in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, Sāṃbāditya is the third.
O Great Goddess, in that field there is the city known as Sāmba; it is the second eternal abode where the Sun is ever-present.
Out of affection for Sāmba and for the sake of showing favor to the people there, the Sun-god, as Mitra, remained there with his twelvefold aspect and with a friendly eye.
Constantly observing the entire world for the sake of its welfare, the Blessed One himself accepts the worship offered according to the prescribed rites.
The Goddess said: Who is this son Sāmba, and whose is he, after whom the city of Ravi is named; or rather, who is this granter of boons of meritorious deeds to whom this thousand-rayed sun belongs?
Īśvara said: "Among these twelve Ādityas who shine forth with great power, he who is known by the name Viṣṇu is renowned throughout all the worlds."
Here, this omnipresent Lord attained the state of Vāsudeva.

To him was born a son named Sāmba, possessed of great strength, by Jāmbavatī. Having been severely cursed by his father, he contracted the disease of leprosy. By him, the Sun-god was propitiated and a city was established under his own name.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, for what reason was this son cursed by his father himself? The cause cannot be a trivial one, since he has cursed his own son."
Īśvara said: Listen attentively to the cause of his curse. There was a venerable sage named Durvāsas, who was born from a portion of myself.
Wandering about, that Blessed One traveled through the three worlds; then he reached Dvāravatī, and the people before him became aware of his arrival.
Seeing that sage who had arrived—tawny-eyed, with matted hair, coarse, misshapen, and likewise emaciated—Sāmba was filled with pride in his own beauty.
He showed him contempt through both sight and touch; seeing his face, the dull-witted one likewise made his own face [like it], for that best of the Yadu clan was arrogant with youth. (15)
Then the illustrious Durvāsas, the best of sages and possessed of great splendor, being enraged, shook his head and spoke to Sāmba.

"Since you, seeing me deformed, were proud of your own appearance, and since you displayed such arrogance toward me in both your movement and your gaze, therefore you shall soon be consumed by the disease of leprosy. (17)

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of a Curse upon Sāmba by Durvāsas," at the commencement of the "Māhātmya of Sāṃbāditya" within the "Middle Pilgrimage," in the "Māhātmya of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," the first part of the seventh section (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: At that very time, the venerable sage Nārada, the mind-born son of Brahmā, who was renowned throughout the three worlds, [arrived]. || 1 ||
He too, a youth who wanders through all the worlds and is honored by the gods, was thus wandering everywhere at his own will.
That best of sages, filled with wrath, used to come constantly to the city of Dvāravatī along with other ṛṣis in order to see Vāsudeva.
Then, as he approached on horseback, all the Yadu princes—those headed by Pradyumna and the rest—stood with their faces bowed in reverence.

Due to the absence of water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the foot-washing (pādya), they performed worship from all sides; however, Sāmba, because that curse was destined to come to pass, [remained as it was]. || 5 ||
He constantly showed contempt for the high-souled Nārada; indeed, he was always devoted to amorous play, being arrogant due to his beauty and youth.
But seeing him so ill-behaved, Nārada reflected: "I shall bring about the auspicious discipline of this undisciplined one."
Having reflected thus, he then spoke to Vāsudeva: "O best of gods, these sixteen thousand women—"
O God, the devotion of all those women is always centered upon Sāmba; indeed, in this world of the moving and the unmoving, Sāmba is peerless in beauty.
"Indeed, even virtuous women always deserve to behold him. Having heard these words from Nārada, Keśava reflected upon them.

"Is that which was spoken by Nārada true? What indeed could be the reality here? For thus it is heard in the world that fickleness exists in women. These two verses were sung of old by Brahmins who knew the hearts of women: (11)
Due to their proclivity for men, extreme fickleness, and inherent ignorance, these women, even when guarded with great effort, indeed act perversely toward their husbands.
They do not examine their form, nor do they take recourse to considerations of age; whether handsome or ugly, they enjoy a man simply because he is a male.
The Lord said: Having reflected thus in his mind, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Nārada: "I do not believe this which was spoken previously."
To the god who was speaking thus, Nārada replied: "I shall indeed act in such a way that you will have faith."
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed once more as he had come; then, after a few days, he returned again to Dvārakā.
On that day, the Lord too, having enjoyed water-sports with the people of his inner apartments, indulged in drinking in private.
In the delightful Raivataka garden, adorned with various trees, eternally perfumed by the flowers of all seasons, and fulfilling every desire.
It was adorned with long ponds filled with various blooming water-lilies, resounded with the cries of swans and cranes, and graced by ruddy geese.
Then that god, surrounded by women and adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, and girdles, takes his delight therein.
Remaining there, he drinks auspicious wine endowed with beautiful fragrances, especially from the hands of excellent women adorned with ornaments on all their limbs.
In the meantime, having learned of this, the women became intoxicated with wine; then Nārada said to Sāmba, "Stay here, O young prince."
"The god summons you; it is not fitting for you to remain here. Thus urged by Nārada, he did not yet comprehend the meaning of those words. || 23 ||
Having gone there quickly, Sāmba offered salutations to his father and took the seat assigned to him by Viṣṇu according to his rank.
In the meantime, all those women there who were of weak sattva-nature, upon suddenly seeing Sāmba, became agitated.
He was not seen before by those inhabitants of the inner apartments; for, due to the fault of intoxication, their memory had been lost to a great extent.
By their very nature, the hips of women with little strength began to drip; moreover, this verse, renowned in the Purāṇas, is heard upon the earth: || 27 ||
Even for a yoginī who is abiding in celibacy, upon seeing an excellent man, her private parts become moistened through negligence.
For this is indeed seen even in the world: even women who are modest, upon consuming liquor, abandon their shame and become fearless. (29)
Through meals containing meat, unctuous foods, drinks such as sidhu, surā, and āsava, and through fragrant perfumes and garments, desire for women flourishes. (30)
A wise man should not give liquor in excess, because women are by their very nature prone to intoxication from the outset. (31)
Then Nārada, having dispatched Sāmba, returned there with great haste, following right upon Sāmba's heels.
Seeing the sage Priyasaumanasa approaching on his own, all those women, though intoxicated with passion, rose up suddenly.
Then, as Vāsudeva looked on, as those women rose up, they tore through their priceless garments, and [the flowers] fell into the vessels.
Sticking to their hips, those [garments] fell off one by one; seeing that, Hari became enraged and then cursed those women.
"O women, because your minds have gone elsewhere, leaving me behind, therefore at the end of your lives you shall not go to the worlds won by your husbands."
Fallen from this world as well as from the path to heaven, you will indeed become defenseless once more and fall into the hands of bandits.
Then, because of the fault of that curse, when Hari had departed for the earth, those women were carried off by thieves from Pañcanada while Arjuna looked on.
O beloved, those women who were of little strength and who were not present have gone to their ruin; such was the case with Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and Jāmbavatī.
"Protected by their own virtue, they have not fallen into the hands of the robbers. Having thus cursed those women, Kṛṣṇa then cursed Sāmba as well.
"Since all these women have become agitated upon seeing your exceedingly beautiful form, therefore you shall contract the disease of leprosy."
Having heard those words of his, Sāmba, filled with shame, spoke these words with a smile, remembering that best of sages.
"O father, I am signless and free from the defects of worldly existence; Durvāsas did not curse me here out of anger, for he would not speak otherwise."
Having spoken thus to the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, Sāmba then became filled with world-weariness and was overcome by anxiety and grief.
He went to Prabhāsa-kṣetra, which destroys all sins; having reached that sacred field in this manner, he performed most severe penance.
Having installed the thousand-rayed god who destroys all sins, he then propitiated him, having undertaken the highest observance.
He worshipped [the Lord] at the three junctions of the day with divine perfumes and ointments; indeed, with devotion, he constantly praised the Lord of Day with this hymn.
Sāṃba said: Salutations to the lamp of the three worlds; salutations to you, the dispeller of darkness. Salutations to the lord of the lotuses; salutations to the enemy of the night-lotus. || 48 ||
Salutations to the foundation of the world; salutations be to you, the sustainer of the world! O God of gods, I bow to Sūrya, the illuminator of the three worlds. (49)
Resplendent as the sun, the protector of the world, this unprecedented and primordial one among the gods—Hiraṇyagarbha, the Great-Souled Puruṣa—is indeed proclaimed to be beyond darkness. (50)
Thus praised, the Sun, with a serene inner soul, appeared before him and spoke to Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī.
O Sāmba, O Sāmba, O you of mighty arms, listen, O son of Govinda! I am pleased by this hymn; choose whatever boon you desire.
Sāmba said: "O best of gods, I, a sinner of very wicked mind, have been cursed by Kṛṣṇa. O Lord, if you are pleased with me, O Master, bring an end to my leprosy. (53)
Śrī Bhānu said: "O highly fortunate one, by my very grace, you shall once again become free from disease, exactly as you were in form before."
"From this day forward, you must not look upon those wives of Viṣṇu under any circumstances; O delight of the Yadus, you must never stand in their sight. (55)
O best of the Yādavas, because they were overcome by jealousy, the powerful and high-souled Viṣṇu indeed bestowed leprosy upon you. (56)
Whoever approaches me and praises me with this hymn, no one born in his lineage shall ever become a leper. (57)
Now, learn correctly the twelve names of Āditya; likewise, there are another twelve, which I shall declare to you in their entirety.
Āditya, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Mihira, Arka, Pratāpana, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Citrabhānu, and Divākara. (59)
Thus, the Sun should be known by these twelve names according to his general designations: Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Aṃśu, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. (60)
