Indra, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya is recorded as the twelfth; thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed individually. (61)
For these indeed always rise up in succession over twelve months: Viṣṇu indeed blazes in Caitra, and Aryaman always in Vaiśākha.
Vivasvat [presides] in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and likewise Aṃśumat in Āṣāḍha; Parjanya in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and Varuṇa in the month known as Prauṣṭhapada.
Indra blazes in the month of Āśvayuja, Dhātṛ in Kārttika; likewise Mitra in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Pūṣan, the maker of day, in Pauṣa.
In the month of Māgha, Bhaga is to be known; in Phālguna, Tvaṣṭṛ shines; and Viṣṇu always blazes with twelve hundred rays.
Aryaman shines with a thousand cows and three hundred; Vivasvat, however, with fourteen; and Aṃśumat with fifteen. (66)
Like Vivasvat, Parjanya, Varuṇa, and Aryaman, Indra shines with eleven hundred [rays], each double the number of the others.
And Tvaṣṭṛ, like Mitra, with a thousand and a hundredfold; during the northern course of the sun, the rays always increase, while during the southern course, the solar rays decrease further.
Thus, abiding within my twelve forms in the center of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, I shall remain renowned as Sāmbāditya until the end of the Manvantara.
O best of the Yādavas, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, eating only one meal a day is prescribed, while on the sixth day, eating only at night is declared.
Having observed a fast on the seventh lunar day in the presence of Sāmbārka, the practitioner of the great vow [should worship] with karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
Having offered the Kundaraka incense, the wise man should worship the Sun; he should also feed the Brahmins with divine food according to his ability. (72)
Thus, he who performs the worship of Sāṃbāditya correctly, being endowed with perfect faith, shall obtain the entire fruit.
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One vanished on that very spot; and Sāmba, having become free from old age, returned once more to Dvārakā.
Thus, O Goddess, has this great glory of Sāṃbāditya been told; when heard, it removes sins and likewise bestows health. (75)

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sāmbāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 101 ||
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess Kaṇṭakaśodhinī, situated two bow-lengths away in the northern direction of that very place.
She who slays the buffalo-demon, of massive form, worshipped by Brahmā and the celestial sages—those Dānavas, thorns to the gods, who were formerly possessed of sin; || 2 ||

One should purify them in every age; therefore, she is known as Kaṇṭakaśodhinī (the Purifier of Thorns). Then, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship her.
O fair-faced one, by means of offerings of animals and flowers, as well as excellent lamps and incense, no enemies shall arise for him for as long as a year.
Whoever beholds her with true devotion, or indeed constantly, even when she has become manifest; |||
The auspicious woman protects him like her own son; of this there is no doubt. || 5 ||
Thus, O Goddess, the sin-destroying majesty of Kaṇṭakaśodhinī has been briefly proclaimed; when heard, it is the supreme provider of protection.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, one should go to the supreme Kapāleśvara, located in the northern direction of that [place], which is worshipped by gods and gandharvas.
Formerly, while the sacrifice of the wise King Dakṣa was in progress, when the Brahmins were seated and the oblations were being poured into the sacrificial fire; || 2 ||
Assuming the form of a rogue, Śaṅkara arrived there. || 27 ||
O Goddess, he was clad in tattered rags, filthy, and grey with dust.
Then all those brahmins, seeing him in the form of a rogue carrying a skull-bowl, became enraged and reviled him with cries of "Fie! (dhik).
"Go away, go away, you lowest of men! 'Sinful one, sinful one!'—for this sacrificial altar is not worthy of one who carries human bones. (5)
Then, O Goddess of the gods, the Blessed One laughed and, having thrown his skull upon the sacrificial altar, vanished; he was not perceived by the wise.
When that one was destroyed, that skull was thrown outside the pavilion; then, O fair-faced one, another of the same form appeared there.
Again and again, as it was thrown down, it was born once more upon the surface of the earth; in this manner, hundreds of thousands, millions, and billions [of times].
When they were thrown there and [the fruits] grew from them, all those sages, filled with wonder and disgusted by his deed, then spoke.
Who else besides Mahādeva, whose crest is washed by the Gaṅgā, is capable of performing such a task, especially in this sacrifice? (10)
Then, praising the bull-bannered god with various hymns, they repeatedly performed oblations into the fire with those Śatarudriya mantras.

Then the god Maheśvara became manifest before them; thereupon they praised the wielder of the trident with various hymns, using diverse mantras declared in the Vedas as well as those spoken in the Purāṇas.
The sages said: Oṃ! Salutations to the primordial nature, to the unconquered Great Soul; salutations again and again to the unobstructed God who is free from desire. || 13 ||
Salutations again and again to the primordial seed, to the one who belongs to the lineage of seers, to the initiator, to the one without interval, to the singular, and to the unmanifest.

Salutations to the Supreme Lord, the stainless and most excellent one, who is adorned with armlets of various and wondrous serpents; salutations to the Soul of the Universe, the cause of the ultimate cause, whose large and wide eyes are like full-blown lotuses.

I take refuge in that primordial God, whom they call the imperishable Brahman—unseen, unmanifest, beginningless, undecaying, and all-pervading—and by perceiving whom one is liberated from the jaws of death. 16.
Thus praised at that time by all those sages whose impurities had been removed, Mahādeva was pleased and appeared before them in person. The God spoke to those sages: "Choose an excellent boon."
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with us, remain intent upon this place; for, O Lord of the Gods, there are innumerable skull-bones here. (18)
O Lord, although they have been repeatedly removed even after having manifested again and again, one who bears the name Kapāleśvara will undoubtedly remain in this place.
O Lord of Gods, while your own linga shall remain until the end of the Manvantara, you yourself should establish your presence in this place under the name Kapāleśvara.
But for those who shall worship you there with incense, garlands, and ointments, their supreme abode shall be one that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Having said, "So be it," that Great Lord remained there; O beautiful lady, the sacrifice of the Lord of Night was then resumed.
O beloved, upon seeing that [liṅga], a mortal shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and be liberated from all sins, even those accumulated in previous births. (23)
This entire majesty occurred during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara; furthermore, in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, there was another [manifestation] which brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

In former times, Maheśāna Hara was addressed as "Kapālī" by Dakṣa; because of that, he brought about the destruction of the sacrifice, and thus he remains in this Manvantara under the name Kapāleśvara.
Then, O lady of excellent hips, during the Sūryasāvarṇika interval, the name of this god shall be Tattveśvara.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the majesty of the deity Rudra, which destroys the sins of all living beings and effects liberation from the bonds of Paśu.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kapāleśvara," in the Madhyayātrā section of the first Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the seventh Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 103 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Koṭīśvara; to the north of that, O Goddess, is the place renowned as Koṭīśa.

O Goddess, in ancient times, in the vicinity of Kapāleśvara, the Pāśupata [rite] was established for all living beings, which destroys sin and grants liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
They perform extensive austerities with their bodies smeared with ashes, wearing crowns of matted hair and girdles made of muñja grass.
All those peaceful Brahmins, who have conquered anger and are practitioners of auspicious yoga, dwell there performing austerities that pervade the sacred field in the four directions.
O Great Goddess, ten million [ascetics], devoted to the recitation of mantras, properly installed that linga near Kapāleśa.
Then, filled with devotion, they worshipped that liṅga; thereupon, the Great God Hara, being pleased, granted them liberation.
O beloved, because crores of sages attained perfection there, the Liṅga became famous on earth by the name Koṭīśvara.
The man who worships that Koṭīśvara with devotion shall obtain the fruit of reciting ten million mantras.
Gold should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he shall obtain the fruit of ten million fire-sacrifices (koṭihoma) as well as the full fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Koṭīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now I shall proclaim another secret, a supreme sacred site that removes all sins of men; I shall describe it to you in detail.
The majesty of the principal deity, the majesty of those who dwell in the Kalpa, Someśa, the slayer of Daityas, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the form of a child. || 2 ||
Arka-sthala, Āditya, Prabhāsa, and Śaśibhūṣaṇa—these six eminent gods reside in the sacred field of Prābhāsika.
Merely by the sight of them, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; one is certainly liberated from the terrible sins accumulated since birth. (4)

The Goddess said: "The greatness of the aforementioned gods has been told by you; however, as for that which was spoken regarding [the deity] at Prabhāsa being 'in the form of a child'—how is that statement to be understood?"
In all other places, the Grandfather appears in the form of an elder; how did he come to this [place], and what is remembered as his majesty?
O Lord of Gods, how is he to be worshipped, and how should the pilgrimage be performed by men? O Master, if you are pleased with me, please explain this in detail. (7)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the majesty originating from Brahmā, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins. (8)
There is no god equal to Brahman; there is no teacher equal to Brahman; there is no knowledge equal to Brahman; there is no austerity equal to Brahman. || 9 ||
So long do they wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering, grief, and fear, until they become devotees of the Grandfather, the eldest of the gods.
If the mind of a living being were attached to the sphere of the senses in the same way that it is [attached] to Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? (11)
The Goddess said: If Brahmā, the teacher of the world, is thus endowed with such greatness, in which location within the great Prābhāsika tīrtha does he reside?
For what purpose did the best of gods come there, at what time, and how is he to be worshipped by the foremost of Brahmins? On which lunar day [is this done]? Tell me this in due order. (13)
Īśvara said: To the northeast of Somanātha, in the southeast direction from Sāṃbāditya, is the supreme abode of Brahmā, like another world of Brahmā.
Indeed, those who dwell until the end of the kalpa remain there for the duration of the kalpa; O Goddess, the Grandfather (Brahmā), staying in that place, remains in the form of a child.
The Lord of the world, the creator of the universe, whose form is pure being and who possesses great splendor, arrived at the auspicious Prābhāsika field when he was eight years of age.
There, desiring to create various offspring, he established a great liṅga and performed severe penance for a thousand divine years. (17)
Then, after some time had passed, the Lord was entreated by Soma, who was completely freed from the disease of consumption and endowed with perfect faith.

Indeed, for the purpose of installing the Liṅga in the auspicious Prābhāsika field, accompanied by Viśvakarman and together with ten million Brahmarṣis, he caused the installation of that supreme Liṅga to be performed according to the prescribed rites.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, having installed the Liṅga Somanātha, he caused abundant sacrificial fees to be given to the Brahmins.
Thus was the Liṅga installed by Brahmā, the creator of the world; and here at Prabhāsa, years passed while he remained in the form of a child.
Two times forty [eighty] years passed for those dwelling in the middle of the field; thus, half a parārdha elapsed for the residents of Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
The Goddess said: "Tell me in detail the measurement of Brahmā’s day, consisting of months and thousands of years, and how his entire lifespan is traditionally reckoned."
Īśvara said: Brahmā is known to have a supreme lifespan; one *parārdha* of it has indeed passed while he was stationed at Prabhāsa-kṣetra, and now a second one is occurring.
When Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrives in the Prābhāsika field at the age of eight years in the form of a child, he is then so described.
O beloved of the gods, at all other sacred fords, the Grandfather (Brahmā) always assumes the form of an old man, except at the Prābhāsika field.
Of all the holy places (tīrthas) that exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and of those which are remembered by Brahmā, the foremost is the one of great splendor situated at Prabhāsa.
Listen, my dear, to those names in every kalpa: in the first kalpa he was Svayambhū, and in the second he existed as Padmabhū.
"In the third [kalpa] he is Viśvakarman, and in the fourth he is Bālarūpin; these are declared to be the principal names of Svayambhū."
He who constantly remembers this shall become a long-lived man.
All the moons, suns, and planets, together with gods, asuras, and humans—the entire triple world perishes at the arrival of the night of Brahmā.
When the next day had dawned, O beloved, the Grandfather, having awakened, carried out the creation just as it had been before.
I shall now declare the measurement of time for Brahmā, the creator of the worlds: one-fourth of a *netrabhāga* is said to be the duration of a *truṭi*.

And from that, O fair-faced one, the duration of a *nimiṣa* should be known as double [a *tatkṣaṇa*]. Fifteen *nimiṣas* are called a *kāṣṭhā* by the wise; and thirty *kāṣṭhās* are declared by the learned to be a *kalā*. (34)
Thirty kalās constitute a muhūrta; fifteen of those make a day. Night is to be known as having the same measure as the day; the two together form an ahorātra.
By those fifteen [days] a fortnight (pakṣa) is formed; by two fortnights a month (māsa) is said to occur. Six months constitute a solstice (ayana), and from two solstices a year (abda) arises.
Forty lakṣas, three lakṣas, and twenty thousand years are to be known as a solar cycle of four yugas (caturyuga). || 37 ||
Seventy-one cycles of the four yugas are declared to be a manvantara; this lifespan of Indra has thus been briefly described to you. (38)
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu; then Auttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata, Arkasāvarṇi, Brahmasāvarṇi, the one named Dharmasāvarṇi, as well as Raucya and Bhūtya. (40)
These fourteen Manus have been enumerated in their proper order; I shall now describe to you, in sequence, all the past and future Indras as well.
Viśvabhuk, Vipaścit, Sukīrti, and Śibi; Vibhu, Manobhū, as well as Ojasvin, Bali, and Balin. (42)
And Adbhuta, Śānti, Ramya, Devavara, Vṛṣa, Ṛtadhāman, Divasvāmī, Śuci, and Śakra—these are the fourteen [Indras]. || 43 ||
All these perish during a day of Brahmā, O beloved; his night is known to be of equal duration—this is remembered as the measure of a Kalpa.
The first is the Śvetakalpa, the second is the Nīlalohita, the third is Vāmadeva, and after that is another, the Rāthaṃtara. || 45 ||
Raurava is declared the fifth; the sixth is remembered as Prāṇa; then the seventh is Bṛhatkalpa, and the eighth is called Kandarpa. (46)
Then the ninth is declared to be Sadyojāta, and Īśāna is remembered as the tenth; Dhyāna is declared the eleventh, and likewise another is Sārasvata.
The thirteenth is indeed the Udāna, and then the fourteenth is the Garuḍa; the fifteenth is to be known as the Kaurma, which is the full moon day of Prajāpati.
The sixteenth is the Nārasiṃha [Kalpa], and after that comes the Samādhi [Kalpa]. The eighteenth is declared to be the Āgneya, and after that the Soma Kalpa.
Bhāvana is said to be the twentieth, and another is Suptamālin; then Vaikuṇṭha, Arciṣa, Rudra, and likewise Lakṣmīkalpa as others.
Then the twenty-seventh was the Vairāja Kalpa, followed by the Gaurī Kalpa and the Andhaka Kalpa; likewise, the Māheśvara Kalpa is proclaimed, wherein Tripura was destroyed.
Likewise, at the end, that new moon day (Kuhū) which is remembered as the Pitṛkalpa—these thirty kalpas, O beloved, are declared to be in one month of Brahmā.
All the past [kalpas] have been described; now the Vārāha [kalpa] is current, wherein on the first lunar day (pratipad) of Brahmā, the earth was uplifted by the Boar.

Thirty *kalpas* are reckoned as a month, and twelve of those constitute a year. According to this measurement of years, Brahmā was then eight years old when Somanātha was brought by Somarāja and installed.
Thus, as he dwelt in that field at Prabhāsa in the form of a child, one *parārdha* passed away and the second is now proceeding.
Thus, this Lord Brahmā, the Self-born One of great majesty, having resorted to the sacred field (kṣetra) because of his childhood, dwells in the midst of Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
He indeed is worthy of worship, salutation, and praise by the wise; he alone should be worshipped at the outset by those desiring the full fruit of a successful journey.
He who worships him with devotion worships me on this earth; he who hates him hates me; whoever is worthy of worship for him is worthy of worship for me as well.
When Brahmā is worshipped, I and Viṣṇu are worshipped; when Viṣṇu is worshipped, I and Brahmā are worshipped. (59)
By my mere worship, both Brahmā and Viṣṇu are worshipped; for Sattva is proclaimed to be Brahmā, Rajas is Viṣṇu, and Tamas is I.
Vāyu is proclaimed as Brahmā, Anala as Rudra, and Āpa as Viṣṇu; the night is Viṣṇu, the day is Rudra, and that which is the twilight is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
O Goddess, I am indeed the Sāmaveda; Brahmā is called the Ṛgveda; Viṣṇu is the Yajurveda, while the Atharvaveda is the support of the lineage.
For I am the hot season, O Goddess; the Grandsire (Brahmā) is the rainy season; and Viṣṇu shall be the cold season—thus he is indeed the three seasons.
I am to be known as the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, Hari is remembered as the Gārhapatya fire, and Brahmā is the Āhavanīya fire; thus, everything consists of these three deities.
I am established in the form of the *liṅga*, while Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the *bhaga*. Brahmā resides within the seed-syllable (*bīja*); Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the waters.

I am the Lord consisting of reality, abiding in the form of space; that which flows from space is the seed established in Brahman. Resorting to his own Brahma-nature, Brahmā is the one who causes the seed to sprout.
Brahmā resides in the center of the navel, and Viṣṇu within the heart; O Goddess, I am in the middle of the mouth—the support of all embodied beings.
He who is I am Brahmā himself; he who is Brahmā is the Consumer of Oblations (Agni). She who is the Goddess is Viṣṇu himself; he who is Viṣṇu is the Moon.
He who is Time is himself Brahmā; he who is Rudra is also the Sun. Thus, O beloved, the Supreme Brahman exists through its particular powers.
The syllable Oṃ is that supreme Brahman, and the Gāyatrī is the supreme Prakṛti; having known both of these, a person does not fall away but is liberated.
O Goddess of the gods, he who thus knows non-duality as the supreme imperishable knows everything; no other, that lowest of men who creates divisions, knows it.
O lady of excellent limbs, he who hates that Supreme Brahman, which is of a single form yet exists as distinct from the state of being an effect, is called a hater of Brahman.
Brahmā is stationed on my right side and Keśava is on my left; O beautiful lady, he who harbors hatred toward those two is one who hates me.
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one should worship Brahmā, Keśava, and Rudra with a single form, with an undivided inner self. (74)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Brahmā," in the Middle Pilgrimage within the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the first section (*Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 105.
The Goddess said: "Tell me truly the procedure for the worship of that Brahman which is proclaimed as non-dual through such a state of being."
O God, in the Prābhāsika field, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) exists in the form of a child; how is he, who possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman, worshipped by the people? || 2 ||
What are the mantras, what is the ritual procedure, and what kind of Brāhmaṇas are there? How does the fruit of the sacred field accrue to the Brahmins residing there? (3)
O Mahādeva, how many kinds of Brahmins reside there in that sacred field? What is their conduct, what is their character, and what is their ultimate goal?
Explain this in detail, [for it brings] great prosperity to the Brāhmaṇas.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess, you who are skilled in asking such a perfect question! Listen with a one-pointed mind to the majesty of the Brahmins, who are the deities."
O Goddess, by hearing which a man is liberated from all sins; whatever twice-born ones have been celebrated throughout the earth bounded by the oceans—(7)
O Goddess of gods, that form of mine is manifest upon the surface of the earth; the Brāhmaṇas and the gods are manifest [here], while the deities in heaven are beyond direct perception.
Brahmins are always dear to me; Brahmins are my own body. He who worships them with devotion always worships me.
Whoever propitiates them with devotion shall also satisfy me.

O beloved, I am undoubtedly those Brāhmaṇas; when they are honored, I am honored, and when they are satisfied, I alone am satisfied. Whoever bears enmity toward them, he bears enmity toward me as well.

Whoever should worship my stone image with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and garlands—even if that person does not worship me, I am indeed worshipped by him through the worship of the Brahmin. (12)
O beloved, as many twice-born ones as there are upon the earth—whether they have observed the vows of the Vedas or have not observed those vows and the Vedas—they too are worthy of worship.
One should not examine the Brahmins residing in the village for a Śrāddha; there is great censure in the examination of Brahmins.
Those who are one-eyed, lame, dark-complexioned, impoverished, or diseased—all these should be engaged in the Śrāddha rite, provided they are accompanied by those who have mastered the Vedas.

Brāhmaṇas are worthy of honor by virtue of their birth, and even more so because of their study of the Vedas; therefore, for the sake of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, Brāhmaṇas should never be censured under any circumstances.
A wise man should not despise Brahmins who are one-eyed, crippled, hunchbacked, impoverished, or even diseased, for they are remembered as my own form.
Indeed, many men, excluded from knowledge, do not know that I wander this earth in the form of a twice-born. (18)
Those who strike brāhmaṇas who resemble me, who compel them to perform improper acts, who send them on errands when they were not to be sent, and who force them into servitude; || 19 ||
The mighty messengers of Yama cut those dead bodies with saws, just as craftsmen cut wood along a marked line.
And those lowest of men who threaten with harsh speech, speak roughly out of anger, and strike them with their feet; || 21 ||
Having struck those dead ones down upon the surface of the earth into the world of Yama, they trampled them with their cruel feet, their eyes bloodshot with rage.
Yama extracts the tongue with tongs glowing like fire for those sinful men who look upon Brahmins with an evil eye. (22)

Those men who are hostile to the Veda, outsiders, and eternal haters of Brahman—against them, by the command of Yama, terrifying crows with huge bodies and adamantine beaks uproot their eyes in a mere moment.
He who strikes a Brahmin so as to cause a wound and draw blood, or causes a fracture of the bone, or even deprives him of his life; || 25 ||
He should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin; no atonement is prescribed for him, as he must pass through fifty crores of hells in succession.
He is cooked intensely for many thousands of years; therefore, O lady of excellent limbs, a Brahmin should always be saluted by men.
Indeed, the twice-born should always be honored with gifts of food and drink; for among all gifts, Brahmins are the rightful recipients of them all. (28)
O Goddess of the gods, no one else is capable [of this]; he who takes it goes to the lowest state. O Goddess, a Brāhmaṇa purified by austerity has his sins removed. (29)
He shall not perish even while accepting the entire earth with its oceans; for there is no such thing as an improper act for a Brāhmaṇa, O Great Goddess. (30)
But he who always abides in the inner self, eternally permeated by the state of being, that Brāhmaṇa is indeed born as a great being from the very moment of his birth. (31)
In this world, all the lords of the world are also worshippers of the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, one should not despise them if one desires a long life. (32)
Enraged, the Brahmins could slay, they could reduce to ashes by their own splendor, and they could even create other worlds as well as other guardians of the worlds. (33)
By those high-souled ones, out of anger, the ocean was made undrinkable; even today, the fire of their wrath does not subside in Daṇḍaka.
These are the eternal gods among gods, the leaders to heaven; by them this path was made, and it is called the Devayāna. || 35 ||
They are to be honored, they are to be saluted; everything is established in them. Indeed, they carry all these worlds across one after another.

The Brāhmaṇas, whose private recitation and austerities are secret, who have praised their vows, who are purified by knowledge and purified by their observances, live without depending on others. (37)
For Brahmins, when provoked, are like venomous serpents; blazing with the power of their asceticism, they could consume even the oceans.
When the Brahmins are satisfied, all the deities are satisfied; they are the refuge of all beings, for they contemplate the path of the supreme self. (39)

Those whose doubts regarding knowledge of the beginning, middle, and end have been severed, who know the distinction between the higher and the lower, and who lead others to the supreme goal—therefore, Brahmins are not to be slain, even if they are always engaged in sinful acts.
He who would destroy all this world, and he who would harm a Brahmin, are equal; such a person is fire, such a person is the sun of great splendor, and when provoked to anger, he becomes poison.
The Brahmin is the first eater among beings, the best of the castes, the father, and the guru; he never spills [his seed], never suffers pain, and never perishes. (42)
For that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed superior to the Agnihotra sacrifice; all the deities abide there, having taken refuge in the bodies of the learned Brahmins. (43)
Therefore, those brahmins should indeed be honored; however, in their absence, images and the like may be used.
Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, a Brahmin is my deity; whether refined or unrefined, he is like fire, the great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled; likewise, even when deprived of offerings to the gods and ancestors, a Brāhmaṇa is not defiled.

O fair-faced one, a Brahmin is indeed worthy of worship, even if he has committed great sins; in every way, Brahmins are to be honored, for they are the supreme deity in every respect. Therefore, with all effort, one should protect a twice-born man who has fallen into distress. 47.

Thus, O Great Goddess, Brahmins are to be honored everywhere by human beings; how much more so those who have conquered their own selves, especially those residing in a sacred field (kṣetra). || 48 ||
Now, I shall explain in due order the distinction in the modes of livelihood for the Brahmins residing in sacred fields who dwell in the four stages of life (āśramas).

Those twice-born ones who know the procedure for the renunciation of the field, as well as the various modes of livelihood in their proper sequence, are the sharers in the fruit of that field. || 50 ||
Listen, O fair-faced one, to how a twice-born man residing in the field should conduct himself according to the various divisions, such as the Prājāpatya and others. (51)
O fair-faced one, there are the Prājāpatyas, Mahīpālas, Kapotas, Granthikas, Kuṭikas, Vaitālas, Padmas, and Haṃsas.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Bakas, Kaṅkas, and Gopālas, O beautiful lady; as well as the Truṭikas, Maṭharas, Guṭikas, and others who are Daṇḍikas.
These are the divisions according to their locations; now hear from me their respective functions.
Non-violence, service to the teacher, study of one's own scriptures, purity, self-restraint, truthfulness, and non-stealing—this indeed is remembered as the vow of Prajāpati. (55)

Because they protect the earth through rites for pacification and so forth, as well as through acts of destruction, nourishment, prosperity, and enmity, they are therefore known as "protectors of the earth" (mahīpāla).
Those who gather up the grains that have fallen on the ground like pigeons, and for whom their livelihood consists of what they have thus picked up, are indeed *sādhakas*, like pigeons. (57)
Those practitioners who, having built a house, abandon it all at once along with their good books, are indeed true *sādhakas* devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 58 ||
Attached to sacred fords (tīrthas), accompanied by their wives, subsisting on whatever they happen to obtain, and endowed with great audacity—these practitioners are known as Vaitālas. || 59 ||

Those who are self-restrained yet attached to desires, who strive for the sake of kingdom, pleasure, and wealth, are known as Padma-sādhakas; they are always devoted to the practice of wandering for alms.
Those who are endowed with the yoga of knowledge and devoted to the practice of non-duality are known as Haṃsas; they are accomplished practitioners whose consciousness has arisen spontaneously.
Those who uphold the world through celibacy, goodness, and likewise through lack of greed, are considered the true Dhṛtarāṣṭras, for they have conquered the universe.

Those who move about in secret, whether for the sake of knowledge, vows, or even dharma, but whose devotion is fixed solely on their own self-interest, are considered *bakas* among practitioners. (63)
Residing by the side of bodies of water for the sake of supreme accomplishment, subsisting on lotus stalks and water chestnuts, those practitioners are known as Kaṅkas.
Those who wander here together with the cows and dwell in the cow-pen, whose very essence is the five products of the cow—those cowherds are indeed the practitioners (sādhakas). || 65 ||
They emaciate their own bodies through kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa penances; those practitioners who consume only a tiny fragment [of food] are considered truṭikas.

Those householders who, having made a wife out of kuśa grass in their hermitage, are devoted to a life of begging for alms and remain pure, are indeed *maṭharas*, practitioners of spiritual realization.
Then those twice-born ones [prepared] eight pills, equal in size to a single morsel of food, produced from bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Those who are engaged in the discipline of their own bodies and remain in the vīrāsana posture at night are declared to be daṇḍins; all this has been told to you. (69)
Whether they be commoners or distinguished, householders or otherwise—I have fully explained the distinctions among those who dwell in the sacred field.
Those inhabitants of the Prabhāsa region who possess such qualities as these should worship the Blessed Lord, the divine Grandfather in the form of a child. (71)
Those who are perpetrators of great sins and those who have been cast out by Brahmins must certainly not touch Brahmā, who is in the form of a child.
Always practicing celibacy, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and mastered his senses—such are the Brāhmaṇas known as those who dwell in the midst of the sacred field. (73)
By them the Blessed Lord, the divine Grandfather in the form of a child, is to be worshipped; by those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas, the Grandfather is to be fully honored.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of Brāhmaṇas," in the Madhyayātrā section of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the seventh Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 106 ||
Īśvara said: Now I shall describe to you in brief the procedure for worship, as well as the various distinct forms of devotion toward that Brahman who has assumed the form of a child.
The procedure for the chariot procession, the sequence of hymns and mantras, and the various forms of devotion arising from mind, speech, and body have been described. (2)

Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or likewise spiritual—that which arises through meditation, concentration, and the recollection of the Vedas—this devotion to Brahman, which brings Him delight, is called mental devotion (mānasī bhakti). || 3 ||
Vocal devotion is said to consist of salutations with mantras, the performance of fire-sacrifices and śrāddha rites, as well as the recitation of prayers from the Āraṇyakas.
By means of vows, fasts, and observances that restrain the mind and the senses, as well as by the *kṛcchra*, *sāṃtapana*, and other penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and so forth; || 5 ||
Bodily devotion of the twice-born is said to be threefold: through fasts prescribed by Brahmā, as well as other auspicious vows.
With cow’s ghee, milk, and curds; with honey, sugarcane juice, and water infused with kuśa grass; and with various perfumes, garlands, and other such offerings.
With incense of ghee and guggulu, fragrant with black aloe-wood, and with ornaments of gold, gems, and the like, as well as with variegated garlands; || 8 ||
With ritual placements (nyāsa), circumambulations, hymns of praise, banners, as well as festivals, with dances, instrumental music, songs, and offerings of all kinds of articles; || 9 ||
Whatever worship is performed by men with various kinds of food, edibles, meals, and drinks, directed toward the Grandfather (Brahmā), that is considered worldly devotion.
The ritual action known as Vedic is that which is performed with portions of Vedic mantras and oblations.

On the new moon day and on the full moon day, the rites pertaining to the Agnihotra must be performed: the ritual consumption, the giving of the sacrificial fee, and the offering of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). || 12 ||

Sacrifices, fortitude, the drinking of Soma, all sacrificial rites, the recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the study of the Saṃhitās—when these are performed with Brahmā as the objective, that is called Vedic devotion. (13)
Constantly devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), possessed of meditation, with senses conquered, subsisting on alms, observant of vows, and having withdrawn all his senses.
Having fixed his concentration upon the heart while meditating on the Lord of Creatures (Prajeśvara), who is seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, red in color and possessed of beautiful eyes.

He who meditates upon the god thus—Brahmā, whose face is radiant, whose waist is well-defined, who is red in color, four-armed, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—he is called a devotee of Brahmā. (16)
And hear from me, O Goddess, the rule prescribed for those who dwell in this sacred field.

Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, unattached, and without possessions, they were devoid of affection even for the four aims of life, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Constantly bestowing fearlessness upon all beings through their threefold actions, they are ever devoted to breath control and dedicated to the meditation on the Supreme.

Those who are constant reciters, ever pure, devoted to the performance of the duties of ascetics, knowledgeable in the rules of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and whose doubts regarding the Dharma have been severed; || 20 ||
Those Brahmins dwelling in the sacred field are constantly devoted to the worship of Brahmā; by them, indeed, the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the form of a child is to be worshipped.

In that manner I shall proclaim it; listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved. Having bathed in a pure sacred ford, wearing white garments and being purified, one should then worship Brahmā, provided with offerings for worship.

Having first bathed [the image] according to the prescribed rite with the waters of the five nectars—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—[one should proceed].
Taking cow's urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

One should bathe [the image] with clarified butter while reciting "tejo'si śukram," with water from Kuśa grass while reciting "devasya tvā," and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā. || 25 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with the five products of a tawny cow mixed with water infused with *kuśa* grass and purified by mantras; this is indeed known as the "Brahma-bath."
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years, by bathing the Eldest of the Gods (Brahmā), one burns it all away; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus bathed Brahmā in the form of a child according to the prescribed rite, the twice-born man should then bathe him with water scented with camphor and agallochum.

Having performed this, one should worship the God through the application of the Gāyatrī-nyāsa; the wise practitioner should place the Praṇava from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet.
One should place the syllable *ta* on the head, the syllable *sa* on the circle of the face, the syllable *vi* in the region of the throat, and the syllable *tu* at the joints of the limbs.
One should place the syllable *va* in the center of the heart, the syllable *re* on both sides, the syllable *ṇi* in the right flank, and the syllable *ya* in that which is known as the left.
One should place the syllable *bha* at the navel and waist, the syllable *go* on both sides, the syllable *de* on the two knees, and the syllable *va* on the two lotus-feet.
Having placed the syllable *sy* on the two thumbs, one should place the syllable *dhī* on the chest; the syllable *ma* at the base of the knees, and the syllable *hi* residing in the secret part.
Having placed the syllable *dhī* upon the heart and the syllable *yo* on the lower lip, the wise one should likewise place another *yo* on the upper lip. (34)
The syllable *na* is at the tip of the nose, while *pra* is situated in the eye; *co* is in the middle of the eyebrows, and *da* is supported by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

O Goddess of the gods, one should indeed place the syllable *yātkāram* at the edge of the forehead; having performed this placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body, O beloved, one should likewise perform it upon the deity.
Having provided all the ritual offerings, one should examine it thoroughly, mixed with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having prepared them with scented water, one should sprinkle all the ritual materials with the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava, and thereafter begin the worship.
One should worship in due order with divine, fragrant flowers such as jasmine and lotuses, as well as aśoka, śatapatra, and bakula blossoms.
Then, with the excellent incense of black agallochum and likewise with supreme ghee lamps, one should there successively offer various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).
With pieces of sugar-candies, *laḍḍukas*, *śrīveṣṭakas*, *kāṃsāras*, and *aśoka* sprouts; with *svastikas*, *ullipikas*, milk-based sweets, sesame *veṣṭakas*, and *kilāṭikas*.
One should cause ripe fruits to be offered with the root mantra, and one should worship the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda.
The wise one should worship knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue in the cardinal and intermediate directions, O Goddess, according to the sequence beginning with Īśāna. (43)

One should worship the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyāsthāna) before Brahmā; then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the heart-mantras, one should proceed in order before the deity.
This verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is proclaimed as the heart; "ṛtaṃ satyam" is declared the crest-lock (śikhā), and one should designate "ud u tyaṃ" as the eye.
"Citraṃ devānām" is thus renowned throughout all the worlds; "brahmaṃs te chādayāmi" is declared to be the armor (kavaca). || 46 ||
The worship of Īśa is proclaimed to be performed with "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ"; one should worship the God with the Gāyatrī mantra consecrated by the syllable Om.
With the syllable Om, one should worship all the others, beginning with the Ṛgveda; Gāyatrī is the supreme mantra, the mother of the Vedas, and the radiant one. (48)
He who, having fasted on the fifteenth day, worships Brahmā with the essential syllables of the Gāyatrī, goes to the supreme abode.
If a twice-born man desires to cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, he should always worship Brahmā at Prabhāsa during the month of Kārttika.
Who, being wise, would not worship him who appears in the form of a child at Prabhāsa, by the mere sight of whom one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice? (51)
O Goddess of the gods, who would not worship Him at whose end of a single day the worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans, go to their dissolution? || 52 ||
He who is the father of all gods and the grandfather of all beings—for this reason, he is to be worshipped by those Brahmins residing in the sacred field.

He who is the form of Rudra and the form of the universe, he alone is the Lord of the worlds; he who, having fasted on the full moon day, worships Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds, according to the prescribed rite, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The chariot procession of the Lord is proclaimed to take place in the month of Kārttika; by performing it with devotion, a human being attains co-residence in the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess of gods, in the month of Kārttika, on the full moon day, the scorcher of foes [Brahmā], together with Sāvitrī and Carman, assumed a four-faced form.
The king should cause it to be paraded throughout the entire city accompanied by various musical instruments; having thus paraded it through the whole city, he should then install it.
Having first fed the Brahmins and having honored Śāṇḍileya, one should place the deity upon the chariot amidst the sounds of auspicious musical instruments.

Having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī at the front of the chariot according to the prescribed rites, and having caused the Brahmins to recite the benedictions, he performed the auspicious Puṇyāha ceremony.
Having mounted the deity upon the chariot, one should keep a vigil with various kinds of performances and abundant offerings to Brahmā and Śeṣa.
"O Goddess, a Śūdra who desires his own welfare must not mount a chariot, especially through unrighteous means—with the single exception of a Bhojaka, my dear. (61)
O beloved, one should place Sāvitrī on the right side of Brahmā; the officiating priest (bhojaka) on the left side, and one should set down a lotus in front.

O Goddess, having thus caused the chariot to circumambulate the entire city to the right with the sounds of musical instruments and the abundant blasts of conchs, the wise man, having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony, should once again station it in its own place.
Whoever performs this pilgrimage with devotion, or whoever beholds it, or even he who pulls the chariot, shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Whoever carries a lamp there, riding upon the back of Brahmā’s chariot, obtains at every step the great fruit of a horse sacrifice. || 65 ||
O Great Goddess, that king who does not cause a chariot procession for Brahmā to be performed is cooked in the Raurava hell for an inexhaustible period of time.
Therefore, one who desires the welfare of the kingdom should, with every effort, personally undertake the chariot procession, especially so.
The wise man should also feed Brahmins who have practiced the path according to the rules, honoring them with unwashed garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
He who offers a lamp in the hall of Brahmā on the new moon day of the month of Kārttika shall go to the supreme abode.
And during all festivals, and especially at all times, the Brahmins should worship this Brahmā, the preceptor of the worlds.
According to the performance of one's duties, those endowed with right faith should worship him with divine offerings, in accordance with the extent of their wealth. || 71 ||
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the supreme majesty of worship, as well as the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra belonging to Brahmā in his form as a child. (72)
I shall recite to him the one hundred and eight names; by bestowing them and by reciting them, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the perfect recitation of one hundred thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī, that same fruit one attains from the chanting of this hymn.
This supreme, divine hymn of praise is a secret that destroys evil; it must not be given to those of wicked intellect, nor likewise to those who are slanderers. (75)
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and possesses a great soul; for in ancient times, this supreme hymn of Brahmā was indeed asked about by Viṣṇu. (76)
O God of gods, O Grandfather, tell me in which various places you should be meditated upon; for you are the best among all who possess complete knowledge. (77)
Brahmā said: "At Puṣkara I am the best of gods; at Gayā, the great-grandfather; at Kānyakubja, Vedagarbha; and at Bhṛgukṣetra, the four-faced one."
In the north is the Creator; Bṛhaspati is in Nandipurī; he is in the form of a child at Prabhāsa; and he is beloved by the gods in Vārāṇasī. (79)
In Dvārāvatī he was Cakradeva; in Vaidiśa, Bhuvanādhipa; in Pauṇḍraka, Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and in Hastināpura, Pītākṣa.
In Jayantī I am Vijaya, and in Puruṣottama I am Jayanta; among the Vāḍas I am Padmahasta, and in Tamolipta I am Tamonuda.
He is Janānanda in Āhicchatrī, Janapriya in the city of Kāñcī, Brahmā in the city of Karṇāṭa, and likewise a Sage (Muni) in Ṛṣikuṇḍa.
Śrīnivāsa is in Śrīkaṇṭha, Śubhaṃkara in Kāmarūpa, Devakartṛ in Ucchriyāṇa, and likewise Sraṣṭṛ in Jālandhara. || 83 ||
Likewise, Viṣṇu is in the one named Mallikā; Bhārgava is in Mahendra; Gonarda is in Sthavirākāra; and Pitāmaha is in Ujjayinī. (84)
Mahādeva is indeed at Kauśāmbī, while Rāghava is at Ayodhyā; Virañci is at Citrakūṭa, and Vārāha is on the Vindhya mountain. (85)
At Gaṅgādvāra he is the best of gods; on Himavat he is Śaṅkara; at Dehikā he holds a sacrificial ladle in his hand; and likewise at Arbuda he holds a lotus in his hand.
In Vṛndāvana he is Padmanetra, in Naimiṣa he is Kuśahasta, in Gopakṣetra he is Govinda, and on the bank of the Yamunā he is Surendra.
In Bhāgīrathī he is Padmatanu, in Janasthala he is Janānanda; in Kauṅkaṇa he is Madhvakṣa, and in Kāmpilya he is Kanakaprabha.
In Kheṭaka he is Annadātā, and in Kratusthala he is Śambhu; in Laṅkā he is Paulastya, and in Kaśmīra he is Haṃsavāhana. || 89 ||
Vasiṣṭha is at Arbuda, Nārada is in Utpalavana, Śrutidātā is at Medhaka, and the Lord of the Yajus is at Prayāga.
The Sāmaveda is in the Śivaliṅga, and Madhupriya is in the monkey; Nārāyaṇa is on Mount Gomanta, and Dvijapriya is in Vidarbha.
In Aṅkulaka he is Brahmagarbha; in Brahmavāha, Sutapriya; in Indraprastha, Durādharṣa; and in Campā, Suramardana.
In Virajā he is Mahārūpa; in Rāṣṭravardhana he is Surūpa; in Kadambaka he is Janādhyakṣa; and in Samasthala he is Devādhyakṣa.
Gaṅgādhara is remembered at Rudrapīṭha, Jalada at Supīṭha, Tripurāri at Tryambaka, and Trilocana at Śrīśaila. || 94 ||
Mahādeva is at Plakṣapura; Vedhanāśana is at Kapāla; Śauri is at Śṛṅgaverapura; and Cakradhāraka is at Nimiṣa. || 95 ||
Virūpākṣa was at Nandipurī, Gautama at the Plakṣa tree, Mālyavat at Hastinātha, and likewise Dvijendra at Vācika.
In Indrapurī he was Divānātha; in Bhūtikā he was Purandara; in Candrā he was Haṃsabāhu; and in Campā he was Garuḍapriya. || 97 ||
In Mahodaya, the great yakṣa is Suyajña; in Pūtaka, he is in the forest; in Siddheśvara, he is white-complexioned; and in Vibhā, he is Padmabodhaka. || 98 ||
The Lord of Umā is at Udaka in the Devadāru forest; Vināyaka is at Mātṛsthāna, and the Lord of Wealth is in Alakā. || 99 ||
Goviṃda is on Trikūṭa, and likewise Vāsuki is in Pātāla; Yugādhyakṣa is at Kovidāra, and Surapriya is in Strīrājya.
At Pūrṇagiri there is Subhoga, and likewise Takṣaka at Śālmali; at Amara there is Pāpahā, and at Ambikā there is Sudarśana.
In Naravāpī he is Mahāvīra, the destroyer of difficulties in the wilderness; in Padmavatī he is Padmagṛha, and in the sky he is Mṛgalāñchana (the Moon). || 102 ||
O Madhusūdana, wherever this hymn of one hundred and eight names is recited, there indeed is my presence at the three junctions of the day.
Furthermore, whoever should behold even one of them in the form of a child obtains the merit of all those aforementioned creators.
O Kṛṣṇa, he who always praises me at Prabhāsa with these names, having attained my abode, Vijaya, rejoices for eternal years.
Whatever evil has been committed through mind, speech, or body—all that goes to destruction by the recitation of my hymn of praise. (106)

Whatever fruit is swiftly attained by men through offerings of flowers, incense, and the gratification of Brahmins, as well as through steady meditation—that same fruit one obtains from the recitation of my hymn of praise. (107)
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, whether committed in this world intentionally or unintentionally, perish at that very moment. || 108 ||
Whoever should hear or recite this hymn, which is dear to me, shall be liberated from all sins and attain his great desire. (109)
I shall tell you another secret; listen, O Kṛṣṇa, according to the truth.
Whenever the lunar mansion Āgneya (Kṛttikā) coincides with the full moon day of Kārttika, that lunar day should be known as the "Great" one at Prabhāsa, for it is dear to me.
If the constellation Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī) should fall on that lunar day, it is the meritorious Mahākārtikī, difficult to obtain even for the gods. (112)

When the moon or Jupiter is in the sign of Taurus and the full moon of Kārttika coincides with the Kṛttikā constellation, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice by beholding him in the form of a child.
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it is difficult to obtain at Prabhāsa, O Hari.
In that yoga, having seen the one in the form of a child at Prabhāsa, even a man burdened by ten million sins does not behold the realm of Yama. || 115 ||
The Lord said: Thus was this hymn spoken by Brahmā to Hari once more; and I have now related to you this majesty whose deity is Brahmā.
The gift of land, which removes all sins of men and accomplishes all goals when heard, should be bestowed there by those desiring the fruit of the pilgrimage. 117.
A water-pot, a white garment, and the sixteen great gifts—these, O Goddess, should be given right there to Brahmā in the form of a child.
When the great festival has arrived, the twice-born should perform the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa); all those Brāhmaṇas, O Goddess, are residents within the sacred field.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Brahmā in the Form of a Child," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Liṅga of the Vasus, located fifty dhanus away from Someśa in the northeastern direction.
O Great Goddess, there stands the four-faced Liṅga, beloved by the gods, named Pratyūṣeśvara, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
By the sight of that deity, the sin arising from seven previous births goes to destruction; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. (3)
The Goddess said: Who was this one named Pratyūṣa, and how was the Liṅga installed? Whose son was he, and how is he renowned? Tell me this, O Śaṅkara. (4)
Īśvara said: O Goddess, Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, is known as Prajāpati; he formerly gave sixty daughters [to Kaśyapa], and ten indeed to Dharma.
Among them, O Great Goddess, one was renowned as Viśvā; she, O Great Goddess, gave birth to eight sons from Dharma.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anala, Anila, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. (7)
Among them, the seventh was renowned as Pratyūṣa; O Goddess of the Gods, desiring a son, he came to the sacred field of Prabhāsa.

Having recognized that field as one that fulfills desires and having installed Maheśvara there, O beloved, he performed extensive divine penance for a hundred years, meditating upon the god Mahādeva, tranquil and with his mind fixed on Him alone.
Then, O Goddess, Mahādeva, the stainless one, being pleased by his devotion, granted him a son, Devala, the best among yogis.
From that time forward, O Goddess of the Gods, by the power of that liṅga, the venerable yogin Devala became a son at dawn.
For this reason, he is known by the name Pratyūṣeśvara.
O Goddess of the gods, the lineage of that man who shall propitiate him, even if he is childless, shall never perish.

O Great Goddess, whoever, with constant self-restraint and true devotion, shall worship the supreme Pratyūṣeśvara at dawn, even the sin arising from the killing of a Brahmin shall go to its destruction for him. (14)
A bull should be given right there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage. || 15 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should indeed keep a vigil there during the night; through that vigil, one obtains the fruit of all gifts and sacrifices.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pratyūṣeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 108.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Anilesvara, located three dhanus to the north-east of it, O beloved.
Indeed, this Liṅga of great power destroys sins through its mere sight; it is celebrated as that which is known as Anila, the fifth among the Vasus. || 2 ||
And having propitiated Mahādeva, he beheld Bhava face to face; endowed with perfect faith, he duly installed a Liṅga.
Thus, by the power of the Lord, his son also became powerful; he was renowned as Manojava, and likewise his movement was unperceived.
Having seen him, a mortal is never again afflicted by disease; nor does he ever become blind, deaf, mute, diseased, or destitute on this earth once he has beheld him. (5)
Whoever should offer even a single flower upon that Liṅga shall always be endowed with happiness and good fortune, and shall possess beauty of form.
Thus, O Goddess, has this greatness which destroys sins been told; by hearing it and approving it with devotion, one prospers in all desires. (7)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Anileśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, one should go to the supreme Prabhāseśvara, which, O Goddess, is declared to be situated to the west of Gaurī’s penance grove.
O Goddess, that great Liṅga was established at a distance of not more than seven bow-lengths by the eighth of the Vasus.
Indeed, one named Prabhāsa, who was devoted to the worship of Śiva and desirous of a son, O Goddess of Devas, came to the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Having installed the great Liṅga, O beloved, he performed extensive penance for a hundred divine years; it is renowned as the Āgneya [Liṅga].
Then, O Great Goddess, because he was endowed with perfect faith, the Blessed Lord Rudra was pleased and granted him whatever he desired in his mind.
Bhuvanā, the sister of Bṛhaspati, was a speaker of sacred knowledge; she became the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
Viśvakarman was her son, the creator of the world and a Prajāpati; he is remembered as the wise architect of the gods and the maternal grandfather of Manu.
Takṣaka was the great destroyer of the splendor of the solar orb; such was the son born to the eighth of the Vasus.
O Goddess of gods, he was intent upon the worship of that Liṅga named Prabhāsa; thus, O Goddess, has this been told to you concerning the indicator of Prabhāseśvara.
He who worships that auspicious [liṅga], which destroys all sins, grants all desires, and bestows greatness, with devotion and endowed with perfect faith—|| 10 ||
Sleeping on the ground and abstaining from food while reciting the Śatarudriya, he bathed at the confluence of the ocean on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, || 12 ||

O Goddess, he who thus performs this great festival of the perfect pilgrimage is liberated from all sins and prospers with the fulfillment of all desires. A bull should be gifted right there by those who desire the full fruit of the perfect pilgrimage. (13)

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Prabhāseśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 110 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Puṣkara forest, situated sixty bows' length away from that [place] in the northeast corner.
There, O Great Goddess, is a pool known as Aṣṭapuṣkara; it removes all sins, O Goddess, and is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined their souls.
There, near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), that great liṅga was formerly established by the wise Rāmeśa; it is known as Rāmeśvara. || 3 ||
By the mere worship of that [liṅga], one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, tell me in detail about the origin of Rāmeśvara; how did Rāma come there, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa?
How is the Liṅga established at Puṣkara, the thief of sins? Tell me this in detail, together with its fruit and its majesty.
Īśvara said: In the twenty-fourth yuga, Rāma was born as the son of Daśaratha with Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest, in order to destroy Rāvaṇa in former times.
Then, O Goddess, after some time, due to the curse of a sage, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who was possessed of great ascetic power, departed together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having departed for residence in the forest, surrounded by divine brahman-sages, he then arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa in the course of his journey.
Having reached that place, being thoroughly exhausted, he sat down; then, when the sun had set, he spread leaves upon the ground.
Then, at the end of the night, O Queen, she fell asleep and beheld her own father, Daśaratha, in a dream, possessing a gentle form and great splendor.
Having risen in the morning, he reported all of that to the brahmins, exactly as he had been seen in a dream by that great-souled one, Daśaratha.
The Brahmins said: "O Raghava, your ancestors, desiring your prosperity and being granters of boons, indeed appear in dreams to one born of their own lineage. (13)
This sacred ford of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is greatly meritorious and well-guarded; it is known as Puṣkara—let a śrāddha be offered here.
"Surely King Daśaratha was longing for this sacred bathing place; therefore, having received the auspicious funeral cake offered by you, he has attained a vision [of the divine]. (15)
The Lord said: Having heard those words of theirs, the lotus-eyed Rāma then invited auspicious brāhmaṇas worthy of the śrāddha ceremony.
He spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood at his side with his neck bowed: "O son of Sumitrā, go quickly for the sake of fruit, intent upon the performance of the Śrāddha."
Having promised "So be it," that joy of the Raghus departed; he quickly brought back various kinds of fruits.
And bilva fruits, kapittha fruits, and tinduka fruits in abundance, as well as badara, karīra, and karamarda fruits, O beloved. (19)
Likewise, there were cirbhaṭa fruits, parūṣa fruits, and mātuluṅga fruits, as well as bright coconuts and those produced from the iṅgudī tree. || 20 ||
Then Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, quickly cooked these; thereafter, at the time of Kutapa, having bathed and being pure, she put on her bark garments.
He summoned the best of the twice-born, Brahmins worthy of the Śrāddha rite: Gālava, Devala, Raibhya, Yavakrīta, and Parvata.
Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Jāvāli, Gautama, and Bhṛgu—these and many other Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas [were there]. (23)
At that very time, those who had arrived for the sake of the funeral rites of Rāma, whose actions are effortless, [were present]; and then Rāma addressed Sītā.
"Come, Vaidehī, give water for washing the feet of the brāhmaṇas. Having heard this, Sītā then entered into the midst of the trees.
Having concealed herself behind the thickets, she remained out of Rama's sight; yet whenever Rama repeatedly called out, "Sita, Sita," [she would respond].
Having learned that she was lost, Lakṣmaṇa, seeing Rāghava overcome with anger, himself performed at that time the rites of expiation appropriate for a Brāhmaṇa.
Then, when the brahmins had finished eating and the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) had been performed, Jānakī Sītā arrived at the place where Rāma was staying.

Seeing her, Rāghava rebuked her with harsh words: "Fie, fie upon you, O sinful woman! Having abandoned the twice-born and this most auspicious ancestral rite, where have you gone, leaving me behind just as the time for the śrāddha has arrived? (29)
Īśvara said: Having heard those words of his, Jānakī was struck with fear.
With palms joined in reverence and trembling, she spoke: "Do not be angry, O auspicious one; do not revile me, O Lord. (31)
Listen, O Lord, why she has gone elsewhere, leaving your presence: today my father and likewise my grandfather were seen by her there. (32)
Furthermore, his ancestors as well as his maternal grandfathers and others were individually established in the various limbs of those foremost of Brahmins. (33)
Then, O descendant of Raghu, shame arose within me there; for there, O mighty-armed one, my father [bestowed] delightful and auspicious [garments]. (34)

"O King of kings, those foods which are indeed wholesome have already been eaten; how then will he eat things that are extremely astringent, alkaline, and pungent? From this, grief has entered me. (36)
For this reason, O scion of Raghu, I vanished out of shame upon seeing my own circle of father-in-laws; therefore, abandon your anger. (36)
Having heard those words of hers, Rāghava was struck with wonder; he performed the śrāddha ceremony especially at that sacred site of Puṣkara.
There, at the vicinity of Puṣkara, within three bow-lengths to the south, he installed the Liṅga known as Rāmeśvara. (35)
He who worships it with devotion, in due order, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, attains the supreme abode where the Lord Janārdana resides. (39)
What is the use of saying more in this regard? Whatever one may bestow on the twelfth day, no reckoning of its merit exists even throughout the three worlds. (40)
O beautiful lady, whenever the fourth lunar day occurs conjoined with Venus or Mars, or the sixth lunar day here, there is great fruit from performing a śrāddha on that occasion.
For as long as twelve years, the fathers and grandfathers, being satiated at Puṣkara by one born of their own lineage, desire nothing else.
In that place, the man who gives a horse endowed with perfect devotion obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 43 ||
Thus, O beautiful lady, I have fully related to you the sin-destroying majesty of the god Rāmeśvara and of Puṣkara.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Rāmeśvara Kṣetra," within the "Majesty of Puṣkara" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 111 ||
The Lord said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Lakṣmaṇeśvara, situated thirty dhanus to the east of Rāmeśa.
O Goddess, that Liṅga, which destroys great sins and is worshipped by the gods, was indeed installed there by Lakṣmaṇa himself while he was on his journey.
He who worships him with devotion through dance, song, instrumental music, fire-offerings, and recitation, remaining established in meditative absorption, attains the supreme goal. || 3 ||
There, food, water, and gold should be given to the twice-born, after having worshipped the Lord of the Gods with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, there is a special significance to worship there; bathing, giving gifts, and recitation performed at that time become inexhaustible in their merit.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Lakṣmaṇeśvara," within the "Majesty of Rāmeśvara Kṣetra," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa Kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa Khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 112.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Janakishvara, situated thirty dhanus to the southwest of Ramesha.
This [liṅga], which destroys the sins of all living beings, was formerly propitiated by Jānakī; having perfectly worshipped Śaṅkara, it was especially installed by her.
Formerly, that very Liṅga was indeed named Vasiṣṭheśa; later, during the Tretā age, it became renowned on earth as Jānakīśa.
Then sixty thousand great sages, the Vālakhilyas, attained perfection there; therefore, it is called Siddheśvara.
O Great Goddess, it is renowned that in the Kali age there is the Yugaliṅga of great splendor; by seeing it, one is liberated from sins arising from suffering and misfortune.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever worships him with devotion after bathing him according to the prescribed rite, shall be liberated from all sins.
And having bathed at the Puṣkara tīrtha, he who, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, should worship that Liṅga continuously for one month; || 7 ||

Day after day, he shall obtain a fruit greater than that of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha). Any woman who worships him on the third lunar day of the month of Māgha—within her lineage as well, misfortune, suffering, and grief shall never arise.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this greatness that destroys sin; when heard, it removes all evils and bestows good fortune.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jānakīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 113 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Vishnu, the destroyer of sins, known by the name Vamanasvamin, who destroys all transgressions.
To the southwest of Puṣkara, at a distance of twenty bows, it is recorded, O Goddess, that when Bali was bound by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Then, O beloved, the one of universal form placed his right foot there; the second was on the peak of Meru, and the third was in the sky.
As far as he threw it upward, so far was it shattered at a great distance; by the tip of his foot, the cosmic egg was pierced, and from there the water emerged.
Then, reaching the surface of the earth at the height of one's own knee, the Gaṅgā, the foot of Viṣṇu, became renowned upon the earth. || 5 ||
Formerly she reached Puṣkara; from Puṣkara that great river [arose]. Space is called Puṣkara, and water is called Puṣkara; therefore that place is renowned as Puṣkara, the abode of Prajāpati.
Having performed his bath there, the man who beholds the foot of Hari goes to the supreme abode where the Lord Hari himself resides.
In that place, O lady of excellent hips, satisfaction for ten million years shall accrue to the ancestors through the offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa); indeed, Hari himself has declared this.
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by the great seer Vasiṣṭha upon seeing the Lord Vāmana; listen to it with a concentrated mind. (9)
Having bathed at the holy site of Puṣkara and then beheld Viṣṇupada, even after having committed a great sin, why should one thereafter feel remorse? (10)
He who, firm in his vows, gives a pair of sandals there to a Brāhmaṇa, ascends an excellent vehicle and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 11 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Vāmanasvāmī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 114 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Puṣkareśvara; and on its very southern side is the excellent Jānakīśvara.
The Liṅga of great power was worshipped with faith by the sage Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, with golden lotuses.
O lady of excellent limbs, that Puṣkareśvara, which destroys all sins, was worshipped there according to the prescribed rite; thus it became renowned.
Whoever worships him with devotion, in due order, with incense, flowers, and other offerings, has effectively performed the Pauṣkara pilgrimage; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Puṣkareśvara," within the "Majesty of Vāmanasvāmī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 115 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess who bestows good fortune, renowned as Kuṇḍeśvarī, located to the northwest of Puṣkara.
O Goddess, thirty bows’ distance from Bhūtanātha toward the southwest stands Pāpadamanī, the destroyer of the flood of poverty.
To the southwest of that [place], situated at a distance of fifteen bow-lengths, is the pool named Śaṅkhodaka, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there in the auspicious waters, those mortals or women, O Great Goddess, should worship her who is renowned as Śaṅkhāvartā.
In the Kali age, she named Kuṇḍeśvarī shall bestow all happiness. O beloved Goddess, in ancient times, one named Śaṅkha was slain by Viṣṇu.
Taking up his great body in the form of a conch shell and filling it with water from sacred fords, he arrived at the holy site of Prabhāsa.
There, having washed the conch and prepared a highly radiant holy site (tīrtha), he filled the conch, which resounded with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.

By his great roar, the Goddess arrived there; approaching that pool, she inquired about the cause [of the sound]. Because of this, she became known as Kuṇḍeśvarī, and the pool is remembered as Śaṅkhodaka.
The man or woman who, endowed with devotion, worships her on the third lunar day of the month of Māgha, shall attain the state of Gaurī.
Those desiring the fruit of the pilgrimage should provide a meal for a married couple there, as well as a bodice, gifts of fruit, and a meal for young women. (10)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaurī at Śaṅkhodakakuṇḍeśvarī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 116.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Hara, the Lord of Bhūtanātheśvara, located twenty dhanus away in the direction of the Lord from Kuṇḍeśvarī.
O Great Goddess, the Kalpa-liṅga indeed exists without beginning or end; formerly, O Goddess, in the Tretā Yuga, it was known as Vīrabhadreśvarī.
O Goddess of gods, it is renowned on earth as Bhūteśvara in the Kali age; formerly, at the junction of the Dvāpara age, millions of spirits (bhūtas) resided there.
They attained supreme perfection through the power of that liṅga; therefore, it became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Bhūteśvara.
There, on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fully worshipped Śaṅkara, he who takes recourse to the southern direction and worships Aghora— || 5 ||
Having become firm and having conquered the senses, being fearless and absorbed in meditation, whatever perfection exists upon this earth arises for him alone.

There, indeed, one should offer gifts of sesame and gold, as well as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), intended for the ancestors, for the sake of their liberation from the state of being a preta.

Thus has been declared this [account] of the Lord of the Sovereign of Beings, which destroys the abundant impurities of the Kali age and is a cause of merit. And whichever person here either recites or listens with devotion to the greatness of the Supreme God is liberated from the floods of sin.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhūtanātheśvara," within the "Majesty of Kuṇḍeśvarī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 117 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Gopyaditya, located thirty bow-lengths away from Bhutesha in the northwestern direction.
O Goddess, the destroyer of the Daityas Bala and Atibala, situated ten bow-lengths to the south-east, stands there as the destroyer of sins.
I shall proclaim its auspicious origin, which removes great sins; by hearing it with devotion, a human being is liberated from suffering and grief. (3)
Formerly, when the immensely radiant Kṛṣṇa arrived at Prabhāsa accompanied by all the Yādavas, numbering fifty-six crores.
Sixteen thousand cowherd girls gathered there; likewise, O beloved, these one hundred and sixty thousand were the sons of Kṛṣṇa.
There, situated in that radiant field which destroys all evil, extending from the site of the Yādavas as far as Mount Raivataka; (6)
Having remained there for twelve years, those mighty ones took possession of that sacred field and all of them individually installed Śiva-liṅgas marked with their own names.
In this manner, all those preeminent Yādavas marked that entire field, extending for twelve yojanas, with banners and liṅgas.

O Goddess, within the space of a cubit in the midst of the sacred field, there stand temples adorned with golden domes and filled with fluttering banners; situated there, they shine like the pillars of fame of Lord Hari.
Then, O Great Goddess, I shall tell you the names of those gopīs who are remembered as the original sixteen; listen to them with a focused mind. (10)
Lambinī, Candrikā, Kāntā, Krūrā, Śāntā, Mahodayā, Bhīṣaṇī, Nandinī, Aśokā, Suparṇā, Vimalā, and Akṣayā. || 11 ||
These arts of the Haṃsa are remembered as bestowing auspiciousness, beautiful, and meritorious; indeed, the Haṃsa is considered to be Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, Janārdana. (12)
O Goddess, these sixteen powers of his are thus proclaimed; he is Kṛṣṇa in the form of the moon, and they are remembered as being in the form of its digits (kalās). || 13 ||
Among them, Mālinī is the sixteenth digit (kalā) with a full orb; beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), the moon moves through these [digits].
O fair-faced one, those sixteen digits themselves take the form of the gopīs; each one of them is individually multiplied by a thousand. (15)
Thus, O Goddess, has this secret born of knowledge been told to you; the man who knows it thus is indeed to be known as a Vaiṣṇava by the wise. (16)

Then, having perceived that they had made their salutations with joined palms, the Yādavas each went to their respective palaces; thereafter, all those sixteen thousand gopīs, having entreated Kṛṣṇa with devotion, established the Sun-god [there].
The sages, beginning with Nārada, as well as those residing in that sacred field, installed the Sun-god there according to the prescribed rite of installation.
Then, when the sun had set, they gave gifts in abundance—cows, land, gold, and garments—to the residents of the sacred field.
Then all those sages, satisfied and joyful in heart, gave a name there to the Sun-god, renowned as Gopyāditya—the deity who removes all sins and bestows great good fortune.
When this had been done, having achieved their purpose and attained great renown, they all returned to Dvārakā together with Kṛṣṇa, just as they had come.
Furthermore, O Goddess, beloved, after an interval of time due to the curse of Durvāsas, they attained the state of Yādava creepers at Prabhāsa, the destroyer of sins.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you of the origin of Gopyāditya; now I shall describe to you, in due order, his majesty arising from worship and salutation.
O Goddess, by the mere sight of Him who was installed by the cowherd girls in this Mitravana, one is liberated from suffering and grief. (24)

Those men who have taken refuge in the cowherd women and Kṛṣṇa attain that same goal through well-performed austerity in this world or through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. (25)
