O Maheśvarī, he by whom every aspect of his being has been placed within the Sun of the Heart is praiseworthy and truly blessed, for he has attained the fulfillment of all purpose.
"Will he, by whom the Sun has been worshipped with a spirit of devotion, be born as a blessed purifier of his lineage and a fortunate one in our family? (27)
O beloved, that man who worships on the seventh lunar day at dawn during the month of Māgha shall deliver seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors.
It cuts away diseases, overcomes evil tendencies, and indeed conquers enemies that are difficult to defeat. || 29 ||
On the seventh [lunar day], one should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing; one should neither bathe with *āmalaka* fruits nor engage in any quarrel whatsoever.

Whatever rite a twice-born man performs while wearing blue or red garments—whether it be bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors—all his great sacrifices become fruitless by the wearing of a blue thread. (31)
If a Brahmin should wear a garment dyed with indigo upon his limbs, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 32 ||
If the juice of any blue substance should enter the pore of his skin, the fallen Brahmin removes that taint by performing three *kṛcchra* penances.
If a Brāhmaṇa should ever enter the middle of the Nīla [river] through negligence, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and a night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 34 ||
If blue wood should be split upon the body of Brahmins and blood is seen therein, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. || 35 ||
If one should, out of ignorance, use a blue twig for cleaning the teeth, the wise have declared that his purification consists in performing two *kṛcchra* penances.
Thus has this been told, O Goddess, regarding the great glory of Gopyāditya; it destroys the sins of all living beings and, when heard, accomplishes all goals. (37)
O Goddess of gods, the merit that is obtained by giving hundreds of thousands of cows in Kurujāṅgala is attained by beholding Gopī-Āditya.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gopyāditya," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 118 ||

Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Mahadevi, the greatly resplendent one, who is renowned on earth by the name Balatibala-daityaghni (the slayer of the Daityas Balatibala). || 1 ||
There, in that sacred field, resides the Goddess who is without beginning or end, surrounded by a retinue of ten million beings, and the destroyer of all the Daityas.
The Goddess said: O Lord, how was it that you spoke of [the goddess] as the slayer of the Daityas Bala and Atibala? And how were the two Daityas named Bala and Atibala struck down?
O Maheśvara, where does that goddess reside, and what is her power? Tell me everything regarding her majesty in full detail.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a narrative that destroys sin; by hearing which, a human being through devotion is liberated from all transgressions.
There was a powerful one named Raktāsura, the son of Mahiṣa; he possessed a massive body and mighty arms, like another Hiraṇyākṣa.
He had two sons named Balātibala; having conquered all the gods, led by Indra and Agni.
In this triple world, they swiftly established a kingdom free from fear; thirty-three heroes are proclaimed to be at the head of their armies.
Fierce in nature, great warriors, leading thousands of akṣauhiṇīs, with shoulders like lions, massive bodies, evil-minded, and possessed of great strength.
Dhūmrākṣa, Bhīmadaṃṣṭra, Kālavaśya, Mahāhanu, Brahmaghna, Yajñakopa, Strīghna, and Pāpaniketana.
Vidyunmālī, Bandhūka, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vibhāvasu, Devāntaka, Vikarman, Durbhikṣa, and Krūra. (11)
Hayagrīva, Aśvakarṇa, Ketumān, Vṛṣabha, Dvija, Śarabha, Śalabha, Vyāghra, Nikuṃbha, Maṇika, and Baka. || 12 ||
Śūrpaka, Vikṣara, Mālin, Kāla, Daṇḍaka, and Kerala—these were the large-bodied Daityas who served as the commanders of their two armies. || 13 ||
In this way, the earth, extending fifty koṭis [of yojanas], was pervaded by them. Having realized this, the gods were then agitated in their minds with fear. (14)
Together with all the celestial sages, they went to the forest of the Himalayas; then, with disciplined minds, they praised that goddess with this hymn.

The gods said: Victory to you, O Imperishable One! Victory, O Infinite One! Victory, O Unmanifest One, free from all affliction! Victory, O Goddess Mahāmāyā! Victory, O You who are saluted by divine sages! || 16 ||
Victory, O Gaṅgā, Sovereign of the Universe! Victory, O Bestower of the Fulfillment of All Aims! Victory, O Brahmāṇī and Kaumārī! Victory, O Sovereign Nārāyaṇī! 17.
Victory to you, O Brahmāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā; victory to you, O Indrāṇī and Maheśvarī! Victory to you, Mother Mahālakṣmī; victory to you, O Pārvatī, who pervades all!
Victory, O Goddess, creator of the world! Victory, O Airāvati, O Bhārati! Victory, O Anante! Victory, O Jaye! Victory, O Goddess Jalāvile! 19.

Victory, O Īśānī! Victory, O Śivā! Victory, O Śarvā! Victory eternally, O you who are worshipped with victory! Victory, O giver of liberation! Victory, O omniscient one! Victory, O bestower of dharma, artha, and kāma! 20.
Victory, O auspicious Gāyatrī! Victory, O Sahyā, O radiant one! Victory, O Durgā, O Mahākālī, O messenger of Śiva, victory over both the conquerable and the unconquerable!
Victory to you, O Caṇḍā, O Mahāmuṇḍā! Victory to you, O Nandā, beloved of Śiva! Victory to you, O Kṣemaṃkarī, O Śivā! Victory to you, O auspicious Revatī!
Victory to you, O Auspicious One who possesses perfection! Homage to you, O Harasiddhi! Victory to Aparṇā, victory to Ānandā, O slayer of the demon Mahiṣa!
Victory to you, O Medhā, O large-eyed one! Victory to you, O Anaṅgā, O Sarasvatī! Victory to you, O abode of all virtues! Victory to you, O Āvartā, O destroyer of the gods! 24.

Victory to you, O you who have perfected all your resolves! Victory to you, O beauty of the three worlds! Victory to you, O slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha! Victory to you, O Padmā, born from the mountain! 25.
Victory to you, O Kauśikī, O Kaumāri; victory to you, O Vāruṇī, O Kāmadā! Salutations, salutations to you, O Śarvāṇī; victory again and again, O Ambikā! (26)
Save us, save us, O Goddess, you who are worthy of refuge, for we have come to you for protection! || 27 ||
O fair-faced one, having been thus praised by all the gods, the Blessed Lady revealed herself, illuminating the horizons with her radiance.

Having paid homage to her, those gods spoke to her, the destroyer of fear: "Having slain the two exceedingly powerful Daityas named Bala and Atibala, as well as their great army, protect us from this immense danger. (29)
Having heard those words of theirs and having granted them fearlessness, she then assumed a wondrous form—three-eyed and crowned with the moon.
The Great Goddess is mounted upon a lion, bearing various weapons and missiles; she has a beautiful face, twenty arms, and resembles a flash of blazing lightning.
Then Ambikā let out a loud roar with frequent bursts of boisterous laughter. || 32 ||
By her terrible roar, the entire sky was filled; the whole earth, girdled by rivers and oceans, trembled.
With breasts as lofty as mountains, she was as beautiful as a young woman overcome by fear; meanwhile, those Asuras also arrived there, accompanied by their fourfold army.
Those who have correctly understood his valor, who are like Time, the Destroyer, and Yama—even the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Daityas, and those who dwell in the netherworld (Pātāla). || 35 ||
All those lords of the Daityas arrived there by the millions; then a great battle took place between the Goddess and the asuras.
O Goddess of the Suras, thirty-three thousand akṣauhiṇī divisions indeed became the cause of an untimely destruction throughout the entire universe. 37.
Twenty-one thousand, eight hundred, and seventy chariots, swift as the wind, along with their followers and warriors, [were destroyed]. 38.
Having slain them with ease, that goddess, remaining unperturbed, led them to their destruction.
Then the earth was covered with the bodies of the immensely powerful Dānavas slain by the Goddess, as well as the bodies of their elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, in that battlefield crowded with the dancing of headless trunks and muddy with flowing fat and bones, the powerful night-stalkers roamed about.
Jackals, vultures, and crows brought about a great slaughter; elsewhere, other night-stalkers, fierce from having drunk blood to satiety, gratified their own ancestors and likewise honored the sages.
Utterly merciless, they devoured elephants, men, and horses; likewise, others crossed the ocean of blood using chariots as rafts. 43.
Thus, in that intense battle crowded with hosts of the enemies of the gods, Ambikā shines resplendent, bearing a bow, arrows, a sword, and a trident.
Crushing the pride of the lordly elephants, trampling the herds of horses, and destroying the armies of the enemies of the gods, she gazes here and there.

Then those heroic lords of the Daityas, beholding that great female ghost—who was joined with eight lions, white as a mountain or a swan, radiant with a brilliant luster, and equal to a bull—became filled with rising rage; and shouting and roaring with a sound like the thundering of clouds, they rushed forward from there.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Alas! while being struck down, some of those asuras entered the ocean, and other dānavas took refuge in the mountains. || 47 ||
Some, having become shavelings and rogues, lived in the forest; professing the dharma of compassion, they adopted the vow of the Nirgranthas. || 48 ||
Some, fearing for their lives, have resorted to heretical stages of life; they are fools devoted to sophistry, devoid of purity, and lacking all regard for spiritual values. (49)
And even today, they are indeed seen here in the world as Kṣapaṇakas, as well as others known as Bhindakas, who have been excluded from the Śiva scriptures.

Indeed, some who observe the Kaula vow are seen here by all people—those who indulge excessively in liquor, women, and meat, who persist in improper conduct, and who merely bear the outward marks of asceticism.
For the most part, those wicked and deceitful ones were devoted to their tongues and genitals; thus, all of them, though joined with Bala and Atibala, were slain by the Goddess.

Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, that Ambikā then took her stand there, accompanied by sixty-four Yoginīs; she, the destroyer of sins, became renowned on earth at Prabhāsa as Balātibalanāśinī.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the Gods, you have mentioned sixty-four Yoginīs; tell me their names, which remove all sins. (54)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great exaltation of the Yoginīs; it is divine, the provider of all protection, and the destroyer of great fears. (55)
First among them were Mahālakṣmī, Nandā, Kṣemaṃkarī, Śivadūtī, Mahābhadrā, Bhrāmarī, and Candramaṇḍalā. || 56 ||
Revatī, Harasiddhi, Durgā, Viṣamalocanā, Sahajā, Kulajā, Kubjā, Māyāvī, Śāmbhavī, and Kriyā. (57)

She is the primordial, all-pervading, pure, accessible through meditative absorption, and transcending the mind; she is both knowledge and ignorance, the great illusion, the central channel (suṣumnā), and the source of all auspiciousness.

O Great Goddess, you are the essence of the syllable Om, the progenitor of the meaning of the Vedas, the auspicious one; you are the Purāṇas, logic, initiation, Cāmuṇḍā, and the beloved of Śaṅkara. (59)
She is Brāhmī, the bringer of peace, Gaurī, the consort of Brahmā, and the beloved of the Brahmins; she is Bhadrā, the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇā, and she who wears the garland of planets and constellations.
Tripurā, Tvaritā, Nityā, Sāṃkhyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Dhruvā, Kalyāṇī, Śobhanā, Nirayā, Niṣkalā, and Paramā Kalā. (61)
She is the Yoginī, the true essence of yoga, accessible through yoga, dwelling in the cave of the heart; she is celebrated as Kātyāyanī, Umā, Śarvā, and Aparṇā.
O Great Goddess, thus have these sixty-four [names] been proclaimed to you; whoever praises Caṇḍikā with devotion by means of this divine hymn, [attains the fruit].
Śarvāṇī protects him like her own son in all calamities, especially on the fourteenth, the eighth, and the ninth lunar days.
O Goddess, those who have undertaken the vows and chant to Caṇḍikā by means of fasting, eating but one meal, or likewise eating only what is unasked for; || 65 ||

Those who practice according to the truth become perfected after half a year or one full year; [this occurs] during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, on the Manvantara-beginnings, and on the Aṣṭaka days.
Having performed a great festival, one should worship the Goddess for the increase of welfare; a devotee of Durgā should wear the golden sandals of the Goddess.

And for the sake of pacifying negligence and obstacles, a man should always carry a razor-knife; likewise, those who have resorted to a demonic disposition [employ] animal flesh and fermented liquors.
Those who worship Ambikā shall become Daityas who enjoy sovereign power; those established in sattvic devotion attain the state of divinity through sattva.

O Goddess, this majesty of the goddess who destroys Bala and Atibala—which accomplishes all aims, resides in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, and increases one's fame—has been told to you in brief as a destroyer of sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Goddess who Slayed the Daityas Bala and Atibala," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Gopishvara, located three dhanus to the north of where the two Daityas, Bala and Atibala, were slain.

Established for the pacification of sins and installed by the cowherd women, it was there that [they] propitiated Mahādeva Maheśvara for the sake of a son; it bestows all desires upon men when worshipped and grants progeny. || 2 ||
The man who worships him on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra with offerings of perfumes and flowers attains his desired fruit.
Thus has been briefly proclaimed the sin-destroying majesty of the god Gopīśvara, who dwells in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gopīśvara," within the "Majesty of the Destroyer of the Daityas Balātibalau," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 120.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Rāmeśvara, which was personally installed there by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
To the northwest of Gopīśvara, at a distance of thirty dhanus, stands a Liṅga of great power that destroys all sins.
O Goddess of gods, when the terrible slaughter of his mother was committed by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, acting in obedience to his father's command; || 3 ||
Then, having felt distress in his mind, Jamadagni, the great ascetic, fell into despondency; thereafter, he attained a state of serenity.
Then, being pleased, he granted a boon and restored Reṇukā to life; thus, although that woman of excellent complexion was brought back to life there, [she remained as before].
Nevertheless, O Goddess, the son of Jamadagni, possessed of great luster and filled with compassion, reached the holy field of Prabhāsa and performed wonderful penance there.
Having installed Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, for more than a hundred divine years, Maheśvara was then pleased.
Remaining right there himself, he granted him everything he desired; thereafter, the great ṛṣi Jāmadagnya attained fulfillment.
Having conquered the earth twenty-one times and slain the Kṣatriyas, the high-minded one established the Pañcanada there at Kurukṣetra.
O fair-faced one, having brought about the complete filling with blood of the kṣatriyas, that mighty one attained freedom from his debt to the ancestors.
Having thus brought about the end of the Kṣatriyas and bestowed the earth upon the Brahmins, he attained his life's purpose, his prowess renowned throughout the three worlds.

That Liṅga was established by him in the auspicious Prābhāsika Kṣetra; whatever man, even if burdened with sin, worships it with devotion, he is liberated from all transgressions and goes to the world of Umāpati.
That man who keeps a vigil there on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, rejoices in heaven like a god.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Jāmadagnyeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 121.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga Citrāṅgadeśvara, situated twenty bows to the southwest of that very place.

O Goddess of gods, O beloved, Citrāṅgada, the lord of the Gandharvas, having recognized this sacred field as pure, performed most formidable penance and, having propitiated Maheśvara, installed a Liṅga there. || 2 ||
Now, he who is devoted to the Bhāva [deities] should fully worship their emblem; he attains the world of the Gandharvas and rejoices together with the Gandharvas. || 3 ||

There, having bathed Śiva according to the ritual on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship him with various flowers, perfumes, and incenses in due order; he shall obtain every desire, whatever is wished for by the mind.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Citrāṅgadeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 122 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Rāvaṇeśvara, situated sixteen bow-lengths to the south-southwest of that [place]. || 1 ||
Established by the Ten-faced one, it destroys all sins; O Goddess, Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, was indeed a most terrible Rākṣasa. || 2 ||
Desirous of conquering the three worlds, he traveled by means of the Puṣpaka chariot. Then, after some time, that Puṣpaka chariot of his—
While traveling through the path of the sky, the Puṣpaka suddenly became motionless; seeing it thus paralyzed, Rāvaṇa was filled with wonder.
He dispatched Prahasta, saying: "Go! What is this? For his movement remains unimpeded throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile."
"For what reason has my Puṣpaka chariot become motionless? Then, O Goddess, he quickly descended to the surface of the earth.
He beheld the Lord of the gods of gods, the illustrious Someśa of great splendor, being praised by hosts of deities by the hundreds and thousands.
Having seen that, O beloved, Prahasta related everything in detail to the lord of the Rākṣasas—everything that he had observed within the sacred field.
Prahasta said: O Lord of the Rākṣasas, O mighty-armed one, O Master, there is your own sacred field known as Prabhāsa, frequented by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.

There, the god Someśvara, Śaṅkara himself, resides, being worshipped on all sides by sages such as those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, those who use their teeth as a mortar, and the Vālakhilyas. || 10 ||
By the power of that god, this Puṣpaka does not move; for that god cannot be transgressed, being indeed unassailable by gods or asuras.
Īśvara said: Having heard those words of his, with eyes wide open in wonder, he descended to the surface of the earth and beheld Someśa.
O Goddess of the gods, filled with supreme devotion, he worshipped [her] with various kinds of jewels, garments, perfumes, flowers, and unguents. (13)
Then, O lady of beautiful limbs, seeing Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, the citizens fled in all directions, terrified by fear.
Everything became empty, and the Lord was established there; at that very moment, an unembodied voice spoke.
O ten-necked one of mighty arms, likewise during the northern course of the sun, at the time of the deity's procession which destroys all sins.
Having arrived from afar, many twice-born men, terrified by the fear of the Rākṣasas, are indeed fleeing in the ten directions. || 17 ||
O Lord of Rākṣasas, do not, out of fear, become an obstacle to our journey. By beholding the Lord Someśvara, a mortal may wash away all the sins committed in childhood, youth, and even old age. (18)
Then that lord of the Rākṣasas, having gone to a secluded and very deep cave, installed a Liṅga endowed with supreme devotion.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, becoming devoted to that, the lord of the Rākṣasas, intent upon fasting, worshipped with all of them.
He kept a vigil before him with song and instrumental music; then, at the time of midnight, an incorporeal voice spoke.
"O ten-necked one, O mighty-armed one, O sinless one, I am well-pleased with you. By my grace, the three worlds shall come under your control. I shall undoubtedly remain ever present here. (22)
And those men who, endowed with devotion, shall worship this Liṅga, O Lord of Rākṣasas, they shall become invincible to their enemies.
"By my grace, they shall undoubtedly attain supreme perfection. Having spoken thus, O lady of beautiful hips, the bull-bannered god became silent.
Rāvaṇa, being highly gratified, repeatedly worshipped Maheśvara and that liṅga; then, mounting the Puṣpaka chariot, he departed for his desired destination, longing for victory over the three worlds.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Rāvaṇeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 123 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Gauri, the bestower of good fortune, who is situated five bow-lengths to the west of Ravanaisha.
There, the goddess Arundhatī herself performed severe penance, devoted to the worship of Gaurī while desiring the blessing of conjugal felicity.
They attained supreme perfection through the power of that goddess on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, O lady of beautiful countenance.
O Goddess of gods, whoever worships her with devotion shall obtain good fortune in another birth; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Saubhāgyeśvarī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 124 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the great Liṅga beloved of the gods, located thirty bow-lengths to the northwest of Rāvaṇeśvara.
The Linga named Paulomīśvara stands there, bestowing all desires and destroying all sins; it was installed by Paulomī.
When the gods standing in battle were destroyed by Tāraka, he seized the entire three worlds and assumed the sovereignty of Indra himself.
Then Śakra, afflicted by great sorrow and agitated by fear, indeed perished; at that time, O Goddess, he was accompanied by his wife Indrāṇī, who was emaciated by grief.
Desiring victory for Indra, she propitiated Śambhu; thereupon, the gratified Mahādeva spoke to that lady of auspicious eyes.
The Blessed One said: "A son shall be born to us, the mighty six-faced one; he shall cause the death of Tāraka, the king of the Daityas."
Go now, free from fever; listen further to my words.
Whoever shall worship this Liṅga situated here, he will surely become my Gaṇa and come into my presence.
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous woman departed for where the king of the gods was stationed—she who was completely liberated from all suffering and freed from all fear of the Daityas.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Paulomeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Shandilyeshvara, located sixteen dhanus to the west of Brahma.
That Linga possesses great power; by the sight of it, sins are destroyed.
The Brahmanical sage named Śāṇḍilya is remembered as the charioteer of Brahmā; he was an ascetic of great splendor, established in knowledge, and a master of his senses. || 3 ||
Having reached Prabhāsa, he performed most severe penance after installing a great Liṅga situated to the north of Someśa.
He himself performed worship for a hundred divine years, O beloved; then, having obtained his desired object, he became one who had fulfilled his purpose.
Endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the rest through the grace of Nandīśvara, a man who beholds him immediately becomes free from sin.
O beloved, whatever sin a man commits in childhood, in old age, or even in youth—whether through ignorance or intentionally—all that comes to destruction by the sight of Śāṇḍilyeśvara.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śāṇḍilyeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Kshemesvara, situated in the northern corner from that [place], in the south-eastern direction from Kapalesha.
Situated at a distance of fifteen dhanus from Kapāleśvara is indeed a Liṅga of great power, which destroys all sins.
In ancient times, there was a king named Kṣemamūrti who possessed great strength; that high-souled one performed austerities there for a long period of time.
Then, having installed the Liṅga with a mind purified by devotion, one attains well-being upon seeing it, and every undertaking is accomplished with safety. || 4 ||
"May I be one whose self is fulfilled in all desires in birth after birth. Thus is the Kṣemeśvara Liṅga renowned as the destroyer of sins.
It bestows all desires upon men and, when heard, grants good fortune; even by the mere sight of it, the merit of a hundred cows is traditionally said to be obtained.
Therefore, one who desires the fruit of the sacred field should always take refuge in that Linga.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kṣemaṃkareśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Sāgarāditya, located to the west of Bhairaveśa as well as Rudra Mṛtyuñjaya.
O Great Goddess, situated not far to the south-east of Kāmeśa, there is a shrine established by the high-souled Sagara which pacifies all diseases and destroys the flood of poverty. || 2 ||
Having propitiated the Sun there, Sagara, the lord of the earth and destroyer of enemies, obtained sixty thousand sons.
O Goddess, this ocean, which is eighty thousand yojanas in length, is proclaimed to be one yojana in width.
In this Manvantara, he was cast by the oceans in the four directions; O Goddess, this name of his is celebrated as "Sāgara" (the Ocean).
By him whose celebrated fame is sung here even now in the Purāṇas, this god Bhāskara, the stealer of waters, was established.
Upon seeing it, one shall not be dull-witted, nor blind, nor poor, nor afflicted by sorrow; one shall neither be separated from what is dear, nor diseased, nor a doer of evil.
O Great Goddess, in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, one who has conquered his senses, having fasted on the sixth day, should sleep at night in front of her.
Then, having awakened on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun with devotion; one should feed the Brahmins with devotion and avoid any stinginess regarding wealth.
Neither by well-performed austerity in this world nor by sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees do men attain that goal which those who have taken refuge in the Sun have reached.
But even if worship is performed with devotion by men using merely sprouts of dūrvā grass, the Sun indeed bestows a fruit that is very difficult to attain through all other sacrifices.
Therefore, with every effort one should worship the Sun alone, just as Janaka and others attained perfection after worshipping the Maker of Light.
The soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the god of gods, and the progenitor of beings—the Sun alone is the root and the supreme deity of the three worlds. (13)
In spring the sun is tawny; in summer it has the brilliance of gold; in the rainy season it is white in color; and in autumn the sun is pale yellow.
In the winter the sun is copper-colored, and in the cool season it is red; thus one should meditate upon the Sun according to the sequence of these specific colors.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, with self-restraint and controlled senses, one should recite the Thousand Names, which destroy all sins.
The Goddess said: "O Lord Śaṅkara, out of your grace, please recite to me the thousand names; or else, proclaim something else that is equal to the thousand names. (17)
Īśvara said: Enough with the thousand names; recite instead this auspicious hymn. Those names which are secret, pure, and auspicious—I shall proclaim them to you; listen attentively.
Vikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, the Illuminator of the World, the Glorious One, the Eye of the World, and the Lord of Planets. || 19 ||
The witness of the world, the lord of the three worlds, the creator and the destroyer, the dispeller of darkness; the sun that heats, the purifier, and he whose vehicle is the seven horses.
Gabhastihasta, Brahmā, and he who is saluted by all the gods—this hymn of twenty-one verses is thus desired for the Great-Souled One.
Bestowing physical health, increasing wealth, and bringing about fame, it is renowned as the "King of Hymns" (Stavarāja), celebrated throughout the three worlds. (22)

And whoever, O Great Goddess, having become purified, praises the Sun at the two twilights—at both sunset and sunrise—is liberated from all sins. With his soul fulfilled by the attainment of all desires, he goes to the world of the Sun. || 23 ||
Thus, O Goddess, has been told this majesty born of Sāgarārka; when heard, it pacifies the flood of suffering and destroys great sins. (24)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sāgarāditya," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Akṣamāleśvara, located fifty dhanus away in the northeast direction from Sāgarārka.
Established there is the Yugaliṅga of great splendor, which pacifies all evils; formerly it was celebrated by the name Akṣamāleśvara, but now it is renowned as Ugraseneśvara. || 2 ||
The Goddess said: "O Lord, regarding that which was previously mentioned by the name Akṣamāleśvara—how did that come to be? Please tell me out of your grace. (3)
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, in former times there was a woman named Akṣamālā, not born from a womb, who was devoted to the dharma of a virtuous wife. 4.
Once, O Great Goddess, when a famine had arrived due to the passage of time, the sages were overcome by hunger and lost their composure.
Desiring food, they all went to the house of the Caṇḍāla; having learned of his store of provisions, they entreated that outcaste.
"O, O, you of great intellect, you of low birth! Protect us by the gift of food—us who have fallen into a danger to our lives, emaciated in body, and tormented by hunger. (7)
"Oh, you are blessed! You are worthy of worship; you are not called an outcaste, since even after this dissolution has passed, grain remains in your house."
In a region struck by drought and when the crops have perished, if one feeds a single Brahmin, it is as if ten million have been fed.
The outcaste said: "Oh, what an incomparable marvel is this that is seen now—that these sages, desiring food, have arrived at my house! (10)
Even the food of a Śūdra should not be accepted by Brāhmaṇas, much less that of an outcaste (antyaja).
He who eats the food of a Śūdra, whether raw or cooked, shall become a village pig or be born into that Śūdra’s family.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as milk; the food of a Vaiśya they call mere food; and the food of a Śūdra is remembered as blood. (13)
The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra, and the acquisition of food from a Śūdra—these cause even one who is blazing [with spiritual merit] to fall. (14)
But that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī) yet does not abstain from the food of a Śūdra—his self, his Vedic knowledge, and his three sacrificial fires perish. (15)
If a Brāhmaṇa dies while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach, that Brahmin is reborn as a Piśāca within six months. || 16 ||
That twice-born man who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice with the food of a Śūdra is born as a Caṇḍāla after death, and even here on earth he is considered a deity belonging to the Śūdra.
But he who eats the food of a Śūdra continuously for one month attains the state of a Śūdra in this very life, and after death, he is born as a Śūdra.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster; the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (19)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds. (20)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen; the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Whatever [sin] would result from eating the food of these [other sinners] a thousand times, that same [sin] results for one who eats the food of a seller of a daughter just once. (22)
Whatever fruit may arise from eating his food a thousand times, that same fruit indeed arises from eating the food of outcastes just once.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, how is it that you, who truly understand dharma, desire to take food from me, a Cāṇḍāla of the lowest nature? (24)
The sages said: He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, accepts food from that source, is not tainted by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud. (25)
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son; yet, while performing the act of warding off hunger, he was not tainted by sin. (26)
But Bhāradvāja, afflicted by hunger along with his son in the lonely forest, the high-minded Bṛhajjyoti, seized many cows.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra, who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma, approached the song and took a dog's haunch from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Desiring dog-flesh during his period of ritual impurity, he did not fall away from dharma; for the sake of preserving his life, Vāmadeva remained unstained by sin.
Knowing this, O Dharmabuddhi, do not hesitate now; give food, give food to us who beg here! (30)
The Caṇḍāla said: "If this task has certainly been accepted by you in this manner, then let this daughter of mine, this maiden, be taken up by you. (31)
"O twice-born ones, if he who is the eldest and the leader among you should certainly marry her, I shall afterwards give you whatever food for the rainy season you desire."
The Lord said: O Goddess, having been addressed thus, the sages, with their necks bowed in shame, reflected upon the matter according to what was right and unanimously chose Vasiṣṭha.

The high-minded Vasiṣṭha, having fully explained the duties for times of distress and perceiving that the time was at hand, married the woman of low birth known by the name Akṣamālā, who was famous throughout the three worlds.
When she obstructed the solar disc with her own splendors, she then became Arundhatī, who is saluted by gods and dānavas.
In whatever manner a woman is united with a husband according to the prescribed rule, she becomes exactly like him, just as a river is by the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained a state worthy of honor when united with Vasiṣṭha, just as Śārṅgī did when united with Mandapāla. || 37 ||
In this manner, in the course of time, the seven high-souled Ṛṣis, accompanied by Arundhatī, arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
They sent forth the sacred fords (tīrthas), which bestow all perfections, toward her.
While they were searching for them, the goddess Arundhatī indeed beheld a single liṅga situated within a thicket of trees. || 40 ||
Having seen that Lord of the gods, she thus remembered her former births: "In my previous birth, while I was situated within the state of passion (rajobhāva), [I acted thus]. (41)
"O Lord of Gods, because Śiva was indeed worshipped here out of ignorance, this twice-born man has obtained the fruit of that action: the status of an outcaste. (42)
O Lord, there is no deity in the three worlds equal to Śambhu, who, even when enraged, bestows sovereignty upon those who practice self-restraint in this manner. (43)
Having reflected thus in her mind, O beloved, she remained devoted right there and worshipped that liṅga for a hundred divine years.
Thus, by his power, Arundhatī is seen within the midst of the sky; for she is the virtuous Satī, who destroys all evil deeds when beheld.
Thus has Akṣamāleśvara been described to you exactly as it is; then, at the end of the Dvāpara age, when the transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśaka) of the Kali age has passed, || 46 ||
The son of the Asura Andha was known as Ugrasena; having reached Prabhāsa, he approached the Liṅga for the sake of obtaining a son.
Having learned of the wonderful majesty of the one named Akṣamāleśvara, and having propitiated Mahādeva for fourteen years, he then obtained a son known as the demon Kaṃsa.
From that time forward, he became the Lord Ugrasena, who destroys the sins of all living beings through both sight and touch. (49)
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual union with the teacher's wife—these are declared to be the great sins; they perish by the sight of him.
On that very occasion, when the auspicious fifth day of the sages (Ṛṣipañcamī) arrives in the month of Bhādrapada, by worshipping Akṣamāleśvara, one is liberated from the fear of hell.
They praise the gift of a cow, as well as food and water, for that purpose, in order to destroy all sins and to attain infinite happiness after death.
Thus, O Goddess, I have narrated to you the origin and majesty of Akṣamāleśvara, which pacifies sins and, when heard, destroys all suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ugraseneśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Pāśupateśvara, situated to the east of Ugraseneśvara, O Goddess. (1)
O Goddess, situated to the southeast of Gopāditya and resting to the south of Dhruveśa, it stands in the eastern part and removes all sins.
Likewise, from Gopāditya comes the Liṅga that grants all desires upon being seen; in this age, it is celebrated by the name Santoṣeśvara.
Because the Blessed One was satisfied there with those ascetics, it became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Saṃtoṣa.
O Great Goddess, Yugaliṅga is a place of great splendor and a station of spiritual perfection; it is the abode of the Pāśupatas and a remedy for those afflicted by the disease of sin.

O illustrious one, four sages attained perfection at that liṅga: Vāmadeva, Sāvarṇi, Aghora, and Kapila; they were fully perfected at that liṅga of the beginningless Lord, which is free from all taint.
O Great Goddess, in the vicinity of that deity, in a forest known as Śrīmukha, there is a station of Lakṣmī frequented by those perfected in yoga.
Among them, the Pāśupatas are the most excellent, being devoted to the worship of my liṅga; and for their residence, that forest was created by the Goddess.

In its center, O lady of beautiful hips, stands a Linga facing the east. In that place dwell the Siddhas of the Pāśupata sect and great sages such as Aghora; by means of this very body, they have gone to the abode of Śiva.
In that radiant field, frequented by gods and siddhas, I always delight in dwelling in that auspicious sanctuary; it is the most beautiful and most beloved of all places. (10)
In that regard, O Goddess, those Pāśupatas who are devoted to meditation on me are all my sons, endowed with the practice of celibacy.
Those Brāhmaṇas were self-controlled, peaceful, and had conquered anger; through the power of that emblem (liṅga), they attained supreme perfection.
Therefore, the best of the twice-born residing in that sacred field should worship him constantly.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, for those who observe your vows in the great sacred field of Prabhāsa—
Please graciously describe their great and meritorious abode, as well as the Pāśupata yoga, and the supreme majesty of the Liṅga.
What is the name of the Lord? How is he to be worshipped by the best of men? And how did the Pāśupatas come to heaven there with their physical bodies? (16)
Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, having shown compassion toward me, O Master.
Īśvara said: O blessed lady, O lady of virtuous vows, you have asked about the great Pāśupata Yoga, as well as its power and that of the Liṅga.
O Goddess of great splendor, those who have taken refuge in my vow at that Linga, which is the primordial name of the beginningless Lord, [attain success]. || 19 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, they long maintain their office and the great Pāśupata vow exactly as prescribed; this causes wonder in me, and my mind runs toward them for the sake of bestowing grace.
Sūta said: O brahmins, having heard the words of Hara, the Goddess was filled with wonder and spoke these words to her husband, the Lord of all the worlds:
"O Lord, I too have a curiosity as to what you did after that; tell me that, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you. (22)
Having heard those words of hers, Mahādeva said to her: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the conduct of my devotees. (23)
And having seen their devotion to asceticism, the primordial Lord of the Gods spoke these words to them as they stood bowing by his side.
Īśvara said: "Go quickly, Nandikeśa, to where my sons are practicing a severe vow that is exceedingly difficult even for me."
By the power of that sacred field and by my constant devotion, those sages of excellent vows attained perfection in their very own bodies.
Therefore, at my word, Nandin, go to the auspicious Prābhāsika; bid them all farewell and bring them quickly to Kailāsa.
"Take this lotus, complete with its stalk and radiant with its bud; having placed it upon the head of the Liṅga, bring the lotus-stalk back here. (28)
Then Nandin was indeed released by Śambhu, the God of gods; he departed from that abode of Kailāsa and arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
And having seen again the linga of the trident-bearing God of gods, and having seen those lords of yogis, he was filled with supreme wonder.
Some there were devoted to meditation, some had taken recourse to yoga; some performed exegesis, and others engaged in philosophical inquiry.
Others perform the worship of the Liṅga, while others likewise offer prostrations; some circumambulate it and others prostrate with all eight limbs. || 32 ||
Some offer praise, while others perform sacrifices of meditative devotion; some perform worship with the auspicious flowers of non-violence.
They perform ablutions with ashes and bathe one another with mouthfuls of water; thus the entire circle of ascetics fell into such confusion.
Then, having beheld such a sight, Nandin was struck with wonder; and having observed everything they did, he reflected upon it all within his mind.
I have come to this region, yet no one looks upon me; I have not been asked by anyone where I have come from or to whom I belong.
"Enveloped by egoism, they all never speak of me anywhere. Having resolved this in his mind, he approached the side of the Liṅga.
Having cut that lotus stalk from the Liṅga and presented it, Nandin worshipped that Pāśupateśvara Liṅga; then, taking the stalk with care, he spoke these words to the sages: || 38 ||
Nandikeśvara said: "By the command of the God of gods, I have come to your side; the Lord of gods issues this order to the circle of the assembly of ascetics. (39)
"You must go to that place where the eternal Lord resides; taking all of you with me, I shall go to the abode of Bhava."
"Arise quickly; let us go to Kailāsa, the best of mountains. Then all those twice-born ones, having become silent, spoke with a sign: "Nandin, you go on ahead; we shall follow behind."
Thus addressed by the sages, Nandin departed with great haste and, with an agitated heart, reported everything that had occurred.
Nandikeśvara said: "O Lord, I indeed went to that place where those yogins were stationed; however, while staying there, I was not satisfied by anyone."
"O Lord, they do not look at me, nor do they speak to me in any way; for I have placed a lotus there upon the head of the Liṅga, O Lord. (44)
"O Great Lord, O God, I have spoken to those lords of yogis: 'By the command of the God of gods, come here without delay! (45)
Having heard these words, O Master, all those great sages there said, "We shall indeed come; do not delay, but go on ahead. (46)
"O Lord, having been told this by them, I have come here quickly. Listen to this, accept it, and do as you wish, O Master. (47)
"O God, you ought to sever this one doubt of mine right now: O Mahādeva, how will they come without me? This is my doubt, O Mahādeva; tell me, O Maheśvara. (48)
Īśvara said: Listen, Nandinī, to this marvel concerning those of purified souls: these Siddhas cannot be seen by any other gods, even including me. (49)
"Those who are permeated by my being indeed attain the yoga of Śaṅkara. Behold this marvel, O Nandin; I shall show it to you now."
That which was brought by you was not sufficient; however, having entered that stalk as if it were minute, they all emerged by the power of their mastery over yoga.
Thus addressed, Nandin, his eyes wide with wonder, beheld the great sages situated within the interior of the pillar like atoms.
Just as atoms are seen situated in the midst of the sun’s rays, so too are the sages seen individually within the center of that stalk.
Having seen this, Nandin, his eyes wide with wonder, was struck by supreme amazement and said nothing further. (54)
Having thus seen that marvel, the Goddess spoke these words: "O Mahādeva, what is being seen? O Maheśvara, why are you so joyful? (55)
When these words had been spoken by the Goddess, Maheśvara spoke this: || 56 ||

Īśvara said: These high-souled ones, disciplined in yoga and established in the Pāśupata yoga, have attained such perfection by propitiating me while I dwell in the sacred field of Prabhāsa; they move about according to their own will. || 57 ||

When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, those sages of great splendor all emerged from the lotus stalk through their yogic power and performed circumambulation of the God who had been brought outside by the Goddess.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, why do these twice-born ones of wicked conduct not see me? This is a great wonder; please tell me out of your grace. (59)
Īśvara said: "Because they are of the nature of *prakṛti*, these perfected ones of great asceticism do not perceive [this]. Having been addressed thus by the trident-bearing God of gods, Girijā—

The woman of beautiful hips became enraged and, with a face flushed with anger, cursed them: "O arrogant ones, because of your lust for women and your wicked conduct, you shall meet your destruction! (61)
When the Kali age has arrived, you will become addicted to accepting gifts from kings, devoted to the worship of deities as a livelihood, and subsisting on the property of the Liṅga.
Attached to courtesans, bewildered, and excluded from all society, you shall exist in the Kali age for the destruction of the property of the gods.
When the curse of the high-souled sages had thus been pronounced, all those lords of the gods propitiated Gaurī.
At the word of the God of gods, she became gracious once again; the Lord too, unable to restrain her, cast her toward the southern quarter.
That stalk indeed fell into the midst of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra; it became that very Liṅga, renowned as Mahānāla.
And when the Kali Yuga has arrived, that which is known as Dhruveśvara is situated to the northeast of that Pāśupateśvara.
Formerly known by the name Anādīśa, he later became Pāśupateśvara; established in the great sacred field of Prabhāsa, he is the destroyer of sins.
This place is supreme and most excellent for the practice of my vow; this Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman, known by the name Anādīśa.
In this place, both spiritual perfection and liberation belong to the Brahmins; of this there is no doubt. By means of this very body, one attains perfection within six months.

Behold this *liṅga* for the sake of liberation from *saṃsāra*; it is difficult for all the worlds to attain and is the supreme bestower of liberation. This *Pāśupata* knowledge is established within this *liṅga*. (71)
And whoever should worship this [deity] with devotion continuously during the month of Māgha, he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and all acts of charity.
Gold should be given there by those who desire the full fruit of their pilgrimage.
Thus, O Goddess, has this greatness of the Lord of Pāśupata, which completely destroys sins and serves to liberate one from the bonds of individual existence (paśu-pāśa), been told. 74.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be worthy of worship by all four castes; moreover, he alone possesses the right to this Pāśupata-Īśvara.
That which was the first purifier of the gods, the all-encompassing Pāśupata vow—this is indeed the ultimate path declared by me, by which the gods go to all the worlds. (76)

Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, having committed theft, or even having killed a Brahmin—one who recites the Rudrādhyāya, covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes, is liberated from all sins.
Having taken the ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should touch the limbs; one should also take the ashes of those residing in the house when the fire has been extinguished.
"Fire is ash; wind is ash; water is ash; earth is ash. Indeed, all this has become ash. One who is not initiated should not touch these eyes. (79)
It should be accepted by Brāhmaṇas, but never by Śūdras; for a Śūdra never has the right to the Pāśupata vow.
Brahmins have the right to the auspicious Pāśupata vow; assuming a brahmin body, I manifest myself age after age.

Whether in the house of a Caṇḍāla, or in a cremation ground, or on the king’s highway, or in the middle of a path, or amidst dried cow dung—those lowest of men who have departed [from this world] reach the state of Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pāśupateśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 130.
The Goddess said: Regarding that which was spoken by you as "Nāleśvara," how indeed did that Liṅga come to be known as Dhruveśvara?
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great glory of Dhruveśvara; having heard this, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
King Uttānapāda had a son named Dhruva, who was high-souled, endowed with wisdom, omniscient, and pleasing to behold.
Once, O Goddess, having reached the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa, he performed extensive and most formidable penance.
Having installed Maheśvara, he worshipped him with true devotion for a thousand divine years, praising him with various kinds of hymns.
I shall proclaim that hymn of praise to you by which I have attained satisfaction.

Dhruva said: I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, who, by the pressing of his lotus feet, held firm the lofty peak of Kailāsa as it was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who himself resembled a peak of Kailāsa.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, by whom even the Asuras and the sons of Danu, together with all the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas, were united [with liberation], yet they were freed from the fruit and the root of that fruit [only through him]. 8.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, under whose eternal control this entire world remains, who enjoys the worlds through his eight very bodies, and who is the cause of the causes of all supreme causes.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who, formerly filled with intense wrath, suddenly severed with the tip of the nail of his lotus-like left hand that fifth head of Brahmā, which resembled a fresh lotus.

Having bowed with devotion at the feet of that bestower of boons and having heard his stainless and unwearied words, the radiant Vivasvat dispels the darkness with his own rays; I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter. (11)

The man who, with self-restraint and a purified mind, recites this hymn of beautiful meaning composed by Dhruva in the assembly of Brahmins, being ever pure and perfected, goes to the beginningless world of Śiva.
O Goddess, as that high-souled Dhruva of purified mind was thus offering praise, I became pleased with him at the completion of a full thousand years.
"O son, I am pleased; may it be well with you. You have now become pure. I grant you divine vision; behold me, free from all distress. (14)
"And whatever supreme fruit has been desired by you in your mind, I shall grant all of that to you; speak quickly before me. (15)

"Whether it be the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Śakra, or any other station that is very difficult to attain—I shall grant it; of this there is no doubt, for I am thoroughly pleased by your devotion. (16)
Dhruva said: "The station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra, which is characterized by return, is all known to me; even in my mind, I do not desire it. (17)
If you are pleased with me, O God, grant me pure devotion; O bull-bannered God, dwell forever within this liṅga.
Īśvara said: "All that was thus requested has indeed been granted in its entirety; and his station is eternal—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (19)
Whoever worships that Liṅga on the new moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

One without a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth; he becomes handsome, fortunate, an enjoyer of pleasures, and an expert in all scriptures; and by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.

He who hears this beautiful fame of Dhruva, who is worshipped by the hosts of Asuras and Suras, goes to the eternal world of Rudra—the storehouse of all happiness, perfectly tranquil, and honored by the lords of the hosts of gods and Danavas. || 22 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Dhruveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 131.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, situated not very far from Someśa in the northeastern direction.
For here, the presiding deity of the sacred seat (pīṭha) is renowned as Siddhalakṣmī.

In the Brahmāṇḍa, there is the first sacred seat (pīṭha) situated at Prabhāsa; O Goddess, beloved, there in that great seat the Yoginīs who move on earth and those who move through the sky sport according to their own will together with Bhairava.
Jālandhara is a great pīṭha, and likewise Kāmarūpa; and Śrī Rudranṛsiṃha is the fourth, the most excellent pīṭha.
Ratnavīrya is a great seat (pīṭha), as is Kāśmīra; O Goddess, he who knows these seats is a knower of mantra.

And among all seats (pīṭhas), it is the supreme seat, the foundation of them all; O Great Goddess, it is known by the name Mahodaya in Saurāṣṭra, where even today the primordial knowledge that assumes any form at will continues to prevail.
The goddess situated on that seat is renowned as Mahālakṣmī; she is the pacifier of all sins and the bestower of auspiciousness in all undertakings.

For that man who worships her on the auspicious Pañcamī according to the prescribed rite with devotion, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—from where could there be any fear of misfortune (Alakṣmī)?
Having taken his stand in the northern direction in the presence of Mahālakṣmī, whoever should recite that queen of mantras known as Siddhalakṣmī, [attains success].

According to the procedure for one hundred thousand recitations, preceded by initiation, ritual bathing, and other rites, it is joined with a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number, using the three sweets (trimadhu), bilva fruits, and clarified butter.
In this way, his fortune undoubtedly becomes manifest; it bestows the desired perfection both in this world and in the next.
Whoever worships her with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the third, eighth, or fourteenth lunar day, for him success rests in the palm of his hand.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddhalakṣmī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, she who is renowned as Mahākālī is stationed right there, upon the great seat (pīṭha) situated below, which is provided with an opening to the netherworld (pātāla).

She who pacifies all suffering and brings about the destruction of all enemies should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite at the dead of night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, with perfumes, flowers, incense, raw meat, and sacrificial offerings.

A woman who is purified in mind should observe the Fruit-Third (Phala-tṛtīyā) there for one year during the bright fortnight, worshipping the Goddess according to the prescribed rite; indeed, fruits must certainly be given to a Brāhmaṇa according to the injunction.
O beautiful goddess, one should indeed avoid these foods at night: flat beans, pigeon peas, mung beans, black gram, and horse gram.
Masūra, rājamāṣa, wheat, tripuṭa, chickpeas, vartala, makuṣṭha, and others of this kind. || 5 ||
O Goddess, those [meats] are not to be eaten as long as she performs the Gaurī-vrata. Listen to me as I describe the fruit of her merit.
In her house, wealth and grain shall never suffer depletion; may she never be miserable, unfortunate, or wretched for seven births. (7)
The vow of Mahākālī has been proclaimed, together with the majesty of the Goddess; it is performed for the destruction of sins and for the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus, O Goddess, has the great glory of Mahākālī been fully described; it is the sacred seat (pīṭha) of the field, O Great Goddess, which bestows the attainment of mantras. || 9 ||

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, one should remain awake there; having offered worship and a bali-oblation upon the pedestal, chanting the desired mantra at night with a tranquil mind, one attains the supreme, wished-for siddhi. (10)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mahākālī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the river Pushkaravartaka, situated not far to the north of Brahmakunda.
Formerly, while a sacrifice for the high-souled Soma was being performed, Brahmā arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa together with the hosts of gods.
Invited by Ṛkṣarāja for the purpose of the installation of Somanātha, he recalled that which had been promised long ago by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
As long as I shall remain in the mortal world for any other reason, so long must the three junctions (saṃdhyās) be constantly worshipped at Tripuṣkara.
At that very time, when the hour for the auspicious moment had arrived, the Brahmins who were experts in astrology declared the favorable time.
Then, knowing that the Grandfather had set out for Puṣkara for the sake of the twilight rites, the Lord of Night indeed spoke these words.
"This very time has been determined by the astrologers as auspicious; let a plan be made so that there may be no delay."
Knowing that the time had now arrived, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being composed in mind, reflected upon the Puṣkara lakes.
O woman of excellent complexion, as soon as they were remembered by Brahmā, those [flowers] appeared right there on the most beautiful bank of the river.
Whirlpools formed there, categorized as great, middling, and small; then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bestowed a name upon her.
"From this day forward, by my grace, this beautiful river shall attain fame in the world by the name Puṣkarāvartakā."
Having bathed here with devotion, the man who shall offer libations to his ancestors will obtain merit equal to that of Tripuṣkara, as well as whatever he desires.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that best of men who offers libations to the ancestors there shall obtain satisfaction for ten thousand kalpas.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Puṣkarāvartaka River," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 134.

Īśvara said: One should behold the Goddess, the bringer of an end to suffering, stationed right there; she who was formerly known as Śītala in the age called Dvāpara, but is now proclaimed in the Kali age as the one who brings an end to the miseries of Kali. || 1 ||
She makes the bodies of children cool and free from disease; because she is worshipped with a spirit of devotion, she is remembered as Śītalā. || 2 ||
For the purpose of pacifying boils and for the sake of children, one should measure out lentils according to the prescribed measure and grind them there.
Having offered [this] before Śītalā, may children be free from disease; may there be the pacification of eruptive boils, scabies, and so forth, as well as of wind-disorders and the like. || 4 ||
One should perform the śrāddha rite right there and feed the Brāhmaṇas there.
Having offered camphor, flowers, musk, excellent sandalwood, fragrant blossoms, and an oblation of milk-rice with ghee to the Goddess, one should cause all of that to be bestowed upon the couple.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, by devotionately offering an auspicious garland made of bilva wood to the Goddess, one shall attain all perfections.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Tilāgaurī, the Destroyer of Suffering," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 135 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Lomaśeśvara, situated seven bow-lengths to the east of Duḥkhāntakāriṇī.
O Goddess of gods, having performed most difficult penance, the great sage Lomaśa installed a great liṅga there in the middle of the cave.
O beloved, when the three and a half crores of heaven-dwellers, headed by Indra, shall go to their destruction, then his destruction will certainly follow.
There are as many Indras as there are hairs on the body; when each Indra perishes in succession, a hair falls from that body.
Thus, by the grace of Īśa, Lomaśa became long-lived; six Brahmās passed away during the full lifespan of Lomaśa.
Whoever worships with devotion that very liṅga adored by Lomaśa, he too attains long life, free from disease, healthy, and happy.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Lomaśeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: One should behold the unsurpassed Kṣetrapāla stationed right there, named Kaṅkālabhairava, who was appointed by Bhairava for the protection of that sacred field against living beings of wicked mind. || 1 ||
He who worships him with devotion, using offerings of food, flowers, and so forth, in due order on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa and on the eighth day of Āśvina; || 2 ||
For that high-souled Puṣkara dwelling in his field, he becomes a remover of obstacles and likewise protects him like a son.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaṅkālabhairava Kṣetrapāla," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: On the western side of that very place, situated at a distance of five dhanus, stands the shrine named Tṛṇabindvīśvara, established through intense devotion.
O Goddess, having performed great austerity, the lordly sage Tṛṇabindu indeed drank only a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kuśa grass month after month.
Having thus propitiated the Lord for many years, he attained supreme perfection in the auspicious Prābhāsika field.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Tṛṇabindīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Citrāditya, located on the southern side of that very place, in the vicinity of Brahmakuṇḍa.

O Goddess of the gods, he possesses great power and is the destroyer of all poverty. O Goddess, in former times there was one named Mitra on this earth, a righteous soul who served as a scribe for all beings and was constantly devoted to the welfare of living creatures.
To him, who approached her during the proper season, two children were born: a son of supreme splendor named Citra, O lady of beautiful countenance. (3)
In that manner, the maiden Citrā became endowed with beauty and adorned with virtuous character.
But while these two were still mere infants, Mitra passed away; then his excellent wife entered the fire along with him.
Then those two wretched boys, protected by the sages, grew up in the great forest, remaining in their vows even as children.
Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, they undertook supreme austerity after installing Mahādeva Bhāskara, the absorber of waters.

The righteous-souled one worshipped with incense, garlands, and ointments; and with the sixty-eight names recounted by Vasiṣṭha, he praised the Lord of gods, the Sun, with palms joined in reverence. || 8 ||
Citra said: Having bowed his head to the god Bhāskara, the lord of the sky, the primordial deity, the master of the world, the destroyer of sins and the eradicator of diseases. (9)
He who has a thousand eyes, a thousand rays, and the splendor of a thousand beams of light.

I shall praise him who is joined with secret names: Muṇḍīrasvāmin at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean in the morning, and Kālapriya, who has taken refuge on the bank of the Yamunā, at midday.
And the original site is situated on the bank of the Candrabhāgā at the time of sunset, where Sāmba himself became perfected while devoted to fasting.
Lohitākṣa is in Vārāṇasī, Bṛhanmukha at Gobhilākṣa, Pratiṣṭhāna among the Prayāgas, and the highly resplendent Vṛddhāditya [is there as well]. 13.
At Koṭyakṣa is Dvādaśāditya, and at Caturghaṭa is Gaṅgāditya; in Naimiṣa and Goghnaka, Bhadra is situated in Bhadrapuṭa.
At Jayā he is Vijayāditya; at Prabhāsa, Svarṇavetasa; at Kurukṣetra, Sāmaṃta; and at Ilāvṛta, Trimantra.
They know Siddheśvara to be at Mahendra, Ṛṇe as Kramaṇāditya, Padmabodha in Kauśāmbī, and Divākara in Brahmabāhu.
One should worship Caṇḍakānti at Kedāra, Timirāpaha at Nitya, Śivadvāra on the path of the Gaṅgā, and Āditya at Bhūpradīpana.
He saw Haṃsa on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Viśvāmitra at Pṛthūdaka, and Naradvīpa of stainless luster in Siddhā at Ujjayinī.
One should worship Sūrya in Kuntīkumāra, Vibhāvasu in Pañcanadī, Vimalāditya in Mathurā, and Saṃjñāditya in Saṃjñika.
In Śrīkaṇṭha, one should remember Mārtaṇḍa; in Daśārṇa, the ten [forms] are prescribed; in Godhana, the god Gopati; and in Marusthala, Karṇa.
Puṣpa is in Devapura, Keśavārka in Lohita, Śārdūla in Vaidiśa, and Vāruṇavāsin in Śoṇa.
And at Vardhamāna is the one named Sāmba; at Kāmarūpa is Śubhaṅkara; at Kānyakubja is Mihira; and at Puṇyavardhana is Mandāra.
He established Kṣobhaṇāditya in Gandhāra, Amaradyuti in Laṅkā, Karṇāditya in Campā, and Śubhadarśin in Prabodha.
One should worship Pārvatya at Dvārāvatī, Himāpaha on the Himavat mountain, Mahātejas at Lauhitya, and Dhūrjaṭi at Amalāṅga.
They know Rohikā as Kumāra, Padmā as Padmasambhava, Dharmāditya as Lāṭā, and Marddakā as Sthavira. || 25 ||
Sukhaprada is in Kauberyā, likewise Gopati in Kosala; Padmadeva is in Kauṅkaṇa, and Tāpana on the Vindhya mountain.
One should know Tvaṣṭṛ in Kāśmīra, Ratnasaṃbhava in Caritra, Hemagarbhastha in Puṣkara, and Sūrya in Gabhastika.
In the village of Tīrthagrāma, he installed Prabhākara at Mujjhāla; in Kāmpilya, Rillakāditya; and in Dhanaka, Dhanavāsin.
On the banks of the Narmadā, there are sixty-eight [sites] everywhere that are superior for visiting the god Bhāskara of immeasurable splendor. (29)
A man who, being capable and pure, rises every morning and either recites or even listens to this, is liberated from all sins.
One who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom; one who desires wealth obtains wealth; one who desires sons obtains sons; and one who desires happiness obtains happiness. || 31 ||
One afflicted by disease is released from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage; whatever desires a person prays for, those very things he attains.
The Lord said: While Citra, whose soul was stainless, was thus offering praise, the omnipresent thousand-rayed Sun became pleased with him after a long time.
He said, "O child, may it be well with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
He said: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, lead me—who possess a sharp intellect—to maturity in all undertakings, as well as to the state of a knower. (35)
"O woman of excellent complexion, Sūrya promised, 'So be it. Thereupon Citra, born of the Mitraka family, attained omniscience."
Having recognized him as being endowed with supreme intelligence, the wise Dharmarāja reflected: "Could this be some kind of messenger? (37)
"Then all success shall be mine and supreme liberation shall come to pass. O beautiful lady, while the King of Dharma was thinking thus, [the goddess appeared].
When Citra went to the Agni-tīrtha in the salt ocean for the purpose of bathing, he was led away by the servants of Yama even as he was entering it.
O Great Goddess, he remained embodied and, devoted to the commands of Yama, became known as Citragupta, the recorder of the conduct of the entire world.
Consequently, O fair-faced one, he became known in the world by the name Citrāditya. (41)
The man who honors one who has restricted his food on the seventh lunar day will not experience poverty or suffering for seven lifetimes.
In that very place, a horse should be given, along with a sword and its sheath, as well as gold to a Brahmin; in this way, one obtains the fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Citrāditya," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 139.
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the river Citrapathā, situated near the Brahmakuṇḍa and in the midst of Citrāditya.
And when Citra, O beloved of the gods, was brought along with his body by the messengers of Yama who were intent on carrying out Yama’s command, he, possessed of great wisdom— (2)
Having understood this, his sister, remaining there in distress, then became the river Citrā, the sister of that great-souled one.
O Goddess, having entered the ocean while searching for her kinsman, the twice-born then gave her the name Citrapathā. || 4 ||
Thus, O woman of excellent complexion, that river arose there.
That man who, having bathed in it, beholds Citrāditya, goes to the supreme abode where the god Divākara dwells.
O Goddess, in this Kali age, the river has gone underground; it may be seen during the rainy season, for its sight there is difficult to obtain.
Bathing and giving gifts, especially, destroy all sins.
Whether he has eaten or not yet eaten, whether by night or by day, on a festival day or at an improper time, and whether he is pure or impure— (9)
O beloved, whenever the river Citrapathā is seen there, its very sight is the authority; time is not the determining factor in that case.
O Great Goddess, upon seeing the river, the ancestors residing in heaven sing Sāman hymns there, and they dance and laugh.
"Someone born in our lineage will perform a śrāddha ceremony here; thus, for as long as a kalpa endures, he shall produce joy for us. (12)
Knowing this, a person should perform a ritual bath and a śrāddha ceremony there for the sake of destroying all sins and likewise for the gratification of the ancestors. (13)
Thus has this been told, O Goddess, how the river Citrapathā, having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, remains there as the destroyer of sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Citrapathā River," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 140 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to where Kapardin is situated. He is located not very far away on the northern side of that very place. O Goddess, he bestows desired objects like another Cintāmaṇi jewel. || 1 ||

O Goddess of the gods, on the fourth lunar day, moreover on a Tuesday, having bathed and worshipped him with various auspicious food offerings, and having gratified the Lord of the Lords of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), one shall obtain all desires. || 2 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kapardicintāmaṇi," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the most excellent Citreśvara, situated at a distance of seven bows to the south-east of that [place].
Indeed, that Liṅga is of great power and destroys all sins; by worshipping Citreśvara there, one shall have no fear of hell.
O Beloved, Citra wipes away his sin that resides upon the cloth; therefore, with every effort, one should always worship Citreśa. Even one who is possessed of sin shall never behold hell.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Citreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Vicitreśvara. It is situated ten *dhanus* away from that very place, slightly toward the south-eastern direction, and it is the destroyer of sins.
O Great Goddess, after performing very difficult penance, that great Liṅga was established by Vicitra through a letter from Yama.
Upon seeing it and indeed worshipping it, one shall be liberated from all sins; and by worshipping it according to the prescribed rite, a man does not become miserable. (3)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vicitreśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the third great Puṣkara. Slightly to the east of that very place, in the direction of Īśāna, there is remembered a smaller pool known by the name Puṣkara. (1)
There, at the time of midday, Sandhyā—the mother of the three worlds—was propitiated by Brahmā, who had gone there for the purpose of installation.
In that regard, whoever performs a bath with a concentrated mind on the full-moon day at that primordial Puṣkara, by him the bath is truly accomplished.
Gold should be given there for the removal of all sins.
Thus has the greatness of your Puṣkara been briefly declared; when heard, it removes the sins of men and likewise grants all desires.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Puṣkara-kuṇḍa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 144 ||
Īśvara said: There itself, one should behold Vighneśa, the destroyer of sins, known by the name Gajakumbhodara, who bestows all spiritual perfections (siddhis). || 1 ||
Having bathed in that pool on the fourth lunar day, a man who, with a restrained mind, worships him with devotion—Vighneśa is pleased with him.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gajakumbhodara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
