Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Yameśvara Mahādeva, established by Dharmarāja and situated to the north of that very place. || 1 ||
O fair-complexioned lady, when Dharmarāja was cursed by the shadow, his foot fell [upon her] and he became overcome with grief.
Then, in the Prābhāsika field, that great ascetic performed penance and installed a liṅga of the trident-bearing God there.
Mahādeva, being pleased with him, then became manifest before his eyes and said: "O Dharma, blessings be upon you; choose whatever boon you desire."
Then Dharmarāja said: "O Lord of Gods, my foot has fallen; by your grace, let it indeed grow back once more. (5)
O best of gods, this Liṅga which has been fashioned by me for you—those living beings on earth who behold it endowed with devotion [shall attain their goal]. || 6 ||
By your grace, may there be for them liberation from sin.
Having said, "It shall be so," Hara vanished; and Yama, having regained his feet, returned once more to heaven.
O best of gods, when that is seen, no fear arises for men regarding the world of Yama, even for those who have committed evil deeds.
On the occasion of the Bhrātṛdvitīyā festival, having bathed in the waters of Puṣkariṇī, one situated near Yameśvara should behold Yameśa.
One should offer a vessel of sesame seeds, a lamp, cows, gold, and so forth, dedicating it to the god Yama; by doing so, one is liberated from all sins.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Brahmakuṇḍa, which was created by Brahmā in ancient times in the south-western quarter of that very place.

When Somanātha was installed by the King of Bears (Ṛkṣarāja), then all the gods, headed by Brahmā, assembled there; for they had been invited by the Moon (Śaśāṅka) for the purpose of the deity’s consecration.
Then the Lord of the Night (the Moon), filled with humility, spoke to Brahmā.
"O best of gods, act in such a way that people may know the installation you have performed; establish a sign originating from yourself."
Having heard this, Brahmā then entered into steady meditation and summoned all the sacred fords (tīrthas), beginning with Puṣkara, from every direction.

Indeed, whatever holy places exist in heaven as well as in the subterranean realm (rasātala) were drawn forth by Brahmā through the power of his asceticism; therefore, it is celebrated by his very name as Brahmakuṇḍa.
It is beheld by fourteen thousand hosts; therefore, this supreme sacred site is difficult to attain for those devoid of devotion.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke to all the gods.

The man who, having bathed in this pool, shall offer libations to his ancestors, that person shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; by its grace, he shall travel through the heavenly world in a celestial chariot.
One should give the gift of a cow, the gift of a horse, and likewise a golden water-pot to a learned Brahmin for the removal of all sins.
On the full moon day, O Great Goddess, and likewise on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the Sarasvatī bathes there for the sake of destroying all sins.
O Goddess, O beloved, the elixir (rasāyana) is indeed perfected there by the water; it becomes effective through instruction, endowed with various colors. 12.
How can a human being continue to suffer the pain, disease, and grief of poverty after reaching Brahmakuṇḍa, which is like another wish-fulfilling tree? 13.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, speak in detail of the great glory of Brahmakuṇḍa; for the benefit of all living beings, O Lord, tell it to me at length.
I have a great curiosity to hear the majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa, for the sake of destroying the suffering of people and as a means to eliminate poverty. (15)
O Blessed One, all human beings, oppressed by suffering and grief, wander through their entire lives, deluded regarding the elixir of immortality.
For their benefit, tell me of Nirvāṇa, the supreme essence, so that here in this world the body may become indestructible from the very beginning. (17)

Endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), possessed of all branches of knowledge (vidyā), able to assume any form at will (kāmarūpa), engaged in purposeful action, and free from all diseases. || 18 ||
Then, O Lord, tell me how a human being may indeed attain the supreme Nirvāṇa and become one who has fulfilled all his duties. (19)

"O Lord of the world, having shown compassion, tell me likewise, O Maheśvara: explain that well-known, divine, and bliss-bestowing Kalpa which culminates in Nirvāṇa and is entirely free from delusion."

Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess, you who act for the welfare of the worlds! In the world of mortals, O Great Goddess, there is this auspicious holy site, the best among holy sites. (21)
That place is renowned as the supreme Prabhāsa, extending twelve yojanas; there dwells the god Someśvara, famous throughout the three worlds.
To its east, it is declared, is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of demons; and there is Caṇḍikā, the Yoginī, surrounded by her female companions.
Then, in the eastern quarter, there is a divine and auspicious place created by the four-faced one, superior to all holy fords, filled with every wonder.
It is always frequented by all the gods, as well as by the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Grahas, and by divine Apsarases, sages, Yakṣas, and Pannagas.
For the sake of accomplishment, for the sake of all desires, and bringing auspicious divine enjoyments, it is renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa because it was fashioned by Brahmā. (26)
In its northwestern corner, Hiraṇyeśa himself is stationed; having propitiated that great god, the supreme Hiraṇyeśvara, [one attains the goal]. || 27 ||

The wise one should quickly recite the great mantra and perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten times its measure; by means of the homa, the mantra is perfected—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. (28)
To the north of that, slightly toward the northeast, O Great Goddess, is the four-faced Kṣetrapa, who bears the form of a Liṅga.
O Goddess, Śaṅkara protects that place in the form of a Liṅga; having propitiated him with effort, one should then resort to the Kuṇḍa.
O Goddess, consisting of all sovereignty and variegated with various colors, the supreme Bhairaveśvara is located at the eastern quarter of the mouth of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O Goddess, she who is foul-smelling and radiant carries the form of the essence (rasa). Indeed, that which is joined with her essence possesses various colors and is variegated.
Cloud-colored, great and divine, and again silver, auspicious; tawny, milk-colored, and as beautiful as the luster of camphor. || 33 ||
When will there be water possessing the luster of musk, bearing the hue of saffron, fragrant and endowed with the scent of sandalwood; and when will there be water from the Rudhira river?
These various flavors are always seen there; for him with whom Mahādeva is pleased, that is accomplished at that very moment.
Silver cast therein becomes like gold; this very place is the supreme elixir (rasāyana) before one's own eyes. 36.
O Goddess, men behold that great wonder instantly; for in the Kali age, they perceive the supreme, divine essence residing therein.
This perfected elixir is accomplished for men, causing the destruction of diseases; it is divine, consisting of the seed of gold, and is the great substance born from the Brahma-vessel.
Now I shall declare it for the benefit of human beings; O illustrious lady, poverty comes to an end at that very moment. (39)
At the very beginning, they first prepare a firm and auspicious copper vessel; one should pour holy water into it, along with copper leaves.
Having placed that jar upon the ground, one should then kindle a fire; in the form of a pit, one should cook it very slowly for six months.
Afterward, having lifted that jar, one should pour water back into it again; one should do this for one month, and then for another month intensely.
Then, having diligently combined all the fragments together, one should again soak them with water and cause them to be churned once more.
If Maheśvara is pleased, gold is produced there.
O Goddess, if the best of men desires success born of the body, he should first perform ritual bathing for three years.
Maintaining silence and self-restraint, and accompanied by the recitation of great mantras, one should diligently worship Hiraṇyeśa, the guardian of the field (Kṣetrapāla).

Combined with the five-fold offerings and joined with meditation and concentration, that which has been cooked with water from a sacred ford is indeed to be drunk; likewise [it is done] at the Udumbara tree.
In this way, within just three years, one's body becomes divine; one becomes radiant, powerful, wise, and free from all diseases.
He shall live for exactly three hundred years, free from suffering, provided that he performs his ablutions there continuously for three years. (49)
One should daily recite the mantra of Vāgīśvarī, accompanied by worship and fire-offerings; for such a person, speech flows forth and the perfection of Sarasvatī shall be attained.
The self-possessed one should utter speech in Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, and Bhūtabhāṣita, like the flow of the Gaṅgā’s current—unwearied, O beautiful woman, continuous and uninterrupted.
Even when debating with thousands of disputants, no fatigue arises for him; by the power of this sacred ford, he becomes a master of all scriptures.

O dear one, all those scholars who are proud and proficient in the sciences of logic (tarka-śāstra) come together with their necks held high due to their learning; yet they are unable even to look upon or speak to my face.
And by such a mere glance, he shatters thousands of disputants. || 54 ||
He swiftly causes the scriptures whose meanings have been fully awakened to be propagated—the pure Pāñcarātra, as well as the Vaiṣṇava and the Śaiva.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Bhūtatantra, the Gāruḍa, the great Bhairavatantra, and the Kula path, O beloved, which is twofold—56.
By the supreme speed of this chariot, one's speech shall become unimpeded; all opponents shall perish like serpents before Garuḍa. || 57 ||
By the grace of Brahmā, he shall experience neither poverty nor disease, nor again any mental suffering; he shall be honored by kings and possess great honor. (58)
Endowed with the power of enthusiasm, the wise man lives like a god; by the grace of this sacred ford, he becomes a donor, an enjoyer, and an eloquent speaker. (59)
Whatever splendor arises among men when they are anointed with oil, such splendor likewise arises immediately upon bathing, by the grace of the holy ford itself.

Whatever sin a living being commits—whether it be slander, ingratitude, the sin of betraying a friend, or the sin of adultery—all that goes to destruction for one who is devoted to bathing at the Kuṇḍa.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by jumping over a pestle or by abandoning his cows, that sin reaches destruction simply by the sight of Brahmakuṇḍa.
Furthermore, whatever sacred fords and deities exist upon the earth, they are all worshipped through the power of bathing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Sin accumulated over seven lifetimes shall go to destruction by the mere sight [of it].
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a preceptor or a cow, and in the theft of others' property—that sin reaches its destruction through the service of Brahmakuṇḍa.
And listen now to the fruit obtained by one who, having bathed, performs circumambulation of the pool exactly fifteen times according to its name. || 66 ||
By him the earth with its seven continents, together with the seven netherworlds and filled with millions of sacred fords, has been circumambulated.
Whoever offers even a mere morsel of food there to the best among those who know the Vedas has, by the power of this sacred site, performed a feast for a hundred thousand.
Having fully worshipped Brahmeśvara and the excellent Hiraṇyeśvara, one should worship the four-faced Kṣetrapāla; thus one shall obtain whatever is desired.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his family and freed from all sins, he indeed goes to the world of Brahmā; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Or, having bathed in the Virañci-kuṇḍa, whoever should recite the Mother of the Vedas according to the rule of one hundred thousand recitations shall be liberated from sins. (71)
He alone is the performer of merit and he alone is the supreme among men, by whom a pilgrimage has been made there at Brahmakuṇḍa, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Eighty-eight thousand sages of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), having taken refuge at Brahmakuṇḍa, worship the god Brahmā.
O beloved, all the sacred fords in the three worlds, including the mobile and immobile beings, roar only so long as men do not behold the Brahmeśvara Tīrtha.
And those men who drink the water in the Brahmakuṇḍa even once—neither verbal, mental, nor physical sin shall ever be transferred to them. (75)
Whatever holy places (tīrthas) exist within the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), one attains their merit by performing a circumambulation of Brahmakuṇḍa.
The high-souled Yājñavalkya, who is of the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, would not abandon that pool, nor would the host of sages. (77)
Thus has the majesty born of Brahmakuṇḍa been briefly proclaimed; out of affection for you, O Goddess of Gods, what else do you wish to ask? (78)
That mortal who hears this, endowed with perfect faith, is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Brahmā. (79)
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the well known as Kuṇḍalasaṃbhava, located on the northern side of that very place, in the vicinity of Brahmakuṇḍa.
O Great Goddess, where the perfected one (Siddha) Rūpakuṇḍalahāraka resides, by bathing there, O Goddess, a man is liberated from the sin of theft.
O Goddess of gods, for seven births there shall be no one born in his lineage; by the power of that bath, no cruel thief shall ever exist there. (3)
Especially on Śivarātri, one should perform rites such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the sake of the liberation of sinners who have been slain by weapons.
The Goddess said: O Lord, best among those who speak, tell me in detail how it was that the form of the earrings attained renown upon the earth. (5)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to this most meritorious narrative that destroys sin; by hearing which, a man is liberated from the sins accumulated over hundreds of births.
Due to the greatness of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, King Sudarśana, who was wise and the sole sovereign of the earth, remained fasting on the night of Śivarātri.

Blessed indeed was he, and rich in wealth, as he protected his subjects with great effort; his kingdom was highly prosperous, graced by Brahmins, flourishing, endowed with abundance, and free from thieves and robbers.
In that delightful country was a blessed and auspicious city, inhabited by the four castes and adorned with city walls.
In that delightful, preeminent city, Sudarśana—endowed with prosperity and born as the son of Hiraṇyadatta by a Gandhāra maiden—ruled a kingdom free from all thorns together with his kinsmen.
His wife was a beloved and virtuous woman, devoted to her husband; she was the auspicious daughter of the King of Kāśī, renowned by the name Sunandā.
Indeed, together with her, that lord of kings always enjoyed pleasures; and as he was thus enjoying those pleasures, a long period of time passed away.
He performed great sacrifices and gave gifts in abundance; thus did his time pass along with his wife, O lady of virtuous vows.
Once, O fair-faced one, on the night of Śivarātri in the month of Māgha, he remembered his former birth and, having called his wife, spoke to her.
Sudarśana said: "O Goddess of beautiful countenance, the Śivarātri vow must be observed by me; indeed, it was by the power of this very vow that the kingdom was obtained by me. (15)
The queen said: "O Indra among kings, you have told me that your power is great; tell me the reason for this, for a wonder dwells within my heart. (16)
The king said: Listen to the majesty of this sacred site resulting from fasting on Śivarātri, in that delightful city of Śiva, the most beautiful gateway to heaven. (17)
At the Āditya-tīrtha in Prabhāsa, that most excellent and desire-granting sacred ford.
O Queen, on the Śivarātri—the most excellent of lunar days—he went to that city, which was endowed with supernatural powers and constantly devoted to the Dharma. (19)
O lady of excellent hips, whatever men were inhabitants of that city and kingdom came there on Śivarātri to observe the fast.
A merchant named Dhana lived there constantly; he was wealthy, righteous-souled, and always devoted to dharma. || 21 ||
Accompanied by his wife, he fasted there on the Śivarātri; his wife was a virtuous woman, endowed with beauty and youth.
With his girdle and necklace swaying, adorned with all ornaments, he lived together with that wife, free from desire and anger.
Standing before Prabhāsa, having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure, one should, free from sleep, worship with devotion according to the prescribed rite. (24)
There, born into a family of virtuous Śūdras who worship the gods and Brāhmaṇas, I was a sinful man who took to thievery in the guise of a thief. (25)
Due to the connection with his past karma, he was always devoted to improper conduct; on that night, however, I remained there in the midst of the people.
O fair-faced one, he remained there coiled up, waiting for a vulnerability; intent on seeking a flaw, he was like a merchant watching for a weakness in his wife.
That night passed for me as I remained awake in that solitary place amidst the sounds of singing, dancing, and other performances, as well as the recitation of Vedic auspicious hymns. (28)
With the sounds of cymbals, as well as with rhythmic hand-gestures and the recitations from books, he remained there indeed for the remainder of the night.
Joined with cessation, being oppressed, she of the pure smile—the wife of a wealthy man, afflicted by the pain of suppression—went outside the temple. (30)
Having torn off her ears, I leaped away and remained within the water; then a great clamor was raised there by the inhabitants of that city.
Then, hearing that tumultuous sound as if their ears were being torn asunder, the guards who carry out the king's commands ran to that place.
Then, while being watched from all sides by them with weapons in hand and torches in hand, the gold situated in my mouth was not obtained.
Then, having severed my head with a sharp-edged sword, they looked on with torches in hand, yet they did not see even a particle of gold.
Having abandoned me, they all departed and reported to the king: "Nothing was obtained there, and we were killed by him at that very moment. (35)
Having spoken thus, they all returned once more to their respective places; meanwhile, his kinsman there remained with a mind terrified by fear.
"O beloved, having dug there to the north of Brahmatīrtha, my head, joined with my body, was buried right there. (37)
But I, having performed my rites at that very same supreme holy site of Prabhāsa, attained the memory of my past lives through the power of Śivarātri.

"O lady of excellent complexion, a kingdom free of thorns and prosperous has been obtained; this is the majesty of Prabhāsa resulting from fasting on Śivarātri. Having attained this fruit, I shall therefore go and observe the fast. (39)
The queen said: "Let us go to that very place where your skull fell. If, when the skull is split open, gold is seen, then I shall have conviction in your words; of this there is no doubt. (40)
The King said: "Indeed, a bone remains for an entire kalpa until the dissolution of the earth. Arise, go; may it be well with you, to the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa. (41)
Having heard those words spoken by the king, he set his mind upon going to observe the fast of Śivarātri.
Then, having mounted a chariot adorned with gold and yoked with swift horses, he went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa together with his wife.
Having performed the vow at Prabhāsa as prescribed, O lady of excellent complexion, one should then go to Brahmatīrtha and extract everything from there.
He himself tore open the corpse and revealed the gold.
Īśvara said: The wife of that king became one who had attained full conviction; she went to the supreme abode where there is the highest auspiciousness. 46.
All the people were also struck with wonder upon seeing that marvelous and extraordinary spectacle.
O lady of beautiful countenance, a river named Citrapathā arose there, to the east of Citrāditya and to the north of Brahmatīrtha.
In that [place], it remains there, destroying all sins. || 49 ||
O Goddess, when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, whoever performs a ritual bath in that well according to the prescribed rules, and especially performs a śrāddha ceremony there—
Having fully worshipped Citrāditya, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 51 ||
Thus has all this been told to you—the great fruit of Śivarātri, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is meritorious, and destroys all sins. || 52 ||
The person who constantly recites this or even listens to it is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Bhairaveśvara, situated to the northeast of Brahmakuṇḍa, which destroys sins; there resides the four-faced Mahādeva for the protection of the holy ford (tīrtha). || 1 ||
Having bathed there in that great pool, the man who worships him with devotion, with controlled senses, according to the rite of the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), [attains the fruit]. || 2 ||
O Goddess, that man shall deliver those families which have passed away and those indeed which are yet to come; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
In this state, neither rebirth nor destruction occurs for him; he constantly travels in celestial chariots possessing a radiance equal to that of the sun.
Constantly surrounded by thousands of women, he sports like a god in heaven.
O Great Goddess, by merely seeing this four-faced Liṅga of great luster, a human being is liberated from all sins.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, one should go to Brahmeśvara, situated to the south of that [Liṅga], which was formerly established by Brahmā near the Brahmakuṇḍa; it is renowned throughout the three worlds and is guarded by my Gaṇas. || 1 ||
Having bathed there on the fourteenth day, and especially on the new moon day, one should perform the śrāddha rite according to the rules and then worship Brahmeśa.
One should give gold to the Brahmins for the pleasure of Śaṅkara as well.
By acting thus, O Goddess, a man obtains the fruit of his birth; he attains vast fame and rejoices with Brahmā, O Beloved.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmeśvara," within the "Majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 150.
Īśvara said: On the southern side of that very place stands the third Bhairava, installed by Sāvitrī in the vicinity of Brahmakuṇḍa. || 1 ||
Having propitiated there the Lord of Gods, the great-grandfather of the deities, she, subsisting on air and taking no food, satisfied Śaṅkara.
Being pleased, O Goddess, the Lord Śaṅkara spoke to that lady of beautiful countenance.
Whatever man, having bathed in this pool, shall worship my liṅga on the full moon day according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order; ||| 4 ||
He chose his service as the best of boons, along with all auspicious things desired by his mind.
Even one joined with great sins becomes liberated from those transgressions; may that bull-bannered Lord become one whose self is enriched by the fulfillment of all desires.
Having spoken thus, O Goddess of gods, he then vanished; Sāvitrī, having established Śaṅkara, went to the world of Brahmā.
Thus has the great glory of Sāvitrīśa been briefly proclaimed; the wise man who hears this shall be liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sāvitrīśvara-Bhairava," within the "Majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 151 ||
Īśvara said: The third Bhairava has been described; now hear of the fourth Bhairava. He is situated three dhanus to the west of Brahmeśa.
It pacifies all sins and grants all desires to men; it is indeed named Nāradeśvara, having been established by Nārada.
Formerly, the venerable sage Nārada was staying in the world of Brahmā; there he beheld a divine great lute endowed with ten thousand strings.
Released by Sarasvatī in the world of Brahmā, it possessed great splendor; therefore, filled with curiosity, he then played it.
From the lutes being played, the Brāhmaṇas fell to the ground; those seven well-known notes, beginning with Ṣaḍja, were produced in their various modulations (mūrchanās).
Seeing them, he was overcome with wonder; carefully setting aside his lute, he asked the god Brahmā, "O Lord, what is this marvel?"
While the lutes were being played, the Brahmins fell to the ground. "Who are these Brahmins, O Lord? Why do they lie here as if dead? (7)
Brahmā said: "O highly fortunate one, these musical notes (svaras), having become faint, have fallen to the earth; by this very act of speaking ignorantly, sin has now been produced by you."
"The sin of destroying seven Brahmins has come upon you. Therefore, O sage, go quickly to the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa."
"Worship the Lord of Gods for the purification of all sins. Having been addressed thus, Nārada there, grieving again and again, [acted accordingly].
Having experienced much despondency, he came to the sacred field of Prabhāsa; there, with great effort, he reached the Brahmakuṇḍa.
O beloved, he worshipped Bhairava for a hundred divine years; thereafter, having become free from all taint, he likewise became a master of song.
From that time onwards, O Great Goddess, that Liṅga became famous in the world as Nāradeśvara-Bhairava, the destroyer of all sins.
O Maheśvarī, he who plays the lute or its notes out of ignorance shall go there for the sake of purifying that sin.
He who, having conquered his appetite, worships Nāradeśa Bhairava during the three periods of the day in the month of Māgha, becomes captivating to the beautiful women of heaven.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Hiraṇyeśvara, situated two dhanus to the northwest of Brahmakuṇḍa.
It pacifies all sins and destroys the flood of poverty; it is located to the east of Kṛtasmara and to the west of Agnitīrtha.
To the southwest of Yameśvara and likewise to the north of the ocean, on the eastern side of that Liṅga, Brahmā performed great penance; he then propitiated the three-eyed God of gods.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, said: "O Brahmā, speak; what boon do you desire from me?"
Brahmā said: "O God, if you are pleased with me, it is my intention that I perform a sacrifice; you ought to tell me of that place which is of great merit. (5)
Īśvara said: From Kṛtasmarā to Brahmakuṇḍa, and from Yameśa to the ocean—having reached this interval, even a sinner is liberated.
O Lord, may the Viṣuvatī [river] always flow there for the sake of meritorious men; wherever that may be, O All-pervading One, fulfill our desire with your mind.
Thus addressed, Brahmā then commenced that supreme sacrifice.
Then the gods, beginning with Indra, who seek their shares, arrived there; and all the sages, desiring their portions, likewise assembled there.
Then he gave sacrificial fees again to those who had come to the sacrifice; thereafter, O illustrious lady, the sacrificial fees being given were exhausted.
Then Brahmā, greatly distressed, meditated with his mind; having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke these words: || 11 ||
"O Lord Virūpākṣa, this sacrifice is certainly not yet completed; O God, because those worthy of sacrificial fees have not been honored, it does not reach fulfillment. (12)
"Act in such a way that they all depart together with their sacrificial fees. Having heard the words of the Grandfather, I then performed meditation. (13)
The goddess Sarasvatī was remembered by me at that time out of a desire for the welfare of the gods; she, who is of great merit, arrived as soon as the goddess was mentioned by me. (14)
"The wealth of Padmayoni has been exhausted and the sacrifice cannot be completed; therefore, by my grace, become a river flowing with gold. (15)
Then, from the Sarasvatī, a stream rose up facing the west; there, thousands of golden lotuses stood tall.
O beloved, having reached Daityasūdana from Agnitīrtha, the auspicious waters of the Sarasvatī filled [the area] with millions of lotuses on all sides by means of a golden current.
Having given those very golden objects as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins, the delighted Brahmā completed the sacrifice together with the twice-born.
Having cast those remaining lotuses upon the ground, he then established the Kanakeśvara Liṅga above them.
Having installed there the Liṅga which is worshipped by all the gods, he bestowed sacrificial fees upon the sages one by one in due order; and to each individual he gave ten thousand golden lotuses.
Then the remaining lotuses were placed upon the surface of the earth in the center of the Brahma-kuṇḍa; indeed, an unmeritorious man does not obtain them.
Even today, the water of that pool is seen to be of various colors; there, through contact with the lotuses below, the water instantly turns to gold.
Having placed golden lotuses beneath it and having installed the Liṅga above, Prajāpati himself then performed its worship with divine golden lotuses; therefore, he became Hiraṇyeśa.
It pacifies all sins and likewise destroys poverty; by seeing Hiraṇmayeśāna, one is liberated from all evils.
Whoever worships that Liṅga on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha has thereby worshipped the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile. (25)
All gifts have been given by him and all the gods have been propitiated by him who has worshipped that Liṅga; it would be as if the entire universe had been gifted by him.
This has been told by me to you out of affection, O lady of excellent complexion; it has not been told by me to anyone else, for it is a great secret, O fair-faced one. (27)
Whoever hears this with devotion or recites it endowed with devotion, shall go to the world of the gods, liberated from all sins.
Thus, O beautiful one, these five highly renowned and purifying Bhairavas situated near Brahmakuṇḍa have been described to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Hiraṇyeśvara," within the "Majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 153 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Pāpavimocana Linga, situated three dhanus to the northwest of Hiranyeshvara. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, this primordial Liṅga, which destroys the sins of all living beings through both sight and touch, was installed by Gāyatrī.
Having reached that Liṅga, whatever Brāhmaṇa, having become pure, recites the Gāyatrī, is liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the man who feeds a married couple and clothes them according to his ability is liberated from all misfortunes.
O beautiful one, he who worships on the full moon day with offerings of perfumes and flowers shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa for seven births.
Thus, O Goddess, has this sin-destroying majesty been told; by the grace of Brahmakuṇḍa, O beloved, it is the most essential of the essential.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gāyatrīśvara," within the "Majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Ratneśvara. Having performed austerities there, O Goddess, that Liṅga which grants all desires was installed by the powerful Viṣṇu, my dear. (1)
The man who, having bathed in Ratnakuṇḍa, always worships Him with devotion using all ritual offerings, shall obtain his desired fruit.
Having performed severe penance here, Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor obtained the Sudarśana discus, the destroyer of all Daityas.
O Great Goddess, this place is always most dear to me; O Queen of the Gods, I dwell there and do not abandon it even during the dissolution of the universe.
O Goddess, that Vaiṣṇava field is known by the name Sudarśana; it is thirty-six dhanus in circumference all around.
O Goddess, whatever base living beings die by the power of time after reaching this interval, they shall go to the supreme state.
Whoever, with Viṣṇu in mind, should give a golden Garuḍa and yellow garments there, shall obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ratneśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 155 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the shrine established by Vainateya, situated three bow-lengths to the north of Ratnesvara. || 1 ||
And Vainateya, O Goddess of gods, having recognized that the sacred field was indeed Vaiṣṇava, installed a Liṅga that destroys all sins.
Whoever worships him with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the fifth lunar day, poison born of serpents shall not affect him for seven births.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and worshipped according to the prescribed rules, one shall obtain all merit and rejoice in heaven like a god.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Garuḍeśvara," within the "Majesty of Ratneśvara" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 156 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the auspicious Satyabhāmeśvara, situated one bow’s length to the south of Ratneśvara.
O Goddess, this pacifier of all sins was established by Satyabhāmā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with beauty and magnanimity. || 2 ||
Having bathed there, that Vaiṣṇava station indeed destroys the sins of men.
On the third day of the month of Māgha, whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever worships him with devotion shall be liberated from all sins.
One who is afflicted by misfortune, sorrow, grief, and likewise by obstacles, shall be liberated; of this there is no doubt, and he shall be united with Satyabhāmā.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Satyabhāmeśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Anaṅgeśvara, situated at a distance of one bow-length in front of Ratneśvara.
That liṅga was installed by Kāmadeva, the son of Viṣṇu; for he knew that this Vaiṣṇava site is the destroyer of sins in the Kali age.
Having seen and worshipped it, one becomes equal to Kāmadeva; he becomes a captivator of the hearts of the celestial women and the Vidyādharīs. || 3 ||
Even in his lineage, there shall be no one who is ugly or unfortunate. || 4 ||
There, O lady of excellent complexion, on the thirteenth day of the waning moon, there is a special worship through a vow, which is the cause for making one's birth fruitful.
A bed should be given there to a virtuous Brahmin, especially to one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu; thus one obtains the full fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Anaṅgeśvara," within the "Majesty of Ratneśvara" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Ratnakuṇḍa, situated seven bow-lengths to the south of Ratneśa; it pacifies great sins and was created by Viṣṇu himself.
Eighty million sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist on earth as well as those in the intermediate space were brought together by Kṛṣṇa and deposited there in great abundance.
O beloved, a single crore of Gaṇas protects that Kuṇḍa; when the Kali Yuga has arrived, it is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined their souls.
Having bathed there, O Great Goddess, according to the rites prescribed by rule, one shall obtain the fruit of a hundredfold Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Especially on the eleventh day, one should cause the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered there; O beautiful lady, his ancestors attain inexhaustible satisfaction.
One should perform a vigil there on the Ekādaśī according to the prescribed rite; O Goddess, one obtains their desired object if their faith is firm.
Yellow garments and a milk-yielding cow should be given there, dedicated to Viṣṇu, for the full attainment of the fruit of the pilgrimage.
In the Kṛta age it is declared to be Hemakuṇḍa; in Tretā, it is named Rāpyanāma; in Dvāpara, it is Cakrakuṇḍa; and in the Kali age, it is remembered as Ratnakuṇḍa.
O beautiful lady, many currents of the Ganges flowing through the netherworld were brought there by Hari, and they remain there.
O Goddess of gods, by bathing there, one obtains the merit of ablutions at all sacred fords.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ratneśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Rājabhaṭṭāraka, the son of Raivata and the son of Sūrya, who is mounted upon a horse and possesses great strength.
O beloved goddess, situated within the center of the field to the southwest of Sāvitrī, a man who beholds it is liberated from all calamities.
O Goddess, that man who worships him on a Sunday coinciding with the seventh lunar day—within his lineage, no man shall ever become poor.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Him even slightly for the sake of dwelling in the sacred field without obstacles, just as a king [worships] for the increase of his horses.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Lord Raivataka King," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 160.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated to the south of that [Lakshmana], sixteen bow-lengths from Ishanalakshmaneshvara, O beloved.
O Goddess of the gods, having recognized that the sacred field was purifying, the Naga king named Ananta established [the shrine] called Ananteśvara.

But he who, O Goddess, having conquered his appetite and subdued his senses, should worship Him on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna according to the rite of the five offerings (pañcopacāra), || 3 ||
Snakes do not bite such a person for fifteen years; nor, O Goddess, does poison spread through his body or even upon his skin.
Therefore, one should worship him with effort, especially on the fifth lunar day.
Therein, the Ananta-vrata should be performed; milk-rice mixed with honey should be offered, and this milk-rice combined with honey should be given as a meal to a Brahmin.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ananteśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga Aṣṭakuleśvara, situated to the south of that [Liṅga] and to the east of Lakṣmaṇeśa. || 1 ||
It pacifies all evils, destroys great poisons, is worshipped by the Siddhas and Gandharvas, and bestows desired objects. (2)
That mortal who worships him according to the prescribed rite on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is liberated from terrible sins and is glorified in the world of the Nagas. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Aṣṭakuleśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 162 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the shrine situated to the east of that, named Nāsatyeśvara, which destroys great impurities.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nāsatyeśvara and Aśvineśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated to the east of that, which pacifies the flood of great sins, is worshipped, and grants all desires.
The one named Aśvineśvara, situated at five bow-lengths [from here], is seen to pacify all diseases and accomplish all goals. (2)
For whatever sick people there are in the world, this is their great medicine; to behold him on the second day of the month of Māgha is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, if one desires the highest good, one should behold it with devotion; for when worshipped, it pacifies the flood of great sins and grants all desires.
"O Goddess, these two lingas were installed by the son of the Sun; on that very day, a self-controlled and excellent man shall behold them. (5)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Aśvineśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Savitri, the Mother of the World, who pacifies great sins and is situated in the northeastern direction from Somesha.
A man who has restrained his self and possesses a disciplined mind should behold her there.
Desiring to perform a sacrifice, Brahmā made Sāvitrī his lawful wife; learning of this through his power, Gāyatrī was overcome with anger.
Then, having abandoned Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, that goddess, tormented by anger toward her co-wife, took refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
She performs extensive penance, difficult even for the gods to endure; that goddess of lovely appearance remains in that very spot even today. || 5 ||
The Goddess said: For what reason was Sāvitrī abandoned by Brahmā in the past? And how was Gāyatrī obtained, and by whom was she revealed to him?
And of what nature was that Gāyatrī whom the Lotus-born One obtained, such that he set aside his wife and fixed his mind upon her alone? (7)
Whose daughter is she, O Lord, and for what purpose was she married? You ought to tell me all of this according to the facts, for I have a great curiosity.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate the great life-story of Sāvitrī—how she was abandoned by Brahmā and how Gāyatrī was married.
In the past, a thought arose in Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest: "The Vedas have been proclaimed by me for the sake of sacrifice; there is no doubt in this. (10)
Satisfied by sacrifices, the gods will grant rain upon the surface of the earth; and from that, all medicinal herbs will come into being on the face of the earth.
From that semen is born; from semen, creation proceeds. For the sake of the creation of all worlds, I therefore perform sacrifice.
Having seen me intent upon sacrifice, those brahmins who are upon the earth shall perform sacrifices by the hundreds and thousands.
Having thus made this resolve for the sake of sacrifice, O beautiful goddess, he established a sacred ford (tīrtha) known by the name Puṣkara.
There was a great sacrificial enclosure for that high-souled one; there all the celestial sages and the gods, led by Indra, were present.
Then the Great Goddess arrived at the sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā); those best of the twice-born who were there also became the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

Sāvitrī, the mother of the worlds, was the wife of that high-souled one; being occupied with household duties, she missed the time for the initiation ceremony. When summoned by the Adhvaryu priest, Sāvitrī spoke these words: || 17 ||
Sāvitrī said: "Even now my attire has not been prepared, nor have the ornaments for the house been brought; neither Lakṣmī, nor Bhavānī, nor Jāhnavī has arrived even yet. (18)
Neither Svāhā nor Svadhā, nor even Arundhatī, nor Indrāṇī, nor any other wives of the gods—how could she go alone? (19)
Having gone there, the high-souled Pulastya spoke to the Grandfather: "O Lord, Sāvitrī does not come; she is absorbed in her household duties. (20)
"Does this ritual activity of yours proceed toward its fruit for the sake of your wife? Having heard that, the initiated one—whether crested, shaven-headed, or clad in a deer-skin—spoke these words.
Tormented by his wife's anger, he spoke to the god Purandara.
"Go, O Śakra, at my command and bring some other wife from somewhere; return quickly so that there may be no lapse of time."
At the command of the Supreme Lord, the destroyer of Bala departed quickly; yet he did not see any woman who was worthy to be borne by the swan-vehicle.
Then, fearing a curse, the wise thousand-eyed one (Indra) saw a certain cowherd girl, endowed with beauty and youth.
Carrying a full pitcher there, she urged him, saying, "It is a maiden. Taking her with him, Śakra then went to where the four-faced God of gods was consecrated, accompanied by Viṣṇu and Rudra.
Madhusūdana, however, performed the formal giving away of the maiden.
Urged by Śaṅkara himself, as well as by Brahmā and the celestial sages, he was then married; thereafter, he performed for her the initiation ceremony just as he had done for himself.
Then the sacrifice was commenced, provided with everything that could be desired.
There, Atri was the Hotṛ priest and Pulastya the Adhvaryu; Marīci was the Udgātṛ, and I, the bull among the gods, was the Brahman.
The members of his assembly, headed by Sanatkumāra, were created, adorned with garments, ornaments, crowns, and finger-rings.
Adorned and equipped with ornaments, three others followed each one individually; thus, there were sixteen such officiating priests (ṛtvij).
"You have been addressed by me at this sacrifice; may I always be favored by you. Let this Gāyatrī, my wife, also be favored at this sacrifice. (33)
Wearing soft garments and visibly veiled in linen cloth, she emerged from the wife’s chamber accompanied by officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas.
Encased in a staff made of udumbara wood and covered with a deerskin, Brahmā entered that sacrificial pavilion together with her.
Īśvara said: At that very time, the celestial women arrived, having been invited to that sacrifice where Sāvitrī was present.
Born of Bhṛgu by Khyāti, the illustrious wife of Viṣṇu—Lakṣmī herself—was invited there and arrived with great haste. (37)
There, the highly fortunate goddess was adorned with yogic sleep and other [attributes]; likewise were the goddesses Kānti, Śraddhā, Dyuti, and Tuṣṭi. || 38 ||
She who is Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, Umā, the auspicious Pārvatī—the goddess who is the most beautiful in the three worlds and the bestower of good fortune upon women. (39)
Jayā and Vijayā, Gaurī and Mahādhanā, Manojavā the wife of Vāyu, and Ṛddhi the beloved of Dhanada. || 40 ||
Likewise, celestial maidens arrived, as did the daughters of the Dānavas born of the lineage of Danu, and similarly the wives of the seven ṛṣis and of other ṛṣis.
The Plavas, the daughters of Mitra, the hosts of Vidyādharas, the Pitṛs, the daughters of the Rākṣasas, and likewise other Mothers of the World (Lokamātṛs). || 42 ||
Sāvitrī desires to go along with the principal brides; likewise, the goddesses beginning with Aditi and the daughters of Dakṣa have assembled there.
Surrounded by them, Brahmāṇī, whose abode is the lotus, was together with them; O fair-faced one, some were taking sweetmeats and others cakes.
Taking fruits such as āḍhakī, niṣpāva, rājamāṣa, and others, they set out toward the presence of Brahmā. (45)
O beautiful one, having taken various pomegranates, citrons, karīra fruits, and likewise other karamardaka fruits, [he went].
Some took safflower and cumin, others dates; still others took utatīs, and yet others took coconuts.
Just as in former times, mangoes filled with grapes were for the sake of amorous enjoyment; likewise, there were auspicious jackfruits, variegated and wonderful. 48.
O fair-faced one, others took walnuts and myrobalans, as well as citrons, fully ripe wood-apples, and cucumbers.
There were many various offerings pertaining to food and drink, as well as another image of a girl made of sugar, likewise dressed in saffron-colored cloth.
O fair-faced one, having taken these and other such vows in the past, all those auspicious women then arrived together with Sāvitrī.
Seeing Sāvitrī arrive there, Purandara was terrified; Brahmā stood with his face cast down, thinking, "What will she say to me? (52)
Viṣṇu and Rudra were filled with shame, as were all the other twice-born ones, the members of the assembly, and likewise the other inhabitants of heaven who were terrified.
Sons, grandsons, sister's sons, maternal uncles, and brothers—these are the gods named the Seasons (Ṛtus), who are the deities even of the gods.
But they were all struck with wonder, thinking, "What will Sāvitrī say? Should the words of Brahmā truly be spoken by a cowherd’s daughter? (55)
Remaining silent while listening to the words of all who were speaking, the fair-complexioned lady did not come when she was summoned by the Adhvaryu priest.
Another was brought by Śakra, and she herself was given by Viṣṇu; she was approved by Rudra and likewise given by her father himself.
"How will that sacrifice come to be, or how will it reach completion?"—while they were thus reflecting, the Goddess Kamalālayā entered.
Brahmā was surrounded by his wife and by officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas; and there, the sacred fires were offered oblations by Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas.
Likewise, in the hall of the wives was Gopī, with silver horns and a girdle, dressed in silken garments and meditating upon the Supreme Lord.
Devoted to her husband, her very life was her husband; she was established primarily in his service, endowed with compassion, large-eyed, and equal to the sun in splendor. (61)
Illuminating that assembly hall like the radiance of the sun, the sacrificial fire blazed forth, and the officiating priests moved about.
The best of the twice-born took the portions of the sacrificial animals; the gods arrived seeking their shares, but the time for the delay had come.
That which is devoid of the proper time must not be performed; if performed [at the wrong time], it shall yield no fruit. This authority regarding the Vedas has been observed by all the wise.
While the Pravargya rite was being performed by Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas, the two milks were likewise offered with mantras by the Adhvaryu priest.

When the twice-born had arrived with their respective invitations and the food was being prepared, the Goddess, seeing this, became filled with wrath; she spoke to Brahmā, who remained silent in the midst of the assembly.
"O Lord, why do you understand it thus? This deed has been performed by you; for out of desire, you have committed this sin by abandoning me. (67)
She is not equal even to the dust of his feet; she has been placed upon his head.
Whatever all the men assembled and seated in the assembly hall say, he performs that very marvel for his masters, whatever they desire. (69)
Out of greed for beauty, you have committed a censurable deed. || 70 ||
O Lord, you felt no shame toward your sons nor toward your grandsons; I consider this contemptible deed to have been committed out of mere whim. (71)
"You are the grandfather of the gods and the great-grandfather of the sages; how has shame not arisen in you as you behold your own body? (72)
"You have caused laughter in the world and are now censured here; if this disposition of yours remains fixed, then stay, O Lord—salutations be unto you. (73)
"How indeed shall I show my face to my friends? How can I say this: 'I have been made a wife by my husband'? (74)
Brahmā said: "I have been commanded by the officiating priests that the time for initiation is passing away; without a wife, no oblation can be performed here—bring a wife here quickly."
"She was brought here by Śakra and given to me by Viṣṇu; indeed, you were taken by me. Forgive this one thing done by me; O lady of noble vows, I shall not commit another offense against you again."
Īśvara said: Thus addressed, she then became enraged and prepared to curse Brahmā: "If I have performed penance, and if my gurus have been gratified... (77)
In all the halls of the Brahmins and in various places as well, those Brahmins will never perform worship for you. (78)

"Except for a single annual worship on the full moon of Kārtika, all the twice-born shall perform [the rites] for you; I swear this to you by the truth. Knowing this, let there be no anger; for that which is destroyed destroys, without a doubt. (79)
Sāvitrī said: "O Śakra, since you have brought this Ābhīrī into the presence of Brahmā, because such an act has been committed by you, you shall therefore receive its fruit."
O Śakra, when you stand in the midst of battle, you will then be bound by your enemies and brought to the ultimate state.
Possessing nothing and having lost your son, you remain in the city of your enemies; having suffered great humiliation, you shall be liberated from it before long.
Having then cursed Śakra, the goddess spoke these words to Viṣṇu as well. || 83 ||
When your birth occurs in the mortal world by the word of your guru, you shall then experience there the suffering born of separation from your wife.
Your wife Sītā was carried away by hosts of enemies to the far shore of the great ocean; yet you did not realize it, your consciousness overwhelmed by grief.
Thus, together with his brother, he will experience the utmost limit of calamity and suffering; furthermore, there will be a long-term association with cattle.
Thus she spoke to Rudra when he was staying in the Dāruvana forest: "Then those sages, being enraged, will cast a curse upon you, O Hara. (87)
"O wretched Kāpālika! You wish to seize our wives; therefore, this adorned Liṅga shall fall to the earth, O Rudra! (88)
Deprived of your manliness and afflicted by the sage’s curse, your wife, who remains on the bank of the Gaṅgā, will console you. (89)
"O Agni, you were previously made by my son to be the consumer of all things; this is the law for the slayer of an embryo—how then can I burn that which is already burnt? (90)
Rudra, as Jātavedas, will inundate you with his seed; and having produced flames within the sacrificial substances, he shall cause you to blaze with his flame.
Then Sāvitrī indeed cursed all the Brāhmaṇas who were the officiating priests.
The acceptance of gifts, the agnihotra sacrifice, wives, and religious labors will all be in vain; out of greed alone, you shall always go to sacred fields and pilgrimage sites.
Always satisfied with the food of others yet unsatisfied in their own homes, they performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing and accepted gifts from the despicable. (94)
Having acquired wealth in vain and likewise having practiced business in vain, there is no doubt that those who die will become pretas because of that. (95)
In this manner, he then cursed Śakra, as well as Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pāvaka, and likewise Brahmā and all the Brāhmaṇas.
Having thus bestowed the curse upon them, she then remained there, steadfast and firm.

Lakṣmī spoke to that female friend, as did the fair-faced Indrāṇī and the other goddesses; she said, "I shall certainly not remain here. I will go to that place where I shall not hear even a sound. (98)
Then all those women departed for their own abodes; Sāvitrī, however, became enraged and prepared once more to cast a curse upon them.
"Since those celestial women have departed, utterly abandoning me, I shall likewise bestow a curse upon them as well, being exceedingly enraged. (100)
"Lakṣmī shall never have a permanent residence in one place; even though she is fickle, O Rudrā, you shall dwell among fools. (101)

"Among the Mlecchas, the mountaineers, the contemptible, the leper-like, the talkative, the arrogant, the accursed, and the evil-souled—in such a man as you shall your dwelling be established by my curse. (102)
Having thus given her a curse, he then cursed Indrāṇī as well.
"O you who have acted wickedly, when Indra has been seized by the word of Tvaṣṭṛ and has departed for the kingdom, Nahuṣa will see you and demand you as his wife. (104)
"I am Indra; why does this lazy woman not attend to me? I shall slay all the gods if I do not obtain Śacī. (105)
"Then you, O wicked one, shall be lost and dwell in misery in the great forest; for you are arrogant, O woman of evil conduct, by my curse. (106)
Then he uttered a curse upon all the wives of the gods.
And not all women will experience the joy derived from offspring; scorched day and night, they will be distressed by the title of "barren woman. (108)
Having thus cursed Gaurī, that goddess Sāvitrī of excellent complexion wept aloud, standing outside her husband’s sacrifice.
She was seen weeping and consoled by Viṣṇu: "Do not weep, O large-eyed one; come, enter the assembly hall, O auspicious lady. (110)
"O auspicious one, having entered this pure sacrifice, take up the girdle and the two linen garments; O Brahmani, receive initiation; O auspicious one, I bow at your feet. (111)
Thus addressed, she said to him: "I will not do as you say; I shall go to that place where I shall not hear that sound."
Having said this much, she who stood on the ground spoke loudly and then ceased.
Viṣṇu, standing before him with his palms joined in reverence, bowed down and offered praise, endowed with supreme devotion.
Viṣṇu said: Salutations be to you, O Great Goddess, who consists of the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; O Sāvitrī, who delivers one from distress, you are remembered as the sevenfold Vāṇī.
O Goddess, you are the future of all hymns of praise, all treatises, and likewise all defining characteristics; salutations be unto you! 116.

You are white, possessing a white form, equal in splendor to the moon; you shine upon the breast of Hari with the radiance of the moon's rays. You are adorned with ears filled with divine earrings. 117.
You are accomplishment, you are likewise supernatural power, fame, fortune, progeny, and intellect; you are twilight, night, and dawn, and you alone are the Night of Doom.
"As the furrow is to farmers, so is she the sustainer of all beings. To Viṣṇu who was thus praising her, the virtuous Sāvitrī spoke:
"O son, you have been rightly praised by me; you shall be invincible. Always, my child, you will be beloved by your father and mother during your incarnations. (120)
Whoever shall always praise me with this king of hymns, being liberated from all defects, will go to the supreme state. || 121 ||
"Go to his sacrifice, my son, and bring it to its long-lasting conclusion."
"At Kurukṣetra and at Prayāga, during future sacrificial rites, I shall remain close to my husband and carry out what you have said. (123)
Having been addressed thus, Viṣṇu went to the supreme abode of Brahmā; but Sāvitrī, O woman of excellent complexion, arrived at Prabhāsa.
Then, when Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī spoke these words: || 125 ||
"O sages, listen to my words in the presence of your husband; I speak with satisfaction, being prepared to grant a boon. (126)
Those men who, endowed with devotion, shall worship Brahmā, for them indeed there shall be clothing, wealth, grain, wives, happiness, and sons. (127)
Having enjoyed uninterrupted happiness, including a home with sons and grandsons, for a very long time, he shall thereafter attain liberation.
Śakra said: "I shall grant you a boon regarding your battle with the enemies; at that time, Brahmā will go to the abode of the enemies and deliver you. (129)
Through the destruction of your sons and enemies, you shall attain supreme joy; a great kingdom, free from all thorns, shall belong to you throughout the three worlds.
O Viṣṇu, when you indeed take an incarnation in the world of mortals, you shall experience supreme suffering along with your brother, as well as the abduction of your wife.
"Having slain the enemy, you shall regain your wife in the presence of the gods; taking her back, you will rule over a vast kingdom and then depart. (132)
Having ruled the kingdom for eleven thousand years, you shall return again to heaven; your fame will be vast in the world, and there will be great affection [for you]. (133)
Gāyatrī spoke this very thing to all those Brāhmaṇas as well.
By bringing satisfaction to you, the deities shall attain contentment; indeed, you all, as the gods of the earth (Bhūmidevas), shall become worthy of worship.
Having performed worship of you and having given gifts many times, you shall cross over all this by means of even a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
O best of the twice-born, by specifically chanting me, the Mother of the Vedas, at Prabhāsa, you shall not incur the faults arising from the acceptance of gifts.
At Puṣkara, all the deities are pleased by the gift of food; when a single Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.
When wealth is placed in your hands, all men shall cross over the sins of killing a Brahmin and whatever other misdeeds there may be.
But by means of recitation and by performing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), you shall be exalted; even a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin perishes at that very moment.
The Gāyatrī destroys the sin produced in ten lifetimes with a hundred recitations, that committed in the past with a thousand, and even the sin of three ages (yugas) with a thousand.
Knowing this, you shall always be worthy of worship when my recitation is performed; of this there is no doubt, and no further deliberation is required in this matter. (142)
All [the deities] are to be worshipped without doubt by means of the three-mora Oṃkāra, especially with the half[-mora], after having recited me along with the Śiras [mantra]. 143.
Abiding in eight syllables, I have pervaded this entire world; I am the mother of all the Vedas, adorned by all the Vedas.
Having known me as the supreme perfection, the best of the twice-born shall behold me; through my recitation, preeminence shall belong to all of you.

A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if he knows only the essence of the Gāyatrī, is better than one who is unrestrained, though he may know the four Vedas, eat all things, and sell all things. (146)

"O best of the twice-born, because the curse of Sāvitrī was bestowed upon you all here, everything given and offered as an oblation here shall produce inexhaustible results; for that reason, O most excellent brāhmaṇas, this boon has been granted to you by me."
Those Brahmins devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice who offer oblations at the three times of day shall go to heaven along with twenty-one generations of their lineage.
In this way, she granted a boon to Śakra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise to Pāvaka, as well as to Brahmā and the Brahmins; having granted the boon at that time, she remained by the side of Brahmā.
Hari, however, explained the cause of Lakṣmī’s curse, as well as the individual curses of all those young women.
Then Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, granted a boon to Lakṣmī.
O daughter, by your residence here, O beautiful one, all shall always be beyond reproach; they will undoubtedly become givers of joy to everyone. (152)
All those who have been gazed upon by you are indeed recipients of merit; their birth, lineage, character, and even their dharma, O lady of the beautiful countenance, [are purified]. (153)
But those men who have been abandoned by you are partakers of suffering; they do not shine in the assembly, nor are they esteemed by other kings. (154)
Indeed, those best of the twice-born offer blessings to them; they treat them with kindness as if they were their own grandson, brother, father, or teacher. (155)

"You are my kinsman, there is no doubt; I cannot live without you. When you are seen, my sight becomes clear and beautiful; my mind is exceedingly delighted—I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (156)
When you look upon such words with discernment, those virtuous people who bring joy to all men will speak them. (157)
"Having reached heaven, Indra will seek you out, O Indrāṇī; for that wicked one was swiftly slain by the word of Agastya before he could see you. (158)
Having attained the state of a serpent, he will entreat that sage: "I am ruined by my pride; O Sage, be my refuge! (159)
Having taken compassion to heart at those words of the king, the blessed ṛṣi spoke these words. (160)
O joy of the Kurus, a king shall be born in your lineage who, upon seeing the serpent's body, will deliver you through his inquiries. (161)

He too, having abandoned his state as a python, will go to heaven once more. When the horse sacrifice has been performed by your husband, you shall go again to the celestial realm; O fair-eyed one, you shall attain this through this boon granted by me.
Then all the wives of the gods were addressed with satisfaction: "Though you may be deprived even of offspring, there shall be no sorrow at all. (163)
Having thus granted these boons, the goddess Gāyatrī, honored by the world, then vanished from sight while everyone was looking on.
Then the goddess Sāvitrī arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa, upon the peak of Kṛtasmara, to the east of Śrī Someśvara.
In the auspicious second Dvāpara of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, a sacrifice was commenced there by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
The high-souled gods and the excellent seven ṛṣis who went to the sacrifice were those who had been praised in the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], yet they were cursed in the past.
From that time onwards, they took refuge in the sacred field of Prabhāsa. || 168 ||

Sāvitrī is the mother of the worlds and the bestower of grace upon the worlds; he who worships her with devotion continuously for one fortnight according to the ritual procedure for the worship of Brahmā, shall certainly obtain a son. (169)
Having bathed at Pāṇḍukūpa and having indeed beheld the five Liṅgas installed here by the Pāṇḍavas, a man shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, he who recites the Brahma-sūktas in the vicinity of Sāvitrī-sthala is liberated from all sins. || 171 ||
Thus has been narrated to you this renowned account that destroys all impurities; whoever hears this with devotion shall go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sāvitrī," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, tell me the life-story of that Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, who is established at Prabhāsa. || 1 ||
Endowed with the greatness of religious vows and accompanied by historical narratives, it brings about devotion to one's husband for women and bestows great fortune and supreme prosperity.
Īśvara said: O Mahādevī, O Maheśvarī, I shall relate the great life-story of Sāvitrī who was established at the site within Prabhāsa-kṣetra; how the vow was performed by Sāvitrī, the princess.
Among the Madras there was a righteous king named Aśvapati, who was devoted to the welfare of all beings and beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside.

Forgiving, childless, truthful, and having conquered his senses, that king arrived for a pilgrimage to Prabhāsa-kṣetra; performing the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites, he came to Sāvitrī-sthala. || 5 ||
There, the king himself, together with his wife, undertook this vow known as Sāvitrī, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
The goddess Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, became pleased with him; she stood there visibly, personified as the syllables "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ."
The goddess, bearing a water-pot, vanished once more; after a long time, a daughter of divine form was born.
Bestowed by the pleased Sāvitrī and likewise through the worship of Sāvitrī, the king gave her the name Sāvitrī itself, according to the command of the Brahmins.
That princess grew like the goddess Śrī personified; Sāvitrī, with her delicate limbs, attained the bloom of youth.
Seeing her with her slender waist and broad hips, like a golden statue—whether she was a daughter of the gods who had arrived there—so did the people perceive her. (11)
That large-eyed Padmā, as if blazing with splendor, performed the vow that Bhṛgu had proclaimed, which was like that of Sāvitrī.

Then, having fasted and bathed her head, and having approached the deity and offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, that woman of excellent complexion caused the Brahmins to recite benedictions.
Having accepted the remaining flowers from them, the princess, the queen who possessed the form of Śrīvatsa, approached while surrounded by her female companions.
Having saluted her father's feet and first offered the remains [of the meal] to him, that woman of beautiful hips stood by the side of the king with palms joined in reverence.
Having seen his own daughter, who had attained youth and possessed a divine form, the king consulted with his ministers regarding his daughter's future and spoke.
"Daughter, the time for your giving has arrived, yet no one chooses me; though I search, I do not see a suitor here who is a worthy match for myself. (17)
"O daughter, act in such a way that I do not become an object of reproach among the gods and others; for this has been heard by me while reciting the treatises on Dharma. (18)
If a maiden sees her menses while still in her father's house and remains uninitiated, the father incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*. (19)
For this purpose I am sending you; O daughter, perform the svayaṃvara yourself. Accompanied by the elder ministers, go quickly and make your choice.
Saying "So be it," Sāvitrī departed from him and went to the delightful penance groves of the royal seers.
Having paid homage by prostrating at the feet of the venerable elders there, he then visited all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and hermitages.
Sāvitrī returned to her home along with her ministers; there she saw the pure celestial sage Nārada before her.
Having bowed to the brahmin seated upon his seat, she, speaking with a smile, related the matter for which she had gone to the forest.
Sāvitrī said: There was among the Śālvas a righteous-souled Kṣatriya, a lord of the earth, known as Dyumatsena; he became blind by fate. (25)
While the noble Dyumatsena was a mere child, his kingdom was seized by his neighboring vassal Rukmin, an old enemy who took advantage of this vulnerability.
He set out for the forest together with his wife, who had a young calf. || 27 ||
"He is his eldest son, grown up in the forest, supremely righteous, truthful, and worthy of me as a husband—thus he was desired by my mind. (28)
Nārada said: "Alas! O King, a great hardship has been undertaken by Sāvitrī; out of her youthful nature, she has chosen the virtuous Satyavat. (29)
His father speaks the truth, his mother speaks the truth; because he speaks the truth, the sages indeed gave him the name Satyavān.
Horses were always dear to him; he would have horses made of clay and even paint horses on a canvas, and thus he was called Citrāśva ("He of the Variegated Horses").
Satyavān was a disciple of Rantideva, equal to him in the virtue of generosity; he was devoted to the Brahmins and truthful in speech, just like Śibi Auśīnara.
Noble like Yayāti, pleasing to behold like Soma, and in beauty like one of the two Aśvins, the mighty son of Dyumatsena was peerless.
"There is one fault and no other: from this day forward, Satyavān will give up his body, his life-span exhausted after one year. (34)
Having heard the words of Nārada, the daughter spoke to the king.
Sāvitrī said: "Kings speak but once; Brāhmaṇas speak but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once—these three things happen only once. (36)
Whether he be long-lived or short-lived, virtuous or even devoid of virtue, my husband has been chosen by me once; I shall not choose a second. (37)
Having made a resolution with the mind, it is then expressed by speech; afterwards it is carried out through action; therefore, the mind is indeed the authority.
Nārada said: "If this is pleasing to you, let it be performed immediately; let the giving away of your daughter Sāvitrī be carried out without any obstacle. (39)

Having spoken thus, he sprang up and ascended to the third heaven; and the king then performed all the marriage rites for his daughter at an auspicious moment, with Brahmins standing by his side who had mastered the Vedas.
And Sāvitrī too, having obtained that husband desired by her heart, rejoiced exceedingly, like a virtuous person who has attained heaven, she of the slender limbs. || 41 ||
Thus, O Pārvatī, as they were dwelling there in that hermitage, some time passed while they remained watching.
As that noble lady Sāvitrī stood there day and night, those words spoken by Nārada remained fixed in her mind.
Then, after a long period of time had passed, the time eventually arrived for King Satyavrata to die.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, at the beginning of the night on the twelfth day, Sāvitrī kept the words spoken by Nārada in her heart as she was counting [the days].
Thinking, "I must die on the fourth day," the beautiful woman remained in the hermitage throughout the day and night, undertaking a three-night vow.
Then, having bathed and offered libations to the deities, she dwelt there for three nights; the sweet-smiling woman then paid homage at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Then Satyavan set out for the forest, taking his axe; Sāvitrī also followed behind her departing husband.
Then, having quickly gathered fruits, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass, he took some dry wood and prepared a load of firewood.
Then, as he was splitting the wood, a pain arose in his head; instantly casting down the load of wood, he hung from the branch of a banyan tree.
Sāvitrī said: "A pain in my head afflicts me; O beautiful one, I wish to sleep for a moment upon your lap. (51)
"Rest, O mighty-armed one," said the sorrowful Sāvitrī; "I shall go to the hermitage that destroys fatigue even later. (52)
As soon as she had placed him on her lap and laid his head upon the ground, Sāvitrī beheld a man who was dark and tawny.
To him, who wore a crown and yellow garments and appeared like the sun itself risen, Sāvitrī then spoke with sweet syllables after bowing down.
"Who are you—a god or a demon—who has come to violate me? O Lord, I cannot be turned away from my own duty by anyone. (55)
Know me, O best of men, to be like a blazing crest of fire.
Yama said: "I am Yama, the Restrainer, who causes fear to all the worlds. (57)
"O devoted wife, this husband of yours has reached the end of his lifespan; he cannot be led away by my servants in your presence, therefore I have come here in person. (58)
Having spoken thus, Yama forcibly extracted from the body of Satyavrata a person the size of a thumb, bound with a noose.
Then he began to set out upon the path frequented by his ancestors; Sāvitrī, the lady of beautiful hips, followed closely behind him.
And because of her devotion to her husband, she was untiring; Yama spoke thus to her: "Turn back and go, Sāvitrī; you have arrived here for only a moment."
O large-eyed one, this path is not followed by anyone.
Sāvitrī said: "Neither fatigue nor exhaustion ever arises in me as I follow my husband in the presence of such a distinguished person."

For the virtuous, the virtuous are the refuge and no other; for women, the husband is always the refuge; for those in the various castes and stages of life, the Veda is the refuge; and for disciples, the teacher is the refuge.
For all living beings there is a place upon the surface of the earth; yet for women, there is no other refuge than their one husband.
Thus, with other very sweet words endowed with righteousness and purpose, the son of the Sun was pleased and spoke these words to Sāvitrī.
Yama said: "I am pleased with you; may it be well with you. Choose a boon, O beautiful lady. She too, with her face bowed down in humility, chose her own kingdom.
Likewise, he obtained the sight of the high-souled father-in-law’s kingdom, as well as a hundred sons for his father and a hundred sons for himself.
Then Dharmarāja, having granted her the boon of her husband’s life as well as eternal success in dharma, sent her forth from that place.
Then, having reached her husband with a joyful heart, Sāvitrī went to her own hermitage together with her husband, free from all anxiety.
And on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, she performed this very vow; by its greatness, O King, the recovery of his sight occurred before him.
Then the king obtained his own kingdom free from all thorns; and her father obtained a hundred sons, as did she herself a hundred daughters.
Thus, the entire greatness of the vow has been recounted by me.
The Goddess said: O Lord, what kind of great vow was that which Sāvitrī performed? And what indeed was the procedure for it during that month of Jyeṣṭha?
Who is the deity in that vow? What are the mantras? What is the fruit, O All-pervading Lord? O Maheśa, tell me in detail this eternal Dharma. (76)
Īśvara said: Listen with devotion, O Goddess of the gods, to the Sāvitrī-vrata; I shall describe it, O Maheśvarī, exactly as it was observed by that Satī.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, O beautiful lady, one should first perform the cleansing of the teeth and then observe the vow of fasting for three nights.
But one who is unable, having subdued his senses, should take a single meal at night on the thirteenth day, eat only what is unasked for on the fourteenth, and observe a fast on the full moon day.
