O lady of beautiful hips, by bathing daily in a pond, a great river, a mountain spring, or at Pāṇḍukūpa, one obtains the fruit of all possible ablutions.
Especially on the full moon day, one should perform a bath with mustard seeds, clay, and water.
O illustrious lady, having taken a prastha measure of sand in a vessel, or else having taken grain such as barley, rice, sesame, and so forth; (81)
Then, having fashioned an image of Sāvitrī, beautiful in all its limbs, in a vessel made of bamboo and wrapped in a pair of cloths; || 82 ||
One should give a golden, earthen, or even a wooden image according to one's capacity; and for Sāvitrī and Brahmā, one should offer two red garments and white ones respectively.
One should thus worship Sāvitrī together with Brahmā according to one's ability, using perfumes, fragrant flowers, incense, food offerings, and lamps. (94)
With ripe *kośātaka* fruits, *kūṣmāṇḍa* and *karkaṭī* gourds, coconuts together with dates, and auspicious *kapittha* and pomegranates; || 85 ||
With rose-apples, citrons, oranges, walnuts, and breadfruits; likewise with cumin, pieces of pungent ginger, molasses, and salt. || 86 ||
One should delight [the deity] with sprouted grains of the seven types of grain arranged in bamboo vessels, and with auspicious silken threads and saffron filaments.
In this way, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, effects her descent.
One should worship her with the Sāvitrī mantra, equal to that of Brahmā; for others, this mantra declared in the Purāṇas is prescribed. || 89 ||
O Goddess preceded by the syllable Oṃ, who holds a lute and a book, O Mother of the Vedas, salutations to you; grant me the state of never being widowed.

Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites, one should cause a vigil (jāgara) to be held there; with the sound of singing and musical instruments, crowds of men and women should spend the night dancing and laughing, accompanied by those expert in the science of dance.
One should also have the best of the twice-born recite the narrative of Sāvitrī until the time of dawn, accompanied by the sentiments and flavors of song.
Having thus performed the marriage of Sāvitrī with Brahmā, he clothed seven couples in white garments.
A house should be given as a gift, complete with all its furnishings; one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas along with the Sāvitrī.
Then, [he gave it] to one who knows the Sāvitrī-kalpa and recites the narrative of Sāvitrī, to an astrologer living by the gleaning of grains, and to a poor man who maintains the sacred fire.
Having thus given according to the prescribed rite, one should invite fourteen couples beneath a banyan tree on that night of the full moon.
Then, at the time of dawn when the morning has arrived, one should bring all the various kinds of food, both solid and soft, to the Sāvitrī-sthala.
Having prepared the cooked food and having diligently performed the protective rite, the wise man should then invite the Brahmins together with their wives.
Having performed the ritual foot-washing of Sāvitrī at that spot, he should cause well-bathed Brāhmaṇas, together with their wives, to sit there.
O Goddess, one should offer food to a married couple in front of Sāvitrī; by that, I am fed there, and I remain here—of this there is no doubt. (100)
Whoever feeds a second [guest], by him Keśava, the granter of boons who is the companion of Lakṣmī, has been fed; he bestows excellent boons upon that person. (101)
Accompanied by Sāvitrī, Brahmā shall be fed on the third day; each single meal there is considered equal to feeding ten million.
O Great Goddess, there, in the vicinity of Sāvitrīsthala, he partook of food prepared with the six flavors in eighteen ways for the sake of the Goddess.

In his family, there shall be no widow, no barren woman, nor any unfortunate woman; nor shall there be a mother of daughters, nor one who is unkind to her husband. Indeed, these eight faults of women shall never exist [in his lineage]. (104)
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort, food that is always free from pungent and dark-colored items should be given before Sāvitrī. (105)
Women should never be given food that is sour or salty; rather, all food should be sweet in five ways, pleasing to the heart, and well-prepared. (106)
There should be cakes filled with ghee and provided with much milk; such cakes are to be made, and the second is the Aśokavartikā.
A third cake should be prepared combined with dates; and the fourth is a saṃyāva cake combined with jaggery and clarified butter.
She brings delight to men and is exceedingly beloved by women; her family becomes endowed with wealth, grain, and people, and filled with hundreds of men and women—of this there is no doubt. (109)
There shall be no fever, nor burning heat, nor suffering born of separation for twenty-one generations through the gift of an Aśoka-wick lamp. 110.
The family of that woman who offers *pūrikās* becomes filled with daughters-in-law, sons, and endless male and female servants.
In this family, there will undoubtedly be daughters accompanied by their daughters-in-law who possess sons, for those young women who have given gifts of *śikhariṇī*. (112)
And the entire family rejoices, filled with all accomplishments; such is the result of the gift of sweetmeats, so said the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 113 ||
And this meal, moreover, is especially distinguished for women who have not yet reached puberty. || 114 ||
O Goddess, in birth after birth, she shall be fortunate, possessed of sons, virtuous, endowed with wealth and prosperity, and a hostess to a thousand guests. 115.
And there were principal drinks that were pleasing and sweet: grape wine, as well as the drink made from tamarind combined with molasses. || 116 ||
Indeed, auspicious water mixed with sugar-candy should be drunk by married women and offered to the twice-born.
One should cause others to be given those very things suitable for their respective castes, as well as fragrant drinks that are appropriate for them. || 118 ||

Having honored them according to the prescribed rite with gifts of garments and bodices, their limbs anointed with saffron and adorned with garlands of flowers, and having worshipped them with perfumes and incense, one should present coconuts.

Having applied collyrium to their eyes and vermilion to their foreheads, and having placed pleasant, fragrant, and soft betel nuts along with their containers into their hands, one should prostrate and bid them farewell.
And afterwards, he himself should eat together with his kinsmen and children.
Alternatively, if one is unable to eat at the sacred site itself, one should go home and eat only after the Goddess has been satisfied.

In this very way, having come to his own abode and performed the śrāddha for the ancestors according to the prescribed rules, preceded by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the ancestors indeed remain satisfied for a day of Brahmā.
O auspicious one, the merit of giving at one's own home is eight times that of giving at a sacred ford; moreover, the base do not witness the Śrāddha offered by the twice-born.
The Śrāddha for the ancestors is prescribed to be performed in a secluded house; if it is seen by a low-caste person, it is destroyed and does not reach the ancestors.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the Śrāddha to be performed in secret; it has been declared by Svayambhū himself to be that which grants satisfaction to the ancestors.
But that rite which is performed through the offering of food to Gaurī and others is declared to be *rājasī*; it bestows fame upon people. (127)
This gift should always be given by one who desires his own welfare; especially so at a *śrāddha*, if he wishes for a result characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*). (128)

O Goddess, this concluding rite (udyāpana) of the Sāvitrī vow must always be performed by men for the sake of purifying all sins. Whether committed unintentionally or intentionally, sin perishes at that very moment.
In this world, however, those by whom that pilgrimage has indeed been performed possess good fortune, wealth, grain, and excellent women of various kinds. (130)
The man who performs this ritual for the pilgrimage with devotion, or even hears of it, is liberated from all sins whatsoever. (131)

On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, at the auspicious site of Sāvitrīsthalaka, whoever performs a circumambulation according to the prescribed rules along with offerings of fruit, [attains great merit].
O Goddess, the man who performs one hundred and eight, or half of that, or half of that again, having circumambulated it there; || 133 ||
And by those men who have committed incest out of ignorance, other sins likewise perish; there is no doubt in this matter. || 134 ||
Those who, having gone to Sthalaka, performed the twilight worship of Sāvitrī with water from the Pāṇḍu-well using the hand of their own wife; || 135 ||

O beautiful lady, he who brings holy water using either a golden pitcher or one made of clay and performs the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) thereby has indeed performed the twilight worship for twelve years. (136)

The fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice is obtained by bathing; likewise, ten times that fruit is gained by giving gifts; furthermore, it is infinite through fasting and likewise through listening to the sacred narrative.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Procedure for the Worship and the Ritual Conclusion of the Sāvitrī Vow," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Bhūtamātṛkā situated there, located to the west of Sāvitrī at a distance of a hundred *dhanus*, accompanied by nine crores of Gaṇas and crowded with ghosts and spirits, and worshipped manifoldly by Siddhas, Gandharvas, gods, and others. || 2 ||
The Goddess said: "Exulting in the thought, 'I am Bhūtamātā,' people everywhere run about in every village and every city, singing, dancing, and laughing. (3)
He prattles like a madman, falls upon the ground like one intoxicated, runs toward others like one enraged, and is indeed dragged along like one dead.
The world, like one seized by wind, brings about the destruction of its own happiness; like a ghost, it plunges into ashes, urine, water, and mud. (5)
Is this the path prescribed by the scriptures, or is it merely worldly? O Lord, my mind is bewildered by this; you ought to explain it to me.

How is she to be worshipped by the men residing in the sacred field of Prabhāsa? Why has the Goddess gone there, and at what time did she arrive? On which day and in which month should her great festival be celebrated? || 7 ||
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you whatever is in your mind; it is my conviction that you are indeed faithful and full of devotion. (8)
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, the daughter of the mountain was then born from Dakṣa’s insult.
Indeed, during the second Dvāpara age, you were given to me by Parvata when our marriage had taken place, O delighter of all the gods.
And formerly, O beloved, accompanied by you on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, I sported with joy using divine playthings; [I,] shining with your firm, high, and swelling hips.

Seeing you, possessed of great luster, with a face like a white lotus, joyful, and appearing as if emerged from the very root and sprout of the tree of Love, I then desired you as you lay upon a costly bed.
O Goddess, when a hundred divine years had passed while you were absorbed in meditation, you then arose and emerged from that state of restraint.
From that water there arose a woman with a cavernous belly, dark-skinned, with a terrifying face, tawny eyes, and disheveled hair.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, her head bound with half a severed corpse, bearing a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skeleton, the auspicious goddess Śivā holds a torso and a skull in her hands. 15.
Clad in garments of leopard skin, with a girdle of tinkling bells, she makes the sound of the ḍama-ḍamaruka drum and fills the sky with her shrieks.
And there were others standing by her side; hear their names from me: they were the friends of that Brāhmaṇa-rākṣasī, and they too were beautiful to behold.
Pervading the earth through ten billion divisions, they are well-established; among them, four are indeed principal, possessing great strength and prowess.
Red-colored, with a large tongue, and truly inexhaustible, she is indeed the doer of evil; born from their lineage are the Brahma-rākṣasas upon this earth. (19)
For these two śleṣmātaka trees are generally the abodes of well-behaved beings; restless like tall palm trees, they dance and laugh.
In this world, they should be known as the primary leaders of living beings; these ones are exceedingly black and roam within the space between the *vyaṃtara* deities. || 21 ||
They move through the sky as high as the tops of trees; of this there is no doubt.
In that very same way, by my power, a man appeared with my own form and ornaments, bearing a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and wrapped in a hide.
Though followed by many terrifying beings with faces like those of lions and tigers, whose mouths scraped the very sky, he remained fearless.
"O Queen, having been born in this manner, he spoke to me while overcome by hunger; therefore, seeing him hungry, I granted him this boon. (25)
"By the touch of your hands, let there be night everywhere; for you both are more powerful at night than by day. Protect the worlds like sons, and let righteousness be upheld. (26)
When I had spoken thus there, O beloved, those two—the hosts of spirits and the Mothers—along with Bhavānī and Bhava, became one in an instant.
Having seen you, O lady of pure smiles, my heart was filled with joy and I spoke to you.
"O auspicious one, look, look at these two born from my own portions—bearers of the loathsome, the marvelous, and the erotic sentiments, and performers of the comic. (29)
Bhrātṛbhāṇḍā, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Udakasevitā—these three names, O Goddess, are remembered as renowned for their prowess in the world. (30)
Then, seeing me with my palms joined in reverence, they spoke to me again: "O Blessed One, in what place shall our dwelling be? (31)
When they had spoken thus, I invited them there with a boon, saying: "In the region of Saurāṣṭra, within Bhārata, there is an excellent sacred field."
It is known as Prabhāsa; it is secure and dear to me, situated to the south of Kūrma and further to the southwest.
In that place where the three constellations Svātī, Viśākhā, and Maitra (Anurādhā) are remembered to be located, one should always remain until the end of the Manvantara.
O beloved of beings, I shall always speak of another means of livelihood for you.
Where there are thorny trees, where there is the niṣpāva creeper, and where the wife is a remarried woman—those are long-lasting dwellings for an anthill.
In that house where there are five men, three women, and as many cows, and where there is a fire fed by fuel in the darkness—in that house is your dwelling. (37)

That place which is inhabited by spirits, ghosts, and piśācas—where there is one ewe, eight young goats, three cows, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants—that is your dwelling in that house. (38)
The *uddālaka* seeds, the flour-cakes, and likewise the vessels such as the cooking pot—whatever was cast here and there, that became your shelter. (39)
O Goddess, your abode is in the pestle and mortar of women, as well as in the udumbara tree; there, too, is your residence where bitter speech is spoken.
Just as grains, both ripe and unripe, are eaten there in that house, so too shall you wander among the branches together with the spirits.
In that house where men place the fire upon the lid of the cooking pot, it becomes the refuge for all manner of ill-omened things. (42)
In whatever house human bone remains for a day and night, there this host of spirits will roam at will. (43)
Enter into those beings who do not proclaim the wielder of the Pināka bow to be superior to all, but instead describe him as being common to all.
And where there is a maiden or a creeper named Rohiṇī in the house, or an Agastya tree, or indeed a Bandhujīva plant in the dwellings; || 45 ||
In whose house there is specifically the karavīra, as well as the nandyāvarta, or the mallikā, that house is indeed fit for the spirits.
The palmyra tree, the tamāla, the marking-nut tree, or even a grove of tamarind; the bakula, a grove of plantains, the kadamba, or even the khadira tree. || 47 ||
For those in whose home there is a banyan tree, or an aśvattha, a mango, an udumbara, or a jackfruit tree—indeed, that is dear to all beings. (48)
Wherever there may be a crow’s nest, whether in a grove or even in a house, and wherever there is an image of a monk in that house or likewise on the right side; || 49 ||
And where the image is situated above, there is the dwelling of the spirits. || 50 ||

One should say that those houses are merely the dwellings of elemental spirits where there is no worship of the Liṅga, where there is no recitation of mantras and the like, and where people are indeed devoid of devotion.
"Enter the home of those mortals who have dirty faces, who wear soiled garments, and whose teeth are stained with grime. (52)
But those who take pleasure in forbidden women through sexual misconduct, and those who engage in sexual intercourse at twilight—enter their house. (53)
What is the use of much talk? Enter the house of those who are excluded from their daily rites and devoid of devotion to Rudra. (54)
He who eats food, as well as food and water, without having first given them to his kinsmen—forsake those men, along with their sapinda and sodaka relatives, from that very moment.
Enter that house, free from fear, along with the elemental spirits, where the wife and husband are at variance with one another.
There is no devotion to Vāsudeva where Hari is never present; there is no chanting, fire-offerings, and so forth, nor is there sacred ash in the homes of those men. (57)
There is no worship even on the festival days, and especially not on the fourteenth day.

And those mortals who, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, are devoid of sacred ash during the twilight, and who do not worship Mahādeva on the fifteenth day—where indeed [can they find merit]? (59)
That house where great festivals, formerly renowned among the citizens and country-folk, are no longer celebrated as before, is not a place for you to dwell.
That house where the sound of the Vedas is not heard, where there is no worship of the guru and so forth, and which is devoid of rites for the ancestors, is known as the home of a ghost.
In whichever house quarrels arise night after night while the children look on and the elders are present before them, enter there joyfully along with the spirits and devour [them]. 62.
"In which month and on which day shall she, who is honored by the world, appear? Thus addressed by her, O Goddess, I spoke to her again, my dear: (63)
On the fourteenth day of the month of Mādhava which falls on the new moon, there shall be for you a great and ancient festival at that place.
At that time, during that great festival, those women will worship her with offerings, flowers, and incense; do not enter their houses. (65)
O Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Mādhava, Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Janārdana! || 66 ||
Those people who [call out] "Nṛsiṃha," "Vāmana," "Acintya," and "Keśava," and who say "Rudra, Rudra," "Rudra," and "Salutations again and again to Śiva"—[they attain liberation]. || 67 ||
They will constantly speak with joy regarding their wealth, houses, and so forth; do not enter their gardens or cow-pens under any circumstances. (68)

O man, do not enter into those people who know the customs of the land and the duties of dharma, who perform recitation, fire-offerings, auspicious rites, and worship of the deities according to the prescribed rules, and who maintain purity while fearing public censure. (69)
The Goddess said: O Lord of the gods, you ought to tell me this: at what time should the worship of Bhūtamātṛ be performed by men who desire happiness? (70)
Īśvara said: This Blessed Lady is everywhere the benefactor of children; she is worshipped through various names, at various times, and with various rites.
From the first day of the lunar fortnight until the fourteenth day in the month of Vaiśākha, worship should be performed with incenses, garlands, and spectacles.
And those who, with devotion, shall sprinkle with handfuls full of water this [image] even when it is broken or has fallen and remains at the foot of an ancient tree; || 73 ||
One should worship with necklaces, threads, vermilion, flowers, and incense; there, the Siddhavaṭa tree is to be honored, and one should deposit a branch of it [there]. (74)
Having observed that [image] worshipped with effort by men desiring auspiciousness, one should feed it quickly with saṃyāva, kṛśara, apūpa, and pāyasa.
The person who performs this rite with a spirit of devotion shall obtain an increase in sons and cattle, as well as physical health. (76)
Neither Śākinīs, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas cause affliction in his house; his children attain growth free from disease. (77)
Now, O Goddess, I shall explain in due order, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), how the festival should be celebrated by men with processions and spectacles.
Through descriptions of the fruits of forbidden actions, through the mockery of heretics, and by means of men intent on laughter with their wondrous gestures, [the truth] is demonstrated. (79)
On the fifth day, however, there is especially a clamor at night; on that auspicious occasion, one should diligently perform a vigil after worshiping the Goddess with effort. (80)
Out of greed for wealth, Viśva has slain his husband, his own teacher; behold him, O people, as he is being impaled upon the tip of a stake! (81)
"You have seen that wicked man who violated another's wife; having had his hands cut off with a sword, he now departs mounted upon a donkey. (82)
Even when his body is shattered by the sword-leaf, he who was adorned with ornaments and seated comfortably on a fine seat goes happily as one who has performed meritorious deeds. (83)
O people, do you not see this supreme traitor to his master, being torn apart by saws with blood gushing from within? (84)
"Surely this is a thief who has arrived, a supreme source of terror to all; struck by blows from the staff, he is being led away by the executioners. (85)
Constantly watched by onlookers and crying out in various tones, he is led away in shackles to be executed, O people, ashamed and with his face cast downward.
You did not see him with white hair and a white beard, bearing a banner of white garments, being struck by Viṭaṅkā and other female attendants.
"Having brought me, a wretched woman, out of my home and led me into his own house, he took his pleasure with me; why does that fool not provide for my maintenance and nourishment? (88)
Adorned with Bhairava ornaments, his leader always has rolling eyes; being drowsy and deluded, he is to be slain here and there. (89)

A sense of world-weariness regarding wealth, fields, and the like has arisen in his heart; for even as a child, he has today taken up the great vow. Do you not see him quickly, with bloodshot eyes and limbs black as a crow? (90)
Having bound others who had entered the hollows of trees with chains, they likewise mangled them into pieces with volleys of arrows and many wooden stakes.
Behold those who have abandoned cries of "victory" and "alas," and who strike with great skill.
"You shall seize this evil-minded woman with her face half-black; behold her with disheveled hair, dancing like a female ascetic. (93)
With her wild eyes and feet, this circle of young girls moves along, performing a violent *tāṇḍava* dance intensified by the deep sound of their anklets. 94.
Wearing a blanket shimmering from a pimple on the surface of her hip, she wanders and dances about, from house to house throughout the earth.
Thus, with such constant incentives and spectacles, he, surrounded by his sons, brothers, and friends, should urge those great men in this manner. (96)
On the eleventh or the ninth lunar day, having lit a lamp, one should place there small bowls (*kuṇḍaka*) made of clay or wood, which indeed serve as representations of the faces.
One should have fashioned various precious images, both fierce and peaceful, for the Mothers such as Caṇḍikā and likewise for the Rākṣasas. (98)
One should likewise have the faces of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and śākinīs fashioned there, displaying various gestures and expressions.
O Great Goddess, on the new moon day, a man should cast [the offering] according to the sequence of worship, preceded by a low-lying path and guarded by many protectors. 100.
Then, at the time of dusk, one should go to where the Goddess is surrounded by people, with loud cries, shrieks, and the chanting of her lineage.

By means of the practice of the hero’s conduct (vīracaryā), one should wander through the city at night; this is called the "hero’s conduct lamp" (vīracaryādīpa), which accomplishes all aims. || 102 ||

One should keep the lamp burning constantly until the fifteenth lunar day (Pañcadaśī). On the fifteenth day, one should perform the great festival of Bhūtamātṛ; as long as that Lord of the House remains in the home, no obstacle shall arise.
Then, after some time had passed, fifty million Piśācas were born from drops of perspiration from the body of Bhūtamātā.
All those Piśācas had cruel faces, tongues like flames, and emaciated bellies; they used their hands as bowls and were fed offerings set apart for them.
Their veins were prominent, they were emaciated, bearded, and clothed in skins; they wore mortars as ornaments, and used winnowing baskets, umbrellas, seats, and garments [for their adornment]. (106)
At night, those Piśācas known as Aṅgārakas, who follow the path of the Mothers, indeed vomit forth burning coals, their hair ablaze.
With mouths gaped wide as far as their ears, long hanging eyebrows, and thick noses, those powerful piśācas indeed dwell in the lying-in chamber.
With hands and feet on their backs, moving with the speed of the wind, those Piśācas were despondent in battle, devouring flesh.
Having seen such piśācas, out of compassion for the miserable and out of pity for those of small minds, I said something to them.

He possesses the power of invisibility within the bodies of living beings, as well as the ability to assume any form at will; he moves during both twilights, and likewise knows their abodes and means of livelihood throughout their lives.
Those houses which are naked, empty, and devoid of inhabitants; those which are dilapidated, as well as those that have been set on fire. || 112 ||
The royal roads, side streets, crossroads, and triple junctions; as well as the gates, watchtowers, exits, and bridges. || 113 ||
O beloved, I gave the paths, rivers, holy fords, sacred trees, great highways, and the dwellings of the piśācas as places of residence.
For those unrighteous people, a livelihood was ordained of old; likewise for those who are devoid of the conduct of the castes and stages of life, as well as for artisans and craftsmen. (115)
They cause remorse among the virtuous and are thieves who betray trust; with these and many other such unjustly acquired riches— || 116 ||
The rites that are undertaken have the Piśācas as their presiding deities; on the day of Madhu-māsa, they are performed with curd, sesame flour, and spirituous liquors.
With cakes, turmeric-flavored rice, sesame seeds, sugarcane, jaggery, and boiled rice, as well as black garments and smoke-colored flowers. (118)
I have fashioned this auspicious goddess for all the bhūtas and piśācas; such is the Mother of Beings, surrounded by hosts of all bhūtas. (119)
The Goddess is established at Prabhāsa, to the north of the ocean; indeed, he who knows this origin of the Goddess, which destroys all evil, [attains his goal]. (120)
His lineage shall never be contemptible, nor shall he ever be overcome by the defects of ghosts, spirits, or demons. (121)
Completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all good fortune, he attains all his desires and becomes the delighter of women's hearts. || 122 ||

Those who honor the Mother of all beings, the Bestower of Fearlessness, with their own smiles, playful charms, and devoted service, become happy—endowed with brothers, servants, sons, and kinsmen, and free from all calamities. (123)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhūtamātṛkā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess Śālakaṭaṅkaṭā, who is situated to the south of Sāvitrī and to the east of Raivata.
She who pacifies great sins and destroys all suffering, worshipped by all the gandharvas, and terrifying with her quivering fangs. || 2 ||
She is the slayer of the exceedingly fierce Daityas, established by Paulastya, the slayer of Mahiṣa, possessing a great body, and stationed in the Prābhāsika field.
The man who worships her on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha shall become possessed of cattle, wise, prosperous, endowed with sons, and highly intelligent.
He who devoutly gratifies her with the gift of cattle, as well as with offerings, worship, and oblations, shall be freed from enemies.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śālakaṭaṅkaṭā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Vaivasvateśvara Liṅga, situated thirty bow-lengths to the south of the Goddess.
Established by Vaivasvata Manu, it grants all desires; near it stands a most wonderful natural pool created by the gods.

O lady of excellent hips, that man who, having bathed there, worships Him according to the prescribed rite with the fivefold offerings, bowing low in devotion and with senses subdued, and recites the hymn according to the Aghora ritual—he shall attain perfection.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vaivasvateśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, the wise one should go to the assembly of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇas) and to Baladevī, who is situated not far from that very place.
The man who worships her on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa with milk-rice, honey, or offerings of divine flowers; || 2 ||
O Great Goddess, his year shall pass happily, being well-honored. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mātṛgaṇabaladevī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Lord said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess Ekallavīrikā, who is situated not very far from me, the solitary hero (Ekallavīra). 1.
Formerly, that very Daśaratha, the ornament of the solar dynasty, having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, performed a most difficult penance.
Having installed a linga there, he propitiated Śaṅkara; he prayed to the God for a son of immeasurable splendor.
Then he gave him his son, a god worshipped in the three worlds, whose fame was celebrated throughout the three worlds under the name Rāma.
Even today, the inhabitants of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar—all the gods, Daityas, and Asuras, as well as great sages such as Vālmīki and others—sing of him here.

By the power of that Liṅga, great fame was attained by the king; whoever worships it according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of the month of Kārtika shall also become illustrious through the offering of lamps and gifts.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Daśaratheśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, from there one should go to that Liṅga, Bharateśvara, which is situated not very far away, located in the northern corner of that [site]. || 1 ||
There was a king named Bharata, a descendant of Agnīdhra, renowned upon the earth; after him, this region is celebrated in the worlds by the name Bhārata-varṣa. || 2 ||
And he performed severe penance in this sacred field, O beloved Pārvatī, for a thousand divine years after having installed Maheśvara.
Desiring a son, that best of men worshipped Śaṅkara; thereupon the Blessed Lord, being pleased, was eager to grant him a boon.
He gave him eight sons and one illustrious daughter; having obtained his desire, that lord of men felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Having divided Bhārata into nine parts, he bestowed them separately upon his sons; from that, the islands (dvīpas) came to be known by their respective names. || 6 ||
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and Aruṇa. || 7 ||
But this ninth island, O beloved, is known as Kumārī; likewise, eight other islands have been submerged by the ocean. (8)
Those situated in places such as villages and those dwelling in the midst of the ocean—of them all, only one now remains, known as Kumārī.
From Bindusaras up to the ocean, extending southward and northward, it is indeed one thousand yojanas in width.
Its length is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas; O Goddess, this is the expansion of that high-souled Bharata.
Bharata, who is honored by the world, performed fifty-six horse sacrifices along the Ganges and thirty on the banks of the Yamunā.
If, by the grace of the Lord, he rejoices in heaven like a god. || 13 ||
Whoever shall worship that installed Liṅga at Bhārata, he will certainly obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and gifts. || 14 ||
The man who beholds him on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation does not see even in a dream the terrible and most dreadful hell.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Bharateśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 172.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the four Lingas situated in a single place, located to the west of Savitri.
There are two pairs of lingas in the east and two facing each other in the west; the first among them is known as the linga named Kuśakeśvara.
The second is Gargeśvara, the third is Puṣkareśvara, and the fourth is declared to be named Maitreyeśvara. || 3 ||
He who, having conquered his senses, beholds these signs with devotion, shall be liberated from all sins and go to the great city of Śiva.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, especially in the month of Vaiśākha, one should diligently perform a ritual bath and feed Brāhmaṇas there.
To them one should give gold and garments according to one's ability; when this is done, O Goddess of the Gods, the pilgrimage becomes complete.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Four Liṅgas beginning with Kuśaka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Kuntīśvara, situated within a hollow in the ground to the east of Sāvitrī. || 1 ||
O beloved goddess, it was established by Kuntī at the sacred site of Prabhāsa; for when the Pāṇḍavas formerly arrived at the field of Prabhāsa, [they performed this rite]. || 2 ||
Accompanied by Kuntī on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), O Great Goddess, they recognized that field as unsurpassed at that time.

The Liṅga established by Kuntī removes the fear of all sins; that man who worships it especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, his soul satisfied with all desires, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O Goddess, whatever verbal, mental, or physical sin has been accumulated, all of that is destroyed by the sight of that Liṅga. || 5 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kuntīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 174 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the auspicious and meritorious Arkasthala, situated in the south-eastern corner from that [place], which destroys all sins.
O Goddess, having seen that, a human being is no longer born subject to grief; O Mistress of the Gods, for seven births, poverty shall never arise.
O beloved, upon seeing him, the ten types of leprosy are destroyed; it is as if the fruit obtained from giving a hundred cows at Kurukṣetra has been attained.
One obtains that same fruit by beholding the Sun at Arkasthala, or by bathing in the Trisaṃgama tīrtha for seven Sundays.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should cause a buffalo to be given there; for a thousand divine years, one is honored in the heavenly world. || 5 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Arkasthala," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Siddheśvara, situated not far from Arkasthala in the south-eastern direction.
Eighteen thousand rishis with vital energy drawn upward attained perfection at that linga; therefore, it is known as Siddheśvara.

Having bathed, fasting and with senses subdued, a man should worship with devotion; having duly honored the God, he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins. With all his desires fulfilled, he goes to the supreme abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess of gods, in the eastern quarter of that very place, Lakulīśa himself remains embodied, having performed severe penance in the past.

Established upon that ground in that place for the pacification of sins, the man who worships him on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation [attains great merit].
O Great Goddess, he is worshipped by all the gods and asuras alike. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Lakulīśa," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 177.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated to the south of that, named Bhārgaveśvara, which destroys all sins.
O Goddess, he who worships him with offerings of divine flowers shall have fulfilled his purpose and become prosperous in all his desires. || 2 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhārgaveśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the sin-destroying Liṅga situated three dhanus to the south-east of Siddheśa; it is named Māṇḍavyeśvara and is the destroyer of great sins. || 1 ||
That mortal who, transcending the senses, performs worship and likewise keeps a vigil on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, shall not return again to the state of mortality.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Māṇḍavyeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: One should behold the auspicious Puṣpadanteśvara situated in that very place; indeed, Puṣpadanteśvara is a Gaṇeśa of Śaṅkara.
He performed severe penance there, and a linga was installed by him.
Upon seeing it, a living being is liberated from the bonds of birth and saṃsāra; one shall obtain all desired objects both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Puṣpadanteśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Kṣetrapeshvara, located near Siddheshvara, not very far to the east.
Having seen that on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, he is not bitten by the nāgas.

One should worship him according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order; and one should feed Brāhmaṇas to the best of one's ability with various kinds of foods, both solid and soft.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kṣetrapāleśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 181 ||
Then one should behold the groups of Mothers, known by names such as Vasunandā and others, situated near Arkasthala, to the south and not very far away.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, he who is self-restrained and of purified soul should worship those Mothers according to the prescribed rite.
He attains prosperity that is difficult for those of undisciplined souls to reach; there he shall behold Śrīmukha, who dwells in that very place and is fond of openings.
On that very day, it should always be worshipped by men desiring spiritual perfection; this has been previously explained by me to you in detail, O beloved.
On that very day, he was worshiped in connection with his pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Śrīmukhavivara of the Vasunanda Group of Mothers," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 182 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Miśratīrtha, the most excellent solar tīrtha renowned as Trisaṅgama. || 1 ||
O beautiful lady, there is the confluence of the Sarasvatī, the Hiraṇyā, and the ocean, which is difficult to reach even for the gods.
Among all the sacred fords there, this is the preeminent and most excellent tīrtha; when the solar eclipse occurs, it surpasses even Kurukṣetra.
Bathing, giving gifts, and recitation performed there all become ten-million-fold more meritorious.
O Great Goddess, from Maṅkīśvara up to the Kṛtasmara Liṅga—within this interval, O Goddess, there are ten crores of holy tirthas.
Even worms, insects, moths, outcastes, or the lowest of men attain heaven; how much more so one whose soul is purified?
In that regard, those who desire the full fruit of the pilgrimage should bestow yellow garments, gold, and fragrant incense upon a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever bathes on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and offers libations to the ancestors, by him the ancestors are satisfied as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
O Goddess, this conjunction of the three destroys great sins; it is difficult to find in the three worlds, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
O beloved, the release of a bull should especially be performed there by the best of men for the destruction of all sins and for the gratification of the ancestors.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Trisaṅgama," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 183.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Maṅkīśvara, situated near the confluence of the three rivers, which destroys all sins.
Formerly there was a sage named Maṅki, the best among those who practice austerities; he, having recognized Prabhāsa as a great sacred field beloved by Śaṅkara, [went there]. || 2 ||
Subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, he performed severe penance for more than ten thousand years, having established Maheśvara [as his object of worship].
Then Mahādeva, being gratified and pleased, granted him a boon; he chose: "If you are pleased, remain established in this very place."
"Reside, O Liṅga marked with my name, for ten million times ten million kalpas. Having said, "So be it," he vanished right there.
From that time onwards, that Liṅga became known as Maṅkīśvara; [it should be visited] on the thirteenth or even the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha.

One should worship [the deity] with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) and shall obtain the desired fruit; those who desire the full fruit of the pilgrimage should indeed give the gift of a cow there.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Maṅkīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 184.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the imperishable Devamātṛ, who, assuming the form of Gaurī, resides in the south-western direction from Maṅkīśa. She is celebrated in the worlds by the name Devamātā Sarasvatī. (1)
And there the goddess Sarasvatī is seated upon a wooden footstool; in the form of Gaurī, she is there with her body resting upon a mare.
The gods protected her like a mother out of fear of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala); therefore, she was designated as "Devamātā" (Mother of the Gods) by the wise in this world.
Whatever man or virtuous, self-restrained woman worships her on the third day of the month of Māgha, shall attain all their desires.
Whoever feeds a married couple with milk-rice, sugar, and other delicacies, shall obtain the fruit of having fed a thousand Gaurīs.
A pair of golden sandals should be given there to a virtuous Brahmin.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Nāgasthāna, located to the west of Maṅkīśa, where the confluence of three rivers occurs.
It was a great opening into the netherworld (pātāla), which destroys the sins of all living beings.
O Goddess, in former times, having heard of Kṛṣṇa’s death by the *bhallūka* arrow at Bhalla-tīrtha, Balabhadra then proceeded to Prabhāsa.
Having realized that this field possesses great power and bestows the accomplishment of all goals, he brought about the destruction of the Yādavas and thereafter attained dispassion.
And having emerged from his body in the form of Śeṣanāgeśa, he then proceeded, going on and on, until he reached the supreme holy site of Traisaṅgama.
Then, seeing the opening that served as the gateway to Pātāla, he entered and quickly went to where Ananta himself was stationed.
O Goddess of the Gods, because he entered this place in the form of a Naga, from that time onwards it has been known as Nagasthana.
To the east of Nāgarāditya, where his body was cast away, that place is even today well known and is heard of as Śeṣasthāna.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, having bathed at that holy ford of the triple-confluence and having worshipped the abode of the Naga on the fifth lunar day while abstaining from food, one should proceed.
Having performed the śrāddha according to his ability and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brāhmaṇa, he is liberated from all sufferings and goes to the world of Rudra.

Whoever feeds a Brahmin there with milk-rice mixed with honey, accompanied by various kinds of foods and snacks, dedicated to Śeṣanāga, has effectively performed a feeding for ten million; of this there is no doubt. (11)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Naga-Sthāna," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 186 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the meritorious Prabhāsapañcaka, the primordial [site] established there which bestows the fruits of all desires. || 1 ||
To the western part of that very place is what is called Prabhāsa; and Vṛddhaprabhāsa is located to the south of that, not very far away.
O lady of beautiful countenance, Jala-prabhāsa is to the south of that, as is Kṛtasmaraprabhāsa, where the Bhairava cremation ground is located.
Thus, he who endowed with devotion beholds these five splendors goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death. || 4 ||
Having reached Prabhāsa, the foremost sacred site renowned throughout the three worlds, one does not return—even though it is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Even for the gods, it is difficult to attain; it destroys even the greatest sins. By performing the water-libation at Prabhāsa on the new moon day for a single night, one achieves this.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Śiva; the sin committed during seven lifetimes [is destroyed] at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Whatever sin a man commits over a thousand births is destroyed simply by bathing in the salt waters of the ocean.
On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, and especially on the fifteenth day, having fasted for a full day and night and having fed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, || 9 ||
Having given a cow and gold to them, saying, "May Śiva be pleased," and having done this, O Goddess, a man shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
The Goddess said: "Regarding this 'Pentad of Prabhāsa' which has been proclaimed by you—how did it originate here? This is a great curiosity of mine. (11)
"Only one Prabhāsa, situated at a sacred ford (tīrtha), has been heard of by us; yet, O Lord of Gods, five Prabhāsas have been proclaimed by you. (12)
You should explain all this doubt of mine to me exactly as it is.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a narrative that destroys sin; hearing which, a human being through devotion attains the supreme goal. (14)
In ancient times, the god Maheśvara, assuming a divine form, beautiful and clad only by the directions (naked), wandered at will over this earth.
And thus enjoying himself, filled with curiosity, he went to the great hermitage of the sages in the Dāruka forest for the sake of alms. (16)
Then, seeing his unsurpassed form as he was wandering about, those women became tormented by desire, their senses agitated. (17)
Then all of them, full of passion, always followed him; some embraced him, while others gazed at him with longing.
Likewise, others, having abandoned their own homes, entreat him.
Having thus seen their true nature, all those great sages were filled with intense anger and cursed that bull-bannered god.

"Since you have come to this hermitage of mine having assumed nakedness, deluding our women and showing no shame at all, therefore, O Bull-bannered One, let your linga fall off this very instant. (21)
Then, at that very moment, as that *liṅga* of Śaṅkara fell, the earth trembled when it struck the ground.
Then all the oceans were agitated and abandoned their boundaries; the mountain peaks crumbled, and all the inhabitants of heaven were terrified.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Mahoragas, and Kinnaras, went to the Grandfather and said, "O Lord, what is the cause of this?"
By him the oceans were agitated so that they flooded the earth; mountain peaks were shattered and the earth trembled. || 25 ||
And terrible omens for the destruction of the world were seen; having heard those words of theirs, the Grandfather [Brahmā] was in the world of Brahmā.
Having meditated for a very long time, he spoke these words: "O best of gods, the Śiva-liṅga has fallen upon the earth. (27)
By the curse of the high-souled Bhārgava sages, the foremost of ṛṣis, when he had fallen to the earth, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, [were shaken].
Since it has reached this state, let us go to that very place; O gods, together with Viṣṇu, let a course of action be devised accordingly. (29)
Then Brahmā and the other inhabitants of heaven went to the Ocean of Milk, where the four-armed Lord lies, absorbed in yogic sleep.
They related everything to him, and then, accompanied by him alone, they went to where the omnipresent Mahādeva was separated from his Liṅga.
Having prostrated themselves, all the inhabitants of heaven spoke with composed minds.
"O Lord, let this Liṅga which has fallen upon the earth be lifted up; for all these great oceans are submerging the earth. (33)
The Blessed One said: "O lords of the gods, this Liṅga of mine was indeed cast down by the sages; however, I am not able to cause any harm to those high-souled ones. (34)
For this is the curse of the lords of the Bhṛgu lineage; therefore, listen to my words: "O all you gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, you must worship [them]. (35)
Therefore, O best of beings, you shall all desire everything through this Liṅga; likewise, all the oceans and the mountains shall go to Prakṛti.
Having placed [the body] in this most meritorious field, all remained composed; then, having lifted it up, all the gods arrived at the sacred site of Prabhāsa.
There they all placed it and then performed worship; the Liṅga was worshipped by Brahmā and by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Then Śakra, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa, as well as the other gods, having worshipped the Liṅga with devotion, spoke as follows. (39)
"From this day forward, by worshipping the linga of Rudra with devotion, we and those who belong to the host of ancestors shall [attain our goal], of this there is no doubt. (40)
Those best of men who, endowed with devotion, shall worship him, will go to the abode of the gods in their own bodies.
In this very place is the first *liṅga*, because it was established by us; its name shall be Prabhāsa, and it will indeed be known as Prabhāsa.
Having spoken thus, all those best of gods departed for the third heaven; and seeing him [depart], many living beings on earth likewise set out for the third heaven.
Then, O beloved, Triviṣṭapa was filled with many living beings; seeing that heaven thus occupied, the thousand-eyed Indra became deeply distressed.
Having understood the power of the Liṅga, O lady of excellent countenance, he then came to the surface of the earth and covered it on all sides with a thunderbolt.
"From that time forward, O Goddess, human beings do not go to heaven. Thus has the great majesty of Prabhāsa been briefly described; it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of all desires. (46)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Five Prabhāsas," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to that place where the self-manifested [liṅga] named Rudreśvara is situated upon the surface of the earth. (1)
To the east of Ādiprabhāsa, situated at a distance of three bows, Rudra, having resorted to meditation, joined his own splendor there.
Then there is the one named Rudreśvara, which destroys all sins; by seeing and worshipping it, one shall attain all desires. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Rudreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: To the west of that very place, situated not far away, is Caṇḍikā Karmamoṭī, accompanied by ten million Yoginīs. O Great Goddess, this is the first of the three seats (pīṭhas), worshipped by the three worlds. || 1 ||
Having worshipped the seat of the Goddess and the Yoginī there on the ninth day, he shall attain all his desires and become beloved by the celestial nymphs of heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karmamoṭī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Hari, the bestower of liberation, situated not very far from Prabhāsa in the south-western direction. || 1 ||
O Goddess, he who has conquered his appetite on the eleventh day and worships [the deity] during the month of Māgha, especially, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 2 ||
Whoever performs fasting there, or undertakes vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others, shall obtain ten million times the desired fruit compared to other holy places.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mokṣasvāmī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 190.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Hara, known as Ajīgarteśvara, situated near Candravāpī and close to Karmamoṭī. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, he who bathes in that [tirtha] and worships that linga shall be liberated from terrible sins and go to the great abode of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ajīgarteśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Linga of great power installed by Vishvakarman, located to the north of Mokshasvamin. 1.
O Goddess, it is situated at five bow-lengths [from here], destroying all sins.
Upon seeing it, a person shall duly obtain the fruit of their journey; verbal and mental sins perish by the mere sight of it.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Viśvakarmeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 192 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Yameshvara, situated not far away in the south-western direction from that very place. || 1 ||
The sight of it pacifies sins and bestows the fruit of all desires. || 2 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Yameśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 193 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga installed by the gods, having recognized the power of this sacred field which destroys all sins.
Having performed severe penance there, the Liṅga was installed by the gods; upon seeing it, O Goddess, a human being becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
There, however, a gift of cows should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; thus, O Goddess, one properly obtains the powerful fruit of the pilgrimage. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Amareśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Then, with self-restraint, one should go to Vṛddhaprabhāsa, situated not very far to the south of Ādiprabhāsa.
The great four-faced Liṅga destroys sins by its mere sight.
The Śrī Devī said: O Lord, how did it come to have the name Vṛddhaprabhāsa? What would be the fruit when it is seen, as well as when it is praised and duly worshipped?
Tell this to me, O Lord, in brief and not in great detail.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, formerly, in the first Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, during the fourth Tretā Yuga, in the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa.
At that time, O Great Goddess, formerly in a previous Manvantara, during the fourth Tretā Yuga, the sages assembled there.
For the sake of seeing Prabhāsa, who was traveling toward the northern region; having seen that god covered by a thunderbolt, O Maheśvarī.
They fell into extreme despondency and then spoke these words: "Without having seen the Liṅga of Śaṅkara, we shall not go home."
"Seeking heaven, we have indeed traveled a great distance; therefore, let us remain right here until the sight of the Liṅga."
Having thus made their resolve, they remained engaged in asceticism; during the rainy season they stayed in the open air, and in the winter they took refuge in the water.

Practicing the austerity of the five fires during the summer, those disciplined celibate students remained so for many groups of years, O Brahmins, until they were eventually overcome by old age. (11)
O woman of excellent complexion, when they had thus reached old age, they were entreated with offers of boons by the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Except for the sight of the Liṅga, they chose no other boon.
But having understood the resolve of them all, the Bull-bannered Lord, becoming intent on compassion, revealed his own *liṅga* to them.
At that very moment, O woman of excellent complexion, that very same linga suddenly rose up, having pierced through the earth.
Having seen him, all those sages departed for the third heaven; then, once they had gone, Śakra became deeply distressed in mind.
He also covered him with a hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Because he went to see those sages while in his old age, it is therefore celebrated on the surface of the earth as Vṛddhaprabhāsa.
O lady of beautiful hips, when that is seen, even today a man endowed with devotion obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (19)
Thus, the light that has arisen there is known as Vṛddha; at that place, a bull should be given as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa by those desiring the full fruit of their pilgrimage.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vṛddhaprabhāsa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 195 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Prabhāsa situated in the water, located not very far to the south of Vṛddhaprabhāsa.
O Goddess, listen to the supreme majesty of that very Lord. || 2 ||
O beautiful lady, when the slaughter of the kṣatriyas was carried out by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, a supreme sense of remorse arose in his mind.
Then, O beloved, having undertaken fierce asceticism, he propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of the gods, for many groups of years.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, appeared before him in person and said: "O you of noble vows, I am here as a granter of boons to you; choose a boon."
Rāma said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then reveal your own linga which has been covered by the thunderbolt during the sacrifice."
Great compassion has arisen in me after killing these many Kṣatriyas; by the sight of your linga, may that compassion of mine be destroyed.
In that way, O Śaṅkara, may all my sin be purified through your grace.
Śaṅkara said: O Thousand-eyed One, my liṅga rose up again and again, yet he covered it with his thunderbolt, overcome by great fear.
I shall never appear before you in the form of a *liṅga*.
"As for what you say to me—that I am overcome by compassion yet enveloped by sin—I shall destroy that for you, O best of the twice-born, simply by my touch. (11)
O Mahāmati, in this meritorious reservoir of water, a great liṅga shall arise in the midst of the water; you should behold it.
"All your distress shall depart and you shall become free from sin"; having spoken thus, O lady of beautiful countenance, he rose up from the midst of the water.
Thereupon, O Goddess, its name became Jalaprabhāsa on the surface of the earth; by merely touching it, a person shall go to the world of Śiva.
Whoever feeds a single Brāhmaṇa of praised vows here, I, along with my wife, have been fed by him; of this there is no doubt. (15)
This origin of Jalaprabhāsa has been recounted by me; when heard, it pacifies sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. (16)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jalaprabhāsa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 196.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the auspicious Jamadagnīśvara, situated not far from the vicinity of Vṛddhaprabhāsa.
Established by Jamadagni, it pacifies all sins; upon seeing it, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from the three debts.
Having bathed in the Nidhāna-vāpī and performed worship there, one shall obtain wealth; for in that place, O beloved, the Nidhāna was obtained by the Pāṇḍavas in ancient times.
By that very treasure, that pond became renowned and worshipped by the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, by bathing in it, an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate; she obtains her desired wishes—thus has it been declared by me to you. (5)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jamadagnīśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eleven thousand verses. 197.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the most excellent Mahāprabhāsa, located to the south of Jalaprabhāsa, which destroys obstacles on the path of Yama.
Listen to its very greatness, and how it came to be upon the surface of the earth.
O Goddess, in the former Tretā Yuga, that was known as the Sparśaliṅga; it is divine, composed of splendor, and bestows liberation upon men through touch. || 3 ||
Then, at a certain time, O beloved, the earth was covered by Vajrin; having come to the earth, O beautiful one, Indra was overcome with fear.
O Goddess, the heat arising from that, emerging unobstructed, assumes the form of a *liṅga* with a crest of flames extending ten crores [of yojanas]. || 5 ||
O Goddess, having established yourself at Prabhāsa-kṣetra, you pierced [the earth] and remained manifest; and having pierced the earth with your thunderbolt, you obstructed it.
Accompanied by masses of smoke, it pervaded that world; thereafter, the entire three worlds were thrown into agitation by the flames.
Then all the hosts of gods and the sages who had mastered the Vedas praised the moon-crested Lord with various hymns declared in the Vedas.

"O best of gods, withdraw your energy which is of the nature of fire! O Lord of the gods, protect [the world] before all the three worlds, including everything moving and stationary, fall into total turmoil and reach dissolution."
Ishvara said: O Goddess of the gods, while the inhabitants of heaven were speaking thus, that splendor entered fivefold, pervading the entirety of the three worlds.
Having pierced the earth there in the form of five rays of light, a great radiance appeared along the path by which he had emerged.
There, O beloved, they established a stone door in a well-chosen spot; and once this opening was closed, the smoke came to an end.
The worlds became healthy once more, and that splendor remained established right there. Thus impelled by me, they installed the Liṅga there.
O Goddess of the gods, that great [being] then took rest there; therefore, it is celebrated as Mahāprabhāsa by the gods and dānavas. || 14 ||
He who worships that Liṅga with devotion using various kinds of flowers goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death. || 15 ||
O Goddess of gods, by seeing it, a man is liberated from sins; O beloved, he obtains his desired objects and whatever is wished for in his mind.
Gold should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa of celebrated vows, and a gift of a cow should likewise be offered according to the rules to that twice-born man.
Having done this, O Great Goddess, one obtains the fruit of birth; one shall attain the exalted fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 18 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Fifth Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity situated to the south of that [place], on the delightful bank of the Sarasvatī, where Smara was created.
O Great Goddess, it is self-manifested and the destroyer of all sins; I shall describe its origin and how it appeared upon the surface of the earth.
O fair-faced one, when Kāma was formerly consumed by me, Rati, having approached that place, lamented in great distress.

Seeing her thus afflicted by grief, I was moved with compassion and said to her, "Do not weep, O auspicious lady; by my grace, your husband shall rise again in due time, of this there is no doubt. (4)
The Goddess said: O Lord, for what reason was that Kāmadeva burnt by you in the past? How did he obtain rebirth? Tell me this in detail. (5)
Īśvara said: O beloved, in former times Dakṣa Prajāpati was your father; he begot a hundred daughters, all fair-complexioned and long-eyed.
He first gave you to me, she who is celebrated as Satī; and he gave ten others to Dharma: Śraddhā, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā.
Anasūyā, Śuci, Lajjā, Smṛti, Śakti, and likewise Śruti; and two wives for Kāmadeva, namely Rati and Prīti. (8)
He gave Svāhā to Agni and then Svadhā to the ancestors; twenty-seven were proclaimed for the Moon, beginning with Aśvinī.
O Goddess, these [wives] ending with Revatī are likewise known among people; however, O Goddess, he gave thirteen daughters to Kaśyapa.
Aditi and Diti, Vinatā and Kadrū as well, Siṃhikā and Suprabhā, and Ulūkī, O fair-faced one. (11)
Anuviddha, Sita, as well as Īrṣyā, Hiṃsā, and another, Māyā joined with Niṣkṛti—these were Dakṣa’s daughters in former times, O high-minded one.
Gaurī, Suprabhā, Vārttā, Sādhvī, and Sumālikā—these five he then gave to Varuṇa, O daughter of the mountain.
Bhadrā, Madirā, Vidyā, Dhanyā, and the auspicious Dhanā—these five he gave to Kubera as wives, O daughter of the mountain.
Jayā, Vijayā, Madhuspandā, Irāvatī, Supriyā, Janakā, Kāntā, Subhadrā, Dhārmikā, and Śubhā. (15)
Knowing the dharma, she gave those maidens as wives to the ten Rudras: Prabhāvatī, Subhadrā, Vimalā, Nirmalā, and Anṛtā. (16)
O beloved, Dakṣa gave twelve daughters to the Ādityas: Tīvrā, Dakṣā, Aruṇā, Vidyā, Dhārapālā, and Varcasā.
Saṃsarpā, Saramā, Guhā, Mālā, Campā, as well as Jyotsnā and Viśvā—these belong to him who is overcome by yogic sleep.
Two daughters, Suveṣā and Bhūṣaṇā, both auspiciously adorned, were likewise given to the Aśvins; one daughter was given to Vāyu—these are the ones proclaimed. (19)
He gave Sāvitrī to Brahmā and Lakṣmī to the high-souled Viṣṇu; then, after some time, he performed a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees.
On Mount Himavat, the great mountain where the Parvata river flows, his sacrificial enclosure was established, abounding in the fulfillment of all desires.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and all the Guardians of the World, arrived at that sacrifice. (22)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed Indra, Varuṇa, and Yama; Kubera, Kumāra, as well as the rivers and the oceans. || 23 ||
The ponds, wells, as well as lakes and pools, and also Suparṇa and those who are the Nāgas—all these were present there in embodied form. (24)
The Dānavas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas, along with their followers and wives, were all masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 25 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, the highly fortunate great sages as well as the divine sages dwell there together with their wives.
Śambhu, who wears a garland of skulls as an ornament and carries the ashes of cremation grounds, was not invited because of his impurity; such was the case with him. (27)
Having arrived from here and there at Kailāsa, the best of mountains, those sisters beginning with Aśvinī spoke these words to you: ||| 28 ||
But why do you remain here so contented, O auspicious one of beautiful waist? We have all set out for our father’s sacrifice, accompanied by our husbands. (29)
"O illustrious lady, we have all been summoned by him as daughters; Dakṣa did not summon you because he fears Śaṅkara. (30)
Having heard their words, Satī, filled with rage, said: "Alas! Shame on you, Dakṣa, of wicked conduct! What shall I say to Maheśvara?"
Having said, "How shall I show my face? he, by means of his own self through the power of asceticism and yoga, cast off [his former form] and remembered nothing else.
Then, seeing Satī remaining without her life-breaths because she had abandoned herself out of indignity, Mahādeva considered himself to be a wearer of skulls (kapālī).
And he dispatched his hosts for the destruction of the sacrifice; those fierce hosts went forth by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Seeing those deformed beings of hideous appearance, innumerable and possessed of great strength, who had been dispatched by Rudra and led by Vīrabhadra, [the gods were terrified]. (35)
Then all the hosts of gods—the Vasus together with the Bhāskaras, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas—possessed of great strength, stood with bows in their hands. (36)
And having set out for battle, discharging sharpened arrows, those Pramathas then encountered one another with the gods.
They released showers of arrows like clouds pouring down torrents of rain; then, by a multitude of their elephants, he was pierced in the heart with a spear.
But from that blow he fell down unconscious; then the elephant Airāvata was struck on the frontal globe with a fist.
Suddenly struck by him, that elephant, uttering terrifying cries, charged with great speed toward the sacrificial enclosure.
The Viśvedevas were rendered breathless by the fierce great arrows; then Vasumān, being more powerful, drew his bow with great force.
At that time on the field of battle, those Ādityas were rendered lusterless by him; in the meantime, the gods were turned away from the fight by him.
Then they sought refuge in Viṣṇu, who was stationed there; thereupon, Viṣṇu, overcome with anger, [addressed] the gods together with Indra.
Seeing that they were all put to flight, he quickly released the Sudarśana. That Sudarśana, the discus of Viṣṇu, rushed forward with great speed.
Suddenly opening her mouth, she indeed drew him into her belly; and when he had been swallowed by that infallible discus, O daughter of the mountain, [the world was filled with darkness].
The Lord Viṣṇu became enraged; with the Śārṅga bow in hand, he rushed forward. Having struck Nandin with ten sharp arrows and Bhṛṅgin with a hundred, [he continued].
Having pierced Mahākāla with a thousand arrows and the Lord of the Gaṇas with ten thousand, he struck Vīrabhadra with tens of thousands of shafts.
Having struck him with his mace until he was overwhelmed and drenched in blood, Viṣṇu, filled with extreme rage, seized him by the feet and dashed him against the ground.
Then, as he was being struck, the Sudarśana discus, though covered in gushing blood, did not deliver a blow to him upon the ground.
O Goddess, Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas, having obtained a boon from Rudra, did not meet his death even though he was struck with a mace.
Seeing him fallen, all those who had been oppressed by the splendor and power of Viṣṇu fled in every direction and went to where the god Maheśvara was.
They related to him everything that had occurred, including the defeat and the prowess of Vīrabhadra; thereupon, Maheśvara became enraged.

Suddenly seizing his trident, he set out with his own hosts toward the sacrificial enclosure of Dakṣa, which was the source of his defeat; there, Viṣṇu himself stood, displaying his prowess alongside Vīrabhadra.
Beholding Maheśvara approaching filled with wrath and considering him invincible in battle, he vanished right there.
Indra, along with the Maruts and the Vasus, as well as Śiva, whose soul was overcome with anger, together with the Kinnaras, then vanished from sight.
O beautiful lady, only the Brahmins remained there in the assembly; they saw Śaṅkara arrived with eyes bloodshot with anger.
Then, filled with fear, they performed oblations on all sides with Rudra-mantras; others, overcome by terror, fled in the ten directions.
Then Mahādeva, having arrived and seen those best of Brahmins, and not seeing the gods there, he destroyed the sacrifice.

Having assumed the form of a deer, he vanished out of fear of Śiva; however, the Blessed Lord Śiva followed behind him with bow in hand. Even today, O Maheśvarī, he is seen in the sky in the form of a star.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, when the sacrifice had been thus destroyed, those Brāhmaṇas who had gone there returned home with their desires unfulfilled, as did all others who were present.
Hara also, his anger having subsided, went to Mount Kailāsa.
At that very time, however, a Dānava named Tāraka was born, a mighty-armed one who destroyed the strength and pride of the gods.

Having conquered all the gods, beginning with Indra, in a great battle, O Goddess, heaven was occupied by them; then they went to the world of Brahmā. O Daughter of the Mountain, the gods, filled with grief, spoke to Brahmā.
O best of gods, we have been expelled from heaven by Tāraka; Indra himself has become [the king], and the Vasus have been treated likewise.
