"The Rudras, the Sādhyas, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Ādityas—O Grandfather, tell us the means for their destruction. (6)

Brahmā said: "It is my opinion that he is indeed invulnerable to all the gods; except for the splendor of Śaṅkara, he cannot be struck down by anyone else. Therefore, go to Maheśvara, the God of gods—may prosperity be yours."
His wife died previously and was born in the house of Himavat; in her a son shall be born who will slay Tāraka. Therefore, for that purpose, you must propitiate the wielder of the trident.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, Kāmadeva was commanded by the gods: "Go to Hara, whose wife has died, and afflict him with your arrows."
By which he, tormented by desire, would become intent on obtaining a wife.
"Let this brother of yours, the charming Vasantaka, go with you. || 10 ||
Having promised "So be it," he went to Mount Kailāsa; then Mahādeva beheld Kāmadeva with his weapon raised.
O Goddess, Rudra, the slayer of Andhaka, having reached Gaṅgādvāra together with Vasanta, beheld [him] right before him.
Having been given the weapon by Kāmadeva, he fled again out of fear; then he went to Vārāṇasī, as well as to Naimiṣa and Puṣkara.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Rudrakoṭi, Kurukṣetra, and likewise Gayā; Jvālāmārga, Prayāga, Viśālā, and the auspicious Arbuda.
O Goddess, wandering thus upon the surface of the earth for many groups of years out of fear of Kāmadeva, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [remained there]. || 15 ||
Then, O Goddess of the gods, the three-eyed God of gods, having dilated his eye, gazed upon Kāma with his third eye.
As he was gazing at him, flames of fire were produced; by those flames, he, together with his bow, was reduced to ashes.
Having burned him and reached the culmination of his wrath, the Blessed Lord Śambhu made his dwelling there in that auspicious Prābhāsika field.
When Kāma had been consumed by fire, Rati, devoted to her husband and overcome by grief, lamented, afflicted by intense sorrow. (19)
"Alas, O Lord, O Master! Why do you abandon your devoted wife? O Lord, why do you forsake me, whose life is her husband, though I am faithful to my spouse? (20)
As she was lamenting thus, an incorporeal voice spoke to her: "Do not weep, O large-eyed one; your husband shall indeed be yours once more."
"By the grace of Śiva, the God of gods, she shall indeed breathe again. Having heard these words, Rati then became composed.
Then the gods, having bowed to Śiva, made this request, O Sovereign Lady: "O Lord, for the sake of accomplishing our purpose, take a wife."
This Kāma has been burnt by you yourself with great wrath; O Lord, without him, creation on the surface of the earth would surely perish.

The Blessed One said: "O best of gods, this Kāma has been burnt by me with my wrath; therefore, he shall move among living beings as one without a body (anaṅga). His vigor and his power shall exist even without a physical form."
The gods said: "O Blessed One, first act so that you may remember the Lord of Rati, for the welfare of all the worlds, so that we may have confidence."
Then the Lord Maheśvara himself remembered Kāma; thereupon that eternal Liṅga rose up from the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, the bodiless god of love (Anaṅga) was powerful there because he had been restored; by him, the daughter of the mountain (Śailajā) was carried off by that high-souled Śaṅkara.
Skanda was born as the foremost of the gods, by whom Tāraka was destroyed; and because he performed his rites of remembrance (smaraṇa) with the fallen linga itself, he became known as Kṛtasmara.
Therefore, he is celebrated on the surface of the earth as Kṛtasmara; upon seeing him, no mortal ever becomes dull-witted, blind, unhappy, or unfortunate, nor does he become poor or diseased. (30)
Thus I have related to you everything that you asked me, concerning how Smara, though previously burnt, has remained endowed with vigor once again. (31)
Īśvara said: Right there, situated to the south of Kṛtasmara, is the pool known by the name Kāmakuṇḍa, where Smara was born once again.

By bathing here at Anaṅgarūpī, one indeed becomes endowed with beauty. There, sugarcane, gold, cows, and likewise garments should be given according to the rules to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.

Thus ends the two hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kāmakuṇḍa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 200 ||
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, in that place is the cremation ground of Kālabhairava, as far as the Brahmakuṇḍa, where the Lord remains mindful of his vow.
There, those living beings who have been burnt and died due to the reversal of time—all of them attain liberation, even if they were perpetrators of great sins.
O Great Goddess, from Kṛtasmara up to where Maṅkīśvara is situated, that is the great cremation ground, O Goddess, which bestows freedom from rebirth.
O beloved, that place where the equinox of living beings occurs is known as Ūṣara; that field is always most dear to me.
Even at the end of a kalpa, I do not leave my beloved Avimukta.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Kālabhairava Cremation Ground," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 201 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Rāmeśvara, located to the south of Maṅkīśa, to the southeast of Kṛtasmara, and to the east of Sarasvatī; it was established by Balabhadra.
O Goddess, it was there that Rāma, having indeed been liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, entered that Sarasvatī river which flows in a reverse direction.
The Goddess said: How was he liberated from his sin? How did that sin come to be in the past? How was that Liṅga installed? Tell me what its power is.

Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the story that destroys all sins; having heard which, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and obtains all desires that are ever dear to the mind.
Having first shown great affection to Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, the wielder of the plow, reflected in many ways: "What deed might constitute a virtuous act? (5)
Indeed, without Kṛṣṇa, I shall not go into the presence of Duryodhana; nor, having taken refuge with the Pāṇḍavas, how could I [approach] King Duryodhana? (6)
"I shall cause the death of that lord of men, who is both my son-in-law and my disciple; therefore, I will go neither to Pārtha nor to King Duryodhana. (7)
I shall immerse myself in sacred fords by my own self until the end of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas is brought about.
Having thus instructed Hṛṣīkeśa, as well as Pārtha and Duryodhana, Śauri departed for Dvārakā, surrounded by his own armies.
Having gone to Dvārāvatī, which was crowded with joyful and contented people, Rāma Halāyudha drank wine together with those who had entered his inner apartments.
Having drunk the yellow beverage and taking his mace in hand, he then went to the prosperous Raivata garden, accompanied by Revatī and the others.
Standing in the midst of a group of women, he proceeded with the staggering gait of one intoxicated; and the hero beheld a forest, beautiful and unsurpassed.
Everywhere it was rich with trees and flowers, crowded with troops of monkeys, endowed with groves of lotuses and ponds, and possessed great forests.
He heard auspicious sounds produced by birds, which were pleasing to the ear, exceedingly sweet, beautiful, and melodious with the intoxication of joy.
He beheld trees rich with jewels of fruit on all sides, radiant with flowers everywhere, and cheered by the songs of birds.

[He saw] mangoes, āgrātaka fruits, bhavya fruits, coconut palms, and satinduka trees; ābalvana trees, yellow pomegranates, and citron trees; jackfruit, lakucha, plantains, and beautiful tāpa trees; as well as pālevata, kusaṃkulla, nalinī, and vetasa reeds. || 17 ||
Bhallātaka, āmalakī, tinduka with its large fruits, iṅguda, karamarda, harītakī, and bibhītaka; || 18 ||
The joy of the Yadus beheld these and other trees, as well as Aśoka, Punnāga, Ketakī, and Bakula trees.
Campaka trees, saptaparṇas, karṇikāras, and sumālatīs; pārijātas, kovidāras, as well as mandāras and indīvaras.
[He saw] flowering *pāṭala* trees, *rambhā* plantains, as well as *devadāru* trees, *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *nicula*, and *vañjula* trees. || 21 ||
They were filled with cakoras, śatapatras, and bhṛṅgarājas, as well as with cuckoos, sparrows, hārītas, and jīvajīvakas.
It was also inhabited by dear young cātaka birds, parrots, and other winged creatures, who were perched there warbling very sweetly in a manner pleasing to the ear.
And there were lakes with lotuses and charming waters, filled with night-lilies, white lotuses, as well as yellow and blue water-lilies.
They were covered on all sides with white water-lilies and lotuses, as well as with kadamba trees, ruddy geese, and water-fowls.
They were crowded with kāraṇḍava ducks, water-fowls, swans, tortoises, and frogs, as well as with these and other aquatic creatures.
Moving along in due order and beholding the delightful sights, Rāma, followed by the women, went to an unsurpassed bower of creepers.
There he saw twice-born men who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—Kauśikas, Bhārgavas, Bhāradvājas, and Gautamas.
And [he saw] the best of the twice-born, born of various lineages, seated and longing to hear the narrative, those great-souled ones.
Upon seats covered with black antelope skins, as well as on grass mats and cushions, they saw him seated in their midst, narrating auspicious stories.

Having observed Rāma, whose eyes were reddened by the drinking of honey-wine, all the twice-born ones—the reciters of the Purāṇas and the foremost among the celestial sages—[recollected] the deeds and activities of the gods.
Thinking, "This one is intoxicated," they rose up with haste, honoring that wielder of the plow, with the sole exception of the one born of the Sūta lineage.
Then the mighty wielder of the plow, his eyes rolling and having agitated all the Dānavas, was overcome with anger and struck down the charioteer.
When that son had been struck down and the station of Brahman had been occupied, all those twice-born ones, clad in black antelope skins, departed from the forest.
Considering himself thus an Avadhūta, Halāyudha reflected: "A very great sin has been committed by me."
For this charioteer, who has been struck down, was indeed seated upon the seat of Brahmā; likewise, all these twice-born ones have departed after looking at me.
The odor of my body is as unpleasant as that of iron, and I perceive myself as a despicable slayer of a Brahmin. (37)
Fie on wealth, and likewise on liquor, which brings about greatness that results in infamy, for by being possessed by these, this very great sin was committed by me. (38)
"I shall perform for you the expiation as prescribed by Smṛti according to the rules; for Manu has indeed set forth the sequence of expiations and so forth. (39)

Recitation and remorse of mind are the purifiers for those who have committed secret sins; austerity and sacred knowledge are the purifiers of the elemental self (bhūtātman), and wisdom is the purifier of the intellect.
Purification from the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśvara) is considered supreme; the purification of the body, however, is achieved through various kinds of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). 41.
Therefore, from this day forward, I shall perform a twelve-year vow, proclaiming my own deed and undertaking the most excellent atonement.
This is the purification for killing a twice-born man unintentionally through ignorance; however, no atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
If a man should ever commit a great sin out of desire, no atonement for it is seen except by leaping from a precipice or entering the fire. (44)
The wise know that expiation is required when a sin is committed unintentionally; however, some say it is also required for what is done intentionally, based on the evidence of the Vedas.

Therefore, for the first [offense], the prescribed rite is performed; for the second, one should perform it twofold; for the third, it is declared to be threefold; but for the fourth, there is no atonement.
One who provides medicine, oil, or food to cows, Brahmins, and others, is not tainted by sin even if misfortune should occur while it is being given.
If any twice-born man should abandon his life for no reason whatsoever, the fault lies with him alone in that matter, and not with the one who gives it to him.
When a Brahmin, though adorned with virtues, kills himself and dies suddenly out of anger for the sake of a house, a field, or similar reasons, he is devoid of merit. (49)
One should observe a vow for three years, or else go to the Pratiloma Sarasvatī for the sake of purification from that sin; this is certain.

If one becomes angry with someone for a specific reason and kills them, but later, being satisfied, causes [the victim] to be restored to life, there is no fault once that person has died, provided the proclamation of both [the offense and the restoration] has been made.
But having killed a eunuch who is a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. Among many people engaged in a single task, all of whom are bearing weapons— || 52 ||
If one person causes another to be killed, all of them are considered killers. If the perpetrator dies while the penance has been undertaken, [the responsibility remains]. (53)
"He shall incur this sin both in this world and in the next; what can I do about him? Where shall I go from this evil-minded one? (54)
"Fie on me, a man of evil conduct who has committed a great misdeed! (55)
Īśvara said: While he was thus lamenting with a mind overwhelmed by grief, an incorporeal voice arose from the sky and spoke.
"O Rama, you must not feel any distress whatsoever. Go to the sacred field of Prabhāsa, where the goddess Sarasvatī resides. (57)
There stands the Sarasvatī, the most excellent of rivers, which has become one with Brahman; she possesses five streams and destroys the five great sins.
O best of men, all the sacred fords within the universe of moving and unmoving beings, such as the Gaṅgā and others, are on one side; among them, the Sarasvatī is the most meritorious. (59)
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin roar only so long as the goddess Sarasvatī, who resides at Prabhāsa, is not seen. 60.
Therefore, go to that very place where the goddess Sarasvatī resides; you cannot be rendered free from stain by thousands of other sacred fords.
Therefore, do not delay; go to the shore of the great ocean and plunge into the Pratilomā at the Prābhāsika shrine to bathe before the Great Goddess.
Worship the omnipresent Lord, the Master, in the form of a linga right there; having installed him, you shall be liberated from the great sin of the body.
Having heard these words, the high-minded Rāma was filled with supreme bliss and set his mind upon going to the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then, accompanied by his own army and provided with all necessary materials and equipment, he arrived at the great sacred site renowned as Prabhāsa.
Having seen the beautiful sacred site at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, he formed a resolve in his heart to bathe there against the flow of the current.
Having summoned the brahmins residing there in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa, the Lord performed the pilgrimage there according to the proper ritual procedure for a pilgrimage.
In the Prābhāsika field, there are various sacred fords extending for twelve yojanas; he performed pilgrimages to them all.
And to each of them he gave various gifts, and likewise he established [the image] below at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean.
Having fashioned a great liṅga in the eastern part and performed the rites of the sacrificial ritual, O Great Goddess, he became liberated from his sins once this was done.

Then, O Goddess, having remained for ten days with his limbs purified, he bathed in that very river and proceeded in reverse order toward Plakṣāvaharaṇa, from the ocean up to the region called Himavat.
Thus, O beloved, Rāma became renowned as one liberated from the flood of his sins, through the majesty of that Liṅga and by the grace of Sarasvatī.
O Goddess, he who worships that Liṅga which removes the fear of sin, and which is called Rāmeśvara, shall also be liberated from his transgressions. (73)
O Goddess, he who especially performs [the rite] on the eighth day according to the Brahmakūrca procedure shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, one should then worship Śaṅkara by the name Rāmeśvara; furthermore, the gift of a cow should be given there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage.
Thus, O Goddess, has the great glory of Rāmeśvara been described; hearing which, a person endowed with perfect faith shall attain heaven.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the great sanctuary of Maṅkīśvara, located to the north of Rāmeśa and in the vicinity of Devamātṛ.
To the south of Arkasthala and to the east of Kṛtasmara, there is a Liṅga of great power that was established in ancient times by Maṅki.
Having seen it, a person shall duly obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
The Goddess said: Who was this Maṅki, O Mahādeva, and how was the Liṅga established? What is the power of that Liṅga? Tell me this in detail. || 4 ||
Īśvara said: Formerly, there was an excellent twice-born man named Maṅki who had a hunchbacked body; having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he performed most intense penance.
Having installed Mahādeva, he remained devoted to the worship of Śiva; yet Hara was not satisfied with him, even though he had been honored for many groups of years.
As he was thus performing austerities, many indeed attained perfection; having propitiated Mahādeva there, they departed from this world for the heavenly realm.
Then, O fair-faced one, great sorrow arose there for Maṅki: "Why does the Blessed One, Maheśvara, find no pleasure in me? (8)
Then, having performed intense renunciation, he practiced fervent devotion; thus, devoted to recitation and meditation, he attained old age.
At the end of his life, Mahādeva was pleased with him and granted him a boon: "I am well-pleased with you, Maṅka; tell me, what shall I do for you? (10)
Maṅki said: O best of gods, what use have I, an old man, for a boon at this time? O Lord, I have a certain great sorrow while staying here. (11)
Śiva said: Listen to the reason why those brahmins worship them so excessively for the sake of fulfilling the vow of those ascetics.
Having gathered flowers of every variety from all sides—those of trees possessing exceeding fragrance—that was not the cause of their joy. (13)
Furthermore, you, though devoted to sacrifices and worship, remain hunchbacked and, despite your great effort, cannot reach the tips of the branches of the trees. (14)
O best of the twice-born, even by offering a single flower with devotion upon the head of the Liṅga, the fruit of a sacrifice is obtained.
To the right of the Liṅga, Brahmā himself is established; to the left is the Lord Viṣṇu, and I am indeed stationed in the middle.
All three are worshipped by him by whom the Liṅga is fully worshipped.
The bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the karavīra, the mālatī, the unmattaka, and the campaka shall instantly become pleasing. || 18 ||

O tiger among the twice-born, my worship is most favored with campaka, aśoka, kahlāra, and karavīra flowers, as well as any others that possess great fragrance; indeed, when worshipped with these constantly, I quickly attain satisfaction.

The Brāhmaṇa said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then let it be so: whatever man comes here, bathes, and sprinkles even just water [upon this place]," || 20 ||

"Indeed, by this liṅga one shall obtain the fruit of all forms of worship. From this day forward, O Śaṃkara, by your grace, may there be the presence here of all trees, whether divine or earthly. (21)
The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, whoever shall perform worship even with water in this liṅga, for him the entire fruit of worship shall accrue."
The presence of all trees shall be here; from this day forward, it shall be known by this name as Nāgasthāna.
Since the presence of all the nāgas is established here, you too, O tiger among the twice-born, shall come into my presence.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there; Maṅki, however, having cast off his body, then went to the world of Śiva.
Thus, O Goddess, has this supreme account of the origin of Maṅkīśa been told; when heard by those endowed with perfect faith, it destroys all sins. (26)

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Maṅkīśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 203.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, please describe to me in detail the majesty of Sarasvatī.
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, what merit is there for self-controlled men who have come on a pilgrimage when they bathe and give gifts at the gateway of the mouth?
What fruit is produced by immersion elsewhere? What is the procedure for a śrāddha, what are the mantras therein, and who are the twice-born priests? (3)
What should be accepted and what should be consumed by Brahmins during the Śrāddha rite? What gifts should be given by men who desire the fruit of their journey? (4)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the sequence of the rules for giving gifts and performing śrāddha; understand from me as I recite the majesty of Sarasvatī. (5)
The meritorious waters of the Sarasvatī, which are difficult even for the gods to obtain, are found wherever they are immersed when mixed with the waters of the ocean.

The Sarasvatī is the most meritorious among all rivers; the Sarasvatī is easy to enter for the happiness of the world. Having reached the Sarasvatī, men are never distressed; they neither grieve here nor in the hereafter.
A man who performs meritorious deeds attains the holy Sarasvata-tirtha, which is difficult to find in the three worlds on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, during the lunar festival.
O Goddess, if the new moon (amā) is found conjoined with the moon (soma) at that very time, what need is there for hundreds of millions of other festival days? (9)
Cāndrāyaṇa penances, Kṛcchra penances, Mahāsāntapana, and Sāntapana penances are prescribed as expiations where the Sarasvatī does not exist. (10)

As long as the bones of one's body remain in the waters of the Sarasvatī, for that many thousands of years shall that person dwell in the world of Viṣṇu; those who do not visit her are to be known as equal to those born blind, the dead, and the lame.
Those places where people do not behold Sarasvatī, though she is present in her radiant form, are merely regions; they are mere holy sites; they are mere hermitages; and they are mere mountains. (12)

Those for whom the goddess Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, flows through the middle, and those who have taken refuge in the holy Sarasvatī, the purifier of the three worlds—they no longer smell the fragrance of the mire of saṃsāra.
Like the science of grammar, she is extensive; like the intellect of the world, she is beloved; and like the mind of the virtuous, Sarasvatī is clear and charming. (14)
That man is base who does not pay homage to this Goddess Sarasvatī, who adorns the three worlds and possesses divine, perfectly pure waters.
The great river Sarasvatī, which has arisen as a ladder to heaven at Prabhāsa, cannot be reached by men who lack merit. 16.
The Candrabhāgā, the Gaṅgā, and likewise the Sarasvatī—those who drink from these three rivers are not humans; they are gods. || 17 ||
"O Goddess, it is indeed true that I have borne the Jāhnavī upon my head; yet among all the rivers in the world, the Sarasvatī is the most meritorious. (18)
In the presence of Sarasvatī, the Rājasūya sacrifice does not shine; indeed, a mere mouthful of her water is superior to the Aśvamedha, for her water is the best of all sacrifices.
Ashes, bones, skin, water, nails, hair, and so forth—even these were shaken away by the winds in the waters of the Sarasvatī.

Those men whom time carries away are not subject to the power of time. O Goddess, what is the use of speaking much or describing it again and again? There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford (tīrtha) superior to Sarasvatī.
In that very place where there is a confluence with the ocean, bathing is difficult to obtain; by bathing and giving gifts there, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Where the waters of the Sarasvatī are agitated by waves like those of the ocean, there mortals who are fortunate will bathe in every age.
Blessed are they, worthy of salutation, and their fame is most expansive—those men whose bodies have been sprinkled with the waters of the Sarasvatī.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence, O Lord of the worlds, please explain in detail the meritorious ritual for the Śrāddha.
At what part of the day, however, should the performer of the Śrāddha perform the Śrāddha at this Sarasvatī-tīrtha in the excellent Prabhāsa-kṣetra? (2)
At which sacred ford (tīrtha) does a performed śrāddha yield great fruit of merit? O Mahādeva, you should explain all of this to me exactly as it is.
Īśvara said: The morning consists of three muhūrtas; saṅgava is likewise of the same duration. Midday consists of three muhūrtas, and aparāhṇa follows after that.
The evening consists of three muhūrtas; one should not perform a śrāddha at that time. That period is named Rākṣasī and is censured for all ritual acts.
The muhūrtas of the day are always known to be fifteen; among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called Kutapa.
Since the sun always becomes dim at midday, therefore its commencement shall yield infinite fruit.
Midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as others such as a black blanket, silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth.
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because they cause torment to such [a person], these eight are thus considered to be renowned as "kutapas."
From one muhūrta after Kutapa until four muhūrtas [after], and for five muhūrtas [in total], this period is desired as the abode of Svadhā.
"Kuśa grasses and black sesame seeds have emerged from the body of Viṣṇu; for the sake of protecting the Śrāddha, so say the dwellers of heaven. (11)

Those residing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) who remain in the water should offer a handful of sesame seeds and water; the performance of a śrāddha is desired by one who holds darbha grass in his hand alone.

In a Śrāddha ceremony, three things are purifying: a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds; and in this regard, three qualities are praised: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
The rhinoceros is called *dauhitra*; that horn which is on its forehead, and the vessel made from that horn, is remembered as *dauhitra*. (14)
Or even if it is a brindled cow that yields milk, the ghee produced from its milk is declared to be "daughter's son's" (dauhitra) for use in rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
The tip of a darbha blade is said to belong to the gods, while that which possesses both root and tip belongs to the ancestors; those kuśa blades that hang down there are remembered as kutapas.
Purification regarding the body, substances, wife, land, mind, mantras, and the twice-born—these seven should be understood as essential, especially at the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
The purification of substances is sevenfold: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.

Wealth acquired through learning, valor, austerity, a maiden, disciples, and so forth, as well as that inherited from one's lineage—these seven kinds of wealth are "white" (pure), and the means by which they are obtained are likewise pure. (19)

Agriculture and trade are considered contemptible; white [merit] is obtained through the practice of crafts. And that which is acquired from one who has rendered assistance is declared to be *śambala*. (20)
That which is obtained through bribery, that which is obtained through violence, and that which is acquired by deceit—this is declared to be "black" wealth. (21)
The śrāddha that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means—by that, those born in wombs such as the Caṇḍālas and Puṣkasas are satisfied.
Whatever scattering of food is performed by humans upon the earth, by that those who have fallen into the state of Piśācas attain satisfaction. (23)
O son, whatever water falls upon the ground from the bathing cloth produces satisfaction for those who have attained the state of trees.
Those drops of scented water which fall upon the surface of the earth provide nourishment for those who have attained the state of gods.
Even when the rice-balls have been offered, those grains of food that remain on the ground provide nourishment for those who have fallen into the state of animals within the family.

And those children in the family who were not cremated, as well as the women who had not yet been consecrated with the funeral rites—they too perished, longing for the scattering and sweeping away [of the ashes]. (27)
Whatever food he eats while wandering, and whatever water he consumes during the day, they attain satisfaction through that very food of the Brahmins. || 28 ||
Those who have attained the state of Piśācas or even the state of worms and insects—now I shall declare the durations; listen to them as they are told by me. (29)

The śrāddha ceremony should be performed on the new moon day, month after month at the waning of the moon; likewise during the aṣṭakās, upon the arrival of a distinguished brahmin, and similarly during solar and lunar eclipses.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the twin months, and the ordinary transits of the sun; on the new moon day and the Aṣṭakās, especially during the dark fortnight.
Under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; when there is an assembly of materials and Brahmins; during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti; and on such days.
On the third day of Vaiśākha, on the ninth of Kārttika, on the fifteenth of Māgha, and on the thirteenth of Nabhasya.
These are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas; what is given on these occasions produces inexhaustible merit.
That seventh day of the month of Māgha, on which the Sun-god, mounted upon his chariot, begins a Manvantara, is known as Rathasaptamī.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, on the fifth of Phālguna, on the fifth of the month of Caitra, and likewise on its final day.

The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the seventh of Kārttika, the full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha—these are remembered as the Manvantara days, which render whatever is given inexhaustible. (37)
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha; the full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha. || 38 ||
Manu and others have recorded these [days] as making what is given inexhaustible; I remember these seven, including the ninth day of Mārgaśīrṣa. (39)
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, at the beginning of each Manvantara, there are twelve [deities] such as Kalpa and Māda who cause what has been given to be inexhaustible. (40)

The daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), ancestral rite for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha) with the offering of pindas (sapiṇḍaka), the rite on the new moon (pārvaṇa), the rite of supreme knowledge (ativijñāna), and the rite at the cow-pen (goṣṭha)—this is the most excellent for the sake of purification. || 41 ||

The ninth is declared to be the limb of ritual action (karmāṅga), and the tenth is remembered as the divine (daivaka). The eleventh is the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), while the twelfth is remembered for the purpose of nourishment (puṣṭi).
Of all the śrāddhas, that performed annually is remembered as the most excellent; that which is performed day after day is proclaimed as the obligatory (nitya) śrāddha.

If one is unable [to perform the full rite], however, the Vaiśvadeva may be omitted and performed with water alone; that Śrāddha which is offered for a single ancestor is called Naimittika (occasional). || 44 ||

That which is performed for the sake of desire is called *kāmya*, intended for the accomplishment of a desired object; that *śrāddha* which is performed on an occasion of prosperity is called *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. (45)
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," this Śrāddha is the Sapindana; whereas the Śrāddha performed on the new moon day is declared to be the Pārvaṇa. || 46 ||
The Śrāddha that is performed in a social assembly is called the Goṣṭhī-Śrāddha; that which is performed for the sake of purifying sin is called the Śuddhi-Śrāddha. || 47 ||

At the time of the impregnation rite, at the Soma sacrifice, likewise at the parting-of-the-hair ceremony, and also at the rite for securing a male child, the Śrāddha is indeed an integral part of the ritual act.
That which is performed for the sake of a deity is called *daivaka*. One who is traveling to another country should perform the *śrāddha* with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).

This should be known as being for the sake of nourishment; the twelfth [day] is remembered as the anniversary of the death (kṣayāha). He who does not perform the śrāddha with reverence on the day of his father's death— || 50 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, O Great Goddess, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother, neither I nor Hari accept his worship at the end of the year.
If a man does not know the day of death, or perhaps at any time, he should perform the Śrāddha on the new moon day in the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa.
Now I shall describe those brahmins who are worthy for the śrāddha; specifically, one who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), a yogi, and endowed with Vedic knowledge.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa, one who knows the Trimadhu, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, a daughter’s son, a son-in-law, a sister’s son, and likewise a father-in-law; || 54 ||

My maternal uncle was devoted to the practice of the five fires and dedicated to asceticism; he was likewise devoted to his father and mother, as well as to his disciples, kinsmen, and relatives. || 55 ||

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas and is a teacher, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts, a relative, a virtuous man, a daughter's son, and the husband of a daughter—[these are those from whom one may accept gifts]. || 56 ||
O fair-faced one, a man should especially not neglect his sister's son, nor even his circle of kinsmen, even if they are fools. (57)
One should not examine Brahmins when a rite for the gods has arrived; when a rite for the ancestors has arrived, one should examine them with great care.
Manu has declared that those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who follow the way of nihilism—such Brahmins are unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

One should not honor at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for a matted-hair ascetic who does not study the Vedas, nor for one who is weak, nor for a gambler, nor for those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers, and those who live by trade in liquor—these should be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors.

A servant, a village-dweller, one who belongs to the king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; || 62 ||

One afflicted by consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has been expelled from the community, a betrayer of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother married first, and one who belongs to a social group (gaṇa)—these indeed [are excluded]. || 63 ||
One who is of bad character, one who is one-eyed, the husband of a Śūdra woman, the son of a remarried woman, the son of an unmarried girl, a gambler, and likewise a drinker of intoxicants—(64)

One afflicted by a chronic disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, a seller of liquids, a maker of bows and arrows, and he who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried; || 65 ||
Mitradhruḍ, Dūtavṛtti, and likewise Putrācārya; Bhramarī, Maṇḍapālī, Citrāṅga, and Piśuna as well. || 66 ||
One who is insane, blind, or deaf; one who reviles the Vedas; one who trains horses, cattle, or camels; and one who lives by means of the lunar asterisms (astrology). || 67 ||
He who is a breeder of birds, likewise one who is a teacher of combat, he who diverts the course of a stream, and he who is devoted to the maintenance of prostitutes; || 68 ||
A messenger who enters houses, one who plants crops, a hunter, one who lives by falcons, and one who defiles virgins; || 69 ||

One who is violent, the son of a *vṛṣala*, a priest for communal sacrifices (*gaṇa-yājaka*), one devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, and likewise one who performs sacrifices constantly [for hire]. (70)

Those who live by agriculture, those suffering from elephantiasis, and those censured by the virtuous; likewise, a butcher of sheep, a keeper of buffaloes, a husband of a woman previously married to another, and those who carry out the dead—these must be avoided with great effort. (71)

Indeed, when other twice-born men are available, one should avoid these lowest of the twice-born—who are of censurable conduct and unworthy of the company—at both [the rites] of offering and reception.
One who is blind from birth, one-eyed, deformed, afflicted with leprosy, the husband of a low-caste woman, or suffering from a sinful disease destroys the fruit of a gift given by a thousand donors.
For as many limbs with which a Śūdra-officiating priest touches the Brāhmaṇas, for that many [limbs] the merit of the donor’s ancestors shall not exist after death. 74.
Having seen first a follower of Mahiṣa, then in the middle a husband of a low-caste woman, and finally a usurer, the ancestors departed in despair. (75)
A wife is called a *mahiṣī*; she who commits adultery while her husband is deceased is known as an *abhicāriṇī*. He who spends the night with such a woman is indeed remembered as a *māhiṣika*. (76)
A Śūdra woman is called a *vṛṣalī*; he who becomes her husband falls from his status due to contact with the saliva from her lips; such a man is a *vṛṣalīpati*. (77)
She who, having abandoned her own husband, takes pleasure with another, is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; a Śūdra woman does not become a *vṛṣalī* [merely by that]. (78)
The Caṇḍālī, the Bandhakī, the prostitute, the girl who has reached puberty, the virgin, the crooked woman, and she of one's own lineage—these seven are proclaimed to be Vṛṣalīs. (79)
But that maiden who sees her menses while still uninitiated in her father's house—her ancestors fall from their station, and she herself becomes a *vṛṣalī*. (80)
But that Brāhmaṇa who, with full knowledge, should choose such a girl [as a wife], one should know him to be the husband of a vṛṣalī, unworthy of the śrāddha and excluded from the company at meals.
A Gaurī maiden is indeed considered the best; a Kanyakā is regarded as middling; a Rohiṇī should be known as equal to her; and a Rajasvalā is the lowest. || 82 ||

A girl before the onset of menstruation is called *gaurī*; once menstruation has begun, she is *rohiṇī*. A girl who has not yet developed secondary sexual characteristics is a *kanyā*, while one who lacks breasts is a *nagnikā*.
A girl of seven years is Gaurī; one of nine years is Nagnikā; one of ten years is a Kanyā; and from that age onwards, she is Rajasvalā (menstruating). 84.
Indeed, by [excessive] condiments she destroys her sons; by [excessive] milk she destroys the family; and likewise, by her menses she destroys the father's desired state and his worlds.
He who marries a woman who has reached her menses should be known as the husband of a vṛṣalī. || 86 ||
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a Vṛṣalī for a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [mantras] for three years.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Examining Brāhmaṇas Unworthy of Śrāddha," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 205.
Īśvara said: Now I shall describe the procedure for the Śrāddha according to the rules of the Pārvaṇa rite; listen with a one-pointed mind in due order, O Great Goddess, my beloved. 1.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder on the previous day, one should first invite the ancestors, saying: "May you kindly perform our ancestral rites for us."
He should dispatch trustworthy men of the same caste to invite the twice-born.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten by those invited by Kṣatriyas and others; likewise, the food of a Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten by those invited by another Brāhmaṇa.

If a Śūdra should give food to Brāhmaṇas, or a Brāhmaṇa should give food to a Śūdra, both of these are persons whose food is unfit to be eaten; having eaten [such food], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man cooks Śūdra food under the pretext of a deposit, that food becomes unfit for consumption and that Brāhmaṇa falls downward.

The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting on the same seat as a Śūdra, and even the acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra—these cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual merit.
Brahmins who have been defiled by the food of a Śūdra, though agitated and longing for pleasure, what can they do when enraged? They are like venomless serpents.

One wearing soiled garments is naked; one wearing only a loincloth is naked; one with two folds [of cloth] but no upper garment is naked; and one who is without any folds or clothing at all is indeed naked. (9)

One should be naked or wear saffron-colored robes; being naked is also considered equivalent to wearing a half-cloth (*ardhapaṭa*). Furthermore, that garment which has its fringes uncut and has been washed with clay [is prescribed].
It is established that [a garment] which is unwashed or dyed with mineral pigment (dhātu-rakta) is pure; yet the fool dwells at his front, while the virtuous man remains far from him. (11)

Gifts should be given to one endowed with virtues; there is no exception for a fool. But that fool who, bypassing a nearby Brāhmaṇa—provided he is not an outcast—honors one who is far away though rich in virtues, shall go to hell.
When a Śrotriya who has completed his Vedic studies and vows arrives at one's house, all the medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking: "We shall go to the supreme goal. (13)

A person who maintains silence during the recitation of prayers at both twilights, while eating, brushing the teeth, performing rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) or the gods (daiva), as well as after voiding urine or excrement, and especially when in the presence of gurus, while giving gifts, or during yoga, attains heaven. || 15 ||
If, in any way, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech during recitations and the like, one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
In giving gifts, bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, eating, and the worship of deities, straight darbha grass is for the gods, while for the ancestors it is likewise doubled.
Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors, there is no defect in the row even if one uses fire, ashes, barley, or water, or even by passing through a doorway. || 18 ||

In the *iṣṭa-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa are remembered; in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, Satya and Vasu are traditionally cited; in the *naimittika-śrāddha*, Kāla and Kāma; and in the *kāmya-śrāddha*, Adhvan and Virocana.
Purūravas and Ārdrava are proclaimed for the Pārvaṇa rite; from the Nyagrodha tree one obtains nourishment, progeny, intellect, wisdom, fortitude, and memory.
The vessel made of Kashmiri wood is said to be a destroyer of demons and a bringer of fame; that made of Madhūka wood is declared to be the highest source of good fortune in the world. (21)
One who performs [this rite] in the Phālguna vessel shall attain all desires, as well as supreme splendor through the Sun and especially renown.
In a *bilva* tree, one obtains prosperity, austerity, intelligence, and constant longevity; likewise, in fields, gardens, ponds, and indeed in all worthy recipients.
While it rains incessantly, for one who uses bamboo vessels [for alms], the merit obtained from these is equal to that gained through gold and silver.
The palāśa, the fruits of the nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, and vikaṅkata; likewise the udumbara, the bilva, sandalwood, and those trees which are fit for sacrifice. || 25 ||
Sarala, devadāru, śāla, and khadira—these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel (samidh). || 26 ||
The śleṣmātaka, naktamālya, kapittha, śālmalī, as well as the nimba and bibhītaka trees, are condemned for use in śrāddha rites. (27)
One should condemn that ground for the performance of a śrāddha ceremony which has unpleasant sounds, is crowded, harsh, infested with living creatures, or possesses a foul odor. || 28 ||
One should abandon the region of Traiśaṅkava for twelve yojanas on all sides, specifically to the north of the great river and to the south of the Kevala.

The country named Traiśaṅkava is excluded from the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha). The Kāraskāras, the Kaliṅgas, and those regions north of the Sindhu, as well as countries where the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) have perished, should be avoided with great effort.
The Kṛta age is said to be the Brāhmaṇa; the Tretā is remembered as the Kṣatriya; they say the Dvāpara is the Vaiśya; and the Kali Yuga is remembered as the Śūdra. (31)
In the Kṛta age the ancestors are to be worshipped, and likewise the gods in the Tretā; the sages always in the Dvāpara, and the heretics in the Kali age.
A wise person should perform the śrāddha in the forenoon during the bright fortnight, but in the dark fortnight, he should perform it in the afternoon, without transgressing the hour of Rauhina.

The Pitṛ-tīrtha (ancestral bathing place) is consecrated at a measurement of one cubit; likewise, the finest Kuśa grasses, cut near their roots, are for the purpose of the sacrificial seat (prastara). Similarly, Śyāmāka, Nīvāra, and Dūrvā grasses are prescribed. Prajāpati, who possesses abundant hair, is the best among those who possess their own fame.
His hair fell upon the ground and turned into kāśa grass; therefore, kāśa grass is always pure and honored in the performance of śrāddha rites.
One who desires prosperity should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) upon them; he should devoutly place warm food before the twice-born.

Except for fruits, flowers, and drinks, a wise man should not place salt or condiments directly into his hand out of affection; indeed, the Rākṣasas consume that which is served with an iron vessel. Having placed the food in the vessels of the twice-born, he should silently perform the formal dedication (saṃkalpa).

For no connection is seen between them [the ancestors] and what is situated in a ladle or similar utensils. Whether one eats like a pig or whether a twice-born man eats from the palm of his hand, the ancestors do not eat that food, nor does he who eats with speech. (40)
One should fashion the funeral cakes according to the measurement described by Vyāsa, so that they fit comfortably into the mouth of a two-year-old calf.
Neither a woman, nor one devoid of knowledge, nor one who has not taken vows should move them; rather, it should be done by the son himself, or by one who desires the highest prosperity.
When the twice-born perform the rite of *svasti* while the vessels remain [unemptied], that food is consumed by the asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed. (43)
One should cause one piṇḍa to float in water, one should present one to the wife, and one indeed should offer into the fire; this is the threefold course.
One should feed a Chandoga at a Śrāddha ceremony and a Bahvṛca at a Vaiśvadeva rite; furthermore, one should feed an Adhvaryu for rites of nourishment and an Atharvaṇa for rites of pacification.

One should seat two Brahmins learned in the Atharvaveda facing east for the rite to the gods; for the rite to the ancestors, one should seat those versed in the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, and the Samaveda facing north.
All varieties of jasmine, mallikā, white yūthikā, all water-born flowers, and the campaka should be offered. (47)
Madhūka, asafoetida, camphor, black pepper, molasses, rock salt, and cucumber are likewise commended for the performance of śrāddha rites. (48)
A Brahmin, a woolen blanket, cows, the sun, fire, a guest, sesame seeds, Darbha grass, and the proper time—these nine are traditionally known as the Kutapas.
One should not perform [this] when there is no fire, at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), during an eclipse of the moon or sun, nor during a gathering, nor likewise when [the sun] has set.
A woman who has reached her menses becomes pure on the fourth day after bathing; she becomes fit for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors on the fifth day.
In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born brahmins, during travel, upon the birth of a son, or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform an *āmaśrāddha*.
One should not perform a śrāddha for those killed by snakes, fanged animals, horned beasts, or reptiles, nor for those who have committed suicide.
Death by the hands of a Caṇḍāla, by water, by a serpent, by a Brāhmaṇa, by lightning, or by fanged beasts—these are the modes of death for those of evil deeds. (54)
Whatever is performed by the eldest alone, having obtained the consent of all, shall be considered as performed by all, provided that the property has been divided.
Whoever causes churning to be performed during the ancestral śrāddha on the new moon day—that buttermilk is equal to liquor, and that ghee is declared to be like beef.
The ancestors eat in due order, as do those who subsist on funeral cakes (piṇḍa). A twice-born man invited to a śrāddha ceremony must not sleep with his wife.
One who has eaten at a Śrāddha should rise early in the morning and perform the cleansing of the teeth; however, a wise person who is performing a Śrāddha should not cleanse his teeth.
The annual śrāddha performed on the anniversary of the death of one's mother and father must not be performed during an intercalary month (malamāsa), according to the words of Vyāsa. || 59 ||
In the case of a birth-rite, a loan-interest rite, a death-rite, a monthly rite for a dependent, and likewise an annual śrāddha, the intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not prescribed as a restriction.

The solar month is prescribed for marriage and similar occasions; the sāvana month is prescribed for sacrifices and the like; but for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies, the lunar month is praised.

On the anniversary of the day of death, the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya) should be performed in that very zodiac sign in which the sun was situated when the twice-born person met with his demise. || 62 ||
The Vaṣaṭkāra, the Homa, the Parvan, and likewise the Āgrayaṇa—these should be performed even in an intercalary month; however, one should avoid optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi). || 63 ||

The establishment of the sacred fire, the consecration of a shrine, sacrifices, gifts, and vows; Vedic observances, the release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, and the girdle ceremony—[these he performed].

One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month (malamāsa); however, being self-restrained, one may perform obligatory and occasional rites during that intercalary period. Likewise, one may perform ritual bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the "elephant's shadow" rite (gajacchāyā), and the śrāddha for the deceased.
Where flavors are praised, where the eaters, kinsmen, and relatives [are the focus], and where there is clamor regarding news of the king and such—these are the characteristics of a Rākṣasa Śrāddha.
If one who has performed a *śrāddha* eats at another’s *śrāddha* while being agitated, his ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*).
Having gone on the following day, he should provide oil, anointing unguents, a bath, and tooth-cleansing sticks to those whose hair and nails have been trimmed.

When the best of the twice-born have been duly invited for offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), a sinner who should transgress against them in any way whatsoever shall go to the state of a pig.
When impurity arises during a rite for the gods or a Śrāddha for the ancestors, the Śrāddha is offered to them either at the end of that period of impurity or in that very instance.

Then, at the conclusion of the śrāddha, one should cause the following benediction to be recited: "May the Nagas be long-lived, as well as the rivers and the three steps of Viṣṇu; by the measure of these, may I attain a long life. (71)
The gods abide in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters. May the waters placed in the hand of a Brahmin be auspicious for us. (72)
Lakṣmī dwells in flowers; Lakṣmī dwells in the lotus. May Lakṣmī dwell in my abode and grant me a joyful mind.
May my merit remain unimpaired; may I have peace, nourishment, and fortitude. Whatever is conducive to welfare in this world, may that always be mine.
"In every case, let there be much to give in the south; so may it be for us. "So be it," they should say, and he should accept that with his head bowed. (75)
A man seeking enjoyment should always offer a piṇḍa into the fire; for the sake of progeny, he should indeed offer the middle piṇḍa to his wife, preceded by the appropriate mantra. (76)
One should constantly cause the highest splendor to be bestowed upon the rays of light; one should desire commands and fame, and should constantly immerse renown in the waters. (77)
Desiring long life, one should cause [food] to be given to the crows; desiring the world of Kumāra, one should cause it to be given to the cocks. (78)
One may even cast [the offering] into the sky while standing facing south; for the sky is the abode of the ancestors, as is the southern direction. (79)
One should avoid performing a śrāddha at night, except when there is the sight of Rāhu; indeed, upon the sight of Rāhu, it should be performed immediately even at the cost of one's entire wealth.
He who does not perform [this] during an eclipse sinks like a cow in the mud; but he who performs it crosses over his sin, just as a boat crosses the ocean.
Black beans, sesame seeds, barley, and rice are excellent; likewise, large barley, *vrīhi* rice, barley, and lentils are superior. (82)
In the rite of Śrāddha, black or white [grains] should always be taken; likewise, the bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, panasa, āmrātaka, and pomegranate [fruits]. (83)
The bhavya, the pigeon, the date-palm, the karamardaka, jujubes with their buds, the bulbous root of the palmyra palm, and likewise the lotus-fiber; || 84 ||
Tamālāsana-kanda, māvela, śata-kaṇḍalī, kāleya, kāla-śāka, mudga-rice, and suvarcala; || 85 ||
Meat, milk, curd, vegetables, the three pungents (vyoṣa), cane-sprouts, as well as kaṭphala, vajraka, grapes, lakuca, and mocaka; || 86 ||
The priya, āmalaka, durgrīva, tiṇḍuka, that which is called madhu, vaikaṅkata, coconut, śṛṅgāṭaka, and parūṣaka. || 87 ||
Long pepper, black pepper, patola, and the fruit of bṛhatī—all these, indeed, should be grown within the boundary of the grove. (88)
And other such flowers as these are used in rites for the ancestors: lentils, the hundred-petaled jasmine, and the flower that is the abode of Śrī.
Varyā, svātiyava, as well as vṛṣa and yavāsaka; vaṃśā, karīrā, surasā, mārjitā, and bhūtṛṇa grasses. (90)
I shall now describe those things that must always be avoided in the performance of the Śrāddha rite: garlic, leeks, onions, the globular radish, the mogara, the vaideha, and the long radish. (91)
If the eighth part of the day has passed and the sun has grown dim, that śrāddha becomes demonic (āsura) and does not reach the ancestors.
If a man performs a Śrāddha when the fourth watch has arrived, he obtains a futile Śrāddha, and the donor shall go to hell. (93)
From the time of sunrise until three muhūrtas have passed, that period is called Prātaḥ (morning); the wise declare the time following that to be Bhaga. (94)

This period of three muhūrtas is called Saṅgava; midday (madhyāhna) likewise consists of [three] muhūrtas on all sides; and thereafter, the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is prescribed as consisting of three muhūrtas. || 95 ||
Furthermore, that which is the fifth part of the day is known as the evening (sāyāhna). || 96 ||

And thus says the Śruti: "When the sun has risen, it is spring; when it is the time of *saṃgava*, it is summer; when it is midday, it is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, it is autumn; and when it sets, it is winter. (97)

Having commenced the Śrāddha during the Kutapa period, the wise man, knowing the ritual rules and adhering to the injunction, should perform the ascent; he must not, however, let the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra] pass by.
The eighth muhūrta is called Kutapa; the ninth is declared to be Rauhiṇa—thus those who know the Śrāddha rites understand.

One should prepare the cooked food for the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday, for the *jātakarman* rite in the morning, and likewise for the sake of the ancestors (*pitrya*) and for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* offering.

O Great Goddess, having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should not perform it for the sake of the ancestors; nor should one perform the ancestral rite (pitrya) within the Vaiśvadeva. Having completed the Śrāddha and having dismissed the Brahmins, [one should proceed]. || 101 ||
Then, O fair-faced one, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, especially in a well-kindled fire provided with abundant sacrificial fuel and oblations.

One should perform the rite for the sake of success when the fire is smokeless and flickering; however, he who offers oblations into a fire that is not yet awakened and is accompanied by smoke [fails]. (103)
It is certain that such a person becomes a blind sacrificer and a bad son; moreover, he is foul-smelling, black, and especially blue in complexion.
One should know that defeat awaits wherever one penetrates the earth [with such a fire] which is radiant, with a tawny crest, and possessing the luster of clarified butter and gold. || 105 ||

A fire that is oily and moving clockwise portends the success of one's undertaking. Likewise, the application of collyrium and ointments, fragrant scents, and the recitation of mantras [are auspicious]. (106)
Furthermore, one should perform the rite with kāśa flowers and obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha); likewise, one should always offer the eight-fold jāti flower and collyrium.
Oil was carefully preserved from black sesame seeds, as were both sandalwood and agallochum, along with tamāla, uśīra, and padmaka.
Guggulu incense is the best, as is the Taurushka incense; white jasmine flowers are excellent, as are lotuses and water-lilies.
And all other fragrant trees that have grown in their entirety, such as the niśigaṃdha, the japā, the bhiṇḍirūpaka, and the kuraṇṭaka. || 110 ||
Flowers should always be avoided in the performance of the śrāddha rite. A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is said to be suitable for the ancestors.
Likewise, even a slight sight of silver bestows merit; so too does the proximity to, the sight of, or the gift of a black antelope skin. (112)
It destroys demons, bestows luster, and secures cattle and sons; now I shall proclaim the mantra, the nectar created by Brahmā. (113)
Salutations to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutations, svāhā, and svadhā—eternal salutations indeed.
Reciting this [mantra] three times at the beginning and end of a Śrāddha ceremony, one indeed obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; this has been recognized and honored by the Brahmins.
Or, while offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one who is concentrated in mind should recite this; the ancestors will swiftly arrive, and the Rākṣasas will flee.
I shall proclaim the Saptārcis [mantra], which bestows all desires and auspiciousness. || 117 ||
I always pay homage to those ancestors of radiant splendor, both formless and embodied, who are meditative and possess divine vision. 118.
Likewise, I bow to Dakṣa, Mārīci, and others who are the leaders of Indra and the rest; indeed, I pay homage to all those ancestors as well as the medicinal herbs.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to the constellations and the planets, to wind and fire, to the ancestors, and to heaven and earth.
Salutations to the seven ancestors; salutations to those in the seven worlds. We pay homage to the Self-Existent Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga.
This which has been spoken by you is served by the hosts of the Seven Sages and the Brahman-sages; for it is supremely purifying, glorious, and a destroyer of Rākṣasas. (122)
Endowed with this method, a man—possessed of supreme devotion, full of faith, and having conquered his senses—should recite [the mantra] three times. (123)
He who, being constantly composed, recites the Saptārcis mantra, shall become the sole sovereign of the earth with its seven oceans.
He who indeed recites the Śrāddhakalpa shall become a purifier of the assembly; he is remembered as one who has reached the further shore of the eighteen branches of learning.
When pleased, the ancestors constantly bestow upon human beings worship, nourishment, memory, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health. (126)
Thus, O beautiful lady, one should perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rite at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean in Prabhāsa-kṣetra, and indeed at Prabhāsa itself.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Śrāddha," within the "Śrāddha-kalpa" section concerning the Confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Ocean, in the first part, the "Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 206 ||
Īśvara said: Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the offerings for the Śrāddha ceremony at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, for the sake of the deliverance of all beings.
Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—all that should be given to the ancestors by those who desire that it be inexhaustible.
The giver of food obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, radiant as the sun, and filled with divine apsarases.
He who gives an unwashed garment during the performance of a Śrāddha rite obtains long life, renown, sovereignty, and beauty. (4)
And he who gives a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, a cow that flows with honey and milk follows after the donor. || 5 ||
He who grants fearlessness to living beings who desire life at a *śrāddha* ceremony surpasses the merit of giving a thousand horses, a hundred chariots, and a thousand elephants. (6)
Whatever jewels exist upon the earth, as well as vehicles and women—a man devoted to his ancestors quickly attains all of that.
In all worlds, at the times of the lunar days, the ancestors and the deities all come toward a man, like cows to a watering trough.
Let them not turn away from you when unhonored during the sacred festival times; let their hopes never be frustrated, neither in this world nor in the next.
Whoever feeds even a single twice-born man in the presence of Sarasvatī obtains the fruit of feeding ten million; of this there is no doubt.
If a man eats another's food on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the merit he has accumulated throughout that month accrues to the giver of that food. || 11 ||

It is taught that one enjoys [the fruit] for six months during the solstice (ayana) and for three months during the equinox (viṣuva). Whatever merit has been accumulated over twelve years—all of that goes to ruin by eating during the conjunction of the sun and moon.

During the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), the first śrāddha lasts for more than a month; during the monthly (māsika) śrāddha, it lasts for three years; likewise, for the annual śrāddha it lasts for six months, and for the half-yearly śrāddha, it lasts for half a year.

Likewise, at a Śrāddha for the collection of bones (saṃcayana), the sins committed by men through their birth and lineage [are removed]; however, for a man who accepts a bed from the deceased, a seller of the Veda, or a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s property, no purification exists. 14.
A usurper of land is not purified even by a thousand tanks, a hundred horse-sacrifices, or the gift of ten million cows. (15)
One who steals a gold māṣa, a single cow, or even half an inch of land, goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the wealth of a poor man, the wife of a guru, and gold—these cause even one residing in heaven to fall. (17)
A cow is equal to a thousand [other gifts], and ten cows are equal to a bull; a vehicle is equal to ten bulls, and a horse is equal to ten vehicles. (18)
A maiden is equal to ten horses, and the gift of land is superior to that; therefore, with every effort, one should never effect her sale.

Especially in a great sacred field that destroys all sins, bathing is prescribed after touching wood from a funeral pyre, as well as sacrificial posts, and after touching one who sells the Vedas. (20)
He who recites the instruction and he who imparts the instruction—both of these are evildoers who shall dwell in the depths of the netherworld.

O Goddess, that man who recites a command at the king’s gate shall likewise become a tree covered in thorns in a saline wasteland; indeed, he who stands at the king’s gate and sells the Vedas [shall suffer the same]. (22)
A sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin has never existed, nor will it ever exist; O Goddess, even while performing a great boon, one should certainly not engage in the sale of the Vedas. (23)
A base twice-born man might rather kill cows and eat choice meat, or live together with Mlecchas, than engage in the sale of the Vedas.
Direct assertion, [giving] conviction, receiving gifts preceded by a question, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and debate—these six constitute the sale of the Veda. (25)
As many syllables as one employs from the Vedas for one's own selfish ends, so many instances of foeticide shall the seller of the Veda indeed incur. (26)
He who, for the sake of Vedic study, gives a gift to a Brāhmaṇa goes first to hell, and the Brāhmaṇa follows immediately after him.

Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and those who are also lacking in hospitality—even if they are twice-born (dvijas) learned in the Vedas, by their conduct they are all indeed Śūdras. (28)
Those who have no Vedic study, those who maintain no sacred fires, and those whose family lacks Vedic learning—all these belong to the Śūdra caste. || 29 ||
O lady of excellent hips, that twice-born man who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of the death of his father or his mother is equal to a śūdra.
One should treat as a Śūdra anyone who eats during a period of impurity following a death, or when the moon and sun are eclipsed, or during the Gajacchāyā conjunctions.

In the case of a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), a sacrifice, one who is self-restrained, an artisan, or one initiated for a rite; and during a sacrifice, a wedding, or a long sacrificial session (sattra)—there is never any impurity (sūtaka) whatsoever.
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, those who are touchable, and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas. (33)
A Brahmin who persists in acts leading to downfall, in improper occupations, who is hypocritical and prone to evil deeds, is declared to be equal to a Śūdra. (34)

One who eats without bathing consumes impurity; one who does not chant prayers consumes pus and blood; one who offers no oblations consumes worms; and one who gives nothing away consumes poison for his meal. (35)
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after eating another's food—the semen proceeds from the food; therefore, those sons belong to the owner of that food. (36)
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster; the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (37)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds. (38)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen; the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (39)

A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if he knows only the essence of the Gāyatrī, is better than one who is unrestrained, though he may know the four Vedas, eat all things, and sell all things. (40)
One falls immediately from one's status by selling meat, lac, or salt; a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk. (41)
Tastes should be bartered for tastes, but salt must never be exchanged for tastes; prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and likewise their equivalents.
Whatever else one does with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or for anointing the body, one becomes a worm in excrement and sinks there along with one's ancestors.
One who, lacking knowledge, accepts cakes, gold, a cow, a horse, land, or sesame seeds, is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood.

Gold and gems drew out his life-force; the earth and the cow drew out his body; the horse drew out his sight; clothing drew out his skin; ghee drew out his luster; and sesame seeds drew out his offspring. (45)
If an Agnihotrin or an ascetic is made to wait even for a moment, then the entire merit of that Agnihotra and asceticism becomes the wealth of the wealthy man [who caused the delay]. (46)
A gift given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood; a gift to a temple-attendant is lost; and to a usurer, it finds no firm foundation. (47)
A Brahmin who is intent on worshipping the gods for the sake of wealth throughout the three worlds is known as a *devalaka*, and he is censured in the offerings made to the gods and the ancestors.
He who, out of lust, approaches the wife of his deceased brother—even if she has been appointed according to dharma—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (49)
He who enters into marriage and the consecration of the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
The man who makes use of another's clothes, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given is a partaker of one-fourth of that person's sin.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), incurs all whatever evil deeds have been committed by the donor. || 52 ||
One should live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*; one may live by means of the *satya* and the *anṛta*, but never by the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*).
Food that is always received is known as *mṛta*; that which is obtained unasked is *amṛta*. Living by usury is *pramṛta*, while agriculture is remembered as *vimṛta*. (54)
Trade involves both truth and falsehood, and one may subsist by that very means; service is called the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
Having entered a base womb, one should avoid the mixing of castes; for human birth is difficult to attain in this world, and the status of a Brāhmaṇa is even more so than that.

Sharing a bed or a seat, eating in the same row, sharing vessels, cooked food, or mixing [with others], officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, [sharing] a common womb, and likewise eating together—this ninefold *saṃkara* (intermixture) has been declared; it must not be practiced with those who are base. (57)
If a Brahmin cannot subsist by his own occupation, he may resort to the duties of a Kṣatriya, or he may perform the work of a Vaiśya; however, he must avoid the work of a Śūdra.
In times of distress, a twice-born man may personally engage in the activities of agriculture and trade; by performing these himself during such a time of calamity, he is purified by bathing.
Having obtained his gain, he should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins; when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that sin of his. (60)

In times of famine, it is taught that the livelihoods of those living by water, cattle, carts, ironworks, begging, usury, and trade, as well as marshlands, mountains, and kings, serve as means of subsistence. 61.
He who, having received wealth even from the wicked, bestows it upon the virtuous, delivers both his master and himself from the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence. 62.

A gift given to a Śūdra is said to yield equal merit; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as yielding twice that; to a Śrotriya, it yields a thousandfold; and to one who maintains the Agnihotra fire, it is infinite.
There is no transgression against a Brahmin for one who does not act according to established order; for indeed, one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
One who is devoid of both learning and austerity must never accept a gift; by accepting one, he leads both the giver and himself to ruin. (65)
Therefore, one who is a Vedic scholar, virtuous, of good character, pure, free from physical deformity, and faultless therein is considered the most excellent among recipients.
Just as water in a skull-bowl and milk in a dog-skin bag are defiled by the defect of their container, so too is sacred learning [defiled] when placed in one who lacks right conduct. 67.
That which is given by passing over a worthy recipient to accept it from an unworthy one is like giving a cow’s daily fodder to a donkey after bypassing the cow.

Therefore, one should protect one's conduct, for wealth that has been spent may come again; one who is diminished in wealth is not truly diminished, but one who is ruined in conduct is utterly destroyed.
First, having given the most excellent gift to the preceptor in due order, one should then give to the other Brahmins according to their worthiness as recipients.
Whatever gift is given by men to the preceptor or to worthy recipients becomes fruitless after death, and they go toward a downward state of existence.
Having shown disrespect to his guru and having provoked his anger, the evil-minded fool, struck down by that dishonor toward his teacher, finds no peace.
In the absence of the guru, one may [approach] his son, or his wife, or his grandson—excluding the son of the daughter—and indeed another who is born of that same lineage.
When one's own guru is heard to be within five yojanas, then a person should not bypass him; he should give gifts to those worthy recipients.
If an ascetic should, out of greed, seek a gift being offered, it must not be given to him by the wise; for greed is not praised in an ascetic. (75)
Having acquired wealth in this world, an ascetic should not practice silence or [worldly] knowledge; rather, he should utilize his enjoyment through charity and his life through celibacy.
Those best of men who have attained [their status] through birth in a noble family and through initiations shall surely obtain good fortune in this world by renouncing [worldly] tastes. (77)
All subjects become long-lived by abstaining from meat. || 78 ||
By wearing garments of bark and rags, having cast aside fine clothes and ornaments, a person attains the lordship of the Nāgas through fasting. (79)
One sports with truthful speech in heaven together with the deities; likewise, through non-violence one attains health, and from giving, fame follows in succession.
Through service to the twice-born, a man obtains a kingdom and an exceedingly abundant state of being twice-born; through service to the gods, he attains a divine form.
From the gift of food, satisfaction arises through all unsurpassed desires; by the offering of a lamp, a man becomes possessed of keen vision.

There shall always be satisfaction from the giving of perfumes and garlands; moreover, those who give salt, sesame seeds, and likewise clarified butter, are born radiant, possessed of enjoyments, and long-lived. (83)

That man who gives a bed to a twice-born man, furnished with variegated cloths, ornaments, and pillows, shall obtain a wife endowed with beauty, possessed of long eyelashes, charming, and adorned with celestial garments.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Consideration of Worthy and Unworthy Recipients," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* section of the *Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya*, within the first part of the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, in the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 207 ||
The Goddess said: "Regarding that which has been declared in the Śruti, 'this is to be given' and 'this is to be given,' I wish to hear in truth the specific distinctions between giving and taking."
Which gifts are praised, and to whom should they be given? O Lord, tell me everything regarding the proper time, the place, and the recipient.
Īśvara said: There are four futile births and sixteen futile gifts; likewise, there are four noble births and sixteen great gifts. (3)
The Goddess said: "O God of gods, O Lord of the world, tell me this in detail."

Īśvara said: Understand from me those four births that are in vain: the birth of bad sons is in vain, as is the birth of those who are excluded from dharma; and the birth of those who go abroad and are always devoted to the wives of others is in vain. (5)
O beloved, those who eat food cooked by others, those who take pleasure in the wives of others, and those who give gifts that cannot be refused, in vain, or with fault—[they go to hell]. || 6 ||

A gift given to one who has fallen from his vows after having ascended [to a high station], wealth acquired through unjust means, a gift to a slayer of a Brahmin, and likewise to one who has fallen or to a thief, is in vain.
Whatever is given to one who causes displeasure to the guru, to an ungrateful person, to a village priest, to a Brahmin in name only, or to the husband of a Vṛṣalī; || 8 ||
That which is given to a seller of the Vedas, to one in whose house a paramour resides, and to one who is conquered by his wife—these are the sixteen futile gifts.
