A good birth belongs to those who have virtuous sons and to those men who delight in righteousness; they do not go into exile, as they turn their backs on the wives of others. || 10 ||
Cows, gold, silver, jewels, and Sarasvatī; sesame seeds, a maiden, an elephant, a horse, a bed, clothing, and likewise land—(these are the gifts). 11.
Grain, milk, an umbrella, and a house equipped with furnishings—these indeed, O Great Goddess, are the sixteen great gifts (mahādānas).
But he who gives out of pride, or likewise out of fear or anger, indeed enjoys the fruit of that gift while still in the womb; of this there is no doubt.
Even in his childhood, he eats what is given for the sake of hypocrisy, out of anger or resentment, and likewise for the sake of wealth.
He who gives at the proper place, at the proper time, to a worthy recipient, and with a pure mind, having acquired the gift through righteous means—he enjoys the fruit of that in his youth. (15)
Wealth acquired by unjust means, bestowed upon an unworthy recipient, and offered with distress or in violation of the prescribed rites—one experiences the fruit of that in old age. (16)

Therefore, at the proper place and time, a person should, with faith and free from deceit, employ wealth acquired through auspicious means for a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rule. || 17 ||

They say that such a person is a worthy recipient—one who is rich in Vedic study, possessed of yoga, tranquil, knowledgeable in the Purāṇas, fearful of sin, generous, patient toward women, righteous, a refuge for cows, and one who has mastered himself through vows.

Truthfulness, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, freedom from envy, straightforwardness, knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and generosity—these are the characteristics of a worthy recipient. (19)
To such a worthy recipient, however, he who bestows a single cow—a tawny milch-cow endowed with all virtues, accompanied by a calf of the same color—[attains great merit].
One who gives a cow with silver hooves and golden horns is honored in the world of Rudra; one who possesses ten cows should give one, and likewise, one who possesses a hundred cows should give ten.

One who gives a hundred [cows] each weighing a thousand [palas], all are recorded as having equal merit. A cow that is well-behaved, endowed with the essence of the moon (soma), young, and full of milk; accompanied by her calf and acquired through righteous means—such a cow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.

One should not cause such a cow to be given away: one that is barren, diseased, deficient in limbs, wicked, old, whose offspring has died, obtained through unjust means, or situated at a great distance. || 23 ||
O Maheśvarī, that man who gives such a cow in dedication to a deity, on the contrary, goes to a lower state and suffers.

One who is angry, afflicted, weak, or diseased should not be given [as a gift], nor one for whom the price has not been paid; for by her, even a slight offense arises toward the Brahmins, and all the worlds of the giver become fruitless. || 25 ||
Even a single gift given to a guest who is tranquil, who maintains the sacred fires, and who is a master of the Vedas, becomes of great merit. (26)
O Goddess, if a Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge sells a cow, he is not praised; such a Brāhmaṇa is not even considered a worthy recipient. || 27 ||
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many; for such a divided sacrificial fee does not benefit the donor. (28)
There, where the palaces are golden and the beds are radiant as the sun, and where there are excellent celestial nymphs (apsarases), thither go those who give cows.
There is no gift equal to land; there is no river equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no dharma higher than truth; and there is no god other than Maheśvara. 30.
Land that is high, stony, uneven, saline, or rugged like a riverbank should never be given away. (31)
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years; the one who seizes it, or even consents to its seizure, shall go to hell for that same duration.
Whatever sin a man commits when distressed by his livelihood, he is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cowhide.
An umbrella, a bed, a seat, a conch, elephants, horses, chowries, women, and land—the fruit of the gift of these is said to be the world of Śiva. (34)

On the day of the sun (Sunday), during a solar transit, at the eclipses of the moon and the sun, during the breaking of a fast, and upon the gift of a cow, a householder who has a grandson need not observe a fast.
If one desires a stable lineage, one should not observe a fast on the new moon, on a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh lunar day, or when a Śata-kratu has been performed. || 36 ||
Just as the bright fortnight is, so too is the dark; there is no difference whatsoever between them. Nevertheless, merit always increases only during the bright fortnight.
If the eleventh day is pierced by the tenth and the twelfth day has come to an end, one should perform the *nakta* rite there; fasting is not prescribed.
He who, having observed the fast on the eleventh day, performs the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day, loses the merit of twelve twelfth-day fasts.
Likewise, during a fast or a śrāddha ceremony, one should not use a wooden tooth-stick; for by the contact of wood with the teeth, one indeed destroys seven generations of one's lineage.

One who does not perform the New Moon (Darśa) and Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa) sacrifices, as well as the anniversary of one's father's death, when they are overlapped by the previous lunar day, falls into hell. || 41 ||

It is declared that there is a loss of one's lineage and one shall encounter misfortune; therefore, I shall explain the procedure for a Śrāddha performed in the absence of wealth according to its true essence.
For even with a single Brahmin, one should perform the Śrāddha consisting of six rice-balls; there, one should offer the six Arghya libations and present them to him according to the prescribed rule.
The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from the mouth; the great-grandfather is situated on the palate, and the maternal grandfather is said to be in the throat. (44)

The maternal great-grandfather is in the heart, while the elder is situated at the navel. O beloved, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, Kuśa grass should be made into a substitute for a twice-born; this is stated after extracting the essence from all the Purāṇas. 45.
This should not be given to an atheist, a slanderer, or one who reviles the Vedas; rather, it should be recited every morning after worshipping Maheśvara.
One should honor and present an umbrella to one who is of noble birth, learned in all the scriptures, and a teacher of this Dharma, like the god Maheśvara himself. || 47 ||
But he who hears even a single verse from an unworthy reciter does not obtain merit; for he is remembered as a thief of the scriptures. (48)
Therefore, a wise person should honor the reciter with every effort; otherwise, his listening to the book will be fruitless. (49)
O Goddess, in whosever house this scripture so difficult to obtain remains, Śiva himself dwells in that person's home together with all sacred pilgrimage sites.
What need is there for much speaking here? One shall become a vessel for liberation. However, this must not be given to a slanderer, nor to an atheist, nor to one possessed of hypocrisy.
This should be given to a peaceful and self-controlled twice-born man who is a devotee of Śiva.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Brāhmaṇas as Recipients of Gifts," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the first part of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 208 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Mārkaṇḍeyeśa, which was established by Mārkaṇḍeya to the north of that [site]. || 1 ||
Not far from the eastern part of Sāvitrī, there formerly lived a great ṛṣi known as Mārkaṇḍeya. || 2 ||

By the grace of the Lotus-born One, he became indeed free from old age and immortal; having gone there, that best of Brahmins, recognizing that field to be supreme, installed a linga of the trident-bearing God of gods. || 3 ||
Having honored him according to the prescribed rite and standing to his right, the sage assumed the lotus posture and then entered into a state of meditative absorption.
While he was thus devoted to meditation, millions and billions of ages passed by, yet the Lord of Sages did not even perceive them.
Then, O Goddess, after a long time, the temple of Śaṅkara remained in a state of ruin, covered by dust raised by the winds.
Then, after some time, the best of sages awoke and saw that entire temple of Śiva covered with dust.
Then, O beautiful lady, that bull among sages, having dug out [the passage], emerged with great difficulty and made a very large door for the sake of worshipping him.
Whoever enters there and worships the Bull-bannered Lord with devotion goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
The Goddess said: "How did Mārkaṇḍa, the best of sages, attain immortality? For this is indeed a source of curiosity; therefore, you ought to explain it. (10)
O Śaṅkara, since immortality does not exist for living beings on this earth—even for the gods—at the end of a kalpa, why has that sage not died?
Īśvara said: Now, therefore, I shall tell you how he became immortal. In a former kalpa, there was a sage renowned as Mṛkaṇḍu. (12)
The illustrious son of Bhṛgu, dwelling with his wife in the practice of austerity, had a son born to him while he was living in the midst of the forest.
Having become five years old, he was endowed with virtues even as a child; then, after some time, a wise man arrived there.
O beloved, he then saw the boy wandering in the courtyard; remembering him, he laughed for a long time, impelled by the future destiny.
His father, a supreme expert in the marks of men (sāmudrajña) who was filled with wonder, saw him and asked the reason for his laughter.
"O Brahmin, why have you smiled upon seeing my son? O Brāhmaṇa, you ought to tell me the reason for that exactly as it is. (17)
Having heard these words of his, the wise Brahmin spoke these words.
"O Sage, this son of yours, though endowed with all auspicious marks, shall meet his death within six months from this day forward. (19)
"If he were to live, he would indeed have attained a long life; therefore, I made this joke. The course of karma is truly manifold. (20)
Having heard these fierce words uttered by the wise man, the boy’s father then performed the initiation ceremony for the vow.
And seeing a brahmin arrive, the seer said to his son: "The three castes must salute him; by doing so, you shall indeed attain spiritual welfare."
Thus addressed, that brahmin indeed performed the salutation; he did not recognize him as being of a lower caste due to his childhood state, O fair-faced one. (23)
Indeed, five months and twenty-five days have passed; at that very time, the stainless Seven Sages arrived.

O beautiful lady, in the course of his pilgrimage, he traveled by that path; and after some time, all those [ascetics] duly addressed that boy, clad in bark and holding a staff, saying, "May you live long! (25)
Having spoken thus, they looked again at the boy whose life was indeed exhausted; knowing his remaining lifespan to be only five days, they became afraid of that falsehood.
Taking the religious student with them, they went into the presence of Brahmā; having placed the boy before him, they bowed down to the Grandfather.
Then that boy also saluted Brahmā; and in the presence of the sages, the boy was told by Brahmā, "May you have a long life. (28)

Then those sages were delighted upon hearing the words from the Grandfather; but the Grandfather, seeing those astonished ṛṣis, said to them: "For what purpose have you come, and by whom was the boy reported? (29)
The sages said: Bhrigu’s son was Mṛkaṇḍa, whose young son had a short lifespan; knowing that his father would die prematurely, he bound the sacred girdle for him.
Then, having been instructed by that Brahmin regarding the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), [he was told]: "Whichever twice-born man you see wandering on the surface of the earth in this world," || 31 ||
O dear son, he must always be saluted; it was by him alone, O best of men, that we were seen by this boy.
O Grandfather, in the course of his pilgrimage to sacred sites, by the turn of fate, he was told by these [sages] who had offered him salutations that he would indeed live for a long time.
"O Lord, he has been brought into your presence and addressed by you in this manner; how then could our speech, together with yours, be false? (34)
Addressing the boy with a smile, the Lotus-born One said: "This boy Mārkaṇḍeya shall possess a lifespan equal to my own. (35)

"At the beginning and likewise at the end of the eon, he shall be my companion. Then the sages, being delighted, took the young sage and released him in that very place where his activities had occurred. (36)
The Brahmins went on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, while Mārkaṇḍeya went home; having reached his home, he then spoke to Mṛkaṇḍa, the best of sages.
"O dear one, I was led to the world of Brahmā by seven sages; at the beginning and at the end of the kalpa, this [man] was declared by Brahmā to be my friend."
"There is no doubt that this boy shall have a lifespan equal to mine. Then he was brought back by them and released toward the hermitage. (39)

"O best of the twice-born, let the fever of your mind depart on my account. Having heard the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, Mṛkaṇḍa, the most excellent of sages, attained supreme joy after that single moment which had been so difficult to endure. (40)
Then, summoning his fortitude, he spoke these words.
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived, since the Grandfather of the worlds has been seen by you, my noble son.
That which even the wise do not perceive through a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices—that very thing has been attained by you, O son, with ease.

Thus was he seen by the lotus-born Brahmā after a long time; O dear one, I have been pained by your suffering day and night, and I could not find sleep, but now that great sorrow of mine has passed away.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 209.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Pulastyeśvara, situated five dhanus to the north of Mārkaṇḍeya.
O Goddess, having seen him and worshipped according to the prescribed rite, a person is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven births; of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pulastyeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 210 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, eight bow-lengths to the southwest of Pulastyeśvara, one should worship with devotion that [liṅga] named Pulaheśvara.
Indeed, by giving a gift of gold, one obtains the full fruit of a successful pilgrimage.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pulaheśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 211 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, eight bow-lengths to the southwest of Pulaheśvara is the one named Kratvīśvara, which bestows the fruit of great sacrifices. || 1 ||
O Goddess, by seeing that [liṅga], a person shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice; for seven births, neither poverty nor suffering shall arise there.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kratvīśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 212.
Īśvara said: Sixteen dhanus to the east of Kratvīśa is the one named Kaśyapeśvara, which destroys even the greatest sins. || 1 ||
O Goddess, by seeing it, a man shall become wealthy and possessed of sons; even one burdened with all manner of sins is liberated—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaśyapeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 213 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, eight bow-lengths from Kaśyapeśvara in the northeast is the one named Kauśakeśvara, which destroys great sins.
Having slain the sons of Vasiṣṭha there, that best of the Kauśikas installed that Liṅga and was thereby liberated from sin. || 2 ||
Having seen and worshipped him, one indeed obtains the desired fruit. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kauśikeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 214.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Kumāreśvara, located not very far to the south of Mārkaṇḍeśvara, at a distance of twenty bows, where it was installed by Svāmin.
Then, O radiant lady, Kārttikeya performed severe penance for the sake of destroying the sins arising from the abduction of another's wife.
Having established a linga there, he was then liberated from that sin; out of dispassion, he abandoned his youth and resumed his childhood once again.
In former times, Sumālī also propitiated him after killing his ancestors; O Goddess, he too was liberated from the sin arising from the slaughter of his forefathers.
This place named Kumāreśvara is indeed worshipped by gods and demons; O beautiful lady, there stands a well before that Kumāra.
Having bathed there, whoever worships the Trident-bearer who is honored by the Lord shall be liberated from all sins and go to the great city of the Lord.
He who gives a golden cock to a twice-born man, dedicating it to his own master, shall obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kumāreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 215 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, fifteen bow-lengths to the north of Mārkaṇḍeśvara is an excellent Liṅga named Gautameśvara. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in former times, having killed his guru, Gautama was afflicted by sin; however, by installing a liṅga there, he was liberated from that sin. || 2 ||
He who, having bathed in the river according to the prescribed rite, gives a tawny cow there and duly worships the Liṅga, is liberated from the five great sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gautameśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 216 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, not very far to the west of Gautameśvara, at a distance of sixteen dhanus, stands Devarājeśvara. || 1 ||
He established that Liṅga, and thereby he was liberated from his sins. Any man who worships it with a concentrated mind shall likewise be completely released from the sin born of human nature.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Devarājeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 217.
Īśvara said: Right there is the Mānava-liṅga, which was installed by Manu. O Goddess, in former times, having killed his son, Manu was overcome with sin. || 1 ||
Recognizing that the sacred field (kṣetra) was a remover of sins, he established the Lord (Īśvara) there; and he became liberated from that sin arising from the slaughter of his son.
The man who worships [it] shall become liberated from all sins. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mānaveśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 218 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, O Great Goddess, in the south-eastern corner near Mārkaṇḍeya, there is a cave-liṅga renowned as Nīlakaṇṭha.
It was formerly worshipped by Viṣṇu and is the destroyer of all sins.
In that regard, whoever worships that sin-liberating liṅga with devotion shall be wise, possessed of sons and cattle, and rejoice upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, O Great Goddess, O beautiful lady, those hermitages of the sages which are seen here even today are situated in the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍeyeśa.
O Goddess of the gods, eighty-eight thousand sages who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) reside there in the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍeya’s hermitage.
And there, the caves of the sages who dwell in those hermitages and perform meritorious austerities are all seen to be endowed with lingas.
There, whoever installs a liṅga in the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍeśa, having delivered a hundred generations of his lineage, rejoices in heaven like a god.
All worlds consist of Śiva; everything is established in Śiva. Therefore, a wise person who desires prosperity for himself should worship Śiva.
A king who is not a devotee of Śiva but is devoted to other gods is like a young woman who, having abandoned her own husband, takes pleasure with others. || 9 ||
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, kings of great supernatural power, as well as all humans and sages, worship the Liṅga.
Liṅgas marked with their own names were installed by Indra and the others in due order at their respective places, and they have been established in great numbers by human beings as well.
By means of this installation, they have crossed over the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of an embryo, and likewise other great sins, through the splendor of Śiva.
In ancient times, having slain Vṛtra and installed Śaṅkara as Māhendra, Śakra was freed from the flood of his sins and thereafter ascended to heaven.

Having established Śiva at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Sūrya became free from affliction; and Soma, having established him at Prabhāsa on the western ocean, likewise became free from disease.
In Kāśī, Āditya likewise, and on Mount Sahya, Garuḍa and Kāśyapa attained supreme establishment after having established the Lord of the World.
For even Ahalyā, whose fault was well known, was then cursed by her husband; yet, after re-establishing Īśāna, she regained her womanhood as well as excellent sons.
Even today, those women and men who, having bathed there, behold Ahiṇyeśvara, are liberated from those defects; of this there is no doubt. (17)
With the exception of Īśvara on the White Mountain (Śvetaśaila), both Bali and Virocana were born as immortals, the foremost among the powerful.
Having slain Rāvaṇa along with his army, Rāma duly installed the Lord of the Thirty-three on the bank of the lord of rivers and streams with devotion. (19)

"Never anywhere shall the earth be devoid of the liṅgas of Svāyaṃbhuva, the Ṛṣis, the Devas, and others. O Vyāpārās, setting aside all else, worship Śiva always! [For] those approaching the city of Death appear as if they were already close at hand. (20)
O Goddess, what is the use of speaking much or describing it again and again? The very essence of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra lies toward the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the god worshipped by the three worlds, named Vṛṣadhvajeśvara, situated likewise to the south.

That which is the imperishable, unmanifest, and supreme beyond which nothing exists; which is attainable through yoga, without beginning or end, and equal to the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva). || 2 ||
O Goddess, it consists of all wonders, is perceivable by the intellect, and is free from affliction; its hands and feet are everywhere, and its eyes, heads, and mouths are on every side. (3)
And Pṛthu, Marutta, Bharata, Śaśabindu, Gaya, and Śibi [worshipped] that god who stands eternally, known as the one whose banner bears the bull.
Rāma, Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, Dilīpa, Bhagīratha, Suhotra, Rantideva, Yayāti, and likewise Sagara. || 5 ||
These sixteen blessed kings, having resorted to the sacred field of Prabhāsa and having worshipped the Lord Vṛṣadhvajeśa with sacrifices, went to heaven.
I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial; I speak the essence again and again: in this worthless, burnt-out cycle of existence, the worship of Śiva is the only essence.
Rebirth, repeated death, recurring affliction, and recurring old age—this cycle, like the turning of a water-wheel day after day, never comes to an end. (8)
Therefore, let that worship of Bhava be performed, which utterly eradicates and severs the knot of Śveta’s worldly existence—a knot otherwise exceedingly difficult to break.
The wish-fulfilling gem is in his house, the desire-granting tree is in his family, and Kubera is his servant—he in whom devotion to Śiva is firmly established.
This very devotion to the Bull-bannered Lord is the prosperity of men in former times; this is the desired devotion; this is the form that brings about the highest good.
By worshipping Maheśvara here even with just five flowers, a human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
A bull should be given there in the presence of the Bull-bannered Lord by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage for the sake of destroying all sins. (13)

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vṛṣabhadhvajeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 220 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Ṛṇamocana; when he is seen, there shall be no debt arising from one's mother and father.
In ancient times, all the ancestors gathered at the divine field of Prabhāsa and remained there for many groups of years, engaged in ascetic penance.
The Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, the Somapās, and likewise the Ājyapās—all of them, being devoted to supreme faith, installed the Liṅga.
Then, after a long time, Maheśvara was pleased with them; having appeared before their eyes, he spoke these words.
I am well-pleased; may it be well with you; tell me what is desired by your hearts.
The Pitṛs said: "Let a means of subsistence be granted to us in this world created by yourself, as well as for the gods, the sages, and human beings upon the surface of the earth."
O Lotus-born One, you alone are supreme in this world for all beings; having come here, the four castes who are endowed with faith [shall attain their goals]. (7)
May they be liberated from their paternal debts and become free from sin; O best of gods, may those whose ancestors have fallen into the state of being *vyantara* spirits [be released].
Those ancestors who have met their destruction by snakes, fire, or poisons—whether they were childless or had sons—if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has not been performed; || 9 ||

For those for whom the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites were not performed previously, nor was the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) performed, and who have been killed by outcastes (*antyaja*), [the following applies]. 10.
Furthermore, those others who have died but were deprived of purification—may they all be satisfied here and attain the supreme goal. (11)
The Blessed Lord said: "Those men who, being devoted to their ancestors, bathe in the holy water and perform the libation for the Pitṛs," || 12 ||
I am the bestower of boons upon them; I shall deliver all their ancestors at that very moment, even if they are shrouded by hundreds of sins—of this there is no doubt.
"Having bathed at this sacred ford, the man who worships the Liṅga installed by you shall be liberated from his debt to the ancestors."
Since one is liberated from debt by the sight of this linga, therefore I have given it the name Ṛṇamocana.
Īśvara said: He who bathes at Ṛṇamocana after placing gold upon his head has truly saved his own soul; it is as if a hundred cows have been given by him.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there. Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there; and one should worship that Pitṛ-liṅga, O Great Goddess, which is dear to the gods. (17)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ṛṇamocana," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 221.
Īśvara said: In that very place stands the Liṅga installed by Rukmavatī; it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. (1)
Having bathed there at that great sacred ford (tīrtha) and having diligently immersed the liṅga, one should cause wealth to be given to the Brahmins; thus, one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Rukmavatīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 222 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga worshipped by the three worlds, known as Gātrotsarga, situated to its south.
There, in that battle, the wise Balabhadra and other highly fortunate Yādavas surrendered their bodies.
Where those Yādavas perished by the serpent of the power of the Brahmanas' curse, this is the sacred field of Puruṣottama, extending for a hundred bows on all sides.
O Goddess, wherever Puruṣottama himself dwells in person, that alone is the Vaiṣṇava field which destroys sins in the Kali age.

O Goddess, that is indeed the supreme secret and the most excellent of all holy sites (tīrthas). O Goddess, formerly in the Kṛta age it was remembered as Pretatīrtha, but when the Kali age arrived, it became known as Gātrotsarga.
To the side of Ṛṇamocana, in the middle of Pāpamocana—by resorting to this middle point, one who dies is liberated from sins.
O Goddess, how can its great and infinite fruit be described? Indeed, by bathing there, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having reached the Aśvattha tree there, Keśava, with his mind fixed in meditative absorption, released his life-breaths—which are so difficult to relinquish—through the aperture of Brahmā.
There, by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, Balabhadra, and Rukmiṇī according to the prescribed rite, one is liberated from the three types of sins.
Having bathed there with devotion, the man who satiates his ancestors becomes a giver of *śrāddha*, and his ancestors are liberated from the state of being a *preta*. (10)

Whether one is a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, a person of wicked intellect, a slayer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—a man who bathes there immediately becomes cleansed of sin.
O beloved, whatever sin a man commits in childhood, in old age, or even in youth—whether through ignorance or intentionally—he is liberated from it by bathing at the sacred ford Gātrapramocana.
There, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), supreme satisfaction arises for the ancestors for as long as a hundred years; so said Hari in the past.
Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, any man who, with a concentrated mind, offers a gift of food there, not even a single descendant in his lineage shall be born as a preta.

The Goddess said: It has been declared that the "Pretatīrtha" (the Tīrtha of the Pretas) follows after the "Gātravimocana" (the Liberation of the Limbs). O Lord of the Gods, tell me the reason for the Pretatīrtha.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the cause of Pretatīrtha; hearing which, a human being through devotion shall be liberated from all sins. 16.
In ancient times, there was a great sage named Gautama of celebrated vows; he arrived at the auspicious Prabhāsa-kṣetra from Bhṛgukalpa.
During the auspicious northern transit of the sun, desiring to behold the illustrious Someśa, he beheld the god Someśvara and bathed in all the sacred fords.
While traveling on a pilgrimage, he then went to Gātrotsarga.
Then, O Goddess, as that Brāhmaṇa reached the boundary, he beheld there a Vaiṣṇava forest dear to Viṣṇu.
And in that sacred field, extending for a hundred bows and enriched with the name of Puruṣottama, he beheld five most dreadful ghosts.
They were mounted upon great trees, possessing massive bodies and being exceedingly fierce; their hair stood erect, their ears were like spikes, and their frames were bound together with sinews.
Seeing those who were fleshless and bloodless, naked, and with blackened bodies, he was struck with terror and thought, "I am ruined! (23)
Having meditated for a very long time and exerting himself with great fortitude, he said: "Who are you, of such deformed appearance, whom I have seen before in the past? (24)
"Never before have I seen you like this; for what reason are you running through the middle of the field, so afflicted by great suffering? This is a source of great curiosity to me. (25)
The pretas said: "O illustrious one, we are pretas who have come here from afar; having heard of this most excellent and meritorious sacred site, we do not obtain entry. (26)
Rendered mangled by blows from the Gaṇas who had become invisible—namely Lekhaka, Rohaka, Sūcaka, and Śīghraga—[they fell]. || 27 ||
I am the fifth, named Paryuṣita, the greatest among evildoers. || 28 ||
Gautama said: "By whom were your names created in their entirety while you were engaged in the state of being ghosts? This is a great curiosity of mine. (29)
The pretas said: "He who writes upon the surface of the earth for a Brahmin who is begging, yet does not recite any reply, is known as a *lekhaka* (scribe). (30)
The second ascended the palace out of fear of the Brahmins; from him was born this one named Rohaka. Listen now, O Brahmin, to the third. (31)
By that sinful man, many Brahmins endowed with wealth were betrayed to the king; therefore, he became renowned on earth as "Sūcaka" (the Informer). || 32 ||
Though constantly entreated by the brahmins, he would always run away quickly; because he never gave anything, he is known as Śīghraga (the Swift-Runner). || 33 ||

"Because I gave stale and poor-quality food to the most excellent Brāhmaṇas, whereas my gift to Brāhmaṇas was always [of] nourishment with sweet food; therefore, I have become known by the name Paryuṣita on the surface of the earth. (34)
Gautama said: "Living beings on earth do not subsist without food. Tell me out of curiosity, what indeed is your food? (35)
The pretas said: "O best of the twice-born, whenever the time for a meal arrives and a battle breaks out, we consume the entire essence of that food. (36)
O best of the twice-born, that food which men eat upon the surface of the earth not smeared [with cow-dung], being devoid of purity—that indeed is our meal. (37)
But he who eats without having washed his feet, or who eats facing the south, or who eats with his head wrapped, the pretas always eat [his food]. (38)
If a dog, a woman in her menses, an outcaste, or a pig beholds the śrāddha, that food becomes our meal. (39)
Having bypassed a Brahmin who has come by hereditary succession and has been honored by his great-grandfathers, he who gives a gift to another with a dissatisfied mind [incurs sin]. (40)

Whatever merit arises from that gift, may it accrue to us. We shall eat in that house where there is always leftover food, where there is constant quarreling, and which is devoid of the Vaiśvadeva offering. || 41 ||
Gautama said: "In what kind of house is there no entry for you? Speak the truth, not untruth; truth is ever consistent with the virtuous. (42)
The pretas said: "O twice-born one, there is no entry for us into that house where the smoke-ascending flame arising from the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is seen. (43)
In whatever house the morning rites of smearing are performed and where the resonance of the Vedas is heard, there we have nothing at all. (44)
Gautama said: By what ripening of karma does a man go to the state of a preta? You ought to explain this to me in detail and exactly as it is. (45)
The pretas said: "Those who steal by falsehood, those who go about while still impure from eating, and those who have killed cows or Brahmins—indeed, they enter the state of being a preta. (46)
Those men who are devoted to backbiting, those who delight in giving false testimony, and those who do not abide by the side of justice, become hungry ghosts (pretas) after death. (47)
Those men who cast phlegm, urine, and excrement into a lake, having attained the state of a preta, wander about. || 48 ||
But those who, when gifts are being given to Brahmins, to cows, or to afflicted Brahmins, cry out "Do not give!", they too become ghosts (pretas). || 49 ||
If a Brahmin should die while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach, he will certainly go to the state of a ghost, even if he were a knower of the six Vedāṅgas.
That man who, intoxicated with pride, yokes three oxen to a plow—especially on the new moon day—is born as a preta.
The man who is an atheist, a reviler, base, one who abandons obligatory and occasional rites, and who truly hates Brahmins, is born as a preta. || 52 ||
A man who betrays trust, a killer of a Brahmin, one intent on the slaughter of women, a killer of cows, a murderer of his teacher, or a patricide is born as a preta. (53)
The man for whom the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites have not been performed, and for whom the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) has not taken place after death, is born as a *preta*.
All this that we were asked, O best of the twice-born, has indeed been explained. Speak further, O foremost of the twice-born, regarding whatever doubt you may still have. (55)
Gautama said: "Tell me in its entirety that ripening of karma by which a man is born as a *preta*; for I have a great curiosity regarding this. (56)
The pretas said: "That man who is devoted to pilgrimages, intent on the worship of the gods, and always devoted to brahmins, is not born as a preta. (57)
He who constantly listens to the scriptures, constantly serves the learned, and constantly consults the elders, does not become a preta. || 58 ||
For this reason, we have all arrived from a very great distance, and we are able to enter this meritorious and most excellent sacred field. || 59 ||
We are despondent in the form of hungry ghosts; therefore, O best of the twice-born, O highly fortunate one, please strive to become the refuge for us all. (60)
Gautama said: "Tell me in its entirety how liberation arises for you; with my heart filled with compassion, I shall strive [to achieve it], of this there is no doubt. (61)
The pretas said: "O Lord, for us who have remained in the state of pretas for a vast period of time, no man whatsoever has come who might become our refuge."
Therefore, go to the Vaiṣṇava field and offer us the śrāddha; by pronouncing our names and lineages, we shall then attain liberation.
Īśvara said: Then that Brāhmaṇa, filled with compassion, went to the house of Hari and performed the Śrāddha for each of them individually.
Whenever that best of the twice-born performed a śrāddha for anyone, that person would come to him in a dream at night and speak these words.
"O best of Brahmins, by your grace I am released from this state of being a ghost. May it be well with you; I shall now depart, for my celestial chariot has arrived. (66)
In this manner, those four best of the twice-born were delivered by him.
Then, when the fifth day had arrived, that best of brahmins performed the śrāddha ceremony for the stale food according to the prescribed rites.
Then, at the end of his dream, he saw a man who had arrived, one who was exhausted, speaking dejectedly, distressed, and sighing again and again. (69)
Paryuṣita said: "O Brahmin, no refuge has been found for me, an unfortunate sinner; for I have seized the wealth that had been collected for the sake of a pond. (70)
Gautama said: Tell me quickly and in its entirety how liberation arises for you; I shall perform it without doubt, even if it should be very difficult to achieve.
Paryuṣita said: "When the northern solstice has arrived, go to that sacred ford dear to Hari and certainly offer a śrāddha for me; from that, there will be a [favorable] destination."

The Lord said: Thus addressed by that ghost, the eminent brahmin sage, when the northern solstice had arrived, went to the holy ford dear to Hari and performed the śrāddha rite according to the rules for the sake of the deceased.
Then, having stayed there through the night, he spoke these words at the end of a dream, his face radiant and wearing a divine garland upon his body.
Paryuṣita said: "O best of the twice-born, by your grace I am liberated from the state of a ghost. May it be well with you; I shall depart, for a celestial chariot has indeed arrived for me. (75)
"I have attained divinity, O best of the twice-born; I am now capable. I grant you a boon, O Brahmin; accept this auspicious boon. (76)

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.

Gautama said: "O granter of boons, if you are capable and if a boon is to be granted to us, then in that place where I saw you, the pretas, in such great suffering, I shall establish a hermitage and perform supreme penance. (78)
Having bathed again at this great sacred ford, I have emerged from my home; there, whoever with devotion and with piety [performs rites] for the ancestors on behalf of the Sun-god... 79.

"Having bathed and offered libations to the deities, he shall perform the Śrāddha rite according to the rules; by your grace, O sirs, may the state of being a ghost never occur even in his lineage, even for one burdened with sin. (80)
Paryuṣita said: "Go to that hermitage there, O best of brahmins; you shall attain supreme perfection and you shall become famous in the world. (81)
In that place, those excellent men who devoutly offer the śrāddha ceremony for their ancestors shall depart for the abode of the gods, seated upon celestial chariots.
Not one born of their lineage shall ever fall into the state of a preta; the wise, firm in intellect, declare that friendship extends for seven steps. (83)
Out of regard for our friendship, listen to what I shall say: your hermitage shall become a sacred place upon the surface of the earth. (84)
"O Lord, may this place, which pacifies all sins and destroys all suffering, become renowned by my name as 'Pretatīrtha'. (85)
Ishvara said: Having promised him "So be it," that best of the twice-born went there and performed every rite according to the path prescribed in the Vedas.
He too, O beloved, having reached heaven, remained there rejoicing; all this is the ancient account concerning this place, Gātramocana.

The man who hears this correctly is liberated from all sins. He who beholds Puruṣottama during the yoga of His reclining and rising, and he who goes there at the time of His leaving His body, shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Puruṣottama-tīrtha and Preta-tīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 223 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga installed by Indra, known by the name Pāpamocana, located to the south of Puruṣottama.
In ancient times, having slain Vṛtra, Śakra was afflicted by the sin of killing a Brahmin; he spoke to the divine sages, asking, "How shall this [sin] depart? (2)
For the murder of a Brahmin is indeed difficult to behold, producing a change of complexion in me; it moves with a foul odor and destroys all vital energy. || 3 ||
Then the hosts of gods and the great sages, headed by Nārada, said to him: "O Lord of Gods, go to Prabhāsa; for that sacred field is indeed the remover of sins."
"Having propitiated Mahādeva there, you shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. Having promised "So be it," O fair-faced one, he went there.
He installed the linga of the trident-bearing God of gods and remained constantly devoted to its worship with incense, perfumes, and unguents.
Then, the foul odor of his body quickly vanished; all its discoloration disappeared, and his physique became most excellent.
Then, becoming joyful in mind, he spoke these words: "The man who comes there and worships him with devotion—" || 8 ||
"His sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin and the like, shall go to destruction. Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one, greatly delighted, departed for heaven.

Released from the sin of killing a Brahmin and being honored by the dwellers of heaven, one should there give the gift of a cow to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin, one should perform a Śrāddha ceremony there.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Indreśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 224 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Anarakeśvara, located in the northern direction from that place, which destroys all sins. I shall proclaim its majesty; listen with an attentive mind, O beloved. (1)

On the surface of the earth, there is a famous city named Mathurā. There, in former times, lived a renowned Brāhmaṇa known as Devaśarman; he belonged to the Agastya lineage, was indeed learned, but was oppressed by poverty.
Then, O Goddess of gods, there was another Brāhmaṇa there, endowed with such a form and age, who had mastered the Vedas and possessed that same name and lineage.
Then Yama spoke to the messenger with the fierce hair on his head: "Go, O messenger, quickly to Mathurā and bring Devaśarman here."
Then, having arrived from there and taken him, the messenger indeed went to that place; seeing him, Yama bowed and spoke to the messenger with great anger.
"O King, this Devaśarman was not commanded by me to be brought to you. There is another Devaśarman; bring him, whose life is spent. And take this long-lived Brahmin there without delay."

Īśvara said: Then the brāhmaṇa spoke: "O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall not go home; being utterly despondent because of poverty for as long as I live, I will spend the remainder of my life right here in your presence."
Yama said: "O best of brahmins, no one ever arrives here out of season; on this earth, no one indeed lives even for a moment beyond their full allotted span."
For this very reason, my name is renowned as Dharmarāja.
On this earth, there is no one who is my friend nor anyone who is my enemy; for even if pierced by a hundred arrows, no one dies before their time. (10)
Even if pierced by the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one does not live when the time has fully arrived; therefore, go, O best of the twice-born, before your body is consumed by fire.
Then that brāhmaṇa said: "O Lord, if you will send me, you ought to answer correctly the single question asked by me. (12)
O Lord, the sight of the virtuous never arises in vain anywhere; this is especially true in your case, and therefore I say this to you. (13)
O Yama, by what action does a human being go to those fierce and most dreadful hells that are seen here? (14)
How many in number are these hells, and what is their measurement? O best of gods, you should explain all of this to me exactly as it is. (15)
Yama said: Listen, O God, I shall declare how many hells exist; by which action a human being goes there, O best of the twice-born. Twenty-one hells are enumerated in my abode. (16)

Those evil-minded ones whose eyes were plucked out by iron-beaked crows were the very same who had gazed upon their wives.
O tiger among the twice-born, you shall always see these other sinners, who were full of passion, fallen into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
For these people are devoted to false testimony and likewise addicted to harsh speech; they [must embrace] pillars made of iron, heated and glowing with the brilliance of fire.
Those evil-minded ones who take pleasure in the wives of others embrace one another in the midst of the Vaitaraṇī river, which is thick with pus and blood.
O best of the twice-born, all those who stand as betrayers of trust are torn into pieces in the terrible Asipatravana hell—those who have fled, abandoning their master when battle was imminent. (22)
Indeed, those lowest of men who delight in betraying their masters and who propound fallacious arguments plunge into blazing heaps of burning coals. (23)
O best of the twice-born, those lowest of men, deprived of the gift of shoes, tread upon a path strewn with iron spikes while crying out in lamentation. (24)
Those who are bound face-down at the top of a tree over a fire, as well as all those lowest of men guilty of the murder of a Brahmin—[all these fall there]. || 25 ||
Those who delight in breaking their vows and who indeed cause harm to those observing vows are devoured by mosquitoes, bedbugs, crows, and birds. || 26 ||
For there are many more such as these who are tormented by the axe—the evil-minded killers of cows and revilers of the gods and Brahmins. (27)

Those who steal the property of others and those who carry off the wives of others are devoured by jackals and by wolves with mouths made of iron. Those sinful ones who, when hungry, eat their own flesh, [suffer likewise]. (28)
"O best of the twice-born, food has never been given by these; they drink blood soaked in fat and pus. They are always intent upon the destruction of Brāhmaṇas and cows. (29)
Bound to the Kūṭaśālmalī trees and tormented by sharp thorns, they remain constantly intent on seeking out the vulnerabilities of others.
But those who are cut by the saw, O best of the twice-born, are indeed those devoted to forbidden food and revilers of their own dharma. (31)
Those who sell their daughters and those who destroy the lives of maidens are indeed cast into the midst of excrement and cooked there by my servants.
Those whose tongues are repeatedly torn out by cruel messengers are indeed those devoted to the suppression of speech and intent upon false speech.
Those who are afflicted by cold and tremble again and again, yet are stealers of the property of gods and especially of Brahmins; || 34 ||
O best of the twice-born, a heavy burden has been placed upon their heads; therefore, O most excellent Brāhmaṇa, they are crying out with terrible shrieks. (35)
Yama said: "O best of the twice-born, thus has all this been fully explained to you—the true nature of the hells and of the karmas, in their proper order. (36)
Go quickly, O illustrious one, as long as the body has not yet been consumed by fire. || 37 ||
The Brāhmaṇa said: O best of gods, tell me everything with full attention—that action by which a human being shall never go to hell. (38)
Those skilled in wisdom say that friendship among the virtuous is established by walking seven steps together; therefore, honoring this bond of friendship, you should speak to me in brief. (39)
Yama said: Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa and beholding the supreme Narakeśvara with devotion, that man does not see hell.
O best of the twice-born, this secret which was established by me while endowed with devotion to Śiva has been told to you out of affection for you. 41.
"This must be guarded with great effort according to my word; of this there is no doubt. Having been addressed thus, the brahmin then departed for the earth of his own accord.
Having regained his body, he then experienced the utmost wonder, recollecting all those words of the wise Dharmarāja.
Having gone there, O lady of excellent hips, he constantly worshipped that Lord for as long as he lived, and thereafter attained supreme perfection.
Therefore, by beholding Him with devotion through every effort, even a man joined with sins does not go to hell. (45)
Whoever performs a śrāddha there according to the prescribed rite on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
There, a black antelope skin should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; for as many as are the number of sesame seeds, for so long is he honored in heaven.
Īśvara said: To the east of that very place, in the southwest of Pāpamocana, is the shrine renowned as Megheśvara, which destroys all sins.
When the fear of drought has arisen, one should perform a propitiatory rite right there; by means of water, the foremost of Brahmins should imbue the earth with the essence of Varuṇa.
Where the Liṅga established by the clouds is constantly worshipped, no fear of drought whatsoever arises there. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Megheśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 226 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga established by Balabhadra, which destroys great sins, located to the north of Gātrotsarga.
O Great Goddess, this great liṅga bestows the fruit of great siddhis; it was installed by Balabhadra according to the prescribed rites for the purification of sins.

He who worships that [deity] with devotion by means of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order, on the conjunction of the third lunar day and the Revatī asterism, shall attain the station of the Lord of Yoga.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Balabhadreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Mātṛsthāna, renowned as Bhairaveśa, which destroys all fear. || 1 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who is self-restrained should worship according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and excellent offerings of oblations.
The Yoginīs protect him on earth like mothers protecting their own son.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, situated to the northeast of Anarakeśa, O Goddess. || 1 ||
[This image], which was self-manifested and brought forth from the midst of the earth by Viṣṇu in ancient times for the sake of the liberation of the Yādavas and for the pacification of all sins.
Whoever performs a ritual bath there by some accumulation of merit, and likewise performs a śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
O Goddess, one shall obtain that same merit which one would acquire by giving away the entire universe, by bathing in the waters of the Jāhnavī on the full moon day of Kārtika.
But when the Kali age has arrived, even a sight [of this place] is difficult to obtain; how much more so, then, are bathing and giving gifts at Prabhāsa in the waters of the Jāhnavī?

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Gaṅgā," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity beloved of Gaṇapati, who is established right there, having been properly appointed by me for that purpose. || 1 ||

O Goddess, on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā dwells one intent on protecting the sacred field; whatever man worships him on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, [attains his desires]. || 2 ||
By means of divine offerings of sweetmeats, flowers, incense, and so forth, in due order, no obstacle arises for him as long as he dwells in that sacred field.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 230 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to where the river Jāmbavatī flows. In ancient times, she who was named Jāmbavatī, the beloved queen of Viṣṇu, asked the virtuous Arjuna: "O best of the Kurus, tell me news."
Having heard those words of hers, Arjuna, sighing repeatedly, spoke these words with a voice faltering with tears. || 2 ||
O blessed lady, we have been abandoned by the high-souled Yādavas.
Of the heroic Baladeva and the high-souled Sātyaki.
Exceedingly cruel and a perpetrator of evil deeds toward other heroes of the Yadu clan, he has arrived here desiring to live, though rejected by Vāsudeva.

Having heard of her husband’s death at the hands of Arjuna, that great chaste lady, radiant as fire, kindled a fire on the banks of the Gaṅgā; then, casting off her massive body, she emerged, having become a river.
Having taken all that ash of her husband from the funeral pyre, the virtuous and auspicious Jāmbavatī then entered the ocean, O Goddess.
O Goddess of gods, whatever woman performs a ritual bath there with devotion, no woman in her lineage shall ever suffer widowhood.
Therefore, with every effort, a man or a woman should perform a ritual bath there; they shall attain the supreme goal. (8)
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the well worshipped by the three worlds, located to the west of that sacred site of the high-souled Pandavas.
O Great Goddess, when the Pāṇḍavas had reached the forest and were wandering upon the surface of the earth, they arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then they dwelt there for some time with composed minds; subsequently, having gone to a highly meritorious sacred field, Kṛṣṇā spoke this.
Thousands of brahmins eat in your house; yet there is no reservoir of water nearby, nor are there so many servants. (4)
Therefore, a reservoir of water should be constructed near the hermitage, where I shall perform my ablutions through your grace. (5)
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, all those Pāṇḍavas together, impelled by the words of Draupadī, dug a well there.
Then the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, having heard that the sons of Pṛthā had arrived from Dvārāvatī along with their kinsmen, came to that very place accompanied by his own relatives.
And with Pradyumna, Sāmba, Gada, Niṣadha, Yuyudhāna, Rāma, and the wise Cārudeṣṇa.
Surrounded by other Yādava heroes who were intoxicated with the pride of battle, all those bulls among the Yādavas gathered together in accordance with propriety.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation and due to a certain other cause, Vāsudeva spoke these words to the son of Pāṇḍu: || 10 ||
O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, what may I do for you according to your desire? Shall it be the kingdom, grain, wealth, or perhaps the destruction of your enemies? (11)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O best of the Yādavas, you are undoubtedly capable of performing all tasks. Previously, you promised that after twelve years, you would do what is pleasing."
O Lord of the World, adored by all the gods, when you are pleased, there is nothing on this earth that cannot be accomplished within the three worlds. (13)
If you are indeed pleased with me, O Lord of all the worlds, then come and remain eternally present here in this well, O Janārdana.
"O Keśava, whatever man comes here and performs his bath with devotion, may he go to the abode of Viṣṇu by your grace. (15)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, "So shall it be," and having taken leave of Yudhiṣṭhira, Kṛṣṇa, who is worshipped by all the worlds, departed for Dvārakā.
Having performed a śrāddha ceremony there, a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha) through the grace of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor. || 17 ||
One obtains half of that merit by libations alone, and one-fourth from bathing; therefore, one should perform a Śrāddha ceremony there with every possible effort.
He who performs a ritual bath and a śrāddha on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, and likewise worships Sāvitrī, shall go to the supreme abode.
A gift of cows should be given there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage. || 20 ||
The Lord said: O Goddess, one who is purified by contemplation should worship five liṅgas in that very place; they were installed, O Queen of the Gods, by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas. || 1 ||
He who worships them with devotion shall be liberated from all sins. || 2 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pāṇḍaveśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 233 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the holy ford renowned throughout the three worlds, named Daśāśvamedhika, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
O beautiful lady, in former times Bharata, having arrived there and considering it an unsurpassed sacred field, performed ten horse-sacrifices.
There, O beautiful lady, the thousand-eyed Indra was satisfied by Somanātha, while the wretched brahmins were gratified with food, drink, and sacrificial fees.

Then all the thirty gods, being well-pleased, spoke to King Bharata: "O mighty-armed one, we are satisfied and have been fully gratified by your sacrifices; choose a boon, O Indra among kings, whatever dwells in your heart. (4)
The King said: "May that man who, having come here, performs his ablutions with devotion, obtain the auspicious fruit of ten horse-sacrifices."

The gods said: "One shall obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices through faith. O Indra among kings, this sacred site on the surface of the earth shall attain renown by the name 'Daśāśvamedhika'; no doubt should be entertained in this matter."
Īśvara said: From that time forward, that sacred site became renowned upon the surface of the earth as Daśāśvamedhika, the destroyer of all sins.
Starting from Gomukha up to Aśvamedhika, relying on the region between Indra and Varuṇa—within this interval, O Great Goddess, the wise know this to be a sacred field (śivakṣetra) of Śiva.
Divine, removing all sins, and resembling a staircase to heaven—that place is proclaimed to be the abode of ten million holy sites (tīrthas).
When one gives up their life there, they rejoice in the world of Śiva; even sinful beings born of animal wombs, such as insects, birds, and wild beasts, [attain this]. || 10 ||
They too go to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells, as do the maternal and paternal ancestors through the offering of water with sesame seeds.
His ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings; for there, in former times, innumerable supreme sacrifices were performed by Brahmā.
And Śakra attained the sovereignty over the gods by performing sacrifices there; likewise, Kārttavīrya performed a hundred sacrifices at that very place in ancient times.
Thus, O beloved, that preeminent place at the very heart of the field bestows the state of non-rebirth upon the creatures who die there.
Furthermore, he who, having purified his soul, performs the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) there, is honored in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the bull's body.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Daśāśvamedha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 234 ||
Īśvara said: One should behold three unsurpassed liṅgas situated in that very place, namely Śatamedha, Sahasramedha, and Koṭimedha, in that order.
To the south is Śatamedha, which bestows the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; it was there in ancient times that Kārtavīrya performed a hundred sacrifices.
Having installed the great Liṅga that destroys all sins, [he established] there in the central part the Liṅga renowned as Koṭimedha.
There, ten million supreme sacrifices were previously performed by Brahmā, after he had installed Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
Situated on its northern side is the place known as Sahasrakratu; there, Śakra, the king of the gods, performed a thousand sacrifices.

Having installed the great Liṅga, the primordial deity of the gods, according to the prescribed rites with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); || 6 ||
O Goddess, he shall gradually obtain the fruit arising from the name of the Liṅga; however, a gift of a cow should be given there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage.
O beautiful lady, ten lakhs of sacred fords (tīrthas) reside there, and likewise, three lingas situated in the center destroy all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Three Liṅgas beginning with Śatamedha," within the "Majesty of Daśāśvamedha" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 235.

Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Durvāsāditya, where Durvāsas performed austerities for a thousand years, abstaining from food, having conquered his appetite, and being solely intent upon the propitiation of the Sun.
Thus, after a long time, the sun-god of divine splendor, having appeared before his very eyes, spoke to the great sage, O lord of men.
Sūrya said: "O Brahmin, do not act rashly; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows! I shall grant you even that which is unattainable, whatever dwells in your mind. (3)
Durvāsas said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of a boon, you should remain in this place as long as the earth endures."
"May this [image] attain fame in this world by the name Durvāsāditya; as for this beautiful image of yours which has been consecrated by me," (5)

O Lord, Master of the Universe, may Your very presence abide in that place; and let Yamunā, Your daughter, also manifest her presence here, as well as Your son, the highly effulgent and mighty Dharmarāja.
Sūrya said: O best of sages, all this that you have spoken shall come to pass; and there shall be another ten million holy sites, such as the Gaṅgā and others, O great sage.
"By my word, O Brahmin, it is certain that he will come to your place; I must remain in this place together with the deities."
O great sage, by the power of the Ādityas who dwell within the belly of the cosmic egg, and endowed with their majesty, I shall remain here.
Whatever fruit is obtained simply by seeing a thousand suns, that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the sight of the Durvāsāditya.
"All living beings shall likewise obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices. Having spoken thus, the Sun then remembered his own daughter, as well as Dharmarāja, the controller of all living beings.
As soon as she was remembered, that goddess, in the form of a river and accompanied by ten million holy bathing places (tīrthas), pierced the surface of Pātāla and rose up there.
And there, the Lord Yama, the wielder of the staff of time, then spoke with affection to Sūrya, the witness of the world.
Yama said: "Let the Lord, the Master of the World, command me and Yamunā; whatever task pertains to the future purpose, I shall perform it without a doubt."
Sūta said: "In this sacred field, you must remain in your own form at my command; furthermore, the protection of sinful living beings here must be carried out with great effort. (15)
The Brāhmaṇas who are householders and devoted to the Sun should always be protected; and you too, O Yamunā, shall be present here together with Koṭitīrtha.
"Dwell here, be well-pleased in this place born of Durvāsas," having spoken thus to Durvāsas there, the Lord of the Gods [remained].

"Thus they spoke, O Goddess; then those sages, their eyes red with anger, looked at one another after being thus deceived by those evil-minded ones. (13)

"From this day forward, in all the households of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas here, no liquor or fermented spirits shall be prepared by any of those residing within the realm—whether for Janārdana, Rāma, or the high-souled Babhru."
And if any man anywhere should do what is known to you in this manner, he shall mount the stake alive, having acted thus together with his kinsmen.

The blazing fire whirls toward the left, emitting distinct flames of blue, crimson, and madder-red.

There, a golden chariot should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, dedicated to Śiva according to the prescribed rite; one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand pilgrimages. || 4 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Hiraṇyā River," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 238 ||

Then, O Goddess, as they were reflecting, sweat arose from the bodies of them all; and because of their restraint, they took it up.
There, a divine maiden with lotus-like eyes was born; she stood before everyone, pervading all the directions.
Then he spoke to all the gods: "For what purpose have I been created? I shall perform that task for you," having heard her words at that time.
They reported her distress and that deed of Ruru to the gods; having heard it, that goddess laughed for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
As she laughed, beautiful young maidens emerged once more, all bearing nooses and goads, with full hips and breasts.
Terrifying all that is moving and unmoving with the mere sound of her shrieks, that illustrious woman followed after the deer along with them.
Then there occurred a tumultuous and terrible battle between them and those [demons], with various kinds of fierce weapons and missiles that brought about the destruction of the enemy host.
By those [blows], all his followers were shattered by the strikes; in an instant they turned their faces away from the fight, and some were struck down. || 14 ||
Then, seeing his army destroyed, Ruru created an illusion called Tāmasī, O Goddess of Gods; yet she was not at all deluded by it.
Then, when everything there had become shrouded in darkness, the goddess pierced the Daitya Ruru in the heart with her spear, and he immediately fell into a swoon.
Then, regaining consciousness after a moment and realizing her prowess, he made an effort to flee and went toward the ocean.
Then that goddess also followed behind that evil-minded one, being praised by hosts of gods, kinnaras, and great serpents.
Then, having entered the ocean and seen that Dānava, she angrily severed his head with the tip of her sword; thereafter, she held a shield and a skull.
She emerged from there once more and arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa, accompanied by an army of many forms and radiant splendor.
The gods beheld that excellent lady bearing a shield and a skull with great amazement; then the gods, standing with palms joined in reverence, offered hymns of praise.
The gods said: Victory to you, O Goddess Cāmuṇḍā! Victory, O remover of spirits! Victory, O omnipresent Goddess! O Kālarātri, homage be to you! 22.
O you of terrifying form, O Śivā, O Vidyā, O Mahāmāyā, O Mahodayā! O highly fortunate one, O Jayā, O Jṛmbhā, O Bhīmākṣī, O Bhīmadarśanā! || 23 ||
O Mahāmāyā, O you of variegated limbs, O auspicious one fond of song and dance! O Vikarālī, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā, O you whose form is Time! || 24 ||

O goddess with a spear in hand, with a staff in hand, with terrible hands, with a fearsome face; O Cāmuṇḍā, with a blazing mouth, with sharp fangs, possessed of great strength; O Goddess seated upon a corpse-vehicle, attended by hosts of spirits! || 25 ||
Thus praised then by all, headed by Śakra, the Goddess, her face beaming with joy, spoke these words.
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever has long been in your hearts; I shall grant all of it, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (27)
The gods said: "O blessed lady, you have accomplished your purpose by the destruction of the Dānava."
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, whoever praises you with this hymn, O all-pervading and eternal Goddess, may you become the bestower of boons upon him. (29)
O Goddess, whoever shall listen with devotion to this account of your origin, being liberated from all sins, may he attain the supreme goal. (30)
O auspicious Goddess, you must always maintain your presence in this sacred field. || 31 ||
Whoever, being composed, worships you here on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina, their undertaking shall always be auspicious. || 32 ||
Ishvara said: Having been addressed thus, the Great Goddess remained intent right there; the gods, their enemies slain, went to heaven filled with joy. || 33 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kumārī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 242 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Kṣetrapāla of great splendor, the deity situated in the northeast, adorned with garlands of mantras.
Having taken recourse to the bank of the Hiraṇyā for the sake of protection, he establishes his guard right there at that sacred field of Hīraka.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, a person should worship him there with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and likewise with the presentation of oblations.
Thus worshipped, the God becomes the bestower of all desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Maṃtrāvali Kṣetrapāla," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 243 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the most excellent Vicitreśvara, which is situated on the bank of the Hiraṇyā and is the destroyer of great sins.
O Great Goddess, after performing most fierce penance, Vicitra established a linga there for Yama.
Having seen that, O Goddess, a man does not behold the world of Yama. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vicitreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to that very place situated above, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, to the west of Parṇāditya.
There stands a very great liṅga established by Brahmā in ancient times; it is renowned as Brahmeśvara and is the destroyer of all sins.

Having bathed there on the second lunar day, fasting and with senses subdued, one should worship the auspicious Brahmeśvara, the Lord of the God of Gods, by name; and if one desires the eternal state, one should offer libations to the ancestors during a śrāddha ceremony.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 245 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Piṅgalī, the destroyer of sins, a river flowing to the ocean located to the west of Ṛṣitīrtha.
O Goddess, by beholding her, a man becomes handsome in form. In ancient times, great sages arrived there with the desire to see Someśvara. || 2 ||
Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa and established themselves on the riverbank, O Great Goddess, those southerners were dark-complexioned and deformed. (3)
Having bathed there in that excellent hermitage and beholding their own forms, they were all filled with supreme wonder as they saw them to be identical to Kāma.
Then they all together, their eyes wide with wonder, said: "Since we have all bathed here and attained a tawny (piṅga) complexion, from this time forward her name shall be Piṅgā."
Moreover, those who perform their ablutions there, endowed with supreme devotion, shall have no one of ill-favored appearance born in their lineage.
By the mere sight of Pitṛmedha, a human being shall obtain its fruit; by bathing there, the merit is doubled, and by offering libations, it is quadrupled.
"Innumerable shall be the fruit for him who performs a śrāddha here. Having spoken thus, O lady of excellent complexion, all the sages then [departed].
All those best of sages divided that riverbank and established sacred fords (tīrthas) everywhere, each as large as a sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta).

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Piṅgā River," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 246 ||
Īśvara said: One should behold the Sun, the destroyer of sins, stationed in that very place; likewise, one should behold the goddess Piṅgalā, who assumes the form of Pārvatī. || 1 ||
He who especially observes a fast on the third lunar day attains all desires; he shall become wealthy and possessed of sons.
Right there, one should behold the one known as Śukeśvara; having seen him, O Goddess, a human being shall be liberated from all sins.
