Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Piṅgalāditya, Piṅgādevī, and Śukreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 247.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place previously mentioned as worshipped by Brahmā, situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī to the west of Parṇāditya.
I shall declare its origin; listen with a focused mind, O beloved, as Brahmā was formerly creating the fourfold collection of living beings.
A woman with lotus-like eyes appeared, richly endowed with a wonderful form; she had a neck like a conch shell, beautiful hair, lips red as the bimba fruit, and a slender waist.
She had a deep navel, beautiful hips, and full hips and breasts; her face was like the full moon, her ankles were hidden, and her countenance was fair.
Neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman possessed such a form as that beautiful woman who was born. || 5 ||
Seeing her endowed with such beauty, Brahmā fell under the power of desire; he then solicited her for the sake of pleasure, O lady of excellent complexion.
Then, O Great Goddess, as he was making his request, his fifth head fell off instantly due to that sin, assuming the form of a donkey.
Then, having realized the great sin arising from lust committed by his daughter, he was filled with supreme remorse and went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Since there is no purity of the body without immersion in a sacred ford, he has bathed in the holy waters of the Sarasvatī, O fair-faced one.
He installed the linga of the trident-bearing God of gods; then, having become free from sin, he returned once more to his own home.
Whoever, having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī, beholds that Liṅga, is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The man who beholds him on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmeśvara," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the god Saṅgameśvara, renowned as "A Hundred Thousand Cows" (Golakṣa), which destroys all sins. || 1 ||
On its very western side is the bestower of the fruits of all desires; for in ancient times, there lived a great ascetic named the sage Uddālaka.
O Goddess of the Suras, having previously reached the confluence that destroys all sins, he performed austerities at the meeting of the Sarasvatī and the Piṅgā.
Then, O beautiful one, as that high-souled one, endowed with devotion, was performing fierce penance, a linga rose up before him.
At that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O mighty-armed Uddālaka, listen to these words of mine."
"From this day forward, my residence shall be here eternally; since this most excellent Liṅga has arisen here at the confluence (saṃgama), its name shall be Saṃgameśvara."
Having performed their ablutions at the world-renowned confluence, those men who behold Saṅgameśvara attain the supreme goal.
Īśvara said: Then he worshipped him day and night without weariness; subsequently, at the end of his body, he went to where Maheśvara resides.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Saṅgameśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga renowned throughout the three worlds, celebrated as Gaṅgeśvara, located to the west of Saṃgameśvara.
O lady of beautiful countenance, when the Gaṅgā was summoned by the powerful Viṣṇu at the time of his own final bath for the purpose of consecration; || 2 ||
Then, having seen that holy field frequented by sages, which was everywhere pervaded by lingas and hermitages of ascetics; (3)
Then Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, flowing toward the eastern ocean and devoted to the worship of Śiva, installed that liṅga.
Upon seeing it, O lady of excellent hips, a person obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; he attains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 5 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gaṅgeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 250 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Śaṅkarāditya, which was established by Śaṅkara to the east of Gaṅgeśvara.
And whoever shall worship him on the sixth day of the bright fortnight will go to the supreme abode where the god Divākara dwells.
The man who, being composed in mind, places red flowers mixed with red sandalwood in a copper vessel and offers this arghya, shall attain supreme perfection and shall never fall into poverty. || 3 ||
Therefore, O lady of beautiful countenance, one should with every effort worship Śaṅkarāditya in that sacred field, who bestows the fruits of all desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śaṅkarāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga renowned throughout the three worlds; there, it is famous as Śaṅkaranātha, the destroyer of sins.
O Goddess, having performed great penance there, Bhānu established [the deity]; and having fasted, he worshipped that Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods.

There, one who has conquered the senses should feed Brāhmaṇas and perform a Śrāddha ceremony; with a concentrated mind, he should give gold and garments to a learned Brāhmaṇa according to his ability. He goes to the supreme abode—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śaṅkaranātha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 252 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Gupheśvara, located on the northern side of the Hiraṇyā river, which destroys all sins. Upon seeing it, O Goddess, a human being dispels the sin of ten million killings.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gupheśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: One should behold Ghaṇṭeśvara, situated in that very place, which destroys all sins; he is renowned as such, worshipped by gods and demons, honored by sages and Siddhas, and the bestower of the fruits of desired objects. (1)
The man who worships him on the eighth lunar day falling on a Monday shall obtain his desired wishes and indeed be liberated from sin.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ghaṇṭeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 254 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the holy site renowned throughout the three worlds, located on the western side of that very place, belonging to the sages of meritorious deeds.
O beautiful lady, even today three-eyed fish are seen there; likewise Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Sumati, and Susakhī.
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, Pratimardana, Raibhya, Bṛhaspati, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, and Bhṛgu. || 3 ||
Durvāsas, Jāmadagnya, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava; Uśanas, Bharadvāja, Yavakrīta, and likewise Trita. || 4 ||
Nārada and Parvata, as well as Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī.
Kāṇva, Gautama, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Akṛtavraṇa, Jamadagni, Rāma, Baka, and others such as these, as well as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana accompanied by his sons and disciples.
Having reached this sacred field of Prabhāsa, O best of sages, those high-souled ones performed various kinds of most wonderful austerities.
Thus, those ascetics of self-restrained nature, endowed with self-control, seek to conquer the eternal world of Brahmā through meditative absorption.
Then, O beloved, at one time there occurred a great drought; indeed, all the people there fell into distress, afflicted by hunger.
Then, when food had disappeared from this world, those who desired to preserve themselves took a dead child and, having fallen into distress, cooked him at that time.
Then King Vṛṣādarbhi, the ruler of the upper regions, seeing those sages suffering there, spoke these words at that time.
The king said: "Acceptance of gifts is seen as an irreproachable means of livelihood for Brahmins; therefore, O bulls among sages, accept a gift from me."
"I shall bestow upon you mung beans, black gram, rice, as well as gems and gold, and whatever else is difficult to obtain. Therefore, all of you, turn back from this supreme sin. (13)
The sages said: "O King, knowing that to be so, how can we accept a gift from you?"
A butcher is equal to ten slaughter-houses; a liquor-distiller is equal to ten butchers; a prostitute is equal to ten liquor-distillers; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. (15)
The Brahmin who, deluded by greed, accepts gifts from kings, is cooked in the terrible hells such as Tāmisra. || 16 ||
"Therefore, go; may it be well with you, O King, along with this gift. Let this be given to others. Having spoken thus, they departed for the forest. (17)
Then, having gone there at the king's command, the ministers scattered udumbara fruits containing gold within them upon the ground.
Then, O lady of excellent complexion, those sages sifted through them; however, having realized that they were heavy, Aṅgiras said, "These should not be taken."
Atri said: "O fool, we were not [as you think]; we were ignorant-minded. We now know these [ornaments] to be made of gold; we have awakened from our stupor. (20)
Vasiṣṭha said: He who accumulates wealth for the sake of dharma is not praised; Vasiṣṭha considers the accumulation of austerity to be the true accumulation of wealth.
Abandon all accumulations, which are the source of calamities for all beings; for no one who possesses accumulations is seen to be free from misfortune. (22)
To the extent that a Brahmin does not accept improper gifts, to that same extent his spiritual luster increases incessantly.
I weighed possessionlessness and sovereignty on a scale; possessionlessness was superior even to sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (24)
Kaśyapa said: This great accumulation of wealth is a misfortune for a Brāhmaṇa; even when deluded by the power of riches, a twice-born man falls away from the highest good.
For the attainment of wealth leads indeed to delusion and to much sorrow; therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon from afar that wealth which is called a calamity.
For even one who possesses wealth for the sake of dharma, that wealth is not seen [to be truly beneficial]; for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. (27)
Bharadvāja said: The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth of an aging man decay; the eyes and ears also decay; but craving alone does not decay. (28)
Just as a seamstress brings together the needle, the thread, and the cloth, so too is craving established as the needle for the thread of saṃsāra. (29)

Just as the horn of a ruru deer grows as its body grows, so too does craving—which is shoreless, difficult to restrain, and always bestowing suffering—always increase when unrighteousness abounds; therefore, one should utterly abandon it.
Gautama said: Who, being contented, is not able to subsist even on fruits? Yet everyone, through the greed of the senses, plunges into calamities. (31)
For one whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere; indeed, for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the entire earth is as if covered with leather.
How can that happiness which belongs to those of peaceful mind, satisfied by the nectar of contentment, belong to those greedy for wealth and of restless mind? (33)
Viśvāmitra said: "If the desire of one who longs for an object is indeed fulfilled, then another desire pierces him even more deeply with its arrow."
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. (35)
A man who, out of greed, longs for sensual pleasures does not thrive in happiness; he is like a man who, having reached the shade of a tree, still desires a palace.
He who dwells alone in the forest is one who has achieved his purpose, not the king who enjoys this earth bounded by the four oceans. (37)
Jamadagni said: "The great man who is capable of receiving gifts but increases his ascetic merit does not perform penance for that gift; rather, it is born back to him a thousandfold. (38)
For those who are capable of receiving gifts but have desisted from accepting them, the very same worlds belong that belong to those who give, even though they do not receive.
Arundhatī said: Just as the lotus fiber is always situated throughout the stalk, so too is thirst—without beginning or end—constantly dependent upon the body.

That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, and which is a disease that ends only with life—happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving. (41)
Caṇḍa said: "Since even these great lords fear accepting gifts from one who is fierce, I too am afraid, like a weakling before those who are stronger. (42)
Paśumukha said: Whatever those who are wise and ever devoted to dharma practice, that very same thing should be done by a learned man who desires his own welfare. (43)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus and having abandoned those fruits containing gold within them, all the sages of firm vows departed for another place.
Then, as they were wandering about, O lady of excellent complexion, they beheld a truly vast lake filled on all sides with lotus ponds.
At that time, the wandering mendicant Śunomukha arrived at that place; together with him, all those great sages bathed there.
Having entered there, they took the lotus stalks and, having placed them on the shore of the lake, performed the meritorious water-libation rites.
Then, having emerged from that water and come together with one another, they did not see those lotus stalks and spoke these words: || 48 ||
The sages said: "O lords of sages, by which evildoer have all those lotus stalks been taken from us, who were tormented by hunger? (49)
Suspecting one another, those best of the twice-born questioned each other; O beautiful lady, they all took oaths according to the prescribed rule.
Kaśyapa said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks become an eater of all things; may he commit the betrayal of a trust; may he become a perjured witness. (51)

Vasiṣṭha said: May he who has sexual intercourse with another’s wife, especially during her season, become a guest to them both; and may he who steals the lotus stalks likewise become their guest. (52)
Bharadvāja said: May he who steals the lotus stalks indeed become cruel, arrogant because of his prosperity, envious, and a slanderer. (53)
Viśvāmitra said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks be constantly devoted to sensual pleasure, may he practice sexual intercourse during the day, and may he be intent upon base deeds. (54)
Jamadagni said: "May he who steals the lotus stalks give his daughter to an old man; may he become the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) and be a perpetual usurer. (55)
Gautama said: "Let him accept gifts from a low-caste person, let him engage in the sale of horses, let him utter insults against his guru, and let him commit the theft of lotus stalks. (56)
Atri said: May that evil-minded one who steals the lotus stalks constantly disregard his mother and father, and may he consult a Śūdra regarding matters of dharma. (57)
Arundhatī said: Let that woman of wicked conduct, who committed the theft of the lotus stalks, eat and sleep before her husband. (58)
Caṇḍā said: "She who acts in opposition to her master, who harbors hatred for dharma, who is intent on hating the virtuous, and who commits the theft of lotus stalks—[may she be born as such]. (59)
Paśumukha said: "May he who steals lotus stalks always go into the service of others, birth after birth, and be devoid of all religious duties and rites. (60)
Śunomukha said: "Let him who steals the lotus stalks study the Vedas according to the rules, let him be a householder fond of guests, and let him speak the truth constantly. (61)
The sages said: "O Śunomukha, this oath which you have sworn is pleasing to the twice-born; you have committed the theft of the lotus stalks for us all."
Śunomukha said: "O twice-born ones, these lotus stalks have indeed been taken by me; know me to be Purandara, desiring to hear about dharma. (63)
O best of sages, through non-attachment the imperishable worlds have indeed been conquered; therefore, request a pure boon, for all this shall undoubtedly be yours.

The sages said: "A man who, having come here, remains pure and fasts for three nights, and having performed his ablutions and offered libations to the ancestors, should perform the śrāddha ceremony with a concentrated mind. (65)
"O Purandara, may he obtain the merit arising from all sacred fords; may he not fall into a lower state, but rejoice together with the gods. Having said, "So be it," Śakra then vanished on the spot.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ṛṣitīrtha," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 255.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should proceed with a concentrated mind to Nandāditya, which was formerly established right there by Nanda of immeasurable intellect.
In ancient times, King Nanda was indeed the bestower of happiness upon all the world; there was neither famine nor disease, nor untimely death among men.
While that knower of Dharma was ruling, there was no fear caused by lack of rain; however, after some time had passed, due to the influence of past karma, [the following occurred]. (3)

Afflicted by a severe case of leprosy, he attained the highest state of detachment. While overcome by that disease, he installed the Sun-god, the Lord of Gods, on the bank of a river, and he was thereby liberated from his ailment.
The Goddess said: Why is this king, a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, afflicted by disease? Even though he is devoted to dharma, from what cause has this onset of illness arisen?
Īśvara said: This powerful King Nanda, who was ever devoted to dharma and right conduct, wandered through all the worlds while seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
A celestial chariot was indeed granted to him by Viṣṇu himself out of satisfaction; it moved at will, possessed a beautiful color, and resounded with the cries of peacocks.
Once, while wandering there, that best of kings arrived at the divine Lake Mānasa, which was frequented by hosts of gods.
There he saw a large white lotus situated in the middle of a lake, and upon it stood a most excellent person, the size of a thumb.
Seeing him covered in red garments, two-armed, and possessing fierce splendor, he said to his charioteer: "Bring this lotus here."
But by bearing this upon my head in the presence of all the world, I shall become worthy of praise; therefore, bring it without delay.
Having been addressed thus by him, O woman of excellent complexion, the charioteer entered and proceeded to seize that lotus. As soon as the lotus was touched, the sound "hum" arose.
And at that very moment, by that sound, the king became a leper, his complexion vanished, and he was deprived of strength and vigor. || 13 ||
Then, having seen the Tathāgata and himself, that bull among men stood right there, afflicted with grief and wondering, "What is this? (14)
While he was thus reflecting, the wise Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and a man of great asceticism, arrived; and the king questioned him.
"O Blessed One, this transformation of my body has occurred; with my self overcome by leprosy, I have no desire to live. (16)
O Brahmin, tell me the remedy for one who is afflicted by disease; is it a vow, or perhaps another practice, or even charity or sacrifice? (17)
Vasiṣṭha said: This lotus, named Brahmodbhava, is renowned throughout the three worlds; by merely beholding it, all the deities shall be seen. || 18 ||
O King, this lotus is seen by the fortunate somewhere or other; indeed, as soon as it is seen, the man who enters the water [attains his goal]. (19)
"Completely liberated from all sins, he shall attain the state of Nirvana. Having seen this, your charioteer entered the water to retrieve it. (20)
O Indra among kings, by your word that man who is diseased shall become dead; even though I am the son of Brahmā, because of that I behold the Supreme Lord.
And coming day after day, you have seen him again; the gods constantly cherish this desire in their hearts.
"Having seen the Brahma-lotus in the mind and having bathed there, when shall we attain the supreme Brahman, reaching which there is no rebirth? (23)
And hear this second reason further, O King, why you have contracted leprosy for desiring to take away the lotus. (24)
Pradyotana himself is established within this womb; it was upon seeing this excellent lotus that this thought occurred to you.
"I bear upon my head this ornament of the world; yet while I was reflecting on this, such evil was revealed by the Lord. (26)
Therefore, propitiate that Sun-god with every effort; through the grace of the God of gods, you shall be liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Go, O Indra among kings, to Prabhāsa, the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds; there, on this earth, success shall swiftly come to afflicted living beings.
Īśvara said: Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, he reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa on the auspicious bank of the Māheśvarī.
Having installed Naṇdāditya, O Goddess, he worshipped him with perfumes, incense, ointments, and likewise with various kinds of flowers.
Then the Lord of Day, being pleased with him, said, "I am the giver of boons. || 31 ||
Nanda said: "Behold me, O best of gods, pervaded by a great leprosy; act, O Sun, in such a way that this may come to an end. (32)
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, remain ever present in this place.
Sūrya said: "O great king, you shall become free from disease this very instant. Furthermore, those men on earth who come here and behold me," || 34 ||

Those who go [to this place] on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day shall attain the supreme goal. On this seventh day, my presence here on a Sunday will occur; of this there is no doubt. I shall depart; may you be happy.
Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One vanished right there.

Having attained freedom from disease and having ruled an unsurpassed kingdom, he went to the supreme abode where the divine Sun-god dwells. Having bathed in that sacred ford and having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) with diligence, a man [attains the same].
Having beheld Nandāditya once again, one shall not return to the state of a mortal; there, one should bestow a tawny cow upon a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Having fasted for a day and night, or likewise having given a cow of ghee, it is impossible for anyone to calculate the measure of his merit.
Thus, O fair-hipped one, the majesty of the God of gods, whose radiance is blazing, has been told to you; it is the destroyer of all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Nandāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Tritakūpa, located three yojanas to the east of Nandāditya.
Formerly, O Indra among kings, there was in the region of Saurāṣṭra a wise man known as Ātreya, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
To him, who approached his wife only during her fertile period, three sons were born: Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, O beautiful lady.
Among them, the youngest was the most learned, having mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; he was endowed with every virtue, while the two elder brothers were fools.
Then, after some time, the best of the twice-born, Ātreya, having performed extensive austerities, met his end according to the law of time.
Then, among them, Trita became the king, being the most virtuous; he took up the burden which his son had previously borne.
The thought arose in him: "How shall I perform the sacrifice? Having invited the best of the twice-born who are established in the performance of sacrificial rites."

Having invoked all the gods, beginning with Indra, according to the prescribed rites, that twice-born man set out for Prabhāsa to provide sacrificial fees for the best of the brahmins; taking his two elder brothers with him, he departed for the sake of the cows.
Whichever house that Trita, a master of the Vedas, would visit, in each of those places he received excellent worship as well as abundant cattle.
Thus, O Goddess, having obtained that wealth of cattle, he set out for home accompanied by his two brothers, having attained supreme contentment.
Trita went before them, and those two brothers followed behind; driving the wealth of cattle, they arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then, seeing that great wealth of cattle brought for the purpose of giving, a sinful thought arose in the minds of the three brothers.
Those two brothers of wicked intent said to one another: "Trita is skilled in sacrifices and likewise proficient in the Vedas."
"Respected and honored everywhere, we two are fools and useless; for Trita will indeed give all this wealth of cattle at the excellent sacrifice. (14)
Whatever has been obtained from our father should be shared equally; therefore, it is indeed proper that the killing of this one who knows the three Vedas should take place right here.
Having thus made their resolution, both brothers set out; Trita, however, went ahead—free from doubt, straightforward, and wise.
Then, O Goddess, a tiger of most fierce appearance rose up there; with its mouth wide open, it let out a terrifying roar. || 17 ||
At his sound, those cows that had been lost fled in the ten directions; in that region, a great and terrible blind well appeared. || 18 ||
On one side was a fierce tiger, and on the other, an extremely dreadful well; seeing this, all those brothers, agitated by fear, fled in every direction.
Then, O beautiful lady, having reached the uneven bank of the well, they stood there until the tiger had gone, and then they set their minds on departing.
Then, O Goddess, O best of kings, Trita was cast by those two brothers into a dreadful well that was dilapidated and devoid of water.
Then, taking that wealth of cattle, they set out with joyful minds; however, Trita fell there into a well devoid of water.

The wise one reflected: "I do not grieve for my life. I have invited the best of the twice-born, masters of the Vedas, for the sake of a sacrifice; all the gods, headed by Indra, are also summoned. Without you, that sacrifice would not take place. (23)
Having mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, O woman of excellent complexion, he reflected thus and commenced a mental sacrifice right there.
Having himself recited the hymns again and again, that best of the twice-born performed an oblation of sand; by that, the deities were gratified.
Having perceived his faith, the deities were once again satisfied; they approached the brahmin standing in the middle of the well and spoke to him. (26)
The gods said: "O Brahmin, we have surely been fully gratified by you through this mental sacrifice; therefore, speak what is in your mind. (27)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O gods, if you are pleased with me, then upon emerging from the well, I shall go to my own home as a sacrificer and perform a sacrifice to the gods. (28)
Ishvara said: Then, commanded by the gods, Sarasvatī emerged from that well, pierced the earth, and filled it with her waters.
Then, having departed, that brahmin went toward his own abode; from that time forward, O Goddess of the Gods, it is called Tritakūpa.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should then offer libations to the ancestors; freed from all sins, one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
O Goddess of gods, the gift of sesame seeds there, especially when accompanied by gold, is highly recommended; O beautiful lady, that holy site is eternally dear to the ancestors.
"O Goddess, those who are remembered as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs and the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, who are divine—verily, their presence is here. (33)
O best of goddesses, by the mere sight of that sacred ford, living beings are indeed liberated from the sin accumulated from birth until the end of death.
Therefore, having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, one who desires his own welfare should perform a ritual bath there with every effort. (35)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Tritakūpa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 257 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Śaśāpāna; to the south of that very spot is a holy ford (tīrtha) that destroys all sins.
O beloved, listen as I tell you the origin of that place, by bathing in which a person properly shall not incur the fear of untimely death.
Having churned the ocean and taken the supreme nectar, the gods went there in haste and drank it according to their desire.
O lady of excellent complexion, as the gods were drinking the nectar there, drops fell upon the earth by the hundreds and thousands.
At that very time, O lady of excellent complexion, a hare arrived there; afflicted by thirst, he entered the water.

Having attained immortality, he grew within the reservoir of waters. Seeing him, all the gods, vying with one another again and again, and perceiving that the water was infused with nectar, became filled with fear and held a consultation.
Human beings shall consume the nectar fallen upon the earth; consequently, they will become immortal—of this there is no doubt to be made.
"This wretched hare has indeed been born in the womb of an animal; yet he competes with us, and therefore fear has arisen from him. (8)
Then the Lord of Night arrived, overwhelmed by disease, and said to all the gods: "Give me the nectar of immortality."
"Having reached this place with great difficulty, I am unable to move further. Then all the gods said, "Everything has been consumed by us."
O Lord of the Night, you have been forgotten; why have you come here after such a long time? O Moon, dispeller of darkness, carry out our request.
"Indeed, abundant nectar has fallen into this water; drink it for us who are drinking. O Lord of the Night, drink all of this reservoir of water! (12)
"And half of it has fallen here; behold this truth. Having heard those words of theirs, the cool-rayed one (the Moon) was filled with haste. || 13 ||
Or, being afflicted by thirst, he drank water mixed with the [milk] of a hare; yet his body remained reduced to mere bones because of consuming that nectar.
At that very moment, he attained nourishment, endowed with supreme luster; for even as his bodily constituents were wasting away, he was indeed nourished by the nectar.
And that hare, having entered his stomach, did not die; even today it is seen there within the body due to its consumption of nectar.
At that moment, endowed with supreme luster, he attained satisfaction and said: "Let this be dug so that there may be water once again. (17)
"Because of our association, this dry pit has become a reservoir of water; therefore, a proper deed has been performed, for this was not the conduct of the virtuous. (18)
Then they all dug until water emerged; thereafter, filled with great joy, they all spoke.
"Since this reservoir of water is joined with the moon (the hare-marked one) and is yellowish-green, it shall therefore be known as 'The Moon’s Hare-Drink' (Śaśāpāna). || 20 ||
The man who comes here and performs a bath with devotion shall go to the supreme abode where the Lord Maheśvara dwells.
Those who, with concentrated minds, shall here bestow food upon the Brāhmaṇas, will obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
"When this is seen, all the gods and all the deities will have been seen. Having spoken thus, all the gods departed for the abode of the gods.
Then, after a long time, Sarasvatī arrived there, having taken up the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), and by her it was once again inundated.
Then, O woman of excellent complexion, that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) became even more pure; therefore, one should perform a bath there with every possible effort. (25)
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Parṇāditya, the Lord of Gods, situated on the northern bank on the shore of the Prācīsarasvatī. || 1 ||

Long ago in the Tretā Yuga, O Goddess, there was indeed a twice-born man named Parṇāda; having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he performed most rigorous penance, worshipping the Sun with supreme devotion.
Then, having gratified the Sun with incense, garlands, and ointments, he remained concentrated day and night, reciting hymns and Vedic chants prescribed in the Vedas.
And as he was meditating in this manner for a long time, the blessed Sun became pleased with him and spoke these words.
I am well-pleased with this austerity, O best of Brahmins, O observer of noble vows! Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—that which has been constantly desired by your mind.
The Brāhmaṇa said: This alone is my desired boon—that the Blessed One himself is pleased; for an audience with you, O Lord of Gods, is difficult to obtain even in dreams.
"If a boon must certainly be granted to me, O Maker of Day, then remain always present here, O Lord Bhāskara."
"By your grace, O Maker of Day, let them go to your world. Having said, "So shall it be," the Sun vanished from sight.

Parṇāda also remained there, intent upon his propitiation. There, in the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform a ritual bath on the sixth lunar day; thereafter, by beholding Parṇāditya, one shall not encounter suffering.
Whatever fruit is obtained from a hundred cows properly given as a gift at Prayāga, that same fruit a mortal attains by the sight of Parṇāditya.
Those who suffer from great leprosy, lameness, and scabies surely possess dull intellects, for they do not know Parṇāditya.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Parṇāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 259 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme deity Siddheśvara, which was established in ancient times by the Siddhas on the western side of that very same [shrine]. 1.
O fair-faced one, in former times the gods known as Siddhas came there and installed a linga for the sake of attaining perfection in all matters.
Then, O Great Goddess, being pleased upon seeing their great austerity, Śiva bestowed upon them all the sovereign powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
He said to me, "I shall always be present here. || 4 ||
Whoever, being a performer of meritorious deeds, shall worship me here on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that person of merit shall go to the supreme abode through my grace.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then vanished from that place; and the Siddhas, arriving there, then worshipped Maheśvara.
Whoever worships him with devotion attains wonderful perfection and whatever they desire, O best of gods; therefore, one should always worship him.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 260 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to where the river Nyaṅkumatī was brought by Śambhu for the sake of establishing boundaries and for the peace of the sacred field.
On its very southern side is the river Sarvapāpapraṇāśinī. Having bathed there properly, the man who performs a śrāddha ceremony shall deliver all his ancestors from hell; of this there is no doubt.

O beautiful lady, O beloved, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, having bathed, one should offer libations with devotion using water, sesame seeds, and darbha grass; by this, it is as if a śrāddha has been performed at the Gaṅgā—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nyaṅkumatī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 261 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Varaha situated there; located to the south of Goshpada, he stands as the destroyer of sins. 1.
The man who worships him on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight is liberated from all sins and shall go to the great abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Varāhasvāmī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to that which is known as Chāyā-liṅga; it is situated to the north of the Nyaṅkumatī river, and is full of great wonders and yields great fruit. || 1 ||

O Goddess, upon seeing it, a man is liberated from the five great sins. O Great Goddess, those most sinful men who do not see it [situated] at twelve and a half cubits [from the source] and three yojanas [in extent], [do not attain liberation].

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Chāyā-liṅga," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, right there is situated a cave that destroys all sins, where the holy-minded sages and Siddhas reside. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, the man who goes there and beholds the cave is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. || 2 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nandinī-guphā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess named Kanakanandā, who is situated in the northeastern direction and bestows the fruits of all desires. (1)
There, on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, a wise person should perform a pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites and shall attain all desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kanakanandā," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Kumbhīśvara, situated not very far to the east of Śarabha-sthāna. Upon seeing it, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kumbhīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place called Gaṅgāpatha, where the Gaṅgā of great current flows, and likewise Śiva as Gaṅgeśvara resides.
O Goddess, that Gaṅgā, who flows to the ocean and destroys sin, is renowned on earth as Uttānā; she is the river that adorns the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, he who bathes there and worships Gaṅgeśa shall be liberated from terrible sins and obtain the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaṅgāpatha and Gaṅgeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Chamasonbheda, where, O beloved, Brahma performed a sacrificial session for ten thousand years.
Having drunk the Soma from the cups, those gods and great sages became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Camasodbheda. || 2 ||
Having bathed there in the Sarasvatī, the man who offers the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa) on the full moon day of Vaiśākha shall obtain merit ten million times greater than that of Gayā.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Camasodbheda," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the great hermitage of Vidura, where Vidura, the embodiment of Dharma, performed fierce penance.
Having installed Mahādeva, the Liṅga that is the Lord of the three worlds, a human being, O Goddess, shall obtain all desires upon seeing it.
The place named Vidurāṭṭālaka, frequented by hosts of Gandharvas, is a station consisting of twelve sites; it is not attained by one of meager merit. || 3 ||
O Pārvatī, there shall never be a lack of rain there; one should behold the divine liṅgas there for the pacification of sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vidura’s Hermitage," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 269 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows; in that place stands the Liṅga known as Maṅkīśvara. || 1 ||
I shall proclaim its origin, which destroys all sins; listen, O illustrious goddess, to the wonder that occurred in the past. (2)
An ṛṣi named Maṅkaṇaka performed supreme austerity; having gone to the eastern region, he restricted his food and was constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Many thousands of years have passed for him, O beautiful lady; then, after some time had elapsed, O fair-faced one, he was pierced.
"We have heard that vegetable juice was produced from his hand by means of the tip of a blade of kusha grass; seeing that great marvel, he was struck with supreme astonishment. (5)
Thinking that he had attained supreme perfection, he then began to dance out of joy; and while he was dancing, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—[was affected]. || 6 ||

O lady of beautiful hips, he did not dance because of the power of that sage. Then the gods, led by Mahendra and preceded by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, said to the slayer of Tripura: "Act in such a way that he does not dance."
The mountains were shaken from their foundations, the ocean was agitated, O Lord, the earth was shattered into fragments, and the trees met their destruction.
The great rivers have gone off their courses, and the planets have strayed from their paths; the three worlds have become agitated until they reach total destruction.
Restrain him for now; no one else is capable of restraining him.
Having promised "So be it," he went into his presence, assumed the form of a brahmin, and spoke these words to that ṛṣi.
"O twice-born one, what is the cause for this joy, and why are you dancing? Therefore, O brahmin, tell me quickly the reason; we have a great curiosity. (12)
The sage said: "O Brahmin, do you not see the leaf falling from my hand? It is for this very reason that I dance; I am perfected, of this there is no doubt. (13)
Ishvara said: Having heard those words of his, O beautiful lady, the Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, struck his thumb with the tip of his finger.
Then, at that very moment, ashes as white as snow emerged from it; thereupon the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, laughed and spoke to him.
"Behold, O Brahmin, how much ash has issued from my thumb! I am not dancing, nor do I feel joy, yet it is so, O best of sages. (16)
Having seen that most wonderful sight, he was struck with supreme amazement; joining his palms in reverence, he spoke with a voice faltering with joy. (17)
I consider no other god to be superior to you, O bull-bannered one; no one else on the surface of the earth possesses such power. (18)
The Blessed One said: "I am known by you, O tiger among sages, best of the knowers of the Vedas. Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—that which is eternally desired by your mind. (19)
The sage said: "O Lord, by means of a great dance, through the grace of the God of gods, let such a method be devised so that there may be no loss of my ascetic merit."
Śambhu said: "O Brahmin, may your austerity increase a thousandfold through my grace; I shall dwell here forever with you, following the East."
The Sarasvatī is exceedingly meritorious, especially in this sacred field; whoever should cast off their body on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī [attains the highest goal].
O tiger among sages, for one who bathes at Prācīna, there is no returning here again; he obtains the abundant fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).

Wasting their own bodies through observances and fasts, those ascetics subsisted on water, fed on air, or lived on leaves; likewise, there were others who slept on the bare ground, each engaged in various distinct disciplines.
Those who, endowed with self-restraint, shall perform their ablutions in this sacred ford, attain supreme perfection, the highest station of Brahman.
Whoever gives even a mere fragment of gold as a gift to an eminent brahmin at this sacred ford shall obtain a fruit equal to Mount Meru.
Those men who shall perform a Śrāddha ceremony at this sacred ford here will certainly go to heaven, accompanied by twenty-one generations of their lineage.
This sacred ford is beloved by the ancestors; those who are gratified by a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) shall go to the world of Brahmā, delivered here by a virtuous son.
Furthermore, they provide food and proceed upon the path to liberation. || 29 ||
O best of the twice-born, those who perform auspicious deeds and behold Sarasvatī as she dwells at Prabhāsa shall also go to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, those men who are devoted to bathing there with sincere intent shall reach the world of Brahmā and rejoice there forever.
Whoever here should offer delightful curd to a Brāhmaṇa, he too, having reached the world of Agni, enjoys most splendid pleasures.
Even he who, out of devotion, gives a woolen shawl to an excellent twice-born man, attains supreme perfection, which is very difficult for other mortals to obtain. (33)
And those men who enter the water here for the destruction of their impurities, one should declare that they shall easily obtain the fruit equivalent to the gift of a cow.
For by performing a bath there with true devotion, a person is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 35 ||
Through the offering of libations and the giving of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), even those ancestors residing in the hells go to heaven, having been delivered here by a virtuous son.
They obtain inexhaustible worlds designated as those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; furthermore, they bestow food upon others and attain the path to liberation.
The Sarasvatī at Prabhāsa has become a ladder to heaven; that great river cannot be reached by men who lack merit.
The Prācī and Sarasvatī rivers are indeed difficult to find elsewhere, especially at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Puṣkara. (39)
Having reached the eastern Sarasvatī, if one seeks another sacred ford, he is like one who, having cast away what is in his hand, attempts to achieve his purpose with his elbow. 40.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, bathing is always prescribed. Whoever offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) there, even with oil-cake and inguda-water, it shall become inexhaustible for the ancestors, and he goes to the world of the ancestors. || 41 ||

Where can there be a delight equal to dwelling by the Sarasvatī? Where can there be virtues equal to dwelling by the Sarasvatī? Having reached the Sarasvatī and gone to heaven, men will remember the river Sarasvatī once again. (42)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished right there; from that time forward, Śaṅkara established his presence in that place.
In this regard, O beloved, these verses were sung of old by the powerful Viṣṇu with a heart moistened by affection toward the son of Dharma.
"Do not go to the Gaṅgā, O son of Kuntī, nor to Prayāga or Puṣkara; go instead there, O best of the Kurus, where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows."
All this that you asked me has been told; what more do you wish to hear regarding the majesty of Sarasvatī?

Thus ends the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Prācīsarasvatī and Maṅkīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 270 ||
Īśvara said: In close proximity to that very place, the Liṅga known as Jvāleśvara is remembered, where the Pāśupata arrow blazed forth by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
Because it was cast down in that place, it is known as Jvāleśvara; by seeing it, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jvāleśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: One should behold the three well-known Liṅgas of the great-souled Tripuras situated right there, in the vicinity of the goddess Prācī. (1)
Vidyunmālī, the one named Tāraka, and likewise the one named Kapola—by seeing the Liṅga installed by them, one is liberated from sins. || 2 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Three Liṅgas of Tripura," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Śaṇḍatīrtha, which pacifies all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. || 1 ||
I shall describe its origin; listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved. In ancient times, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, had five heads.
For some particular reason, his head was severed by me; there, from the blood of Brahmā, the river Gaṅgā was born.
Because great palm trees rose up there, it is known as Tālavana; then, the skull of Brahmā became stuck to my palm.
The bodies of both myself and my bull turned black; then, fearing sin, I went to many sacred fords (tīrthas).
My sin did not go anywhere; then, having come to Prabhāsa, I beheld the goddess Sarasvatī, the Eastern One, in that sacred field (kṣetra).
There, my bull entered the midst of the water to bathe; at that very moment, it attained whiteness, and I too was liberated from the sin of killing.
Then a skull fell, stuck in the middle of my hand; that very place became established as Kapālamocana in the form of a Liṅga. || 8 ||
Furthermore, whoever offers a śrāddha there in the presence of the goddess Prācī, his maternal and paternal lineages, numbering one hundred generations each, shall likewise be satisfied.

And he shall remain satisfied for as many as seventy kalpas. O Goddess, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, whoever performs a śrāddha there, taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti—
When offerings are made according to one's means to a worthy recipient in accordance with the prescribed rite, one's ancestors shall remain satisfied for as long as a thousand yugas.
The gift of food and gold, as well as the gift of a cow with a white blanket, should be given there according to the prescribed rite for the purification of all sins.
O Goddess, when the bull that was black in form attained whiteness, it became renowned as Śaṇḍatīrtha, worshipped by the three worlds.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Sūryaprācī, which possesses great splendor, which pacifies all sins, and which bestows the fruits of all desires. (1)
Having bathed there, O Great Goddess, one is liberated from the five great sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sūryaprācī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Three-eyed Lord (Trilocana), who is situated near Ṛṣitīrtha and destroys all sins; he was worshipped by the sages of old on the northern bank of the Nyaṅkumatī.
O Goddess, where there are three-eyed fish and the water resembles crystal, a man who bathes there is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, one should observe a fast and likewise keep a vigil at night.
One should perform the morning Śrāddha and worship Śiva according to the rules; O Goddess, one shall dwell in the world of Rudra for thirty thousand years.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Trinetreśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the vicinity of Ṛṣitīrtha; for there is a supreme field known by the name Devikā, which fulfills all desires.
There was the Mahāsiddhivana forest, crowded with sages and perfected beings, filled with various trees and creepers, and adorned with mountains.
With divine campaka and bakula trees, with clusters of excellent aśoka blossoms, and with fragrant punnāga, kiṃkirāta, and nāgakesara flowers. || 3 ||
With *mallikā* and *utpala* flowers, with *pāṭalā* and *pārijātaka*, with mango, *campaka*, and *kapittha*, as well as with *bilva* and *panasa* fruits.
It was adorned with dates, jujubes, and other fruits, as well as with citron, pomegranate, jambīra, and divine oranges.
It was being sung to by peacocks and cuckoos, as well as by bees; and it was frequented by deer, bears, boars, lions, tigers, and other such creatures.
It was filled with beasts of prey of various forms, as well as mountain caves and deep ravines; it was frequented by hosts of gods and asuras, siddhas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and pannagas.
It was crowded with many Apsarases, Uragas, and Nāgas; some were praising the Lord, while others were dancing before him.
Some released a rain of flowers, while others played musical instruments; some laughed with joy, and others likewise roared.
Others likewise stand with their arms raised, while others, absorbed in that [state], meditate; such is the place, O Great Goddess, on the auspicious bank of the Devikā.
I am always established there under the name Umāpatīśvara, throughout every age, at the completion of every kalpa, and likewise during every manvantara.
O Goddess, I never abandon the auspicious bank of the Devikā, for it is difficult to find in all this world, sacred, and truly dear to me.
And while I was staying with you in that place, O fair-faced one, because my body was joined with Umā, I became known as Umāpati.
On the new moon day of the month of Puṣya, one who is composed in mind should offer a śrāddha; O Pārvatī, I do not see any exhaustion of that which has been given on that occasion.
By the mere sight of it, a thousand killings of Brahmins are destroyed; there, a wise person should bestow cows, land, gold, and garments. (15)
O beautiful one, that alone is the supreme son who, having gone there, offers the śrāddha for his ancestors; for him, there is truly no end [to his merit].
Summoned by all the gods for the purpose of bathing, that best of rivers became known as Devikā; therefore, she is the destroyer of sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Umāpati at Devikā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Right there, one should behold the mountain known by the name Bhūdhara, because he lifted up the earth and supported it with the tip of his tusk.

And by him was described Bhūdharatīrtha, situated on the bank of the Devikā; [the Lord] whose feet are the Vedas, whose tusks are the sacrificial posts, whose teeth are the sacrifices, and whose mouth is the sacrificial ladle.
Agni-jihva (Fire-tongued), Darbha-roma (Darbha-haired), Brahma-śīrṣa (Brahma-headed), and Mahātapas (Great ascetic); he has day and night as his eyes and the Vedāṅgas and Śrutis as his ornaments.

He is without beginning or end, with a sacrificial ladle for a beak, possessing a great voice like the sound of Sāman chants; his body is the sacrificial hall, he is radiant, and he is adorned with various initiations.
The yogi has the *dakṣiṇā* as his heart; he is great, resting upon the *mahāsatra*; the *upākarma* is the ornament of his lips, and the *pravargya* is the whorl of his jewelry. || 5 ||
Having assumed the form of the Sacrificial Boar, whose path of movement through various meters was a stride following the sequence prescribed by Brahmā, he remained stationed in that place.
Indeed, on the new moon day of the month of Puṣya, or on the eleventh day, or when the rainy season has arrived and one knows that the sun has entered Virgo; || 7 ||
One should consecrate the milk-rice mixed with jaggery and the sacrificial food soaked in jaggery with the mantra: "Obeisance to you, O ancestors, for the sake of essence; [this is] the food. (8)
The clarified butter is offered with the mantra "tejo 'si śukram"; the curd with the "dadhikrāvṇa" mantra; the milk with the mantra for the clarified butter; and likewise the various side dishes.
The twice-born man should cause all kinds of food and edibles to be given by Mahendra; having recited the mantra for a year, he should offer water with that [mantra].
Having thus fed the Brahmins, one should cause the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to be given; he who performs the Śrāddha there according to this procedure— || 11 ||
His ancestors remain satisfied for as long as fourteen Indras endure; even without performing a śrāddha at Gayā here, one obtains the fruit of a Gayā-śrāddha.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Bhūdhara-Yajñavarāha," within the Devikā-Māhātmya, in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-Kṣetra, in the seventh part (Prabhāsa-Khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 277 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place renowned as Śūlasthāna, located on the beautiful bank of the Devikā, where Bhāskara, the drawer of waters, resides.
There, Vālmīki, the bull among sages, performed severe austerities; there the great sage, the brahminical ṛṣi named Vālmīki, attained perfection.
O beloved, it is there that the Seven Sages were seized by that very sage; and on the western side of that very place are the twice-born ones, headed by Marīci.
The Goddess said: "How did Vālmīki attain perfection, and how did he set his mind upon theft? How were the Seven Sages robbed? Tell me this, O Śaṅkara. (4)

Īśvara said: O Goddess, formerly there was a twice-born man known by the name Śamīmukha. While he was living as a householder, a son was born to him; he was named Vaiśākha and was born with a fierce disposition.
Except for one thing—service to his teacher—that twice-born man performed no other auspicious deed daily, from daybreak onwards.
Then, after a long time, his two beloved parents reached a state of old age; overwhelmed by it, they were to be supported by him.
Having constantly traveled on his path and plundered the worlds according to his power, he took wealth and supported his parents and his wife as well.
Then, after some time, as he was traveling along that path, he saw the Seven Sages who were intent on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Seeing them, he raised his staff and, rebuking them with harsh words, spoke to all of them repeatedly, saying, "Stay! (10)
Then those sages were tranquil, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal; they were impartial toward enemy and friend alike, and entirely free from anger and passion.
"Aṅgiras spoke these words: 'May our meeting with him and our conversation with the sages not be in vain.'"

Aṅgiras said: "O thief, listen to my words with focused attention for a moment. For the sake of your own welfare, I speak the truth to you. Tell me everything: who are those dependent upon you for support?"
The thief said: "O Sage, I have two aged parents, a wife who is childless, and a single maidservant; I am the sixth. There is nothing else besides these."
Aṅgiras said: "Go and ask all those who have become fat on wealth acquired through sin: 'I am the one who commits the sins, while you all are merely the consumers. (15)
"Tell me quickly, to whom will that sin belong? Having gone there, he questioned his parents, and they spoke thus: || 16 ||
The parents said: "One person commits sins, yet the multitude enjoys the fruit. Those who enjoy are set free, while the doer alone is stained by the fault. (17)
That dull-witted man who performs unwholesome deeds for the sake of his family—surely the self is not dear to that most sinful person. (18)
Īśvara said: Having heard their words, his mind filled with fear once more, he paid homage to them and spoke again to his parents. (19)
"Whatever inauspicious act I perform that may be harmful to you both, tell me whether you must partake in even a portion of it, or not. (20)
The parents said: "O son, in our earlier years we were indeed to be protected by you; but in our later years, it is we who must be properly protected by you once again. (21)

This mutual law has been declared by the Lotus-born One: "Whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed by us two for your sake, we alone shall experience all of that here; there is no doubt in this. (22)
Moreover, dear child, whatever merit or demerit you yourself perform, you alone shall experience all of that in the next world, and no one else. (23)
One inevitably experiences for oneself the results of actions performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious; therefore, a wise man should perform virtuous deeds.
"O son, whether by means of theft, agriculture, usury, trade, or service, you must provide our food day and night; there shall be no fault on our part, my son. (25)

Having heard those words from them, he then spoke to his wife; she repeated that very same speech which had been uttered by the elders previously. Thereupon, Vaiśākha, the best of sages, attained a state of world-weariness.
Thus reproaching himself again and again, he was deeply afflicted by grief: "Fie on me, a doer of evil deeds who has always delighted in sinful actions! (27)
The man who commits sin while abandoned by discernment and deprived of the company of the virtuous, and who does not serve the wise—for him, his own self is not dear; this is my conviction. (28)
Having thus resolved in his heart, he went into the presence of the sage and spoke with gentle words, respectfully saying, "Please proceed."
"Let this seat be taken up, as well as the water-pot; and likewise all these bark garments, rags, and deer-skins. (30)
"O best of sages, may my offense be forgiven—me, who am wretched and miserable, separated from the company of the virtuous, and a fool. (31)
"From this day forward, I myself have desisted from this fierce, cruel, and wicked deed which is censured by the virtuous; therefore, tell us how we too may attain cessation from this action. (32)
By means of your grace, may I attain liberation from sin; whether it be through fasting, or mantra, or religious observance, or self-restraint. (33)
The sages said: "Well asked by you, dear child; listen with a single-minded focus to the truth. Having condensed it, we shall proclaim it to you, but it must not be told by you to anyone."
By reciting that, you will certainly attain liberation from the nature of sin; this four-syllabled mantra, *jhāṭaghoṭa*, should be proclaimed by you. (35)

"Remover of all sins for men and bestower of the fruits of heaven and liberation"—thus was he addressed at that time by those bulls among sages; he remained constantly devoted to his silent recitation, and those bulls among sages departed.
O Goddess, as he, devoted to his guru, was thus reciting incessantly on the auspicious bank of the Devikā, meditative absorption (samādhi) arose within him. || 37 ||
Then hunger and thirst were destroyed, and his body attained purity.
In respect to a mantra, a sacred ford, a brahmin, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a guru, whatever one's disposition is toward them, such will be the success that occurs.
This Supreme Self is pure by its very nature, just as it is beneficial; yet, having encountered the contact of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it undergoes modification, just like a crystal.
And just as a barren female bee, having found a tiny living creature somewhere, places it in her own abode and meditates upon it with focused concentration, so too [should one meditate]. || 41 ||
But that living being, nourished by that meditation, becomes such [as it meditated]; or even if born from another womb, it is likewise, according to the illustration given by the wise. (42)
If one who has been instructed by the Guru falls into doubt, that unfortunate person does not attain success, just as [one might fail to find] a treasure.
In this manner, many thousands of years passed for him as he remained devoted to his recitation, having attained the state of immortality.
Then, in the course of time, he was enveloped by an anthill, so that he was completely covered on all sides and indeed did not perceive it.
Then, after some time, those sages gathered together; having looked upon that region and rendered mutual assistance, they all spoke to one another, joining hand in hand.
The sages said: "It was here that this thief, Vaiśākha of terrible appearance, arrived—he by whom we all were robbed while gathered in this place. (47)
While they were thus conversing, they heard a distinct and supreme sound from the middle of the anthill; thereupon, they were filled with curiosity.
There they dug into an anthill, which was like a mountain, using wooden spades. || 49 ||
Then those best of sages beheld Viśākha there, repeatedly chanting that very same four-syllabled mantra.
Knowing him to have attained that state of meditative absorption, the Brahmins thoroughly crushed his body as it lay there asleep with medicinal herbs approved for their application.
Then he said to all the sages, "O twice-born ones, let your own wealth be taken; that which was seized by me, of unrefined intellect, belongs to you. (52)
"O best of the twice-born, let all of you go on pilgrimage; I have granted you leave. Having gone there, my parents and likewise my wife must be told this by you. (53)
Having completely renounced all attachments, Viśākha became such that he no longer desired to see you as he did before.
The sages said: "O sage, many years have passed while you have been dwelling here; all those relatives of yours, as well as the others who were your family members, have met their death. (55)
O best of sages, we have arrived at this place after a long time; you have undoubtedly attained perfection through this mantra.
"Since you have resorted to an anthill while meditating on the mantra with one-pointed concentration, therefore you shall be known by the name Vālmīki upon the surface of the earth. (57)
The goddess of speech, Svachchandā Bhāratī, shall reside at the tip of your tongue; after composing the poem Rāmāyaṇa, you will then attain liberation.
Viśākha said: "O tigers among the twice-born, please accept this gratuity for my preceptor out of favor, so that, having become free from debt, I may perform very great penance. (59)

The sages said: "O Brahmin, this is our fee (dakṣiṇā) for you, who have attained perfection; with your self fulfilled by the accomplishment of all desires, O sage, we too have accomplished our purpose."
Choose another boon, whatever dwells in your mind. || 61 ||

Vālmīki said: "If you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then tell me quickly: which deity resides here on the beautiful bank of the Devikā, bestowing the fruits of all desires? (62)
The sages said: "Listen with a focused mind, O Brahmin, to which deity is established here. Behold this neem tree, O Brahmin, with its many spreading branches. (63)
At its root stands the Sun, born from a portion of Brahmā at the beginning of the kalpa; worship him, for he is the presiding deity of this place.
This area of one *gavyūti* is declared to be the domain of the Sun; for those who reside in this place, heaven shall certainly be theirs. (65)
"From this day forward, O best of Brahmins, this place shall be known as Mūlasthāna, the abode of the Sun; O best of Brahmins, you must establish your residence here."
From this day forward, O best of Brahmins, this sacred site situated on the bank of the Devikā shall attain supreme renown upon the surface of the earth.
"O Brahmin, since we were robbed while formerly staying at Mūlasthāna, this place shall indeed become famous in the world by the name 'Mūlasthāna'. (68)
In this place, those men who with devotion perform their bath at the confluence of the Sūrya on the northern bank shall go to heaven.
O best of the twice-born, by offering libations with water mixed with sesame seeds, the ancestors will attain satisfaction equal to that of a śrāddha performed at Gayā.
In this place, those excellent men who, endowed with perfect faith, shall offer a śrāddha with devotion—even if only with vegetables, roots, or fruits—[shall attain the highest goal]. (71)
The ancestors of those [who perform this] will attain liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even those who are insects, moths, birds, domestic animals, or wild beasts, when afflicted by thirst, shall attain the supreme goal through contact with the water.
O best one, out of affection for you, we ourselves shall undoubtedly be present here in the month of Śrāvaṇa on the full moon day. (74)
On that day, whoever shall satiate the ancestors with water offerings, his eighteen types of leprosy will perish at that very moment.
Kapāla, udumbara, indramaṇḍala, vicarcikā, ṛṣyajihva, carma, ekakiṭibha, sidhma, alasaka, and vipādikā; || 76 ||
Dadrū, vitā, ruci, sphoṭa, puṇḍarīka, with kākaṇa, pāmā, and carmadala—these indeed are the eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha). || 77 ||
"They shall go, there is no doubt," having said this, they vanished; the sage then worshipped the Sun and thereafter composed the Rāmāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should behold that God, who bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, and one should hear this narrative, which destroys all sins. (79)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Original Site of Devikāmāhātmya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Cyavanārka, situated in the eastern part of Hiraṇyā, which was established by Cyavana. || 1 ||

It bestows all desires upon men when worshipped according to the prescribed rites; and whatever man shall praise the Sun on the seventh lunar day according to the ritual injunctions [shall likewise obtain his wishes].
Endowed with perfect faith, listen, O Great Goddess, having become pure and composed, to those one hundred and eight names.
"Wait a moment, O Goddess of gods; I shall tell you everything in its entirety, just as it was previously told by Dhaumya to the high-souled son of Pṛthā. (4)
The eight hundred names have been declared; listen to them, O high-minded one: Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitṛ, and Ravi. || 5 ||
He is the rayed one, the unborn, time, death, the creator, and the maker of light; he is earth, water, fire, ether, and wind, the ultimate refuge.
Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Budha, and Aṅgāraka; Indra, Vivasvat, Dīptāṃśu, Śuci, Sauri, and Śanaiścara. (7)
Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Skanda, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama; the fire of lightning and the digestive fire, the lord of all splendors—[these are his forms]. || 8 ||
He is the banner of Dharma, the creator of the Vedas, the limb of the Vedas, and the vehicle of the Vedas; he is the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, and the refuge of all the immortals.
The maker of years, the horse-mounted one, the wheel of time, and the fire-god, he is the divisions of time: the kalās, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, fortnights, months, days, and nights. (10)

The Puruṣa is eternal, the Yogi, both manifest and unmanifest, the ancient one; he is the overseer of the worlds, the lord of creatures, the architect of the universe, and the dispeller of darkness. || 11 ||
Varuṇa, Sāgara, Aṃśu, Jīvanta, Jīvana, Arihā, Bhūtāśraya, Bhūtapati, and Sarvabhūtaniṣevita. || 12 ||
The creator, the fire of dissolution, the originator of all, the stainless one; the infinite, Kapila, the sun, the granter of desires, and the one whose face is turned in every direction. || 13 ||
Victory, freedom from dejection, the bestower of boons, served by all the elements; equal, golden-hued, the source of beings, swift-moving, and the sustainer of life. || 14 ||
Dhanvantari, whose banner is smoke, the primordial god, the son of Aditi; the twelve-fold self, the lotus-eyed one, who is father, mother, and grandfather. (15)

He is the door to heaven, the door to progeny, the door to liberation, and the celestial realm; he is the creator of the body, the tranquil self, the soul of the universe, and the one whose face is turned in every direction; he is the soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle self, endowed with a friendly form.
This hundred and eight names of the Sun, who is worthy of praise and possesses immeasurable splendor, was indeed proclaimed by the wise Śakra. (17)
From Śakra, Nārada received it, and after him, Dhaumya; having obtained it from Dhaumya, Yudhiṣṭhira attained all his desires. || 18 ||
Whoever should daily recite these names of the Sun, who is worthy of praise and possesses immeasurable splendor, shall obtain all their desires. (19)

Worshipped by gods, ancestors, humans, and yakṣas; saluted by asuras, night-stalkers, and siddhas; possessing the radiance of excellent gold and fire—you too, bow down for the sake of your welfare to the Sun. (20)

That man who, with a concentrated mind, recites this at sunrise, shall obtain sons, as well as accumulations of wealth and jewels; that person always attains the memory of past lives, as well as mindfulness and intelligence.

The man who, with a pure mind and concentrated focus, recites this hymn to the best of gods, is liberated from the intensity of the forest fire of sorrow and shall obtain all desires as wished for by his heart. (22)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the One Hundred and Eight Names of Sūrya and the Majesty of Cyavanāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme Cyavaneśvara; the Liṅga situated right there is the destroyer of all sins.
Where Sukanyā was given by Śaryāti to that great ṛṣi, and where he brought to a standstill the army that had been afflicted by the pain of thirst.
O Goddess, this place of Śaryāti’s sacrifice shines forth; situated in the midst of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, it is the manifest destroyer of sins.
There, Kauśika directly partook of the Soma together with the Aśvins; and the descendant of Bhṛgu, a man of great asceticism, became enraged at Mahendra.
And the powerful Cyavana paralyzed that Vāsava, and he obtained Sukanyā, the princess, as his wife.
The Goddess said: How was the Lord Pākaśāsana obstructed by him? And for what reason did Bhārgava, the great ascetic, also become enraged?
And how, O Brahman, did you make the two Nāsatyas drinkers of Soma? May your holiness relate all that to me exactly as it occurred.
Īśvara said: There was a son of the great sage Bhṛgu named Cyavana; having reached Prabhāsa, that great muni performed penance. (8)
O beautiful lady, O fair-faced one, the one of great splendor stood for a very long time in one spot like a pillar in the posture of a hero.
O Goddess, in the course of a long time, that anthill became completely covered with creepers and swarmed with ants.
Thus restrained on all sides like a lump of clay, that wise one performed severe austerities while covered by an anthill.

Then, while he was away on a journey, a king named Śaryāti arrived at the great sacred field of Prabhāsa, which destroys all sins, in the course of a pilgrimage with the desire to behold the illustrious Someśa.
He had four thousand women as his wives, but he had only one daughter, the radiant Sukanyā by name.
Surrounded by her friends and adorned with all her ornaments, she, while walking about, approached the anthill of Bhārgava.
And that fair-toothed woman, beholding those delightful trees there, sported surrounded by her companions as she gathered them.
