On account of his beauty, his youth, and the intoxication of drinking wine, he broke off the branches of the forest trees that were in full bloom. || 16 ||
The wise descendant of Bhṛgu beheld her alone, without her companions, clad in a single garment and adorned with ornaments, moving like a flash of lightning. (17)
Beholding her in that secluded place, the Brahman-sage of supreme luster, though his throat was parched, took delight, being endowed with the power of asceticism. (18)
He spoke to that auspicious woman, but she did not hear him at all. Then Sukanyā saw the two eyes of Bhārgava within the anthill.
Driven by curiosity and the force of her deluded intellect, she said, "What indeed is this? and pierced his two eyes with a thorn.
Pierced by her, he became extremely enraged and, with eyes full of supreme fury, he then overwhelmed Śaryāti’s army with excrement and urine.
Then, seeing his army distressed by the suppression of its excrement and urine, and observing them in such a state, the king was filled with remorse.

"By whom has an offense been committed here today against this high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu, who is constant in austerity, aged, and especially prone to anger? Whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly, tell me this without delay. (23)
Thereupon all the soldiers said: "We do not know of any harm we have done; may you investigate the matter as you wish by every possible means. (24)
Then that protector of the earth himself questioned his circle of friends with both gentle and harsh words, yet they did not acknowledge [the truth] at all.
Then, seeing that army approaching them and her father also distressed, Sukanyā spoke thus: || 26 ||
"O father, everything here was seen by me blazing within the anthill; though it was radiant, out of ignorance I pierced it from nearby. (27)
Having heard this, Śaryāti quickly went to the anthill; there he saw the descendant of Bhṛgu, advanced in asceticism and advanced in years. (28)
Then that lord of the earth, with palms joined in reverence for the sake of his own army, said: "You ought to forgive that which was done by this girl out of ignorance."
Then Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu, spoke to the protector of the earth regarding her who was endowed with beauty and nobility, yet shrouded by greed and delusion.
O King, having accepted that very daughter of yours, I shall forgive [the offense], O protector of the earth; I tell you this truth.
Ishvara said: Having understood the words of the Rishi, Sharyati, without hesitation, gave his daughter to that high-souled Chyavana.
Having accepted that maiden, the Blessed One indeed became gracious; and when his grace was attained, the king returned to the city together with his army.
Sukanyā, too, having obtained as her husband that blameless ascetic, constantly attended upon him with affection, through austerity and self-restraint. (34)
Serving the sacred fires and her guests without malice, that woman of beautiful countenance quickly propitiated Cyavana.

Thus ends the two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cyavaneśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 280 ||
Īśvara said: Then, after some time had passed, O beloved, the two Aśvins, the gods among gods, beheld Sukanyā uncovered as she had performed her ritual ablutions.
Seeing her, whose limbs were beautiful like the daughter of the king of the gods, the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, then ran toward her and spoke.
"To whom do you belong, O lady of beautiful thighs? What do you intend to do in this forest? I wish to know you; tell me the truth, O beautiful one. (3)
Then Sukanyā, having dressed herself, spoke to those two best of gods: "Know me to be the daughter of Śaryāti and the wife of Cyavana."
Then the two Aśvins, laughing, spoke to her once again: "How is it that you, having been recognized by your father, were given away and have come to this forest?"
You shine in the expanse of the sky like the lightning of the clouds; indeed, O beautiful woman, we do not see anyone equal to you even among the gods.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing exquisite garments, O lady of faultless limbs, leave this man who lacks discernment.
O auspicious lady, why is it that you, being such as you are, would worship one on this earth who is worn out by old age and excluded from the nature of desire? (8)
O lady of pure smiles, since he is incapable of protecting or nourishing you, do you abandon Cyavana and choose one of us two.
"Do not spend your youth in vain for the sake of a husband, O lady who resembles a celestial child. Thus addressed, Sukanyā spoke these words to those two gods: ||| 10 ||
"I am devoted to my husband Cyavana; do not entertain such doubts. They both spoke to her again: "We are the two best of divine physicians. (11)
"We shall make your husband young and endowed with beauty; therefore, choose one among him and us as your husband. (12)

"In this matter, O slender-waisted one, bring about peace between us. At their words, O Goddess, she approached the descendant of Bhṛgu and spoke the message that had been addressed by them to the son of Bhṛgu.
Chyavana said that speech to his wife, "Let her be honored. Thus addressed by Chyavana, Sukanyā then spoke to those two.
"O goddesses, let that which has been spoken by you two be performed quickly. Thus addressed there by her, Sukanyā, the two physicians said to that princess: "Let your husband enter the waters. (15)
Then Cyavana, desiring beauty, quickly entered the water; O Goddess, the two Aśvins also then entered the water after him.
Then, after a moment, they all emerged from that lake; they were all young men of divine form, wearing polished earrings.
Wearing divine attire and increasing the delight of the mind, they all spoke together: "O auspicious lady, choose one of us."
"O blessed lady of excellent complexion, this is our desire; therefore, O most beautiful one, choose him whom you desire. (19)
Having observed them all standing there, assuming identical forms, she reflected with her mind and intellect and, O Goddess, chose her own husband.
Having obtained his wife, Cyavana, established once more in youth and beauty, spoke these words with great joy to the two Nāsatyas: ||| 21 ||
"Since I have been made by you both endowed with beauty and possessed of youth, and having become old, have obtained my own wife—tell me what you desire, and I shall surely perform it for you. (22)
The Aśvins said: "We two are the physicians of the gods, yet Śakra does not grant us the right to drink the Soma; therefore, make us drinkers of the Soma. (23)
Cyavana said: "I shall make you both worthy of a share in the sacrifice and drinkers of the Soma."
Īśvara said: Then those two Nāsatyas, their minds filled with joy, departed for heaven; Cyavana and Sukanyā, too, sported like gods.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cyavaneśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 281 ||
Īśvara said: Then, having heard that Cyavana was of the same age [as his daughter], Śaryāti, who was staying at Valabhī, felt his heart overflow with joy.
Delighted, he set out for the hermitage of Bhārgava together with his army, [finding] Cyavana and Sukanyā, who was as joyful as a daughter of the gods.
King Śaryāti, a great ocean of universal bliss, arrived; honored by that sage, the lord of the earth sat down there with his wife, and the high-minded king engaged in auspicious conversation.
Then, O Goddess, Bhārgava spoke to him, consoling him: "O King, I shall perform a sacrifice for you; prepare the necessary materials."
Thereupon, O Great Goddess, Śaryāti, the lord of the earth, being exceedingly delighted, honored those words of Cyavana.
On an auspicious day suitable for sacrifice, one rich in the fulfillment of all desires, Śaryāti caused an excellent sacrificial ground to be prepared.
In that very place, O Goddess, Cyavana caused the descendant of Bhṛgu to perform a sacrifice; and there, O Maheśvarī, many wonders occurred.
Then Cyavana took the Soma for the two divine Aśvins; Indra restrained him, saying, "Do not take the draught for those two."
Indra said: "It is my opinion that neither of these two, the Nāsatyas, is worthy of the Soma; for they are the physicians of the gods and are thus censured by their very office."
Cyavana said: "Do not despise these two high-souled ones, who possess beauty, wealth, and splendor, and who have today made me ageless like a celestial being."
Why indeed do you not look upon other gods with equanimity? O Indra, scorcher of foes, know that even the two Aśvins are gods.
Indra said: "How do these two physicians, who perform manual labor and possess the power to assume any form at will, deserve the soma here while wandering among mortals in this world? (12)
Ishvara said: When Vasava repeated these very words again and again, disregarding Shakra, the descendant of Bhrigu then seized the planet.
Then, seeing that the most excellent of beings was about to seize the Soma from the Aśvins, the god Indra, the slayer of Bala, spoke these words.
If you yourself take the Soma for the sake of these two, I shall strike you with my thunderbolt, which is of terrible form and unsurpassed.
Having been addressed thus, that descendant of Bhṛgu looked at Indra himself and duly took the excellent draught of Soma for the two Aśvins.
Then Indra, the lord of Śacī, struck him in anger with his thunderbolt; however, Bhārgava paralyzed the arm of him as he was striking.
Then, having paralyzed [the gods], Cyavana, possessing great splendor and seeking the fulfillment of his purpose, offered oblations into the fire with mantras, intent on harming the god.
There, at the sacrifice, by the power of that sage’s asceticism, a great asura named Mada arose—possessing great heroism, a massive body, and immense strength.
His body cannot be described even by gods and asuras; there exists nothing here equal to his form in its dimensions. (20)
His mouth was terrible, with great fangs that were difficult to behold; one of his jaws rested upon the earth, while the other reached up to heaven.
Furthermore, those four fangs of his were each a hundred yojanas long, while his other teeth were ten yojanas in length.
Shaped like ramparts and appearing equal from base to summit, they are called "Mountain-like" (Parvata-saṃkāśa) and measure tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of yojanas.

His eyes resembled the sun and the moon, and his eyebrows were like the God of Death; with a flickering tongue as mobile as lightning, he licked his face; with mouth wide open and a terrible gaze, he seemed to be swallowing the world by force.
Desiring to devour him, he rushed furiously toward Śatakratu, covering the worlds with the sound of his great and terrible roar.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Occurrence of the Great Asura named Madana, Created by Cyavana for the Destruction of Śakra Who Was Intent on Discharging the Thunderbolt to Obstruct the Sacrificial Portion of the Nāsatyas," within the *Cyavaneśvara-māhātmya*, in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 282 ||
The Lord said: Seeing that Mada approaching with a terrible face, like Death himself with his mouth wide open, intent on devouring him, the god Śatakratu [spoke]. || 1 ||
With his form paralyzed by fear, repeatedly licking [his lips], he, afflicted by terror, bowed down and spoke to Cyavana, O Great Goddess: || 2 ||
"O Bhārgava, from this day forward, these two Aśvins shall be worthy of the Soma; I tell you all this as the truth. (3)
O ascetic, let not your exertion be in vain; and I know, O brahmin-sage, that you will not act falsely.
"O Bhārgava, these two Aśvins are worthy of Soma exactly as they were made by you today; yet, let your own prowess be manifested even further."
"Thinking that fame for Sukanyā and for her father would arise in this world, I have therefore ordained this manifestation of his prowess. Therefore, grant me your favor; let this be as you desire."
When the high-souled Cyavana was addressed thus by Śakra, his anger quickly subsided, as did the pride of the lord of the gods.

The powerful deity then divided intoxication (mada), which had been created again and again in the past, among drink, women, dice, and hunting. Having thus distributed intoxication and having gratified Śakra with the moon, [he departed].
O lady of excellent complexion, having caused that king to sacrifice together with all [the gods] including the two Aśvins, and having made his valor renowned throughout all the worlds; || 9 ||
In this sacred field within the great forest, he sported with Sukanyā; O Goddess, this place associated with him bears the name Cyavaneśvara.
The Liṅga, which destroys great sins, was installed by Cyavana; one who worships it according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 11 ||
Therefore, the sages attend upon that sacred ford of the Moon—the sages known as the Vaikhānasas and likewise the Vālakhilyas.

In this month of Āśvina, especially on the full moon day, a man should perform a śrāddha according to the prescribed rite and feed the Brāhmaṇas individually; he shall obtain the fruit of ten million holy places (tīrthas), of this there is no doubt. || 13 ||
O Goddess, the man who hears this narrative that destroys sins shall be liberated from all the evil accumulated throughout his entire life.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cyavaneśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Sukanyāsaras, where the two Aśvins, along with Cyavana, submerged themselves, O Ambikā; for it was there that Cyavana became equal in form to the two Aśvins.

Because the beautiful Sukanyā obtained her desire there through the power of bathing in that lake, it is known as Kanyāsaras. A virtuous woman who bathes there, especially on the third lunar day, [attains her desires].
For seven thousand births, he shall not suffer the ruin of his home; nor shall his husband be poor, crippled, wretched, or blind.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Sukanyāsaras," within the "Greatness of Cyavaneśvara," in the first section, the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 284 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go again to the river Nyaṅkumatī; having performed the Gayā-śrāddha there at the excellent holy site of Goṣpada.
Then one should visit Varāha, and from there proceed to the abode of Hari; having bathed at the confluence of the ocean, one should worship the Mothers there.
From there, one should first proceed toward the Nyankumati river and the ocean, and then to the divine hermitage of Agastya, which is remembered as "the dispeller of hunger."
There, having subdued both Ilvala and Vātāpi, the venerable sage liberated the Brāhmaṇas from their calamities and granted them a dwelling place.
This is indeed the hermitage of Agastya, most excellent and dear to Agastya, situated on the delightful bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, which destroys all sins.
The Goddess said: For what reason was Vātāpi subdued here by Agasti? What was the power of that Daitya, the slayer of Brahmins? And for what reason did anger arise in the high-souled Agasti?
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent complexion, in ancient times there was a lord of the Daityas named Ilvala in the city of Maṇimatī, and Vātāpi was his younger brother.
That son of Diti spoke to the Brahmin endowed with ascetic power: "O Blessed One, grant me a single son who is equal to Indra."
That Brahmin did not wish to give him such a son; consequently, the son of Diti became exceedingly angry with that Brahmin.
Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, that evil-minded Daitya Vātāpi, who could assume any form at will, instantly took the form of a ram.
Having prepared the food, he feeds the Brahmins there, yet he intends to kill them; he summons them with his voice, and once they have arrived, they go to their destruction.
He, moreover, having regained his body, appeared alive once more. Then Vātāpi, having turned him into a goat and prepared it well, fed the brahmin and then summoned him back again.
Having burst through the side of that high-souled Brahmin, Vātāpi emerged from the twice-born’s belly, laughing all the while.
Thus, O Goddess, having fed the Brahmins again and again, he would tear open their bellies and kill many twice-born ones in that manner.
Then all the Brahmins, terrified with fear, fled; they went to the hermitage of Agastya and spoke [of this] before him. || 15 ||
"O Blessed One, hear our words which bring us great fear; O Lord, we have all been invited by Ilvala. (16)
That food is undoubtedly the very form of death for us; therefore, O Blessed One, protect us, whose minds have become despondent with fear. (17)
Then, having reached Prabhāsa, that great sage beheld those two foremost of Daityas there, who were slayers of Brahmins and devoted to sin.
Seeing the great asura Vātāpi prepared in the form of a ram, he said: "Give me food; I am hungry. (19)
When they were thus addressed, they then offered a welcome to the sage: "O Blessed One, I shall provide you with an extensive meal. What is the quantity of your food? I shall cook that much. (20)
Agastya said: "Cook some food, O lord of Daityas; there will be some satisfaction. "So be it," the lord of Daityas replied, O great sage, as he prepared the cooked meal.

"Be seated upon this seat; eat as you please, O Sage. Thus addressed, the great sage, muttering the Aghora mantra which brings about the end of the kalpa, took his place upon the preeminent seat and sat down.
Ilvala, the lord of the Daityas, as if laughing, surrounded him and made a heap of food measuring a hundred cubits.
Then Agastya, with a joyful mind, swallowed two mouthfuls, having assumed that great form which he had displayed when drying up the ocean.
Then he consumed that entire meal, including Vātāpi; once the Asura had finished eating, Ilvala called out to him.
Then he gave food to the high-souled Agastya; he [Agastya] reduced all that food, along with the Dānava, to ashes.
The great sage reduced Ilvala to ashes with a fist of wrath; then, letting out cries of "Alas! Alas!", all the Daityas perished.
Then Agastya, of great luster, having summoned the foremost of the twice-born, gave that place, filled with the wealth of the lords of the Daityas, to them.
Then, O Goddess, because hunger was removed there from the Dānavas by Agastya, that place of the twice-born came to be known as Kṣudhāhara.
To its west, not very far away, stands the shrine renowned as Gaṅgeśvara, which was established by Gaṅgā.

Formerly, O Great Goddess, when the high-souled Agastya was about to consume Vātāpi, he summoned Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins, for the sake of purifying himself from all the evils arising from devouring that Daitya. || 31 ||
Then, O Goddess, Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins, arrived; she purified that sage and remained established in that place. || 32 ||

In the beautiful hermitage of Agastya, which removes the fear of sin for men, one who beholds Gaṅgeśvara there is liberated from the sin arising from eating forbidden food; by means of bathing, giving gifts, chanting prayers, and so forth, there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaṅgeśvara at Agastya’s Hermitage," within the "Majesty of Nyaṅkumatī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 285 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Bālārka, the destroyer of sins, which is not very far to the north of Agastya’s hermitage, O Goddess. || 1 ||
O beloved, because the Sun performed his penance there while still a child in ancient times, he became famous on the surface of the earth by the name Bālārka.
Having seen that [image] on a Sunday, a man shall not be born with leprosy; nor shall children ever suffer from afflictions born of disease.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bālārka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the auspicious Ajapaleshvari, situated not far to the east of the abode of Agastya.
Indeed, Ajāpāla, the best of kings born in the lineage of Raghu, propitiated the Goddess there, who brings [beings] under the power of sinful diseases.
The protector of the earth indeed caused diseases in the form of goats to roam there; he established that [tirtha] there under his own name as the destroyer of sins.
The man who worships her with devotion on the third lunar day according to the prescribed rite shall obtain strength, intelligence, fame, learning, and good fortune.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ajāpāleśvarī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 287 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place renowned as Bālāditya, located two *gavyūtis* to the east of Agastya’s station.
O Goddess of the Gods, to the south of that place stands the site known as Bālārka, measuring one *gavyūti* in extent, together with the Sapaṭikā. || 2 ||
And there, the wise Viśvāmitra propitiated the Vidyā after having installed three Liṅgas and likewise consecrated the Sun-god.
He performed the practice for the sake of knowledge and attained perfection from the Sun; therefore, that Lord became renowned as Bālāditya.
O Goddess, having seen that [liṅga] which steals away the sins of the sun, a person does not encounter poverty as long as he lives. || 5 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bālārka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 288 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, to the south of that very place, at a distance of only one gavyūti, the sin-destroying Gaṅgā flows down to the netherworld (Pātāla). || 1 ||
O woman of excellent complexion, when summoned by Viśvāmitra for the purpose of bathing, O Great Goddess, one who bathes there is liberated from all sins.
There, having beheld Gaṅgeśvara as well as Viśvāmitreśvara, and having gazed upon Bāleśvara, one shall obtain all desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Three Liṅgas Named Pātālagaṅgeśvara, Viśvāmitreśvara, and Bāleśvara," within the "Majesty of Bālārka" in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 289.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme abode of Kubera, where in ancient times, O Goddess, Kubera became the perfected one (siddha) and the giver of wealth (dhanada). || 1 ||
In former times, a Brāhmaṇa lived in that place in the guise of a thief; through the power of his devotion, he was indeed made the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) by me in the past.
The Goddess said: How did that lowest of men, having become a Brāhmaṇa, take the form of a thief? O Lord of Gods, tell me how he became the giver of wealth (Dhanada). (3)
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, regarding that matter, I shall relate everything that occurred during the Uttama Manvantara, which indicates the majesty of Śiva.
O Goddess, there was once a certain twice-born man renowned as Devaśarman; residing in the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he lived on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī river.

Constantly devoted solely to the affairs of sons, fields, wife, and so forth, he then abandoned his household life and, deluded by greed for the sake of wealth, wandered over this earth with its villages and cities.
His wife, who had tremulous eyes, had gone out from his house; she was always acting according to her own will and was constantly infatuated by the god of love.
Once, by the power of fate, a son was born to her from a Śūdra; he was evil-minded, utterly unrestrained, and was therefore named Duḥsaha.
Then, after a long time, that sinful man—driven by his name and past actions, afflicted by calamities, and likewise abandoned by his kinsmen—[fell into ruin].
Seeing the materials for worship in a certain temple of Śiva placed at the entrance of a place full of many defects, he entered there with the desire to steal them.
It is said that as soon as the lamp was nearly extinguished and the wick was severed, he applied the wick-end for the purpose of searching for the substance.
Having awakened and risen there, the man, who was performing the worship of the deity, cried out loudly with his iron club as a weapon, "Who is this? Who is this? (12)
And that foolish son of a Śūdra, out of fear for his life, fled; deeply distressed, he reviled both his own birth and his actions.
Slain by the city guards on the earth, he died and in due course was born as a king in the region of Gandhāra, renowned by the name Sudurmukha.
There he was devoted to singing and instrumental music, intensely addicted to courtesans, a fool who caused distress to the people, and excluded from all dharma.
However, he was always worshipping the linga inherited through the lineage of his kingdom with flowers, garlands, incense, food offerings, perfumes, and so forth, but without mantras.
And at all times, he should offer many lamps, brightly blazing with wicks, in the principal temples of the deities.
Once, that powerful man, addicted to hunting, wandered about; having arrived at the holy site of Prabhāsa, he was moved by his former latent impressions.
Struck by enemies in battle on the auspicious bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, he had all his sins destroyed through the performance of the worship of Śiva.
Then he became the son of Viśravas, renowned on earth; he was that very one of great splendor, the powerful lord of all sacrifices.
The righteous-souled Kubera, endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, installed a linga to the east of the Nyaṅkumatī river. || 21 ||

To the west of Kaubera, on the auspicious bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, he worshipped the one renowned as Somanātha, who is like Īśāna himself, and praised that granter of all desires with devotion through this hymn.

May that Great Form of Maheśvara protect you constantly—that form which is the root-source of sacrifice, possessing a gourd with lofty fruits and hundreds of millions of cosmic eggs; the measure of which neither the Grandfather Brahmā nor Hari, stationed within the universe, knows—what then can be said of other gods? (23)

I bow to the unborn, ancient God, who is served by Indra and the king of the gods; whose eyes are equal to the moon, the sun, and fire; whose emblem is the lordly bull; and who is the cause of dissolution and the rest. (24)

To him who is the Lord of all, the sole friend possessing the three powers, attainable through yoga, the abode of the world, the source of wonder, possessed of infinite power, born of knowledge, and preeminent in the quality of fortitude; || 25 ||

I bow to Śambhu, the sole lord of the world, who holds the Pināka bow, the noose, the goad, and the trident in his hands; who wears matted hair, whose roar is like the thundercloud, who has a dark throat, and who shines with the luster of crystal.

To the skull-bearer, the garlanded one, the primordial god, the wearer of matted locks, who has terrifying serpents for his necklace; to the illuminator, the thousand-formed, the thousand-headed, the distinguished Puruṣa.

That which the virtuous describe as the imperishable, devoid of qualities, immeasurable, the singular light; that which is far-reaching, the object of knowledge, praised by the blameless, situated within the hearts of all, and supremely pure. (28)

I bow to Rudra, who resembles radiant light, who wears the young moon upon his crest, whose fierce face flashes with brilliance; he is the fuel for Time, the granter of desires, free from attachment, seated upon the throne of Dharma, and established in the two natures.

Those masters of yoga and supreme ascetics meditate upon Him who is beyond the senses, whose arms are the universe, who has conquered all enemies, who transcends the three qualities (*guṇas*), who is unborn, desireless, composed of darkness (*tamas*), consisting of the Vedas, a portion of pure consciousness, the Lord of Prajāpati, Indra invoked by many, the primordial one whose form is the singular sound of the future.
I, being liberated, bow down again and again to you, the God who severs the bonds of saṃsāra. || 31 ||

I bow to that inconceivable Vāmadeva, whose incomparable face, power, and majesty, as well as the true nature of that Supreme Person, are not fully understood even by Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha (Brahmā), and the other gods. || 32 ||
Having propitiated that Śiva of fierce form, the blessed Agastya drank the ocean; Dilīpa also obtained all his desires—I take refuge in him, the source of the universe. (33)

O Lord of Devas, O Deliverer, lift me up who am without a protector; O Śambhu, you are indeed compassionate and merciful. O Lord of Umā, rescue this wretched one submerged in the ocean of suffering; you are Bhava, you are Śaṅkara.

In heaven, the hosts of gods—Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra—sport at will while offering him worship; I praise that Śarva, I bow to him here, I mutter his name, and having sought refuge, I revere him who is worthy of adoration. (35)

Having praised the Lord in this manner, he ceased; at that very moment, Rudra, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, the boon-granting god who slew Andhaka, bestowed three boons upon Vaiśravaṇa: friendship, the status of a guardian of the quarters as his fourth, and sovereignty over the wealth of the inhabitants of heaven.
Because here, on the auspicious bank of the Nyaṅkumati, you have properly worshipped me according to the prescribed rites after having fashioned an image made of earth. (37)
Therefore, that place shall become famous by your very name; it will be known as Kuberanagara, which bestows joy upon me. || 38 ||
The Liṅga installed by you to the west of this place, according to the prescribed rites, is remembered as Somanātha, the Lord of Umā. (39)
Whoever worships that [deity] according to the prescribed rite on the auspicious Pañcamī day, his prosperity shall endure for seven generations.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Kubera’s City and the Greatness of Somanātha Established by Kubera," within the *Nyaṅkumatī-māhātmya*, in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 290.
Īśvara said: To the north of that place known as Kaubera resides the great goddess Bhadrakālī, the bestower of desired objects. (1)
At the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the great goddess Bhadrakālī, accompanied by Vīrabhadra, was the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 2 ||
Whoever worships that Goddess on the third day of the month of Caitra, nine crores of Cāmuṇḍās will become well-worshipped for him; he shall obtain good fortune, victory, and prosperity. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhadrakālī," within the "Majesty of Nyaṅkumatī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 291 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, O Great Goddess, to the north of the place known as Kaurava, Bhadrakālī performed a most difficult penance.
Endowed with supreme devotion, she installed Ravi on a Sunday coinciding with the seventh lunar day (Saptamī), using red flowers and unguents.
Whoever worships it with devotion shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices and be liberated from diseases arising from wind and bile, as well as from many other ailments.
A horse should be given as a gift right there by those desiring the full fruit of their journey.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bhadrakālī and Bālārka," within the "Majesty of Nyaṅkumatī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 292 ||
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent complexion, from that station of Vaiśravaṇa, in the southwest direction, Kubera himself is ever present as the destroyer of all poverty. || 1 ||

Adorned with the eight treasures, beginning with the *makara*, one should worship it with devotion on the fifth lunar day using perfumes, flowers, and unguents. For such a person, the attainment of incomparable treasures occurs without obstacle. (2)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kubera," within the Account of the Origin of the Abode of Kubera, in the *Nyaṅkumatī-māhātmya*, within the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 293 ||

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated to the east of Kaubera. Five *gavyūtis* away from there, O Goddess, is the site known by the name Puṣkara, where, O Great Goddess, a fisherman who was a killer of fish attained perfection (*siddha*).
The Goddess said: "Tell me in detail how he indeed attained perfection. O Maheśvara, God of gods, please speak out of your grace. (2)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to what occurred in the past during the Svārociṣa Manvantara. There was a certain man of wicked conduct, a fisherman who killed fish.
Once, while wandering, that wicked man went indeed to Puṣkara; there he beheld the abode of Śaṅkara, crowded with creepers and trees.
In the month of Māgha, afflicted by the cold and carrying his wet net, he, being distressed, ascended the palace out of a desire to seize the heat of the sun.
Then, he spread out that wet net on the tip of the palace flagpole in order to dry it with the rays of the sun.
Then, O Goddess, having gradually fallen from the palace due to his dull-wittedness, he suddenly died, O Goddess, in that sacred field of Śiva.
After a long period of time, that net became so extensive that banners were fastened to it with cords, and thus it came to be upon that auspicious palace.

Then, by the greatness of that banner, he was born on earth as a wise king, renowned as Ṛtadhvaja, in the region of Saurāṣṭra; for he wandered the earth in a chariot with a glittering banner at its peak.

His soul overcome by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, the powerful king ruled his kingdom; thereafter, that lord offered nothing else whatsoever to the abode of Śambhu except for a white, beautiful, and variegated banner.
Then the king, remembering his former births, came to the sacred field of Prabhāsa; there he found a sanctuary provided with a network of banners.
He caused a temple to be built for the god Ajogandha, who had been previously propitiated, as well as various implements for Śiva.
He constantly worshipped that sin-destroying liṅga with devotion; the high-minded one ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
Then, by the power of that Liṅga, he went to heaven after some time; therefore, having gone there with effort, one should worship the Liṅga. || 14 ||
Having bathed in the western pool at Puṣkara, the thief of sins, where in former times Brahmā performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.
And having summoned the sacred fords (tīrthas) from Puṣkara there, O beautiful lady, and having placed them in that pool near Ajogandha, he installed a great liṅga by the name of Ajogandha.
O Great Goddess, at Tripuṣkara, in the pool that destroys sins, one should give a golden lotus there to an eminent Brāhmaṇa.
Having worshipped the God according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings, one is liberated from all sins, even those accumulated over seven lifetimes. (18)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ajogandheśvara," within the "Majesty of Puṣkara" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 294 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, O beloved, in the northeastern quarter, at a distance of five *gavyūtis*, is the unsurpassed abode of Indra, where the lake of the Moon is located.
Therefore, O Goddess, situated not far from there in the northern direction is the place where the Moon-water (Candrodaka) is found, which destroys old age and poverty.
Its increase occurs with the waxing of the moon, and its waning occurs with the moon's decline; even in that age of sin, this is sometimes observed.
O Great Goddess, if one who has committed a thousand sins bathes there, he attains this state; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
There, his mind was rendered dejected by the curse uttered by Gautama, as he was terrified of the great sin arising from his illicit union with Ahalyā.

And in ancient times, O Goddess, Indra performed a sacrifice there with abundant sacrificial fees; having installed the Lord Śiva for thousands of years, it became known by the name Indreśvara, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed at Candratīrtha, having satiated the ancestors and the deities, and having worshipped Indreśvara, a man is liberated; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Indreśvara within the Majesty of Candrodaka Tīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 295.
Īśvara said: "Therefore, at a distance of seven *gavyūti*s in the south-eastern direction, there is a place named Devakula, where the gods assemble."
O Great Goddess, because it was there in the past that the linga of the perfected sages was cast down, and from which [it originated], it is therefore known as Devakula.
To its western direction flows the great river Ṛṣitoyā, O Goddess, beloved by the sages and the destroyer of all sins.
Having bathed there properly, a man should offer oblations to his ancestors; he shall bring satisfaction to his ancestors for seventy thousand years.
Gold should be given there, as well as a deer-skin and a woolen blanket; whatever is given on the new moon day of Āṣāḍha certainly bears fruit.
It increases sixteenfold until it reaches the full moon.
Gold, as well as a deer-skin and a woolen blanket, should be given there; one is liberated from all sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the River Ṛṣitoyā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 296 ||
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, tell me in detail the great majesty of the Ṛṣitoyā.
How did it acquire the name "Ṛṣitoyā" on the surface of the earth? And how did she come again to the auspicious Devadāru forest?
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, with attention; I shall declare my words concerning the majesty of Ṛṣitoyā, which destroys all sins. 3.
O lady of excellent limbs, in the meritorious Devadāru forest, hundreds and thousands of sages endowed with ascetic power dwell.
O beloved, as they lived there, a great deal of time passed; having increased through sons and grandsons, they remained settled, pervading the entire region of Dāruka.
Having come together, they all reflected among themselves: "Let us place the Vāḍava fire upon the head of the highly meritorious Sarasvatī."
After a long time, he will go to the sacred field of Prabhāsa, leaving behind his ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth, except for that which flows toward the ocean.
It brings no joy to our hearts even during bathing, giving, and recitation; therefore, we shall go to the abode of Brahmā and petition him.

Īśvara said: Having thus invited them, all those sages, radiant with ascetic power, went to the world of Brahmā to behold the god Pitāmaha; they praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, with various hymns.

The sages said: Salutations to the one whose form is the Praṇava, the creator of the universe; salutations again and again. Likewise, let there be salutations to the Supreme Self, the protector of the universe. (10)
Likewise, salutations to Him who is the destroyer of that very [universe], whose nature is Brahman; O Grandfather, salutations to you; O eldest of the gods, let there be salutations to you.
O Four-faced One, salutations to you; O Lotus-born One, let there be salutation to you! Salutations to you, Virañci; salutations to Vidhi, to Vedhas. (12)
O Consciousness and Bliss, salutations to you; O Hiraṇyagarbha, salutations to you; O you whose vehicle is the swan, salutations to you eternally; O Lotus-seated One, let there be salutations to you.
While those sages of sublimated vital energy were thus offering praise, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke with supreme delight.
"Welcome indeed, O best of the twice-born! I have already done you a favor by means of this divine hymn; now choose an excellent boon. (15)
The sages said: "O God, O best of the gods, a river that destroys sins is sought by us for our consecration; grant us this supreme boon. (16)
Īśvara said: Thus addressed by those sages resplendent with austerity, Brahmā then looked toward all the rivers who were present in embodied form.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, as well as the goddess Sarasvatī, the Candrabhāgā and the Revā, and likewise the Śarayū and the Gaṇḍakī. || 18 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, there are also the Tāpī, the river Godāvarī, the Kāverī, the Candraputrī, the Śiprā, and likewise the Carmaṇvatī.
O fair-faced one, the Sindhu, the Vedikā, and all the rivers stand there in embodied form—all pure and destroyers of sin. (20)

Seeing that all the rivers were flowing toward the earth, the Grandfather (Brahmā) fixed his gaze upon his water-pot in the delightful Devadāru forest at Prabhāsa, the most excellent sacred field; they then entered into that water-pot.
Brahmā said: "All these highly meritorious rivers have been held within the water-pot of Brahmā; out of compassion for the sages, let them enter the earth. (22)
"O twice-born ones, if I abandon even one, another will surely be angry with me; therefore, I shall release them all, who have made their home in my water-pot. (23)
Īśvara said: Then Brahmā released [the waters], and the great rivers situated there also released them; having released them, Brahmā spoke thus to all the sages again and again.
Since rivers of great velocity, consisting of water and eager for my consecration, were released by me when entreated by the sages; || 25 ||
She shall be known by the name Ṛṣitoyā upon the surface of the earth; she is the goddess beloved by the sages and the destroyer of all sins.
Īśvara said: Thus, O Goddess, the river known as Ṛṣitoyā, which is pure and auspicious, arrived at the Devadāru forest, O lady of beautiful countenance. (27)
The goddess was brought to the ocean by sages who had mastered the Vedas, amidst the sounding of musical instruments and drums and the auspicious chants of the Vedas.
The Goddess is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to attain in three places: at Mahodaya, at the great pilgrimage site (mahātīrtha), and in the presence of Mūlacaṇḍīśa. || 29 ||
Where that river flowing eastward meets the ocean, and where the water of the sages is found—what more could one seek beyond that? (30)
Those men are always blessed who drink that water, wherein their bones dissolve within the space of six months.
In the morning the Gaṅgā flows, and likewise in the evening the Yamunā.
At midday, the Sarasvatī flows joined by a thousand rivers; in the afternoon, the Revā flows; and in the evening, the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) flows.
The man who, knowing this, is skilled in bathing there and performs the śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rules, shall partake in its fruit. || 34 ||
Thus has been briefly described the great glory of Ṛṣitoyā, which removes all sins of men and bestows the fruits of all desires. (35)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Ṛṣitoyā," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: To the west of Ṛṣitoyā, at a distance of just one gavyūti, there is the place named Saṅgāleśvara, which destroys all sins.
There, Prayāga is hidden, as are the deity Mādhava, the goddess Jāhnavī, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī.
O fair-faced one, there are many other sacred fords there as well; by bathing, seeing, and worshipping them, one shall be liberated from all sins.
Pārvatī said: O Maheśāna, saluted by all the gods, tell me how Prayāga, the king of holy places (tīrtharāja), is the eternal Viṣṇu. || 4 ||
How is it that the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī, as well as many other sacred fords (tīrthas), exist, O Bull-bannered Lord? || 5 ||
They arrived right there in the presence of Saṅgāleśvara. What is the meaning of this name "Saṅgāleśa"? Tell me, for I am curious.
Īśvara said: "O beautiful goddess of the gods, formerly, when the Liṅga fell and all the deities assembled, there were three and a half crores of meritorious [sites]."
This Prayāga, the king of holy places, has arrived; it conceals itself, surrounded by millions of other sacred sites.
Then the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived there and beheld that king of holy places with their divine vision.
Filled with millions of sacred fords, pure and destructive of sins, they were overcome with great sorrow upon hearing of the falling of the Liṅga.
Then, O Goddess, all the best of gods, beginning with Brahmā, stood there.
At that very time, however, the eternal Lord Rudra, devoid of joy, arrived and spoke these words.

Listen to my words, O gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu: My unsurpassed Liṅga has fallen due to the curse of a sage; therefore, worship that Liṅga for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (13)
Having spoken thus, O beloved, Mahādeva remained in that place; there, it is remembered, are three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
The fourth is named Trisaṅgama, where there is a confluence of rivers: that of the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and likewise the daughter of the Sun.
One crore of holy fords (tīrthas) is established in Brahmakuṇḍa, and likewise, one crore is proclaimed to be in Vaiṣṇavakuṇḍa.
It is proclaimed that there are one and a half crores [of deities] celebrated in the Śivakuṇḍa; the Brahmakuṇḍa is in the west, and the Vaiṣṇavakuṇḍa is remembered as being in the east.
That which is situated in the middle portion is celebrated as the Rudrakuṇḍa; O fair-faced one, it is there that the Gaṅgā emerges from the center of the pool.
And where she is united with the daughter of the Sun, that is called Trisaṅgama; between these two, in a subtle space, Sarasvatī remains hidden there.
In these [places], Prayāga, the leader of all sacred fords (tīrtha), is eternally present. O lady of beautiful countenance, whatever man comes here during the month of Māgha—
O beloved, one should bathe at the time of dawn when the sun is situated in Capricorn; listen now to the fruit obtained when the sun has slightly risen.
By the first bath alone, a man who is endowed with perfect faith and has conquered his senses completely dispels the evil committed through the mind.
Verbal [confession] is by the second; bodily [confession] is by the third; that arising from association is by the fourth; and the secret [confession] is by the fifth.
One removes minor offenses (upapātakas) by means of the sixth bath alone. || 24 ||
O fair-faced one, by performing the consecration of the sacrificial pits seven times, even great sins are always washed away by men.
He who bathes for the entire month at Prayāga, known as Gupta—the merit of that cannot be described even by Brahmā and the other gods in ten million kalpas.
O beautiful lady, whatever sacred fords exist at Prabhāsa, this ford is the most beloved among them all, the destroyer of all sins.
For the sake of their protection, these Mothers must indeed be worshipped there by me with great effort, using various auspicious food offerings.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, with a mind endowed with faith, O Goddess, their followers—bhūtas and pretas by the millions—[assemble]. (29)
One should worship those Mothers for the destruction of their fears; by bathing in this sacred ford (tīrtha), a man casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whosoever performs a śrāddha ceremony with devotion for the sake of the ancestors, that best of men shall deliver the host of his father’s kin and the host of his mother’s kin.
A bull should be given there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage; for him who performs the pilgrimage in this manner, the reward is infinite.
Thus has the greatness of Guptaprayāga been told to you; having heard it and rejoiced, a person shall attain the abode of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Guptaprayāga," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 298 ||
Īśvara said: On the southern side of that very place, situated not far away, Mādhava stands there, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.

He who, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, having fasted and subdued his senses, worships him with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and unguents, goes to the supreme abode that grants freedom from rebirth.

In this regard, a verse was sung of old by Brahmā, the creator of the world: "The man who, having bathed in Viṣṇukuṇḍa, worships Mādhava, shall go to the supreme abode where the Lord Hari himself resides. (3)
Thus has this entire majesty of Viṣṇu as the deity been recounted; it bestows all desires upon men and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mādhava," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 299.
Īśvara said: To the north of that very place, situated slightly toward the northwest, there is the shrine named Saṅgāleśvara, which destroys all sins.
There, O beloved, both Brahmā and Viṣṇu were intent upon the worship of the Liṅga; and Śakra, endowed with great splendor, likewise worshipped the Liṅga.
Varuṇa, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), Dharmarāja, and Pāvaka, together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Guardians of the World, were present on all sides. || 3 ||
The great liṅga named Saṅgāleśvara was propitiated; having worshipped it and witnessed its supreme majesty, they all [did so]. || 4 ||

And they spoke suddenly, O Goddess, filled with supreme bliss: "Since it has been established by the hosts of gods who have assembled here, its name on the surface of the earth shall be Saṅgāleśvara. (5)
Those men who worship the deity named Saṅgāleśvara—none in their lineage shall ever become destitute.
Whatever fruit is obtained from giving a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra, that same fruit one attains from the sight of Saṅgāleśvara.

Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā) and performed his bath according to the prescribed rules, the man who performs the śrāddha for the ancestors while free from anger—his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings (yāvadābhūtasaṃplavam).
And that sacred field is half a krośa in circumference all around; it bestows all desires upon men and destroys all sins.
O Great Goddess, in this field, living beings—whether superior or middling—who meet their death in due course of time, they too attain the supreme goal.
O Great Goddess, those men who, having undertaken a fast unto death, shall give up their lives, will certainly merge into the Supreme Lord.

Those killed by a cow, those killed by a twice-born man, and those killed by fanged beasts; those who are suicides and those who have died from snakebite—[these are the ones for whom this rite is intended].
Those who have lost their lives upon this bed, and those who are devoid of purity, [attain liberation] at this most meritorious tīrtha, which grants freedom from rebirth.

When sixteen Śrāddhas have been offered, and the rite of releasing a bull has been performed, and the Brahmins have been fed according to the rules, liberation will surely follow; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, all the gods departed for heaven.
The greatness of Saṅgāleśvara has thus been briefly told to you; when heard, it removes sins as well as miseries and sorrows. (16)

Thus ends the three hundredth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Saṅgāleśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 300 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Siddheshvara, situated not far away in the eastern direction of that very place.
When the gods had assembled together and quickly installed the auspicious Śivaliṅga, which removes all sins and is enriched with the name Saṅgāleśvara; || 2 ||
Then all the hosts of Siddhas, having propitiated the bull-bannered Lord, installed a Liṅga that bestows all supernatural powers.
Then the hosts of Siddhas praised Śiva with various hymns at that place called Tatsiddheśvara, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, said, "Request an excellent boon. Thereupon, having offered their salutations, they all spoke to the moon-crested Lord: (5)
Whatever man comes here, bathes according to the prescribed rite, worships Siddhanātha, and recites the Śatarudriya; || 6 ||

O best of sages, one should recite the Aghora mantra, the Gāyatrī, and that of Maheśvara; by reciting them for no more than six months, one will certainly attain the supernatural powers (aiśvarya) such as atomization (aṇimā) and complete perfection.
Ishvara said: Having spoken thus, "It shall be so," Hara vanished. A man, having worshipped Siddheshvara, should indeed mutter the Aghora mantra. || 8 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, at the dead of night, that man who remains fearless and maintains fortitude shall attain success.
Thus, O Goddess, has been narrated this majesty of the god Siddheśvara, which destroys sins and bestows the fruits of all desires. (10)

Thus ends the three hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Gandharveshvara, situated five bow-lengths to the north of that very place.
O Great Goddess, having seen it, a man becomes handsome; having bathed and worshipped even once the Liṅga established by the Gandharvas, one attains all desires and becomes sweet-voiced. || 2 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gandharveśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme deity in the north; he who propitiates that god, the destroyer of great sins.

On its very western side, at a distance of three bow-lengths, there stands an excellent Liṅga installed by the Nāgas, headed by Śeṣa, who were endowed with great ascetic power after they had propitiated Mahādeva. || 2 ||
O beloved, poison does not affect the body of one who propitiates that God, who was formerly propitiated by the serpents, for as long as that person lives.
The serpents become gracious toward him and never cause him harm; therefore, a man should worship that liṅga with every effort.
There, on the highly meritorious western bank of the Gaṅgā, O lady of excellent complexion, many Liṅgas have been established by the sages.
Having seen and worshipped them, a person is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.

Thus ends the three hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Uttareśvara," within the "Majesty of Saṅgāleśvara," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 303 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, situated seven bow-lengths to the northeast of Saṅgāleśa.
In that [lake], O beloved, there are always three-eyed fish that dwell in the water; they are seen even in the Kali age—this I have spoken as the truth, the absolute truth.
Having bathed in it, O Great Goddess, one is liberated from the five great sins.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard those words of his, the virtuous Girijā was struck with wonder and spoke to him whose crest-jewel was the trembling moon.
Pārvatī said: O Śiva, how did Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, arrive there? And how did the aquatic fish come to have three eyes?
Tell me this in detail, O Lord, if I am dear to you.
Īśvara said: Listen, O auspicious Goddess, for I shall speak since you ask me; it is my conviction that people will become believers and full of faith.
When Mahādeva was indeed cursed by the sages, who were shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and filled with anger, on account of some other cause; || 8 ||
Then all those sages, realizing that Maheśvara had been cursed, and seeing that the entire world as well as themselves were devoid of joy, [were filled with grief].
Having propitiated the Supreme Lord who had assumed the form of an elephant, the twice-born ones joyfully led him to a lofty place.
From that time forward, even though Maheśvara was ever gracious toward them, they all constantly considered themselves to be supreme offenders against Śiva.
Having arrived quickly from Mahodaya to that great sacred ford, everyone performed most formidable austerities in the presence of Saṅgāleśvara.
Having worshipped all those named Saṅgāleśvara according to the prescribed rite, [there were] Bhṛgu, Atri, as well as Maṅki, Kaśyapa, and Kaṇva.
Gautama and Kauśika, as well as Kuśika of great asceticism, Śūkara, Bharadvāja, and Bhārgava of great asceticism. || 14 ||
Jātūkarṇya, Vasiṣṭha, Sāvarṇi, Parāśara, Śāṇḍilya, Pulastya, and Vatsa of great asceticism; || 15 ||
These and many other great sages, indeed innumerable, [were there]. || 16 ||
Having reached Saṅgāleśvara at Prabhāsa, the destroyer of sins, they constantly perform penance after having installed Maheśvara.
Then, after a long time, all those bulls among sages, while in meditation upon the Three-eyed One, failed to perceive Maheśvara.
Those ascetics, whose wealth was their austerity and who were devoted to penance, attained a three-eyed state; looking at one another, they were filled with apprehension regarding the Three-Eyed One.
Having realized through meditation that the god had attained the state of having three eyes, they praised Maheśvara with various hymns, regarding him as such. || 20 ||
Cakru and Ugra performed penance for the sake of worshipping the trident-bearing God; while they were indeed performing that penance, Maheśvara was filled with compassion.
He said to all those sages, "Listen to this supreme boon; O best of sages, I am pleased by your penance and your worship. (22)
The sages said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, you ought to grant us a boon; O Hara, bring the Gaṅgā with speed for our consecration."
Having performed our ablutions in it, we, though we have committed offenses against you, shall attain purity upon the surface of the earth through the state of ignorance. (24)
The Lord said: "You are the purifiers of the pure and the sanctifiers of sanctifiers; I shall bring the Gaṅgā herself for the satisfaction of your hearts. (25)

"O best of sages, through your purity, the three eyes have been produced," having spoken thus, Śambhu, his eyes motionless in meditation, then remembered in a mere moment Gaṅgā, who is filled with schools of fish.
As soon as she was remembered, the goddess Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, pierced the surface of the earth and arrived there, filled with schools of fish.
When the sages beheld the auspicious Gaṅgā filled with fish, those fish, upon being merely seen by them, attained the state of having three eyes.
Īśvara said: "O Brahmins, by the sight of you, [the gods] have attained the state of having three eyes. This is an illustration for all, and a demonstration for the worlds. (29)
The sages said: "O Mahādeva, by your grace, may the progeny of fish in this pool always possess three eyes in every age. (30)
Whatever man comes to this sacrificial pit and performs a ritual bath, and gives gold, cows, clothing, and likewise sesame seeds to a Brahmin; || 31 ||
"May he, the three-eyed one, be born especially on the new moon day. Having said, "It shall be so," Hara vanished from sight.
The Brahmins, filled with satisfaction, all departed for Mahodaya.
Thus has this supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā been told to you, O Goddess; when heard, it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of all desires. (34)

Thus ends the three hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gaṅgā Situated Near Saṅgāleśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the shrine situated to the east of that [Tīrtha], named Nāradāditya, which destroys old age and poverty.
O Goddess, three hundred dhanus to the west of Mūlacaṇḍīśa, Nārada worshipped the Sun, the drawer of waters; at that very moment, his body became freed from old age.
The Goddess said: "How did Nārada, the bull among sages, come to be overtaken by old age? How was the Sun propitiated by him? Tell me this, O Śaṅkara. (3)
The Lord said: When Nārada, the bull among sages, arrived at Dvāravatī, he then beheld all those sons of Viṣṇu who were possessed of great strength.
While they were playing with one another in the midst of that royal palace, they all, filled with humility, saw Nārada approaching.
They paid their respects according to custom, yet they were in a hurry because Sāmba was absent; seeing him so ill-mannered, Nārada spoke.
"O Sāmba, son of Hari, because you are intoxicated with pride in your body, you shall receive a terrible curse in a very short time."
Sāṃba said: "What purpose is served by bowing down to sages who have conquered their own selves? By bestowing blessings upon them, a diminution of their ascetic merit occurs. (8)
O Nārada, son of Brahmā, not even a trace of that which is indeed the true nature of the sages exists in you; what more than this can be said?
Neither wife nor sons, nor grandsons or great-grandsons; neither house nor even door, nor indeed cows nor calves [are yours]. (10)
The mind-born son of Brahmā, though established in celibacy, constantly performs what is improper; why is his nature such? (11)
Without war you have no happiness, and there is no happiness without quarrel; whether it be of such a kind or that, even verbal dispute is always dear to you.
Nārada performs bathing, twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, and libations for the ancestors and the gods; other Brāhmaṇas perform different rites.
"Since you, arrogant because of your youth, will curse me, therefore you too, O brahmin-sage, shall be possessed by old age. (14)
Thus cursed at that time, O Goddess, Nārada, the best of sages, went to a secluded, pure place, free from thorns and bones. || 15 ||
Seated upon an excellent seat covered with a black antelope skin on the delightful bank of the river Ṛṣitoyā, the great sage established [the image].
He praised with various hymns the Sun, the dispeller of darkness, the beautiful image of Sūrya that destroys all poverty.

Salutations to you whose nature is the Rigveda; salutations to you who are the abode of the Samavedas. Salutations to you whose body is the singular form of knowledge, and who have shaken off all darkness.
Salutations to the Supreme Self, who is the nature of pure light, formless, and stainless in essence; who is the most excellent, the most worthy of choice, and the all-pervading.
Salutations to the embodiment of bliss whose nature pervades the entire universe; to the one who is purified as the cause of all, and who is the ultimate goal for those with minds of wisdom.
Salutation to you who are the essence of all things, whose form is light yet unperceivable; salutation to you, O Bhāskara, and likewise salutation to the Maker of Day.
Ishvara said: As he was thus praising him with his heart before him, O Queen of the Gods, the eternal Eye of the Universe appeared. Greatly pleased, he spoke to Narada, the bull among sages. (22)
Sūrya said: "Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever dwells in your mind; being pleased with you, I shall grant it even if it be very difficult to obtain. (23)
Nārada said: "O God, O Divākara, if you are pleased, may I, though possessed of the age of a youth, have a body endowed with old age through your grace. (24)
O Dispeller of Darkness, may there be no fear of disease for that man who beholds you on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day, through your grace.
Īśvara said: Having spoken thus, "It shall be so," the Sun vanished from sight. O Goddess, this entire majesty of the deity Nāradāditya, which destroys all sins, has been narrated to you. (26)

Thus ends the three hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nāradāditya," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Sāmbāditya, located to the north of that [place], which destroys all sins.
There, having performed austerities and propitiated the Sun-god, Sāmba obtained a beautiful body through the grace of the Thousand-rayed One.
When the son of Jāmbavatī was cursed by his father out of anger, he then propitiated Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one.
For the sake of favoring the curse, Viṣṇu, the son of Jāmbavatī together with Sāmba, having assumed a gracious countenance, spoke to him.
Go to the supreme region of Brahmā in the Prābhāsika field, on the delightful bank of the Ṛṣitoyā river, adorned with Brāhmaṇas.
"In that regard, O dear son, I shall grant you a boon in the form of the Sun," thus was Sāmba addressed at that time by the powerful Viṣṇu.
He went to the beautiful and auspicious city of Śiva in the Prābhāsika field; there he propitiated the supreme god Bhāskara, the drawer of waters.
Then, having praised him in many ways with hymns of praise, he propitiated him.
Ravi replied to Sāmba: "I am indeed pleased by your hymn of praise. Go quickly, O best of men, to the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā."
Thus addressed, he then arrived at the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā river, where the Brahman-sage Nārada was indeed performing austerities.
Having gone there, the son of Hari spoke these words to those Brāhmaṇas who were residing in that elevated place.
Sāṃba said: "This indeed is the portion of Brahmā in the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa; those Brāhmaṇas who reside here are indeed remembered as the most excellent on earth. (12)
"O Brahmins, at your word I shall propitiate the Sun; for this very place was previously ordained for me by Viṣṇu. (13)
The Brahmins said: "O Sāmba, success shall be yours; worship the Sun. Having been told this by the Brahmins, he then entered the temple of Prabhākara.
The son of Jāmbavatī, along with Sāmba, constantly propitiated him; and seeing him devoted to asceticism, the great and compassionate Viṣṇu [appeared].
Filled with affection for his son, he indeed reflected thus: "Just as Rudra is the bestower of sovereignty, so too is Viṣṇu the giver of liberation."

For just as the Lord of the Gods (Indra) is remembered as the bestower of heaven when worshipped with sacrifices, just as water combined with earth and ashes is a purifier, and just as fire is by nature a burner, so too is Gaṇeśvara the remover of obstacles. || 17 ||
Just as the daughter of Brahmā is for men in the granting of unimpeded speech, so too there is no other deity besides the Sun-god who bestows freedom from disease.
Although that pure god Bhāskara has been propitiated by me in many ways, he does not grant me the boon because of my curse.
Having reflected thus, the lotus-eyed Lord Viṣṇu, Janārdana, being pleased with him, assumed the form of the sun.

Standing in the very presence of him who is known as Aparanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu himself appeared visibly there as the Sun, the Maker of Day; and being supremely pleased, the Giver of Boons spoke to those of meritorious deeds.
"Enough of this distress for you, O Sāmba; why do you perform such penance? I am pleased with you, O son of Hari; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. (22)

Sāṃba said: "O Bhavānī, O Lord of the gods of gods, O you whose garments and ornaments are manifest before my eyes! By your grace, Nirmala’s body has been freed from leprosy. Please remain forever present and stationed in this beautiful place. (23)
Sūrya said: "O Sāmba, now your body shall become stainless. Any man who comes here on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, intent upon fasting and remaining awake during the night," (24)
The eighteen types of leprosy as well as other diseases born of sin shall never occur in the lineage of that great-souled one. (25)

That man who, having performed his ablutions, being endowed with devotion and having conquered his senses, worships the greatly radiant Sāmbāditya on a Sunday, becomes free from disease, wealthy, and possessed of sons. || 26 ||
To the northeast of that very place, situated slightly toward the north-east, is a meritorious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that destroys sins, filled with clear water.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rules, the wise man should perform the śrāddha rite; he should feed the brāhmaṇas and worship Sāmbāditya.
With his every desire fulfilled, he is glorified in the world of the Sun. || 29 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Sāṃbāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 306 ||
Īśvara said: Slightly to the east of Sāṃbāditya, situated somewhat toward the southeast, is the one named Aparanārāyaṇa, than whom there is none higher on earth. || 1 ||
O Goddess of the gods, that Sun-god, who possesses the nature of Viṣṇu, assumed another form and, in the form of Viṣṇu, granted a boon to Sāmba. || 2 ||
In former times, Viṣṇu was indeed renowned by the name Aparājita; [this occurred] according to the prescribed rite on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
One should worship the lotus-eyed Lord there, who is of the nature of the sun; he becomes liberated from sins and prospers with all his desires.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Aparanārāyaṇa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 307 ||
Īśvara said: Prior to that Nārāyaṇa, there existed something established as Īśāna, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mūlacaṇḍīśa. || 1 ||
O beloved goddess, where our linga was formerly cast down by the sages with eyes red with anger, it attained the state of being the hundredfold Mūla-caṇḍīśa.
O Goddess, the first [liṅga] was the Liṅgodbhava, which fell due to the anger of the sages; whatever sages were staying there in the Devadāru forest, [they were the ones who caused it].
After some time, O Great Goddess, I arrived there; O Goddess, out of a desire to test them, they became enraged, and then, O Queen of the Gods, they cursed me by causing my linga to fall.
The Goddess said: "How did these twice-born ones come to have their true nature destroyed by anger? Tell me this, for my curiosity is great. (5)

Īśvara said: O Goddess, in former times, having assumed the form of Ḍiṇḍi in the Dāruka forest, I became a naked mendicant in the holy hermitage of the sages. Seeing me begging for alms in the hermitage, all those wives of the sages [were struck with wonder]. || 6 ||
Having fallen under the sway of desire and having abandoned what is dear from every side, they beheld him with an upward-pointing *liṅga*, wearing a crown of matted hair.
"Begging with his limbs smeared with ashes like another fish-bannered god (Kāma), all our wives have been thrown into agitation by this Diṇḍin."
"Therefore, we shall cast a curse upon you," the sages then said. Then those whose wealth is austerity took the water for the curse and performed their twilight devotions.
"Let this linga, which is seen to be perpetually erect, go downwards. When this was said, the linga fell there in my temple.
That liṅga, renowned in the three worlds by the name Mūlacaṇḍīśa, having seen it fallen, those ascetics, their minds overcome with anger, began once more to strike Ḍiṇḍin.
Some with seats in their hands, others carrying water-pots, and still others holding sandals, ran behind him.
And Dindi, having become invisible, said to you, O slender-waisted one: "Behold these ascetics whose minds are overcome by anger."
For this reason, O sinless Goddess, I did not grant favor to those wrathful ascetics at your word.
In the meantime, not seeing Diṇḍin, all those sages became joyless and went to see the god Pitāmaha.
Having seen Virañci, the lord of the gods, free from all feverish distress, all the sages bowed their heads and spoke straightforwardly.
"O Blessed One, there is a certain ascetic in the form of a mendicant who, it is said, has entered [the city] to beg for the purpose of destroying [my] wife. (17)
That man of evil conduct was cursed by us, and his linga was struck down; when it fell, ours likewise fell as well.
"He has departed because of that cause; since that emblem has fallen, we all remain devoid of joy. Please explain the reason for this. (19)
Brahmā said: "This great deed which has been performed by you is unseemly—you who, out of envy, were intent on killing Rudra, who is exceedingly handsome."

Having abandoned these excellent women—the Asurī, Dānavī, Daivī, Yakṣiṇī, Kinnarī, as well as the Vidyādharī, Gandharvī, and the charming Nāgakanyā—even among those who belong to you, [they have turned their minds]. || 21 ||
O twice-born ones, you do not at all know her who brings delight to everyone—the mistress of the three worlds, endowed with supreme beauty. (22)
Having abandoned her, how can he bring joy to the wives of the sages? For Rudra was indeed entreated by her while he was bestowing grace upon the seers.
By those words of Pārvatī, her mind was set upon inquiry; for he is the Lord of even the fourteenfold multitude of living beings.

That lord of the senses, having been cursed by you in the form of Diṇḍi, has caused this entire abode of his qualities—the realm of gods, animals, and humans—to be likewise cursed and remain devoid of joy. (25)
"By this curse of yours, a great calamity arises; otherwise, the Liṅga, once fallen, cannot attain elevation even through worship. (26)
When this had been said by the Lord, the brahmins spoke to the Grandfather: "Where is he to be seen by us? Tell us according to the truth. (27)
Brahmā said: He resides in the form of an elephant, stationed at the hermitage of Kubera; go there, approach him, and gratify that wielder of the Pināka bow.
Having heard these words of his, all those ascetics, numbering ten million, set out immediately with joyful hearts.
They reflected upon seeing that auspicious region, where Rudra, known as Pitāmaha, dwells in the form of an elephant in the hermitage of Kubera.
Perceiving the ascetics, whose wealth was their penance, to be thirsty and with throats parched by hunger, Gaurī took some cow's milk and stood before them out of compassion.
Bearing on her head a braid that was black, curved, glossy, and long like a female serpent, the fair-complexioned Gaurī was joined with the essence of cow's milk.
She said to all those sages: "That which was brought by me from the mountain is cow's milk, possessing the fragrance of wood-apple fruit and resembling nectar. (33)
Thus addressed by her, the brahmins said to that large-eyed woman: "Having bathed, we shall all drink the cow's milk brought by you."
Then, having heard that, the goddess likewise prepared an excellent, beautiful pool for the purpose of bathing, which was filled with hot water.
There, they all bathed together and were liberated from their great fatigue; having spent the day, they gathered for the purpose of drinking cow's milk.
Having fashioned auspicious leaf-cups from the leaves of the *divākara* tree, they all sat down in order and drank the cow's milk.
Then, for the sake of satisfying those hungry sages, he filled their leaf-cups with cow's milk as if with nectar.
Gaurī filled it once more, and having drunk, they attained satisfaction; freed from hunger, thirst, and fatigue, they stood as if born again. (39)
Then, with their minds composed, they realized: "This one known as Gopālī has arrived here as Gaurī for the sake of bestowing grace upon us. (40)
Having bowed their heads, they all said to that slender-waisted woman: "O Umā, tell us where Rudra is staying so that we may see him at once."
