Thus addressed, those great-souled ones beheld that mighty elephant, who, having attained the state of an elephant, was moving about with great strength.
"Indeed, he should be accepted by you according to your own devotion and as it pleases you. Having received those words, O twice-born ones, they gathered together in one place.
With a purified inner self, he went to see that elephant; where the Brahmins were gathered together, there was a highly auspicious holy site known as Saṅgameśvara, famous everywhere from of old.
Then, desiring to see that great elephant, they set out from there, completely abandoning their water-pots and arming themselves by their own efforts.
The sacred ford where those water-pots were abandoned is called Kuṇḍikā; it removes all sins of men and bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
Then, having reached the hermitage of Kubera, those best of sages beheld that elephant situated within a grove of coconut trees.
With joyful minds, they began to seize him with their own hands; the elephant cast off those ascetics who were clinging to his trunk.
Some [women] had them clinging to their limbs on all sides, yet they remained free from fear; thus he was again acted upon by all of them like gnats.
Established in the forest, the elephant of Hara performs various sports; then, completely casting off that form consisting of a fierce elephant, Rudra [assumes his own nature].
Furthermore, he assumed another beautiful form as Dindi, accompanied by the loud proclamation of the word "Victory! and auspicious Vedic chants.
Furthermore, that place where the Liṅga of great prosperity was raised up by him is called Unnata; it is the best among all excellent locations.
Assuming the form of an elephant, the one of great strength remained in that place; indeed, in the form of Gaṇanātha, he stood tall in the world.
Assuming the form of a ḍiṇḍi, Rudra said to those whose wealth is penance: "Tell me here what must be done for you by me."
Thus addressed by them, who were devoted to all forms of knowledge and action, he replied: "By your grace, may all living beings be filled with joy, just as they were in the past."
"O Lord of the gods of gods, whatever has been done by us with deluded minds should be forgiven; O Lord of the Suras, through your grace, may you be gracious toward us. (56)
Having been told by him, "So be it," they were all freed from their fever; then those sages fashioned a linga in imitation of his form, and all those sages, free from envy, offered hymns of praise.

Forgive us, O Lord of the gods of gods; grant us your favor. Enter into dissolution within this liṅga known as Mūlacaṇḍīśa. O Lord of the gods of gods, your portion must indeed be received here at the three times of day.
Īśvara said: The goddess is called Caṇḍī, and I am remembered as her lord; the Liṅga is known as its root because it fell here.
Therefore, it shall become famous as "Caṇḍīśamūla. Even with hundreds of vast wells, step-wells, and tanks— || 60 ||
The merit that arises from all those performed acts is obtained simply by the sight of the Liṅga; it is the same fruit of merit one would attain by giving away the entire universe.
O Goddess, one obtains that merit from the sight of Mūlacaṇḍīśa; there, sixteen gifts indeed should be given by the best of men.

"O best of the twice-born, all that I have spoken shall come to pass exactly so. Go to the Dāruvana forest, O Brahmins, all of you whose wealth is asceticism. Commanded by me, all of you, O twice-born ones, go to the Dāruvana."

Then, O Maheśvarī, having received my great words of supreme significance, all those sages were filled with joy; and having gone to that Dāruvana forest, those whose wealth is their austerity once again performed severe penance.
For this reason, O Goddess, the Liṅga known as Mūlacaṇḍīśa, which destroys the sins of men and is adorned with a crescent moon, [is established]. (65)

O Goddess, because you performed this unsurpassed act of removing the fatigue of the sages whose souls were parched by thirst through the gift of milk from your udder, that [place] became a pool on the surface of the earth known as Taptodaka.
He who bathes in the waters of the Ṛṣitoyā and worships Caṇḍīśa shall become powerful on earth, a sovereign lord of the worlds.
O Goddess, this greatness of the deity Mūlacaṇḍīśa has been briefly proclaimed to you; when heard, it destroys all sins.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Greatness of Mūlacaṇḍīśa in the Arising of the Taptodaka Kuṇḍa," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 308 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Vinayaka, renowned as Chaturmukha, situated to the north of Chandisha. (1)
In a certain spot toward the northeast, at a distance of four bow-lengths, one should worship that [liṅga] with great effort; thus, one is liberated from all obstacles.

Having worshipped the Four-faced One there on the fourth lunar day with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, including various kinds of food and sweetmeats, one shall become a partaker of spiritual accomplishment.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Caturmukha-Vināyaka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 309 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, situated at a distance of two bow-lengths in the northwestern direction, is the one named Kalaṃbeśvara, who destroys all sins. (1)

Having seen and worshipped it, one shall be liberated from all sins. On a Monday coinciding with the new moon (amāvāsyā), that very place bestows great merit; those desiring the fruit of merit should provide food for the Brahmins there. || 2 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kalaṃbeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 310 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Hari Gopālasvāmin, situated twenty dhanus to the east of Caṇḍīśa.

It pacifies all sins and destroys the flood of poverty; having seen and worshipped it, especially in the month of Māgha, and having performed worship and a night vigil there, one shall go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the three hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gopālasvāmī Hari," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 311 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, O beloved, eight bow-lengths to the north of that place, one should behold the Sun-god Bakulasvāmin, who destroys all suffering.
If a man performs a vigil on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, he attains all his desires and is glorified in the world of the Sun.

Thus ends the three hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bakulasvāmī," in the first section on the Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 312 ||

Īśvara said: Therefore, situated sixteen *dhanus* away in the northwestern direction, there is indeed the northern sun (*uttarārka*) by name, which immediately produces conviction. By performing the *niṃbasaptamī* rite, one is liberated from all diseases. (1)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Uttarārka," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 313 ||
Īśvara said: Now, situated one *gavyūti* to the south-east of Devakula, on the shore of the ocean, is the delightful and unsurpassed Ṛṣitīrtha. || 1 ||
O Goddess, even today sages remain there in the form of stone images; they are seen by humans as the destroyers of all sins.

There, on the new moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) is especially attained by low-born men who are endowed with faith, as well as the performance of ritual bathing.

At the confluence of the Ṛṣitoyā, bathing and performing śrāddha are very difficult to obtain; there, those best of sages praise the gift of cows. One should cause food to be given to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity.

Thus ends the three hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mūlacaṇḍīśa and the Confluence of Ṛṣitīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Marudāryā, which possesses great splendor and is situated half a krośa to the west of that [place]. || 1 ||

A person should diligently worship the Goddess—who is honored by the Maruts and who bestows the fruits of all desires—with fragrances, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite on the seventh and especially the Mahānavamī days, for the sake of accomplishing all their wishes.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Goddess Marudāryā," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now, at a distance of five *gavyūtis* to the east of Devakula, in the midst of Śambarasthāna, there is one renowned as Kṣemāditya. || 1 ||
O Goddess, having seen him, a person shall attain the fulfillment of their welfare and goals; when worshipped on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, he grants all desires.
Thus has been described the establishment of the sacred sites (tīrtha) in the location of Devakula.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kṣemāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 316 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess Kaṇṭakaśoṣiṇī, situated to the north of the temple and to the south of the high mound.
I shall describe its origin; listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved. On the southern side of Unnata, the best of the twice-born perform sacrifices.
Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Kaṇva, Maṅki, Sāvarṇi, and likewise Jātūkarṇya. (3)
Vatsa, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Viṣṇu, Śātātapa, and Parāśara; || 4 ||
Śāṇḍilya and Kauśika, Gautama and Gārgya, Dālbhya and Śaunaka, as well as Śākalya and Gālava. || 5 ||
Jābāli, Mudgala, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka, Viśvāmitra, Śatānanda, Jahnu, and likewise Viśvāvasu.
These and other sages performed various sacrifices after constructing a sacrificial enclosure on the auspicious bank of the river Ṛṣitoyā.
It resounded with the dances of gods and gandharvas, the music of flutes and lutes, the chanting of the Vedas, and the sounds arising from sacrifices, oblations, and the agnihotra fire.
Everything was enveloped in incense and honored with the fragrance of clarified butter; it was graced by divine sages and the best of the twice-born who were masters of the four Vedas.
Having seen such a place, the exceedingly powerful Daityas emerged from the midst of the ocean for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice.
Deceitful, with massive bodies, dark-complexioned, and pot-bellied; they had long eyebrows, beards, and tips of the nose, with red eyes and red hair. || 11 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, all the Daityas had assembled at the sacrifice; seeing them of fierce form and terrifying appearance, all the sages [were struck with fear].
Some fell upon the ground, while others, with sacrificial ladles in their hands, fell into the fire; some entered the hall of the wives, and others likewise entered the oblation-hall.
The officiating priests, however, stood in the midst of the assembly hall, observing silence.
O Goddess, when this had thus occurred regarding the high-souled sages, then the Adhvaryu, possessed of great splendor, took recourse to fortitude with reverence.
Having placed the sacrificial offering fit for the Agnihotra rite, the knower of mantras offered oblations into the well-kindled fire for the purpose of destroying the Rākṣasas.
O Goddess of the gods, as soon as the oblation had been offered, a Śakti arose at that very moment, radiant with great splendor, equipped with a trident and a spear, and holding a shield in her hand.
By her, those Daityas who were destroyers of the sacrifice were slain; then the sages praised her with various hymns of praise.
The goddess, becoming exceedingly gracious, replied to those sages: "Choose a boon, O munis; I shall grant you an excellent boon. (19)
The sages said: "O crusher of asuras, every task has indeed been accomplished by you; our sacrifice has been protected by you. If a boon is to be granted by you to us," (20)

"Stay forever in this place out of a desire for the welfare of the sages; since the thorns—the Daityas—have been withered by you, let your name from this day forward be Kaṇṭakaśoṣiṇī, O Goddess, and may it remain so here eternally. (21)
The Lord said: "Having spoken thus, 'So shall it be,' that Goddess then vanished. A new person shall worship me on either the eighth or the ninth lunar day."
No fear arises for him from Rākṣasas or Piśācas; that man shall attain supreme perfection—of this there is no doubt. (23)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaṇṭakaśoṣaṇī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 317 ||
Īśvara said: Not far from it, situated in the eastern quarter, is indeed a Liṅga of great power that destroys all sins.

That [liṅga] is rich with the name Brahmeśvara and was installed by Brāhmaṇas. Whoever bathes in the waters of Ṛṣitoyā and worships that liṅga shall become a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, freed from the state of dullness. || 2 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 318 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the most excellent site called Unnata, located on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā river in the northern direction of that very place.
O Great Goddess, I forcibly bestowed this place, together with all its boundaries and well-guarded by the hosts of Caṇḍīs, upon the Brahmins. || 2 ||
The Goddess said: O best of gods, how did he come to have the name Unnata? And how was it bestowed by you with force, and what were its boundaries?
Tell me all of this in brief, and not in excessive detail.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a narrative that destroys sin; having heard which, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from all transgressions.
All this, which is the cause for the secret signs of the locations, was previously declared in the third [chapter], concerning the sacrificial pit of Brahmā that indicates the summary of creation.
Nevertheless, I shall speak to you; listen in brief, O Pārvatī. || 7 ||
Furthermore, where the Liṅga is raised up at Mahodaya, that place is called Unnata, the best among all excellent locations.
Alternatively, the gate of the Prābhāsika [region] was indeed elevated in the east; that is declared to be "the Elevated" (Unnata), the best of places for those who possess a worthy station.
That place where the great seers are preeminent through both knowledge and austerity is called Unnata, the best among all excellent locations.
When the Brahmins, having propitiated Mahādeva known as Mūlacaṇḍīśa in the temple, returned once more to Mahodaya; || 11 ||
For sixty thousand years, the great seers performed austerities, meditating upon Maheśāna, the supreme one who is without beginning or end.

O Pārvatī, while those [sages] numbering ten million were performing austerities on the delightful, pure, and sin-destroying bank of the Ṛṣitoyā river, I went back to that very place once more, having become a mendicant, O beautiful lady. (13)
O lady of beautiful countenance, I was then observed there by all those ascetics who see the three periods of time and are free from both defects and passion.
As soon as he was seen by the brahmins, Maheśvara stopped; saying, "O God, where are you going? You are known," the twice-born pursued him.
Meanwhile, the sages arrived, proclaiming "O Lord of Lords!", running along and illuminating the ten directions with their own ascetic power.
They behold only the linga; they do not behold Maheśvara.
And whoever beheld the Liṅga known as Mūla-caṇḍīśa, at that time all those sages went to heaven in their physical bodies.
When the triple heaven was seen to be pervaded by the performer of a hundred sacrifices, other sages, radiant with asceticism, likewise arrived there.
Having reached this interval and arrived upon the surface of the earth, Śatakratu covered the Liṅga with his thunderbolt.
Eighteen thousand sages with sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) remain here, yet they do not behold this unsurpassed Liṅga.
But Śakra, suddenly seen accompanied by his very thunderbolt, vanished as soon as they uttered their curse; thus was Purandara destroyed.
Seeing those sages filled with anger, the Blessed Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, spoke to the munis, consoling them with sweet words.
"How is it that you, O best of the twice-born, who are always devoted to peace, have become dejected? Having made your faces cheerful, listen to my words. (24)
O you who are endowed with knowledge, why do you think much of heaven, where some are called Vasus and others likewise Ādityas? (25)
Likewise, some are designated as Rudras, and there are also two others known as the Aśvins; among these, one is proclaimed as Indra, their sovereign lord. (26)
Since men fall from that which they have attained by the measure of their own merit, heaven, being thus joined with suffering, is not desired by the wise. (27)
For this reason, O Brahmins, do as I say: accept this beautiful and highly radiant city for your residence. (28)
O twice-born ones, let the Agnihotra oblations be offered to the deities at all times; let them be worshipped with various sacrifices, and let the honoring of the ancestors be performed. (29)
Hospitality should be practiced constantly, and likewise, the study of the Vedas.
O best of Brahmins, for those who act thus constantly, even without the accumulation of knowledge, liberation will come at the end through my grace.
The sages said: "We are incapable of providing protection; we have conquered our appetite for food and are devoted to austerity. Desiring to show devotion to you, what can we do here with a city?"
The Lord said: "Your devotion to the Supreme Lord shall always endure; accept this beautiful city and carry out my word. (33)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, with his eyes slightly closed, called to mind Viśvakarman, the best among all masters of the arts.
As soon as he was remembered, Viśvakarman stood before him with palms joined in reverence and said, "May the Lord command me; I shall carry out your word."
Īśvara said: "O Tvaṣṭṛ, let a beautiful and auspicious city be built for the sake of the brāhmaṇas."
Thus addressed, Viśvakarman, having surveyed the earth on all sides, bowed down and spoke to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
I have examined this ground; however, a city is not appropriate here, for there is a temple of the gods and likewise the falling of a linga. (38)
Ascetics should dwell here; it is not appropriate for householders.

O Maheśvara, householders accompanied by their sons and wives should dwell at a sacred ford for three nights, five nights, seven nights, or even for a fortnight, a month, a season, or as long as a year.

But when the master of the house dwells in a sacred place for more than six months, contempt arises toward him due to the fickleness of his mind; then all the religious merits of that householder perish. (41)
Thus addressed by Viśvakarman at that time, the god Śiva, having praised his words, spoke to him again.

"I do not like dwelling here among householders who are Brahmins, where the Linga has been raised on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā. Therefore, O Tvaṣṭṛ, best of artisans, construct a city there. (43)
Having heard those words of his, Viśvakarman, filled with haste and surrounded by tens of millions of artisans, went there and constructed a city.
O beautiful goddess, having beheld that city renowned in the world as Unnata, Śiva became joyful in mind; then, summoning all the Brāhmaṇas, he spoke with his neck bowed in reverence.
This excellent and delightful place was fashioned by Viśvakarman; it is said to be surrounded on all sides by thousands of villages.
On all sides of the city, the region known as Nagnahara is considered meritorious; it extends for eight yojanas in both length and breadth.
The region where Hara wandered at will while naked is called Nagnahara by people; they say it is a most meritorious place.

To the east is the Śāṅkarī Āryā, and to the west is the Nyaṅkumatī; to the north is the Kanakanandā, and to the south it extends as far as the ocean. Having reached this interval, the region is known as Nagnahara.
This entire region has been described by me as being eight yojanas in length and breadth, and likewise level and elevated.
"Accept this preeminent city; be gracious, O best of the twice-born! Herein shall be both devotion and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (51)
Having been addressed thus, all those brahmins then spoke to Maheśvara.

The Brahmins said: "It is not possible to render void the command of the Lord, the Supreme Soul, for those who are devoted to austerity and the Agnihotra sacrifice and who are distinguished by their study of the Vedas. (53)
Who is our protector in this terrible Kali age? Who is the giver, who bestows health, and who indeed will grant liberation? (54)
The Lord said: "Abiding in the form of Mahākāla at this most auspicious tīrtha, I shall utterly destroy your enemies once I have been properly propitiated."
The exalted Lord of Obstacles shall be the destroyer of impediments; he is the very embodiment of Gaṇeśa, the bestower of wealth and the lord of treasures. (56)
Even when properly propitiated, he will grant you wealth; Durgāditya shall be a constant bestower of health.

It shall be of great fortune and a bestower of great bliss for you; when Brahmā is properly propitiated, he will always grant you all your objectives in every undertaking, as well as all desires and liberation. (58)
The Brahmins said: "O best of gods, if all the holy fords (tīrthas) reside in Saṅgāleśvara-tīrtha, as well as in the auspicious Devakula," || 59 ||
"O Maheśvara, even in this most terrible Kali age, you must remain for our purification; therefore, we accept [your presence], and not otherwise."
Having promised "So be it," he gave them that excellent city, adorned with seven-storied palaces as radiant as the moon, joined by various villages and surrounded on all sides by boundaries.
Sūta said: Having thus given the city to them, the Lord Maheśvara beheld Viśvakarmā standing before him with palms joined in reverence.
Viśvakarman said: "O Mahādeva, behold this city, which resembles a celestial city; having ascended the golden ground, it has been constructed through your grace. (63)
Having heard the words of Viśvakarman, the Blessed Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, ascended the chariot-seat together with all the great sages.
He gazed upon the beautiful city adorned with ramparts. All the sages offered praise to Tripurāntaka, who was stationed there. Mahādeva said to them, "Choose an excellent boon."
The sages said: "O Mahādeva, if you are pleased and bear the name Sthalakeśvara, O Hara, remain forever upon this ground, gazing upon the city."
Thus addressed by them, O Goddess, the Lord has always remained in this place; in the Kṛta age he was made of jewels, and in the Tretā age, of gold.
In the Dvāpara age, it was said to be made of silver, and in the Kali age, the site is made of stone; thus the Lord resides there under the name Sthalakeśvara.
Mahādeva is always to be worshipped by those dwelling in elevated places; however, on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, there is a special significance to the vigil (jāgara) held there.
Thus, O Goddess, has this great account of Unnata been told; when heard, it removes the sins of men and bestows the fruit of all desires. (70)

Thus ends the three hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Unnatasthāna," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 319 ||
Īśvara said: To the east of that, situated slightly toward the southeast, are two highly meritorious Liṅgas installed by Viśvakarman. || 1 ||
When Tvaṣṭṛ indeed arrived there to build the city, he first installed Mahādeva and then constructed the city.
And having constructed a beautiful city by the power of this *liṅga*, that Viśvakarman indeed reinstalled the *liṅga* once again.

At the beginning of any ritual action and at its conclusion—whether during a journey, a marriage, entering a house, or similar occasions—one attains success instantaneously by worshipping the two Liṅgas.
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort, one should worship the pair of Liṅgas with fragrant nectar-like waters, various offerings of food, and diverse oblations.

Thus ends the three hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Two Liṅgas," within the "Majesty of Unnatasthāna" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 320 ||
Īśvara said: Now I shall proclaim to you that supreme secret place, which removes all sins for men who dwell in elevated regions.
The majesty of the preeminent deity Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, who dwells in a lofty station, and who assumes the form of a child—by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins. (2)
The Goddess said: "Regarding that which was stated, that he is in the form of a child—tell me, how is that so elevated? For in all other places, the Grandfather (Brahmā) is in the form of an elder."
In what place does he reside, and for what purpose did he go there? O best of Brahmins, tell me in due order how he is to be worshipped by the lords of sages and on which lunar day.
Īśvara said: To the west of Ṛṣitoyā and to the northeast of Sthalakeśvara is the supreme abode of Brahmā, like another world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are always to be worshipped in Prābhāsika; Brahmā is situated in the portion of Brahmā on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā.
At the Rudrabhāga and at Agnitīrtha, the eternal Rudra is to be worshipped; on the beautiful Raivataka mountain, Hari in the form of Dāmodara is to be worshipped.
Requested by Soma, the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived in the form of a child, eight years of age, at that most excellent and elevated place.
Having seen the best of the twice-born, the omnipresent Lord Brahmā remained stationed in that place.
There is no god equal to Brahmā; there is no teacher equal to Brahmā; there is no knowledge equal to Brahmā; there is no austerity equal to Brahmā. || 10 ||
They wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering, grief, and fear, as long as they do not become devotees of the Grandfather, the eldest of the gods.
If the mind of a living being were to be fixed upon Brahman in the same way that it is attached to the realm of sensory objects, who would not be liberated from bondage? 12.
Brahmā is known to have a maximum lifespan of a *parārdha*, and for him who resides in the elevated station, the first half has indeed passed; now the second half will come to pass. (13)
When that Grandfather (Pitāmaha) comes from the world of Brahmā to the elevated place, being eight years old and in the form of a child, he is then so described.
In other places belonging to the Brahmins, the Grandfather (Brahmā) appeared in the form of an elder; that elevated site was fitting and always dear to Brahmā. || 15 ||
O best of men, having first bathed according to the rules in the Brahmakuṇḍa, one should worship Brahmā in the form of a child with flowers, incense, and other offerings.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmā at Unnatasthāna," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 321 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the shrine situated to its south, named Durgaditya, which destroys all sins.
When she had fallen into misfortune, that goddess who destroys suffering propitiated the Sun for the removal of her distress.

Then, after a long time, the Sun-god was pleased with her; the deity spoke these sweet words to the immensely radiant Durgā: "Choose a boon, O Goddess of Devas, for I am satisfied by your ascetic penance."
Durgā said: "O Lord of the Day, if you are pleased, destroy this multitude of my miseries."
Sūrya said: "In a very short time, the Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, will attain the supreme Liṅga at the excellent, elevated place."

“O Goddess, my name here shall be Durgāditya. Having spoken thus, O Great Goddess, the Sun vanished right there. One should worship Durgāditya on the seventh lunar day (saptamī) when it falls on a Sunday.
O Goddess of the gods, all his sufferings and various types of leprosy go to destruction through the worship of Durgāditya.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Durgāditya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should behold that which stands to its south, renowned as Kshemesvara, situated on the bank of the Rishitoya.
His name was formerly proclaimed as Bhūtīśvara; O Goddess, in the Kali age, his name is proclaimed as Kṣemeśa. || 2 ||
Having seen and worshipped him, one shall be liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kṣemeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Lord said: Therefore, one should behold Vināyaka, the bestower of all perfections, situated slightly toward the northwest in the northern direction. || 1 ||

O Goddess, he who was previously described by me as my friend Dhanada, the protector of treasures in the form of Gaṇanātha, remains in this place, O beloved, for the sake of bestowing spiritual perfections upon the worlds.
On the fourth lunar day, O Goddess, if one worships according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of food and sweetmeats on a Tuesday, his success will certainly be attained.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaṇanātha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Vinayaka on the delightful bank of the Rishitoya, which wards off all obstacles.

He who is the presiding lord of the hosts of gods and the manifest destroyer of Tripura, having assumed the form of an elephant, stands upon the elevated earth in the great sacred field of Prabhāsa, surrounded by crores of his attendants.
Therefore, with every effort, for the sake of ensuring that the journey remains free from obstacles, one should always propitiate the Lord of the Gaṇas with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
And on every fourth day, a great festival should be performed by all the city-dwellers for the sake of achieving the welfare and security of the kingdom.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Unnatasvāmin," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Mahākāleśvara situated to the north of that very place; he is the supreme bestower of protection against all [evils]. || 1 ||
Bhairava, assuming the form of Rudra, is the presiding deity of this city; one should perform a great worship on the new moon and the full moon days.
Having bathed at Mahodaya, a man beholds Mahākāla; he becomes wealthy in this world for seven thousand births.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mahākāla," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," within the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, one should go from there to Mahodaya, which is situated to the northeast.
Whoever bathes there according to the prescribed rite and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods, for him there exists no fear arising from the fault of accepting gifts.

It brings great prosperity and bestows supreme bliss upon the twice-born who are devoted to receiving gifts and whose minds are attached to sense objects; it grants liberation even to them, and for that reason it is known as Mahodaya.

O Great Goddess, for the sake of protecting that [place], the Mothers have been appointed and are stationed there to the north of Mahākāla; having first bathed in that [water], a man should worship those Mothers.
Thus, O Goddess, I have declared this most exalted Mahodaya, which removes all sins for men and bestows liberation through its consecration.
That holy site (tīrtha) extends for half a krośa all around in a circle; its center is of great essence and is always beloved by the sages.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Mahodaya," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Therefore, situated in the northwestern direction is the destroyer of sins, renowned by the name Saṅgameśvara, where the sages have gathered together. || 1 ||
In the eastern direction of that very place is the Kuṇḍikā, the destroyer of sins, where the Sarasvatī arrived joined with the Vaḍavānala fire.
Having bathed in the Kuṇḍikā and worshipped Saṅgameśvara, O Great Goddess, for thousands of births there shall never arise any separation from fortune, sons, and beloved ones.
One is liberated from all sins committed from birth until the end of life.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Saṅgameśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now, at a distance of one *gavyūti* from that temple of the gods to the north, there is a place renowned upon the surface of the earth as "Uttamasthāna."
To the north of that, at a distance of twelve bow-lengths, stands the elevated Vighnarāja, the destroyer of all obstacles.
When properly worshipped on the fourth lunar day with fragrant scents, fruits, and sweetmeats, he grants all desired objects, and one shall become victorious throughout the three worlds. || 3 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Unnata-Vināyaka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 329 ||
Īśvara said: Three yojanas to the north of that elevated place is Taptodakasvāmī, where Tala was formerly slain.
O Goddess, after waging war for a hundred years with the powerful Viṣṇu, the lord of the Daityas then became Talasvāmī.
Having bathed in the Taptakuṇḍa, a man should worship Talasvāmin; by performing the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, he obtains the fruit of ten million pilgrimages.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Talasvāmī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place renowned as Kālamegha; from there, [one should visit] the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapa) in the form of a Liṅga, situated in the eastern direction. || 1 ||
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, he should be worshipped with offerings by men; in the Kali age, he is truly a wish-fulfilling tree who bestows all desired objects.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kālamegha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Therefore, O beloved, five *dhanus* to the south of that place, there are even today, O fair-faced one, pools of heated water (*taptodakuṇḍa*).
Twenty-five dhanus to the east of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) resides the goddess Rukmiṇī, the destroyer of all sins.

Having bathed in the Taptodaka pool, which destroys ten million killings, one should then worship the goddess Rukmiṇī, the bestower of gold. For women, the ruin of their homes shall not occur for seven births.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rukmiṇī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: To the east of Balabhadra, there stood an excellent river; there, the Linga of Bala named Durvaseshvara was installed. || 1 ||
It is seen to pacify all sins and bring about all happiness; and having bathed here on the new moon day, whoever offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) [attains great merit].
By worshipping the deity named Durvāseśvara there according to the prescribed rite, one shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Having obtained the fruit of ten million sacrifices, one shall attain all desires; for there are many Liṅgas established by the sages in that place.
"By seeing, touching, and worshipping it, one shall be liberated from all sins. Thus, O Goddess, has this foremost of sacred fields been described to you in due order. (5)
From Bhadrā’s western [gate] to the east, in due order from the beginning, has been heard that which pacifies evil and bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Then, the location of the field's boundary is called Madhumatī; therefore, the location in the south-western direction is called Khaṇḍaghaṭā.
There, near the shore of the ocean, is the god Piṅgeśvara; there is a group of seven wells where, O Queen of Gods, the hands of the ancestors are seen even today on every festival day.
Having performed a śrāddha there, a man obtains a fruit ten million times greater than at Gayā; of this there is no doubt, provided that it occurs on the new moon day of the month of Soma (Māgha).
Not far from that very place, the confluence of the Bhadrā is recorded; it is declared to be the eastern confluence relative to the western confluence.
O Goddess, whatever merit one obtains at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean in the east or the west, that same merit one shall obtain there at the confluence of the Bhadrā.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Piṅgeśvara and Bhadrā at Madhumatī," within the "Majesty of Taptodakasvāmī" section of the first part, the "Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya," in the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 333 ||
Īśvara said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, I ask you something out of devotion and once again out of curiosity.
O Lord, as for that great glory of Talasvāmin which was described by you—what is the reason there, O Lord, why Tala was struck down? || 2 ||
Who is this one known as Tala? What is his power and what is his ultimate goal? From what place did he arise, and how was he born? Tell me this.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret that destroys sin; that which has not been told to anyone, I shall declare to you in its entirety.
Even the gods do not know the cause of its origin; O Goddess, in the former Kṛta Yuga, he was celebrated as Govinda.
In the Tretā age, Svāmī Vāmana was the Lord of Praise; in the third [age], O Great Goddess, he is proclaimed as Talasvāmī in the Kali Yuga.
Likewise, O beloved, Taptodakasvāmī is another name for him; now, O dear one, I shall describe his origin to you.
O beloved, in former times there was a Dānava named Mahendra who assumed a fierce form; by him alone penance was performed for ten million years.
Possessed by the power of asceticism, he conquered the gods along with Indra; having thus defeated all the gods, he returned at that time.
He requested a most terrifying battle with me; then there occurred a great war that brought about the destruction of the universe.
Then, O fair-faced one, from my body in that great battle, a flame arose out of anger, and in its midst, that Tala appeared.
By him was seen that great Indra, roaring and taking refuge in a mountain cave.
"O fool, why do you roar? Fight with me!"—when this was said there, O Goddess of the Gods, the battle commenced with him.
When that battle between those two, Tala and Māhendra, had commenced.
By means of a blow from his joined palms, executed with the prowess of Rudra and through a wrestling match of noble deeds, the mighty Mahendra was struck down.
Then, seeing him fallen, Tala was filled with amazement; perceiving that he was lifeless, he then began to dance out of joy. || 16 ||
While he was dancing there, O lady of beautiful hips, everything both stationary and moving trembled due to his power and valor.
Then the earth, oppressed by the weight of the burden and pressed down upon its surface, was utterly terrified along with the gods, asuras, and humans. (18)
All the mountains were shaken, the great oceans were agitated, the trees met their destruction, and the rivers abandoned their currents. (19)
The sun and other luminaries lost their brilliance and did not shine; the three worlds became agitated by the power of that dancing on the ground.
Then all the hosts of gods went to Rudra for refuge; having related the events exactly as they occurred, Rudra then spoke to them.
"O gods, my palm is not to be slain, for it is established as my son. Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, who dwells in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa, [he departed].
Named Stutisvāmī, he was situated before Durvāsas, established in the eastern part in the vicinity of Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
"O gods, go there to the vicinity of the Taptodakuṇḍa; for in every kalpa, that Dānava is indeed pierced by that very [lake]."
When this was said, the gods then arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa; there those deities went to where the lord of Taptodaka resided.
Having seen Nārāyaṇa there, the gods, filled with faith, praised Janārdana, the God of gods, with supreme devotion.
"O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, protect us gods! We have been driven from our abode by the power born of Rudra’s splendor, which arose from the wrath of Mahendra."
We reported our entire mission in the presence of Rudra; thereafter, we were all dispatched by Rudra, the Supreme Lord. O Mahādeva, we are here at your side; O God, please be our refuge.

Having heard their words, Janārdana, the god of gods, the mighty-armed one who is dear to the sacred field of Prabhāsa, made an effort for the sake of slaying the Dānava and for the protection of the gods. (29)
Then, having summoned the Daitya from the midst of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, O Goddess, he waged a battle that caused the dissolution of the universe.
Then all the gods, surrounded by their own armies, waged a most great and hair-raising battle against the Daitya.
Then, seeing the exceedingly powerful Daitya who resembled a mountain, Garuḍa, whose vehicle he was, spoke with restless side-glances.
"O mighty-armed Daitya, grant me a wrestling match! Having seen your pair of arms, I have no desire for [any other kind of] combat. (33)
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, the Dānava Daitya, whose splendor was like that of the Destroyer at the end of time, raised his hand and then rushed forward.
Then a battle commenced between the two, each desiring victory over the other: with their shanks they bound each other's feet, and with their arms they locked in a grip of the arms.
Binding throat with throat and likewise belly with belly, in that interval the gods became filled with fear.
Then, overcome by that affliction, Viṣṇu remembered Hara; at that very moment, the mighty Rudra arrived and asked, "What shall I do? (37)
Viṣṇu said: "O Śaṅkara, Lord of the gods, I am exhausted by this wrestling match; prepare hot water here now to dispel my fatigue. (38)
Then, in a mere moment, I shall strike that terrible palm.
Īśvara said: O Kṛṣṇa, in the beginning, during the Kṛtayuga, that which was formerly performed by Umā for the sake of destroying the fatigue of the sages—the Taptoda [lake]—was constructed there.
Due to the power of that Daitya’s sin, it became cool once again; then, at the conclusion of the kalpa, it was brought back to heat.
Having spoken thus, Maheśvara then gazed at the god with his third eye, which was adorned with a garland of flames.
The sacrificial pit was pervaded on all four sides by that mass of flames; because of this, it became famous on the surface of the earth as Taptodakuṇḍa.
Then, here on earth, Nārāyaṇa washed his excellent body; through that washing of the god, his fatigue came to an end.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, the god, with a satisfied mind, remembered ten crores of sacred fords (*tīrtha*s), and having duly cast [the water] there and bathed, he departed.
Then he engaged in a great and most terrifying battle with Tala; he struck the Daitya Tala on the head with a blow of his fist.

When that tumultuous battle had commenced, the worlds together with the earth trembled; the gods were terrified, the quarters of the sky did not shine, and the world was swooning, enveloped in a great darkness.
"The Siddhas have perished; may Hari, the destroyer of sins, indeed bring peace to this world! 'Save us!'—thus do the hosts of great sages and the terrified beings cry out, O Goddess of gods. (48)
Then, indeed, by means of wrestling, the Dānava was thrown to the ground; having seized his throat with his foot, he was struck with a sword.
Then the Daitya, whose neck was seized by Viṣṇu, laughed; the lotus-eyed Lord said to him, "What is the cause of this laughter? (50)
"One attains joy at an increase and becomes sorrowful at a decrease"—this is a worldly verse, O Daitya, but for you it is the very opposite.
Thus addressed, the Daitya then replied to Janārdana: "By means of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, and by various kinds of Vedic study... (52)
That supreme state which is attained through constant observances of fasting, ritual bathing, charity, recitation, and the like—when these are pure and joined with yoga—is [attained]. (53)
"By that wicked disposition of mine, I attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. When this was said, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu became intent on granting a boon.
He spoke these supreme words to Tala, the leader of the Daityas: "Choose a boon, O lord of Daityas, whatever resides in your mind. (55)
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the Dānava requested: "O Upholder of the Earth, act in such a way that my name shall endure in the world. (56)
May the sin of whoever beholds you with devotion on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa be destroyed. || 57 ||
Having said, "It shall be so," the god was filled with joy; various drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.

O highly fortunate lady, when Viṣṇu’s head was [restored], the worlds became established in well-being. Then all the hosts of gods, filled with joy, danced; devoted to Nārāyaṇa and imbued with delight, they spoke. || 59 ||
This is that great sacred ford, the destroyer of all sins; it removes the fatigue of Viṣṇu and purifies even the murder of a Brahmin and other such offenses.
Nārāyaṇa is stationed there, and Śaṅkara is there as Bhairava, renowned by the name Kālamegha in the form of the protector of the field (Kṣetrapāla).
I shall describe the procedure for its pilgrimage: having gone there, O Great Goddess, a pure man should remember Viṣṇu, who is known as Talasvāmī.
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, one should praise Viṣṇu with the Ṛgvedic verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and one should perform the libations and other rites with the "sahasraśīrṣā" mantra.
Having thus bathed according to the prescribed rite and offered the arghya to Janārdana, one should worship Him with perfumes, flowers, garments, and floral unguents.
One should smear it with honey and sugarcane juice, and with saffron mixed with camphor, uśīra, and musk.
Thereafter, one should wrap [the image] with garments and offer excellent food offerings (naivedya); then, a vigil (jāgaraṇa) accompanied by the hearing of the Dharma should be performed.
A bull should be given there, along with gold and a pair of garments; one should cause these to be bestowed upon a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and is a master of the Śruti.
Then, O beautiful lady, one should observe a fast on that day, and having paid homage to Janārdana, one should behold Rukmiṇī.
By acting thus with devotion, a person obtains the fruit born of their birth; they obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and all acts of charity. (69)
And thus, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords and religious vows; one shall uplift the host of one's fathers as well as the host of one's mothers.
It shall be the destruction of all sins committed since birth; neither suffering, nor poverty, nor misfortune shall arise.

O Goddess, the fruit that is obtained by giving a thousand gold pieces to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is attained by bathing in that pool for as long as seven lifetimes, through the sight of Talasvāmī.

Thus, this supreme life-story of Talasvāmin was heard of old by the assemblies of perfected great seers; having heard its power in the presence of the god Tala, one obtains everything desired by the mind.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Talasvāmin," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, one should go to the west, to the auspicious bank of the Nyaṅkumatī; situated facing the southern direction is a tīrtha of great splendor.
O Great Goddess, there is a place renowned as Śaṅkhāvarta, where a self-manifested stone, variegately marked, red in its interior, and most beautiful, exists.
Even though it was severed, it is still seen there, deeply red; for that place is called Viṣṇukṣetra, where Śaṅkha was slain in ancient times.
O Goddess of gods, when the Vedas were stolen, the powerful Viṣṇu created the holy site of Śaṅkhodaka; it is seen there in the shape of a conch shell.
O Goddess, having bathed there, a man is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; even for a Śūdra, the status of a Brahmin arises for seven births.
Having first gone to that very place, one should then proceed to Rudragayā; there, a gift of a cow should be given by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śaṅkhāvarta Tīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Goṣpada Tīrtha, where a man, having performed a Śrāddha, obtains a fruit seven times that of Gayā; of this there is no doubt, provided his faith be firm.
O Great Goddess, it was there that Pṛthu, having performed a Śrāddha, delivered his father, the great lord named Vena, from a sinful womb. || 2 ||
The Goddess said: In what place is that sacred ford (tīrtha) situated, and of what nature was its origin? And how was that King Vena uplifted from his sinful birth?

"How is it that merit seven times greater than Gayā is produced there? What is the procedure for the śrāddha, what are the mantras, and who are the brahmins there? O Lord, you ought to explain this curiosity of mine exactly as it is. (4)
Īśvara said: O Goddess of gods, this secret which you have inquired about—this sacred ford (tīrtha) is not to be disclosed in this age of sin, O beloved.
Nevertheless, O Goddess of the Suras, out of affection for you I shall proclaim it; one should not speak this to a sinner, nor indeed to one devoted to mere logic.
Not for an atheist, O Queen of Gods, nor for one who is not a seeker of gold; there exists, O Goddess, the great and meritorious river Nyankumati.
O Maheśvarī, she was brought by me for the sake of establishing a boundary for this sacred field; she stands established to the south of Parṇāditya as the destroyer of sins.
O Great Goddess, situated not far from the northern side of Nārāyaṇa’s abode, there is in its center a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds.
The place known as Goṣpada is famous for removing ten million sins of men; it is situated not far from, but very close to, Goṣpada.
The lord of serpents named Ananta, who was self-manifested upon the surface of the earth, was appointed by Viṣṇu for the protection of that sacred ford.

The ancestors, who are terrified of hell, long for sons, thinking: "That son who goes [to heaven] like one entering a cow's footprint will be our savior. And upon seeing a son in that cow's footprint, there shall be a festival for the ancestors.

"Having touched even the water with his feet, will he not give it to us? Might there be someone born in our lineage who would offer us a handful of water? Having reached the sacred site of Prabhāsa, at the excellent Goṣpada Tīrtha. (13)
"May there be someone in our family who would diligently perform a Śrāddha ceremony even once with the meat of a rhinoceros, or else with black potherbs. (14)
May he be one who has offered even a lamp as small as a cow’s hoofprint to our family; by that, our light shall endure until the end of the aeon. (15)
O ancestors, he who offers even a hundred morsels of food at Goṣpada becomes a father of sons; by staying there for even a single day, he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
A man should himself offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for his ancestors and for himself as well; even with the oil-cake of the iṅguda fruit, O fair-faced one, by that he shall be liberated.

What is the use of the knowledge of Brahman or of yogic practices, and what is the use of dying at Gograha? What is the use of residing at Kurukṣetra if one goes [to heaven] even from a cow’s footprint? 18.
Visiting a sacred ford once and offering a funeral cake once are difficult to achieve; how much more so, then, to be permanently established at this sacred ford? (19)

That sacred ford (tīrtha) extends for half a krośa, and even half of that half is difficult to attain. One who performs a śrāddha ceremony in its midst obtains merit seven times greater than that of Gayā.
He who performs the *śrāddha* at Goṣpada is indeed freed from his debt to the ancestors; especially by performing it at Padamadhye, he shall uplift a hundred generations of his lineage.
For one who has merely set out from home toward a journey even as short as a cow's footprint, there is a staircase for ascending to heaven at every step for the sake of the ancestors.
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is prescribed with milk-rice, honey, parched grain flour, ground meal, or with sacrificial oblations (caru) consisting of rice and other grains.
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the cow-pasture, even if they are only the size of a śamī leaf, or by offering bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, one leads one's ancestors to heaven.
The fruit that a man obtains by offering a ball of food at Goṣpada cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. || 25 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the auspicious procedure for a pilgrimage, as well as the rules for undertaking a journey; listen with perfect faith. (26)
If a man should go to a sacred ford (tīrtha) with the desire for the fruit of a Gayā-śrāddha, that wise man should undertake the journey according to such a procedure.
Having become pure through the practice of celibacy, with hands and feet restrained, full of faith and free from atheistic doubt, the wise man should then proceed to the sacred ford.

A person should not associate with an atheist at that sacred ford (tīrtha). Equipped with all necessary provisions and endowed with materials suitable for a śrāddha rite, one should go to the sacred ford accompanied by virtuous people, holding Gayā in high esteem within his mind.
Thus, that twice-born man who proceeds while avoiding the acceptance of gifts undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at every step. (30)

Having bathed there in the Nyaṅkumatī for the sake of spiritual perfection and the liberation of one's ancestors, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods and others according to the prescribed rule.
May all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—the gods, sages, Manus, and humans—as well as the ancestors, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.

Having thus satisfied [the ancestors] according to the rule and performed the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, a man should perform the Śrāddha ceremony together with the Piṇḍas, following the procedure prescribed in his own [Tantra]. || 33 ||
Having invited there the Brahmins who are learned in the scriptures and free from defects, and having thus performed the hospitable rites, he should utter this mantra: || 34 ||
Kavyavāḍ, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman; the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa Pitṛ-deities—may these highly fortunate ones come, for you shall be protected by them here. (35)
O grandfathers, I have come here as the giver of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for my own fathers and those who were born in my lineage, my kinsmen. || 36 ||
Having spoken thus, O Great Goddess, one should utter this mantra.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather; the mother, the grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother. || 38 ||
The maternal grandfather, the great-grandfather, and likewise the great-great-grandfather—may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible. (39)
Oṃ, salutations to the Sun, the Sustainer, who possesses the forms of the lotus, Mars, and the Moon; having thus bowed and worshipped him, one should then recite this hymn of praise. (40)
There, near the footprint of a cow, with well-cooked sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the protectorless ancestors while reciting the sacred mantras.
For those who have died in my family and for whom no destination is known, and for those who have gone to Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra—for their deliverance, I offer this pinda.
For the sake of delivering those who have gone to the worlds of the pretas, existing in various states of torment, I offer this piṇḍa. (43)
And those who have entered the womb of animals, those who are insects or reptiles, or those situated in the womb of trees—to them I give this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have been led by the governors of Yama to innumerable states of torment, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 45 ||
Those who are not kinsmen in this life but were kinsmen in another birth—may they all attain satisfaction forever through this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas, may they all forever attain satisfaction through this rice-ball offering.
May this pinda be for the liberation of the ancestors—those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, or on earth—as well as kinsmen and others who have died and remain uncremated.
Those who have died in the paternal lineage and likewise in the maternal lineage, as well as those other kinsmen of the teacher, the father-in-law, and relatives who have passed away; || 49 ||
Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have fallen into neglect, as well as those born blind or lame; || 50 ||
To those who were deformed, those who died in the womb, and those unknown or known within my lineage—to them this funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me shall indeed reach as an inexhaustible offering.
"May my ancestors be liberated from the state of being a preta forever; may whatever cow's milk mixed with honey, ghee, and milk-rice [be offered]. (52)
One should approach this inexhaustible Goṣpada-tīrtha; there, one should cause the Vedic study and all the Purāṇas to be recited.
One should recite, according to one's ability, various hymns to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra, as well as the hymns to Indra, the Soma-sūktas, and the Pāvamānī verses.
Likewise, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], the Jyeṣṭhasāman with the Raurava, as well as the Śāntikādhyāya and the Madhubrāhmaṇa. (55)
Furthermore, he should recite there the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and whatever else brings pleasure to the Brahmins and to himself. 56.
Thus, in the midst of the Nyaṅkumatī, at the excellent Goṣpada Tīrtha, having offered the funeral cakes according to the rules, one should again recite this mantra: || 57 ||
May the gods, headed by Brahmā, and the preeminent sages be my witnesses: having reached this sacred ford, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors.
"O best of gods, I have come to this sacred ford for the sake of ancestral rites; may you all be witnesses that I am now liberated from the three debts. (59)
Having thus circumambulated Goṣpada, the most excellent of holy fords, and having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the river.
In that case, O beloved, a gift of a cow should be given, and likewise a black antelope skin, on the Aṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of the day of death.

In this case, the śrāddha for the mother is performed separately, whereas elsewhere it is performed together with the husband; however, in the Vṛddhi-śrāddha and at Gayā, the order begins with the father and so forth, including the mother.
Just as at Gayā, so too here the śrāddha must be performed by the best of men; therefore, this very place was called Guptagayā by Viṣṇu himself.

Through the gift of fragrance, one obtains fragrance; through the gift of flowers, good fortune; through the gift of incense, the attainment of a kingdom; and through the offering of a lamp, radiant splendor.

By the gift of a banner, one's sins are destroyed; the performer of the pilgrimage shall attain the world of Brahmā. By offering the funeral cakes at a Śrāddha, Viṣṇu will indeed lead the ancestors to the higher worlds.
Whoever feeds a single Brahmin of praised vows there at the great holy site of Gopracāra, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Thus, the ritual for the Śrāddha has been briefly described to you; now I shall relate to you an ancient history.
O Goddess of the gods, listen with perfect faith to all of this: the life-story of King Vena and that of the high-souled Pṛthu, and how his liberation from that birth as a Cāṇḍāla came about. 68.
This meritorious teaching must never be told to one who is malicious, nor to one who is wicked, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who seeks harm, nor to one who observes no vows. (69)

He who listens without malice to this secret, proclaimed by the sages—which leads to heaven, brings fame, prolongs life, confers fortune, and is equal in authority to the Veda—[attains these rewards]. (70)
And that mortal who, having paid homage to the Brahmins, causes this account of the origin of Pṛthu Vainya to be heard, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
This king, the protector of dharma, shone with a splendor equal to Atri; for he was the Prajāpati named Aṅga, born from the lineage of Atri. (72)
His son was Vena, who was not at all righteous; he was born as a Prajāpati from Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu.
Due to that fault of his maternal grandfather, he, whose face was like the personification of Time (Death), cast Dharma behind him and became evil-minded.
He established the eternal order endowed with righteousness; yet, having transgressed the Vedic scriptures, he became devoted to unrighteousness.
While he was ruling, the subjects were devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of "vaṣaṭ"; that king caused a drum to be sounded throughout his own realm.
"No gift should be given, nor should sacrifice be performed while I rule the kingdom; such was the cruel vow made when destruction was imminent. (77)
I am to be praised and worshipped by the best of the twice-born with all sacrifices; sacrifices are to be performed for me, and offerings are likewise to be poured into me. 78.
Then the great sages, headed by Marīci, being enraged, spoke to him who had transgressed all bounds and was intent on oppressing his subjects.
"Do not commit unrighteousness, O Vena; this is not the eternal dharma. You were born in the lineage of Atri; you are undoubtedly a Prajāpati. (80)
"I shall protect the subjects"—this was the vow you previously made. To all those Brahman-sages who were speaking thus, he then replied: (81)
Vena, the evil-minded one, skilled in speech, laughed and said: "Who else is the creator of dharma, or whose words am I to listen to? (82)
"Who else on earth is equal to me in heroism, learning, austerity, and truth? Surely you do not know my true self in its reality. (83)
He is the source of all worlds and especially of all phenomena; thus, with his body, his devotion, and his sacrifice, he [pervades] the earth.
"I can create and I can swallow; there is no need for hesitation here—[only] when I am unable [to do so], being stupefied by a pillar and by intoxication. (85)
In order to bring him back to his senses, the great sages, being enraged there, slew that exceedingly powerful King Vena with an Atharvaṇa mantra.
Then, having become exceedingly enraged, they churned his left arm; and from that which was being churned, it is heard in the sacred tradition (śruti), he was first born.
O beloved, at that time there was a man who was exceedingly short and dark; O beloved, he stood before him with joined palms, filled with fear.
Seeing him thus seized and distressed, they said, "Sit down" (niṣīda); because he sat down, he indeed became the Niṣāda, the founder of the lineage, possessed of great prowess. (89)
He also created the fishermen, who were born from the sin of Vena, as well as others who dwell in the Vindhya mountains, namely the Tuṃbaras and the Khasas.
Those born from the sin of Vena, who took delight in unrighteousness, were further increased; then the great sages once again [took] the right hand of Vena.
Like kindling sticks, those who were filled with fury churned him; from his hand, Pṛthu was born, resembling a blazing fire.
Because he was born from the palm of Pṛthu’s hand, he was therefore named Pṛthu; and he blazed with a body like the fire itself in its manifest splendor.
Taking up the Jāgava bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents, as well as a sword and a brilliantly shining armor for the sake of protection, he remained vigilant. || 94 ||
O Great Goddess, upon his birth, all living beings everywhere became exceedingly joyful, and Vena ascended to the third heaven.
Then all the rivers and oceans, having brought jewels from every direction, presented themselves before the king for his consecration.
And the blessed Grandfather, together with the ṛṣis and the immortals, as well as all beings, both stationary and moving, in every respect. (97)
Having assembled, they then consecrated the son of Vena as the lord of men; thus consecrated by the gods, including Aṅgiras and others, he was possessed of great splendor.
In the supreme sovereignty, the illustrious and majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena, was established; his subjects were not delighted by his father, but they were delighted by the son of Vena.
From his great affection, the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him; and as he was about to march toward the ocean, the waters stood still before him.

Even the mountains crumbled, yet there was no obstruction to the movement of banners; the earth yielded crops without being ploughed, and food was prepared by mere thought; cows yielded all desires, and honey was found in every hollow.
At that very time, moreover, the Magadha was born again from the sacrificial vessel used for the Vaiśvadeva offerings while the Sāmavedins were chanting.
Because he was born among the Sāma-singers, he is therefore called Magadha; and Bṛhaspati [offered] a mixed oblation with the oblation of Indra. || 103 ||
When he offered oblations for Indra, from that [offering] it was born; therein negligence arose, as well as the need for expiation in ritual acts.
The sacrificial offering of the Guru, which was mixed with and overwhelmed by the remaining oblation, produced a corruption of the syllables through the inversion of high and low tones.

A sacrifice was performed for her by one born of the Kṣatriya lineage upon that Brāhmaṇa woman; therefore, because of this similarity with the former case, they are proclaimed to possess equal dharmas. || 106 ||
For this is the middling duty of a Kṣatriya: subsisting by means of the true nature of reality; whereas the practice of chariots, elephants, and horses, as well as medicine, is the lowest.
The two of them were summoned there by the great sages for the sake of the story of Pṛthu; all the munis said to them, "Let the king be praised. (108)
"Since this lord of the earth is indeed consistent with his past deeds," the Sūta and Māgadha then said to all those ṛṣis.
"We two please both the gods and the sages through our own duties; yet you do not know his deeds, nor his characteristics, nor his fame. (110)
"O twice-born ones, compose a hymn of praise for this radiant king"; thus were the two appointed by the ṛṣis, saying, "Let him be praised with future [events]."
The deeds that the mighty Pṛthu performed later were composed into songs by the panegyrists, the Sūtas and Māgadhas, as they offered praise.
Then, having heard the matter, the well-pleased Pṛthu, lord of subjects, gave the coastal region to Sūta and the Magadha country to Māgadha.
From that time forward, the protectors of the earth were praised by bards and chroniclers, and they were extolled with benedictions by bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists.
Seeing him, the subjects and the great seers were exceedingly pleased and said: "This son of Vena, the lord of men, has been ordained as the provider of livelihood for you. (115)
Then, according to the words of the great seers, "You are the provider of our livelihood," the subjects flocked to the illustrious Vainya.
Thus urged by his subjects, that powerful one, desiring to act for the welfare of his people, took up his bow and arrows and struck the earth.
Then, terrified by the fear of Vainya, the Earth fled away, having become a cow; Pṛthu took that running cow and pursued her.
Having traveled through the worlds, beginning with the world of Brahmā, out of fear of Vainya, she then saw Vainya before her, with a bow raised in his hand.
With blazing, sharp arrows endowed with radiant splendor, [he struck] that high-souled one of great yoga, who was unassailable even by the immortals.
Finding no protection, that goddess—who is always worthy of worship by the three worlds—sought refuge with Vainya alone, with her hands joined in reverence. (121)
And he said to him: "Do you not perceive that the killing of a woman is unrighteous? O King, how will you sustain the subjects without me? (122)
O King, the worlds are established in me; by me this universe is sustained. Know this, O Ruler of the Earth: without me, all creatures would perish.
O protector of the earth, if you desire to act for the welfare of all creatures, you truly ought not to kill me; listen to these words of mine.
All undertakings that are commenced with skillful means succeed; O King, having slain me, you will certainly not be able to protect the subjects.
"I shall be compliant; abandon your anger, O one of great luster! For they say that women are not to be slain, even if they have entered the womb of an animal. (126)

When the destruction of a single, most wicked evildoer of cruel deeds results in the welfare of many, that killing bestows merit; since this is so, O protector of the earth, you ought not to abandon righteousness.
Having heard such words, the righteous and mighty king restrained his anger and spoke this to the Earth: || 128 ||
And he who, out of desire, should kill one person—whether for his own sake or for the sake of another, whether it be one or many—therein lies a sin. (129)
But when many prosper happily upon the death of one, there is indeed no sin at all for him who has slain that person. (130)
Therefore, O Earth, for the sake of my subjects, I shall slay you if you do not today carry out my word for the welfare of the world. (131)
Having slain you today with an arrow for turning away from my command, I shall sustain the subjects here by expanding myself.
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, abide by my word and constantly restore the living beings to life, for you are indeed capable; of this there is no doubt.

"Indeed, become my daughter; in this way, I shall restrain this great arrow of terrible appearance that has been discharged for the purpose of killing you. Having been addressed thus, the great virtuous lady then replied to the son of Vena.
"O King, I shall accomplish all this without a doubt; however, provide me with a calf so that, out of maternal affection for her offspring, I may flow with milk."
And make me level everywhere, O best of all sustainers; so that, flowing forth, I may nourish milk everywhere. (136)
Īśvara said: Then he cleared away the masses of rocks in every direction with the tip of his bow; by that means, the son of Vena caused the mountains to increase.
In the past *manvantaras* that have passed, the earth was likewise; by its very nature, it possessed both level and uneven regions. (138)
For indeed, in the original creation, the surface of the earth was not uneven; nor did there exist any differentiation between cities and villages. (139)
There were no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade routes. || 140 ||

Indeed, this [account] occurred previously during the interval of Cākṣuṣa; and now, in this Vaivasvata interval, there is the origin of all this, wherever indeed there was an evenness of the earth in some particular place.
In each of those places, the subjects indeed lived at all times; it is said that the food of the people consisted of fruits and roots. 142.
We have heard that at that time, the birth of all these beings in this world occurred with great difficulty from the son of Vena onwards.
Having then designated the lord Cākṣuṣa Manu as the calf, Pṛthu milked the earth for crops into his own hand.
By him, this earth was indeed milked of its crops, using Manu Cākṣuṣa as the calf and the earth itself as the vessel. || 145 ||
By that food, those subjects indeed always subsisted at that time; and it is heard from the sages that the Earth was milked once again.
Soma was the calf for them, and Bṛhaspati was the milker; the Gāyatrī and all other meters were indeed the vessels. (147)
At that time, their austerity and eternal Brahman became milk; then, by the hosts of gods led by Purandara, [it was churned]. || 148 ||
Taking a golden vessel, this earth was milked; Maghavan was the calf, and Savitṛ became the milker. (149)
Milk is said to be the essence of nourishment and honey; by it the deities subsist. Furthermore, it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the ancestors.
Taking a silver vessel, [he offered] "Svadhā for imperishable satisfaction. Among them, the powerful Vaivasvata Yama became their calf. 151.
The Lord, the blessed Master, became the milker for the ancestors, and it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the Asuras.
Taking up an iron vessel and summoning all his strength, Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was among them, possessed of great majesty. (153)
The two-headed priest of the Daityas, the son of Diti, milked the illusory milk that brings satisfaction to the Daityas. || 154 ||
Therefore, even today, all these highly powerful Asuras, masters of illusion, continue to exist through illusion; this is their supreme strength.
And it is heard that the Nāgas, having made Takṣaka their calf, milked her, taking a gourd vessel for the great poison-milk. (156)
O Great Goddess, Vāsuki, the son of Kadrū and of great renown, was indeed the milker for all those serpents and snakes in every respect. (157)
Indeed, those fierce ones of massive bodies and virulent poison subsist by that [poison]; they have that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their strength, and that as their refuge. (158)
Furthermore, having milked this earth into an unbaked earthen vessel, with Vaiśravaṇa as the calf and the Yakṣas and Puṇyajanas as the attendants; || 159 ||
The milker is Rajatanāga, who moves at will by means of the wish-fulfilling gem; he is the lord of Yakṣas, possessed of great splendor, self-controlled, wise, and of great asceticism. || 160 ||
Sustained by those Yakṣas through their powerful Vasus, the Earth was milked once again by the Rākṣasas and Piśācas. (161)
Brahmopendra was indeed their milker, originating from Kubera; the calf was the powerful Sumālī, and the milk was blood itself. || 162 ||
Milked into a skull-bowl, you vanished from sight by the Rākṣasas; with that milk, the Rākṣasas sustain themselves here in every way.
Then, having made Caitraratha the calf, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases milked the Earth, which possessed pure fragrances, upon lotus leaves.
