O Goddess, Vatsa Ruci was their calf, and the auspicious son of the sage was the milker; it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the mountains.
Then the medicinal herbs in embodied form and various kinds of jewels were the milk; Himavat was their calf, and the great mountain Meru was the milker.
For his vessel was made of stone; by him the mountains were established. It is heard that the Earth was milked again by trees and creepers.

Taking a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood—which sprouts again even when cut or burnt—the milker is the flowering *śāla* tree, O illustrious lady, and the calf is the *plakṣa* tree. The Earth, the source of all beings, is the cow that milks all desires. (168)
This very earth is the supporter, the ordainer, the sustainer, and the bearer of wealth; we have heard that she was milked by Pṛthu for the benefit of the worlds. (169)
This earth, renowned as Medinī, extending to the edge of the ocean, was the foundation and the very source of the world of moving and unmoving beings. (170)
Because she formerly held the fat and flesh of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, she supports all things; therefore, she is celebrated as Vasudhā.
Then, because she accepted the status of being the daughter of the wise King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, she thereafter came to be called "Pṛthivī" (the Earth).
The earth, adorned with garlands of cities and mines, has been made famous, well-divided, and beautified by the king, who has milked it with great effort.
Such was the power of that king Vainya, the best of monarchs; thereafter, he delighted the earth through righteousness.
Then the word "rāja" (king) arose on earth because of his power to delight (rañjana); having obtained the kingdom, that son of Vena, the ruler of the earth, began to reflect.
"My father was indeed most unrighteous, a destroyer of sacrifices and other sacred rites; to what place has he gone, and how is that place to be known by me? (176)

How indeed should the funeral rites for him who has been slain be performed by the Brāhmaṇas? And how may his destination be secured through the power of the performance of sacrifices and acts of charity? (177)
While he was thus reflecting, Nārada arrived; having offered him a seat and prostrated before him, he questioned him.
O Blessed One, you know the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of all the world; my father was of wicked conduct and a reviler of the gods and Brahmins. (179)
Struck down by his own karma, O Brahmins, my father has reached the other world; to what place has he gone, dear ones—to a pit of hell or indeed to heaven? (180)
Then Nārada, having perceived this with his divine eye, said: "Listen, O mighty-armed King, to where your father resides. (181)
In this region, there is a desert named Maru, devoid of water and trees; in that most terrible land, O best of men, was your father, Janaka. (182)
Born among the Mlecchas, afflicted by consumption and possessed of leprosy, he eats the leftovers of the Mlecchas and is covered with worms and ulcers. (183)
Having heard those words of the high-souled Nārada, he then let out a cry of "Alas! Alas! and fell down unconscious.

Afflicted by grief, he reflected: "How should this be done by me? As that high-souled one was thus reflecting, an idea occurred to him: "In this world, he who protects his father is called a son. (185)
"How indeed shall my father be liberated from sin by me?"—having reflected thus, he then questioned Nārada.

"O Blessed One, you have related all the deeds performed by my father. O best of the twice-born, tell me by what action—whether through vows, gifts, austerities, or a pilgrimage to sacred fords—his liberation might be attained. (177)
Nārada said: "Go, O King, lord of men, to the principal sacred fords (tīrthas), bringing your father from that desert region to them. (188)
"O Great King, go to that place where the gods with their powers and the stainless sacred fords (tīrthas) reside; O Lord, undertake a pilgrimage there."

"Know this to be the truth: thus shall your father attain liberation. Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, the king entrusted the burden of his kingdom to his minister and departed for heaven.
Having gone to the desert land, he indeed beheld him in the midst of the Mlecchas, overwhelmed by a great case of leprosy and by consumption.
Seeing that very place, extending for a distance of one *gavyūti*, empty and devoid of humans, the king was deeply distressed and spoke these words: (192)
"I shall lead this sick man, the Mleccha, to my own home; there I will make him free from disease, if you agree. (193)

Having understood this, all those Mlecchas, with every limb bowed in prostration, said to that man who was supremely compassionate: "O Lord of the World, lead us away quickly! O Protector, it is by the power of our good fortune that you yourself have arrived here."
O Lord, the worlds afflicted by foul odors have been made happy by you; therefore, having summoned men suitable for carrying the palanquin, [you prepared to depart]. (195)
Then, having heard those compassionate words of the king, they reached many millions of sacred fords, beginning with Kedāra.
Wherever Vainya went accompanied by Vena, there too a great cry of distress was heard from the sacred fords (tīrthas).
"Alas, O Fate! An enemy approaches for the sake of our destruction; where shall we go now?"—such was their thought again and again. (198)
Even at the mere sight of him, the holy places and the gods, uttering cries of "Alas! Alas!", flee and perish at that very moment.
In this manner, the king indeed undertook a pilgrimage for three years; yet liberation was not seen by him, and consequently, he fell into supreme grief.
Then the dispatched servants [went] to Kurukṣetra, which possesses great splendor; for if one goes there, liberation from sin occurs once again. || 201 ||
O beloved, having taken the palanquin upon their shoulders, they went to Kurukṣetra; having carried it there and set it down at Sthāṇutīrtha, they departed.
Then, at midday, that king, desiring to perform his bath with devotion, likewise performed there the sixteen gifts for his father.
Then, as he was desirous of giving to the Brahmins, being full of faith and devoted to that purpose, Vāyu spoke these words from the intermediate space: || 204 ||
"Do not act rashly, my son; protect the holy ford with great effort. This man is completely surrounded by terrible sin. (205)
This wicked man of evil conduct, who reviles the Vedas and is joined by hundreds of Brahman-murders, will bring ruin to this sacred place.

"Do not destroy the sacred ford, O Lord; it will result in great sin. Hearing these words of Vāyu, he was afflicted by great sorrow; tormented by grief and distressed by the suffering of his father, he spoke. (207)
And with his arms raised, he cried out again and again, "O Fate! for he was utterly enveloped by terrible sin.
"Since even by this means it is not possible to make him pure, I shall perform an expiation for the sake of my father; of this there is no doubt. (209)
Having heard these words of his and having exercised great compassion, the sky-dwellers spoke again with a voice arising from the atmosphere: || 210 ||
"O King, O best of monarchs, casting aside your grief, listen to these words, by which there shall be a great destruction of the sins of this Janaka. (211)
There is a great perfected field renowned as Prabhāsa, which pacifies all sins and destroys even the most heinous crimes.
The principle of Brahmā, the principle of Hari, and the third, the principle of Rudra—[all these reside] in that very great field of Prabhāsa, which is dear to Śaṅkara.
The Śākteya, Cāndra, Saura, Sārasvata, as well as the Āgneya and Vāruṇa—these are remembered as the unsurpassed sacred fields (kṣetra). || 214 ||
Whatever holy fords and sacred regions exist within the cosmic egg shall all come to Prabhāsa when the Kali age has arrived. (215)
Eighty-eight hundred million hosts of Śaṅkara’s attendants, stationed there, protect that sacred field of Prabhāsa.
This meritorious Sarasvatī is indeed found everywhere; however, at Prabhāsa, she flows in five streams and is difficult to attain even for the gods.
The fifth stream of that river and its banks belong to the Yamunā; situated in the middle of it is the sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned as Goṣpada.
There, in the center, is the Pretaśilā, which grants liberation to the departed spirits; there, in ancient times, twenty-eight crores of pretas attained release.
The primordial Rudragayā is remembered as a sacred ford (tīrtha) that grants liberation even to sinners; in the Kali age, it is renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Goṣpada.
When the Mothers of the World emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, they then arrived together with the gods at the vicinity of the sacred ford.
And there, upon the stone surface of the Nandā, his hoofprint was submerged; seeing the stone marked by hooves as well as marked by the region of his knees. || 222 ||

All the gods, filled with wonder, questioned the cow Nandini: "O Goddess, what is this that is seen upon the surface of the Preta-shila? How has this exhaustion arisen for us, and why this stumbling? (223)
Nandinī said: "O gods, this foot of mine, resting upon the stone, shines like another orb of the moon situated in the courtyard of the sky. (224)
"From this day forward, O gods, in the three worlds including all that is mobile and immobile, it shall become famous in the world by the name 'Goṣpada' (the Cow's Footprint)."
O gods, whatever man comes here and performs a ritual bath and a śrāddha ceremony, his merit shall be seven times that of Gayā.
Neither the day of the week, nor the lunar mansion, nor the time is the cause there; whenever a sacred ford (tīrtha) is seen, that moment is equal to a thousand auspicious festival days (parvan).

Alternatively, O Pārvatī, if you have a desire for the sacred festival days (parva), listen to these from me: during the solstices (ayana), the equinoxes (viṣuva), the pairs of junctions (yugma), and at the ordinary transits of the sun (arkasaṃkrama).
On the new moon day and on the Aṣṭakā days, especially during the dark fortnight, and under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī, when materials and a worthy Brāhmaṇa are available.
On the day of Gajacchāyā, during Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti, when the chowries are held [in honor], on the third day of Vaiśākha, and on the ninth day of Kārttika; || 230 ||
The fifteenth day of Māgha and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas; or rather, [these are auspicious] at those times.
And at the beginning of a Manvantara, a wise person should perform a Śrāddha there; likewise on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja and the twelfth day of Kārttika.
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada; the new moon of Phālguna, and likewise the eleventh day of Pauṣa. (233)
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the month of Māgha, the eighth dark lunar day of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon day of Āṣāḍha. (234)
The full moon day of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Jyeṣṭha, as well as these beginnings of Manvantaras, cause what is given to be inexhaustible. (235)
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, on the fifth of Phālguna, on the fifth of the month of Caitra, and likewise on its final [fifteenth] day.
The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the seventh of Kārttika, and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa—these seven are the beginnings of the Kalpas.

"May there be satisfaction for a kalpa through this śrāddha performed at the beginning of the kalpa," having spoken thus, Nandā, who brings joy to the gods, vanished instantly like a lamp extinguished by the wind. (238)
Having seen this marvel, all the gods together with Indra, as well as the Brahman-sages and the celestial sages, sang this ancient verse: || 239 ||

Oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred ford and the power of Nandā’s asceticism! By giving even a single funeral offering (śrāddha) here, one obtains a fruit seven times greater than that of Gayā.
Having spoken thus, the gods then performed the funeral rites and other ceremonies; they obtained the fruit as previously described by Nandinī.
In this manner, O Indra among kings, you too should go quickly to Goṣpada; having performed the śrāddha and other rites there, you shall obtain your desired fruit. || 242 ||
O King, this father of yours is remembered as the foremost among sinners; he cannot be uplifted by hundreds of other holy places, except for Goṣpada.
Therefore, O Great King, go; do not delay. Having heard this, the king then arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
There, placing at his head Brahmins who were established in their stations and well-versed in the majesty of sacred fords (tīrthas), the great king proceeded to the Nyaṅkumatī river.

They showed the king that sacred ford (tīrtha), the footprint situated upon the Pretaśilā rock. Having seen that stainless tīrtha, his eyes wide with wonder, he constructed sacrificial pits, altars, and pavilions for the successful performance of the sacrifice.
Then the sacrifice was commenced according to the rules, with abundant sacrificial fees; his ancestors appeared before him in person, radiant as blazing fire.
Then, having established faith through ancestral rites and sacrifices of great merit, those Pitṛs, being satisfied, spoke these words to that best of kings: ||| 248 ||
"You are blessed, O King; you are meritorious, and we are even more blessed by you, since we have been uplifted by you through the performance of a śrāddha at this sacred site. (249)
Having spoken thus, all those ancestors together with Vena, seated upon excellent celestial chariots, departed for the abode of the gods.
As he was departing, Vena said to that broad-chested king: "O King, in another birth, I have existed in four previous lives."
"I was a leper, a sinner of evil conduct, and one who ate the leftovers of a Cāṇḍāla; now, liberated from that sin, I am going to the abode of the gods. (252)
Therefore go, O illustrious one, and enjoy the kingdom for a long time; every task that is performed by a son has been accomplished by you.
Having heard this, the king then rejoiced together with his kinsmen; he gladdened the Brahmins with gifts of land, gold, and other riches.
There was nothing in this world that the king did not give away, having witnessed the power of the sacred ford and the direct manifestation of his ancestors.
Having thus performed his duty, that king returned to his own place; having enjoyed the entire earth, he attained heaven after death. || 256 ||
Such is the power of that Prabhāsa field, which destroys all sins; it is there that sacred fords arrive and deities reside by the millions. (257)
Having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, he who seeks another holy site is like one who, having cast away what is in his hand, tries to lick it with his elbow. 258.
And the ancestors spoke this ancient verse to her, O beloved: "If your son is unable to go to Gayā by any means, then you must with effort go to the supreme holy site of Goṣpada. (259)
"May there be born in our lineage someone who will offer us a śrāddha here with bulbs, roots, fruits, oil-cakes, or even water. (260)

Having bathed there with diligence, one should respectfully invite Brahmins who are most learned in the Vedas and, according to the prescribed rules, feed them with great care at a śrāddha ceremony; then, for the sake of the ancestors' satisfaction, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) must be performed.
There is no need for a specific lunar day, nor a constellation, nor indeed a festival or the like; one should always go there with a mind endowed with faith. (262)

There is no restriction regarding time there, since the vision [of the deity] is the authority; for in that place, O beloved, it is difficult to obtain access on the third day of the dark fortnight (Akṣayatṛtīyā).
On the full moon day of Kārttika, on the seventh day of Māgha, or on the Padmaka festival.
A gift of gold, a gift of cows, clothing, silver, clarified butter, and sesame seeds should be given there by one who is disciplined and desires the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Thus, O Goddess, has this secret of the sacred ford, which brings great prosperity, been told to you. It must not be spoken of to those of wicked intellect, to sinners, or to those of cruel mind.
It should be given to one endowed with faith and devoted to service toward his ancestors; at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, the knower of the Purāṇas should especially recite it with devotion.

By this, satisfaction for twelve years is produced for the ancestors. It should be heard constantly with self-restraint by men who fear hell; it should always be recited with devotion before Brahmins while they are eating. (268)

A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors; by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare. (269)
This is a secret, a treasury of glory; this is exceedingly dear to the ancestors. This is eternally for the sake of immortality in the Vedas, and it removes the great sins of men. (270)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Goṣpada Tīrtha," within the "Greatness of the Nyaṅkumatī River" section of the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the first part of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 336 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the supreme abode of Nārāyaṇa, located on the auspicious shore of the ocean to the south of Goṣpada.
Near the Nyaṅkumatī river, at that place which destroys all sins, Keśava himself resides, remaining there throughout the duration of other kalpas.
Indeed, for the sake of uplifting the ancestors in this fierce Kali Yuga, when the Lord Hari effects the destruction of the Daityas.
He would always remain in that house for the sake of rest; therefore, it became renowned on the surface of the earth as the "House of Nārāyaṇa."
In the Kṛta age he is named Janārdana; in Tretā, Madhusūdana; in Dvāpara, Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and in Kali, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O subduer of enemies, whenever the four ages (caturyuga) arrive again and again, he establishes the order of dharma and returns to that same place.
He who, fasting on the eleventh day, beholds that Lord, surely beholds the eternal station, the infinite abode of Hari.
Therefore, yellow garments should be given to the best of the twice-born; and those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage should properly perform the ritual bath and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Thus has been told to you that which possesses great power, arising from the abode of Hari’s sign; the wise person who, being self-restrained, either hears it or recites it, attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nārāyaṇagṛha," within the "Majesty of Nyaṅkumatī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 337 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated on the bank of the Devikā, renowned as Jāleśvara, which is saluted by gods and demons.
When the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived during the Dvāpara Yuga, there was a Liṅga named Jāleśvara situated on the bank of the Devikā.

It is worshipped by the daughters of the Nāgas, yet mortals do not behold it; it is composed of great splendor and jewels, with a radiance equal to the orb of the moon. By the mere remembrance of that deity, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
The Goddess said: How did it come to be named Jāleśvara, and at what time did that occur?
O Lord, what virtues are proclaimed to arise from dwelling together with the virtuous? What worlds and what merits [are attained]? Tell me all of that.
The Lord said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Nābhāga and Āpastaṃba, the treasure-house of austerity.
Formerly, the great seer Āpastamba, a self-possessed leader among the twice-born, was always observing a fast; at that time, the Blessed One became Rambha.
Having permanently cast off anger, greed, delusion, and malice, he entered the body of water in the middle of the Devikā river.
Having correctly understood [the truth] in that delightful Prābhāsika field, which is dear to Śiva, a great length of time then passed while he was dwelling there.
While he remained like a pillar through the power of supreme meditative yoga, fishermen once arrived at that place.
Having spread out their very great net, all of them pulled it with force; then the fishermen, arrogant in their strength, [dragged] that great fish.

Therefore, they rescued the son of Brahmā from the water; seeing him blazing with ascetic power, the fishermen, overwhelmed by fear, prostrated themselves with their heads and spoke these words aloud: || 12 ||
The Niṣādas said: "O you of noble vows, you ought to forgive us for the sin we have committed out of ignorance. Or rather, what pleasing service may we perform for you today? Please command us. (13)

Seeing that great slaughter of fish being carried out by the sages, he was overcome with supreme compassion and, filled with grief, spoke to the fishermen: sa munistanmahaddṛṣṭvā matsyānāṃ kadanaṃ kṛtam | kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo dāśānprovāca duḥkhitaḥ || 14 ||
What indeed could be my means [to achieve this], for alas, all remain intent upon their own self-interest; even the minds of the wise are devoted solely to their own welfare. (15)
When even the wise, relying on their own self-interest, remain absorbed in meditation, where then will these beings afflicted by suffering find happiness in this world? (16)
Those seeking liberation declare that person who desires to experience only miseries to be indeed more sinful than the sinful.
"What indeed might be the means by which I, possessing a suffering self, having entered within all beings, might become the experiencer of all their sufferings? (18)
Whatever merit I possess, may that go to them; and whatever evil they have committed, may all of that come to me. (19)
It is my conviction that he in whom no compassion arises upon seeing the blind, the wretched, the maimed, the helpless, and likewise the diseased, is a demon.
He who, though capable, does not protect living beings who have fallen into mortal danger and are overwhelmed by fear, incurs that very sin himself. (21)
They say that whatever happiness arises for afflicted people, heaven or even liberation does not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
Therefore, I will not abandon these miserable and deeply distressed fish and move even a single step; how much less shall I go to the abode of the thirty gods?
Īśvara said: Having heard these words of the sage, those fishermen were filled with agitation and reported everything exactly as it had happened to Nābhāga.
Having heard of that from him, Nābhāga also went there in haste to see the son of Brahmā, accompanied by his ministers and his family priest. || 25 ||
Having duly honored that god-like sage, the king said: "O Blessed One, tell me what I may do at your command."
Āpastamba said: "O King, these fishermen, who live in misery and are overcome by great exhaustion, say: 'Give us my price, whatever you deem appropriate. (27)
Nābhāga said: "O Blessed One, I shall give a hundred thousand [gold pieces] as the price to the Niṣādas for the one named Nigraha, just as the son of Brahmā has stated. (28)
Āpastamba said: "O King, I am not to be restrained by you with hundreds of thousands; let a fitting price be paid—deliberate on this together with your ministers. (29)
Nābhāga said: "O best of the twice-born, let ten million be given as the price to the Niṣādas; if even this is not sufficient for you, then more shall be given. (30)
Āpastamba said: "O King, ten million or even more is not a fitting price for me; let a suitable price be given, and deliberate upon it together with the Brāhmaṇas. (31)
Nābhāga said: "Let either half the kingdom or the whole kingdom be given to the Niṣādas; I consider this to be the price, O twice-born one, or what else do you think? (32)
Āpastamba said: "O King, I do not deserve half the kingdom or even the whole of it; let a fitting price be given, and deliberate upon this together with the sages. (33)
Having heard those words of the great seer, Nābhāga became despondent; afflicted by grief, he reflected along with his ministers and his domestic priest.
Then a certain rishi there, Lomaśa of great asceticism, said to Nābhāga: "Do not fear; I shall propitiate that sage for you."
Nābhāga said: "Tell me the price, O illustrious one, for this high-souled sage; save me from this [debt], along with my kinsmen, family, and relatives. (36)
The Lord Rudra might consume the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving; how much more so a lowly human being who is utterly devoted to the objects of the senses? (37)

Lomaśa said: "O great king, you are indeed worthy of praise, honored by the world, and the best of the twice-born; the cows are divine as well. Therefore, let a cow be given by you as the price for this. (39)
Having heard those words, the king, together with his ministers and his priest, was filled with great joy and spoke these words to the sage: || 39 ||
"Arise, arise, O Blessed One! You have been purchased, there is no doubt. This is the most fitting price for you, O best of sages. (40)
Āpastamba said: "I rise up, O King, well-pleased; I have been properly purchased. I see no price for cows that is more supreme or purifying on earth. (41)
Cows should always be circumambulated and worshipped; for these goddesses, the abodes of auspiciousness, were created by the Self-born One himself. 42.
The fire-sanctuaries of Brahmins and the temples of the deities are purified by cow-dung; what could be more excellent than that? (43)
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—these five purifiers of cows sanctify the entire world. (44)
Cows are always before me, and cows are indeed behind me; cows are in my heart, and I dwell in the midst of cows. 45.
A person who, being self-controlled and pure, recites the mantra in this manner at the three junctions of the day, is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world. || 46 ||
Every day, one should devotedly provide grass for the food of the cows; by failing to do so and eating oneself, one falls into a miserable state.
By him who gives daily fodder to cows, the sacred fires have been properly offered, the ancestors have been gratified, and the gods have been honored. (48)
The mantra: "O daughter of Surabhi, goddess worshipped by the world, abiding in the station of Viṣṇu; everything has been given by me—may you accept it, being well-pleased. (49)
By protecting young children, by scratching the cows, and by guarding those who are exhausted or afflicted, a man is glorified in heaven. (50)
For cows are proclaimed to be the beginning, the middle, and the end of a mortal; they always provide for the gods milk, clarified butter, and nectar.
Therefore, cows should always be given as gifts and constantly worshipped; for they are indeed constructed like a staircase for the attainment of heaven.
Having heard this supreme majesty of cows, those Niṣādas prostrated before the high-souled Āpastamba and then spoke to him.
The Niṣādas said: "Conversation, sight, touch, as well as praise and remembrance—these are indeed purifiers of the virtuous; so we have heard. (54)
Conversation and even sight of you have been shared by us; therefore, show us favor and accept this cow. (55)
Āpastamba said: "I accept these cows from you; you are now freed from sin. O Niṣādas, go to heaven together with the fish drawn from the water. (56)
If, having inspired joy in living beings even through a censurable act, I should see hell, I would dwell in heaven itself. (57)
Whatever merit may have been performed by me through the actions of mind, speech, and body—by that, may all those afflicted by suffering go to a fortunate rebirth. (58)
Then, by the grace of that great seer of purified soul, the Niṣādas, together with the fish, went to heaven because of his words.
Seeing those fishermen departing for heaven along with their fish, the king, together with his ministers and servants, spoke this out of wonder: || 60 ||
Those who seek their own welfare should serve the virtuous, who are like sacred waters; even a moment’s attendance upon them here shall not be fruitless. (61)

One should always sit with the virtuous, engage in noble conversation with the virtuous, and conduct oneself according to the vows of the virtuous; one should not perform even the slightest act with the wicked.
Through these encounters with the virtuous, even these fishermen have attained heaven like meritorious men.
There the sage Āpastamba and the high-minded Lomaśa gratified the king with various desired boons.
Then he chose Dharmabuddhi, who was very difficult to find; and saying "So be it," the two of them joyfully gave their consent to that king.
"Oh, you are blessed, O Indra among kings, for your mind is devoted to dharma! Dharma is very difficult for men to attain, especially for those who rule the earth. (66)
If a king, though intoxicated by pride, does not abandon his own duty, then who in the world could be superior to him? (67)
Birth is certain for kings at all times, and delusion is likewise always certain; from delusion, hell is certain. Therefore, the wise censure kingship.
For men who are greedy for sense-objects highly prize sovereignty, but the wise regard that very thing as being like hell. (69)
Therefore, O Great King, if you desire an eternal state for yourself, you must not indulge in pride, which destroys both worlds. (70)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, those two great-souled ones departed for their respective hermitages; and Nābhāga too, having obtained the boon, entered the city filled with joy.
O Goddess, this power arising from Devikā has been described to you; and at that time, Bhava was established as Jāleśvara by the sage.
Because that best of sages fell into the net of the fishermen, he became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Jāleśvara.
Having bathed there, O Great Goddess, by worshipping Jāleśvara, Āpastamba, Nābhāga, the Niṣādas, and those who live by catching fish [were liberated].
By the power of Devikā, they went to heaven along with the fish on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra. (75)

He who offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the ancestors on that day finds no end to his merit. A gift of a cow should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; likewise, the greatness [of the place] should be heard and Jālakeśvara should be visited.

Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the well renowned throughout the three worlds, situated on the beautiful bank of the Devikā; it is filled by the mere utterance of the syllable "Huṃ."
From there, O beautiful lady, the water flows downward again; there, in ancient times, one named Taṇḍi resided on the bank of the Devikā.
O Great Goddess, devoted to the worship of Śiva, he performed penance; while he was thus performing penance in that region, O lady of beautiful countenance, (verse 3).
O beloved, an old blind deer came to that place and fell into a great, bottomless pit devoid of water.
Seeing him, that sage, overcome with compassion, maintained his vow of silence; yet there, O beautiful lady, he uttered the sound "huṃ" again and again.
Then, O beloved, by the sound of the syllable "Huṃ," that pit was filled; thereafter, the deer emerged from the water with great difficulty.
Assuming a human form, he questioned that Ṛṣi, having reached a state of supreme wonder regarding the fruit of action that grants all desires.
Having fallen into the state of a deer there and subsequently having become a human being, that best of the twice-born spoke of the greatness of that water.
Therefore, I have attained human form; there is no other cause for this here. Then that water entered back into the surface of the earth.
Then that sage, filled with curiosity, uttered the syllable "Huṃ" once more; the well was filled again with water just as it had been before.
Then, having performed his bath and likewise the libations to the ancestors, and considering that place to be the best of sacred fords (tīrthas), he attained the supreme goal.
Even today, when that "hum" is uttered, a flood of water flows forth; and any man who goes there with devotion—even if he is devoted to sin—[is purified].
That man who, having bathed there and become pure, performs a śrāddha ceremony, does not obtain rebirth as a human being on the surface of the earth. || 13 ||
He is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the ancestors; he delivers seven generations of his lineage, both past and future.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to that place where the great liṅga Caṇḍīśvara is situated, which destroys all sins.

There, O beautiful lady, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, he who, intent upon fasting, performs a night vigil (prajāgara), goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.

Thus ends the three hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Caṇḍīśvara," within the "Majesty of Devikā" section of the first part, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," in the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 340 ||

Īśvara said: From there, one should go to Āśāpūra, the stainless Vighnarāja. Situated to the northwest of Śaśibhūṣaṇa, he is the destroyer of obstacles. Because he fulfills one's hopes (āśā), he is remembered as Āśāpūraka.
O Goddess of Devas, it is there that Rāma, along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, having propitiated Vighneśa, obtained their desired wish. || 2 ||
And there, O Goddess, having propitiated the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Moon formerly obtained that which he desired: the destruction of all skin diseases.
Likewise, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, having worshipped the Lord of Gods there, one should feed the twice-born with sweetmeats (modakas).
One obtains the desired accomplishment through the grace of Vighnarāja; indeed, O Great Goddess, [this was done] by me in the past for the protection of this sacred field.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, he was appointed as the destroyer of obstacles for those who were about to depart.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vighnarāja Āśāpūra," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 341 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, situated not far to the south-southwest of that [place] is a sin-destroying Liṅga, established by Soma himself. || 1 ||
Right there is the Amṛtakuṇḍa, which is known as Kalākuṇḍa; having bathed there, whatever man shall worship Candreśa, [he shall attain his goal]. || 2 ||
He shall obtain the fruit of a thousand years of austerity; O Goddess, right there is situated a lake fashioned by Candra.
To the east and west of Candreśa, extending sixteen *dhanus* in width—that which lies to its east has been fully described, beginning with the granting of liberation.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Caṇḍreśvara-Kalākuṇḍa Tīrtha," within the "Greatness of Āśāpūra," in the first section, the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 342 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Kapileśvara, located to the east of Śīrābhūṣaṇa and to the west of Koṭitīrtha.
To the south of Jaradgaveśa and likewise to the north of the ocean—this is indeed the field of Kapila, which is not attained by men lacking merit.
O Goddess, in ancient times, Kapila performed great austerities at this place for more than ten thousand years after having installed Maheśvara.
The goddess Kapiladhārā, the great river, was summoned there; she is seen even today by the meritorious in the midst of the ocean. || 4 ||

Having bathed there, O Great Goddess, especially on the sixth day of the month of Kārttika (Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī), one should cause a tawny cow to be given as a gift; one shall then partake in the fruit of giving ten million cows.
This is remembered as the expiation for all sins; by worshipping Kapileśvara, one obtains the merit of ten million maidens.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, it is a marvel! I desire to hear the ritual procedure for Kapila-Ṣaṣṭhī, beginning with the rules for gifts, mantras, and so forth. (7)
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, if even one such [day] as this—endowed with the conjunction [of planets]—is obtained by men within the span of their birth and life, what more can I say? (8)
If Tuesday falls on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, and that sixth is a Vyatīpāta yoga occurring under the asterism Rohiṇī, it is known as Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī.
Having bathed in that sacred field, or at an auspicious site of the sun, with earth, white sesame seeds, and at the auspicious confluence of Kapilā; || 10 ||

Having performed his ablutions and recitations, he should thereafter offer an *arghya* oblation to the Sun with water mixed with red sandalwood and *karavīra* flowers. Having placed the *arghya* vessel upon his head, he should present it with this mantra: ||| 11 ||
Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, who has illuminated the three realms; salutations to you, O Veda-rayed one, accept this water offering; homage be to you! 12.
Having circumambulated and worshipped Kapileśvara and the sun, [one should perform the rite] in a consecrated and auspicious place adorned with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
One should place a flawless jar filled with sandalwood water, endowed with the five jewels, and accompanied by dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Covered with a pair of red garments and joined with a copper vessel, the chariot is indeed made of gold-leaf and adorned with various wonderful patterns.
One should have an image of the Sun fashioned out of one pala of gold; having placed it upon a water-pot, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers. || 16 ||
In the pavilion consecrated by the fire-sacrifice (homa) in the presence of Kapileśvara, one should worship the god Āditya with his own names as they have been declared.
O Āditya, Bhāskara, Ravi, Bhānu, Divākara yourself, Prabhākara—salutations to you; deliver me from this worldly existence.
Since you bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, therefore grant us peace.
The prayer mantra: Homage, homage to you, O giver of boons, Lord of the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajus Vedas; homage be to you who possess all forms, the abode of the universe; homage be to you! 20.
O Goddess, your milk is nectar, pure and bestowing nourishment here in this world; by your grace, human beings are liberated from all sins. (21)
O Goddess of great radiance, produced by Brahmā from the sacrificial fire-pit; salutations to you, O auspicious Kapilā, who are worshipped by all the gods. || 22 ||
O Goddess, who embodies all the gods and consists of all sacred fords, O Auspicious One, lead me yourself—who am honoring the donor—to the world of Brahmā.
The mantra for worship: Having thus performed the worship of the tawny cow and the Sun residing within the water-pot, one should bestow both upon a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas. (24)
One should cause it to be given to Vyāsa, the devotee of the Sun, with this mantra. || 25 ||
May the divine-formed Sun-god, the eye of the world, the twelve-fold soul, together with Kapilā, grant me liberation. || 26 ||
"Since you, O Kapilā, are meritorious and the purifier of all the world, being bestowed together with Sūrya, become the bestower of liberation upon me. (27)
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's means, or even half of that, or again half of that; endowed with such a fee, one should present that cow. || 28 ||
The man who performs the rite known as the Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī according to this procedure obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 29 ||
Whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—that entire fruit one obtains who observes the Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī vow.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of tawny cows on the occasion of a solar eclipse, that same fruit shall be multiplied ten millionfold. || 31 ||
O woman of excellent complexion, he who observes the Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī vow dwells in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the bodies of ten million cows.
"Whatever sin has been accumulated in the past, whether through knowledge or ignorance, all of that goes to destruction; so said the sage Kapila. (33)

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ritual for the Kapilā-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," within the "Greatness of Kapi-ladhārā and Kapileśvara," in the first section, the "Greatness of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 343 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the sin-destroying Liṅga situated to the north of the northeast of Kapileśvara.
The shrine named Jaradgaveśvara is established by Jaradgava; it destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||
O Goddess, the river Aṃśumatī is situated right there; having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to be given.
It shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors for more than a full hundred million years; a bull should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Then one should worship the god Jaradgava with perfumes and flowers, as well as with the essence of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and incense of guggulu.

With hymns of praise, prostrations, and circumambulations day and night, one should feed the Brahmins there with various kinds of foods and delicacies; by feeding even a single person, it is as if ten million have been fed.
In the Kṛta age, that sacred ford (tīrtha) is celebrated by the name Siddhodaka; however, in the Kali age, it is celebrated as Jaradgaveśvara.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jaradgaveśvara," within the "Majesty of Aṃśumatī," in the first section, the "Majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra," of the seventh book, the "Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa," of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Hāṭakeśvara Liṅga, located sixty-three dhanus to the east of Jaradgava.
O Goddess, Nala indeed established it under the name Naleśvara, together with Damayantī, having recognized that field as most excellent. || 2 ||
O Goddess, having seen that [liṅga] and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, a person is liberated from the sins of the Kali age and shall be victorious in gambling. || 3 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Naleśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 345 ||
Īśvara said: Therefore, O Great Goddess, the Sun-god is situated in the south-eastern direction; in the previous kalpa, he was remembered as being joined with Karkoṭaka. || 1 ||

By the mere sight of him, all the deities become delighted. He who worships according to the prescribed rite on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday with incense, perfumes, and ointments is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karkoṭakārka," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Hāṭakeśvara Liṅga, located two hundred dhanus to the east of Naleśvara.
In that place, there is a grove named Agastyāmravana situated three hundred dhanus to the northeast of Cintāmaṇi; it was there that the high-souled Agastya formerly performed penance.
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, tell me everything in detail—at what time [did this occur]? || 3 ||
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent complexion, in ancient times there were fierce hosts of Daityas known as the Kālakeyas, who brought about the destruction of the three worlds.
Then they were all slain by the powerful Viṣṇu, who dwells in the sacred field of Prabhāsa under the name Daityasūdana.
Having assumed the form of a tiger named Cakramukhī, he indeed killed her in that form; thereafter, he became the slayer of the Daityas.
Those who remained after the slaughter, overwhelmed by fear, entered the edge of the ocean; then they consulted together: "How can the gods be oppressed? (7)
May those who exist here on the surface of the earth as upholders of dharma—those devoted to austerity and sacred study, and those intent upon sacrifice and charity—attain their goal. || 5 ||
Then, O beloved, having made an agreement and emerged from the ocean at night, they slaughtered there the ascetics who were devoted to sacrifice and charity.
O Great Goddess, at that place in Prabhāsa, extending for twelve yojanas, was the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha and of the great-souled great seers.
Five thousand and seven hundred ascetics were devoured by Raibhya, and five hundred and sixteen by Viśvāmitra.
Seven hundred of Cyavana's disciples, two hundred of the sage Jābāli's, and six hundred of Vālakhilya's were killed by those evil-minded ones in the holy hermitage of the Vālakhilyas.
Wherever a sacrifice may take place, they go there at the arrival of night and devour the officiating priests engaged in that sacrifice and its offerings.
Then everyone on the surface of the earth became agitated with fear, and no one understood the movements of the Daityas.
At night those sages sleep, having retired to their comfortable beds; but at dawn, during their sacrifice, there remains for them only a heap of bones.
Then, religious rites were abandoned by all human beings on the surface of the earth; the world became devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of "vaṣaṭ."
Then other ascetics, joined together at night and bearing weapons, appeared; for when Dharma had been destroyed, the inhabitants of heaven were oppressed.
Exclaiming, "What is this?", they went for refuge to Brahmā, saying, "O Blessed One, all these ascetics as well as those who are devoted to knowledge [are in distress]. (18)
O Great-grandfather, on this earth all those who have lost their religious duties are devoured by something at night and go directly to death. (19)
O Lord, he who practices dharma during the day meets death at night; on this entire earth, there is no recitation of the Vedas nor the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call.

"Because of the non-existence of the Dharma, we have all fallen into the greatest doubt. Having heard those words of theirs and having reflected, the divine Grandfather spoke to all the gods who were beset by supreme doubt: 21. "We have all fallen into the greatest doubt because of the non-existence of the Dharma. Having heard those words of theirs and having reflected, the divine Grandfather spoke to all the gods who were beset by supreme doubt.
The Dānavas known as the Kāleyas, who perform terrible deeds, having reached the ocean, began devouring the ascetics.
And because they cannot be destroyed for your destruction, you must strive for their destruction; otherwise, our own destruction will come to pass. (23)
Go quickly to the surface of the earth to where Agastya resides, who is constantly devoted to the practice of vows in the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Born from Mitra and Varuṇa, he is capable of drinking up the ocean; he must be propitiated by you, O best of beings—drink the sea!
Then, when he has done so, all those lowest of Dānavas shall become subject to your slaughter, O lords of the three heavens. || 26 ||
Īśvara said: Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, all the gods approached the sacred field of Prabhāsa and sought refuge with Agastya. (27)
The gods said: "Protect, protect, O best of the twice-born! The three worlds have fallen into peril, devastated by the Kālakeyas who have taken refuge in the ocean. (28)
"O best of the twice-born, dry it up for the benefit of the inhabitants of heaven; O Lord, no other man is capable of performing such a deed."
Īśvara said: Thus addressed by the hosts of gods, Agastya, the bull among sages, went toward the ocean together with the deities, filled with joy.
Being sung of by the Gandharvas, being praised by the Kinnaras, and being extolled by the gods, he spoke these words.
"For the sake of protecting the three worlds, I shall dry up the great ocean; O gods, you shall behold this great spectacle, including its fish and sea-monsters."
Having spoken thus, the venerable sage Agastya, the best of the twice-born, took a mouthful of the entire ocean, the lord of rivers.
When that great ocean was swallowed by the high-souled one, the Dānavas, terrified with fear, wandered here and there.
Being struck there by the gods with extremely sharp weapons, others, intent on flight, went toward the wilderness.
When the Daityas had been mostly slain, they quickly entered Pātāla, having torn open the surface of the earth and being drenched in blood.
Then the delighted thirty gods spoke to Agastya, the best of sages: "All that we desired has been accomplished; let the ocean be filled once again."
Agastya said: "O gods, the water has been digested by me and likewise rendered impure. For there shall arise in the lineage of the Raghus a most excellent king. (38)
Known as Bhagīratha, the best among all wielders of weapons, he shall bring the Gaṅgā there solely for the sake of his kinsmen.
"From the world of Brahmā, the best of rivers shall come, and by it he will be filled. Having spoken thus, the sage returned to his own abode together with the gods. (40)
Then, when he had reached his own hermitage, the gods spoke these words: "O Brahmin, O sage, we are thoroughly pleased with this deed of yours."
"Tell us what you desire; even if it should be very difficult to obtain, what can we do? (42)
Agastya said: "For twenty-five billion Brahmās, I shall remain as a dweller of celestial chariots at the summit of the southern sky."
"Whatever man comes here to my auspicious hermitage, in the vicinity of Hāṭakeśvara, in the excellent Prabhāsa-kṣetra;"
May he who duly performs his ablutions there attain the supreme goal—having descended from Pātāla, Maheśvara in the form of a Liṅga. (45)
Whoever should worship that which has been established by me through the power of my asceticism, for him there will certainly be, day after day, the fruit of a hundred cows.
Whatever mortal should worship me, accompanied by Lopāmudrā, and with a concentrated mind offer the respectful oblation (arghya) according to the prescribed rule using kāśa flowers; || 47 ||
And when the autumn season has arrived, let him attain the supreme goal, along with me, Lopāmudrā, and Hāṭakeśvara.

By worshipping at the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand cows. O best of men, whatever twice-born man performs a śrāddha here at the northern solstice, his reward shall be equal to the entire merit of a śrāddha performed at Gayā.
The Lord said: "So be it," having thus spoken to them, all the gods, including Vāsava, then departed for their own abodes with joyful minds.
Therefore, with every effort, when autumn has arrived, a person should go to the hermitage of Agastya and worship Hāṭakeśa.

This is the Kalpa-liṅga named Agastyeśvara, beloved by the gods; whoever listens with devotion to this account of the sage’s deeds is instantly liberated from the sins committed during a day and night.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Hāṭakeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Nāradeśvarī in the west, who dwells in the vicinity of Nāradeśvara and destroys all misfortune.
Whatever woman, with a concentrated mind, worships the Goddess on the third lunar day, no woman in her lineage shall be possessed of misfortune.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nāradeśvarī," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the goddess Maṃtravibhūṣaṇā, who was worshipped by Soma in ancient times in the vicinity of Bhīmeśvara.
Whatever woman worships her according to the prescribed rite on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, she is liberated from all miseries.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mantravibhūṣaṇā-Gaurī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Vishvesha Durgakutaka, located to the east of Bhalla-tirtha and to the south of Yogini-chakra.
Propitiated by Bhīma, he became the granter of all desires according to the prescribed rites on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
Whoever worships that deity with perfumes, flowers, and water-offerings, for him there shall be no obstacle for one year; of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Durgakūṭa Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go from there to Kauraveśvarī, who was propitiated in ancient times by him [the Kuru king] after whose name Kurukṣetra is so called. || 1 ||

She was propitiated by Bhīma after he had performed the protection of the sacred field; that auspicious goddess protects the man who worships her with effort on the Mahānavamī day as if she were her own son—of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||
Food must be given there to the husband and wife, without a doubt; she, being praised, is then satisfied with divine delicacies and well-prepared meals.

Thus ends the three hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kauraveśvarī," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 350 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Suparṇelā Bhairavī, located five hundred bow-lengths to the south of Durgakūṭa.
O Goddess, in ancient times the nectar was carried away from Pātāla by Suparṇa; having seized it there, he indeed released it while the Nāgas were looking on.
Then, having seen that she was protected by the side of the Naga, the Goddess was thereafter known on the surface of the earth as Suparṇelā.
The earth is indeed called Ilā, established by Suparṇa; therefore, she is known by the name Suparṇilā, which destroys all sins.

Having bathed right there in Suparṇakuṇḍa, a person should worship her; he should give food to the Brahmins, and that man shall not die from calamities. A woman shall have living children and be adorned by her offspring.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Suparṇelā," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 351 ||
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Bhalla-tirtha, located on its western side where the four-armed Vishnu resides.
In that delightful Mitravana, measuring half of a half-yojana in extent, was the place where the powerful Viṣṇu had cast off his body.
O Great Goddess, in age after age, at the beginning of kalpas and manvantaras, Viṣṇu’s abiding place is in that very spot; his delight is nowhere else.
The wise know that Vaiṣṇava is the primordial field among all fields; it contains three and a half crores of the most excellent holy places (tīrthas).
O beautiful lady, those [powers] exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; there itself, the Gaṅgā herself is present in embodied form.
For the purpose of Viṣṇu’s universal dissolution and for the welfare of living beings, [he established] Gaṅgā, Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
"Having abandoned the city of Dvāravatī, Hari dwells right here; O Goddess, I perform his funeral rites in age after age."
O beloved, having gone there myself on the twelfth lunar day of the month of Nabhasya, I perform that rite according to the prescribed rules, accompanied by the most eminent of Brahmins.

Having bestowed gifts there according to the rules upon those who have mastered the Vedas, and having bathed right there according to the prescribed rite on the occasion of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), || 9 ||
Having gratified the ancestors with devotion, one is liberated from all sins; and having worshipped Viṣṇu there and kept a vigil during the night. (10)
But by making offerings such as lamps, one becomes fulfilled in one's purpose. || 11 ||
Now, O beloved, I shall relate to you an ancient account concerning him: after the powerful Vāsudeva had withdrawn all the Yādavas, [he departed]. (12)
When Durvāsas smeared his feet with milk-rice (pāyasa), Janārdana, who pervades all things, became one whose body had attained the nature of a diamond (vajra).
Having gone to the shore of the ocean, he became established in meditative absorption, restraining all his sensory currents and settling the self within the Self.
In the meantime, there arrived the son of a fisherman named Jarā, who held an arrow in his hand; he was a sinful man, a killer of fish, with an exceedingly dark body.
Then, seeing from afar one born of the Niṣāda race, he mistook him for a deer seeking the footprint of Viṣṇu and released an arrow at him.
Then, having gone into his presence, he beheld one who was four-armed, of massive body, and bearing a conch, a discus, and a mace.

Seeing that person, who resembled a dark cloud and for a moment appeared like a white lotus, he became terrified with fear and, trembling with palms joined in reverence, said: "O Lord, I did not recognize you as one who bears such a divine form. (18)
O best of gods, I have pierced you at the tip of your foot out of ignorance; O Lord, you ought to forgive me, for it does not behove you to be angry here. (19)
Viṣṇu said: "O auspicious one, the end of my curse has been brought about by you today through the falling of this arrow. Therefore, O one of great luster, go to heaven by my grace. (20)
And whatever other supreme men come here and behold me, they shall go to that highest abode where I am eternally established.
"O auspicious one, since I have been pierced by you with a crescent-headed arrow (bhallaka) on the sole of my foot, this place shall therefore become renowned as Bhallatīrtha."
It was proclaimed as Harikṣetra in the former Svāyambhuva Manvantara.

The Lord said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished, and the hunter also went to heaven. Those who shall perform their bath here, endowed with supreme devotion, will go to the world of Viṣṇu out of my grace and with my favor.
Those who, devoted to their ancestors, shall perform the Śrāddha ceremony here, their ancestors, being duly gratified, will attain complete satisfaction.
Therefore, having reached that supreme field with every effort, one should bathe in the Bhallaka Tīrtha and behold the four-armed Lord.
Those who, arrogant due to the strength of their devotion to me, do not bow to Vāsudeva, my beloved, should not be known as my devotees; for they are indeed sinners.
For even one who has become my devotee, if he eats on the day of Ekādaśī, that person of sinful intellect must not perform the worship of my liṅga.
Whatever lunar day is dear to Viṣṇu, that lunar day is dear to me; he who does not fast on it is more wicked than the most wicked. (29)

Likewise, he who—whether a woman or a man—worships me with devotion on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the vicinity of the Bhalla-tīrtha, for him there shall be no destruction of his home for thousands of births.
Thus, O Goddess, has this majesty of Viṣṇu’s Bhalla-tīrtha been told, which destroys sin and annihilates all transgressions. (31)
There, in the vicinity of Viṣṇu, to the northwest is an excellent pitcher; it is the famous Bhalla-tīrtha, where Hari was struck by a bhalla-arrow.
There, garments, footprints, and cows should be given according to the prescribed rite to the foremost of Brahmins by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage. (33)

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhalla-tīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 352 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Kardamāla, a holy site renowned throughout the three worlds that destroys all sins.
In that terrible single ocean, when all things moving and stationary had perished, and when the moon, sun, and fire had vanished and the luminaries had gone to their dissolution; || 2 ||

O fair-faced one, seeing the earth gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), the Lord Janārdana assumed the form of a boar; lifting the earth with the tip of his tusk, he established it in its own place upon his head.
Having raised him up, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these words.
O Goddess, it was while remaining in this very place that you were rescued by me; my residence here shall forever remain constant.
O lady of beautiful countenance, those who shall offer libations to the ancestors at Kardamāla will have satisfied them until the end of the kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious lady, those who perform a śrāddha ceremony there with vegetables, roots, or fruits, will indeed have performed a śrāddha at all sacred fords.

O twice-born ones, whatever human being bathes at this sacred ford and beholds me—even those humans who die as mere insects or moths—upon death they go to the third heaven by virtue of that meritorious act.
Then they are born on the islands in wealthy and noble families; that water which issued forth from your body by the piercing of your tusks [is what they drink]. || 9 ||
Having bathed there, O Goddess, a person is not born into the womb of an animal. || 10 ||

Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to the wonderful event that occurred there in the past. A herd of deer, greatly terrified and harassed by hunters, entered the Kardamāla lake and immediately attained human form. || 11 ||
Then those hunters, their eyes wide with wonder upon seeing them, asked those mortals in great agitation, O lady of excellent complexion.
"By which path did the herd of deer that arrived depart? Then they said, "We, who were actually humans, arrived here in the form of deer. (13)

"This is the power of this sacred ford; indeed, we do not know our own cause [of liberation]. Then those hunters, O highly fortunate lady, having cast aside their bows and arrows and bathed there, were released from all sins.
Pārvatī said: O Blessed One, tell me in detail of the great glory of Kardamāla; [tell me] its origin, its ritual injunctions, and the boundaries of the sacred field, in due order.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to this secret concerning the origin of Kardamāla; it is a hidden treasure of all the Brahman-sages, and you must not give it to anyone.
Formerly, when the single terrible ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished; when the moon, sun, and wind had vanished and the luminaries had gone to their dissolution.
Brahmā beheld this entire world as a single ocean; within it, the earth was submerged and had reached the depths of Pātāla.
Then, O lady of excellent countenance, that Sacrificial Boar, having assumed a body composed of sacrifice, lifted up the entire earth with the tip of his tusk.

Īśvara said: The Veda is his feet, the sacrificial post his tusks, the ritual sacrifices his teeth, and the offering-ladle his mouth; fire is his tongue, the *darbha* grass his hair, and Brahman his head—such is he of great ascetic power.

Īśvara said: Day and night he was intent on his eyes; the Vedāṅgas were his ear-ornaments; the clarified butter was his nose; the sacrificial ladle was his tongue; and the great sound of the Sāmaveda chanting was his voice. (21)
The Prāgvamśa was his body, radiant and surrounded by the initiations (dīkṣās) of Mātrā and the others; the Yogin had Dakṣiṇā as his heart, and he was the great Mahāsatra festival.

His lips are radiant with the Upākarma rite, his ornaments are the Avarta marks of the Pravargya ceremony; his paths of movement follow the various Vedic meters, and his strides are the sequential steps prescribed by the Brahmanas.
Having become the sacrificial boar, he then lifted up the earth; as he was lifting the earth, the tip of his tusk emerged outward.
In that Prābhāsika field, it was smeared with mud; because its tip of the fang was thus [smeared], O Goddess, it is therefore remembered as Karddamāla.
At Daṇḍodbheda Mahākuṇḍa, where the fang is well-situated, the water drawn up by that fang is equal to the merit of bathing in ten million Gaṅgās.
Therein lies the eternal Viṣṇu-field, measuring only one gavyūti. Those who have gone to another land and die at Daṇḍodbheda indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu for as many thousands of kalpas.
But he who, O Great Goddess, should behold the Boar at Kardamāla—even if he is burdened by ten million acts of violence—shall attain the supreme goal. (28)
O beloved, by the sight of him, the sin committed during ten lifetimes is destroyed; likewise, the accumulation of sins committed throughout thousands of other births [is destroyed]. (29)
But Kardamāla, having seen the Boar, shall meet his destruction; [he shall give] thousands of crores of gold and hundreds of crores of cows.

The merit that one obtains by making a gift from a single sight of Vārāha in this most terrible Kali age, which brings fear to all living beings—that liberation does not arise elsewhere except at the Saukara-kṣetra.
O Goddess, this most essential majesty of Karddamāla, which destroys all sins, has been declared to you in brief.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, O beloved, one should go to Devagupteśvara, located to the northwest of that place, where Soma performed penance.
Having become hidden from leprosy, he stood with his face cast down in shame for a thousand divine years in the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then Śiva, the lord of all the gods, became manifest before his eyes; being pleased with Candra, he likewise brought about the destruction of his waning.
Then the Moon, having installed a great liṅga worshipped by gods and demons, became completely freed from the disease of consumption.
Because he performed penance in secret, he is remembered as Gupteśvara; the Lord removes all skin diseases even by sight or by touch.
O Goddess of the gods, whoever especially worships that Liṅga on Mondays, not even a single person with leprosy shall be born in his lineage.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gupteśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the deity Bahusuvarṇaka, located in the place called Bahusuvarṇaka to the east of the Hiraṇyā river.
Where the son of Dharma performed an exceedingly difficult sacrifice, he installed a linga of great luster, which was named Bahusuvarṇa.
They know the one named Sarveśvara as the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices; there itself is situated the Liṅga, filled with the waters of the Sarasvatī.
O lady of excellent hips, he who bathes there and offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) uplifts ten million members of his lineage and is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whoever worships him with devotion using perfumes and flowers according to the prescribed rite, for him there is the fruit of ten million-fold worship; thus said Sadāśiva. || 5 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Bahusuvarṇeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Śṛṅgeśvara, located in the vicinity of Śukasthāna, which destroys all sins. || 1 ||
Having bathed right there according to the prescribed rites, a person should worship Śṛṅgeśa; he shall be liberated from all sins, just as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was in ancient times.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śṛṅgeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Īśvara said: Therefore, in the north-eastern direction from that place is remembered Koṭinagara. Situated one yojana to its south is the great Liṅga Koṭīśvara, which bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices. || 1 ||
Whoever bathes there according to the prescribed rite and worships that Liṅga shall be liberated from all sins and obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Koṭīśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 357 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the holy ford named Nārāyaṇa; in the northeastern direction of that very place is the step-well celebrated as Śāṇḍilya.

Having bathed right there according to the prescribed rite, whoever worships Śāṇḍilya on the day of Ṛṣipañcamī with due ceremony—even a devoted wife—shall certainly be liberated from the fear of the impurity of menstrual flow, whether she has touched it or not.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Nārāyaṇatīrtha," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Shringasaras. (1)
And there the deity named Śṛṅgāreśvara is established, where Hari, accompanied by the Gopīs, performed amorous dalliance according to the prescribed rites.

And he is named Śṛṅgāreśvara, the destroyer of floods of sin; whoever worships Bhava stationed in that place according to the prescribed rite shall never again be joined with poverty or suffering in this world. || 3 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śṛṅgāreśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to Ghatika-sthana, situated on the bank of the Hiranya, where in ancient times a perfected sage attained realization.

O fair-faced one, by means of a single channel through the power of meditative yoga, Mṛkaṇḍu established a Liṅga right there, known by the name Mārkaṇḍeśvara; it pacifies all sins merely by being seen or even worshipped.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mārkaṇḍeśvara," in the first section, the *Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ishvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place known as Mandukesvara; indeed, a Linga established there bears the name Mandukyayana.
There, O Goddess, is Koṭihrada, as well as Śiva Koṭīśvara; and there also resides the host of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇa), who bestows the fruits of one's desires.
Whoever bathes in the Koṭihrada tīrtha and worships that Liṅga, and likewise worships the Mothers right there, is liberated from suffering and grief.

Therefore, O Goddess of gods, one yojana to the east lies the stainless place renowned as Tritakūpa, which destroys all sins; for it is there, O Goddess, that the abode of all sacred fords (tīrthas) is established.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭihrada and Maṇḍūkeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 361 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place situated two gavyūtis to the north of Goṣpada, which is renowned as Valāya. || 1 ||

There, O beloved, one should also worship the *sthāna-liṅgas* of the eleven Rudras according to the prescribed rites—namely those known by names such as Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and others—and thereby one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Eleven Rudra-Liṅgas," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place named Tuṇḍapura, situated on the bank of the Hiraṇyā, where that Gharghara pool is located.
There is the deity Kandeśvara, where my matted locks were bound; having bathed there, the man who properly worships that deity shall be liberated from terrible sins and attain auspicious sovereignty.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Hiraṇyātuṇḍapura, Ghargharahrada, and Kandeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 363 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the excellent Saṃvarteśvara, located to the west of Indreśvara and to the east of Arkabhāskara.
Having seen that Mahādeva and bathed in the waters of the Puṣkariṇī, a human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Saṃvarteśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 364 ||
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the north of the Hiraṇyā river, where there are divine places of perfection (siddhisthāna) where the great ṛṣis have attained perfection.
Indeed, it is not possible to recount all the many lingas there; however, among them, one hundred and more lingas are remembered as preeminent.
O Goddess, on the bank of the Vajriṇī there are nineteen liṅgas; O Goddess, on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī there are one thousand two hundred more.
O Varārohā, O Goddess, during the previous Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, there were preeminently sixty excellent Liṅgas on the banks of the Kapilā.
Furthermore, O Goddess, there is no count of liṅgas on the Sarasvatī; thus, the five-faced one is adorned with a garland of liṅgas.
O Goddess, it was told at Prabhāsa that the Sarasvatī has five streams, by whose flows the sacred field is divided over an extent of twelve yojanas.
In that regard, water originating from ponds, wells, or wherever else may be found—know that it is indeed Sārasvata; blessed are those who drink it.
Wherever a man bathes, being fully endowed with faith, he obtains the fruit of bathing in the Sarasvatī; there is no doubt about this.
That which was declared as the Sparśaliṅga, renowned as Śrīsomeśa, is indeed a portion of that very Śaṅkara among the liṅgas of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra.
Having worshipped any linga whatsoever situated in the center of the sacred field, and recognizing it as Śrī Someśa, Someśa himself becomes worshipped. || 10 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Miscellaneous Local Liṅgas," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now I shall fully describe to you the most exalted Kṣetragarbha, the majesty of that Vastrapatha where the Raivataka mountain stands.
Dāmodara is at Raivataka, and likewise Bhava is at Vastrāpatha; this is known as the Raivataka-kṣetra and the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra. || 2 ||
There stands the Suvarṇarevā river, which destroys all sins; there Kṛṣṇa himself resides, known as Dāmodara.
There stands the Mṛgīkuṇḍa, which destroys great sins; where, by performing a śrāddha even once, the ancestors attain satisfaction for a thousand crores of kalpas, desiring no further rebirth.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, tell me in detail of the great glory of Dāmodara, the majesty of the interior of the sacred field (kṣetra) which is situated in the form of a pericarp.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate concerning Dāmodara Hari an ancient history (itihāsa) formerly narrated by the sages who dwell in the Kalpa.
On the auspicious, delightful, and holy bank of the Gaṅgā, crowded with inhabited regions, constantly frequented by sages, and certainly bestowing the path to heaven.
There, the Brahmins who possess knowledge worship with various sacrifices; the seers do so through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, while other people worship through charity alone.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who desire heaven resort to that divine water, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
There, a powerful king named Gaja, the lord of all people, abandoned his kingdom and went forth for the purpose of consecration by the waters of the Gaṅgā. || 10 ||
His wife was virtuous, faithful, possessed of a son, and endowed with beauty; devoted to her husband, she too went along with that very husband.
