She was named Saṃgatā, and she was as skillful as Dakṣāyaṇī; while they lived there in this manner, ten thousand years passed away.
Then the highly illustrious sage named Bhadra arrived there, accompanied by many Brahmins devoted to the practice of recitation and fire-offerings.
Having abandoned the path of worldly existence and desiring to conquer the path to heaven, they resorted to the Gaṅgā and, having cleansed the impurity of their own souls, burst it asunder.

Having offered water to the spirits and having worshipped Janārdana, while the sages headed by Bhadra were going to the riverbank, they saw the king and his elephant, which resembled a noble elephant. || 15 ||
By that very king, the sages whose impurities had been destroyed were beheld, just as the Seven Sages are seen in heaven by the wise King of the Gods.
And having observed that sage, he said: "Fifteen steps have been taken; please come here to my palace, for you are worthy of honor. (17)
"Let everyone together behold my illustrious wife; having performed her worship, let them follow whatever path resides in their minds. (18)

"Go there, O highly fortunate ones, you who are meritorious and desirous of merit. Thus addressed by the king, those sages, filled with curiosity, went to that bright palace which resembled the city of Purandara. 19.
Having offered them various seats, that wise woman sat down together with the king of kings, positioned before him.
Having joined his palms in reverence toward the sages of meritorious deeds, the auspicious king spoke these words, which were auspicious and well-composed.
The earth was filled with wealth, adorned with cities and towns, as well as mountains, oceans, rivers, and lakes. || 22 ||
It was crowded with villages, formidable crossroads, and herds of cattle; it was teeming with jewels among men, jewels among horses, and jewels among elephants.

This [state] belongs to those who have not renounced worldly objects, who enjoy sense-pleasures, and who do not know the supreme knowledge, within this most terrible cycle of existence that causes repeated rebirth. (24)

O auspicious one, O lord of brahmins, men fall again and again like leaves; tell me the truth, O observer of noble vows, regarding that deed by which one attains the stainless heaven through either charity or austerity.
Bhadra said: "Sacred fords are full of water, and the gods are made of stone and clay; those who do not perceive that which resides within themselves do not perceive the Supreme. (26)

There are many sacred fords (tīrthas) and holy shrines; there are rivers with meritorious waters and likewise oceans that are pure. The earth bestows great merit at every place and at every step. (27)
O Indra among kings, O best among the wise, if you possess knowledge [of him who is] Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, as well as the bearer of the conch and the mace; || 28 ||
The four-armed, mighty-armed slayer of the Daityas at Prabhāsa; Vārāha, Vāmana, Nārasiṃha, and Balārjuna.
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, and indeed Puruṣottama; likewise Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Gadāpāṇi. || 30 ||
Rāghava, the subduer of Śakra, Govinda, the bestower of great merit, Jaya, Bhūdhara, and Janārdana, the God of gods; || 31 ||
To the supreme god Śrīdhara, Hari, as well as Yogīśvara, Kapileśa, Bhūtanātha, and Hari, the Lord of Śvetadvīpa; 32.
And likewise, O lord of the people, Nara and Nārāyaṇa dwelling at Badarī-āśrama, as well as Padmanābha, Sunābha, and Hayagrīva.
To Dvijanātha, Dharānātha, and likewise Khaḍgapāṇi; to Dāmodara, who dwells in the waters, the Lord Hari who removes all sins.
For these very places belong to the God of gods, the wielder of the discus; wherever one goes to them, there one is liberated from all sins.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, as well as the goddess Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī and the Gomatī, the Tāpī and likewise the Kāverī; || 36 ||
The Narmadā, the Śarmadā, and likewise the river Godāvarī; the Śatadrū as well as the Vindhyā, the Payoṣṇī, and the Varadā. || 37 ||
The Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, and the Gaṇḍakī which destroys fierce sins; the Candrabhāgā, the Vipāśā, and the Śoṇa—each mentioned again and again.
These and many other auspicious rivers originate from the Himavat; having bathed in them, a man goes to heaven, freed from sin. (39)
Forests such as Nandana and mountains such as Mandara—by the mere utterance of their names, indeed, sin goes down to the netherworld.
The elephant said: "O auspicious one, you have spoken well; this narrative is like nectar. O knower of all dharma, I ask you something indeed. (41)
O observer of noble vows, tell me in which month, on which day, and at which sacred ford (tīrtha) heaven is enjoyed by men in succession, and how it becomes imperishable.
"Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, study of the scriptures, and worship of the deities—by what means indeed does one attain imperishable heaven? You should tell me that. (43)
Bhadra said: "Listen, O tiger among kings, as I relate this story; having heard it, O best of men, a person is liberated from sin. (44)
This was previously told to the sages by the high-souled Nārada.
Thus questioned by all of them, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke with great joy in a voice resonant like the sound of clouds and kettledrums.
O bull among men, I heard this during an assembly on the beautiful slopes of the Himalayas; I shall relate it to you, as you desire to hear it.
For indeed, all other sacred fords lead only to rebirth; however, there is that one ford which grants imperishable worlds—of that I shall tell you.
O best of kings, having stayed in Kānyakubja during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, neither man nor woman grieves; they go to the highest heaven. 49.
If that full moon day of Pauṣa is observed at Arbuda, one rejoices in heaven with one's ancestors for a hundred million years.
If a man performs the Śrāddha for his ancestors at Gayā on the full moon day of Māgha, he becomes the fourth [companion] even to the three gods.
A man who dwells for one night on the slopes of the Himalayas during the month of Phālguna goes to the supreme abode where the Lord Janārdana resides.
Those wise and most excellent men who perform the Śrāddha at Prabhāsa on the full moon day of Caitra do not become mere mortals here, but are joined by those born of noble lineage.
O beloved of the waters, whatever man performs [this rite] at Caturbhuja on the full moon of Vaiśākha, as well as at Avantī, he attains the supreme goal.
Those who perform a Śrāddha at Tritakūpaka on the full moon day of Jyaiṣṭha when it is joined with the Jyeṣṭhā constellation shall dwell in the abode of the gods for three Yugas.
The man who stays for fourteen days by the river in the forest of Vrajeśa goes to Vaikuṇṭha in heaven.
On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, by performing ritual bathing, giving gifts, reciting prayers, and offering ancestral rites at the eastern ocean, a man does not grieve.
Likewise, by worshipping the moon-crested Liṅga at the sacred site of Prabhāsa in the month of Bhādrapada, a man thereafter becomes a possessor of a divine Liṅga.
Whoever performs a ritual bath and offers a Śrāddha at the Candrabhāgā river during the month of Āśvina has secured for himself a place in heaven for thousands of Yugas.
The best of sages meditate upon him who has four arms and eight syllables; what is the use of saying more here? O Gaja, I shall explain it to you.
A holy place equal to Dāmodara has never existed, nor will it ever exist; among months, Kārttika is the best, and within Kārttika, the Bhīṣmapañcaka.

Even there, O King, the twelfth day is supreme at Dāmodara’s waters. What is the use of many other holy places, sacred fields, or great forests? Having bathed at Dāmodara, a man is liberated from all sins.
The elephant said: "O auspicious one, you have spoken what is most auspicious, like another elixir of life. I desire to hear further of the great fruit of this sacred ford."
What are the countries, what is their extent, which rivers and which mountains are there? What people dwell there, and who are the ascetic sages? (64)
Bhadra said: "O conqueror of enemy cities, the earth is filled with wealth, surrounded by the ocean, and adorned with cities, villages, and gods."
Vārāṇasī and Prabhāsa are the confluence of the white and the black; thus are these essential holy places (tīrthas), for they remove death.
Those who indeed remember "Dāmodara" wherever they may be, they dwell in the abode of Hari and never depart from there.
In the vicinity of Somanātha, there is the great mountain Udayanta; on its western side, however, is that which is known as Raivataka.
A river flows there from Kāñcanaśekhara; its minerals are red, white, blue, and likewise black. (69)
Some stones have the form of elephants, others resemble buffaloes; some have the shape of chickpeas, and others have the appearance of *gokṣura* plants.
There are trees, creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants in great numbers; all of them consist of gold—their roots, flowers, fruits, and leaves.
Indeed, the evil-minded man does not see; he sees only through his own sin. That mountain is constantly frequented by men devoted to the practice of alchemy.
Then, by Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and those outside following the Shudras, many birds there uttered both auspicious and inauspicious cries.
Swans, cranes, ruddy geese, parrots, cuckoos, and peacocks; deer and lords of monkeys, as well as swans and tigers. (74)
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), those beasts, birds, and reptiles do not act wickedly; they meet their death in due course of time.
All, having ascended celestial chariots, go to the abode of Hari; there, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth are brought down by the wind.
By touching the water of that river, everyone indeed attains liberation; O King, that river emerged from Pātāla after piercing through the earth.
Previously, a king of serpents had come by that path to bathe at the Dāmodara-tīrtha, which destroys both Yama and death.
Having returned from heaven, Candra also performed a most excellent sacrifice; freed from the disease of consumption, he went back to heaven free from ailment.
And Bali, having arrived during the month of Kārtika, gave gifts according to the prescribed rite, as did Hariścandra, Nala, and Nahuṣa.
Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa, and others performed deeds most difficult to accomplish, having bestowed many gifts: elephants, cows, horses, and chariots.
He gave oxen, gold, land, various kinds of jewels, parasols, vehicles, and garments to the foremost of the Brahmins.
Having offered foods mixed with flavorful juices before Dāmodara, they went to the world of Viṣṇu and do not return to the surface of the earth.
He who, endowed with devotion, offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water to the twice-born at that sacred ford, goes to the one who reclines upon the waters.
And he who gives even a handful of raw grain to one distressed by hunger, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, goes toward Soma.
Having placed before Dāmodara mountains made of food, which have been honored with fruits and flowers, one should offer a lamp together with its wick.
Having attained this difficult-to-reach state, one shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage; even by giving [an offering] merely four finger-breadths wide before Dāmodara.
Through such giving, one is honored in the heavenly world for thousands of yugas. Do not go to the back of the Himalayas, nor to Malaya, nor to Mandara.
Go to Mount Raivataka where Dāmodara resides; having performed a month-long fast before Dāmodara, the twice-born man [shall attain his goal]. (89)
He does not return at the end of time but goes to the city of Dāmodara. Furthermore, whether it be a man or a woman who practices fasting, he shall transcend all worlds and attain the abode of Hari.
Five hundred obstacles always reside there, acting to destroy the Dharma; a man should not go there.
That great mountain is always served by Pradyumna, Balarāma, and Śaineya (Sātyaki), with maces, discs, and other weapons, numbering in the hundreds of lakhs.
Indeed, women with faces like the beautiful moon—fair, dark, and slender-waisted—constantly sport before Dāmodara.
They possessed shapely hips, beautiful hair, and were radiant with large, elongated eyes; they had lovely cheeks, graceful forms, fine armpits, and beautiful breasts.
Radiant, with beautiful calves, lovely feet, and handsome toes, the princesses laugh and take their pleasure upon that mountain. (95)
Competing with one another, they each separately give safflower for their pair of feet, saffron, and yellow bodices to the Brāhmaṇa women here. (96)

In the month of Kārtika, on the day of Hari, one should offer food to be chewed, food to be eaten, drinks, foods to be licked, foods to be sucked, and slimy substances, as well as betel-leaf combined with flowers.
Having beheld the Revatī-kuṇḍa, one should bestow the highest fruit; that virtuous woman becomes possessed of sons, endowed with prosperity, and fortunate.
Having done this, that night passes without sleep, accompanied by the most meritorious sounds of Vedic chanting and the recitations of the Bhārata narrative.

With sounds of "huṃ," clapping of hands, and rhythmic beats repeated again and again, O King, women speaking the various dialects of the land stood in the midst of the circle of beauties before Dāmodara, engaged in laughter and dance.
He who constructs a temple of Śiva as a palace made of five stones is honored in the heavenly world for five thousand years.
Having fashioned [an image] joined with ten stones and placed it before Dāmodara, one sports and frolics in heaven for ten thousand years.
O great king, he who constructs a mansion with a hundred stones—a beautiful and bright temple—goes to the abode of Hari. (103)
Having constructed a thousandfold caitya endowed with many forms, one transcends all worlds and attains the supreme Brahman.
One should place a five-colored banner atop the house of Dāmodara; for as many divine years as there are spans of that banner, he shall go to heaven.
Within a distance of two gavyūtis from that place is the auspicious field of Vastrāpatha, seeing which many great sins are dissolved. || 106 ||
O King, having worshipped the god Bhava, who brings about the destruction of the cycle of existence, one attains that state from which there is no return. (107)
O best of kings, both man and woman are glorified in the world of Śiva. Having heard those well-spoken words of Bhadra, [he was filled with joy]. (108)
Then, when Lord Dāmodara had arrived to perform the Kārttikī festival, [he was accompanied] by Brāhmaṇas, the most eminent knowers of Brahman, who were well-versed in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Accompanied by Kṣatriyas who knew the duties of the warrior class, by Vaiśyas devoted to charity, and by Śūdras, King Gaja arrived at that sacred ford.
Having bestowed many gifts and offered oblations into the sacrificial fire, the king, being fully composed, duly performed there numerous sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and the Aśvamedha.

Thereupon, he dwelt there with the sages to perform austerities. Some brahmins remained standing on their heads, inhaling smoke while facing downwards; others subsisted on dry leaves, and others indeed lived on fruit alone.
Some other twice-born ones eat roots, while others subsist on water; some gaze at their own [limbs], and likewise others lie in water.

Others are practitioners of the five fires, and others are consumers of powdered stone; some, being purified, mutter the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; others [mutter] Sāvitrī in their minds, and others the goddess Sarasvatī.
For the hymns are indeed purifying and were created by Brahmā; others then resided there, contemplating the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this alone is firmly established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times. (116)
In this existence so difficult to cross, no one other than the Blessed One has been propitiated; indeed, there is none greater than Mahādeva who protects one from falling.
The planets, beginning with the moon and the sun, undergo coming and going; yet even today, those who meditate upon the twelve-syllable mantra do not return.
Those sages who are unchanging, as well as others who desire to conquer the world of the gods, attain that station from there, and likewise their seed becomes burnt away.
By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" are uttered even once, the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation.

Having performed eating once a day, as well as eating at night, not begging for food, fasting, and other such practices before Dāmodara, they become fulfilled in this world until the dissolution of all beings.
While that king remained there together with the sages, thousands of celestial chariots arrived at that very spot.
There, Gandharvas, Apsaras, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras—all mounted upon celestial chariots by the hundreds and thousands—were present. || 123 ||
Together with all his subjects and accompanied by his wife, that king ascended the celestial chariot and went to that state which is free from all suffering.
The person who constantly recites this, or even listens to it, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme Brahman. || 125 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Dāmodara," in the second section, the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go again to the sacred field of Vastrāpatha, which is the entire essence of Prabhāsa, the navel of the field, and dear to me. || 1 ||
Where the Lord Bhava himself, the cause of creation and destruction, resides—he who is the presiding authority over the earth and the primordial Master of all principles.
That self-existent Bhava, the bestower of prosperity, resides there at Prabhāsa; because this world comes into being from him, he is remembered as "Bhava."
Whoever performs a pilgrimage even once more to the field of Vastrāpatha, having immersed himself there in its sacred fords (tīrthas), becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Then, having beheld Lord Bhava and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, that best of men shall partake in the fruit of a pilgrimage to Kedāra.
Having seen Bhava in the month of Caitra, one is not born again on earth; or else, having properly seen Bhava in the month of Vaiśākha, one is liberated.
Whatever fruit is obtained at Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, or on the Narmadā, that same fruit is attained by beholding Bhava day after day for even half a moment.
Dwelling there is difficult to attain, and the sight of you is difficult to obtain; for such a person, there is no state of being a ghost, nor the agony of Yama or of hell.
O lady of excellent complexion, those whose lives have departed while dwelling in Bhava’s abode are the most blessed even among the blessed, and the deities even among the gods.

For those whose minds are set on Vastrāpatha and whose resolve is firm in existence, they praise the gift of cows there, as well as the feeding of Brahmins; and by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) right there, one shall bring about satisfaction until the end of the kalpa.
Thus has the majesty arising from Bhava been briefly told to you; when heard, it pacifies sins and bestows the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Origin of the Vastrāpatha Field," in the second section on the Majesty of the Vastrāpatha Field, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 2 ||

Īśvara said: Now, although there are tens of millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) in the field of Vastrāpatha, nevertheless, I shall tell you the essence, which brings about the great prosperity of all sacred fords.
In Dāmodara, the river known as Svarṇareṣā is proclaimed; likewise, Brahmakuṇḍa and Brahmeśvara are recorded to be in that very place. || 2 ||
Kālamegha is fully proclaimed [there], and Bhava is remembered as Dāmodara; Kālikā is celebrated there at a distance of exactly two gavyūtis.
Indreśvara is located in that very place, as is Mount Raivata; and Ujjayanta is also there, where the deity Kumbhīśvara is remembered to reside.
And Bhīmeśvara is right there; from that point, the field is of great splendor, known by the name Tailasāraṇika, which in the Tretā age was called Haimamāraka.
That sacred field is proclaimed to be five *gavyūtis* in extent; and right there is Mṛgīkuṇḍa, which destroys all sins.
O Goddess of gods, this field of Vastrāpatha has been described by me to you once more in brief as a mine of jewels and a treasury of gems. (7)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Pravaratīrtha," in the second section, the Vastrāpathakṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the place renowned as Dunnāvila, located a yojana to the west of Maṅgalasthiti, O Goddess. || 1 ||
O beloved, in that very place where the demon Dunnaka was formerly devoured and cast off by Bhīma, there is a divine cavern leading to the path of the great Pātāla.
The ritual procedure for that was previously declared in the *Pātālottarasaṃgraha*; therein are many liṅgas and sixteen sites of the Siddhas.
O beloved goddess, that place was formerly a mine of gold; O goddess, men desiring prosperity should go to that place.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Site of Dunnāvillahṛdgiri," in the second section, the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should go to the Liṅga situated to the west of Maṅgala, namely Gaṅgāsrota, as well as Surārka in particular. || 1 ||

O Goddess, if there is a desire for the fruit of the pilgrimage, one should go to them according to the prescribed rite; having bathed, one should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there in accordance with the truth, and likewise, abundant food along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.

Thus, O beloved, I have narrated to you this auspicious account which destroys the flood of sins of the Kali age; when read in its entirety, it brings about the great rise of all holy places and utterly destroys the accumulation of evil.
This destroyer of sins must not be given to one of evil intellect; rather, it should be heard according to the prescribed rule, as set forth in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Gaṅgeśvara," in the first section, the Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Now I shall fully describe [the rite] one should perform to the west of Maṅgala; there one should behold Siddheśvara, the bestower of all accomplishments.
In that very place is Cakratīrtha, which bestows the fruit of ten million holy sites; there is also the self-manifested Lokeśvara, formerly known as Indreśvara.
Having seen that according to the prescribed rite, O Goddess, one should then proceed to the Yakṣa Forest, located to the west of Maṅgala, where the Goddess herself resides.
The highly fortunate Yakṣeśvarī, who bestows desired objects, should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite; thereafter, one should proceed again to Vastrāpatha.
Having gone to Mount Raivataka, one should perform the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites; for there alone exist crores of sacred bathing places (tīrthas), such as Mṛgīkuṇḍa and others.
O Goddess, that which is at the peak of Yadbhukti is indeed remembered as Sīmāliṅga; O bestower of boons, ten crores of holy places (tīrthas) are situated there.

Where indeed the Yādavas, who are perfected beings (siddhas) in the Kali age and whose forms are wisdom, reside, there alone stands a liṅga measuring a hundred thousand times ten million (śatasahasrārbuda).
There, at the very spot where the lordly elephant stood, are the wells of nectar; likewise, there on that most excellent mountain Raivata, are seven sacred pools.
The goddess Ambikā is stationed there, as are Pradyumna and Sāmba; on that mountain in the form of a linga, there are tens of millions of sacred fords (tīrthas).

Mṛgīkuṇḍa is also right there, as is Kālamegha; Mahodadhi himself stands there in the form of the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), and Dāmodara is also there, as is Bhava, the leader of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 10 ||
Pārvatī said: O Lord of Gods, as you speak, I have heard of your sacred fords—the Gaṅgā, the meritorious Sarasvatī, and the great river Yamunā. (11)
The Godāvarī, the Gomatī, the river Tāpī, and the Narmadā; the Sarayū, the Svarṇarekhā, and the sin-destroying Tamasā. || 12 ||
I have heard of all the rivers that flow into the ocean, which are all meritorious, as well as the divine forests of liberation and those sacred fields.
By your grace, I have heard of those cities that bestow liberation, belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as to the Sun, the Moon, and Varuṇa.
There are many abodes belonging to the deities and the sages; yet, O Lord, Prabhāsa has been described by you to me as the most meritorious. (15)
Therefore, regarding that field Vastrāpatha which was described by you as superior, I did not at that time ask the reason for it while listening to you previously.
Now that I have heard everything, I am at ease; tell me the cause. First, speak of the power of the sacred field and of Bhava.

In what region is that sacred ford (tīrtha), and by whom was Śiva established there? How did the Lord Rudra, being self-manifested (svayaṃbhū), himself remain stationed there? O Lord, a great wonder dwells within me; tell me that now.
Īśvara said: First hear the power of the sacred field of Vastrāpatha; afterwards, O fair-faced one, hear the majesty of Bhava. 19.
In the great field of Kānyakubja, there was formerly in the age of merit a renowned king named Bhoja, who was righteous and governed his subjects according to dharma.
Large-eyed, long-armed, wise, eloquent, and sweet-spoken, he was endowed with all auspicious marks and beheld many wonders. || 21 ||
Once, having returned from the forest, the forest-guardian said this: "O Lord, while wandering in the forest, a marvel was seen by me just now."
On a mountain, in a rugged region thick with many trees, I saw a woman with the face of a deer who had joined a herd of wild animals.
"The fool leaps like a deer and is always seen in that very same place. Having heard these words, the king was pleased and gave him wealth.
"O commander of the army, I shall depart this very moment with you, taking my divine four-legged horse, two garments, and golden ornaments. (25)
"Let ten thousand horses and many kinds of snares set out; let the foot soldiers go everywhere and surround this best of mountains."
"No deer whatsoever must be killed, for that female deer is to be protected; on this earth, a woman wearing the guise of a female becomes a deer. (27)
Where will that wretched woman go, oppressed by my forces—an army devoid of weapons and missiles, consisting only of forest guards as its followers? (28)
Within a single day and night, the powerful Bhojarāja himself, mounted upon his horse, arrived at the front of the many afflicted people.
Moving silently on his feet and communicating through signs and gestures, the king himself surrounded the mountain with snares.

Accompanied by the forest guardian, he beheld a herd of deer. That female deer stood in the midst of the bucks; though her body was that of a woman, she had the face of a doe. The young woman moved like a deer and ran along with the other deer. (31)
Upon smelling the scent of aśvagandhā, the leaders of the deer herds became terrified; agitated and bewildered at that moment, they all fled in the ten directions.
But the woman with the face of a deer, who was leaping along with several other deer, fell into a snare unconscious.
Surrounded by his people, King Bhojarāja, accompanied by the superintendent of the forces, slowly beheld a great marvel with the deer.
Then a great clamor arose, accompanied by sounds of supreme joy; the king brought the doe back to Kānyakubja along with the deer.
Clad in divine garments and adorned with celestial ornaments, a woman seated in a human vehicle entered, surrounded by deer.
Accompanied by musical instruments and the chanting of Vedic hymns, he is led to the royal palace; he is beheld on the road by the people of the countryside at the king's residence. (37)
Being led by the citizens who spoke of this great wonder, that female deer reached the king's palace when an auspicious moment arrived.
O Indra among kings, the people were restrained by the words of the doorkeeper; the commander-in-chief departed for his own residence, taking the army with him. (39)
The king, too, having reached his own home, bathed and worshipped the deities; he then caused that doe to bathe and anointed her with divine perfumes.
Her limbs were smeared with saffron, she was draped in divine garments, and she was adorned with divine ornaments, each placed in its proper position as was fitting.
In a secluded and solitary place, the king spoke to the beautiful-eyed woman: "Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And for what reason are you here with these deer? (42)
"Why is your body that of a woman, yet your face that of a doe? Explain all of this to me, for my curiosity is great. (43)
Although addressed in this manner, Sulocanā did not speak at all; like one who is mute, she neither understood nor ate. || 44 ||
The protector of the earth does not eat; he does not hold his kingdom in high regard; he has no concern for his wives, nor for horses, elephants, or chariots. (45)
That very kingdom is yours, those wives are yours, those elephants and that great wealth are yours—wherein the mind sports, intoxicated by the passion for women. (46)
Deluded by her, the king summoned his doorkeeper and said, "Bring the family priest, the preceptor, the brahmins, and the teachers here quickly. (47)
Thus commanded by the king, the doorkeeper himself went forth to summon the astrologers, the masters of mantras, the physicians, and likewise the tantrikas.
Having summoned the best of the twice-born, he arrived with speed and informed the king: "O Lord, the brahmins have assembled. (49)
"Admit the wise gatekeeper who has arrived, for he is devoted to my welfare. Thus urged by the king, that intelligent man did accordingly.
Having first risen, paid his respects, and honored them, the king, intent on his purpose, spoke to those who were seated upon their thrones.
How can this single marvel even be described? For you all know it yourselves, whether from common experience or from the scriptures. (52)
How did she come into being, and of what karma is this the fruit? By what means could human speech arise within her? (53)
"How will she herself come to have a human face? Let all this be considered further by the attentive twice-born ones and then be explained. (54)

The brahmins said: "O Lord, there was a most excellent twice-born man named Sārasvata in Kurukṣetra; with his senses conquered and his vital energy drawn upward, he performed austerities on the banks of the Sarasvatī. (55)
"Commanded by him, the deer herself will tell you everything. Having heard these words, the king went to the brahmin Sārasvata.

Having seen him bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī at Prabhāsa and intent on meditation, the king circumambulated him, prostrated before him with his eight limbs touching the ground, and sat upon the earth with palms joined in reverence and his senses subdued. (57)
Having heard of the movement of human footsteps and having understood the cause, Sārasvata then spoke to that king who was intent on devotion.
Sārasvata said: O King Bhoja, may it be well with you; I have understood the reason for this: a woman with the face of a deer was indeed brought by you from the forest. (59)
"This is indeed a great marvel that dwells in your mind; however, once the young woman has been instructed by me, she will tell you everything. (60)
"O Great King, I know her conduct and the nature of her birth; it would be a marvel for the world to hear it related by her own lips. (61)
Having given these instructions, he departed swiftly by means of a chariot with the splendor of the sun; in just two days and nights, O King, he reached the palace.
Having entered and seen the doe where the fawn-eyed woman was staying, Sārasvata was recognized by her as a twice-born man who knew the Dharma and was all-knowing.
The female deer said: "He indeed knows everything—the cause and its nature, as well as that which is present, that which is yet to come, and that which has occurred within the three worlds. (64)
By this, my death in a previous birth was known: penance was performed by me at Vastrāpatha, the great field, in the abode of Bhava. || 65 ||
Having shaken off all impurity and having produced knowledge through diligent effort, he became liberated from old age and death and directly perceived existence.
Lord Bhava was pleased with him and learned the cause of the holy site; he declared that what had been commanded by me must be told regarding the cause of his birth.
While she was thus absorbed in thought, the Brahmin arrived; overcome with the desire to prostrate before him, she fell down in a swoon.
Then Sārasvata, through his knowledge, understood that cause; "Let the twice-born ones quickly bring a jar filled with water! (69)
All medicinal herbs, sprouts, dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), incense, sandalwood, cow dung, honey, and clarified butter. || 70 ||
Thus commanded by the twice-born, [the materials] were brought with haste at the king's order; then, having smeared a portion of the ground and having arranged a svastika there— || 71 ||

There, having performed the fire-rite and placed the Vedas into the pitcher, he installed Indra therein and the guardians of the quarters in their proper order; having offered oblations into the fire and prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), he performed the worship of the planets.
Then, having placed water in a golden vessel, the Guru himself performed the consecration upon the jars during an auspicious moment that fulfills all desires.
Once she had been sprinkled by him with the water intended for bathing, the girl became conscious and saw everything with her eyes.
He hears everything and knows the conduct of his previous birth; the Guru offered him a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) the size of a jujube fruit.
After she had enjoyed [the food] with effort, he then performed the cleansing; thereafter, the Guru imparted knowledge into his ear in human speech.
Having given the sacrificial fee to her guru, that deer-faced woman then related her entire life story from her previous birth to King Bhoja.
Having first paid homage to his guru, as well as to the Brāhmaṇas and the Kṣatriyas, he began to recount what had occurred in his previous birth during childhood.
The female deer said: "O King, you should not despair after hearing what I have spoken. You shall be born as the son of the Lord of Kaliṅga in the seventh place from here. (79)
"When your father died, you, being but a child, were consecrated by your own ministers; for I am indeed born as the daughter of the King of Vaṅga. (80)
"O King, O Lord, you married me when I was given by my father; since I am the best of women, you have made me your chief queen. (81)
Having been born as a youth, he gradually became violent and cruel; he was not skilled in the Vedas or the Shastras and was utterly devoid of compassion and righteousness.
Greedy, arrogant, and full of great wrath, he is excluded from truthful conduct; being evil-minded, he recognizes neither God, nor the Guru, nor the Brahmins. (83)

For his subjects were indeed disaffected because he was a destroyer of Brahmins; his entire country was plundered by neighboring kings, and taking his whole army with him, he marched forth for battle.
O Lord, I went along with him; a battle broke out with the kings, and his soldiers were defeated; they fled and disappeared in the ten directions. (85)
Abandoning his own duty, the king became intent on flight; as he was departing, the monarch was tormented by his enemies.
"O best of kings, that wicked-souled speaker of 'Thine' (tavāsmi), who was an opponent of the world, has been slain; having taken his body, I have entered the fire. (87)
For one who has died in this manner, there is no higher destination; he is tormented in hell. If a wife, taking hold of her deceased beloved, should enter the fire, [she likewise falls]. (88)
She delivers even the most sinful person until the dissolution of all beings; having brought about the destruction of sins in this world, she is thereafter glorified in heaven. || 89 ||
Therefore, O King, you were born as a Brāhmaṇa in the land of Mālava; and there, O King, I was born as his Brāhmaṇa wife. (90)
He became prosperous with wealth and grain, and likewise possessed of abundant living means; yet his father died, his mother died, and he was deprived of his brothers.
Though rich in wealth and grain, the greedy man wanders upon the earth; likewise, the Brahmin who is exceedingly wrathful and devoid of Vedic study [wanders]. || 92 ||
Neglecting his baths, twilight prayers, and other duties, this deceitful man begs for alms from people; yet though he says, "I offer supreme devotion," he becomes angry with me.
He has no continuity of lineage, for he is solely intent on guarding his wealth; he neither gives, nor eats, nor offers oblations—he merely guards it.
A Brahmin who is excessively greedy does not perform the libation with sesame seeds, nor does he offer worship to Viṣṇu even when the month of Kārttika has arrived. (95)
The Brahmin offers a lamp continuously for one month; he does not eat leafy vegetables and maintains a single meal a day without interruption. (96)

O best of kings, when the month of Nabhasya has arrived and its dark fortnight has begun, he who does not perform the Śrāddha at home, being devoid of ritual bathing and libations, [is a sinner]. (97)
That Brahmin does not know his father’s day, nor even a single continuous fortnight; he eats elsewhere even when the anniversary of the death has arrived. (98)
Even during the transit [of the sun] into Capricorn, he does not give kṛśara-rice; nor does he give sesame seeds, gold, silver, cloth, or fruit, nor vegetables, leaves, flowers, or likewise firewood.
The cows do not even receive their daily fodder; how then will liberation come to pass? When the sun has entered its southern course, they do not go for refuge to Viṣṇu.
The Brahmin gives a cow during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Even a single cow, well-milking, provided with cloth, bells, and ornaments, and accompanied by her calf, grants liberation to the donor and brings prosperity to his lineage. (102)
For as many years as there are hairs upon her body, he is glorified; surrounded by hosts of Siddhas in the abode of Brahmā, he dwells there with a splendor equal to the sun.

He does not build a temple for the gods, nor does he construct a step-well, a well, a pond, or a reservoir; he performs no meritorious marriage, renders no aid to the virtuous, nor does he build a dwelling for the righteous or for the twice-born. (104)
He always buries his wealth underground, and he knows nothing of the Dharma or his own lineage; for I am devoted to him—how indeed could I abandon my beloved? (105)
"O Lord, while living in this manner, he has met his end; yet out of greed for wealth, I have avoided death. (106)
O Lord, while watching as my entire store of wealth was seized by kinsmen, after a long time I died in the house of a brahmin.
O best of men, O king, a white serpent appeared in that region; and right there, I was born as the daughter of a Brahmin.
When her eighth year had arrived, she was married by a twice-born man; O King, in that very house there dwells a serpent belonging to me. (109)
Bitten at night by a great serpent with the thought, "She is my wife," the husband died; nevertheless, the serpent was struck down with clubs by the Brahmins.
Having bestowed widowhood upon me, both the Brahmin and the serpent have died; then, having been filled with great grief by my father and mother, my head was shaved. (111)
Wearing white garments and devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, she was intent on fasting for a month at various sacred pilgrimage sites.
The serpent was born as a crocodile in the Godāvarī at the abode of Śiva; meanwhile, I went with my kinsmen to see the deity Bhīmeśvara. || 113 ||

O King, while I had entered the water to bathe surrounded by all the people, I was then seen by a crocodile: "This is my wife, my beloved. O King, I was seized by the crocodile to be taken into the depths of the water.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose as the people became agitated on all sides: "By whom has this makara been struck down with a blow from a spear? (115)
With the face of a fish, I remained there; dead, I was dragged out by people. Having applied fire and cast me into the water, the people took the ashes and went home. (116)
Due to the killing of a woman, he was born as a hunter; then, by the power of a sacred ford, he attained a human birth in that very same great forest.
Those who meet death from fire, water, snakes, elephants, lions, bulls, fish, or even from boils, have gone to hell.
One who destroys oneself, a destroyer of an embryo, a killer of a woman, a slayer of a Brahmin, one who gives false testimony, a seller of a maiden, and he who observes a vow falsely; || 119 ||
He who sells a Vedic sacrifice, he who is a drinker of intoxicants, a twice-born man who betrays the king, a thief of gold, and one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa; || 120 ||
The killer of a cow, the embezzler of a deposit, he who seizes the boundary of a village, and the woman who deceives her husband—all these go to hell. (121)
O King, by the power of dying as a fish, she was born as a female curlew in the forest; meanwhile, a hunter wanders in the Godāvarī forest, tracking deer.
In the forest, a passionate curlew, eager to desire me with joy, saw me as he was wandering; then, having drawn his bow, he [struck me] with an arrow.
"O King, the curlew was killed and died; I have been lost from my place. Then, in that very forest of Godāvarī, she beheld him in such a form. (124)

Then the sage, seeing that contemptible deed—the killing of the krauñca while it was not engaged in sexual union but intent on conversing with its mate—cursed the hunter: "Since you have slain the krauñca, you shall therefore become a lion. (125)
The king was satisfied by that disciplined sage who stood before him; the sage spoke in his presence: "My word shall not prove false. (126)
I shall grant my grace to you while you are situated in the form of a lion, for the sake of your liberation; in the land of Surāṣṭra, on Mount Raivataka, you shall become a lion.

"O God, liberation is ordained for you as certain in the great field of Vastrāpatha. Having spoken thus, that sage departed toward Bhīmeśvara; meanwhile, due to hearing those harsh words, the hunter gradually met his death.
And that female curlew, having gone into the middle of the forest due to separation from her mate, died by the power of fate and was born as a doe on Mount Raivataka.
Constantly intoxicated with passion, she took delight in the company of a herd of deer; meanwhile, in the great forest of that mountain, there lived a lion who was a hunter. (130)
A lion, tormented by desire, once saw a doe wandering nearby; from that moment on, both the lion and the doe wandered constantly together in the forest. (131)
By the turn of fate, the lion also thought, "She is mine," yet, due to his predatory nature, he proceeded to seize her. (132)

Thus addressed by Gaṇeśa, those led by Prajāpati [spoke].
The gods said: "You must certainly recognize our authority; the mantras are indeed our share. (114)
The mantras said: "O gods, you have become shrouded in darkness, your minds struck down by darkness, since you do not worship Maheśvara, the king of the sacrifice. (115)
"Ishvara is the lord of all beings; Hara is the body of all the gods. The Gaṇa said: "Since he is worshipped in all sacrifices, why would Dakṣa not worship him? (116)
The mantras were not made authoritative by you who are arrogant in your strength; therefore, because they are unbearable, I shall today destroy your pride.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the bull among the Gaṇas, went to that sacrificial hall; and the furious lords of the Gaṇas uprooted the sacrificial posts and hurled them away.
The Lord of the Gaṇas seized the Prastotṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu, and all those terrifying beings threw them into the current of the Gaṅgā.
The resplendent Vīrabhadra, undaunted in spirit, paralyzed the hand of Hari that was armed with the thunderbolt, as well as those of the other inhabitants of heaven.
Likewise, having effortlessly plucked out Bhaga’s eyes with the very tips of his fingers, he struck down the seven-horsed Sun with blows from his fists and staffs. || 121 ||
And likewise, the powerful Lord of the Gaṇas, smiling, playfully overpowered the god Candra with his big toe.
Having effortlessly cut off both hands of Vahni and torn out his tongue, he struck even the sages and the lords of sages on the head with his foot.
Likewise, the one of great strength, having paralyzed the Sudarśana discus, pierced Viṣṇu—who had arrived together with Garuḍa—with sharpened arrows.
Then Bhadra created many thousands of numerous Garuḍas, even more powerful than Vainateya; they all rushed toward Garuḍa.
Seeing them, the wise Garuḍa became intent on flight; situated there, Mādhava moved with speed like a cow oppressed by a lion.
When Vainateya and Viṣṇu had vanished, the lotus-born Brahmā arrived and restrained Vīrabhadra, the beloved of Śiva.
Out of reverence for the Supreme Lord, he propitiated him; yet those gods did not perceive Rudra, who had arrived there, as being invisible.
That god was recognized by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Dadhīci; the blessed Brahmā, Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, and the dwellers of heaven offered him praise.
In particular, Dakṣa, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, praised the goddess Pārvatī, who shares half the body of the Lord, with various kinds of hymns.
Then the Blessed Lady, smiling, said to Maheśvara: "You alone are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector of the world. (131)
"The Lord should show favor to Dakṣa as well as the gods. Then the Lord Kāpardin, Nīlalohita, Hara, smiling, spoke to the prostrate gods and to Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas.
"Go, all you deities; I am pleased with you. You are to be worshipped first in all sacrifices and in all divine rites. (133)
And you too, O Dakṣa, listen to my words which provide protection from all [evils]: having abandoned this desire for worldly existence, become my devotee with diligence. (134)

"By my grace, you shall become the Lord of the Gaṇas at the end of the Kalpa; until then, remain at ease in your own offices by my command. Having spoken thus, he vanished from the sight of Dakṣa of immeasurable luster.
Dadhīci beheld Śiva and requested him regarding the release from the curse: "How shall they cross over the curse given by me at your command? (136)
Śiva said: When the Kali age has arrived, there will be those outside the three Vedas; yet those Brahmins who recite the Vedas shall go to heaven.
Those Āgamas composed by Viṣṇu which are recited by the twice-born shall also go to heaven through my grace; of this there is no doubt. (138)
Due to the influence of the Kali age, for those who do not possess [this] recitation, the practice of the duties of a householder and the worship of me must be performed. (139)
I must certainly effect their liberation from sin; covered in ashes, I wander for alms when midday has passed. (140)
Wearing a mass of matted hair, peaceful, with a mendicant’s bowl in his hand, that twice-born man who gives me alms goes to heaven. (141)

"Whether it be sandals, or an umbrella, or a loincloth, or a water-pot—whatever man gives these to ascetics is liberated from his sins. Having granted these boons to Dadhīci, he spoke together with Viṣṇu.
Rudra said: "He who is your friend is my friend; he who is your enemy is my enemy. O Viṣṇu, he who worships you certainly worships me. (143)
He who praises you praises me; he who is dear to you is dear to me. Wherever I am, there you are; there is no mutual difference between us.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O Supreme God, it is exactly as you have said; it must be told just so, for previously I beheld You with a body that was half-woman and half-man."
"This is not a woman that I have seen; rather, it was my own form that was seen—bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace in its hands, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers. (146)
I beheld the second half [of the Lord], marked with the Śrīvatsa, clad in yellow garments, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, holding a trident in his hand, and possessing three eyes.

Joined with the crescent moon, wearing matted locks and carrying a skull-cup, I have attained a state of oneness; as it was before, so it is now. Gaurī does not perceive me, and I likewise do not perceive her.
Īśvara said: There is no difference between us two; we are both of one and the same form. He who knows this knows [the truth], and he goes to Satyaloka. || 149 ||
Having spoken thus, he went there to Kailāsa, the best of mountains; Kṛṣṇa also reached Mandara for some purpose concerning the gods.
In the meantime, this king of the Daityas, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, by the grace of Mahādeva, was harassing the three worlds. (151)
Having obtained immortality from Hara, he, blinded by lust, did not see at all the goddess who bore a portion of Hara’s body—she of divine form and beautiful eyes. || 152 ||
He perceived it as "mine" and begged Hara for it; Hara, too, being preoccupied with his own task, abandoned Mount Kailāsa.
Having reached Mount Mandara to see the god Janārdana, he consulted with one another and left the goddess there on Mandara.
The Goddess remained in the abode of Nārāyaṇa, surrounded by hosts of goddesses; meanwhile, Gautama was defiled by the sin of killing a cow.
For the sake of purifying him, Hara, assuming the form of a mendicant, arrived at the house of Gautama, while Andhaka went to Mount Mandara.
The wicked one begged Pārvatī for battle and fought with Viṣṇu; though defeated by all the Gaṇas, the Daitya could not see the Goddess. || 157 ||
Assuming the form of a woman, that Kṛṣṇa protects Gaurī in the palace; there, Hari created a hundred Gaurīs by means of his illusory power.
These excellent women of divine form were born from the body of Viṣṇu; Andhaka did not recognize them at all, wondering, "Is this Gaurī or Pārvatī? (159)
A delay occurred there as he was deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu; meanwhile, Śiva arrived, having performed the purification of Gautama.
Gautama was purified by mere alms-food; then Rudra, becoming enraged, engaged in battle with Andhaka.
This immortal one was born from Hara; though impaled upon a most dreadful stake, while standing on that stake he offered praise, and Maheśvara was pleased with him.
He granted him the status of Gaṇeśa until the dissolution of all beings; Kṛṣṇa himself gave him Umādevī, who was identical in form to his own.
Other women in the form of Gaurīs have been dispatched to the earth; having assumed names for yourselves, you shall be worshipped in the world. (164)
Those who shall worship these [goddesses] will worship Śivā; those who shall worship Śivā are worshipping Hara and Hari.

Taking Umā with him, Hara, who is worshipped by gods and asuras, ascended his bull and departed for the mountain; meanwhile, after Andhaka was slain, Hari sported with Ramā, and the gods approached the king of the gods.

Those who hear the wonderful life-story of the high-souled ones—Brahmā, Īśa, and Nārāyaṇa, whose minds are meritorious—are liberated from the sins born of the Kali age and, honored by hosts of celestial attendants, shall go to heaven.
While time was passing in this manner, on Mount Kailāsa, Hara was being offered many boons by the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Daityas.
The great asura named Tāraka was fierce, having received a boon from Brahmā; by him the entire world was pervaded, and the gods were destroyed in battle.
He created that Kārttikeya, the son of Umā, born from the seed of Rudra, to be slain by the son of Mahādeva in battle.
He was consecrated as the commander-in-chief by all the gods, including Indra and the others; yet even he was struck down by that same turn of fate by the one named Tāraka.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, was delighted in the company of Umā and surrounded by Nandin, Bhadra, and others.
Accompanied by Skanda, who has the face of an elephant, and by the Lord of Wealth, Śivā then slowly spoke to the God who was intent on laughter.
O Śaṅkara, by what means will you be satisfied—by what gift, austerity, or observance of mortals? (174)
O Lord of Gods, by what action or again by what mantra, by what bath or by what incense are you pleased? (175)
"By what flower, O Lord, by what leaf, O Śaṅkara, by what hymn of praise, or indeed by what act of daring, are you satisfied? (176)
With what food offering and with what oblation are you pleased, O God? By what austerity or by what respectful offering (argha) are you satisfied, O Lord? (177)
"These sixteen questions have been asked by me; tell me their resolution."
Śaṅkara said: "Well asked by you, O Goddess; I shall speak that which is dear to me. This method of Śiva-worship is performed according to the word of the Guru. (179)
O Goddess, the gift of fearlessness to all living beings is dear to me; truth and austerity are likewise declared to be so, as is the avoidance of the wives of others. (180)
O Goddess, this self-restraint is dear to me; such action brings delight to the world. This mantra, "Mayaṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," has been accepted by me. (181)
O Goddess, completely liberated from all sins, he is dear to me; the abandonment of sin is my bath, and guggulu incense is dear to me. (182)
The flower of the thorn-apple is for me; the bilva leaf is dear to me. The praise "Śiva, Śiva" is mine, as is the act of daring in battle. (183)
I manifest myself before that man who does not fear; he who offers the "haṃtakāra" (the call of "haṃ") to cows, that is my favorite offering.
O beautiful one, supreme delight arises in me through the final oblation; for service to those who are beloved, even if it be difficult, is dear to ascetics and practitioners of austerity. (185)
O Great Goddess, O my beloved, that *argha* which is offered to the Sun at sunrise, at midday, and likewise at sunset, is dear to me.

Of what use are gifts, or what use are austerities, or what use are sacrifices devoid of true feeling? O Goddess, even a small amount that is given with devotion—characterized by compassion, truthfulness, mercy, and non-stealing, and free from hypocrisy and malice—is dear to me.
While he was thus speaking on subtle questions as they had been set forth, Viṣṇu himself arrived there accompanied by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said: "O Maheśvara, I am not able to protect you while you grant so many boons to the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas."

Afterwards, they undergo transformation and, alas, become fit to be slain by me. O God, since a man attains liberation through a mere leaf, a flower, the syllable *oṃ*, or even Śiva himself—who would not practice devotion to Bhava? (190)
Even those gods, Indra and the others, who nourish themselves with sacrifices—the twice-born do not sacrifice for them; you are satisfied by the gift of alms alone. (191)
Rudra said: "I have no business with Indra and the others; what will Brahmā do for me? By whatever means possible, you must now protect the subjects."
This is indeed my own nature; how could I venture to abandon it? I have been joined by you, O Brahmā, and by the gods, in this task of granting boons. (193)
What has been lost this very moment, apart from the Goddess who stood before you? Having abandoned my form, I wander alone. (194)
Having spoken thus, the god Śiva vanished right there. When that Śiva had departed, a very great agitation arose in that place.
Umā spoke to Indra and the others, as well as to the hosts of Brahmā and Viṣṇu: "What is there now for me to do with you who are devoid of Śiva? (196)
In the meantime, whatever other gods were assembled there, as well as the ṛṣis, the siddhas, and likewise Nārada and Parvata—197.
The Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and other rivers, as well as the Nāgas and Yakṣas, having assembled and deliberated with Brahmā and the others, [asked]: "How will this come to pass? (198)
Viṣṇu said: "Let them go together to that place where Lord Śiva has gone; by the command of Śiva, let those men go to heaven with little effort."
May men go to the world of truth (Satyaloka), may the gods go to the surface of the earth; and may Śaṅkara grant boons to the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Daityas.
I must inflict punishment upon those who cause harm and those who would destroy the Dharma; when Śiva is pleased, I shall establish the order for those destined for heaven.
Those men who, having abandoned the dharma of the three Vedas, worship another dharma, shall go to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
When Śiva had become invisible, he entered the forest of the mountain; having cast off his two divine garments, he took his stand amidst the peaks.
Having cast off his elephant hide and abandoned his form, the god Maheśvara, in the guise of Sthāṇu, pierced the surface of the earth and remained there.

Because he exists as self-born (Svayambhū), he is therefore Hara (the Withdrawer). In the meantime, all the gods did not perceive Maheśvara, who is beyond knowledge, beyond the creative powers (kalās), and situated outside of divine meditation.
When the gods were agitated and the sun, wind, sky, water, and earth were all disturbed, they remained in their respective places and praised Umā’s God of Gods, the Lord of the Suras.
Whether in heaven or on earth, in the nether regions, among gods or mortals, or among reptiles; whether in gross or subtle forms—just as it is, so must our word be spoken in truth. (207)
Then all the gods, including Nandin, Bhadra, and others, as well as Indra and the rest, set forth with Gaurī at their head.
Accompanied by Skanda, the Goddess herself went forth mounted upon a lion; and the eternal Viṣṇu went forth, having ascended Garuḍa.
The Lord Brahmā, mounted upon a swan, followed behind; the King of the Gods himself went forth, having mounted Airāvata.
The Gaṅgā, the goddess Sarasvatī, and the great river Yamunā have departed, as have all the deities, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, and the Kiṃnaras. || 211 ||
In brief, they all went to where the god Maheśvara was; having ascended the mountain peak, the goddess Ambā remained stationed there.
Having dismissed Garuḍa, Viṣṇu remained on Mount Raivataka; then the Goddess performed a hymn of praise, while the well-restrained [sages] sang songs.
Though trampled by Airāvata’s feet, that mountain did not waver; thereupon, the king of serpents emerged, having pierced through the surface of the earth.
Through that opening, all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā entered; then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods offered praise from every side.
Then the Blessed Lord Bhava, the god Hara, beheld that form.
Then all the gods were delighted, as were Ambā and those Gaṇas; [Śiva], being greatly rejoiced, said, "O Goddess, let us go to Kailāsa."
Īśvara said: "If all the gods and likewise the rivers beginning with Gaṅgā are pleased, let Viṣṇu and Ambā remain right here on Mount Raivataka."
The Sarasvatī, Yamunā, and Revā are all established within this [place]; because its water has the appearance of gold, that river is called Svarṇarekhā.

This field is Vastrāpatha; may Lord Bhava reside here. This sacred site (tīrtha) has been described by me as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. A man or a woman who bathes here is released from all sins.
Having spoken thus and having then deposited a portion (kalā) into Bhava, the god Śiva departed for Mount Kailāsa while all the gods were looking on.
Then, having placed the digit (kalā) called Ambā upon the mountain from the mouth of Skanda, the Goddess herself, mounted upon her bull, departed together with the God.
Nārāyaṇa himself resides on the delightful Raivataka mountain; Viṣṇu is always present on that mountain at the beginning of a kalpa and at the beginning of a yuga.
Having stayed for many nights and having accomplished the destruction of the Daityas, the Lord sported on Mount Raivataka until the dissolution of all beings.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by him in the form of Narasiṃha; having killed him, he then went there and released Narasiṃha.
In the form of the Great Boar, Hiraṇyākṣa was struck down; having abandoned that very form, the Lord of Gods remained on Mount Raivataka.
Having established Pṛthu as the ruler of the earth for the sake of the gods' purpose, O King, that deity, honored by the immortals, dwelt upon Mount Raivataka.

Having arrived here in former times, Pṛthu performed the worship of the God; then a rosary was placed around his neck by Pṛthu himself, and Pṛthu personally gave the name "Dāmodara" to the Lord of Gods.

The supreme deity Bhava is stationed at Vastrāpatha; Dāmodara is established on Raivataka; the goddess Ambikā resides upon the mountain peak; and all the gods are established all around them. || 229 ||

The lords of the field, the protectors of this most excellent sacred ford, have been released by the God from the proximity of worldly existence. Those men who behold the supreme deity named Bhava are liberated; they depart from the earth and go to heaven.
O King, I have related to you the origin of the field Vastrāpatha and of Bhava; what else do you wish to hear? || 231 ||
Whoever hears or recites this narrative in its entirety, being completely liberated from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world. || 232 ||
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of an embryo, and the violator of the guru’s bed—by bathing in the waters of Svarṇarekhā, one is liberated from all sins. (233)
And those insects, moths, and others, as well as golden lines (gold-dust) that die in the water, being liberated from all sins, go to the abode of the gods. || 134 ||

He who bathes in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, performs the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), and offers the ancestral oblation (śrāddha), and worships the Lord of Vastrāpatha, goes to the world of Brahmā. || 235 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Origin of Bhava," in the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya of the seventh section (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pārvatī said: Oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha), of Mount Raivataka, of Bhava, the God of gods, and likewise of Vastrāpatha!
The Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the Gomatī, and the river Narmadā—all these were present in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, as were Brahmā and Indra.
The residence of the gods, headed by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara, was established there for as long as the day of Brahmā lasts.
O Śaṅkara, through your grace, I have heard in full detail all this regarding the power of sacred fields and pilgrimage sites that you have spoken.
O Lord Maheśvara, tell me what the lord of men did after obtaining the doe—both Bhojarāja and that sage Sārasvata.
Īśvara said: Among all those women, she was preeminent in beauty, generosity, and virtue; she was eternally joyful, peaceful, and always a bringer of auspiciousness.
Among women, she is made a mother, a sister, a friend, a daughter, or one who increases social bonds; likewise, among men, she is made a father, a brother, a teacher, or a son. (7)
Having obtained such a virtuous wife, the lord of men was delighted; having praised the sage Sārasvata, the king spoke these words. (8)
The King said: "O Lord, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Sūrya, Indra, Agni, and the host of Maruts have been gratified by you through your celibacy and austerity."
"You are my supreme deity; you are my father, mother, teacher, and lord, for you have described to me my entire previous birth as if it were before my very eyes."
The land of Surāṣṭra is renowned, and there is the great mountain Raivataka; the self-existent Lord Bhava is heard of as being in the sacred field of Vastrāpatha.
On the summit of Mount Ujjayanta, Gaurī, Skanda, and Gaṇeśvara all remained for the duration of a day of Brahmā, meditating upon Bhava.
Having established Vāmana in the city near Śiva Siddheśvara, and having conquered and bound the demon Bali, he himself remained on Mount Raivataka.
All this is a marvel if it is seen by those who are still living; for through the performance of a pilgrimage, Lord Hari appears at Vastrāpatha.
Having renounced my kingdom, my beloved sons, and my infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants, and having established my son upon the throne, it is certain that I must depart. (15)
Through your grace, everything has been heard; if it is seen, then by following the procedure for the pilgrimage, Lord Hari is reached at Vastrāpatha. (16)
Having transcended the world of the Sun, the world of the Moon, the world of Indra, the city of Hari, and the world of Brahmā, I shall go to the abode of Śiva.
Having heard these various words from the lord of men, the sage’s hair stood on end with joy; desiring to know everything about the king, the sage restrained the monarch.

Sārasvata said: "O King, even at home, the gods headed by Hara and Viṣṇu reside in water, in *darbha* grass, and in sesame seeds; therefore, O King, you must restrain your mind from the desire to see many other lands. (19)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by the Sage Sārasvata to King Bhoja, Who Was Eager to Undertake a Pilgrimage to the Sacred Field of Vastrāpatha," in the second section, the *Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 10 ||
Īśvara said: Having heard the words of the Brahmin Sārasvata, King Bhoja, his face turning pale, took hold of his feet and spoke these words. (1)
"O Sage, you must not speak thus; my departure is certain. Tell me how this pilgrimage, which bestows merit upon men, may be performed. || 2 ||

What is to be grasped and what is to be abandoned? What is to be given and what is not to be given? Regarding the pilgrimage sites, fasting, bathing, and the sequence of rules for twilight ablutions; as well as worship, sleep, and recitation at night—tell me all this in brief. (3)
Sārasvata said: "O King, if you are to go to Mount Raivataka in the land of Surāṣṭra, I shall describe the procedure for the pilgrimage; listen with a one-pointed mind."
Having taken up the strength of Bṛhaspati and having fully gratified the Sun, he surrounded everything on his left and behind him, and purified the day.
O King, having ascertained the moon's ascendant from the strongest planet relative to the birth sign, and having obtained auspicious omens, kings should set forth.
One should always go to a sacred ford (tīrtha); indeed, all months are auspicious, and all lunar days (tithis) are excellent for bathing, giving gifts, worship, and other such rites.

On the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, at the end of the month on the full moon day, during the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), and during eclipses—these times are declared for the worship of Bhava.
Having left Mount Kailāsa along with the Goddess and the assembled gods, Bhava emerged from the earth on the fifteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
On that very day, the goddess Svarṇarekhā emerged from the bed of the river and reached the path of Vāsuki, destroying all sins.
The great mountain Ujjayanta, trodden upon by Airāvata’s feet, flowed forth pure water in many streams produced from the elephant's tread.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, gathered together at the great sacred field of Vastrāpatha with a spirit of devotion toward Śiva.
O King, hear the measurement of the field of Vastrāpatha: it is where the garments and ornaments fell to the ground as Hara was casting them down. (13)
The gods have designated that much as the sacred field of Vastrāpatha; to the north lies the Bhadrā river, extending for two yojanas to the east.
To the south is the site of Bali, along the river Ujjayanta; and to the west is the confluence of rivers beyond the city of Vāmana.
This field of Vastrāpatha bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; its extent should be known as four yojanas. (16)
O King, on the fifteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, Bhava is worshipped with devotion in the world of Śiva, and one dwells there for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Therefore, O King, when spring has arrived, undertake the journey; having restrained your senses, become pure, bathe, and remain self-controlled. (18)
That man who, having abandoned elephants, horses, and chariots, travels on foot, goes to the abode of Śiva by means of the Puṣpaka celestial vehicle.
Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for, or by subsisting on alms-food, or water, or fruit; || 20 ||
He who passes [his time] through fasting, through hardship, and by subsisting on vegetables, goes to heaven being fanned by hosts of beautiful women and by the Gaṇas.
Without bathing, having avoided anointing his feet on the road, bearing dirt, with a wasted body, staff in hand, and with senses conquered; || 22 ||
If a man, though afflicted by cold, heat, and water, remains intent on the remembrance of Śiva and proceeds, he goes forth having pierced through the solar orb.

O King, by this means one leads seven generations on each side—seven from the mother’s side and seven from the father’s side—even if they are situated in hell, to an imperishable state in the abode of Śiva.
When a man goes to a plundered land covered with deer skins, or if he counts the extent of the ground measured by the length of his staff; || 25 ||
In a waterless place in the forest, tormented by thirst within the midst of water, he made Śaṅkara his refuge and rendered his own mind steady.
O King, having obtained the earth girt by the seven islands and clothed by the ocean, he performed many sacrifices and gave away that land as a sacrificial gift.
Residing in a celestial palace on the seventh level, possessing a divine body and the form of Hara, he gazed slowly upon the earth, having performed auspicious adornments.
A man whose full breasts are touched by the arms of deer-eyed women, through the diversion of song and instrumental music, shall go to Satyaloka. (29)
Having restrained the force of his arms or having bound his feet very slowly, the man, observing silence and abandoning all illusion, goes to the abode of Śiva.

Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed, or even an ungrateful person—he is released from his sins; having died, he shall attain liberation.
Having abandoned mother, father, country, brother, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as village, land, and home, and having practiced restraint of the senses; || 32 ||
Having received the purificatory rites of Śiva, a man wanders upon the earth to behold numerous sacred fords and meritorious shrines.
At which auspicious sacred site or holy place, having severed the bonds of saṃsāra and having given the gift of fearlessness, does one utter "Śiva, Śiva"? (34)
O lord of men, if he remains in a solitary and secluded place, intent on the remembrance of Śiva, they go there to pay him homage.
All the deities come to observe his signs, wondering, "When will this Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) be led away by throngs of celestial chariots? (36)
But when, in due time, he attains the state of the five elements, his body composed of the aggregates being gazed upon by celestial beauties, he is led away by those women reeling with intoxication.
Worshipped by Surendra, Sūrya, Agni, Dhaneśa, and Rudra, and assuming the form of Śiva, the devotee of Rudra quickly leaves the worlds of the gods and others and dwells in the abode of Śiva. (38)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Procedure for the Pilgrimage to Vastrāpatha," in the second section, the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 11 ||
Sārasvata said: He who carries Ganges water, honey, clarified butter, saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, guggulu resin, bilva leaves, and bakapuṣpa flowers— || 1 ||
Walking on foot with a pure body, having placed his burden upon his shoulder, he bathed at the sacred ford and [worshipped] Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the beloved Śaṅkara.
He who, having seen [it], reports it, is liberated from all bonds; that man attains the status of a Gaṇa until the dissolution of all beings.
Accompanied by his wife, friends, sons, brothers, kinsmen, or other men, he goes to the sacred ford (tīrtha) while meditating upon the Lord.
Having fashioned an auspicious image of the deity, well-established and mounted upon a chariot, it should be worshipped with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron.

O King, he worshipped him with various flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as with songs, dances accompanied by musical instruments, and many kinds of laughter and rhythmic movements.
If a man goes away while bestowing land, gold, cows, water, food, clothing, grass, fuel, or even his beloved wife; || 7 ||
Seized by the grasp of the hands of celestial nymphs, having reached the Nandana grove, he enjoys auspicious pleasures as long as the moon and stars endure.
A man who wanders through a sacred ford (tīrtha) may lose his life due to diseases; however, by beholding the deity at the ford, one obtains the full fruit of having visited the sacred site.

Having reflected upon the various defects of saṃsāra, he is liberated from bondage even toward wife, sons, and friends; having realized that the Puruṣa is bound by the primary elements (pradhāna), he makes his own body all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
O lord of men, having burned away the sins accumulated from birth until the end of life, that man beholds the ancient, all-pervading, radiant Bhavodbhava; he is liberated.

At a sacred ford (tīrtha), the word of a Brahmin is to be accepted; having bathed, one should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), worship, and other rites. Darbha grass, sesame seeds, sacrificial food (haviṣya), and ritual applications performed with faith [yield great fruit].
Agastya, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the auspicious hundred-petaled flower; camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, saffron, and a leaf of Tulasī. (13)
Upon funeral cakes the size of bilva fruits, on ground illuminated by lamps, one should offer betel leaf, fruit, and food offerings, along with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water.

Whatever is intended by mortals at a sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes infinite; likewise during the solstices, the equinoxes, the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), and during eclipses. || 15 ||

At the end of the month, during the dark fortnight, on the anniversary of the death of one's father or mother, under the Gajacchāyā yoga on the thirteenth lunar day, or whenever wealth is obtained, O best of the twice-born, [one should perform the śrāddha].

One should perform the Śrāddha rite at home for the sake of liberation from the debt to the ancestors; however, it is a hundred times more meritorious when performed by a river that flows to the ocean. (17)
O King, [one should perform this] at Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, on the Gaṅgā, at Piṇḍatāraka, at Prayāga, at the Gomatī, and before Bhava, Dāmodara, and Agni.
If a man performs a śrāddha at sacred fords such as the Narmadā, he is liberated from all sins, and his ancestors attain a happy state.
Having attained a most excellent lineage and enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures, he ascends a divine celestial chariot and, at the end, goes to the abode of the gods.
One should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha at the birth rites and other sacrifices, at marriage, during sacrificial rituals, and at the commencement of the installation of a deity. (21)
All the deities are satisfied, and the ancestors of men are satisfied; in the home of one who performs the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, every auspiciousness arises.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication and the like, deceit, envy, malice, lack of discrimination, and improper reflection; (23)
Egoism, arbitrariness, fickleness, greed, O King, as well as excessive exertion, lack of exertion, negligence, malice, and rashness; (24)
Laziness, procrastination, consorting with the wives of others, eating too little, fasting, grief, and theft—O best of kings—[these are the causes]. (25)
If a man lives while constantly avoiding these faults in his home, he is an ornament of the earth, of the region, and of the city.
He is illustrious, learned, and of noble birth; he alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). For him, the ritual bathing at all sacred fords occurs perpetually.

Then, for one who has abandoned all faults, the full fruit of the sacred ford arises. Bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, burnt offerings, libations to the ancestors, gods, and sages, the ancestral rite, and the worship of the deity—all these bear fruit for one who has abandoned all faults. (28)
Whether at Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, or at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean; or at Gayā, at Rudrapada, or at the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (29)
O King, at Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Kṛṣṇa, Gomatī, Piṇḍatāraka, Vastrāpatha, the holy mountain, and likewise at Dāmodara; || 30 ||
At Bhīmeśvara on the Narmadā, at Rāmeśvara and other sites according to the Skanda Purāṇa, at Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, and at Vārāṇasī, [the worlds] Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ [are attained].
If a person goes even once to the Kālindī and Mathurā, he is liberated from all faults, including those such as the killing of a Brahmin committed by him.
Whether it be a worm, an insect, or a bird; or even a pig; or a donkey, a camel, an elephant, a horse, a deer, a lion, or a reptile—(33)
O King, whether through knowledge or ignorance, all those who die in these places are performers of meritorious deeds; having enjoyed great happiness in heaven, they [attain liberation].
All of them are born among the four castes due to the bondage of karma; however, by quickly abandoning the bondage of karma, men attain liberation once again.

They rejoice because of dying at a sacred ford (tīrtha), after which the enjoyments of heaven come to an end, having reached the land of action (karmabhūmi) of great prosperity within the region of Bhārata.
It was endowed with many wonders and adorned with numerous mountains; all the rivers, including the Gaṅgā, were joined there along with the oceans.
