At every step there are treasures and numerous sacred fords (tīrthas), by the mere remembrance of which all sins are destroyed. (38)
Many paths to the netherworld (pātāla) and the path to heaven are seen; the sun is seen in the sky, and Hara is seen in the heart. (39)
Through meditation, through the yoga of knowledge, through austerity, through the word of the guru, through truth, and indeed through courage, the three worlds are perceived.
Those men who do not perceive the surface of the earth, the netherworld (pātāla), and the heavenly realm through the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, are deceived in this world. (41)

Those who are not detached from women, being addicted to passion and deprived of their senses, perceive the body of beautiful women as one thing, yet it is conceived by them as something quite different.
Attached to their birthplaces, living beings are born again; having fallen once more from the path of liberation, they are born in the wombs of animals.

Those of impure mind who, having acquired wealth, do not offer even a single cowrie shell to a preeminent Brahmin after performing worship—those lowest of men, struck by fate, are as good as dead. (44)

Having obtained a well-nourished body and youth free from decay, those men who do not go to the Gaṅgā and other sacred waters have neither mother nor father, neither son nor kinsman, nor wife, sister, nor daughter. (45)

But how is it that the one who goes alone does not suffer? It is because the fool does not know Maheśvara, the Lord of Existence. Those lowest of men who, even after bathing, do not behold Hara Maheśvara, are indeed robbed by fate.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Pilgrimage," in the second section on the Greatness of Vastrāpatha-kṣetra, within the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 12 ||
Sārasvata said: Having severed both auspicious and inauspicious karma, one should then desire auspicious liberation; for otherwise, this auspicious task cannot be accomplished by men. (1)
Rising again and again, one should bathe and personally worship Hari and Hara; one should speak the truth, act for the benefit of others, and give gifts according to one's capacity.
One should fear slandering others and avoid the wives of others; one should refrain from seizing gold or land, and from taking what belongs to Brahmins or the gods. (3)
One should not utter anything unpleasant even in one's mind toward Brāhmaṇas, women, kings, children, the elderly, ascetics, nor toward one's father, mother, or teachers.

One must have full knowledge of place and time, and distinguish between those who are worthy recipients and those who are not; one should not disclose the secrets of men, nor [keep] buttermilk, fire, fuel, and sour gruel [in public view]. || 5 ||
Householders should give medicine and vegetables to those in need on the eleventh, fifteenth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days.

On the new moon day, during the vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), during eclipses, on the vaidhṛti yoga, on the anniversary of the death of one's father and mother, and on the days of the ancestors' passing; || 7 ||

On the day of the beginning of a Yuga or the commencement of a Manvantara, a great festival should be celebrated at home, or one should go to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), since the merit gained there is a hundred times greater than that at home.
One should achieve mastery over the senses, avoid liquor and gambling, and a householder should diligently avoid disputes, travel, and warfare. (9)
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, worship of the gods, and honoring the twice-born—all these become inexhaustible if they are performed according to the prescribed rules.
Even a single cow, adorned with garments and ornaments, yielding milk, accompanied by her calf, and young, should be offered to a preeminent brahmin. (11)

Having attained the land of Bhārata and an excellent human birth, that fortunate man who gives a cow pierces the solar orb and travels by means of a celestial chariot, escorted by cows and other beings.
Even a sinful and base person who has committed sins throughout seven lifetimes is liberated from all transgressions by one who gives a cow.
When he is led bound along the path of Yama by the servants, then Nandā approaches and beholds him as if he were her own son.
Having conquered those messengers standing at a distance by a mere roar of "huṃ," he takes that giver of cows and proceeds to the abode of Śiva.

The bull is declared to be Dharma; by him who is liberated from it, one is truly liberated. In the midst of cows, one should offer [oblations] to all the ancestors, dedicating them to Hara or to Hari. || 16 ||
On the day of Brahmā, one’s residence arises in the city of Sūryabrahma; [he obtains] a firm, humped, excellent, young bull capable of bearing burdens. (17)
By giving a plow-ox capable of bearing the yoke to a Brahmin on sacred festival days, a man ascends it and goes to Goloka in the presence of Śiva.
Having given a horse equipped with a saddle and a bit, one rejoices in heaven for the duration of a Brahma-day by the power of that king of horses.
"By the gift of an elephant, he shall be led by the lord of elephants to the Nandana grove; he shall become the king of the entire earth bounded by the oceans. (20)
By giving a house together with its furnishings to a brahmin who is a householder, one obtains a divine celestial chariot that fulfills all desires in the Nandana grove.

Gold is the supreme substance upon the earth; the gods rejoice if it is given as a gift. Even the Sun grants him a beautiful celestial chariot, and he wanders here [in heaven] for as long as that lasts.
Silver is exceedingly dear to the ancestors; by giving it, a person attains purity. He obtains the world of Soma for as long as the sages remain bound to the earth. (23)
Having offered betel leaves filled with sandalwood and camphor, as well as precious fruits, flowers, and garments, he goes happily to heaven with the hosts of gods to dwell with the Moon.
He who should offer water, oil, ghee, milk, sugarcane juice, and honey, together with dates, sugar-candy, grapes, vātāma, and cumin; || 25 ||
Having given darbha grass, unbroken rice, earth, cow dung, dūrvā grass, sacred threads, sesame seeds, skins, and a sun-skin basket, one becomes renowned in heaven for a long time.
If food that has been prepared is given from one's own meal when it constitutes a fourth part, that is called *hantakāra*; by giving that, one certainly goes to the abode of Dhruva.
Every day, food is given to the cows in proportion to one's own consumption; by giving this daily provision to them, a man goes to the abode of the gods. (28)
Whatever sin has been committed by means of the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, and the broom, the householder washes away by giving alms every day.
A morsel of food constitutes true alms; that house where this is given constantly is a true home, while any other appears like a cremation ground. (30)
Having given water-pots filled with prepared food, along with an umbrella, sandals, a water-pot, a ring, and garments, a man goes to heaven.
O lord of men, that man who gives a vehicle to the weary, a drink to the thirsty, and food to the hungry, goes to the third heaven in a celestial chariot while being praised by divine nymphs.
Food soaked in ghee should always be given according to one's ability; for since the vital breaths consist of that very substance, living beings are thereby nourished. (33)
For the affliction of hunger is great in the world, and food is known to be its remedy; therefore, it is pacified by that, and thus excellent food should be given. (34)
Food, clothing, fruit, water, buttermilk, vegetables, ghee, honey, leaves, flowers, as well as sandals, a patched garment, a staff, and a water-pot.
An umbrella, a vessel, a vow, sacred knowledge, a rosary, worship of the gods, a maiden, kusha grass, a sacred thread, seeds, medicinal herbs, and houses. || 36 ||
Grain, a field, sacrificial vessels, a yoga-band, and sandals; a black antelope skin, the gift of wisdom, and the narration of instructions on dharma. || 37 ||
Now, this should be given continuously; by that, great spiritual merit shall arise. Having brought about the destruction of all sins, the donor goes to the abode of Śiva.
At a śrāddha ceremony, householders who are of noble birth, masters of the Vedas, free from anger, habituated to bathing, and devoted to the customs of their own country should be fed. (39)
Having been invited on the previous day, those twice-born who are free from worldly desire, devoid of greed, and free from disease—but not those who act as village priests—[should be chosen]. (40)
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) must be presented before them according to the prescribed rite; for a Śrāddha performed by one devoid of faith is as good as not performed at all.

Therefore, those endowed with faith and free from anger should perform the śrāddha. A forest-dweller, a celibate student, a traveler, and one visiting sacred pilgrimage sites [should likewise do so]. 42.

A guest should be honored at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite during the performance of a Śrāddha ceremony; ascetics should always be honored by householders according to their own capacity. (43)
O best of kings, I shall now describe the procedure for the pilgrimage along with its history.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śrāddha, Giving, and Other Rites," within the "Description of the Procedure for Pilgrimage" in the "Greatness of Vastrāpatha-kṣetra," the second part of the seventh section (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 13 ||
Sārasvata said: In ancient times, in the city of Vāmana within the great sacred field of Vastrāpatha, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha was consumed by grief for his son.
He came to perform austerities on the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river, in the water of the Svarṇarekhā river located in the northeast corner of the city.

When, having bathed and meditated, he contemplated the god Śiva with his mind, then Rudra—the three-eyed one whose banner is the bull—arrived. "O great sage, I am pleased with you; tell me what I shall do. (3)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Mahādeva, if you are pleased and a boon is now to be granted to me, then you should remain here as long as the moon and stars endure."
O Lord, you must always effect the destruction of the sins of those men who perform evil deeds and bathe here.
O Lord of Gods, lead those men who, despite being doers of evil deeds, worship the Three-eyed One, to the abode of Śiva by means of celestial chariots.
Sārasvata said: Having replied, "So be it," the god Hara vanished right there. After slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu, the mighty Narasiṃha gave the three worlds to Indra and himself went to Kālarudra.

In his lineage was born Bali, who was exceedingly superior in strength. Possessed of great power, Bali brought the earth under a single umbrella; the earth was rich with crops, well-watered, and yielded grain without being ploughed.
The flowers were fragrant and the fruits were succulent; the trees bore fruit up to their very trunks, and there was honey in every leaf-cup.
All the twice-born were masters of the four Vedas; the Kṣatriyas were skilled in warfare; the Vaiśyas were devoted to service toward cattle; and the Śūdras were intent on rendering obedience.
The regions were characterized by virtuous conduct and were free from calamities and diseases; all the people were joyful and well-nourished, ever blissful and always industrious.
With their limbs smeared with saffron and agallochum, well-attired and beautifully adorned, they were liberated from the miseries of poverty and death, becoming long-lived.
With the regions illuminated by lamps, mortals roam even at night as if it were day, just as gods move about in a celestial abode.
The asura Bali ruled a kingdom on earth that was like heaven; the royal palace resounded constantly with the music of wedding festivities.
The Daitya enjoyed the earth just as the king of the gods enjoys heaven; at that time, the lord of the gods was constantly gratified by Bali with sacrifices.
There is no mutual war between the gods and the dānavas; there is but one ruler of the earth, and there is no war upon the surface of the earth. 16.
There is no battle between Hari and his enemies, nor with elephants; there is no eternal conflict between snakes and mongooses, nor between cats and mice. (17)
Having wandered through the three worlds, Nārada reached the Nandana grove, where the entire world—both stationary and moving—had attained a state of loving-kindness.
He did not see the battle anywhere in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; meanwhile, a great pain arose within his belly.
I have no need for bathing and the like; what purpose is served by libations? My entire endeavor is otherwise, through recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth. (20)
That is their bath where elephants fight with the clashing of their tusks; that is their twilight when the earth is adorned with slain headless trunks.
Where carnivorous beasts are satiated by the blood flowing from the frontal globes of elephants split open by the blows of spears—that kind of libation is dear to me.
Those Kṣatriyas, who were unassailable by elephant-heads, have been slain in battle; that is the sacrificial fire-offering where elephants and the best of men are offered as oblations.
This sacrifice of Nārada in the fire of sound is renowned throughout the three worlds; it is performed with [offerings] whose feet, heads, and hands are severed, and whose entrails dangle out.
Whatever spot on the surface of the earth is honored by me is my constant worship of the gods; what need have I for the gods in heaven, or for humans on the face of the earth? (25)
But why do the serpents in Pātāla not fight with one another? I shall act in such a way that [they do so] on the surface of the earth, even against the lords of the gods, Indra and Upendra.
"May Bali go to the netherworld (rasātala), and may my word come true: [I shall never abandon] Hari Dāmodara even at the cost of my life or my kingdom. (27)
When he satisfies him with effort, he will become Indra; having been the slayer of Vṛtra, the lord of the gods, he will then fall from his kingdom.
When, having gone to Vastrāpatha, one worships Bhava with devotion, then even a lord of the gods becomes further freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 29 ||
By means of this recitation of the mantra, his abdominal pain was pacified, and Nārada went suddenly into the presence of the King of the Gods.
Having ascended his lion-throne and being established in the Nandana grove, Hari, the king of gods and possessor of great strength, sits surrounded by the deities.
While gazing at that celestial beauty Rambhā as she danced, the god, filled with wonder, beheld Nārada approaching.
"Aha! The venerable Nārada appears to me as one who acts in contradiction; for why does he not dance when there is dancing, and why does he not sing when there is singing? (33)
While Hari was still lost in thought, "Let the instruments be played according to the rhythmic measures," the sage arrived, intent on sprinkling him with water.
Leaving his lion-throne and rising, Hari stood before him; having greeted him with a welcome, he then spoke to Nārada.
"O Great Sage, welcome to you today; from where have you come? Are you well in your bathing, twilight prayers, and fire-offerings? (36)
Thus addressed, Nārada smiled and then spoke to Hari: "If this is granted to me, what further need have I for anything else? (37)
O Lord of Heaven, I see no place for you as a mere spectator; I have no need for your sovereignty so long as it belongs to Bali.
All the planets, beginning with the Sun, are joined with the measurement of time; drenched by the oblation, the clouds rain joyfully upon the earth. (39)
There is no death from disease and the like; Yama is constrained by Dharma.

That lord of men enjoyed the earth under a single umbrella; he was constantly praised by throngs of *cāraṇas* and bards as "Lord of the Three Worlds," "Great King," "Skilled in the Science of Warfare," and "Lover of the Breasts of the Fortune of the Three Worlds. (41)
"Brahman! Kṛṣṇa! Hari! Bhūman! Indra! Sūrya! Lord of Wealth! Lord of the Enemies of the Gods! Lord of the Suras!"—thus is he celebrated by throngs of celestial bards and panegyrists.
Without war, the hosts of Daityas laugh; intoxicated elephants trumpet in their madness; men mounted on chariots wander about; and army commanders take pleasure with women in their homes. (43)

The sky shines with the smoke from the sacrificial fires, and the earth shines with the color of gold; yet the world is empty of the Vedas, while the celestial abode of Bali shines with hosts of Daityas.

"Bali does not know you to be the lord of the gods, nor do all the gods who partake in Bali’s sacrifice; you yourself must consider him your enemy in your heart. What I have told you is what is appropriate for you. (45)
Rambhā does not shine in the assembly; Menakā does not even consider you [her equal]; Tilottamā, too, regards King Bali as the lord of the gods.
Urvaśī herself approaches him; that fair-haired woman speaks with him, yet Mañjughoṣā, having turned her face away, does not look at you. 47.
Pulomā does not experience a thrill of horripilation without Bali; and Mantharā, having gone before Paulomī, praises Bali.
Nārada, Parvata, Hāhā, Hūhū, and Tumburu—these praised the kingdom of Bali in the presence of Rudra, as I have heard.
Satisfied by offerings of clarified butter, the sages in the abode of Brahmā praised that very thing in the presence of Brahmā; thus has it been related by me.
"What Bṛhaspati tells you must not be spoken by me to you; considering Bali to be powerful, Indrāṇī looks for him among the paintings. (51)
At these words, the lord of the gods, overwhelmed with anger, then moved forward; he said to his charioteer, "O driver! Bring the elephant, the thunderbolt, my sword, my armor, and the chariot! (52)

May Sūrya with his chariot, the Maruts with their elephant, Rudra with his bull, and the son of Sura (Kubera) with his buffalo, cause musical instruments to sound for my battle today; may Caṇḍī and Gaṇeśa set forth with haste.
Seeing the lord of the gods enraged, the wise and noble-minded Bṛhaspati, having gone into the midst of the sages, spoke words appropriate for the occasion.

The four methods of policy, beginning with conciliation (sāma), were proclaimed by Manu in ancient times; since these matters are to be accomplished through conciliation, let the rod of punishment not be cast down.
Therefore, let the best of the gods summon Upendra and consult with him; for the entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving, is dependent upon him.
When undertakings have failed, his good and bad fortune must be declared; he alone should first go forth upon this earth for the accomplishment of his own purpose.
Having been thus requested by the gods, the Lord of the Suras acted accordingly; then Viṣṇu, having arrived from Satyaloka, went to Mount Mandara.
"Let those sages go there to bring Janārdana. Thus addressed, Nārada, who had come from heaven to bathe, arrived at Mount Mandara.
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha arrived at the abode of Hari.
On the mountain, that Nārada performed his bath in the waters of the Gaṅgā and observed the twilight rites; while he remained there, the great sages, the Vālakhilyas, were filled with joy.
Then, having saluted him with humility, Nārada said: "The sages have arrived at Mount Mandara to take Viṣṇu to the abode of the gods."
"It is also fitting for you to grant an audience to the sages. Having heard these words, those great sages were filled with joy.
Before them, Hari saw the Vālakhilyas—dwarfish beings the size of a thumb's joint—who had gone to the waters of the Gaṅgā to bathe in the abode of Hari.
Then, by the power of their destined task, they laughed at all the Vāmanas; these were all the Vālakhilyas, sons of Brahmā, who were firm in their praised vows.
Filled with shame yet overcome by anger, they spoke loudly to one another: "By some divine purpose, this one will become Vāmana. (66)
Having been enlightened and propitiated by all the sages and Viṣṇu, they said: "Tell us, when will there be liberation from worldly fortune for Viṣṇu? (67)
When Vastrāpatha becomes superior to Prabhāsa, then there will surely be an increase extending throughout the Dhruva-maṇḍala; likewise, the field of Vastrāpatha will become superior to Yava.
Having seen the god Someśvara, you will be freed from all defects; your power to accomplish the impossible shall become firm.
He who beholds Somanātha at Vastrāpatha truly beholds; there, Indra and Upendra are seated together on an excellent throne, embracing one another.
Viṣṇu said: "O King of the Gods, what is your business? I shall certainly perform it for you."

Indra said: "In the lineage of Hiraṇyakaśipu, there was a Daitya named Bali of great strength; by him all this has been pervaded, and the gods have been deprived of their share of the sacrifices. (72)

O Keśava, let the entire world of mortals go to the world of the gods, provided that Bali—who remembers their former enmity—does not undergo a transformation; meanwhile, let him remain in Pātāla, deprived of his kingdom.
"May there be some king on the surface of the earth in the lineage of the Sun and Moon. (74)
Sārasvata said: Having heard these words and reflected upon them himself with his mind, Janārdana said to the sages, "I shall do so," and then spoke to them.
"Let the sages go there and perform the great sacrifice; I shall come there myself and accomplish that offering."
Having been addressed thus, all the sages departed for the sacrificial pavilion; the great twelve-day sacrifice, accompanied by all the ritual fees, was commenced.
O King, there is the famous land of Surāṣṭra, the sacred field of Vastrāpatha; to the southern region of that place lies the great city of Bali, which is perfected.

A sacrifice in which one's entire possession was given as the sacrificial fee (sarvasvadakṣiṇa) was commenced outside the sacred field. All the sages were invited by Śukra to the sacrificial rites; Bali, being exceedingly joyful, bestowed various kinds of gifts at the sacrifice.

In all golden vessels, abundant food is served; a learned Brāhmaṇa guest is honored even with one's entire possessions. Through giving, a sacrifice becomes complete; without giving, it is in vain. (80)

At that very time, Viṣṇu assumed the form of a dwarf; he was a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas traveling on a pilgrimage to sacred sites in the Middle Country, possessing a large belly, short arms, a lame foot, and a massive head.
He had large jaws, thick calves, and a thick neck; he was exceedingly gluttonous, wore white garments, and had his topknot tied. He carried an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.
He wandered over the surface of the earth to see many sacred fords; eventually, that twice-born man arrived at the field of Vastrāpatha in the region of Surāṣṭra.
On the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā, Vāmana reflected: "Should I first go to see Lord Someśvara Śiva after having seen Bhava? (84)

"Then, having worshipped Someśvara, I shall afterwards go to Mandara. Having become intent on this thought and reflecting upon his duty with his mind, he resolved: "Remaining here, I shall certainly worship Somanātha. (85)
In the great field of Vastrāpatha, people constantly worship Someśvara in vain; likewise, I must certainly act in that same manner. (86)
The best of countries, the best of mountains, the best of sacred fields, and the best of rivers. (87)
The divine forest shall indeed be the best among forests, and Bhava shall be the highest among the gods, when the god Someśvara emerges by piercing through the earth.

Then, in that divine mango grove, this field is even more excellent than Yavādhika; on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one intent upon the practice of fire-sacrifice [should go there].
With his arms raised at the time of the sun, he beholds Bhava for as long as the Lord of Day has not yet reached the midpoint of its course and remains lingering. (90)
Scorched by the heat of the fire on his limbs, he beheld Śaṅkara—Somanātha, the peaceful Śiva, who is saluted by all the gods—with an offering mixed with flowers and water, O beautiful lady. (91)
Sārasvata said: Then, having pierced the earth, the Lord of Gods himself, Mahādeva Someśvara, remained in the form of a *liṅga* for as long as the day of Brahmā lasts.
Someśvara said: "By my grace you have attained perfection; your purpose shall be accomplished. Having been addressed thus, Vāmana replied to the god Maheśvara.
Vāmana said: "O Mahādeva, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then let this divine Linga remain here before me."
But whoever shall worship the Svāyaṃbhuva Liṅga in my city of Vāmana—whether he be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a killer of a cow, or a murderer of a child—[he shall be purified].
One who has betrayed his guru or stolen gold is liberated from all sins; he who, being faultless, worships Hara-Someśvara even once [is likewise freed]. 96.
Having died, he ascends a celestial chariot, surrounded by divine women; being praised by the guardians of the quarters, let him go to heaven, the abode of Śiva.
"May he go beyond the world of Brahmā to the world of Rudra. Having said, "So be it," Somanātha vanished right there.
Having manifested the self-existent Liṅga Somanātha as Vāmana, and having attained knowledge and achieved spiritual growth, he went to behold Bhava, the Destroyer.

All rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, are situated within the waters of the Svarṇarekhā. Those men and women who hear this account of the origin of Someśvara—the destruction of all their sins occurs for them; of this there is no doubt. (100)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Someśvara," in the second section, the *Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 14.
Sārasvata said: Then that brahmin Vāmana, having attained knowledge through the worship of Bhava, went to that beautiful forest belonging to Mount Raivataka.
There were various kinds of trees with long branches and laden with fruit—banyan, udumbara, and bilva trees, as well as sarja, arjuna, and kadamba trees.
Palāśa, aśvattha, and nimba; dhava, aṭī, and vāruṇī trees; śamī, kaṅkola, and liṃba; as well as bījapūra and pomegranate (dāḍima). || 3 ||
The jujube tree, the neem, the betel nut, the plantain, the śallakī, the śivā, the palmyra palm, the hintāla, the śirasa, the bījaka, the bamboo, and the khadira; || 4 ||
Ajagāsanas, Gāgucchās, Iṅgudīs, Koraveṅgudas, Brahmavṛkṣas, Kurubakas, Karañjas, and Putrajīvins; || 5 ||
Aṅkolla trees, pāribhadra trees, kalaṃba trees, and likewise panasa trees; ujjvala trees, haridrā trees, and gaṅgaḍīvāyu trees.
Tesuṇḍakas, śirīṣas, kharjūrīs, karavaṃdikās, sevālīs, śālmalīs, śālas, madhūkas, and vibhītakas; || 7 ||
Harītakya trees, Kaṭāhas, Karyaṣṭas, Āṭarūṣakas, Vikacchavas, Kapitthas, Rohiṇīs, and Vetrakadrumas. || 8 ||
Madanaphala trees, nirguṇḍī, pāṭalā, and naṃdipādapa trees; clove, cardamom, and lavali creepers; santāna trees and agaru trees.
Then Vāmana saw sandalwood trees, camphor trees, kalpa-trees, and the best of mountains—shady trees worshipped by the gods.
For those whose shadows are not obstructed at sunrise or sunset, the destruction of all sins occurs merely by the sight of them. || 11 ||
Those people who have performed meritorious deeds are within the range of his vision; beholding them, he then went from those trees to Mount Raivataka.
As long as the brahmin gazed at its lofty peak, he beheld upon its summit a wondrous sight that struck terror into the world.
He sees five men standing amidst smoke and flames—black-limbed, moving through the sky, fierce, and adorned with black aloe-wood.
Mounted upon dogs, with trunks like those of elephants, wearing girdles, holding swords and shields in their hands, and possessing the terrifying sound of hand-drums (ḍamaru).
They made the mountains resound with the placement of their rattling feet; their forms were radiant with howls, and their hair was matted like kāśa grass.
Their palates were occupied with mouthfuls of the essence of human flesh and fat; their fierce eyes were intent on perceiving the scent of people. (17)
By the power of his divine vision, attained through the practice of the five fires, that best of Brahmins, who knew the succession of duties to be performed, beheld the gods.
These five lords of the field were created by Mahādeva; possessing great strength, they dwell eternally on Mount Raivataka.
Just as that mountain restrains mortals from acting according to their own whims, so too do they not perceive Hari, Hara, the river, or the goddess, as they perceive the mountain.

Having seen and recognized [him], and having meditated upon the god Maheśvara, he offered praise: "Victorious is that body marked by the meditation on battle against the wicked lords of the Daityas, which those brothers bear, possessing prowess equal to five Indras. (21)
Born from the mouths of Rudra, they were skillful and the destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; they were delighted by the submarine fire which had been terrified by the oblations licked up by them.
The gods had their limbs smeared with saffron, agallochum, and camphor, and were beautifully adorned; they were intoxicated by the fragrance of wine and engaged in dancing and singing.

Victorious are those guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapālas), who are weary from wandering through the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), whose movements are startled by their own fragrance, who possess the speed of thought, and who travel at will.
Satisfied by these words, they stood before the twice-born man themselves, saying: "I am one [foot], and the other is the formidable mountain. (25)
The third is Meghanāda, the fourth is Siṃhanāda, and the fifth is Kālamegha; I am he. Tell us, what shall we do for you? (26)
The twice-born one said: "If you are pleased with me, and if a boon is certainly to be granted, then [O gods], you must remain established here for me until the final dissolution."
With one foot first placed upon the mountain slope out of great joy, he dwelt on that mountain during his stay, and there he encountered Giridāruṇa.
Having been propitiated, that granter of boons established himself there; then Meghanāda himself went to the summit of Mount Ujjayanta.
The delightful Bhavānīśaṅkara was likewise entered by Siṃhanāda; he himself was presented before Bhava at Vastrāpatha itself.
On the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river, the mighty Kālamegha established a sacred ford (tīrtha) in ancient times for the benefit of all the worlds.
O Indra among kings, in ancient times at the beginning of the Yuga, Vāmana himself went there and worshipped the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), and all the gods assembled together.
They arrived in the land of Surāṣṭra at the meritorious Raivataka mountain for the protection of all the worlds and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Then a garland of victory was placed upon Viṣṇu’s neck by the best of the gods; and the supreme name of Hari, "Dāmodara," became renowned.
There, at the outset, on a day in the bright fortnight of Kārttika beloved of Viṣṇu, having fasted together with the gods, that holy place was created by Viṣṇu.
The meritorious river Svarṇarekhā, embodying all sacred fords (tīrthas), stands there; it is holy, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and granting the realm of Viṣṇu. || 36 ||
Dāmodara at Raivataka bestows supreme bliss; he is the washing away of all sins and the destroyer of disease and poverty. (37)
Those who behold [the deity] with celestial chariots are led to the abode of Viṣṇu; one should not perform the Kārttika vow at home, especially the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
The twelfth day after the five [days] is most excellent; it should be observed by people while Dāmodara is in the water. When Kārttika has arrived, the morning bath must be performed.
A month-long fast should be observed by ascetics, celibate students, virtuous women, and widows who desire the state of liberation.
By eating only once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for, or by fasting, or again by the kṛcchra penance, or by subsisting on vegetables; || 41 ||
Viṣṇu should be worshipped in the month of Kārttika by men devoted to the offering of lamps; if this month is passed by human beings intent on celibacy, [it becomes most meritorious].
Then one dwells in the city of Viṣṇu together with Viṣṇu; when the Bhīṣmapañcaka has arrived, five fasts must be observed.
Beginning from Ekādaśī up to the fifth day, the full moon, and so forth—this group of five days is declared to be the remover of all sins for human beings.
Of all months, even more than the five beginning with Kārttika, the Ekādaśī of Kārttika is meritorious when dedicated to Dāmodara. (45)
In the month of Kārttika, sweet food, sacrificial oblations (haviṣya) drenched in ghee, gold, silver, clothing, water, food, and fruits should be given.

At the end of the month, various gifts should be given: a cow, sesame seeds, and flowers. Whatever merit is found in all forms of giving, and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords—[all that is obtained by this]. (47)
O King, whatever fruit is obtained by men through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha or by one who offers funeral cakes at Gayā, that same fruit arises for them upon seeing Dāmodara.

Having performed his bath on the eleventh day, he should be intent upon the worship of the deity; having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then with water from sacred fords (tīrtha).
Having worshipped with water mixed with saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, and camphor, and then with fragrant lotus flowers, || 50 ||
Having offered many bright *mālatī* flowers and *tulasī* leaves, as well as a cloth and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should burn incense thoroughly.
One should offer a lamp with ghee, or even with oil in the absence of ghee; various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) should be presented, as well as fruit and betel leaf.

O King, worship of the temple should be performed by means of the offering of flags and other such acts; thereafter, a cow together with her calf, which carries one across the ocean of worldly existence, should be given as a gift.
Then, having performed a circumambulation accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments, as well as the recitation of the Vedas, Purāṇas, commentaries, and divine narratives; || 54 ||
A vigil should be observed before the deity, and lamps should be offered upon the ground; seven mountains made of the seven grains should be prepared, each accompanied by a lamp.
Filled with fruits, betel, and cooked food, these [gifts] were prepared by learned, Vedic-scholar householding Brahmins who were weary from their labors.
O tiger among men, the Vaiṣṇava narrative must indeed be heard by women as well; in this manner, the vigil (jāgaraṇa) should be observed by those who are free from passion and anger.
Having kept a vigil at night, when the orb of the sun has risen, one should bathe during the morning twilight (pūrvasaṃdhyā) and then perform the midday rites.
Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and human beings according to the prescribed rites, and having performed the śrāddha for the ancestors, he should give gifts according to his own capacity.
Having again worshipped the god Dāmodara with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should worship the divine Narasiṃha and Vainateya as well.
Having kept a vigil at night and awakened Madhusūdana, men should perform the breaking of the fast upon reaching the time for eating on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Having fed the Brahmins together with his sons and kinsmen, he should give food according to his ability to the disabled, the blind, and the miserable.
At Dāmodara, Raivataka, and in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river—he who performs a pilgrimage there, listen to the fruit of his merit. || 63 ||
A slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, one who destroys the boundaries of a village, a traitor to the king, a traitor to his guru, and he who observes false vows; || 64 ||
He who gives false testimony, he who misappropriates a deposit, the Brahmin who kills children or women, and he who neglects the twilight prayers and ritual bathing; || 65 ||
One who steals the property of gods or Brahmins, one who sells the Vedas, one who sells his daughter, and one who reviles gods and Brahmins; || 66 ||
A Brahmin who betrays trust, one who eats the food of a Śūdra, a hunter, one who violates another's wife, and one who misappropriates what has been given by himself; (67)
He who indulges in sexual intercourse before the proper time, as well as he who destroys a dam, and he who does not approach his own wedded wife when she has bathed after her menses; || 68 ||
A young Brahmin widow shall not be one who retains what she has heard; O King, these and many others are great sinners. (69)
Having bathed in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā and beheld Hari as Dāmodara, and having performed a vigil at night, one is liberated from all sins.
But those of evil deeds who have come to this vigil do not go to the city of Hari at that sacred ford on the ocean of saṃsāra.

In whatever manner a man passes through the night vigil, in that very manner he is meditated upon in the city of Viṣṇu; indeed, for the sake of his residence in the world of Viṣṇu, he is welcomed by the gods in a home resounding with the sounds of drums and songs.

Bearing maces, swords, conchs, and lotuses, four-armed and assuming forms that humble the pride of the Daityas, they proceed through the sky while being praised by celestial beauties, their bodies joined with those of the sky-dwellers.

In the Vārāha-kalpa, at the beginning of the first Yuga, Dāmodara became renowned on Mount Raivataka; this is that river, the most excellent of streams, and this is that Hari, the creator of the world. (74)

The man who reads or hears this Purāṇa is led by the hosts of gods, praised by them, to the abode of Madhusūdana in celestial chariots; there, with four arms and the arms of divine damsels placed around him, he is escorted. (75)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrī Dāmodara," within the "Procedure for the Pilgrimage to the Tīrthas Proclaimed by Sārasvata," in the "Majesty of Vastrāpatha-kṣetra," the second part of the seventh section, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 15 ||
The King said: Then that dwarf Brahmin entered the dense forest; what did he do there alone? Tell me that wonder. || 1 ||
Sārasvata said: Then that brahmin Vāmana, having gone to Mount Raivataka, bathed according to the prescribed rites in the waters of the river Svarṇarekhā.
Having worshipped the Lord with devotion using fragrant flowers, incense, and other offerings, O King, he stood alone before Him in the solitary forest.
It was filled with all kinds of beings, crowded with crawling reptiles, resounding with the cries of many voices, and made to ring out with the calls of peacocks.
In that place, delightful with the cries of cuckoos and resounded by the calls of wild cocks, illuminated by fireflies and shaken by monkeys; (5)
In some places it was stilled by forest fires, in others it was filled with flowering trees; there, the branches reached toward the sky and were free from the heat of the sun.
In that place where boars were bewildered and terrified by the slaughter of hunters, and which was expert in providing standing ground for the joyful winds of the kṣatriyas; || 7 ||
He remembered Hari in his mind, who is endowed with many wonders; perceiving him as if terrified, Narasiṃha arrived.
Standing before that brahmin for the sake of his protection, he said: "O brahmin, you must not fear; tell me, what shall I do for you? (9)
The Brahmin said: "O Narasiṃha, if you are pleased and a boon is to be granted by you to me, then protection must always be provided here for all those dwelling at this sacred site."
"You must always remain before the God for as long as there are fourteen Indras. Having said to him, "So be it," Hari then acted accordingly.
Therefore, that Narasiṃha is worshipped in the presence of Dāmodara; he has made the forest pleasant and he protects the sacred site (tīrtha).
In that forest, no dwelling with spirits, ghosts, and the like occurs; through the power of Narasiṃha, the fear arising from lions and other beasts has been destroyed. (13)
On the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, when the breaking of the fast was performed, he paid homage to Dāmodara and then departed to see Bhava.
Having bathed on the fourteenth day and worshipped Bhava with devotion, the sin born of worldly existence is reduced to ashes through the worship of Bhava. (15)
Through the sight of the God, he became one whose accumulation of sins was destroyed; he stood before Bhava and likewise before Vastrapatha in a state of peace.
Having worshipped that Kālamegha, he then proceeded to Vastrāpatha; there he fully honored the deity with mantras declared in the Vedas, according to the prescribed rites.
With incense, lamps, food offerings, and other gifts, that Vāmana performed everything; having completed a hundred circumambulations, he stood before Bhava.
As long as he gazed at everything, he beheld Mount Ujjayanta, the best of mountains, the brother of Maināka.
In the land of Surāṣṭra, there stands a mountain famous from the beginning of the Yuga, the first to exist; it is endowed with other mountains and adorned with rocks and trees.
Seeing him, that Vāmana reflected upon subtle dharmas that require little effort but yield great results, bestowing the fortune of sons.
When one's own duties are necessarily performed, they yield their fruit; having seen a river flowing toward the ocean and having bathed in it, one is liberated from sins. || 22 ||

Having touched a cow, having bowed to a Brāhmaṇa, and having fully honored his teachers and deities, as well as an ascetic, a mendicant, one who is peaceful, a learned Vedic scholar, and a celibate student; || 23 ||
By feeding their father, mother, sister, her husband, daughter, son-in-law, nephew, grandson, as well as friends, relatives, and kinsmen, householders are liberated from all sins.
May kings, elephants, horses, mongooses, chaste women, bulls, mountains, mirrors, milk-trees, and those who constantly bestow food be for your protection. (25)
These men, who are always speakers of truth, purify merely by being seen; having heard their discourse on the Vedas and Dharma, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. (26)
Having remembered Hari and Hara and having performed ablutions on the bank of the Gaṅgā, one should go to the vigil for Viṣṇu and give gifts according to one's capacity.
Having offered betel-leaf, flowers, a lamp, food offerings, and Tulasī leaves, as well as song, dance, and instrumental music in the temple of the Lord; || 28 ||
These subtle dharmas are said to lead to great prosperity when practiced; therefore, I behold this auspicious king of mountains, the abode of all the gods. (29)
For those men who go to the peak, heaven is within the palm of their hand.
Having understood this, Vāmana ascended the summit of the mountain where water had gushed forth due to the trampling of Airāvata's feet.
Then that Vāmana went to the peak situated in the sky to see Bhavānī, the mother of Skanda, who had ascended the summit.
In whatever measure men ascend this best of mountains, in that same measure all embodied beings are liberated from their sins.
Having formed this resolve, the brahmin went to the mountain peak; there, a devotee of Bhava, he beheld Bhavānī, the mother of Skanda.
Then Skanda addressed them as "O Mother," and likewise all other deities, all humans on earth, and all serpents in the netherworld (pātāla).
Therefore, she is renowned as Ambā and is worshipped on the mountain peak; having been honored with various excellent and diverse fruits by the twice-born, [she bestows her grace]. (36)
Standing on that mountain peak which reached up to the sky, filled with curiosity, he remained alone upon that summit with his arms raised upward.
Having gazed upon the entire earth with its mountains and oceans, [he beheld] the primordial, eternal god Bhāskara, whose nature consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Consisting entirely of splendor, the god of all gods, saluted by the deities, wandering without support, and the cause of the measurement of time. || 39 ||
As soon as the brahmin saw him, he beheld Śaṅkara—the god Bhava, naked and completely covered with stones.
The god, possessing the form and appearance of a Buddha, omniscient and adorned with virtues, emaciated in limb, with matted hair, gentle, stood himself upon the path of the sky. || 41 ||
The illustrious Śiva said: Listen, O Vāmana; I am pleased and shall grant you various boons. Your prosperity shall pervade the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.

The Vedas and whatever else, such as song and dance, shall manifest before you; your power to accomplish the impossible shall become firm. However, go to Vastrāpatha and perform a pilgrimage to its sacred sites.
Vāmana said: O Mahādeva, tell me specifically, O Lord, about those holy places that exist in Vastrāpatha, if you have compassion for me. (44)
Rudra said: In the northwestern corner of Vastrāpatha is a divine lake; on its western side is a Jālī tree with dense foliage.
In the center, there is a linga made of clay within a bilva tree, where that hunter formerly went and attained perfection in my city.
By the mere sight of it, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed; indeed, it was there that Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, was liberated from the guilt of Brahmin-slaughter.
Therefore, in the northern quarter, there is a Liṅga established by Dhanada, renowned throughout the three worlds; there resides the Goddess Triśūlinī.
By the mere sight of whom his son Nalakūbara had his hand ensnared by a noose, he made the trident-bearing god [Śiva] his own deity. (49)
In the south-western corner of Bhava, the Gaṇa known as Heraṃba was established by Yama when he first installed the Liṅga.
His majesty was wondrous; Citragupta, being greatly amazed upon seeing it, came to behold that deity made of clay as of old.
O best of the twice-born, he also fashioned a linga in that sacred field, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Citragupteśvara.

To the west, the noble-minded Prajāpati, with a loud sound of the syllable *cakāra*, [established] that Liṅga known as Kedāra situated on Mount Raivataka; then Prajāpati himself remained there upon the mountain peak.
Rudra said: I shall recount the majesty of Indreśvara; listen to that, which is famous in the northeast corner and known to me as belonging to Bhava. 54.
Vāmana said: "O Lord, why has Indra arrived here, and how did Hari worship Hara? Tell me this story in full detail."
Rudra said: "In former times, a hunter attained perfection through keeping vigil on Śivarātri; he then reached the world of Śiva, where a celestial chariot accompanied by attendants arrived. (56)
Having ascended that all-pervading, most beautiful vehicle, which resounded with the songs of celestial women, he arrived to behold that city of Hari. || 57 ||
In that [battle] where a conflict arose between the Gaṇas and the servants of Yama, the King of the Gods, perceiving him approaching, reflected: || 58 ||
He is worthy of worship by all, including Citragupta, Yama, and others, just like Hara; for Indra has mounted his elephant, and Yama [has mounted] his buffalo.
Having placed his pen behind his ear at the command of Yama, Citragupta then summoned all the attendants who had been brought from the surface of the earth.
Tormented by their own transgression, they departed facing the south. Hospitality must be offered even when a hunter comes to one's house. (61)
"If he departs without being honored, Hara will surely curse me; therefore, I shall perform worship so that Śaṅkara may be pleased."
He saw the god who had arrived to visit him standing nearby, seated upon a celestial chariot, possessing the form of Hara and radiating a splendor equal to ten million suns.
He was being praised for his deeds concerning Śiva and Śivarātri, performed during the vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.

"Thus, O Lord of the Gods, everything on the surface of the earth is born. Having spoken thus to Purandara, that beautiful-eyed woman of the celestial nymphs raised her hand and restrained the lordly elephant.
O Lord of the Gods, what is the use of giving many gifts, what use are vows, what use is the worship of deities, what use are yogas, what use are austerities, and what use is celibacy? (66)
What is the use of offering funeral cakes at Gayā or dying at Prayāga? What is gained by going to Someśvara, the Sarasvatī, or the Somaparvan festival? (67)

What would be gained by those who have gone to Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu? What would be achieved by the gift of gold equal to a tulā-weight or by the recitation of the Vedas? || 68 ||
What is the use of that rite of releasing a bull by which all sins are destroyed? What indeed does the gift of a cow accomplish, and likewise the gift of water? (69)

What kind of fruit is obtained during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the transits of the sun; and what kind of fruit is obtained when a vigil is performed on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha? (70)
Yama, seated upon his buffalo, speaks with his voice: "Behold the majesty of Rudra; O Citragupta, reflect upon it! (71)
This is that hunter by whom Hara was worshipped in the past; now hear of the famous sacred site Vastrāpatha in the land of Surāṣṭra.
There is Mount Ujjayanta and likewise Mount Raivataka; I have heard that a great Jāli (enclosure) exists between the two of them. || 73 ||
The linga is made of clay, and it was worshipped by him during the night; he had come for the purpose of performing a night vigil.

How then can this be told by us, for those gods know it themselves? These excellent women, having come from Indra’s abode to the Nandana grove with great speed, choose one another as their preferred suitor to behold.
A certain man, with a body possessing the splendor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, approaches to behold the city of the Lord of the gods; he is my husband—is he also your husband? (76)

Awakened in the palace of the king of gods by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, and paṭahas, the women ask one another: "Is this the god Hara, or a man in the form of Hara? What is it, what is it between us two? (77)
Some sing, some laugh, some dance, and some recite; others speak with many words joined with shouts of "Victory! in the presence of their teacher. (78)

One woman praises Śiva, while another likewise praises Śivā; then yet another asks: "What indeed is the fruit of the bilva leaf? Or is this fruit of yours from fasting, or is this fruit of yours from the loss of sleep? (79)
Various kinds of words were heard from them in the Nandana grove; and immediately after that, news concerning the world of Brahmā and other realms was brought forth.
Filled with curiosity, the Lord of the Gods spoke again to the hunter: "In which region and on which mountain is the Jāli-liṅga located? Show it to me. (81)
The hunter said: "In the land of Surāṣṭra, there is a famous region where the Sarasvatī, bearing the submarine fire upon her head, entered the salt ocean. (82)
Where that Gomatī flows, where Gandhamādana dwells, where Ujjayanta, the best of mountains, and Mount Raivataka are located. || 83 ||
There lies the sacred field of Vastrāpatha; there resides Bhava. There, O best of gods, stands a clay linga in the midst of a thicket.
Indra said: "You must go there together with them; I myself shall worship you. Furthermore, O hunter, show me the Liṅga within the thicket."
Whatever sin arose from the violation of others' wives and so forth during the slaughter of the Daityas, and that which was produced at the killing of Vṛtra—all that I now wash away.
Having spoken thus, they all together reached the summit of the mountain; and having abandoned their vehicles, they set forth on foot.
The king of elephants arrived at the summit of Mount Ujjayanta; for a specific reason, he placed his forefoot upon its peak.
Trampled by him, the best of mountains discharged pure water; the water born from the elephant's foot shall remain forever stable.
Thus it was spoken by the Lord of the Gods out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; all gathered there where Jāli was stationed. (90)
Having worshipped with various flowers on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, and having kept a vigil on that night, he became the pure Hari.
Having worshipped Hari at Vastrāpatha and having installed Indreśvara on Mount Raivataka, he returned to his own abode.
The hunter also arrived at the abode of Hari by means of a celestial chariot; having spoken thus, the god Bhava vanished right there.
Then Vāmana also performed an immersion in that holy ford (tīrtha), assuming the same form as the sky-clad Śiva who had been seen within the solar disc.
Seated in the lotus posture, gentle, and thus meditating upon Him there, he installed the great image and worshipped it for a day.
Then, having attained success for the sake of accomplishing his heart's desire, that Vāmana gave him the name Nemināthaśiva. (96)
Then, at the western part of Bhava, on the ground near the sacred site of Vastrāpatha, Vāmana made his dwelling.
Therefore, this holy place (tīrtha) was declared superior even to barley by the gods, including Indra; for Indra, having approached before Bhava, performed [this rite] as a god.
By your command, this sacred ford shall be six times more radiant than Prabhāsa; by the command of Śiva, it shall become a sacred ford six times superior to all others. (99)
All this has been told; what else do you wish to ask? || 100 ||
The King said: "This incomparable power of Śivarātri has been proclaimed; it was heard that in the past, even by that hunter, this was performed unknowingly. (101)
Now tell me, O Lord: how should other people perform it? What is to be accepted and what is to be abandoned on Śivarātri? Please tell me this. (102)
Sārasvata said: Having attained a human birth and having recognized the Great Lord Maheśvara as God, one should always observe Śivarātri, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (103)
O King, such merit as this arises from performing it even once; for those mortals who perform it constantly, their merit is infinite.
This vow should be performed every year for twelve years; however, if it cannot be performed because the life of men is fickle, [then it may be done otherwise]. || 105 ||
Then, O King, this vow is completed in twelve months; its commencement is made on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha.

Then it should be performed month by month, and it is completed at the end of the month of Pauṣa; however, if some obstacle should arise in the interim due to the turn of fate, [the procedure remains as follows].
There shall be no violation of the vow; furthermore, it must be performed immediately thereafter. Specifically, having fixed the number, exactly twelve [recitations] should be performed. (108)
In this world, an action performed—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is never lost; on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having first performed the morning rites, [one should proceed].
The rule of fasting should be undertaken, and bathing in a river is prescribed; in its absence, one should perform a bath in a pond or similar body of water according to one's ability. (110)
One should not perform an oil massage, nor should one go anywhere; however, one should practice visiting sacred fords (tīrthas), and arriving there during that time is auspicious.
Śivarātri should always be observed by men at a self-manifested (svāyaṃbhūva) liṅga; in its absence, at a highly meritorious liṅga that is more than a hundred years old.
Whatever [liṅga] is on a mountain, in a forest, at the edge of the ocean, by a river, or in a temple of Śiva—that is indeed the Svāyambhuva Liṅga, established there of its own accord.

A linga made of sand, salt, and so forth, when worshipped, is remembered as bestowing fruit; having worshipped it diligently with flowers, incense, and other offerings during the day, a man [attains his goal]. (114)
One should avoid liquor, gambling, women, and clipping the nails; those devoted to celibacy and tranquility should observe the fast.
At night, having gone before the deity, seven mountains should be fashioned, adorned with cooked food, fruits, betel, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
A lamp should be offered with ghee for the purpose of destroying sins; for the greatness of the lamp is to be known as that which bestows liberation. || 117 ||
Lamps should always be offered by men in their homes and in temples; day and night, as well as at the twilights, a lamp should be lit according to one's ability. (118)
The gods on earth are satisfied with even a slight illumination; therefore, at the time of the Śrāddha rite, a lamp must first be offered to the ancestors.
One should keep vigil at night so that sleep does not come; this power of Śivarātri should be heard in the presence of Śiva. (120)
The extensive life-story of Śiva should be heard at night; likewise, singing, dancing, and instrumental music should be performed in the presence of Śiva.
In this way that night is passed, since the primary requirement is the vigil; indeed, during that vigil at night, gifts should be given according to one's ability.
Having bathed again at dawn, the worship of Śiva must be performed; and the ascetics (yatayas) should be honored with food, clothing, and other such gifts.
Householders must provide food for ascetics; twelve, eight, four, or even just one may be fed.
Even a single celibate student who knows Brahman and worships Śiva is equal to thousands [of others] in terms of devotion when he is fed at one's home.

Free from pungent and salty flavors, the food should be eaten by those who have restrained their speech directly upon a leaf-plate; first, however, food must be given to one's sons, friends, and wife.
By this procedure, Śivarātri should be observed by those who maintain the vow of Śiva; when these twelve [days] are complete, then indeed there are vessels of sesame seeds.
Twelve [cows] should indeed be given to the preceptor, Brahmins, and kinsmen; at the conclusion of the vow, a firm black cow accompanied by her calf must be presented.
She should be given clothed in garments and adorned with ornaments, decorated with bells and jewelry, along with a finger-ring, clothes, an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.

A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor and to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity. Having performed this, food should then be provided to the ascetics; having offered various kinds of sweet foods and asked for their forgiveness, one should dismiss them. || 130 ||
Thus, for one who acts with truth, no sin exists; having obtained an excellent lineage and enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures, [he attains liberation]. || 131 ||
Mounted upon a divine celestial chariot and surrounded by divine women, he is led to the abode of Śiva amidst the sounds of music and singing.
Thus has this meritorious Śivarātrivrata been described by me; by performing it, the destruction of all sins of people occurs. (133)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śivarātri," in the second section, the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The King said: "This wonderful narrative has been heard by me through your grace, concerning how Nārada, having seen Nārāyaṇa and Śakra on Mount Mandara," [1]

O Sage, tell me in detail what the Lord of Sages did next; O Master, satisfy me—who am tormented by the illusion arising from the path of worldly existence—with the flood of the nectar-water of your narrative.
Sārasvata said: Then Nārada, having understood that the god had been cursed previously by the twice-born Bhṛgu, realized, "This shall not be otherwise. (3)
O Lord, let that which is to be and that which is present be considered; for this Viṣṇu, having become a dwarf (vāmana), will go to that city.
"Afterwards, he will perform the pleasing task of subduing Bali; otherwise, how can we remain while this most formidable battle is currently underway? (5)
All the battles between gods and dānavas, as well as those among daityas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, reptiles, and birds, were brought to an end.
There is no strife born of co-wives for me, as my fortune has reached its end; the Lord of the Gods was previously restrained by my preceptor—what can I do? (7)
"This man is my venerable preceptor; therefore, I do not curse him. However, since my effort for the sake of battle does not succeed, what shall I do? (8)
Due to some stroke of fate, human effort may not succeed; nevertheless, a wise person must still exert effort toward their goals. For destiny sometimes bears fruit even without human exertion.
What was said is useless, since success comes from effort; having gone to Bali, I shall speak in such a way that he will engage in battle.

"If he does not listen to my words, I shall surely curse him. Having said this, Nārada went with speed to the palace of Bali; in the mere twinkling of an eye, he stood in the sky with his two disciples.
Upon that seven-storied palace, which was as massive as a mountain and exceedingly brilliant, a divine assembly hall was constructed by Viśvakarman.
Upon that [throne] was a divine lion-throne; there sat King Bali, surrounded by all the Daityas who were intent on bold laughter and conversation.
In a celestial palace, he was surrounded by sages and tranquil Brahmins, as well as by Uśanas himself, along with his sons, friends, and wife.
Fanned by divine chowries held in the hands of celestial nymphs, the lord of the Daityas was being praised by the Cāraṇas.
While they remained there, intoxicated with pride, those leaders of the Daityas and Dānavas, all of whom were desirous of battle, consulted with one another.
Rising up again and again, they speak boldly with the gods, saying, "All this, which was ours, has now gone to the three worlds."
Without the intelligence of Śukra, how could the great-souled lord of the Daityas attain victory in battle with the king of the gods, even if they were to share mutual affection? (18)
Why does Bali not request Airāvaṇa, who is ever-intoxicated? And why does Divākara not surrender his clever horse? (19)
As long as the greedy lord of wealth is not overcome on the field of battle, he will not surrender that treasure which has been accumulated by the gods.
The ocean does not reveal its treasures from the depths of the underworld as long as we do not churn it by hurling Mount Mandara against it.
Just as the digits of nectar are consumed sequentially from the moon by the gods, why does the one whose nature is water not give a portion of Bali? 22.
The cool breeze from the celestial river, perfumed by the filaments of lotuses, blows gently in heaven, yet it does not blow so [gently] in the palace of Bali.
Clouds raised by Indra’s bow release water upon the earth; then, impelled by Bali’s sword, they return from the earth back to heaven.
"Upon our surface of the earth, Yama causes people to die; not so in heaven, nor in the netherworld. Behold, oh, the nature of cause and effect! (25)
That Citragupta himself inscribes our lifespan, livelihood, sons, and happiness upon our forehead; even for the gods, there is nothing equal to that.
The seasons of rain, cold, and heat are currently prevailing upon the earth; indeed, terrified, they wander on the ground, neither in heaven nor in the netherworld.
"O gods and dānavas, you are all sisters' sons born of the same vigor. We are established upon the earth; why are we [inferior], and by whom have you been placed above us? (28)
While the ocean was being churned, the lord of the Daityas was deceived by the gods; on one side stood all the gods, and on the other side stood Bali.
And when the jewels have appeared, whatever kind of fortune belongs to whom—such as elephants, horses, wish-fulfilling trees, and those who bestow groups of cows, moons, and tuskers.
"Indeed, after the gods had taken the nectar, we were appointed to drink it; yet you, being excessively arrogant, do not realize that you have been crushed by this [pestle]. (31)
"The nectar remaining after it was drunk has been held by the gods in Satyaloka! Oh, how extremely crooked are the gods; why is the remainder not given back? (32)
Thinking that this is nectar and ambrosia, we have been deceived of the true elixir; those by whom ghee has never been seen consider even sesame oil to be desirable. (33)
The number of Viṣṇu’s crooked deeds cannot be calculated; nevertheless, that which was performed by those who were satisfied and delighted is now being told.
Fair-limbed, beautiful, with lovely eyebrows and full, elevated breasts; she had beautiful hair, a moon-like face, and eyes reaching to her ears.
Her waist is marked by three folds and can be grasped even by a child's fist; her feet are like land-lotuses, and she is adorned with arms like creepers.
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all auspicious marks, that goddess, who fascinates the three worlds, was born during the churning for nectar.
For him from whom she first arose from the nectar, that [nectar] belongs to him for certain; and he who possesses that beautiful-eyed woman has the three worlds under his control.
Deluded by her, all the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas abandoned the churning and prepared to seize her. || 39 ||
"One woman and many gods, dānavas, daityas, and rākṣasas—a very great dispute has arisen as to how this shall be resolved. (40)
Having arrived, Viṣṇu seized them all by the arm and restrained them, saying: "O sirs, why indeed is this mutual dispute being waged for his sake? (41)
An undertaking for the sake of nectar perishes for the sake of a woman; having first made an appointment, she was kissed again by Viṣṇu. (42)
Bearing a divine form, wearing garlands and adorned with a forest-wreath, his body illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having placed a beautiful garland in her hand, Viṣṇu stood before them; raising his arm for everyone to see, Hari spoke these words: || 44 ||
"Let everyone fashion the earrings; let them remain seated upon their own thrones. Having gazed [at him] as she pleases, let Lakṣmī offer the bridegroom’s garland. (45)
He who, being excessively lustful, shall cause the disruption of the *svayaṃvara*, deserves to be put to death by all united together, just like one who covets another's wife. (46)
"May the sin committed by him who violates another's wife result in his own wife being put to death; and may it be so for anyone else who acts likewise—let this be proclaimed. (47)

Knowing Hari to be common to all, she said, "So be it," and acted accordingly: "He who is chosen as your husband from among the gods, dānavas, daityas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas—he shall truly become yours. (48)
Having first deluded her by casting a glance and drawing her toward him, he performed that primary enchantment of women: the gazing with a steady look.
In this very way, whatever is said into his ear while placing a hand there, that which a woman, tormented by the arrows of love, holds in her heart; (50)
In this matter, someone should choose that very [course]; of this there is no doubt. Previously, when a quarrel had arisen, it was for the sake of turning Hari back from that [course].
When she was seized by all of them, she would not release Hari at all; she said, "You alone are my husband; let me go, depart far away! (52)
Then Viṣṇu, having cast [the weapon] far away, entered the host of the gods; and then all of them, having addressed me, departed for their respective abodes.
Vijayā first announced all the gods in their proper order; she then looked at him and, having deliberated, released him. (54)
Śiva is indifferent, peaceful, the beloved of Gaurī, and three-eyed; the three-eyed one is eternally intent on meditation and never looks upon another woman.
When her friend said, "This is your grandfather," she then bowed and departed; having gone far away and observing silence, she did not look back.
"Leave Āditya, who is like a lotus; leave Dahana, whose nature is fire. The wind blows far away, for my father Varuṇa is there. (57)
The Lord of the Gods, being attached to the face of Paulomī, does not please me.
Inflicting killing, binding, cutting, piercing, punishment, and dragging away, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, does not assume a gentle form.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, daityas, pannagas, and rākṣasas.
Then, having seen those most fierce [beings], he proceeds; that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) was seen by him as he gazed upon him with a face whose eyes wandered to the corners of his ears.
Overwhelmed by an excess of good fortune, it was beautiful, enchanting to the senses, and marked by the breaking out of horripilation and drops of perspiration.
Though gazed upon with eyes of wrath by the lords of the gods, dānavas, and daityas, Rāmā chose the beautiful one; she then personally bestowed the garland upon him.
Seeing that conduct of the gods, the Daityas said to one another: "Behold the division among the gods; they have all gone to heaven themselves."
"You humans shall go to the depths of Pātāla; the gods shall go to the surface of the earth and the three worlds; we shall not go to heaven. (65)
"Let human Kṣatriyas rule the kingdom upon the surface of the earth; for if the world is protected, Pātāla may indeed be abandoned. (66)
It was not auspicious that it was performed by certain Rākṣasas born of Daityas and Dānavas; what more need be said? King Bali was the sovereign of the three worlds.
"Then, having distributed the jewels, let the kingdom be shared equally; while they were thus boasting, they beheld Nārada. (68)
He was approaching from the sky like a second sun, holding a staff as thick as Brahma’s rod and carrying a book of battle.
He wore a black antelope skin and was peaceful, holding a parasol, a lute, and a water-pot; his excellent girdle consisted of three strands of muñja grass tied with knots.
He bore the form of Brahmā, was peaceful, adorned with divine rudrākṣas, and hung with a garland of threads knotted according to the elapsed kalpas.
Today, who—proud with the ego of birth—is engaged in a dispute between Brahmā and Śiva, while his mind is intent on contemplation? (72)
Seeing that Nārada had arrived, they stood before him in amazement and said: "O Lord, let your favor be bestowed; please come to my home. (73)

"I am blessed, I have performed meritorious deeds, since you have come to my home. Having been addressed thus by Bali, the Brahmin entered the palace of the Asura; having offered him a seat, water for his feet, and the guest-offering (arghya), the twice-born was duly honored.
Having entered together, all the Daityas and Dānavas lay down; then the Daitya Bali, accompanied by Śukra, spoke to Nārada.
"This kingdom, these wives, these sons, and I myself are my offering. Tell me what you require here; giving is my foremost vow. (76)
Nārada said: Those Brahmins who are satisfied with devotion alone are true Brahmins, the deities of the earth; but those who, though honored according to their means, beg again, are base.
I have been honored by you and am delighted; I have no need for wealth. I am pleased with your kingdom, as well as with your sacrifices, gifts, and religious observances.
"O Bala, I perceive some displeasure caused toward you by the gods; for even though he is being honored by you, the King of the Gods is not satisfied. (79)
"All the gods cannot endure your sovereignty upon the surface of the earth; because of your conflict with the gods, I have become a source of distress even in heaven. (80)
That Kṣatriya who, having first girded himself for battle, advances against the army in the lands of the enemy, is victorious and his kingdom prospers. (81)
"I have heard that the destruction of your kingdom will come to pass; knowing this, let what is appropriate be done immediately. (82)
Bali said: "O Lord, tell me those qualities by which a king governs his kingdom; you must also tell me that worthy recipient to whom gifts should be given by me. (83)
Nārada said: A king endowed with twenty-six qualities governs the kingdom; he obtains the fruit of sovereignty—listen, for I shall tell you of that. (84)
One should practice the Dharma without harshness; one should abandon affection for the non-believer; one should pursue wealth without cruelty; and one should pursue pleasure without arrogance. (85)
One should speak kindly without being fawning; one should be brave without being boastful; one should be a giver without being miserly; and one should be bold without being harsh. (86)
He should not form alliances with the ignoble, nor engage in strife with his kinsmen; he should employ spies through trustworthy agents and carry out his business without causing oppression.
One should not speak of one's wealth in times of adversity, nor should one speak of one's own virtues; one should not take from the virtuous, nor should one take refuge with a wicked person.
One should not inflict punishment without investigation, nor should one reveal one's secret counsel; one should not bestow gifts upon the greedy, nor place trust in those who have done harm.

A king should keep his wives well-guarded by trusted attendants, and he himself should be protected by others who are compassionate; he should not indulge excessively in women, and he should eat what is wholesome, not what is unwholesome. (90)
Free from theft, one should honor those worthy of respect and serve the guru without deceit; one should worship the Divine without hypocrisy and desire prosperity that is not ignoble.
One should serve [the teacher] with affection, being skillful and knowledgeable of the proper time; one should always speak words of consolation, showing favor and never censuring.

One should not strike a Brahmin, nor, having slain enemies, should one leave no remnant of them. One should not give way to anger without cause, and one should be gentle even toward those who do harm.
Thus, if you desire prosperity in this world, you should remain long in the kingdom; [therefore, attend to] austerities, Vedic study, charity, pilgrimages, and the stages of life.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the self-awakening attained through yoga. You must cultivate detachment from worldly existence and perform the worship of Brahmins. (95)
"One should sacrifice with various sacrifices; Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is to be meditated upon. Having arrived here by chance, I shall go to the Raivataka mountain. (96)

There dwells the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, and there flows the river that purifies the three worlds; there also stands the Śivā tree, endowed with many flowers and fruits. Having gone there, I shall perform that vow which is dear to Viṣṇu.
Bali said: Who is this one named Raivataka? What is the vow that is dear to Viṣṇu? And which trees are declared to belong to Śiva? Tell me all that. || 98 ||
Nārada said: O Lord of Daityas, in ancient times at the beginning of the Yuga, the mountains were created with wings; later, after reflection, Brahmā made them immovable once again.
Great-bodied beings leap up and fall down at will; even Meru, Mandara, and Kailāsa remain firm and stable by his word alone.
Those who were not restrained, however, were made stable by Indra; on the southern peak of Meru is that mountain known as Kumuda.
Divine, winged, golden, and surrounded by celestial trees—above it stands the divine city of Viṣṇu, created by Viṣṇu himself.
In its center is a divine house wherein Lakṣmī always resides; on a peak of Mount Meru is a beautiful city, and therein is a delightful mansion.
There dwells that Lord Bhava, where Bhavānī is established; there is the delightful assembly hall of Maheśvara, made of gold and adorned with jewels.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, surrounded by the gods headed by Brahmā; in that city, Viṣṇu always goes to see the god Maheśvara.
Because it was adorned everywhere with golden water-lilies (kumudas), the gods who assembled there gave it the name Kumuda.
Once, the Lord Rudra arrived at that mountain to behold from its beautiful peak that city protected by Viṣṇu.
Seeing Hara arrived at his home, he was honored by Hari; Gaurī, having been worshipped by Lakṣmī, remained there filled with joy.
As the two of them sat upon a single seat consulting with one another, Hara perceived the cause and related everything to Hari.
"This city must be built by you on Mandara, the best of mountains; I am not to be questioned regarding the reason, for it shall certainly come to pass. (110)
"Only Hara knows the cause; no one else at all does. Having said, "So be it," they both remained there, as did that Parvata.
Seeing that Rudra had arrived, Kumuda came forward in person, saying: "I am blessed, I have performed meritorious deeds, for he has come to my home."
"O best of mountains, what boon do you grant me?"—being thus addressed by the two of them, that mountain of deluded intellect chose a boon from them. (113)
Because it will serve as the cause for a future task, it shall not be in vain; wherever I am, there you two must dwell—let this be my boon.
"Having come into my presence, you must remain for a day of Brahmā. Having said, "So be it," both Hari and Hara departed together with their wives.
Listen now to what occurred at the beginning of the Kumuda kalpa regarding the origin of that fifth Manu, formerly renowned by the name Raivata. || 116 ||
There was a highly fortunate rishi renowned as Ṛtavāk; at the end of the Revatī [yuga], a son was born to that great-souled man who had been childless. (117)
He performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules, as well as the initiation and others; yet that king remained devoid of virtuous conduct.
From the moment he was born, that sage suffered from a most formidable and persistent affliction of chronic disease.
And his mother, afflicted by the disease of leprosy, fell into great distress; the sage, being sorrowful, wondered, "What is this? || 120 ||
But a foolish son of dull intellect causes suffering to his father; especially when he goes astray, that indeed brings sorrow upon sorrow. (121)
For human beings, childlessness is better than having a bad son; for it does not bring benefit to friends, nor does it lead to the satisfaction of the ancestors.
A good son dwells in the hearts of his parents day after day; fie upon the birth of that evildoer who brings sorrow to his parents! 123.
Blessed are those sons who are esteemed by all the world, who act for the benefit of others, who are peaceful, and who are devoted to virtuous deeds. (124)
