For a living being, having a bad son leads to hell and not to heaven; for such a son brings no peace, lacks joy, and is overwhelmed by suffering and grief. 125.
A wicked son indeed causes distress to his friends and joy to his enemies; moreover, he brings premature old age upon his parents. 126.
Nārada said: Thus, with his mental state burning due to the conduct of his exceedingly wicked son, the sage questioned the aged Garga.
Ṛtavāk said: "In former times, the Vedas were studied by me according to the prescribed rule with great devotion; having completed my studies, I took a wife. (128)

For those rites pertaining to the Śruti and Smṛti, and so forth, which ought to be performed with one's wife, have been duly accomplished according to the injunctions and in accordance with his desires. || 129 ||

"O Sage, this child was conceived for the sake of obtaining a son; yet he has fallen away from the status of a male. Is this due to his own fault, or the fault of his mother, or mine? O wise one, tell me, for he has been born as a bringer of sorrow to us because of his wicked character. (130)
Garga said: "O best of sages, this son of yours was born at the end of the Revatī asterism; therefore, he has been born for your sorrow during this evil time. (131)
This transgression of yours belongs neither to his mother nor to his family; rather, another cause for misconduct has come to an end with Revatī. (132)
The Gaṇḍānta occurring between Revatī and Aśvinī, as well as between Āśleṣā and Maghā, and between Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, is declared to be fraught with danger.

"Those men, women, and horses who are born under the three Gaṇḍas do not remain in the house for long; even while remaining, they are terrifying. Having been addressed thus by Garga, the extremely irascible king became exceedingly enraged.
Ṛtavāk said: "Since my only son was born at the end of the Revatī [nakṣatra]," || 135 ||
"Does Revatī not know that this brahmin will curse me? Therefore, let Revatī fall from the sky, burning with flames! (136)
Nārada said: When those words had been thus spoken by him, the constellation Revatī fell down.
While all the world looked on, their minds filled with wonder. || 137 ||
By the power of the Lord’s will, the constellation Revatī fell upon the mountain peak; it descended all around the Kumuda mountain.
He arrived in the land of Surāṣṭra and fell upon the auspicious ground where the great mountain Ujjayanta, the son of Himācala, is located. || 139 ||
In the past, a mutual friendship was established between you and Kumuda; wherever you shall abide, there I too will certainly remain. (140)
Having thus resolved, he then took the water of the Gaṅgā along with that of the Yamunā, as well as the meritorious water of the Sarasvatī, and arrived to sprinkle him.
They remained together until the dissolution of the world; and because of his falling there, that mountain Kumuda became known as Raivataka.
O Lord of the Earth, the golden Kumudādri is exceedingly beautiful on the entire earth, having been produced again from the cyavana of Revatī.
O King, that best of mountains was born with an outer luster like that of a lotus; yet in its center, that supreme mountain was the color of Meru, being made of gold.
Then Mount Raivataka begot a daughter, born with the splendor of Revatī and possessing a face like that of Revatī.
A royal sage named Pramucu beheld that beautiful woman; O best of kings, he gave her the name Revatī, as if she were his own daughter.
That excellent woman became renowned everywhere as Revatī; she was a place consisting of all splendor and a refuge for the waters of all holy pilgrimage sites.
The waters of the Sarasvatī remained there in those hollows, joined with the currents of the Gaṅgā as well as those of the Yamunā—those three [rivers] being present there. || 148 ||
There is the famous Revatī-kuṇḍa, where Revatī was born; by remembering it, seeing it, or bathing there, the destruction of all sins occurs.
That young woman was raised by that high-souled Pramuñca; she attained her youth upon that Raivataka mountain.
Then, seeing her endowed with youth, the sage Pramuca reflected in solitude: "Who will become her husband? (151)
Having repeatedly offered oblations into the fire, that best of the twice-born questioned his preceptor: "Be gracious to me and tell me, who shall become her husband? (152)
"There is no one else like her in this lineage; what shall I do? Having risen from the sacrificial fire-pit, the Fire-god (Havyavāhana) spoke thus. 153.
Listen to my words, O Brahmin, concerning him who shall become her husband: he will be born in the lineage of Priyavrata, endowed with great strength and prowess. (154)
The son of Vikramaśīla, born from the womb of Kālindī, shall be named Durdama; he will indeed become the lord of the earth and her husband. (155)
In the meantime, that king Durdama arrived; desiring to hunt deer on the mountain, he did not see the sage at home. He cried out, "O beloved, where has my father gone? Come, tell me the truth! (156)
Nārada said: Standing in the fire-chamber, he heard those pleasant words: "Who is this addressing me as 'dear one' in my own house? (157)
The sage beheld the high-souled King Durdama; seeing Durdama, the sage rejoiced and spoke to Gautama.
"Bring water for honoring and water for the feet for this disciple who is endowed with discipline; first, let this king, who has arrived after a long time, be attended to. (159)
"The son-in-law is now a king, and my daughter is worthy of him. Thereupon, the king reflected upon the matter of his son-in-law.

In accordance with the prescribed rite, the king accepted the *arghya* offering by the command of the twice-born. Then the great sage, the brahmin, [addressed] him as he sat upon his seat, having received the *arghya*.

He addressed the eminent king with these relevant words: "O King, is all well in the city, in the treasury, the army, the allies, the servants, the ministers, and the subjects; and likewise, O mighty-armed one, is it well with yourself, upon whom everything is established? (162)
And your wife who stays here in this place is well; tell me of the welfare of the others who are in your home.
The king said: "By your grace, there is no misfortune anywhere in my kingdom. O sage, I am filled with curiosity; who is my wife here?"
Pramuca said: "O best of kings, do you not know that Revatī is your excellent wife? How is it that she, who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, has been forgotten by you? (165)
The king said: [I shall give you] Subhadrā, Śāntapāpā, likewise Kāverītanayā, Sūrātmajānujātā, and Kadambā, who possesses excellent offspring. (166)
"I know Vipāṭhā and Nandinī as my wives staying in my house; I do not know at all where my wife Revatī is. (367)
The sage said: "O best of kings, she who was just now called 'Priyā' is indeed your beloved Revatī; her name shall not be otherwise."
The king said: "There is no fault committed through one's disposition; let those words of mine be forgiven. O best of the twice-born, once they have issued from the mouth, I have no power over them."
The sage said: "There is no fault caused by your disposition; I understand this, so act accordingly. You were described to me by Agni; today you shall become my son-in-law."

By these and other such words, the king considered Revatī to be his wife; meanwhile, the sage, prepared to perform the marriage according to the prescribed rites, said to the father of the maiden: "O Father, listen to something from me. (171)
"O father, if you wish to perform my marriage with my husband, then by your grace, let the constellation Revatī perform my marriage. (172)

The sage said: "O blessed lady, the constellation Revatī is certainly not situated in the sky in conjunction with the moon; there are other constellations as well, O fair-browed one, that are suitable for marriage. (173)
The maiden said: "Father, without him, time appears incomplete to me; Father, how can there be a marriage for one such as I when it is incomplete? (174)
Pramuñca said: "The ascetic known as Ṛtavāk became enraged toward Revatī; by him, in his anger, that bear was struck down. (175)
It is known to you that I have already promised her to him as his wife; if you do not desire the marriage, a great crisis has come upon us.
The maiden said: "That sage is indeed a speaker of truth; why did he himself undergo such penance? Am I not the daughter of my father, who was not [neglected] by you, O wretched Brahmin? (177)
The sage said: "You are not the daughter of a mere Brahmin-scholar; there is no ascetic superior to me. You are my daughter and must be given by me; I am unable to do otherwise. (178)
The maiden said: "If my father is an ascetic, then why is this marriage not performed once again by placing me upon that star in the sky? (179)
The seer said:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours. O auspicious lady, be full of joy; I shall place the constellation Revatī upon the path of the moon for your sake. (180)

Then, by the power of his asceticism, that great sage, the best of the twice-born, restored the constellation Revatī to its former state as conjoined with the Moon; and having performed the marriage of his daughter, he spoke to his son-in-law: || 181 ||
"O protector of the earth, let that which pertains to your marriage be told; what may I give you? Even if it be difficult to obtain, I shall give it, for I possess great ascetic power. (182)
The king said: "O sage, I am born in the lineage of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu; by your grace, I choose you as my son to be the sovereign of a Manvantara. (183)
The sage said: "There shall be a protector of the earth possessed of great strength and prowess; having bathed in Revatīkuṇḍa, Revatī will give birth to a son. (184)
Having done this, the king departed, and she gave birth to a son; he was given the name Raivata and became that Manu, the king.
And he said at that time: "On this Raivataka mountain, women shall perform ablutions; their sons will be very powerful, long-lived, and free from suffering and poverty. (186)
Nārada said: O King, when this was said, Parvata became elongated and fell; these two were recognized as the gods Hari and Śaṅkara together with their wives. || 187 ||
As soon as they were remembered, the two arrived; because they had been bound by him previously, it was decided that "you two must remain wherever I am. (188)

Therefore, those two gods, Viṣṇu and Hara, were stationed on that best of mountains; on the delightful Raivataka mountain and in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river, Revatī worshipped the god Hari, and he spoke to her.
"And by your word, O Brāhmaṇa, your conjunction with the Moon shall take place in the sky; choose another boon as well, whatever resides in your heart, for I am pleased. (190)
Revatī said: "O Lord, you should always remain on Mount Raivataka; wherever I have performed my ablutions, there those people shall bathe. (191)

"May their residence be in Viṣṇupura"—this was the boon chosen by me. "So be it," he then said, and remained on Mount Raivataka; Dāmodara himself, four-armed, also took up his abode there along with Rudra.
All the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, remained together with Viṣṇu; indeed, when the ocean of milk was being churned, a tree emerged.
Because she crushed the gods and demons, she is known as Sāmardakī; O King, Lakṣmī always resides in this tree, as if in her father’s house. (194)
The tree known as Śivālakṣmī is resorted to by the best of the gods; that tree is indeed remembered as Vaiṣṇava by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā. || 195 ||

In ancient times, he was released by all of them after being meditated upon on Mount Raivataka; those who shall perform the pilgrimage of this tree on the day of Hari [shall likewise attain liberation]. (196)

O best of kings, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, their sons and grandsons shall become preeminent in virtue; in the end, they shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt. (197)
Bali said: "How is this Vaiṣṇava vow, which is dear to Viṣṇu, to be performed? Tell me by what ritual the night vigil (jāgaraṇa) should be observed. (198)
Nārada said: Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, one should bathe in a river, a pond, a large well, a small well, or even at home. (199)
Having gone to a mountain or even to a forest where that auspicious goddess is found, she should be worshipped with beautiful flowers at night, and men should perform a vigil.
One hundred and eight fruits should be used for circumambulating it; having circumambulated the mountain, the men should then eat the fruit.
A water-pot filled with water, accompanied by a vessel, should be prepared; sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) should be provided, and a lamp should be lit according to the prescribed rite. || 202 ||
In this manner, those intent on listening to the sacred narratives should remain awake; thus, embodied beings are liberated from the sins born of the Kali age and produced by the body. (203)
At the end of their bodies' lives, all those men are honored in the abode of Hari.
Sārasvata said: Having spoken thus to the Daitya, Nārada departed for Mount Raivataka. The lord of the Daityas deliberated: "What should be done by me now? (205)
"O best of gods, conflict with the gods does not please me. (206)

The ministers said: "For those Kṣatriyas who abide by their duty, there is no great forbearance in their homes; they will consider even one who is powerless as such, because they come to him of their own accord. Therefore, we shall go together ourselves to the Lord of the Gods."
Having heard this, he first sounded the drum at the abode of the gods; then, taking up their armies, the Daityas set out for Mount Meru.
Where that delightful city of the King of the Gods is situated to the east; having learned that the army was approaching on Mount Meru. (209)
O King, the divine army set out at the command of the king of the gods; on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru, there was mutual combat.
When the entire army of the gods was joined by the army of the Daityas, a battle resembling the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) then took place between the two.
Having mounted Airāvaṇa, the king of the gods arrived; having mounted his chariot, the lord of the Daityas arrived; others likewise assembled for battle. || 212 ||
Since the gods are partakers of sacrifice, they do not desire war; thus, even upon seeing Bali, Airāvaṇa did not move from his position at the front in the battle.
Surrounded by the elephants of the quarters, he turns his back and flees from the battle—that arm with which Bali made his solemn resolve during the sacrifice.
With that [weapon], he indeed repelled all the gods in the encounter; being thus warded off, they turned their faces away and departed—what could the king of the gods do? || 215 ||
The vajra does not perform its function, nor does it move when released from the hand. || 216 ||
In this way, many battles took place between those two at that time; the exceedingly powerful Daityas could not be slain in battle even by the gods.
The gods stood with their hopes fixed on Bālāka, but they were awakened by their preceptor; all those immortals and deities were thus restrained by Śukra.
Having learned that the fifth incarnation of Hari, Vāmana, was present, the Lord of the Gods, exceedingly joyful, ruled his kingdom in Amarāvatī.
The lord of the Daityas danced in battle; he worshipped the gods in his own home; the Daityas retreated to Pātāla, while men ruled the kingdom.
Then all the hosts of gods, together with the deities, deliberated: "The Daitya rules over the two worlds; the Lord of the Gods rules over heaven. (221)
Vāmana must endure this on Mount Raivata only so long as the task of the gods—who, though conquerors of the Daityas, have maintained silence—is accomplished.
From the moment Vāmana was born upon the surface of the earth, from that time forward, ill omens appeared for the Daityas. || 223 ||
Having entered the city, that jackal howls discordantly at night; crows wander through the city, crying out incessantly day and night. || 224 ||
Black, fierce serpents with virulent poison slither through the houses; herons, vultures, and cranes wander in confusion, circling above the city.
Fetuses are born deformed in women, cows, or does; there is no ghee or milk at all, and oil is not found in sesame seeds. (226)
The people of the countryside were constantly fighting with one another; there was a woman who was dark, with a terrifying face, long hair, and piercing eyes.
Unrecognized, she went weeping toward her home in the city; "Who is this? Why is this ascetic smeared with ashes not recognized? (228)
The ascetic, observing a vow of silence and naked, goes before him from house to house; behind him, he beats the ḍamaru drum most fiercely and utters the sound "hum."
Clouds enraged out of season release abundant water; their wombs filled with raindrops, the mountains roar loudly. (230)
An earthquake occurred and a conflagration of the quarters also arose; and the entire pack of dogs, having gathered together, raised their muzzles high.
The owl constantly shrieks at night within the city, uttering its cry; the destruction of Bali’s kingdom has occurred, and a comet has risen in the sky during the night.
A piercing with stakes is seen made upon the solar disc; in the sky crowded with headless trunks, the moon does not shine. (233)
He who was born at the transition of the Yugas was born under the conjunction with Rohiṇī; by people of superior merit, the constellations are counted during the day. (234)
A reversal of seeds occurred among the earth, women, cows, and female deer; horses suddenly neighed, yet the elephants did not display rut.

The counsel deliberated by ministers is leaked when the kingdom is on the verge of ruin; it is like a fire fed with offerings of ghee that blazes up even when no longer being sacrificed into by the twice-born.
A fierce, purifying wind blows, causing the trees to whirl in its vortex; banners blaze atop the shrines, and the sky becomes grey with dust.
These and many other powerful portents occurred in the house when Vāmana was born, following the arrival of Nārada.
Furthermore, a terrible thing occurred: the sight of dreams by day; when the Daityas were arming themselves, they fell down and continued to fall. (239)
Having seen such omens regarding his army, Bali does not advance; he remains constantly at home and rules the kingdom.

There was no comfort for his body; he suffered from aching limbs and a headache. Afflicted by fever, he could not sleep, nor did he eat or drink. What he ate did not digest, and everyone in the world was thrown into great agitation.
Seeing the world in such a state of reversal, Bali, his mind agitated and distressed, consulted with the brahmins, asking, "What is this? (242)
Having summoned Śukra and seated him in the assembly hall, the Daitya, endowed with supreme devotion, inquired after his welfare and said: "All this has become contrary; explain that to me. (243)
"O Guru, that which was spoken to me by Nārada shall come true; together with the Brahmins, please prescribe for me the rites to pacify these portents. (244)

Śukra said: "To pacify the portents, a sacrifice should be performed in which one's entire possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Let it be conducted for twelve years together with Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. (245)
"May the ṛṣis, the brāhmaṇas, and those sages who are celibate students come to this great sacrifice, even those who reside far away. (246)

"To the east of the city, a sacrificial pavilion (yajñamaṇḍapa) should be constructed. O King, whatever gift is desired by each person, that should be given by you. Having said, "I shall do so," he became intent upon the sacrifice. || 247 ||
Having summoned all the brahmins who were skilled in the rites of sacrifice, they undertook the initiation for the sacrifice in which every possible sacrificial fee was bestowed.
"If a Brahmin asks me here for my everything, I shall give it; if asked, I will give even my body, sons, friends, and wife. (249)

"Gifts must always be given by me to the Brahmins during this sacrifice; even if I am forbidden, I must not remain still, for it is my firm resolve that I shall give. If, when asked, I do not give, then my sacrifice will be in vain. (250)
Having constructed a divine pavilion extending for many yojanas, gifts such as food and clothing were distributed there. (251)
The seven sages descended from the sky to the surface of the earth; all the brahmins who exist on the earth arrived there from every direction.
And the Kṣatriyas, having arrived with various kinds of wealth, presented it to the king once the sacrificial rites had commenced. (253)
Actors, dancers, and beggars arrived from as far as the ocean; the sound of singing and musical instruments was mingled with the resonance of the Vedas.
When begged with the words "Give! Give!", the three worlds were made deaf; there was no word "Do not give," nor even the slight phrase "Give a little. (255)
Whatever object anyone requests, that very thing is given to him there; for there is no brahmin who asks him excessively.
And for the sake of food and clothing, the twice-born do not accept gold, gems, silver, nor likewise horses, chariots, and elephants. (257)
The twice-born do not accept houses, cattle, land, or villages; content with the kingdom of Bali, what would they do with wealth? (258)
In this manner, the great sacrifice proceeds, in which one's entire possession is given as the sacrificial fee.
Others dance, sing, recite, and praise the sacrifice accompanied by abundant gifts; Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the planets, the Sun, and the Moon were propitiated with oblations and mantras.

Some praise Bali, others the Guru, some the Hotṛ priest, and others the attendants; yet even for Prajāpati or the Lord of the Gods, it would not suffice, and he will surely depart. Having bestowed the kingdom upon the foremost of the twice-born, he shall go to the netherworld (rasātala) accompanied by his sons and friends.
"Thus do the Brahmins speak; the Daityas hear them and say, 'What is this they are saying? Standing before Bali, they speak together: 'Bali, being delighted, gives whatever is requested.'"

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Bali’s Sacrifice," in the second section, the *Vastrāpathakṣetramāhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 17 ||
The King said: When Vāmana arrived at the great sacred field of Vastrapatha, what did he do from that time forward? Tell me that in detail.
Sārasvata said: O best of kings, Vāmana took up residence before Bhava after bathing in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā and worshipping Bhava with devotion.
Seated upon an excellent seat covered with a black antelope skin in a solitary, pure place, free from thorns and bones.
Having assumed the lotus posture, the wise and best of the twice-born became motionless; fixing his neck in its place, he gazed straight at the tip of his nose.
Having abandoned anxiety for his home, fields, wife, and wealth, and having cast off the illusory power of Viṣṇu, he remained silent with his senses subdued.

Without food, having conquered anger and being liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra, the twice-born placed his arms in the lotus posture with his eyes slightly closed; perceiving the mind to be exceedingly fickle, he made it steady within his heart.
Through the practice of gradual training, he unified within himself those distinct vital airs known as prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Having thus placed it in the heart and grasped it at all the joints, he brought it to the station of Brahman and firmly united it with Brahman.
When, having taken in the external air, one fills the body, that is to be known as *pūraka* (inhalation); now I shall describe *recaka* (exhalation).
O King, when the internal air gradually moves to the outside, that is to be known as *recaka* (exhalation); through the cessation [of movement], it becomes *kumbhaka* (retention). || 10 ||
When yogis know the twenty-five principles (tattvas), they are liberated from all sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes. || 11 ||

The King said: What are the principles? Who is the embodied soul? Tell me, what is to be known by yogis? And how does one become endowed with yoga, having brought about the true nature of knowledge? (12)

Īśvara said: From that [Prakṛti] arose Nature (prakṛti), and from that came the intellect (buddhi); from that arose the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from that the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka). Thus, this Prakṛti is eightfold.
Know that there are exactly five sense organs and five organs of action; the mind is the eleventh, and there are also the five great elements. (14)
In the Sāṃkhya system, the group is proclaimed in detail as sixteenfold; there are twenty-four principles (tattvas), and the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
He who says "give" within the body perceives both the body and the self; they find that Supreme Self, the twenty-sixth, beyond the twenty.
Those various types of postures and so forth should always be understood first; when they perceive within their heart a light resembling the flame of a lamp. (17)
Those in whom the true nature of arisen gnosis exists are called yogins by the wise; first, it wears away old age, and diseases perish far away. (18)
When the destruction of all sins has been exhausted, he meets death afterwards; yet, once dead, no man exists in this world, provided the yogin knows this for himself. (19)

Then, having closed the gates, he releases the ten vital breaths; having brought about the destruction of merit and sin, the breaths of the yogis depart, and they attain the sovereignty of the powers such as *aṇimā* in the abode of Śiva.
By means of this yoga of meditation, a person perceives existence; everything conceived by the mind is fully attained through the vision of existence.
While the brahmin Vāmana was thus seated in the presence of Bhava, he then beheld Nārada descending from the sky.
Vāmana said: "O great sage, is it well with you today? For what reason have you come? I bow to you, O great sage; you are indeed Brahman in the three worlds."
Nārada said: "I have arrived from the heavenly world; what can I say regarding your welfare?"
The day of Brahmā is filled by the comings and goings of the Sun; at the end of the day, night arises, and during the night, the deities perish.
What need is there to speak of the world of mortals, where beings die day after day? The sky has become filled with smoke, and the gods have gone to the abode of Bali.
The seven sages, practicing celibacy under Brahmā, went there; and Hāhā, Hūhū, Tuṃburu, as well as Nārada and Parvata, also went.
The hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas arrived at Bali’s palace; Bali himself was performing a sacrifice for the pacification of portents.
I wish to go to that very place to see the sacrifice in the house of Bali; Bali has performed nine thousand sacrifices, falling short by one.

When this [sacrifice] is completed, the entire realm of the Daityas shall be restored; for some extraordinary undertaking has been commenced in this sacrificial rite, by which I shall grant whatever is requested by the twice-born themselves.
Even if it must be withheld from me, let my word be true: I shall give up even myself, my wife, my kingdom, and my dear sons. (31)
"If I do not grant what has been requested, let my sacrifice be in vain. By these words, a great headache arose within me; having made such a promise, how will this sacrifice be completed?
I saw no means of destruction; I wandered through the three worlds until, recognizing you as the one who brings about my ruin, I have come before you. (33)
"Act now in such a way that the sacrifice is not rendered incomplete. || 34 ||
Vāmana said: "O great sage, listen to my words: what power do I possess? Who am I, and why should I act, now that the gods have assembled at the sacrifice? (35)
"How can all these sages and brahmins be rendered fruitless? Furthermore, O Brahmarṣi, Lord of Brahmā, hear my words. (36)
Neither wife nor sons [bring you joy]; why is your nature such that you find no happiness without war, nor any happiness without strife? (37)

Whether it be of such a kind or otherwise, even idle talk is always dear; likewise are bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, and the libations for the ancestors and the gods. (36)
"Nārada does one thing, while the Brāhmaṇas do another; curiosity has arisen within me as well, O Great Sage—speak quickly! (39)
Nārada said: Listen, O Vāmana; when the Pādma Kalpa had passed and at the end of the night, the cosmic egg was pervaded by water, and nothing else existed.
The God of gods reclines upon the waters, and he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa; he is Brahmā and he is Śiva—there is no distinction between them one another. (41)
When they became divided, then those three deities also became divided; thus, having become divided, they were then established as the three [Vārāhakalpas].
The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara consist of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas; thus Brahmā performs creation, and Hari protects it.

Hara withdraws everything—the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving. Having thus set things in motion, the Lord of Gods sat upon an excellent seat on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa and consulted one another.
"Among these three, which god is the best? Who is the eldest? Who is superior in qualities? There is no fourth who knows [this]; suddenly those three stood there. (45)
The light arising from them became unified in the sky; joined with the measurement of time, that solar orb began to revolve.
"I am the eldest! Indeed, I am the eldest!"—such was the dispute between Hara and Brahmā. From the anger of those two as they contended, I was born from the mouth of the Lord. (47)
"O Lord, how is it that you do not know what was said by Brahmā at that time: 'In the past, your ten incarnations, beginning with the Fish and the Tortoise, were for the sake of sporting'? (48)
Having gone there, she was restrained by Rudra with the words, "A quarrel is not fitting for you. Viṣṇu likewise performed those ten incarnations.
"O best of the twice-born, I was born from the mouth of Brahmā at the beginning of the kalpa; since my birth arose from a quarrel, therefore quarreling is dear to me. (50)
"O Hari, how can a creation be performed by me, a Vedāntin, when at the beginning of the kalpa, Brahmā himself previously reflected [upon it]? (51)
"I do not know where the lost Vedas have gone; nor do I know whether the earth remains in its place or has sunk below. (52)
"I no longer have the power to move within the water; you must protect the creation by means of your ten incarnations. (93)
"You shall become a great fish, a water-dweller, in a mighty river; having taken up the Vedas, you must give them to me with speed. (54)

And so the Lord assumed the great form of a fish in the waters and, in ancient times, brought back the Vedas and gave them to Brahmā; then, having again assumed the form of a tortoise, you shall support Mount Mandara.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu [replied]: "Lakṣmī will choose you as her husband; formerly, I witnessed your wondrous deeds during the churning."
When the earth reached the netherworld (rasātala), it was no longer visible; for the sake of establishing a place for the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), it could not be seen there either. || 57 ||
"Assume the form of a boar," he was urged by Brahmā himself; having assumed the form of a great boar, he went beneath the earth.
And then, having lifted up the earth with the tip of his tusk, Viṣṇu restored it to its proper place, just as one might lift a clump of musta grass from the surface of the ground.
Indeed, the third incarnation of Hara was truly captivating, by which he supported that vast earth together with its mountains.
I shall indeed describe the fourth [incarnation], the most terrible Narasiṃha. The Ādityas are the sons of Aditi, while the two sons of Diti were of great strength.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu and the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa [ruled]; all the gods were stationed in heaven, while the Daityas and Dānavas dwelt in Pātāla.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu ruled over the kingdom in Rasātala, while the sons of Manu were established upon the surface of the earth by the gods and Dānavas.
O twice-born one, having transgressed that established order and having conquered the lord of the gods, Hiraṇyakaśipu ruled the kingdom upon the surface of the earth.
Having taken possession of the earth consisting of seven islands, he, desiring to seize Amarāvatī, enjoyed it while being honored by his sons and grandsons.
That dull-witted man tormented his sons, headed by Prahlāda; while the other sons were being made to recite, Prahlāda also recited that same thing.
Indeed, by the recitation of which that demon experienced such agony, he no longer respected the gods because of his sovereignty over the two worlds.
Pleased by his ascetic penance, the Lord Brahmā granted him a boon: "O best of gods, you shall possess immortality from both gods and men. (68)
May my death never come from anyone whatsoever; were it to happen, may he be partly a lion and partly a man, or one who is a mountain-bearer. (69)
"Therefore, pierced by your claws, I shall not die upon the surface of the earth. Having said, "So shall it be," Brahmā departed in amazement.
As time passed, a great conflict arose within him: "What will the gods do to me? What need have I for Viṣṇu? (71)
"I am always to be worshipped with sacrifices; what will Rudra do to me?"—while he was thus behaving, Prahlāda praised that Hari.
He remembers that very Hari by whom his death is brought about; and when he is being restrained, he cries out, "Hari! Hari! (73).

I ever remember Viṣṇu, the sole leader of the world, who has four arms, holds a conch, a mace, and a sword, is clad in yellow garments, and is marked with the Kaustubha gem; he who grants liberation the very moment he is remembered. (74)
Agitated by these words, the Daitya commanded the other Daityas: "Kill that wicked one by means of elephants, serpents, water, or fire! (75)

Prahlāda said: Viṣṇu is in the elephant, Viṣṇu is in the serpent, Viṣṇu is in the water, and Viṣṇu is in the fire. O Daitya, Viṣṇu resides in you and Viṣṇu resides in me; without Viṣṇu, even the hosts of Daityas do not exist.

When, even though being slain, he did not meet his death anywhere, and when Hiraṇyakaśipu’s chest was scorched by the fire of his wrath, he then placed his son upon the tip of his mouth in order to instruct him.
With harsh words, he prepared to kill his own son; "Fie on you! You praise Nārāyaṇa; if you praise him again, you praise my enemy! (78)
"I shall pluck your head like a flower with my excellent sword! I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, I am Rudra, and I am Indra—choose a boon! (79)
"O child, setting aside your own father, whom else do you praise?"
When the boy did not study nor praise his own father, Prahlāda was struck with a heavy staff and urged again: "Speak, my disciple! Give me a single word as my teacher’s fee. (81)
Since my master is pleased with me, he bestows abundant wealth.
Prahlāda said: Strike me first; I shall do as you say, O Guru, so that I may praise Viṣṇu, by whom this triple world with its moving and unmoving beings is pervaded. (83)
May that Viṣṇu, who is the creator, the nourisher, and the peaceful one, be gracious to me. Viṣṇu is Brahmā, Viṣṇu is Hara, Viṣṇu is Indra, Vāyu, Yama, and Anala.

The principles beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) reside within the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa; he is established within the body of the father, within the body of the guru, and likewise within my own body. (85)
Knowing this, how can I praise a dying man who is the lowest of men? (86)
The Guru said: "O disciple, who among men is the lowest? One who is base from birth until death. Why do you not praise your father as he dies, instead praising Hari, Hari?"
Prahlāda said: He who does not utter the two syllables "Ha-ri" while eating, sleeping, traveling, suffering from fever, spitting, or in battle—even at the moment of death—is the lowest of men.

In times of fear, in the royal court, in battle, during illness, in sexual union, in the forest, or when incapacitated, in renunciation, or at the moment of death—those fools and lowest of men who remain on the ground remember only their mother and father. (89)
I have no mother, I have no father, and I have no kinsmen or people; there is no one at all except Hari. Whatever is appropriate, let that be done.
Enraged by these and other such words, the Daitya rose up to kill him; then his mother arrived and stood before her son. (91)

"Brothers, kinsmen, and sisters say to me: 'Do not speak of Hari; I am your mother, this one is your sister, and these are your brothers and kinsmen—O child, remain with those who are assembled here for many days. (92)
Prahlāda said: Who is my mother? Who is my sister? Who are my brothers? And who is my father? O Mother, hear from me about my kinsmen; they always remain together. (93)
She whose urine was drunk by me and whose feces were much consumed in my belly—she is our mother; it is impossible to describe hell before her.
This second person created by Viśvakarman is not a mere phantom; for there is no man like you in whose heart Hari does not dwell.
"I think it is certain that for ten months he will drink urine while being satisfied; how could there truly be brothers even in the womb? (96)
How will that wretched mother restrain them as they fight? An old kinsman is seen acting like a wise man toward his enemies.
Why is it called "family" (kuṭumba), and why is it that one both comes and goes? Furthermore, this bondage of family leads us to hell. (98)
"I have another mother, another father, and other brothers; having realized that sisters and kinsmen are merely worldly relations, one attains liberation. (99)
Nature (prakṛti) is our mother, and intellect (buddhi) is said to be our sister; from her the ego (ahaṃkāra) is born, by which the notion "I am" is inferred.
The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are my brothers who go along with me; this is our nature (prakṛti), and my own kin are but a transformation (vikāra). || 101 ||
The person who is the twenty-fifth and the driver of these is my father; Hari, the Supreme Self, resides within this body.
If that Hari is seen within the heart-mind at the time of dissolution, his very state of sovereignty, characterized by the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, arises.
That kingdom which you consider desirable is, for me, always equal to blades of grass, wherein Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, Anila, and Anala are not worshipped.
He who is seen directly, yet wanders without support—he alone is the Blessed Viṣṇu, who resides in these [forms] within the sky. (105)
All these planets that are situated, as well as these constellations, are bound to Dhruva; by the word of Viṣṇu, they all do not fall to the surface of the earth.
"Since destruction at the proper time has been ordained for all by Him Himself, having reflected thus, I have no fear of death from you. (107)
At the conclusion of those words, his father struck him with his foot and said: "Where is he? I shall kill him first, and afterwards you who speak like a monkey. (108)
Prahlāda said: The elements, beginning with earth, are indeed the Lord Hari himself. On land and in water—what need is there to say more? The entire universe is permeated by Viṣṇu.
Hari resides in grass, wood, a house, a field, in wealth, and in the body; he is known through the yoga of knowledge—can he indeed be seen with the physical eye? || 110 ||

He goes to the abode of Brahmā or to the netherworld (rasātala), and in an instant he wanders upon the surface of the earth; he smells the fragrance, performs everything, hears, and knows—all this is Viṣṇu here. 111.
Thus addressed, he abandoned his innate illusion, rose from his lion-throne, firmly girded his loins, and drew forth his radiant sword. (112)

Having struck him with the tip of his sword-blade, he spoke these unbearable words: "Now, O wretch, remember Viṣṇu! Otherwise, your head shall fall to the ground like a ripe fruit from a tree—along with its blazing earrings."
"If you do not show me that Viṣṇu emerged from this pillar," [said Hiraṇyakaśipu]. But Prahlāda, casting aside his fear, made a lotus-seat upon the ground.
Having raised his neck and restrained his heavy breathing, he stood facing death, meditating upon the god Hari within his heart.
O Lord, I then witnessed a marvel on earth from the sky: a garland of flowers went of its own accord and settled upon Prahlāda’s neck. (116)
The sky was being pervaded; what indeed has been done thus by the people? Suddenly, the crowd was agitated by the sound as it broke away from the pillar. (117)
The earth might sink into the netherworld, or the sky might descend to the ground; would my head fall to the earth, as if struck by a blow from a sword? 118.
Then, a terrifying lion’s roar issued forth from that pillar; all the Daityas fell to the ground, rendered unconscious by the sound.
The sword and shield fell from Hiraṇyakaśipu’s hand; he did not know again and again what this was or what it meant.
As soon as he stood up and looked, he beheld that Hari: a man standing below and a terrifying lion above.
With a mouth made terrifying by its fangs, as if licking the very sky, his blazing body tossed his head from the tip of his tail.
With a roar produced from his great throat like a thundering cloud, with the ends of his hair bristling upward, he was difficult for even the gods and asuras to behold.
Then, seeing Narasiṃha, she fell again upon the ground; seizing him by his mass of hair, she whirled him through the sky.
Having whirled him around a hundred times, he dashed him against the earth; yet that lord of the Daityas did not die, due to the power of Brahmā’s boon.
Then Hari was loudly reminded by the gods stationed in the sky; bringing the Daitya to his knee and joyfully gazing upon his chest, he [acted].
Having placed his two lotus-marked arms in readiness, he caught the sound "Victory! Victory! from the Yakṣas and the gods within his ears.
With his nails, which resembled kunda flowers, he tore open the chest of the Daitya—a chest scarred by the blows of the thunderbolt and hardened by a mass of bones.
With his chest pierced, the lord of the Daityas died and fell; then the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, became filled with joy.
O Keśava, through your grace, as well as through the grace of Śaṅkara, satisfaction has arisen within me when the three cities were consumed.
Now that Hiṇyākṣa has been slain and brought down in due time, she has been born again; yet now I have no satisfaction—where shall I go, and what shall I do? (131)
"On earth there are kṣatriyas who do not fight with one another; O Lord, why is it that there is no war between the gods and the dānavas? (132)

"Now the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, are pervaded by Bali. I do not know what your fifth incarnation will do; this is the time for the subjugation of Bali, so show yourself, O Janārdana! (133)
Sārasvata said: Having heard all of this, Vāmana spoke to the sage.
Vāmana said: Listen, O Nārada, to what occurred when Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain; Prahlāda, who was exceedingly devoted to Viṣṇu, was made the king of the Daityas. || 135 ||
By him, sovereignty was exercised upon the surface of the earth for many years; yet even as he ruled, there was indeed conflict with the gods.
Even while recollecting his former enmity with the Daityas, he did not look upon them with ill will; having fathered many sons, he ruled over a prosperous kingdom.
From Virocana, Bali was born; when he was still a child, having recognized Hari in solitude through a certain yoga, [he attained his goal]. (138)
Having abandoned his kingdom and beloved sons, he went to the mountain peaks; Janārdana made his body endure until the end of the kalpa.
On account of the kingdom, a great dispute arose among many Daityas and Dānavas as to who among them should become their king. || 140 ||
Nārada said: "The sons and grandsons of Hiraṇyākṣa who are exceedingly powerful—Virocana and the others who are most mighty—" (141)
The powerful Vṛṣaparvan also presented himself for the sake of the kingdom; as did Indra, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Varuṇa, Vāyu, Sūrya, Anala, and Yama. || 142 ||

In strength, form, endurance, and other such qualities, they would not be equal to the Daitya; yet, by virtue of his magnanimity and other noble traits, as well as his progeny, he surpassed even the Asuras. (143)
Being incited by Śukra, they fought with one another whenever the Daityas remembered the wickedness [displayed] during the seizure of the nectar.
"Why do the deities withhold the nectar that remains from their drinking? It is not for us!"—thus resolving, they fight one another. (145)
At no time does the battle come to rest, because many Daityas and Dānavas are intent upon this single task.

Having drunk the nectar, the gods became immortal and they are victorious; yet in battle, Viṣṇu is superior in strength to the gods, dānavas, daityas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas—tell me the reason for this. (147)

Vāmana said: "Janārdana is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, without beginning or end. He alone is that auspicious God (Śiva), and he is also designated as Brahmā. O King, whenever a task for this One arises in the world—"

Taking recourse in his body, they perform the work of death; since Viṣṇu is the granter of boons who makes the entire universe pay tribute to him, therefore Viṣṇu is superior in strength, and there is no one else like him.
Viṣṇu is intent upon protection; what need is there for others who possess only the eye of flesh? All the gods, beginning with Indra, are merely performers of Viṣṇu’s work. (150)
Having performed the act of creation, Brahmā then departed, and Hara established himself on Kailāsa; Viṣṇu could not be found by the gods, who wandered throughout the three worlds.
Whenever anyone in this world behaves contrary to the natural order, Janārdana, having arrived, surely effects his destruction.
O mighty-armed one, you are not like the mind of Nārada; I shall relate that divine story which removes all sins. (153)
Formerly, when those Daityas were disputing for the sake of the kingdom, Prahlāda himself approached them and established an agreement.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, long-lived, and exceedingly strong, he is devoted to sacrifice, ever joyful, possessed of many sons, and very difficult to conquer. (155)
He who knows Viṣṇu to be invincible does not fight with the gods; for him who is devoted to all, there is no death in battle. (156)
He never makes his own word go in vain; he is the one who shines with splendor in the midst of all his sons and grandsons. (157)
"Once consecrated by Śukra, he shall be your king. Having said, "The preceptor's word is authoritative," he departed and returned once more to where he had come from. (158)
And so, those Daityas and Dānavas together—Virocana and the others, including sons and grandsons—personally performed it. (159)
Having examined each one individually with full knowledge, the Guru said: "Prahlāda has described these qualities, O Virocana, but they do not exist in you."
O sage, even among other Daityas, Vṛṣaparvan was not such as these sons of Bali and the others were when observed by Śukra; for having examined them all, Śukra saw such virtues only in Bali.
Seeing that Bali was superior in strength, they reported it to the Daityas: "O Daityas, Bali is superior in virtue; how should my task be carried out? (162)
By some stroke of fate, Bali will become Indra; for as is the father in this world, so shall the son be.
If there were no son, it would certainly have been the same for the grandson; however, Prahlāda was a great yogi, a Vaiṣṇava, and beloved of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Virocana, some of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s virtues [remain]. If Virocana, the elder brother, is made king, O Asuras, Narasiṃha will surely come and kill him. (165)
Even Virocana, fearing death, relinquished his kingdom; all the virtues of Prahlāda were established within the body of Bali.
Having thus made this agreement, they consecrated Bali in the kingdom; for he who is Prahlāda is indeed Viṣṇu, and he who is Viṣṇu is himself Bali.
Therefore, made a friend by the gods and freed from all conflicts, the gods and asuras brought everything into a state of unity under the kingdom of Bali.
Having heard his speech as well, the Vālakhilyas arrived at my palace; Indra was cursed by them, and I was made a dwarf.
Having propitiated them, I spoke to them, and they said, "After the subduing of Bali, there will be a liberation from my curse for you. (170)
You too have a curiosity for battle, yet Bali performs a sacrifice; there is no restraint over the gods, for they have all assembled at the sacrifice.
"He is performing a sacrifice for me; who can bring about his destruction? And I have been born as Vāmana, while Nārada is filled with curiosity. (172)
"All this is occurring contrary to my mind; nevertheless, by means of gradual application, I shall make everything auspicious. (173)

Nārada said: "O Lord of Gods, show me favor; I have a curiosity regarding battle. When Kṣatriyas are slain in combat by a single Brāhmaṇa, then, as was previously told to me by my father, that war shall take place. (174)
"You are born as a Brāhmaṇa; when will you engage in battle? Laughing, Vāmana said, "It shall come true for you. (175)
Having become the son of Jamadagni and having made Maheśvara my preceptor, I shall slay Kārtavīrya along with many kṣatriyas.
"At Samantapañcaka, I shall create five lakes of blood; there I will satiate my fathers and grandfathers. (177)
"I shall make myself a field of merit; you will come there, and a supreme, pleasing spectacle will take place in the battle. (178)
When the Kṣatriyas again seize the earth from the Brāhmaṇas, at that very moment I shall slay them and restore the earth once more.
Having conquered the earth again and again twenty-one times, I shall lay down my weapons; weary of the business of war, I shall dwell in delightful forests and upon mountain peaks.
In Laṅkā, the mighty Rāvaṇa will rule the kingdom when he bears the name Trailokyakaṇṭaka. || 181 ||
Then Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and the increaser of Kausalyā’s joy, will go together with his brothers to the sacrificial pavilion in the future.
"Having struck down Tāḍakā and having taken Subāhu away from the sacrificial hall, I shall depart from the sacrifice for Sītā’s svayaṃvara. (183)
Having broken the bow of Maheśvara, I shall marry that Sītā; having renounced the kingdom, I will go to the forest for fourteen years.
"The sorrow born of Sītā’s abduction shall be my first [task]; I shall make that Rākṣasī in the forest devoid of her nose and ears. (185)
Having slain the fourteen thousand Triśiras, Khara, and Dūṣaṇa, I shall kill the Rākṣasa Mārīca who has taken the form of a deer.
Having burned the vulture Jaṭāyu, I shall go forth with my wife taken; then, having established friendship with Sugrīva and slain Vālin, I shall depart.
I shall cause the ocean to be bridged by the monkeys headed by Nala; I shall surround Laṅkā and I shall slay the Rākṣasas.
Having slain Kumbhakarṇa in battle, and then having slain Meghanāda in the fray, he killed the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa while all the Rākṣasas looked on.
Having returned to Ayodhyā and established a kingdom free of all obstacles, I shall bestow upon Vibhīṣaṇa the city of Laṅkā, which was fashioned by the gods.
"Having entrusted the kingdom to my son, I shall go to Amarāvatī together with my brothers, accompanied by the wondrous life-stories of Kāla and Durvāsas. (191)
When the Dvāpara age arrived, the earth, burdened by many Kṣatriyas, was unable to support its weight and prepared to sink into the netherworld.
At that time, the great asura Kaṃsa will rule the kingdom in Mathurā; so too will Śiśupāla, Jarāsaṃdha, and the great asura Kālanemi. (193)
O Sage, at that time Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva and the great asura King Bāṇa, along with their wealth of elephants, horses, and steeds, shall be slain by me.
In the Kali age, clouds contain but little water and cows yield but little milk; there is no ghee in the milk, and truth exists not among men. (195)
People afflicted by thieves and tormented by diseases do not find a protector, even when they have reached the state of battle. (196)
In the month of Kārttika, small rivers flowing westward dry up; likewise, there is no Ekādaśī vow, nor is there a fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) on which Kṛṣṇa is present.

No one will recognize even one who has displayed his prowess in his own home; everyone will be afflicted by poverty and deprived of the twilight ablutions. All this will occur in the Kali age, as it did not in the three preceding ages.
A son abandons his father and mother to attend to his wife; no one is a teacher or a kinsman to anyone else—does anyone ever serve another? 199.
To the very extent that Kali spreads across the surface of the earth, to that same extent all people will become uniform in character.
When everything is oppressed by barbarians and devoid of the twilight prayers and ritual bathing, I shall indeed become a Brāhmaṇa renowned as Kalki in the future.
"Having carried out the destruction of the Mlecchas, I, with Yājñavalkya as my domestic priest, shall perform a sacrifice with abundant gold for the sake of expiation. (202)
There will be my incarnations, and among them there will be war; at present, the gods will not engage in battle with the powerful one.
That lord of the Daityas is performing a sacrifice for me; Bali must not become subject to my slaughter. He is undertaking a vow of giving away all his possessions at this great ritual.
Sārasvata said: Having spoken thus to Nārada and dismissed him, the Lord then went forth to witness the sacrifice performed by Bali for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose.
Vāmana, having gone to the city and looking from house to house, went to the houses of the Brāhmaṇas and begged for food.
A Brahmin who is constantly devoted to bathing and intent upon the study of the Vedas obtains alms and food at the house of another twice-born man as a dwarf. (207)
At delightful crossroads and in temples of the gods, he sits surrounded by people, shaking his broad hips.
Shaking his thick head, he with the stout shoulders and large jaw dances to the measure of the rhythm and sings most enchantingly. (209)
Vāmana recited the four Vedas in the assembly of the twice-born; likewise, all the sons of the Daityas and the Brāhmaṇas [did so]. 210.
They attended upon the charming Vāmana day and night; then Vāmana was led by all of them into the sacrificial pavilion.
"You must certainly request a site for a small monastery; then there will be great welfare for us, as well as for the country and the city. (212)
Vāmana was entreated by all the sons of the Daityas and the twice-born: "O Vāmana, you must always dwell in the city of the lord of the Daityas."
Sārasvata said: Having replied, "So be it," Vāmana entered the sacrificial pavilion; thereafter, a great clamor was raised at the gate by the doorkeepers.
Standing together with many Brahmins, he remained reciting the Vedas; then, indeed, a great sound of the Vedas arose within the sacrificial pavilion.
When the two Daityas had first entered, they informed the Daitya: "O Lord, a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a dwarf has arrived at the sacrifice to see you."
Out of curiosity, he entered the doorway for a moment, so that Vāmana might come into your presence all alone. (217)
O God, the desireless Vāmana remained right there for some time, producing the sound of the four Vedas from his single mouth. || 218 ||
Delighted, Bali spoke these words: "Admit this man at the gate; I shall honor this best of Brahmins and give him whatever he desires. (219)
I remember the words of the Smṛtis which my teacher spoke: "One vessel consists of Veda; another vessel consists of austerity. (220)
Whatever worthy recipient shall come, that recipient he will deliver; while the sacrifice is being performed, a sacrificial fee must be given by me.
"Vāmana is not to be questioned; let my word be true. Having heard this, the preceptor Śukra restrained that Bali.

Śukra said: At the door, all the twice-born should be honored, as well as the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others; likewise the deaf, the dwarfs, the hunchbacked, and those who are diseased or harsh. (223)
Let Vāmana be worshipped at the gateway with gold, silver, and garments; for the birth of four [types of people] is in vain, and their sixteen kinds of gifts are likewise in vain.

The birth of those who are childless is in vain, as is that of those who are excluded from dharma; so too is the life of those who eat the food of others and those who are devoted to the wives of others. || 225 ||
One who desires his own welfare should not give wealth acquired by unjust means; likewise, a gift given to one who is not a Brahmin, or to one who has fallen from his high status, is fruitless. (226)
When a twice-born man has neglected the twilight prayers, when he is ruined, fallen, or a thief; likewise, when he causes displeasure to his guru, or is turned away from his father and mother.

And that which is given to a Brahmin in name only, that which is given to the husband of a Vṛṣalī woman, to a seller of the Vedas, to an ungrateful person, and to one who officiates as a priest for an entire village; 228.
That which is given to one conquered by a woman, and likewise to a snake-catcher, and that which is given to attendants—these sixteen gifts are in vain. (229)
Sārasvata said: "In the meantime, Bali said: 'O Guru, you should not speak thus. Whosoever studies the Vedas, he is Viṣṇu himself who has come to me. (230)
No delay should be made when a Vedic scholar has arrived at one's house; [one should honor him] by rising from one's seat, by welcoming words, and by washing his feet. (231)
A householder should provide food according to his capacity; for when Vāmana departs from the pavilion unhonored, [the consequences are dire]. (232)
Then this sacrifice, in which one's entire possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, becomes futile. In the meantime, Vāmana was brought into the presence of Bali.
The Daitya beheld Vāmana approaching in the form of Viṣṇu, his body blazing with radiance, tawny-hued, and resembling the sun.
Rising up, he went forward facing him and, having offered salutations, stood before him, saying: "I am blessed, for in my sacrifice a twice-born one equal to Viṣṇu has arrived."

Bali, having been brought into the center of the altar, offered him a seat; and having given water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), and a grass mat (viṣṭara), Bali worshipped him with sandalwood paste, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and stood before him.
Having quickly offered him the madhuparka and a cow, and after Vāmana had then smelled the madhuparka, [the king performed the remaining rites].
"Welcome," said Bali; "May it be well with you," replied the twice-born one. "I have come as a petitioner; tell me, O Lord, what shall be given? (238)
"O Daitya, O best of the twice-born, give me land; how much is it, O Lord of Daityas? Let three paces be given to me for the sake of my dwelling. (239)
"Having constructed a divine hermitage, I shall instruct my disciples. "The threefold transmission has been given to you," Vāmana said. (240)
"‘Do not give it,’ said Śukra; Viṣṇu himself is eternal. Delighted, Bali said to Śukra: “What recipient could be greater than this? (241)
Having placed the sacrificial grass (darbha) with unbroken rice grains in his right hand, Bali performed the ritual application; however, the Guru did not do so, nor did he place water in his hand.
All the sages were struck with wonder, as were the Hotṛ priests, the members of the assembly, the Brāhmaṇas, the young students, the Daityas, wives, sons, and kinsmen. || 243 ||
When it is said, "It is given, it is taken," why does one not release the water? Water is offered into the hand for Vāmana and for the sake of discernment (viveka). 244.
That gift which is given with words but not carried out through action, having cast the sacrificer into the hell of putridity, there is no atonement.
Uśanas said: "O Lord of the Daityas, this Vāmana is Hari; by some stroke of fate, he has arrived to see you. (246)
"I do not know whether he will do something unpleasant or even pleasant; let the words of the sacrificer be heard, O Guru, descendant of Bhṛgu. (247)

At the times of giving, it is proclaimed by both the sacrificers and the twice-born: "I am Indra, the twice-born am Viṣṇu, and the material object is the deity Āditya; so how could that not be given by me, saying 'May Viṣṇu be pleased'? (248)
Having spoken thus, Bali gave water into the hand of Vāmana; then, saying "What is this?", he stood outside the pavilion.
Even in the middle [of the earth], that brahmin Vāmana became as large as Bali; he was given a hand by the lord of the asuras in order to take three paces.
The sacrificer and the twice-born were seen by the gods and others at the sacrifice; Vāmana grew exceedingly large, having assumed a four-armed form.
Nārada also arrived and spoke: "O Bala, what has been done? Accompanied by your two disciples, you stand before me and dance with joy. (252)
"Accept the sacrificial fee, O Lord," Bali said along with his wife; "What have I not gained today, that Janārdana accepts [this offering]? (253)
Having reduced his wealth by half, he begs for three things from the earth; O Madhusūdana, one should be content with whatever remains. (254)
Seeing Hari growing in size as he traveled through the sky, the Brahmins, sages, and gods praised the Blessed Janārdana.
The celestial sages said: Victory to you, O God! Victory, O Infinite One! Victory, O Viṣṇu! Victory, O Acyuta! Victory, O Fish; salutations to you! Victory, O Tortoise, supporter of the earth! 256.
Salutations to you, O Varāha; salutations again and again, O Narasiṃha. Salutations to you, O son of Jamadagni; be victorious, O Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Victory to Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory to the Son of Devakī! I bow to Buddha and to Kṛṣṇa; I prostrate myself before Kalki.
Sārasvata said: Nārada, having ascended to the sky, dances and praises [the Lord], as do the yogis Sanaka and others who laud Janārdana. || 259 ||
When Kṛṣṇa had gone into the intermediate space and was increasing in size before the city of Bali, everyone stood with their faces turned upward and gazed at the sun.
Having first appeared in the form of an umbrella, Hari subsequently ascended upwards; the sun shines like a crest-jewel upon the head of Hari.
Gazed upon intently by the Daityas, Hari appeared like a tilaka-mark upon their foreheads; as he grew larger, he appeared like earrings upon their ears.
And in the heart of the increasing Hari, he acts as the Kaustubha gem; Indra and the other deities, the Rudras, and the Vasus remain stationed in the sky.
Furthermore, where Hari is situated above, there the sky is not considered to exist; at that time, a garland of forest flowers was placed upon his neck by Vāsava.
The entire earth trembles, as does the solar disc situated in the sky; O Daityas, being terrified, you gaze upon the sun—what will happen? (265)
The sun-like Viṣṇu became like a lotus at his navel and like a girdle at his waist; thus nourished, he took two steps.
There is no room for a third; the entire universe has been fashioned. Then the Creator of the world, the Day-staff, acts as the Staff of Brahmā. || 267 ||
The feet of Viṣṇu are worshipped, praised, and honored by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, humans, uragas, and pannagas. || 268 ||
Indeed, that righteous-souled one, whose rod of punishment was restrained, was repeatedly sung of by the Gandharvas; was he not himself fashioned by Hari as the axle-rod for the wheel of the stars?
Having conquered this world, the gods have made the Gaṅgā their banner-staff; this staff-like foot of Trivikrama certainly serves as a staff for his fame.
Having been seized with force by Hari and carried to the summit of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), his foot will pass out with speed, having pierced through its top.
To that extent, this momentum of the cosmic egg is designated as Virāṭ; for he, being the form of all seeds, is called the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 272 ||
Therefore, all this has come into being, situated at the tip of your foot; having split the cosmic egg, you must not go outside.
Along with him, Hari’s foot split the cosmic egg; the cosmic egg became shattered even by the mere withdrawal of His foot.
When that [egg] was split, the water of Brahmā pervaded the three worlds; then Gaṅgā, born from Viṣṇu’s foot, issued forth from his head.
The goddess who floods the three worlds and was herself borne by Rudra is worshipped as the celestial river Svarṇadhunī in heaven; yet, having gone to the earth, she is known as Gaṅgā. (276)
When she reached Pātāla, she became renowned as Tripathagā; by the mere remembrance of her, the destruction of all sins occurs. (277)
By the mere sight [of it], one obtains the fruit of a complete horse-sacrifice; by the mere act of bathing, the sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed.
The man who, having bathed, worships the two deities Hari and Hara, transcends the world of Indra and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 279 ||
Having drunk the water from Viṣṇu’s feet and having realized the fundamental principles, the self-controlled embodied soul, after fasting for a day dedicated to Viṣṇu, attains liberation.
Abiding in the state of beings whose nature is pure and free from passion for the planes of birth, they sever the bonds of saṃsāra and go to that supreme goal. || 281 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Subduing of Bali," in the second section, the *Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The King said: Having taken the sacrificial fee from the Daityas, what did Mahāviṣṇu Janārdana do? Tell me; for my curiosity is great indeed. || 1 ||

Sārasvata said: Thus praised by the gods, Lord Hari took hold of the earth and banished Bali once the sacrificial rite was completed. Having received the sacrificial fee at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the ritual then became fully accomplished.
When the third step was not yet fully completed, the omnipresent Lord approached Bali and spoke, his lower lip slightly quivering.
O Lord of the Daityas, when there is a debt, there arises a bondage of terrible appearance. Fulfill that requirement of mine; otherwise, O sir, accept imprisonment.
Having heard those words of Murāri, Bāṇa, the son of Bali, came forward and then addressed that Vāmana, who possessed a universal form.
Having made the earth very small and having assumed a dwarf body, how did you go forth in your universal form after requesting only three paces?
If you ask for a third stride, O Lord of the World, then assume dwarfhood once more; Bali will grant that step.
To one such as the dwarf Bali offered water, to that very same kind it should be given; but what need is there to speak of one who possesses the universal form?
O Maheśvara, this universe was created by you, and tribute exists within the universe; the virtuous do not accept it through deceit.
O Lord of the World, if you consider this world to be yours, then recognize Bali as one who has transgressed all bounds and is averse to devotion toward you.

Having been cast out by means of a noose around the neck, by whom indeed can you be restrained? The Lord of Cows appoints another cowherd for protection; what then does the former cowherd do while grazing his well-fed cattle? (11)
When these words had been spoken by the son of Bali, the Blessed One Janārdana, the primordial creator, spoke this speech.
"Regarding those words which have just now been spoken by you, a child, listen to my reply, which is joined with its underlying reasons. (13)
"Previously, your father was told by me: 'Give me three paces [of land] according to the proper measure'; that very thing has now been fulfilled. (14)
"O son, does your father Bali not know my authority? These three steps were taken for the very benefit of Bali himself. (15)
Therefore, O son of Bali, because a great amount of water was given by your father into my hand, he shall dwell in Sutala for the duration of a kalpa.
O Bāṇa, when the Manvantara of Śrāddhadeva has passed and the Sāvarṇika period has arrived, Bali shall become Indra.
Having thus addressed Bāṇa, the son of Bali, the divine Trivikrama approached Bali and spoke these words in sweet syllables.

The Blessed Lord said: "O King, since the sacrifice was performed with incomplete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), go to the great netherworld; dwell there in the nether realm named Sutala, free from all affliction."
Bali said: O Lord, for me who resides in Sutala, how can there be the sight of your feet, worship, and enjoyment, so that I may dwell in happiness? (20)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lord of Daityas, I dwell eternally within your heart; therefore, having obtained your vision, I shall remain once more in your presence."
Likewise, when the great festival of Śakra has concluded, there shall be another meritorious festival there known as Dīpapratipad.
There, O tiger among men, joyful, well-nourished, and well-adorned people will diligently honor you with offerings of flowers and lamps. (23)
O Daitya, there shall be a most meritorious festival on the surface of the earth marked by your name; therefore, you shall be happy for a year.
Furthermore, those men who shall be endowed with firm devotion and worship you according to the prescribed rite, they too shall become partakers of happiness. (25)
"Just as your kingdom is now, so too shall that Kaumudī be," having spoken thus, he settled the lord, who was intoxicated with wine, along with his wife in Sutala.

Taking up the earth, he went swiftly to the abode of Śakra, which is frequented by hosts of immortals; for the conqueror of Madhu, having given the triple heaven to Maghavan, made the gods partakers of their sacrificial portions.
The Great Lord, the master of the universe, vanished even as the lords of the earth were looking on.
Having thus seized the kingdom, it was entrusted to Bali, the son of Manu; and by his own command, those Daityas were dispatched to other continents.
Those who had their abode in Pātāla were settled right there; supreme joy arose among the gods at the subjugation of Bali.
Furthermore, Vāmana set his mind upon dwelling there; in that sacred field, in his own city, Vāmana indeed took up residence.

Sārasvata said: O lord of men, this meritorious, pure, and sin-destroying manifestation of Vāmana has been told to you; by remembering it, hearing it, or reciting it, one's sin goes to destruction and merit is attained. (32)
Īśvara said: Having heard these words of Sārasvata, that Bhoja king, having bowed to the best of sages, worshipped him with devotion. || 33 ||

Then, having performed the pilgrimage to the field of Vastrāpatha along with his retinue according to the prescribed rites, that Bhoja, the best of kings, attained fulfillment and in the end went to the supreme state.
Thus, I have described to you this most meritorious Vasrāpatha in the sacred field of Prabhāsa; by hearing and reciting it with supreme devotion to Viṣṇu, one attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
Just as sins are shaken off by plunging into the waters of the Gaṅgā, so too is there the destruction of evils through listening to the Purāṇas.

This supreme secret has been told to you; it must not be spoken to one who is devoid of devotion to Hari, nor to one who delights in censuring the twice-born, nor to an extreme sinner, nor to one who is disloyal to his guru, nor to one whose mind is intent on committing evil. (37)
Whosoever is a man who, having cultivated meditative practice, recites this with certainty, his devotion to Śiva and Kṛṣṇa will certainly become unwavering. (38)
Through devotion to that, the Supreme Person attains all his goals. One should give cows, land, gold, and ornaments to the reciter of the Purāṇa.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one incurs poverty. By reciting, hearing, or causing this to be heard three times, one shall attain all desires. (40)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion of the Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya, Preceded by the Dialogue between Sārasvata and Bhoja and the Description of the Greatness of the Pilgrimage to Vastrāpatha-kṣetra, Following the Narration of the Account of the Boon Granted to Bali by Vāmana," in the second section (Vastrāpatha-kṣetra-māhātmya) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: Om, salutations to the Infinite, the Subtle, the one accessible through knowledge, the Pervader; to the Pure, the Universal Form, the God of gods, Śambhu. (1)
The sages said: "The expansion of the lineages of Soma and Sūrya has been recounted by you, as well as all the Manvantaras and the various kinds of creation. (2)
Now we wish to hear about the supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrtha). O high-minded one, which are the meritorious sacred fords upon this earth? (3)
Sūta said: There are various sacred fords (tīrthas) in this world whose number is not known; formerly, their number was calculated as three and a half crores.
The sacred fields, rivers, mountains, and likewise the streams, have attained supreme majesty through the power of the asceticism of the sages.
Among them is the sinless one named Arbuda, which removes all sins; it remains untouched by the defects of the Kali age due to the power of Vasiṣṭha.
Just as all sacred fords (tīrthas) purify through bathing, giving, and other such rites, Arbuda removes all the sins of men by its mere sight alone.
The sages said: What is the extent of the place named Arbuda, and in which region is it situated? Or how has it become renowned upon the surface of the earth through the greatness of Vasiṣṭha?
Which are the principal sacred sites (tīrthas) that exist on Mount Arbuda? Tell us everything in detail, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall also fully relate the sin-destroying narrative and the majesty of Arbuda, exactly as it was heard by me.
The celestial sage named Vasiṣṭha, born from the Grandfather (Brahmā), formerly reached the surface of the earth and performed most rigorous penance. || 11 ||
He was self-restrained, restricted in his food, and devoted to the welfare of all beings; during the rainy season he lived under the open sky, and in the winter he dwelt within the water.

Practicing the five-fire austerity during the summer and devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, he eventually acquired a milch cow well-known as Nandinī; she was indeed auspicious and a granter of all desires.
Once, while wandering upon the surface of the earth in search of grass for her bed, she fell into a terrible, bottomless pit shrouded in darkness.
At that very time, O best of sages, the Lord of piercing rays set, yet Nandinī had not yet arrived.
With her milk, that twice-born sage, firm in his vows, daily performs the fire-oblation in the well-kindled fire both morning and evening.
Then the brahmin, lost in thought and certain that he would face the fear of penance, looked about in that forest, both on level ground and on uneven terrain.
Having reached that pit, he heard the sound of the earth's burden; the best of sages said to her, "O auspicious one, how have you fallen? (18)
"I have come out from the sacrificial fire out of agitation to look for you. She replied, "O brahmin-sage, while eating, I was searching for grass. (19)
"O Lord, I have fallen here; save me from this most unbearable distress. Having heard those words of hers, that sage entered into meditation.
He meditated upon the river Sarasvatī, the purifier of the three worlds; as soon as she was thus meditated upon by that sage with his mind, she appeared there at that very moment.
It filled that chasm on all sides with pure waters; then, when the chasm was completely full, Nandinī emerged from it.
Filled with joy, she went together with the sage toward the front of the hermitage.
Having seen that deep chasm in the middle, the wise great sage reflected upon how to completely fill that pit.

O Brahmins, as he was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind: "By bringing a mountain and placing it here, this chasm will be filled; therefore, I shall go quickly to Himavat, the best of mountains. (25)
That very mountain, the upholder of the earth, shall send [another] here, by which that chasm may be filled by that great-souled one.

Then that sage went to Himavat, the best of mountains. Seeing Vasiṣṭha approaching, Himavat, with a joyful mind, honored him with the rites of *arghya*, *pādya*, and other offerings, and spoke as follows: || 27 ||
Welcome to you, O best of sages! Today my life has become fruitful, since you, who are worthy of worship by all the inhabitants of heaven, have arrived at my home. (28)
"Speak your business, O best of sages; I shall surely grant it even at the cost of my own life. Let your command be given to me. (29)
Vasiṣṭha said: In the vicinity of my hermitage, there is a most dreadful pit; it is bottomless, and there the excellent cow Nandinī fell.
Therefore, having been drawn here with great effort out of fear of falling once again, I have come into your presence; no other king is worthy [of this]. (31)
Therefore, dispatch some excellent serpent, a supporter of the earth, to that place; send forth such a one by whom that chasm may be completely filled.
Himavat said: "O Sage, tell me what the dimensions of the chasm are in terms of its width and length; having reflected upon them, I shall dispatch a certain mountain of that same size."
Vasiṣṭha said: It is two thousand [yojanas] in length and three thousand in breadth; there is no end to its number below, O best of mountains.
Himavat said: "How did such a great chasm come to be formed by that measurement? I have a great curiosity regarding this; tell me everything in detail. (35)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Commencement of the Account of the Cavern Situated Near the Hermitage of Vasiṣṭha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vasiṣṭha said: In former times there was a sage named Gautama, a man of great asceticism; Ahalyā was his beloved and illustrious lawful wife.
At that time, the sage taught his disciples by the hundreds; once they were perfected in learning and Vedic study, he then sent them forth to their homes.
Moreover, another disciple of his, a wise man named Uttaṅka who was devoted to his guru, lived in his hermitage.
He did not dismiss him even though he was overwhelmed by old age; for Uttaṅka, due to his status as an excellent disciple, did not even perceive that his head had turned grey.
Although he was occupied with his duties and had reached the further shore of learning, after some time he went outside for the sake of firewood.
