Having taken up many [materials], he went to the supreme hermitage; then he cast that heap of wood down upon the surface of the earth.
Then he saw a single white matted lock stuck in the wood; seeing it, he was overcome with grief and reflected piteously.
"Fie, fie upon my ruined life! For what purpose does it exist? Being so intent on worldly affairs, I, a fool, did not even take a wife. (8)
"The extinction of my lineage will come about through the laxity of my evil mind. Then, having been seen by the preceptor’s wife, Uttaṅka was filled with grief.
His suffering was thus quickly reported to Gautama; Gautama, having said "So be it," addressed him with gentle words. (10)
"O child, go home and perform the Agnihotra and other rites according to the prescribed rules together with your wife; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Thus addressed by the Guru, he replied to the Guru: "O Master, request a fee; I shall give it without doubt."
Gautama said: "O child, you have always rendered great service to me; by that alone my fulfillment has been attained—of this there is no doubt. (13)
Uttaṅka said: "O Lord, there is something that ought to be accepted by you; I feel great satisfaction. O best of sages, through your grace, I have reached the further shore of knowledge. (14)
Gautama said: "O son, nothing should be accepted by me; I am satisfied with your service. I do not desire wealth from you; go happily to your home."
Thus addressed by his preceptor, he also spoke to his mother: "O mother, let me take something; grant me my satisfaction. (16)
The wife of the guru said: "Go to Saudāsa, my son; carry out my command immediately. Madayantī is his beloved, his lawful wife, and highly illustrious. (17)
"O son, bring the earrings of Madayantī quickly; otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you if you have not returned by the fifth day. (18)
Thus addressed by the preceptor’s wife, he then set out in haste and reached the house of Saudāsa, where he beheld him with the face of a tiger.
Seeing the brahmin who had approached for the purpose of eating him, he then said: "O brahmin, I shall indeed eat you; there is no doubt about this. (20)

Uttaṅka said: "O lord of men, you must certainly eat me; listen to me for a moment, O father! Give me the earrings, and having given them to my teacher, I shall return; then eat me, but do not let me go without having accomplished my purpose. (21)
Saudāsa said: "Go, O twice-born one, to my beloved who dwells in the inaccessible palace; having reached her with great effort, [inform her] out of fear for your life. (22)
"Let her be requested on my behalf; she will give you the two earrings. O best of the twice-born, you must not act otherwise than what is true. (23)
Vasiṣṭha said: Having approached Madayantī, that best of the twice-born spoke: "O Queen, give me the earrings; Saudāsa has commanded you."
Madayantī said: "O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, my doubt regarding the earrings still remains today. O twice-born one, bring some token of recognition and show it to the king. (25)
Having gone there quickly, he requested a token of recognition from the king.

Saudāsa said: "O best of the twice-born, go and speak these words of mine to that virtuous woman—those [deities] without whom there is no good rebirth and who indeed lead one to a miserable state. Then she will surely give you the two earrings adorned with jewels. (27)
Vasiṣṭha said: Taking the token of recognition, he went and presented it to her.
Then he said to him, "O twice-born one, take my two earrings; O best of the twice-born, exert yourself and let them be taken. (29)

"O twice-born one, Takṣaka always desires these two earrings for you. Having agreed, saying "So be it," and taking them with eyes wide open in wonder, he returned out of curiosity and spoke these words to the king: [30]
"O King, although I obtained the two radiant earrings through my supernatural powers, I did not understand the meaning of the words; therefore, I have returned once more. (31)
Out of curiosity, O King, tell me as it truly is regarding your own purpose: by what things is there no good rebirth, and who lead one to a miserable state? (32)
Saudāsa said: "O Brahmin, when propitiated, the twice-born grant a happy state; when dissatisfied, they immediately bestow a miserable state, as happened to me in the past. (33)
"This is the extent of my curse from the high-souled Vasiṣṭha: 'When someone shall cause you to be questioned [regarding this matter],' [then you shall be freed]. (34)

Then you will undoubtedly be liberated from your fault; for by your grace, O best of the twice-born, I have indeed been released from the curse and have attained the state of pure goodness (sāttvika). Go, O Brahmin, salutations be to you!
Vasiṣṭha said: Released by him, Uttanka quickly set out on the road; as he went along, overcome by intense hunger, he saw bilva fruits.
Then, having tied his two earrings together and placed them upon the ground on a black antelope skin, that sage, overcome by hunger and desiring fruit, climbed up [the tree]. (37)
At that very moment, Takṣaka, the best of serpents, took the earrings and quickly departed toward the south.
Then Uttaṅka, subsisting on fruit, descended to the surface of the earth and searched everywhere with great speed and intensity.
Seeing that he had arrived before him and drawn near, that best of serpents entered a fierce cave enveloped in darkness.
Uttaṅka also reached the cave; having entered that place shrouded in darkness, he took up his wooden staff and, filled with anger, began to dig there.
Seeing him thus afflicted, possessed of afflictions, and burdened by his heavy task, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, placed the thunderbolt upon the tip of his staff.
Then he quickly tore open the surface of the earth and entered the netherworld (pātāla), wandering about in search of the earrings.
There he saw a horse, entirely white and endowed with excellent qualities. He was told by it: "Touch my private parts; then the task will be accomplished."
He did so quickly, and from that smoke arose; O mountain, the netherworld was everywhere pervaded by that fire.

Then all the serpents, becoming greatly agitated, rushed forward with Takṣaka at their head; having arrived together with the earrings, they gave them to Uttaṅka, and after bowing down, they departed for their homes.
Vasiṣṭha said: Then, O best of the twice-born, I, who am Agni, spoke thus to Aśvastha: "I am he whom you previously propitiated at the command of your preceptor. (47)
"Knowing that you have arrived here in distress, I, devoted to compassion, have come; O Blessed One, mount upon my back quickly in every way. (48)
"I shall lead you to where the Guru, the abode of all virtues, resides. Having mounted his back, he set out toward the hermitage. (49)
At that very moment, he arrived at the residence of Gautama; at that same time, however, Ahalyā had finished adorning herself.
Having bathed and approached her husband, the virtuous woman spoke these words: "Uttanka has not arrived today; I shall certainly pronounce a curse. (51)
When she perceived that he was negligent in his duties, at the conclusion of her speech, Uttanka appeared.
With a serene face and joyful, adorned with his two earrings, he prostrated before her with devotion and offered the earrings to her. (53)
Upon seeing him, that virtuous woman immediately placed [the earrings] upon her ears; then she quickly dismissed Uttaṅka to his own home.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus was that chasm produced on account of Takṣaka and Uttaṅka, just as I have constantly been thinking regarding the filling of the pit for the sake of the cow.
Therefore, you must quickly fulfill this; no one else is capable of this task here. O best of mountains, perform my work swiftly and without doubt. (56)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Uttanka, the Disciple of Gautama," within the account of the origin of the Cleft (Vivarotpatti-vṛttānta), in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, Himācala reflected upon that task regarding the filling of the chasm.
Having reflected for a long time, that best of mountains said this to the sage: "Tell me, what indeed is the means for the mountains to go there?"
In the past, Śakra cut off the wings of all [the mountains]; therefore, O best of sages, consider the certain course of action for this matter.
Vasiṣṭha said: "There is indeed a means to lead the great mountain there; this son of yours, Nandivardhana, is renowned in that place."
His friend, known as Arbuda, was most dear to him—a powerful nāga, the best among living beings, who could travel through the sky. || 5 ||
He, indeed, moving upwards, will undoubtedly lead [him] away in an instant; knowing him to be so in all his actions with ease, I have come here.
Let an order be given for him; you ought not to cause him suffering. If you must certainly be devoted [to me], then send him there immediately.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Himavat, the supporter of the earth, who was devoted to his son, was overcome with great sorrow and began to reflect.
"Our son Maināka has entered the ocean out of fear; however, Vasiṣṭha has now come to take away our eldest son by all means. What should we do now? How will our welfare be secured? (9)
On one side is the intense fear of a curse, and on the other is the sorrow born of my son; let there be separation from my son rather than a curse originating from a twice-born man. (10)
Having made this resolution, he said to Nandivardhana: "Go, my son, at my word, toward the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha."
"There is a terrible chasm there; fill it quickly by taking Arbuda, the best of living beings, as your companion."
Naṃdivardhana said: "O Lord, that region is wretched, devoid of fruits and roots; it is instead abundant with palāśa, khadira, dhava, and śālmali trees. (13)
"O best of mountains, neither do rivers flow there, nor are the inhabitants virtuous; rather, they are cruel kings, beasts, and various Bhilla tribes. I am not fit to go there by any means. (14)
Then Vasiṣṭha spoke to the terrified Nandivardhana: "You must not fear anything whatsoever in that region due to wickedness."
My residence shall always be upon your head; there shall be sacred fords, rivers, deities, and holy sanctuaries.
And there shall always be trees of various forms, endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as auspicious deer and birds. (17)
I myself shall bring Maheśvara for your sake; then all the gods, including Vāsava, will indeed remain there.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Naṃdivardhana was greatly delighted; having approached the serpent Arbuda, he spoke these words. (19)
In this matter, O friend, may you be blessed; since you are endowed with humility, I consider this task arising from the brahmin to be what must be done by you right now. (20)
Arbuda said: "O son of the mountain, out of affection for you I shall go there; and I will undoubtedly dwell right there together with you. (21)
But out of affection, O brother, listen to the words I shall speak; if I am held in your esteem, you must not act otherwise than out of this affection.
"May I become famous by the name 'Man' (Mannāman); I choose nothing else. Then he, having made that vow, mounted upon him, and after bowing to his parents, set out together with the sage.
It was filled with auspicious divine trees, abounding in rivers and waterfalls, frequented by sweet-voiced birds, and inhabited by gentle deer.
Released from Arbuda by the word of the sage right there in that chasm, that most excellent mountain went entirely down until its very peak reached the surface.
In that cavern, the great-souled Arbuda was liberated; and when it was filled, the bull among sages was fully satisfied. || 26 ||
And he said to the Naga Arbuda: "Choose a boon, O you of noble vows! I am well-pleased with you, O auspicious serpent, because of this deed."
Arbuda said: "O great sage, this alone is our boon—that you are pleased with us. O best of the twice-born, if something must certainly be granted, then hear it."
And let this waterfall with its pure water on this very peak attain renown everywhere on earth as "Nāgatīrtha. (29)
"O Sage, out of affection for my friend, I shall dwell here forever; by your grace, let a human being go to heaven after bathing there. (30)
Even a woman who is barren, O Brahmin, if she performs merely the ritual bath, shall become possessed of sons and endowed with happiness and good fortune.
Vasiṣṭha said: Even she who is barren shall obtain a son endowed with all auspicious marks, provided she performs a mere bath in this full water.
And she who performs worship with fruits on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Nabhas shall become a mother of sons, even if she is a hundred years old.
Those who perform their ablutions here in this sacred ford with devotion shall go to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
And those who, with concentrated minds, perform a śrāddha ceremony here on the fifth day of the month of Nabhas, shall obtain the fruit of this sacred site.
Sūta said: Having thus granted him the boon, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha approached Naṃdivardhana and spoke these words.
"Choose a boon, my child; I am well-pleased with you, O sinless one. Out of your humility and affection, I shall grant everything, even that which is very difficult to obtain. (37)
Naṃdivardhana said: "O best of sages, let your previously spoken word be true; may your presence be established here forever. (38)
"By your grace alone, may it come to pass that I become renowned on this earth as 'Arbuda'—this is the desire that dwells in my mind. (39)
Sūta said: Having replied to him, "So be it," the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, impelled by his words, established his own hermitage there.
It was filled with jackfruit, campaka, mango, priyaṅgu, bilva, and pomegranate trees, frequented by various birds, and served by gods and gandharvas. || 41 ||
The best of sages remained there together with Arundhatī; that most excellent of munis summoned the Gomatī by means of his ascetic power.
Having bathed in which, even men who have committed extreme sins go to heaven, especially during the month of Māgha when the sun is situated in Capricorn.
Those who shall perform their ablutions there will go to the supreme goal.
The person who especially makes an offering of sesame seeds in the month of Māgha remains in heaven for as many years as there are sesame seeds. || 45 ||
What is the use of saying more here? One should simply perform the ritual at the sacred site itself. || 46 ||
Having beheld the face of Vasiṣṭha, there is no rebirth; Arundhatī is to be worshipped, and she is especially worthy of worship. (47)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Filling of the Cavern by Mount Nandivardhana at the Command of Vasiṣṭha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having established his own hermitage there, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha performed most severe penance for the sake of Śambhu’s dwelling.
That sage became one who subsisted entirely on the fruit of the season; thereafter, for two hundred years, he lived on withered leaves.
For five hundred years he lived on water alone, and thereafter for a thousand years he subsisted on air.
In summer he was a practitioner of the five fires, in winter he dwelt in water, and during the rains he lived in the open air; thereafter, he performed [the penance] for a thousand years.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased with that great-souled ṛṣi, immediately split that mountain and a liṅga rose up before him. Seeing it, the sage was overcome with wonder and uttered a hymn of praise.
Salutation to Śiva, the pure, the all-pervading, and the immortal; salutation to you, the one with matted hair; salutation to that triple-formed one.
Salutations to the gross, to the subtle, to the all-pervading Great Soul; salutations to you who bear the sword, salutations again and again to the three-eyed one.
Salutations to you, the bearer of the crescent moon; salutations to him whose garment is the directions; salutations again and again to you, the eight-formed one who holds the Pināka bow in hand.
Salutations to you whose form is knowledge; salutations to you who are attainable through knowledge. Salutations to you whose body is knowledge and who consists of all knowledge. || 9 ||
O Lord of Kāśī, salutations to you; repeated salutations to Giriśa! Salutations to you, Mahādeva, whose form is the cause of the universe. || 10 ||
Obeisance to you, O beloved of Gaurī; obeisance to you, whose nature is Śiva. Obeisance again and again to the three-eyed one, who is the very form of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. || 11 ||
Salutations to you, the Great Soul, who possesses manifold forms and is pure; salutations to the one whose nature is the universe and who consists of all the gods.
Sūta said: At that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke: "I am well-pleased with you; may it be well with you, O observer of noble vows! Choose a boon."
Having spoken thus, he split the mountain, and immediately a linga rose up before him.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Śaṅkara, may your presence always abide in this linga. Previously, I made a promise here to the high-souled Naga; O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased, make my word true."
The Blessed Lord said: "From this day forward, O best of Brahmins, my presence shall abide in this linga; by your word, everything shall come true."
O best of sages, whatever mortal shall praise me with devotion by means of this hymn on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina, [shall attain my grace].
O best of sages, for the sake of my pleasure, Śakra sent the river renowned as Mandākinī, which purifies the three worlds. (18)

To the north of the God, there is a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that exists eternally. O best of sages, he who bathes in it and beholds my Liṅga goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
"Since my Liṅga has emerged after piercing through Acala, it shall attain fame in the world by the very name Acaleśvara. (20)
Due to the majesty of this Liṅga, it shall never move; in every way, this Liṅga of mine will not be displaced even at the end of the dissolution.
Sūta said: Having spoken these words, Maheśvara ceased; Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and the other lords of sages were also exceedingly delighted in their souls. || 22 ||
Then, by means of his ascetic power, the Brahman-sage caused Śakra and the other gods, as well as sacred fords and shrines, to arrive at that best of mountains.
Then, being gratified, the best of the gods made his dwelling there.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Acaleśvara," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "O Sūta, tell us in detail the greatness of Arbuda; curiosity has arisen within us, so relate it as it truly is for our welfare."
Sūta said: Formerly, there was a lordly sage, Pulastya, the best of ṛṣis; having gone to the house of Yayāti, the king bowed to him and spoke.
Yayāti said: "Welcome to you, O best of sages! My life has become fruitful today. Please, out of favor, tell me the story concerning Arbuda."
O best of the twice-born, tell me the procedure for the pilgrimage and its fruit regarding that mountain famous on the surface of the earth known by the name Arbuda.
O you who are devoted to pilgrimages, tell me everything in detail; therefore, O best of sages, speak so that I may undertake the journey.
Pulastya said: O King, this Arbuda, the best of mountains, consists of manifold dharmas; it is impossible to describe it in full detail even in hundreds of years.
I shall describe to you, in brief, those foremost among the sacred fords (tīrthas). Among them, the first is Nāgatīrtha, which bestows all desires upon men.
O King, listen to this ancient account which is most wonderful and supreme, for it bestows sons and good fortune especially upon women. (8)
A Brāhmaṇa woman named Gautamī, virtuous, saintly, and devoted to her husband, having encountered widowhood in her youth, was dedicated to pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having reached Arbuda, she entered the Nāgatīrtha; she had previously come there to bathe, having immersed herself in those waters.
Accompanied by her son, the leader arrived at that sacred ford; O King, she performed various kinds of service for her there.
With all kinds of ritual implements, darbha grass, and various flowers, Gautamī, distressed for her son, then began to reflect.
"Blessed indeed is this son who always performs service for her; blessed is she who is joined with a son, while shame upon me, who am destitute of a son! (13)
"Separated from my husband and deprived of my son, I am deeply distressed. Then, O best of kings, she emerged from that water.
Even without union with her husband, she immediately became pregnant; endowed with the signs of pregnancy, she was filled with shame before virtuous people. (15)
He set his mind on death and kindled the fire; at that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke.
The voice said: "O Gautamī, you ought not to enter the sacrificial fire; there is no fault in this matter for you, owing to the power of this sacred ford. (17)
Whatever a man or a woman standing in the midst of the water desires in their heart, they obtain that very thing which was thought of; there is no doubt in this matter. || 18 ||
"O daughter, having seen her son, a desire for a son was formed in your heart; surely a son will be born to you from within your womb. (19)
"Therefore, desist; may it be well with you; you are faultless, O devoted wife. Then, O King, the virtuous Gautamī desisted from death.
Having heard the voice from the sky spoken by the messenger of the gods, and seeing her pregnancy without having seen her husband, she spoke these words: || 21 ||
"Aha! This power of the sacred ford appears unprecedented to me; for there, conception occurs in women even without semen or menses. (22)
"I shall not go anywhere else, having left this supreme holy place (tīrtha). Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman then resided there forever.
O tiger among kings, she indeed gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks there on the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
Furthermore, O King, for him who performs the śrāddha, his lineage does not perish; never shall a preta be born in his family.
O best of kings, for that man who performs his bath there free from desire and offers a śrāddha, eternal worlds are attained.
Any woman who offers flowers and fruits at this very sacred ford shall become blessed with sons, fortunate, and shall attain good fortune. || 27 ||
One who is free from desire attains heaven, which is difficult even for the gods to reach; therefore, one should perform his pilgrimage with every effort. (28)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nāgatīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to Vasiṣṭha, the treasure-house of austerities, by seeing whom a human being may properly attain the state of having fulfilled his purpose.
There is a pool there, filled with water and removing the sins of men; in that pool, O best of kings, by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha— || 2 ||
And Gomatī was brought there by means of ascetic penance, O best of kings; a man who bathes there properly is completely liberated from his sins.
O King, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there with the grain of the sages shall deliver all his ancestors belonging to both lineages.
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by the high-souled Nārada, after he had bathed in that holy water and beheld that best of sages.

O best of kings, what is the use of performing śrāddha at Gayā, or what is the use of other elaborate sacrifices, for that man who, having reached the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, performs a śrāddha—he shall deliver all his ancestors along with himself.
In that very place, near Vasiṣṭha, is the virtuous Arundhatī, who is especially worthy of worship and bestows all desires upon men.
Whatever sin has been committed in childhood, in old age, or even in youth, it is immediately destroyed for men by the sight of Vasiṣṭha.
The man who, with a concentrated mind, offers a lamp before Vasiṣṭha, is born endowed with happiness and good fortune, and becomes radiant.
He who, devoted to fasting, spends even a single night there, goes to the supreme abode where the stainless Seven Sages dwell.
He who, with a concentrated mind, performs the three-night rite in the presence of Vasiṣṭha, goes to Maharloka, freed from old age and death. || 11 ||
But he who performs the month-long fast in the presence of Vasiṣṭha also attains liberation; he does not go to the ocean of worldly existence.
He who, being composed, offers libations to the sages on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, goes to the world of Brahmā.
That man who recites the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times in the presence of Vasiṣṭha shall be instantly liberated from all sins committed from birth until death. || 14 ||
If one endowed with faith worships Vāmadeva there, O King, that person immediately obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 15 ||
Therefore, with every effort, that great sage should be beheld by those who are pure and endowed with faith; they shall go to the supreme state.
Therefore, O King, one should worship Vāmadeva with one's whole being.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vasiṣṭha’s Hermitage," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the most meritorious Acaleśvara; by seeing it, a man endowed with faith attains perfection.
In that place, whatever man performs a śrāddha on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, whether in the month of Āśvina or Phālguna, he goes to the supreme goal.
But he who, standing in the southern direction, worships with devotion using flowers, leaves, and fruits, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 3 ||
That man who performs libations there with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) shall attain the presence of the God and reach the world of Śiva. || 4 ||
The man who offers a prostration at the conclusion of the circumambulation—his sins are destroyed with every step of that circumambulation. || 5 ||
In that regard, O Mahāmati, listen to this truth which was formerly a marvel: it was heard by me in heaven from Nārada in the presence of Śakra.
There, the twice-born Śuka first built a nest in a tree; by his coming and going, he performed circumambulation of that nest.
And yet, O Great King, although born from the womb of a bird, that parrot did not [die] through devotion; rather, after a long time, he met his death.
Born in the lineage of the Pārthivas, he was known as King Veṇu; O great king, he remembered his former births and was the destroyer of all enemies.
Remembering that power indeed arising from circumambulation, he approached Acaleśvara and then performed a circumambulation.
Day and night, O Great King, he does nothing else; he exerts no effort whatsoever toward asceticism, nor in any way toward the offering of food.
He was not always intent on offering flowers, incense, or circumambulations; however, after some time, sages arrived there.
Nārada, Śaunaka, Hārīta, and likewise Devala; Gālava, Kapila, Nanda, Suhotra, and King Kaśyapa. (13)
These and many others, devoted to divine vows, some perform the ritual bathing of that Liṅga with devotion. || 14 ||
Others performed various kinds of worship, while others, composed in meditation, recited prayers; some danced, O lord of kings, and others likewise sang.
Some offered oblations, while others performed hymns of praise; then, having witnessed that supreme marvel, they circumambulated the king who was intent on the rite of circumambulation.
Then, overcome with great curiosity and desiring to know the cause arising from the circumambulation, they spoke these words.
The sages said: "O best of kings, why are you always intent upon circumambulating this deity specifically? You ought to tell us the truth. (18)
"You do not offer abundant and beautiful water to the Liṅga, nor flowers, incense, and the like, nor various hymns of praise. (19)
O lord of the earth, you are capable of [bestowing] other gifts as well; it is our curiosity that you should explain all of this to us exactly as it is. (20)
Veṇu said: "O best of the twice-born, listen to all that I shall relate; it is the truth, specifically concerning everything that occurred in a previous body."
Formerly, I was a parrot living in this palace; at that time, O Lord, I performed circumambulations of the deity day and night. (22)
By his grace and through its power, I have become one who remembers my past births; now, with supreme devotion, I perform this circumambulation.
"I do not know what fruit I shall obtain today through the grace of this god; for this reason, O sirs, I perform no other act whatsoever. (24)
Pulastya said: Then, having heard the words of Veṇu, the sages of celebrated vows, their eyes wide with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (25).
Then all those great sages and all the munis there became intent on circumambulation, endowed with supreme faith.
That illustrious king Veṇu also, by the grace of Śambhu, attained the eternal abode that is difficult even for the gods to reach.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Acaleśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the great lake Bhadrakarṇa, where even today many rocks resembling the three-eyed god (Śiva) are seen.
In the western part of that very place is the Liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow; by beholding it there, a human being becomes like the Three-eyed Lord.
In former times, there was one named Bhadrakarṇagaṇa, a favorite of Śiva; by him this Liṅga was installed and this very lake was constructed. || 3 ||
Then, at one time, he fought in battle with the Dānavas in the presence of Śambhu, accompanied by various hosts.
When Skanda was lost, the army slain, and Vīrabhadra defeated, they fled, terrified by fear, once Mahākāla had been conquered.
A powerful Dānava named Namuci, who was even more powerful, wielding a sword and shield, swiftly rushed toward Maheśvara.
But Bhadrakarṇa, seeing that Dānava immediately after, as he was falling toward him, stood facing him and said, "Stay! Stay! (7)
Having cut his sword with a razor-sharp blade and even his shield, the mighty one, overcome with rage, struck the Daitya between the breasts, O King.

Then, struck by him and entering into dense darkness, he fell upon the surface of the earth like a tree broken by the wind. Having met his death, that Daitya remained there bowing to Hara. Seeing him established in truth, Maheśvara was then pleased.
The Blessed One said: "I am well-pleased with your heroism and especially with your righteousness. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—that has always resided in your heart."
Bhadrakarṇa said: "O best of gods, since this liṅga has been installed by me at Arbuda, let your presence be here; remain steadfast in this lake."
The Blessed Lord said: "On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, my presence shall always be especially manifest in the lake and in the Liṅga."
Having bathed in Bhadrakarṇahrada, he who beholds the Three-eyed One with a concentrated mind shall certainly go to my eternal abode.
Therefore, one should perform a ritual bath there with every effort; and having worshipped that linga, he goes to the world of Śiva. || 15 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bhadrakarṇahrada and Trinetra," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, celebrated as Kedāra, which removes all the sins of men.
O King, a man who bathes there where the holy Mandākinī joins with the Sarasvatī is liberated from all sins.
Listen, O King, to this ancient history as it truly occurred, sung in many ways by the sages on Arbuda, the best of mountains.
Ajapāla, the best of kings, born of the Solar dynasty, protects the earth consisting of seven islands; of this there is no doubt.
That king had no elephants, no infantry, nor horses; he had no chariots, O Great King, nor were there such treasuries.
O King, he did not take taxes from his subjects that were excessive; devoted to the welfare of all the world, he ruled his kingdom in such a manner.
If someone should somehow commit an offense upon the surface of the earth, the weapons would instantly go to him and inflict punishment upon him at that very moment.
Thus, while this lord of men remains upon the earth, the world rejoices in happiness within a kingdom from which all thorns have been removed.
When the lord of men is present, the rain-cloud pours forth at will, the crops are full of sap, and the cows yield abundant milk.
Then, at a certain time, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha arrived at his house on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having seen him, he honored him according to the path prescribed by the scriptures, with rising to meet him and salutation, as well as with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites.
Thus honored by him with supreme devotion, O King, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, sat down comfortably and rested; then he recounted stories of royal sages as well as divine sages.
Then, O best of kings, at the conclusion of a certain conversation, he, endowed with humility, questioned that sage of celebrated vows.
The cowherd said: "O Brahmin, by the power of your ascetic practice, you know everything—the past, the future, and likewise the present. (14)
"O bull among sages, a curiosity has arisen in my heart; please show me favor and, out of your grace, tell it to me. (15)
Vasiṣṭha said: "Speak, O tiger among kings, whatever dwells in your mind; I shall tell you all of it, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (16)
The king said: By what ripening of karma has this supreme kingdom of mine become forever free of thorns, secure, and endowed with all objects of desire? (17)
O great sage, there is no one in my kingdom who is dejected, nor afflicted by suffering, nor seized by disease; indeed, there is no one who is poor.

"This woman is my virtuous wife, dearer to me than my own life. Her mind is fixed on me, her life is dedicated to me, and she is ever devoted to my welfare. O Brāhmaṇa, tell me everything that was thought by her in full detail. (19)
O Sage, O best of sages, is this by the power of giving, or of vows and sacrifices, or of asceticism, or of religious observances and restraints? (20)
"O best of the twice-born, my curiosity regarding the merit performed in a previous birth is indeed great; please relate it to me in detail out of your grace. (21)
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O protector of the earth, everything shall be told to you in detail; you should feel neither anger nor shame, O high-minded one.
O King, in another body, she was born into the Śūdra caste; this virtuous woman, who was previously of the Śūdra caste, has indeed become your wife. (23)
Then, after some time, O Great King, when a famine had arisen and food was exhausted, the entire world was afflicted by hunger.
Then, having ascended with difficulty to a certain mountain waterfall, you went together with your wife to another foreign land.
You have seen a beautiful and auspicious grove of lotuses; having bathed there and drunk the water, the ancestors and the gods were fully gratified.
For this was indeed thought by him in his mind: "Taking these lotuses, I shall sell them so that I may obtain food in every way. (27)
Then, taking many lotuses with his wife, he went to where many people had gone, O best of kings. (28)
No people, afflicted by famine, will accept anything from you; you have wandered everywhere, become exhausted, and have reached a state of world-weariness.
Then, at the close of day, having taken refuge in a certain cave and laid down lotuses upon the ground, he fell fast asleep, overcome by hunger.
At that very moment, however, there reached his ears the sound of the recitation of the Vedas and Purāṇas by the foremost of the twice-born.
Having heard that, he rose up immediately; then, realizing it was the time for vigil, he took lotuses and went with his wife right there to the temple of Śiva.
There, a courtesan named Nāgavatī, devoted to Śivarātri, kept a vigil at night at Kedāra with supreme devotion.
O Lord of Men, a maidservant standing by her side was questioned by you: "O girl, for what reason is there a night vigil before the God? (34)
She said, "On the night of Śivarātri, this courtesan of excellent complexion, named Nāgavatī, performs a vigil with devotion during the night. (35)
He who, endowed with faith and devotion, performs a night vigil after having worshipped Mahādeva, goes to the supreme state. || 36 ||
The man who, having observed a fast, worships the Three-Eyed Lord with lotuses, goes to the realm of Rudra, served by hosts of celestial nymphs.

"One who possesses desire obtains even those desires that are very difficult for even the gods to attain. Therefore, you give me these lotuses and three palas of gold; having received their price, provide sustenance for my life. (38)
Then you were told by your wife: "O Lord, while gold is being taken, the price for these must not be accepted by you under any circumstances. (39)
"Indeed, the fast undertaken by both of you was born of necessity due to the lack of food; therefore, it is certain that Hari is to be worshipped today with these very lotuses. (40)
"Today you must do this: let the gold of this [woman] be abandoned. Having heard the words of his wife, Śiva was honored by them with lotuses. || 41 ||
O Great King, with faith and accompanied by your wife, you performed a vigil before Śiva in the temple of Śiva. (42)
O best of kings, O great monarch, the hearing of the Purāṇas took place there on Śivarātri, and Śiva was worshipped with lotuses.
O great king, you have likewise performed a night vigil with devotion before Kedāra with a one-pointed mind. (44)
Then, when morning had dawned, O Great King, you performed your alms-round and took your meal-offering (pāraṇā) before Śiva together with your wife.
Then, after some time, you passed away according to the law of time; and this wife of yours entered the fire together with you.
Born from that [lineage], O Great King, you became the daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa; and in the city of Vaideha, O best of monarchs, you were born as a king. (47)
O best of kings, you shall be renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Ajapāla, and you will be dear to all living beings.
For this reason, this wife, who is as dear to me as my own life, was born again for you, since you ask me about her. (49)
O lord of the earth, by the majesty of that god Kedāra, your kingdom shall be a source of happiness for men and likewise free from all thorns.
O Great King, you have obtained [this power] through the grace of Kedāra, by which you protect the earth even though you are devoid of an army. (51)
Pulastya said: Having heard those words of his, that king, the lord of the earth, filled with wonder, set his mind upon going toward Kedāra.
Having gone to that delightful mountain and having worshipped that Lord, he became fully devoted to Śivarātri every year.
Having established his son in the kingdom, he then went to Arbuda; thereupon, by the power of that place, he attained liberation along with his wife.
O lord of the earth, all this greatness of Kedāra has been narrated to you; it bestows auspiciousness upon men and destroys every sin. (55)
O high-minded one, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna is renowned on this earth as Śivarātri. (56)
O great king, O monarch, one should perform his pilgrimage there in every respect; one should perform the worship of Kedāra.
O King, he who observes a fast and performs a vigil there on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha goes to the world of Śiva.
Those who, having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī which fulfills all desires, behold Kedāra, shall go to the supreme goal.
Whoever drinks the pure water at the pool known as Kedāra shall deliver fourteen ancestors—seven preceding and seven following generations.
And whoever should constantly hear this with supreme devotion, O King, he too shall be liberated from sins through the power of Kedāra. (61)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kedāra," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Yayāti said: "O Brahmin, it is heard that Kedāra is on the Himālaya mountain; from there the Gaṅgā has emerged and entered the eastern ocean. (1)
Likewise, the goddess Sarasvatī emerged from the mango tree and, having taken up the subterranean fire (vaḍavānala), reached the western ocean.
"How did you come here, and what is this curiosity regarding Kedāra? O Brahmin, tell me everything in detail; it is wonderful to me. (3)
Pulastya said: "O great king, this which you ask us here is indeed true. Listen attentively to how it happened, exactly as it was heard by me."
O best of kings, in former times the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, the celestial abodes such as Kedāra, and the gods led by Śakra were all with me.
O Indra among kings, all the great seers went to Brahmā; there they all engaged in various and distinct discourses on dharma.
And in that assembly of the gods, O King, all sacred fords, holy fields, forests, and groves were present.
Then, in the course of conversation, Indra, filled with curiosity, spoke to the Four-faced One and questioned him, O best of kings.
Indra said: "O Blessed One, I now desire to hear about the meritorious majesty [of this place], as well as the distinct measurements for all the ages, beginning with Kṛta."
Brahmā said: O Lord of the Gods, the measure of a Yuga is declared to be one hundred and seventeen lakhs, together with twenty-eight thousand years; this is called the Kṛta [Yuga].
The age known as Tretā is said to consist of twelve hundred thousand years, measured by an additional ninety-six thousand.
Eight hundred and sixty-four thousand [years] are proclaimed; after that, indeed, is the age named Dvāpara, as celebrated by the gods. (12)
O best of gods, it is said that the measurement of a Yuga consists of four hundred and thirty-two thousand Kali ages.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma has four feet and Janārdana is white in color; in that age, there is indeed neither famine nor disease anywhere.
And then righteousness is performed; there is no untimely death for men. Without a plough there is no harvest, yet cows yield abundant milk. (15)
O Thousand-eyed One, in that age, lust, anger, fear, greed, envy, and malice never exist at any time.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, Dharma was born with three feet; the men in that age were long-lived, and Janārdana was red in color.
In that [age], sacrifices proceed which grant the desired objects to living beings; and in that [age], no inclination toward desire and the like arises among men.
Through austerity, celibacy, ritual baths, various kinds of gifts, as well as sacrifices, recitations, and burnt offerings, there shall be sustenance for men there.
Then the third age, called Dvāpara, is described; at that time, Dharma became two-footed, and Janārdana was yellow in color.
In the Dvāpara age, O best of gods, recitations, sacrifices, and austerities are performed with a desire for fruits; and the world is characterized by both truth and falsehood. (21)
There, the rulers of the earth fought one another upon the surface of the earth; yet those who were well-purified, having worshipped Janārdana with sacrifices, went to heaven.
Thereafter, the terrible fourth age, Kali-yuga, sets in; dharma remains with only one foot, and people become terrified even of daily worship.
Viṣṇu becomes black in color, and an abundance of sin prevails; likewise, illusion, envy, desire, anger, and fear arise.
Likewise, kings will be greedy for wealth and possessed by hundreds of lusts and delusions; men there will have short lifespans, and the earth will yield little grain. (25)
Likewise, cows will yield little milk, and the twice-born will be devoid of truth; the people there will be deceitful, devoted solely to the pleasures of the tongue and the genitals.
Likewise, in the Kali age, people will be devoid of truth and sinful; therein, at the sixteenth year, men will have grey hair.
O Lord of the Gods, women will become pregnant at twelve years of age, and there will gradually arise a mixture of castes.
Indeed, all castes and stages of life will become uniform; sacrifices will go to ruin, as will the eternal family dharma.
O best of gods, all sacred fords (tīrthas) touched by barbarians (mlecchas) there will become useless and devoid of power in every respect.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, the sacred fords situated there spoke this to Brahmā: || 31 ||
The sacred fords (tīrthas) said: "How shall we fare when the terrible Kali age has arrived? O Lord of Gods, tell us our place, for we must certainly remain forever. (32)
Brahmā said: Arbuda is the best of mountains; there, the Kali age does not exist. Therefore, one should go there along with sacred fords (tīrthas) and shrines.
Even one who has committed a great sin as vast as an arbuda, if he gazes upon Arbuda, shall be liberated from the defects of the Kali age and attain the supreme goal.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, O King, the four-faced one went to the world of Brahmā; thereafter, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) departed during the Kali age.
Out of fear of the Kali age, the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the Yamunā, and the Puṣkara lakes remained stationed on the ground at Arbuda, the lord of mountains.
Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and likewise Brahmāvarta—those three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist upon the surface of the earth.
Their dwelling was established on the mountain named Arbuda; thus did Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī arrive there. (38)
There, peaceful men shall duly attain supreme nirvāṇa; and by performing a śrāddha ceremony, O great king, their ancestors go to heaven. (39)
Listen, O Great-minded One, to that wonder which occurred there in the past: there lived on the bank of the Sarasvatī a sage named Maṅkaṇaka. (40)
That virtuous soul, free from desire and anger, performed austerities; while he was thus engaged, once he happened to sneeze.
The bile fell there and it appeared as if made of blood; seeing that, the sage Maṅkaṇaka became exceedingly delighted.
Realizing, "I have attained perfection," he then performed a dance; while he was thus engaged, the entire world, both stationary and moving, [was affected].
There, even the oceans, having fallen into agitation, were tossed about; everyone, abandoning their household duties, was struck with wonder. (44)
O best of kings, O foremost of monarchs, as that excellent sage was thus dancing, all the worlds danced as well by his power.
Then all the hosts of gods, having gone to the Destroyer of Kama, said: "O Maheśvara, act in such a way that he does not dance at all."
Then, addressed by Śambhu in the form of a brahmin, that best of the twice-born was asked: "O Brahmin, you have performed austerities; why now do you dance? (47)
Maṅkaṇaka said: "O Brahmin, do you not see that blood and bile are present within me? Since my blood and bile have become perfected, I have attained success."
"For this reason, O twice-born one, I dance out of joy. Having been addressed thus by him, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [spoke]. (49)
O best of kings, he struck his own thumb with his forefinger; then, from that thumb, there issued forth ash as white as a lotus stalk.
Then he said to Maṅkaṇaka: "Behold, O Brahmin, from my hand pure ashes have emerged; behold, O twice-born one, my wonder! (51)

Pulastya said: Having seen that and being struck with wonder, the brahmin, recognizing him to be the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), knelt upon the ground and spoke these words: 52. Pulastya said: Having seen that, the brahmin was struck with amazement; recognizing him to be the one whose banner is the bull, he went down to the earth on his knees and spoke these words.
Maṅkaṇaka said: "Surely you are Mahādeva himself whom I have beheld; be gracious to me. You have been ascertained by me; this dwells within my heart. (53)
"This power which has been displayed by you to me does not belong to anyone else; O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, show compassion and deliver me. (54)

Śrī Mahādeva said: "O best of Brahmins, I have been rightly understood by you; there is no doubt in this matter. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—since you have performed such excellence in dancing."
Maṅkaṇaka said: "Those who perform their ablutions here in the Sarasvatī with concentrated minds shall, through your grace, obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (56)
Śrī Mahādeva said: Those who, with concentrated minds, perform their ablutions here in the Sarasvatī shall go to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
O best of the twice-born, those who perform a śrāddha here at the world-renowned confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī shall attain the supreme goal.
Those who give gold here to an excellent brahmin according to their ability shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme goal.
Having spoken thus, O King, Maheśvara, the God of gods, vanished.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of All Tīrthas to Arbuda Mountain due to the Influence of the Kali Age," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the supreme deity Koṭīśvara, by beholding whom a human being may properly attain the highest perfection.
Listen, O lord of the earth, to that wonder which occurred there in former times: in the south, excellent sages numbering in the tens of millions [resided]. (2)
Competing with one another, they all arrived at Arbuda with ease, each thinking, "I shall see the Lord of the Mountain first; I shall see him first."
The Brahmin who arrives later will become like a dog; he will be more wicked, devoid of devotion, and lacking in faith.
Thus competing with one another, they arrived at Arbuda with ease; thereafter, all of them became self-controlled and perfectly devoted to their vows.
All those ascetics were peaceful and proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas; having fully understood their desire, the Destroyer of Kama [approached them].
Overcome by supreme compassion and out of a spirit of devotion, Maheśvara established himself in that place, manifesting ten million of his own liṅgas.
O best of kings, at one and the same time, Maheśvara was seen individually by all the sages, numbering in the tens of millions.
Then all those sages, seeing Maheśvara together with her, their eyes wide with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (9).
All those twice-born ones, filled with devotion, praised him with Vedic hymns; then Śambhu, pleased with them, spoke these words.
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "O all you sages, I am indeed pleased with your supreme faith. Let a boon be chosen quickly by each of you individually."
The sages said: "O Lord, this alone has been the boon cherished in the hearts of us all: let the supreme fruit arise from seeing you all at once."
Śrī Mahādeva said: "The sight of me shall not be in vain, especially for a Brāhmaṇa; those who behold me shall obtain the fruit born of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites."
The sages said: "O Maheśvara, O Bull-bannered One, if a boon must certainly be granted to us, let a single Linga consisting of ten million [parts] be created."
"O Bull-bannered Lord, grant us this boon: that upon seeing it, men may obtain the fruit born of ten million lingas. (15)
Pulastya said: While the sages of purified souls were thus offering their prayers, the Liṅga suddenly emerged, having burst through that best of mountains.
At that very moment, O lord of the earth, an incorporeal voice spoke out of supreme compassion toward all those sages.
The Voice said: "My Liṅga, named Koṭīśvara, shall attain renown in the world; and whoever shall worship it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha," (18)
O Brahmins, for that man from the Deccan who performs a śrāddha here, the fruit shall be a millionfold.
The fruit of that [action] shall be ten-millionfold, equal to a śrāddha performed at Gayā; therefore, my liṅga must be especially worshipped by human beings. (20)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, O lord of the earth, that voice ceased. Then all those sages [honored her] with perfumes, incense, and ointments.
O King, they worshipped that great Liṅga with supreme faith; having worshipped it, they all attained perfection through the grace of the Liṅga.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Koṭīśvara," in the third section on Arbuda, within the seventh section on Prabhāsa, in the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Rūpatīrtha, which removes all sins of men and bestows beauty and good fortune.
In that regard, O Great King, there was formerly a most excellent Apsaras renowned in the world by the name Vapuḥ, who attained perfection as has been related of old. (2)
In former times, there was a certain Ābhīrī woman who was deformed, with a distorted face, a protruding belly, a crooked neck, and thick teeth and hair.
Once, while wandering on Mount Arbuda to gather fruit on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, she fell into a mountain torrent.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, endowed with celestial limbs, lotus-eyed, with beautiful hair, she was marked by all auspicious characteristics.
O Great King, she was born through the power of this sacred ford; at that very moment, Śakra arrived there.
On that best of mountains, while there for the sake of sport, he beheld that woman of beautiful eyes; then, pierced by the arrows of Kāma, he spoke to that woman of slender waist.
Indra said: "Tell me, O lady of beautiful hips, who are you? For what purpose have you come here? Are you a goddess, or the daughter of a Naga, or perhaps a Siddha or a Vidyadhari?"
"O lady of beautiful brows, my mind has been captivated by you, who have lotus-like eyes. I am Śakra, the lord of all the gods; accept me, O lady of lovely smiles. (9)
The woman said: "O Lord of the Thirty-three Gods, I am an Ābhīrī woman with many husbands; having come here for the sake of fruit, I fell into a mountain torrent."
"Having bathed, I have attained this beautiful and auspicious form; for you are indeed difficult even for the gods to obtain, let alone for those born as mortals. (11)
"All those gods are under my control; why do you desire me? O Lord of the Thirty-three, O Sovereign of the Gods, enjoy me as you wish. (12)
Pulastya said: Having been addressed thus by her, Śakra then desired her; having withdrawn his passion, he spoke to that woman of slender waist.
Indra said: "Choose a boon, O auspicious lady, whatever dwells in your heart. I am pleased by your modesty and shall grant you an excellent boon. (14)

The noble lady said: "Whether it be a man or likewise a woman, whoever performs a ritual bath with devotion on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, all the deities shall be pleased. (15)
"May they be born with a beauty difficult even for the gods to attain; O Thousand-eyed One, Lord of the Gods, lead me to the abode of the immortals. (16)
Pulastya said: Having said "So be it" to her, the lord of the gods took her and, together with her, went toward the celestial realm in a celestial chariot.
O best of kings, because she obtained that body (vapuḥ), that excellent Apsaras became known by the name Vapuḥ.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, all the gods perform their ablutions in that reservoir at dawn, filled with devotion.
There, O lord of men, at that time, other celestial maidens as well as the wives of Siddhas and Yakṣas are present for him who performs his bath.
And he shall obtain such a form as was previously obtained by her; there all the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas shall come to be.
In the eastern direction of that very place, there is a most beautiful cave, where the maidens of Pātāla come and perform their ablutions.
Having bathed there and taken water, they enter that cavity; therein, upon the pedestal of Vaināyaka, is great water produced from stone.
By being joined with that water, a person becomes perfected; for whoever takes that water and goes wherever he may, [he attains success]. || 24 ||
Neither in heaven nor on the surface of the earth can it be assailed by anyone; there, at the entrance of the cave, stands a tree named Tilaka.
By means of its flowers and fruits, every undertaking of his becomes successful; by either eating them or wearing them, a human being becomes a perfected one (siddha). || 26 ||
In that cave, however, the stones on all sides resemble conch shells; when touched by that water, they become made of gold.
If a barren woman drinks water there mixed with sesame seeds, even if she is a hundred years old, she will immediately become pregnant. (28)
Even a mortal seized by disease who performs a bath there becomes healthy immediately, and one possessed by a planetary spirit is liberated.
The affliction caused by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas is instantly destroyed; when touched by that water, every evil deed perishes. (30)
Even those who are insects, moths, piśācas, birds, or wild animals—whosoever are touched by that water shall immediately attain a good rebirth.
Yayāti said: "O Brahmin, this marvelous majesty of Rūpatīrtha which has been described by you is one that has never occurred before, nor will it ever occur again. (32)
O Brahman, what is the reason that this is remembered as superior even to all else? Tell me everything in detail, for my curiosity is indeed great. (33)

Pulastya said: O best of kings, in former times Aditi performed penance there when Indra had been deprived of his kingdom and Bali was the leader of the three worlds. Then, O best of kings, the four-armed Lord descended into Aditi.
When that great Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Asuras, was born, Aditi remained hidden at the entrance of the cave out of fear arising from the Dānavas.
As soon as he was born, Hari was placed by her in that waterfall; from that, the sacred site attained purity and became the bestower of desires upon men.
And there is no other cause, O King; this which I have spoken is the truth: on the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Trivikrama was born there.
The Tilaka tree, the foremost of all trees, was nurtured like a son; it was constantly served by Aditi with auspicious waters from her own hand.

Thus has this entire, supreme majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha) been recounted to you. Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath there; it bestows all desires upon men, both in this world and in the next. (39)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rūpatīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds, situated to the northeast of the royal sage Ambarīṣa, which destroys all sins.
In that very place, at the time known as Kali, Hṛṣīkeśa himself, honoring his word, indeed resides personally at the sacred ford.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was once a protector of the earth named Ambarīṣa; he propitiated Hari and performed most difficult austerities.
At that sacred ford, that lord of kings, with his senses conquered and his food restricted, remained for a thousand years subsisting on fruits alone.
Then, O King, for two thousand years he subsisted on withered leaves; thereafter, for another two thousand years, he lived solely on water.
O King, for three thousand years he subsisted on air alone, contemplating the Lotus-eyed One in his mind, filled with faith.
Then, at the end of ten thousand years, O best of kings, the Blessed Viṣṇu was pleased and granted him a vision.
Having assumed the form of the Lord of the Gods and mounted the elephant Airāvata, he said to King Ambarīṣa, "I am the giver of boons."
Indra said: "Choose a boon, O King—may it be well with you—whatever is desired by your mind. Having seen you endowed with devotion, I have come here without a doubt."

Ambarīṣa said: "O slayer of Vṛtra, you are unable to grant me liberation. By your grace, O Lord of Gods, the three worlds remain under my control. Welcome! Depart, O Lord of Gods; no boon is pleasing to me."
"In every way, the four-armed one, being pleased, will grant me a boon; then I shall accept it. Go, O God, salutations to you! (11)
Indra said: "Choose a boon, O royal sage, whatever dwells in your mind; for I am the lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Three-eyed One, O best of kings. (12)
"I am the sovereign even over other gods and indeed over the three worlds; therefore, by my grace, choose a boon that is very difficult to obtain."
O Indra among kings, since I am pleased, all the deities are pleased. O King, follow my word and accept this most excellent boon.
Ambarīṣa said: "O slayer of Vṛtra, you are the king of all the gods and likewise the lord of the three worlds; I am the king of the earth consisting of seven islands."
"O dear one, know me for certain to be a true devotee of Hṛṣīkeśa; and when Hṛṣīkeśa has arrived, he will undoubtedly grant you a boon. (16)
Indra said: "O protector of the earth, if you do not accept my boon while I am offering it, I shall hurl my thunderbolt at you, having resolved upon your destruction. (17)
Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed one, licking the corners of his mouth, took the thunderbolt in his right hand and whirled it around.
As he was wandering in this manner, great portents occurred; then, mountain peaks shattered on all sides. (19)
Then the sky was covered by clouds that shook the earth; nothing at all could be seen there, as everything was enveloped in total darkness.
At that very moment, however, that king, who was fond of Hari, closed his eyes and became absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then the Lord of the World, being pleased, became manifest before his very eyes; at that very moment, he became Airāvata and Garuḍa.
Hṛṣīkeśa, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud to that best of kings who was absorbed in meditation.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am well-pleased with you, O child, O lord of men, for you are devoted to none other. Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—even if it be very difficult to obtain. (24)
Ambarīṣa said: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then become the granter of a boon to me, O Hari, for the sake of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. (25)
Pulastya said: Then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke to Ambarīṣa, the lord of men, concerning the very extensive yoga of knowledge, which is the cause for the destruction of saṃsāra.
"O King, upon whose birth a man is immediately liberated from saṃsāra"—having heard this, that monarch, bowing properly, spoke to Keśava.
Ambarīṣa said: "O Blessed One, this yoga which has been described by you to me in detail is difficult for men to understand, O Lord, especially in the Kali age. (28)
Moreover, O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, if you are well-pleased with me, please tell me of Kriyā-yoga for the sake of delivering the worlds. (29)
Pulastya said: Then, O best of kings, Keśava Janārdana explained the yoga of ritual action (kriyāyoga) to that lord of men as was appropriate.
Having heard that, Ambarīṣa, with a joyful heart, spoke these words: || 31 ||
Ambarīṣa said: "O Blessed One, O Mādhava, if you are pleased with this form, O Lord of Gods, may you always remain present in my hermitage. (32)
"Since I worship this single image of yours according to the prescribed rites, people shall worship you as the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace. (33)
Pulastya said: Thus addressed by Mādhava, he constructed a temple for Hari and worshipped the image with perfumes, flowers, and unguents.
Then, after a long time, the Blessed One arrived at the temple of Viṣṇu in that very same body, accompanied by his sons and kinsmen.
Even today, O King, by virtue of the monarch's truthful word, Lord Viṣṇu remains ever present there at that time in the Kali age.
From that time forward, O Great King, the practice of Kriyāyoga in the form of images has been established upon the earth during the age known as Kali.
O King, he who worships Hṛṣīkeśa with devotion at Arbuda attains the same world as Viṣṇu through the grace of Hari, O King.

O Great King, O Ruler, he who always performs the vigil on the eleventh day, remaining without food before Hṛṣīkeśa, shall go to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (39)
Whatever merit is gained from the gift of a Kapila cow at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika, a mortal obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Hṛṣīkeśa.
Whether it be during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, when the day of Hari has arrived, he who beholds Hṛṣīkeśa shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship according to the prescribed rites. He who, devoted to the vow, properly worships Hṛṣīkeśa there for four months is not born again.
O best of kings, one person visits all the sacred fords, while another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period.
One person bestows all kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins; another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya.
One person might give a thousand maidens in marriage according to the prescribed rites, while another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period. (45)
One may give unsurpassed gifts at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse; another, being composed, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period.
One person performs sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with sacrificial fees, while another, being composed, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya observance.
One, having gone to the Himalayas, casts off his own body; another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya.
One may abandon the body at a sacred bathing place by leaping from a cliff, while another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period.
One man gives up his life by fasting unto death, while another, composed in mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya.
One person, having become expert in knowledge upon hearing it, speaks of the knowledge of Brahman; another, being composed during the Cāturmāsya, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa.
O best of kings, one performs the śrāddha at Gayā for the sake of his paternal ancestors, while another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period.
One person, composed in mind, performs a thousand cāndrāyaṇa penances; another, likewise composed in mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the four months of the rainy season.
One man might perfectly observe a vow of austerity for a thousand years, while another, being composed, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya period.
One Brāhmaṇa may recite the four Vedas perfectly, while another, with a concentrated mind, beholds Hṛṣīkeśa during the Cāturmāsya.
What is the use of saying much more here? Listen in brief, O King: on one side may be everything, but on the other side is the sight of Hari.
Therefore, with every effort, one should remain in the presence of Hari at the sin-destroying site of the royal sage Ambarīṣa. (57)
On one side is Hṛṣīkeśa, and on the other side is Karṇikeśvara; O best of kings, whatever mortals and men die between those two [are liberated].
Even having committed great sin, they go into the presence of Hari; by beholding Hṛṣīkeśa, they immediately attain liberation.
O King, he who offers even a single flower to Hṛṣīkeśa shall be endowed with happiness and good fortune both in this world and in the next.
He who, out of devotion, shall apply anointment to Hṛṣīkeśa, will go to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.

And whoever, with a concentrated mind, performs the sweeping in front of it, shall rejoice in the world of Viṣṇu for as many hundreds of years as there are particles of dust there; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O best of kings, O monarch, he who offers a lamp before Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika—
In whatever measure the sin accumulated in other births becomes manifest, in that same measure it shall perish entirely from his body.
Whoever shall perform worship of Hṛṣīkeśa with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), or with curd or milk, is not born again.
Therefore, with every effort one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa; O King, by doing so, a human being attains liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra.
Worship should always be performed especially for Hṛṣīkeśa.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Hṛṣīkeśa," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 13.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the supreme deity Siddheśvara, who grants success to living beings and was established in the past by Siddha himself.
There, a Siddha named Viśvāvasu performed great penance for many years, remaining devoted to Śiva with supreme faith.

Having conquered anger, overcome pride, and subdued the activities of all his senses, at the end of those thousands of years, the Blessed Lord whose banner is the bull was pleased and appeared in person before that king.
Mahādeva said to him, "O King, I am the giver of boons."
The Blessed Lord said: "Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells in your mind; being pleased, I shall grant it to you, even if it be very difficult to obtain. (5)
Viśvāvasu said: O Śaṅkara, best of the gods, having meditated upon this liṅga with firm resolve in his mind, let him attain all his desires through your grace.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, "So be it," he vanished on that very spot. Then, by going to Siddheśvara, one attains perfection by the thousands.
By the power of that linga, people obtained all their desired objects; consequently, all religious rites on the surface of the earth fell into ruin.
No one performs sacrifices with rituals, nor does anyone bestow gifts; yet, by the grace of Siddheśvara, men on earth attain perfection.
O best of kings, when sacrifices and gifts had been abolished, all the thirty gods, headed by Indra, fell into supreme distress.
Having learned of the obstruction to the sacrifice, Vāsava covered it with his thunderbolt so that no success could arise from its interruption.
Nevertheless, O best of kings, in the presence of that Lord of Siddhas, success in one's actions arises and the destruction of sin occurs. (12)
O best of kings, that man who touches [the deity] on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight, on a Monday, shall become a perfected one (siddha).
Even today, spiritual perfection is attained; this which I have spoken is the truth. Therefore, having gone to Siddheśvara and having bowed there, one shall go to a good state.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Śukreśvara, which was established in ancient times by Śukra; upon seeing it, a human being is immediately liberated from all sins. || 1 ||
O best of kings, having seen the Daityas formerly defeated by the gods, the wise brahmin Bhārgava reflected upon them.
"How shall the Daityas, having conquered the gods, attain great glory? By propitiating Śaṅkara, I shall go to the perfection desired by my mind. (3)
Having thus made his resolve, he went to Mount Arbuda; reaching a cavity in the earth, he performed most rigorous penance.
Having installed the Śiva-liṅga, he worshipped it incessantly with incense, perfumes, and ointments, endowed with supreme faith.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Blessed Lord Śiva was pleased; having granted him a vision, he spoke these words.
Śrī Mahādeva said: "I am well-pleased with you, O Brahmin, because of your devotion, O best of the twice-born. Choose a boon—may it be well with you—even if it should be very difficult to obtain."
Śukra said: "If you are pleased, O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant me that knowledge by which living beings, even when confronted with death, continue to live. (8)
Pulastya said: O best of kings, having bestowed that knowledge upon him, Śiva spoke again to Śukra: "Choose another boon from me."
Śukra said: "That man who, endowed with faith, touches this [Liṅga] on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika and then worships the Liṅga," || 10 ||
By your grace, may he have no fear of premature death; may he attain his desired objects in this world and in the next. (11)
Pulastya said: Having said, "So be it," he vanished right there; Śukra also [beheld] the Dānavas slain by the gods many times in battle.
And by the power of that knowledge, the sage restored them to life; before him was this great, stainless pool that destroys all sins.
A man who bathes there is completely liberated from his sins; O Indra among kings, by performing a śrāddha ceremony there, the ancestors go forth satisfied.
They are satisfied by water alone; how much more so by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas)! Therefore, one should perform a ritual bath there with every possible effort.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śukreśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the sin-destroying holy site known as Maṇikarṇikā, which is renowned throughout all the worlds.
O King, in that mountain cave where the great ṛṣis, the Vālakhilyas, attained perfection, a most beautiful pool was constructed by them.
O lord of men, listen to the truth regarding that great wonder which occurred there while those sages of purified souls were seated.
A certain Kirāta woman named Maṇikarṇikā was exceedingly dark, with deformed eyes, formidable, and of terrifying appearance.
Afflicted by thirst, she arrived there when the sun had reached the meridian; and when the sun was swallowed by Rāhu, she entered the water.
At that very moment, while the sages were looking on, the slender-waisted woman emerged, possessing a body of divine form.
Then her husband arrived, intent on searching for her; afflicted by grief for his wife, he questioned that woman of beautiful limbs.
"O slender-waisted one, if my wife has arrived here and been seen by you, tell me quickly, O beautiful lady; this boy was born of her."
Afflicted by thirst and overcome by hunger, he weeps again and again; if she is seen, let it be told, O fair-browed one—for without her, he will die.
The woman said: "O beloved, by the power of this sacred ford, I have become your wife and have attained this divine form, which is very difficult even for the gods to obtain. (10)
And you too, O sinless one, perform your bath in this water with haste; you shall attain a supreme form, just as it has been attained by me.
Then, O King, having entered that waterfall together with his son while the sun had set, he became deformed once again.
Having met her death through suffering in that very same body of water, she then, out of grief for her husband, resolved upon dying herself.
Having prepared the funeral pyre, he ignited the fire along with it. Then those sages, seeing that woman of auspicious limbs who was possessed of such conduct, [were amazed].
Overcome with supreme compassion and filled with wonder, O best of kings, they all spoke to her upon witnessing that act of hers. (15)
The sages said: "O beautiful woman, you have attained a divine form that is very difficult even for the gods to obtain; why then do you follow this most wicked man?"
The woman said: "O best of Brahmins, I am a devoted wife, always dedicated to my husband; what shall I do with beauty without my own husband? (17)
Whether he be ugly or handsome, poor or lord of wealth, for women there is but one husband as their master and refuge; there is no other in the three worlds. (18)
"O best of sages, this boy has come to you for refuge; as for me, united with my beloved, I shall enter the fire. (19)
Pulastya said: Then all those sages, having understood her firm resolve and looking at one another, were overcome with supreme compassion.
Then those lords of sages restored her husband to life, endowed with a beautiful form and marked by divine characteristics.
At that very moment, a celestial chariot desired by his mind arrived there instantly, filled with divine maidens.
Then that couple, having prostrated before those sages of purified souls, set out toward heaven.
Then those sages said to that woman at Maṇikarṇikā: "Choose a boon, O auspicious lady; we are all pleased with you."
Pleased by her devotion to her husband and especially by her truthfulness, our sight never becomes fruitless in any way whatsoever. (25)
Maṇikarṇikā said: "O sages, if you are pleased with me and joyfully grant me a boon, let this great liṅga that is here be known by my name. (26)
This alone is my desired goal; there is no other purpose. Through the grace of all of you, I shall now go to heaven. (27)
The sages said: "So be it; let your fame endure in this sacred ford and linga, O fair-faced one. This holy site has indeed become known as Maṇikarṇikā, bearing your name."
Pulastya said: Accompanied by her husband and her son, she reached heaven; there, the Vālakhilyas, who were devoted to austerity, were especially established.
In that regard, when a solar eclipse occurs, whoever performs rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts, their fruit shall be equal to that of Kurukṣetra. || 30 ||
