O King of kings, whatever desire one contemplates while performing a bath there, that very thing one attains, provided one is endowed with correct meditation. (31)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath there; at the sacred ford, one should give gifts according to one's ability and offer libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Maṇikarṇikeśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Paṅgutīrtha, which destroys all sins, where in former times penance was performed by a lame Brāhmaṇa.
O best of kings, formerly there was a twice-born man named Paṅgu in the lineage of Cyavana; due to his state of being lame, he was unable to move upon the earth.
O King, once, while he was appointed to household duties, that cripple was unable to go and experienced extreme suffering.
Then, abandoned by them, he went to Mount Arbuda; having reached a certain lake, he performed most rigorous penance.
Having installed a liṅga right there, he worshipped that Lord with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth, being fully endowed with perfect faith.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva, that best of the twice-born named Paṅgu became a consumer of air alone, constantly engaged in the recitation of mantras and the performance of fire-sacrifices.
Then, O best of kings, Mahādeva was pleased and spoke these words to the Brahmin who was lame, O great king.
Īśvara said: "O you of noble vows, Mahādeva is pleased with you; choose a boon. I shall grant you everything, even if it be very difficult to obtain."
The lame man said: "O Lord of the Gods, let this sacred ford (tīrtha) become famous by my name; O Śaṅkara, by your grace, let my state of lameness depart here."
"May you always remain present here together with your wife. Having been addressed thus by him, he then spoke these words to the Brahmin:
Īśvara said: "O best of the twice-born, this sacred ford (tīrtha) shall be known by your name; O most virtuous one, through the power of your asceticism, this tīrtha will attain renown."
Likewise, my presence shall be there on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra.
Pulastya said: Merely by bathing, that brahmin attained a divine form. There, Mahādeva, the Great Lord, remained together with Gaurī.
On that day, O best of kings, one should perform a bath there; he shall be liberated from lameness and attain a divine form. (14)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Paṅgutīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 17 ||
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Yama-tīrtha, which liberates living beings from hells and destroys their sins.
In former times, O best of kings, there was a king named Citrāṅgada who was exceedingly greedy; he did not perform even the slightest meritorious deed.
He was exceedingly cruel, wicked, a harasser of gods and Brahmins, constantly a stealer of others' wives, and likewise a thief of others' wealth.
Devoid of truth and purity, and possessed of deceit and envy, he once became intent on hunting while mounted upon Mount Arbuda.
Exhausted from wandering and distressed by hunger and thirst, he reached a lake there that was filled with clear water.
It was filled with lotus ponds, teeming with crocodiles, water-monsters, and fish; it was frequented by various birds, enchanting, and very extensive.
Afflicted by thirst, he entered that very body of water; at that very moment, O best of kings, he was seized and devoured by a crocodile.
For his sake, terrible hells were fashioned by Yama; then, having been led there, that worst of evildoers was cast into them by the messengers of Yama.

By his touch, all those residing in hell attained happiness; filled with wonder, those messengers reported to Dharmarāja the account of what had occurred in hell—the emergence of happiness for those dwelling there.
Then Vaivasvata said: "On earth there is Mount Arbuda; there is my very dear sacred site where penance was performed by me."

"In that regard, he has met his death; this is the cause for his brilliance here. They replied, "This is indeed true; he died on Mount Arbuda. That lowest of kings was seized there by a crocodile and met his end. (11)
Yama said: "Let this man be released quickly; no other people are to be brought who have died at my holy ford, which destroys all sins."
Then, O best of kings, released by those servants at the command of Yama, he joyfully reached heaven, being served by hosts of apsarases.
But he who, endowed with devotion, performs his bath there, goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath there on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, where Yama attained perfection.
On that very day, O King, a man should properly perform the śrāddha rites; his ancestors shall remain in heaven until the end of the kalpa.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Yama-tīrtha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the sin-destroying holy site (tīrtha) beloved by Hari in his Boar incarnation, which always bestows the happiness of residence.
In the Vārāha incarnation, the Earth was lifted up there by Hari, who said to her, "Remain firm; you must never fear."
"And I shall go from here again to the auspicious Vaikuṇṭha; choose a boon, O blessed lady, whatever you desire, however difficult it may be to obtain. (3)
The Earth said: "O Bearer of the Conch, Discus, and Mace, O Hari, if a boon is to be granted to me, then remain forever in this sacred ford in this very form."
Hari said: "O Goddess, at your word, I shall remain forever on the mountain named Arbuda in this very form, devoted to the welfare of the world."
In front of me is a meritorious lake filled with perfectly pure water; on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should remain there with a concentrated mind.
Having bathed there with devotion, a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; and there, men endowed with faith shall perform the ancestral Śrāddha rites.
The ancestors attain satisfaction [there] until the dissolution of all beings; therefore, one should perform the ritual bath there with every effort.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, O King, Govinda, whose banner bears Garuḍa, vanished. On that day, O best of kings, one should perform the vow after bathing.
O King, he who, intent on devotion, performs the libation and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), goes to the realm of Viṣṇu along with his ancestors.
Having gone there to that most excellent of Brahmins, they praise the gift of charity; O best of kings, he who performs the gift of a cow at this sacred ford [obtains great merit].
A human being remains in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the cow; therefore, O King, one should perform the gift of a cow with all one's soul. 12.
On the eleventh day, one should especially perform an excellent bath; one should give gifts according to one's capacity, and such a person attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vārāha Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to Candreśa at Prabhāsa; for it was there in ancient times that splendor (prabhā) was obtained by the great-souled Candra.
O King, in ancient times, all twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, headed by Aśvinī, were married by the Moon.

And among them, he constantly took delight with Rohiṇī alone; all the other daughters of Dakṣa were abandoned by Candra and became deeply distressed. Going to their father and bowing down, they spoke with eyes clouded by tears: ||| 3 ||
O Lord of Creatures, we have been abandoned by our husband, though we are faultless; therefore, filled with great sorrow, we have come to you for refuge. (4)
O best of gods, become our refuge and act for the welfare of all; having instructed this Candra, who is devoted to Rohiṇī, [depart].
Pulastya said: Having heard their words, he went to where the Maker of Night was and said, "Behold my daughters all with equal regard."
Then Candra, overcome with shame, replied to him: "O Dakṣa, I shall do as you say; go, salutations be unto you."
Then, when Dakṣa had departed, the Moon, devoted to Rohiṇī, abandoned all the maidens born of Prajāpati.
Then, having returned, all of them, being deeply distressed, spoke again to Dakṣa: "Indeed, your word was not heeded by the evil-minded Candra."
Tormented by the misery of misfortune, we shall die without a doubt; even with this life, death is certain.
Pulastya said: Then, filled with rage, Dakṣa went and spoke to the Moon: "O Candra, since my word was not heeded by you, O sinner! (11)
"Therefore, you shall meet your destruction by consumption; of this there is no doubt. Having thus pronounced the curse, Dakṣa then departed for his own abode.
Afflicted by consumption (yakṣman), the Moon waned day by day; being emaciated and deprived of luster, the Moon reflected thus: || 13 ||
"What must be done by me in this most terrible curse? And how shall I worship Śiva, the granter of all desires? (14)
Having thus made this resolve, he went to Mount Arbuda and performed austerities, having conquered his anger and being devoted to recitation and burnt offerings.
When ten thousand years had passed, Mahādeva, being pleased with him, said, "I am a granter of boons," and then he granted him a vision of himself.
Īśvara said: "Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind; I shall grant it to you, O Candra, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (17)
Candra said: "O best of gods, O destroyer of Tripura, bring about the destruction of my disease! O Lord of the world, this body of mine is pervaded by consumption. (18)
Īśvara said: "O Candra, by the curse of Dakṣa, consumption has taken hold in your body; for it is not possible to make that curse of the high-souled one otherwise. (19)
Therefore, at my word, look upon all those maidens of his simultaneously; O Moon, your disease shall depart.

O Moon, in the dark fortnight there shall be waning for you, and in the bright fortnight there shall be waxing. Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever other desired thing is very difficult to obtain.
Candra said: O Śaṅkara, whatever man here performs a bath with devotion during a lunar eclipse on a Monday, let him go to the supreme goal.
O Lord of Gods, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), may my ancestors go to heaven; O Lord of Gods, by your grace, let this sacred site (tīrtha) become a bestower of liberation.
Īśvara said: O Maker of Night, there shall be men right here who are free from sin, because you have obtained radiance at this sacred ford of pure water.
Therefore, this shall become renowned as Prabhāsa-tīrtha, where, when a lunar eclipse occurs—especially on a Monday—[great merit is attained].
Those men who perform their ritual bath here shall attain the supreme goal; likewise, those men who perform the śrāddha ceremony and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) here [shall do so].
O Candra, for them there shall be merit equal to that of performing a śrāddha at Gayā; likewise, O Soma, gifts should be bestowed by people during your eclipse.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, Virūpākṣa vanished on the spot; and Candra too enjoyed all the wives born of Dakṣa.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Candraprabhāsa Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Piṇḍodaka, the sacred ford where penance was performed by the twice-born Piṇḍodaka.
Long ago, O Mahāmati, there was a brahmin named Piṇḍodaka; he was dull-witted and of little intelligence, and was taught by his preceptor. (2)
O Lord of the Earth, being unable to study due to a state of dull-wittedness, he attained supreme detachment and arrived at a mountain cave.
At that very time and in that very place, Sarasvatī, accompanied by the diversion of her lute, approached him in that secluded spot.
Seeing that brahmin distressed and filled with world-weariness, the Great Goddess, overcome with compassion, spoke these words: ||| 5 ||

Sarasvatī said: "O Brahmin, why are you distressed? You appear as if detached from the world. Why do you not rejoice in your heart? For what reason have you come here? Speak quickly, O illustrious one; I dwell in your presence. (6)
Piṇḍodaka said: "O illustrious lady, having fallen into a state of world-weariness after being insulted by my preceptor, and being devoid of knowledge, I now desire death. (7)

"O lady of beautiful countenance, the goddess Sarasvatī does not dwell upon the tip of my tongue; there is no other cause for this here than death for me. Since I have been seen by you unexpectedly, I shall therefore depart elsewhere. For death is better for me than a life of silence."

Sarasvatī said: "O twice-born one, I am the goddess Sarasvatī; I always dwell on this excellent mountain at the onset of night on the thirteenth lunar day. Therefore, ask for whatever boon you desire, even if it be very difficult to obtain."
Piṇḍodaka said: "O Vāṇī, by your grace, omniscience is indeed my desire; O lady of pure smiles, let this sacred ford attain fame by my name. (11)
Sarasvatī said: "From this day forward, you shall indeed be omniscient in this world; likewise, this sacred ford (tīrtha) shall attain renown by your name. (12)
Whoever performs a bath here at the onset of night on the thirteenth lunar day shall become all-knowing, even if he be of very dull intellect. (13)
"O best of the twice-born, my residence shall be here forever; therefore, a bath must always be performed by those who are well-composed. (14)
Having spoken thus, the goddess then vanished right there; and Piṇḍodaka, having become omniscient, went to his own home, astonishing all the people by resorting to that sacred ford (tīrtha).

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Piṇḍodaka Tīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to Śrīmātā, who is praised by the gods and who grants all desires to men both in this world and in the next.
And that omnipresent power, by which this entire world is pervaded, chose to dwell there on that mountain in person.
Formerly, in the age of the gods, there was a Dānava king named Kaliṅga; he was free from old age and death, and he struck fear into the gods.

By him all this triple world, including the mobile and immobile, has been pervaded; by the power of his strength, heaven was conquered by him, and he reached the world of Brahmā accompanied by all the gods.
By that Daitya, all gods and humans were terrified; that Daitya, named Kaliṅga, indeed became Indra himself.
O lord of men, by him all the Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and divine sages were established among the Daityas according to their respective fitness.
All those Dānavas themselves consumed the sacrificial portions; thereafter, all the gods went to Mount Arbuda for the sake of performing penance.
Even today, the Devatā-khāta remains renowned throughout the three worlds; there, all are devoted to their vows, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits.
Out of supreme fear, they remained there meditating in an unmanifest state; some among them were practitioners of the five fires, devoted to their vows.
Some eat but once a day, others are without food, while others still subsist on air; some observe monthly fasts, and others are devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Some were devoted to the Kṛcchra and Sāṃtapanīya penances; others were Mahāpārākiṇas; some subsisted on water, some on air, some drank foam, and others drank heat.
Others were devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, while others were absorbed in meditation; O lord of men, [they worshipped] with offerings of food, oblations, perfumes, and incense.

Worshipping the supreme power, the Goddess, for the sake of their own purpose—thus, O King, for all those established in their vows whose souls were purified by austerity, there arose liberation from the bondage of karma.
Then, O best of kings, when a thousand years had been completed, the Goddess appeared in person, assuming the form of a young maiden.

O Great King, first there appeared a terrifying form of smoke; then a flame, and then a maiden adorned with white garments and unguents. Upon seeing her, the gods then offered praise with their palms joined in reverence.
Homage be to you, O Goddess who pervades all; salutations to you, who are worshipped by all! Salutations to you, O Kāmaga, O Inconceivable One, O Refuge of the Thirty-three Gods! || 16 ||
Salutations to you, O Supreme Goddess, the source of Brahman; salutations again and again! Salutations again and again to the half-mora syllable, and even to its half and half again.

Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed Mother of the Universe; salutations again and again. Salutations to you, O Goddess who grants boons, whose nature consists of the qualities of passion, goodness, and darkness.

O Goddess, while abiding in your own true nature, you are the very characteristic of worldly existence; you are intellect, you are fortitude, you are patience, you are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, and you are forgiveness.
You are growth, you are the goal, the agent; you are Śacī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī; you are Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, invincible and the destroyer of sins.
And whatever else exists here, O Goddess of the Gods, known as the three worlds—that form of yours, O Goddess, is established upon the mountains. (21)
Just as wood is pervaded by fire and as cloth is pervaded by thread, so is the world pervaded by you; you remain hidden, yet present everywhere.
Pulastya said: Thus praised, the Mother of the World spoke to those best of gods: "O most excellent of deities, let the boon desired by you be requested from me quickly."
Why do you remain here in concealment, situated in the midst of a chasm? For my devotees, there is no fear even throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
The gods said: "O Goddess, we have been repeatedly defeated in battle by Kaliṅga. By him, this entire triple world, including all mobile and immobile beings, has been pervaded. (25)
"The sacrificial portion that was ordained for us Daityas has been taken away; by that means heaven has been seized and all the gods have been expelled. (26)
"O highly fortunate one, act in such a way that Śakra may regain his own position after having slain the Daityas; this is the boon desired by us. (27)
The Goddess said: "O best of gods, just as you were created by me, so too was this great Asura; there is no difference whatsoever between the two of us."
"Therefore, I shall ward them off from the third heaven, including Śakra and the others. Having spoken thus, O King, the woman of beautiful limbs sent them forth.
"O messenger, abandon heaven quickly for the sake of the Daitya Kaliṅga. Having gone there, he spoke these words with conciliation to the Daitya Bāṣkali.

The messenger said: "That goddess who is omnipresent, whose form is Śakti, who possesses a pure smile, the illustrious Mother, the Mother of the worlds, the supreme one worshipped by the gods—pleased with them, the goddess spoke these words to you: 31.
"Go quickly to your own abode; let Śakra go to Triviṣṭapa. By my word, O best of Dānavas, you shall not possess the status of a god. (32)
Pulastya said: Having heard the words of the messenger, that Dānava, intoxicated with pride, [spoke].
Thinking himself to be the Lord of the World, he spoke these words with pride. || 33 ||
Bāṣkali said: "Who is Śrīmātā? Who are the gods? I will not abandon heaven because of them. I do not know her nor them; go and speak to them on my behalf. (34)
"I shall by no means grant you heaven; for even in the most terrible enmity, a messenger must remain unslayable even by kings. For this reason, O messenger, I do not deprive you of your life. (35)
O messenger, if you show me Śrīmātā, then I shall grant her all her desires; I speak this truly.
I will go with you to that place where she resides; I shall bring her under control, for my word is true. (37)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, that Dānava, intoxicated by pride and overwhelmed by great wrath, quickly departed for Arbuda with his messenger.
Seeing Bāṣkali approaching, the gods led by Śakra, though being restrained by the Goddess, then became intent on flight.
Overcome by great fear, they fled in all directions; then Bāṣkali arrived, surrounded by a vast army.
Where Śrīmātā resides on the mountain named Budabuda, the lord of men sent a messenger and spoke to him.
Bāṣkali said: "Go, O best of messengers, and speak to the beautiful-smiling Śrīmātā: 'O lady of lovely hips, become my wife; I shall always remain under your control. (42)
"For my entire kingdom shall come under your control; otherwise, I shall overpower you along with all the foremost of the gods. (43)
O lady of beautiful countenance, what is Indra, who possesses little prowess, or what are the others? The thousand-eyed one is not my equal, nor are the gods and asuras my equals.
Pulastya said: Having heard this, O lord of the earth, that messenger then went and reported everything exactly as it had been spoken by him.
Then, having heard this and smiling, the beautiful woman reflected: "This lord of the Daityas has been rendered free from old age and death by Śambhu."
"How can I effect his subjugation for the sake of the goddess?"—while she was thus reflecting toward the Dānava, he arrived there swiftly, overwhelmed by desire. (47)
Then, with a glance, that goddess looked upon the lord of the Dānavas; thereupon, a firm resolve arose within her.
Then, O best of kings, that goddess laughed softly; from her mouth there emerged an exceedingly terrifying army.
There were elephants, excellent horses, and various kinds of infantry; there were also thousands of warriors mounted upon a thousand chariots.
By them, the entire army of the lord of the Dānavas was struck down with weapons, even as that Daitya and Asura stood motionless watching.

When that army force was destroyed, Indra and the other inhabitants of heaven spoke these words to her: "O Goddess, you ought to slay the Dānava; as long as he lives, O Goddess, our sovereignty in heaven shall not exist. (52)
Pulastya said: Having heard those words of theirs and knowing him to be exempt from death, he himself gave a great peak of the mountain and placed it upon him.

O King, that Śrīmātā, the mother of the world who can assume any form at will, has settled there for the welfare of the worlds; even today she dwells in person upon that excellent mountain, bestowing the fulfillment of the desires of men.
At that very time, all the gods, together with Indra, were filled with great joy and praised that Great Power (Mahāśakti), the destroyer of fear.

Then, O lord of men, the Goddess became gracious toward them there; "O all you gods, go to your respective abodes, freed from affliction! Having gone to your own places, may you all protect [the world], free from suffering. || 56 ||
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Gods; speak what is in your heart. Being pleased by your devotion, I shall grant you all of it. (57)
Indra said: "O Goddess, eternal one, who art compassionate toward devotion, if you are pleased with me, then please remain right here in heaven for as long as I, the Lord, am present."
O Goddess of gods, eternal one, compassionate toward devotees, I shall rule the kingdom, for I am undecaying and immortal, O Sovereign of the Suras, since [the boon was granted] by the Daitya. (59)
It was fashioned long ago by Hara, by which it remains immovable; through your grace, may the three worlds be free from affliction.
"Having assembled here on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, we shall all worship you; having beheld you, may they go to a good state. (61)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed Indra, accompanied by all the gods, reached heaven joyfully through the power of that goddess.
That goddess also remained there, desiring the welfare of the gods.
O King, he who beholds her on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra goes to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death. (64)
O lord of men, what is the use of vows, observances, or even gifts? All of these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit of beholding him.

O lord of men, when those two divine sandals were placed there by her, whoever beholds them shall never again behold this cycle of worldly existence; he attains all desires both in this world and in the next.
Yayāti said: O best of the twice-born, at what time were the sandals placed here by the Goddess, and for what reason? Tell me everything in detail.
Pulastya said: O best of kings, all men who perform righteous deeds, upon beholding that goddess, attain the two kinds of supreme perfection.
At that very time, O King, the rites of sacrifice, charity, and the like, as well as those arising from pilgrimages and vows, were lost upon the earth. (69)
All those hells belonging to Yama became empty; and the gods, deprived of their sacrificial shares, fell into a state of misery.
Then, O best of kings, all the gods assembled there; having gone to Arbuda, they spoke to the supreme goddess Śrīmātā.
The gods said: O Goddess of the Suras, all rituals beginning with the Agniṣṭoma have perished; therefore, we are exceedingly tormented in the world of mortals by that deed.
"O Goddess, upon seeing you, even sinners attain perfection along with their ancestors; therefore, by your grace, may we also attain prosperity. (73)
The Daitya Bāṣkali does not go forth; you must act accordingly.

Pulastya said: Having heard those words of theirs and having reflected for a very long time, O Indra among kings, he placed his two sandals made of stone there and spoke to all the gods who had fallen into distress: 75. Pulastya said: Having heard their words and having reflected for a very long time, he placed his two sandals made of stone there and spoke to all the gods who had fallen into distress, O Indra among kings.
The Goddess said: "O gods, at your word, this best of mountains has indeed been abandoned by me; I have placed my sandals there for the sake of protecting it from Bāṣkali. (76)
O best of gods, that Daitya, overwhelmed by the weight of my sandals, will not be able to move from his place; he shall be rendered paralyzed just as I have done.
This entire treatise has been composed by me for the sake of the sandals, as a spiritual work for the benefit of living beings upon the surface of the earth. (78)
Whoever worships my sandals with devotion according to this scriptural method shall attain perfection arising from the vision of me.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, I shall always dwell here at Arbuda for a full day and night, well-concealed within a mountain cave.
This mountain is dear to me, and my mind was not set on abandoning it; nevertheless, it has been completely relinquished out of a desire for your welfare. (81)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, that goddess, being praised on all sides by gods and kinnaras, departed for heaven after leaving behind those two auspicious sandals.
Even today, yogins devoted to meditation attain perfection, being fixed upon that and having offered their lives to it, just as occurred from the manifestation of the Goddess.
O protector of the earth, all this that you asked me has been told to you—the meritorious account of the origin of the Śrīmātā and the two sandals.
O Great King, that man who recites this with devotion or praises it, being intent upon knowledge, is liberated from all sins. (85)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrīmātā," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Śuklatīrtha, which formerly attained its renown from the presence of the group of fishermen.
O lord of the earth, formerly there was a washerman named Śamilākṣa; O lord of the earth, he used to throw clothes into the midst of indigo.
Then, having realized that his clothing was merely a mockery, he became overcome with fear and set out for another country, accompanied by his own family.
Then, O King, his beautiful daughter, a friend of the fisherman’s daughters, overcome with great sorrow, ran toward her mother.
With a voice faltering with tears, he informed her of the danger arising from the garment and his departure for a foreign land.
The fisherman’s daughter also, filled with sorrow at her [the queen's] suffering, spoke while her voice was choked with tears and she sighed again and again. (6)
The fisherman’s daughter said: "O beautiful one, there is a great remedy known to me in this matter; by its certain performance, both you and your father will be free from fear."
O fair-browed one of excellent complexion, there is a waterfall here at Arbuda; there my brothers and other fishermen dwell.
And whatever else is thrown there into that auspicious water, all of it becomes white; behold my body is such as this.

O slender-waisted daughter, by immersing all those garments of the fishermen in that water, your father will quickly wash them right there in the water, and they will attain a state of perfect whiteness.
"You should not feel any fear in this matter; go and restrain your father who has set out for a foreign land—there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (11)
Pulastya said: Having heard her words, the daughter quickly went and reported everything to Janaka; thereupon, he attained great satisfaction.
Rising quickly in the morning, O king of kings, he ran toward that waterfall; indeed, as soon as those garments were thrown by him, [they fell].
Then, having been immersed in that water, those garments became exceedingly white and attained a supreme luster upon being seen.
Then, overcome with wonder, he took those [objects] and quickly reported the incident and its origin to the king.
Then, filled with wonder, that king threw other garments dyed with indigo into the water of that waterfall.
All things became pure and became distinguished; then, having recognized that supreme holy place, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite.
Having renounced his kingdom, that lord of the earth performed austerities in that very place; then, through the power of this sacred site, he attained supreme perfection.

O King, the man who performs a śrāddha ceremony there on the eleventh day uplifts ten generations of his lineage and thereafter goes to heaven; by that very moment, freedom from sin arises simply through bathing.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śuklatīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to where the goddess Kātyāyanī, the destroyer of the Dānava Śumbha, dwells in the midst of a cave.
In ancient times, there was a great Daitya named Śumbha upon the surface of the earth; having defeated the gods on the field of battle, he pervaded the entire world.
By virtue of a boon from Śaṅkara, that Daitya was incapable of being slain by gods, Dānavas, or Rākṣasas, as well as by all other living beings on earth, with the sole exception of women.

Then, O Lord of the World, all the hosts of gods went to Mount Arbuda and performed austerities for the sake of slaying Śumbha; they propitiated the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods, who had manifested her visible form.
Then, appearing before their field of vision, she, being pleased, said: "I am a granter of boons; tell me, what shall I do for you? (5)
The gods said: "O Goddess, everything has been seized from us by the very wicked Śumbha. O auspicious one, destroy him; he can never be slain by others in battle."
O Goddess, we were previously protected by you from Bāṣkali.

"O Mother, there is no other refuge for us except you, O lady of beautiful smiles. Pulastya said: Having been addressed thus by the gods, the goddess went to the abode of Śumbha; filled with rage, she challenged him to battle, rebuking him again and again.
When she requested a battle, the Daitya, O King, recognizing her to be a woman, treated her with contempt and then dispatched his Dānavas.
"Let this wicked woman of harsh voice be seized alive; let a cruel punishment be inflicted at my command—of this there is no doubt. (10)
Then, at his command, the Dānavas went quickly from there and, surrounding him on all ten sides, began to revile him.
Then, by her mere glance, those Daityas were reduced to ashes; thereupon, Śumbha, filled with rage, arrived there in person.
Raising his sword, the terrifying one cried out, "Stay! Stay! But he too, O Great King, was likewise gazed upon by the Goddess.

He was instantly reduced to ashes like a moth in a fire; when he was slain, O best of kings, the remaining Daityas, filled with fear, pierced through the netherworld (rasātala) and went to Pātāla. || 14 ||
Then all the hosts of gods praised that sovereign of the deities and said: "Choose a boon; tell us whatever dwells in your heart. (15)
The Goddess said: "O best of gods, I shall indeed remain on that very mountain, Arbuda; for that mountain, known by the name Arbuda, is always dear to us. (16)

The gods said: "Beholding you stationed there, mortals go to the third heaven even without sacrifices or gifts; thus, heaven has become overcrowded. O Queen of the Gods, there is no other cause here for this prohibition."

The Goddess said: "O lords of the gods, I shall remain there in a secluded and beautiful cave within that mountain; for only a few living beings will come into the range of my vision as they proceed toward that peak. (17)
The gods said: "If this is indeed your desire, O goddess of pure smiles, do so. We shall always behold you there on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, O pure one."
Pulastya said: Having been addressed thus by the Goddess, the gods departed for heaven with great joy; and that Goddess too, O King, went to Mount Arbuda there.
Having reached the interior of the cave, she dwelt there constantly for the welfare of the world; delighted in that secluded place, she was difficult to be attained by gods or men.
O Indra among kings, he who beholds her with a concentrated mind on the eighth day of the bright fortnight always obtains his desired object, even if it be very difficult to attain. (22)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Kātyāyanī," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Pulastya said: Thereafter, O King, one should go to the Piṇḍāraka tīrtha, which destroys all sins, where in former times penance was performed by the Brāhmaṇa Maṅki, and who, O King, attained perfection through the power of this very tīrtha.
Long ago, O King, there was a Brahmin named Maṅki; he was a fool, ignorant of the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, and possessed of very dull intellect.
Then, O best of kings, on that beautiful mountain, the queen protected the people during the performance of the Piṇḍāraka rite.
Then, after some time, he acquired wealth; having obtained it with great difficulty from afar, he subsequently purchased a pair of oxen for a small sum.
Then, O best of kings, he tamed that pair of oxen; however, O King, by the power of fate, his pair of oxen became untamable.
O King, having reached a tethered camel that stood firmly by its neck, the camel then rose up in haste, intent on flight out of fear.
O Lord of the Earth, seeing that pair of oxen hanging from his neck was indeed a most great wonder, for it portended the destruction of that very pair of oxen.
Maṅki, having attained detachment, abandoned his village and went to the forest; O best of kings, he went to a certain waterfall on Mount Arbuda.
O King, he performed his bath at the three periods of the day and the supreme recitation of the Gāyatrī; by that means, he became free from sin and attained divine vision.
At that very time, however, Śaṅkara emerged along that same path with Gaurī for the sake of sporting on the beautiful mountain.
O King, having been suddenly seen by that high-souled Piṇḍāra, he prostrated before him; thereupon Śaṅkara spoke to him.
"Let my sight not be in vain; let a boon be accepted from me, O twice-born one! Whatever is desired, O great king, even if it should be very difficult to obtain. (12)
Piṇḍāraka said: "O Lord of Gods, O Destroyer of Tripura, I am your attendant; O All-pervading One, act as you see fit, for nothing else dwells in my heart. (13)
"May this Piṇḍāraka Tīrtha become famous by my name. (14)

The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, at the end of your body, you shall become one of our attendants (gaṇa). This place here shall become a sacred ford (tīrtha) known by the name Piṇḍāraka."

"O Mahāmati, on this Great Eighth day I shall enter [the water]; and those who perform their ablutions when the eighth day has arrived, they shall go to the supreme abode where I am eternally established. (16)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished on that very spot. Maṅki then performed penance day and night at Piṇḍāraka.
Then, after a long time, having abandoned his body, he went to heaven; there, where the Blessed Lord Rudra resides, he became a Gaṇa.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the ritual bath accompanied by mantras.
O Indra among kings, the gift of a queen should especially be made on the eighth lunar day by one who desires what is always desired in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Piṇḍāraka Tīrtha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the pilgrimage site renowned throughout the three worlds, located on that sin-destroying mountain named Naikakala.
Listen, O lord of the earth, to that wonder which occurred there in former times: a king named Sumati arrived at Mount Arbuda.
O protector of the earth, during a solar eclipse he went to the Kanakhala tirtha; for the sake of the brahmins, he brought back gold that was indeed of pure quality.
O King, a great quantity [of it] fell into the water through the negligence of that monarch; and though he was intent on searching for it, it was not recovered by him.
Then, having bathed, he returned home filled with remorse; subsequently, after a long time, he came there once again.
When the sun was eclipsed, he went to that place for the purpose of bathing; then the wise one reflected: "In this very place, at that time, [my father]... (6)
Gold fell from his hand, yet it could not be recovered by any means whatsoever.
Pulastya said: As he was reflecting thus, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O Indra among kings, there is no destruction here, neither in this world nor in the next."
The ancient gold that was produced here has become ten-millionfold; yet you have felt great remorse regarding the loss of that wealth.

Therefore, O best of kings, the number [of merits] has arisen for one who acts thus, as well as for one who is unattached. Those here who are endowed with faith, and especially those who will diligently perform the śrāddha with gold, [shall obtain great merit]. (10)
They will bestow [it] upon the Brāhmaṇas; its number is not known. Search for it here in this region; you will find it, of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
O King, having heard that voice which had arisen there from the sky, he searched in this region and found that gold.

Having attained great satisfaction from that abundant merit, ten million times more pure than before, and having recognized the power of that sacred ford, he, filled with compassion, bestowed it upon thousands of Brahmins for the sake of his ancestors and the gods.
Then, by the power of that gift, that lord of the earth became a yakṣa named Dhanada, the bestower of various kinds of wealth.
O King, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there during a solar eclipse, his ancestors, being well-satisfied, shall attain gratification for an entire kalpa.
O Lord of the Earth, by bathing, the sages, the gods, and the great serpents attain satisfaction; and the destruction of sin occurs instantly. (16)
Therefore, O best of kings, one should perform a ritual bath there with every effort, as well as give gifts and perform a śrāddha ceremony according to one's capacity. (17)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kanakhala Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha, where in ancient times the discus was released by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Having slain the Dānavas in battle and performed his ablutions in a beautiful waterfall, Viṣṇu washed himself with that water, and by that act it attained purity.
O lord of men, those ancestors of one who performs the śrāddha ceremony there during the sleeping and waking festivals of Hari attain satisfaction for an entire kalpa.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Cakratīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the most meritorious Lake Mānuṣa, where a man who bathes properly is always born as a true human being.
Even after committing many sins, one does not attain the state of an animal; O lord of men, hear that wonder which occurred there in the past.
Having encountered a herd of deer surrounded on all sides by hunters, those deer, terrified with fear, entered into the midst of the water.
Having immediately attained human birth and likewise remembered their former lives, at that very moment those hunters arrived.
All of them, bearing bows and arrows like the very servants of Yama, O King, questioned the deer who had attained human form.
"A herd of deer has arrived at this place near the water; tell us quickly by which path they went, for we are all exhausted, especially by hunger and thirst. (6)
The men said: "We are all deer who have taken on human form; this is the truth, without a doubt, through the power of this sacred ford."
Pulastya said: Then, O King, all those Śabaras cast aside their bows; having bathed in that water, O monarch, they immediately attained perfection.
Then, O King, best of monarchs, Śakra, having seen that holy place which removes all sins, filled it everywhere with dust.
Even today, O lord of men, those humans who perform a ritual bath there on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight of the month of Budha shall not fall into the state of an animal.
They shall obtain the entire fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice through the giving of śrāddha offerings.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Manuṣyatīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Paulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the excellent Kapilātīrtha, where a man who bathes properly is liberated from all sins.
In ancient times, there was a king named Suprabha, a slayer of enemy heroes, who was constantly addicted to hunting and devoted to the injury of deer.
Neither toward women, nor toward pleasures, nor toward horse-drawn carriages, nor toward elephants did he have such passion as he had for the crushing of deer.
Once, O best of kings, that monarch, while pursuing deer, went to Mount Arbuda; there, on a mountain ridge, he beheld a doe surrounded by her young.
As she was suckling the breast of her child, who was full of affection for her milk, she was suddenly pierced by him with that straight-jointed arrow.
Then, seeing the king with his bow grasped and about to fix a second, perfectly stainless arrow, she became a doe. (6)
Then, consumed by anger, she replied to the king: "This which you have practiced today is not remembered as the duty of a Kshatriya."
O King, a deer should not be killed while lying down, nor one intent on mating, nor one suckling its young, nor one afflicted by disease; and the same applies to a doe accompanied by her fawn.
O lowest of kings, having encountered your arrow, my son has perished along with me; thus, today my death has come upon me in its entirety. (9)
"O lord of the earth, because I have been slain by you through unrighteousness, therefore you shall become a fierce tiger right here on this mountain peak."
Pulastya said: Having heard of that great sin, the king, overwhelmed with fear, then sought to appease that doe whose life was at its end.
"O auspicious one, out of lack of discrimination and being merciless, you have been killed by me. Therefore, O noble deer, grant liberation from the curse to me, who am wretched. (12)
The doe said: "But when you see the milch cow named Kapilā, through conversation with her, you shall return once more to your natural state. (13)
Having spoken thus, the doe, tormented by the strike of the arrow and especially by her affection for her son, gave up her life before the king. (14)
Then that king immediately became fierce-faced; he turned into a tiger with ten formidable paws, sharp teeth, and claws, and, overwhelmed by rage, began to devour his own army. || 15 ||
Then, O King, those soldiers who remained after the slaughter, deeply distressed, returned to their own homes there, reporting what had occurred among the people in the city.
They announced the news in the squares and at the triple-junctions, saying how that king had indeed attained the state of a tiger on Mount Arbuda.
Having heard those words of his, they consecrated his son of great prowess, renowned by name and possessed of immense luster, upon the throne.
Then, after some time, O best of kings, a herd of cows accompanied by cowherds and cowherdesses arrived at that mountain peak, afflicted by thirst. (19)
There, one cow had strayed from her herd out of a thirst for grass; she was known as Kapilā and used to lead her own herd. (20)
O King, she who always grazed upon grass with uncut tips then reached a deep, empty, and terrifying cave in the mountain.
There, a tiger with a mouth formidable with fangs approached her; seeing that wicked beast, she was struck with terror like a doe.
Seeing her weeping in grief as she remembered her milk-drinking son tied up in Gokula, that lord of beasts spoke to her.
The tiger said: "O cow, why do you weep in vain? Having encountered me, no one's life remains, O fool; therefore, remember the deity you hold dear. (24)
Kapila said: "O tiger, out of fear for my own life, I do not weep at all; rather, it is my young son, who drinks milk, who awaits me in the cow-pen. (25)
"Even now he does not eat the grass; therefore I am overwhelmed with grief. O tiger, I weep out of love for my son; I swear this by my own soul. (26)
"O Lord, having given my young son milk, and having seen and questioned my own people, I shall return again, if you so permit. (27)
The tiger said: "I do not believe that you will go to the presence of your own son, see your own herd of cows, and then return here again. (28)
"You speak thus to me out of fear; there is no fear equal to that for one's life. Therefore, O cow, you will not come back out of fear for your life. (29)
Kapila said: "I shall return by means of oaths; hear this truth from me. O lord of beasts, if you have confidence in me, then release me. (30)
The tiger said: "Tell me those oaths, O blessed lady, by which you will return; then, having gained confidence, I shall either release you or not. (31)
Kapila said: "If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin which belongs to one who deceives a Brāhmaṇa accomplished in the study of the Vedas. (32)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin which arises for those men who are intent on betraying their guru.
Whatever sin arises from killing a Brahmin or killing a cow, may I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again.
May I be tainted by that sin which lies in betraying a friend and that sin which lies in deceiving a teacher, if I do not return again. 35.
"May I be tainted by that same sin if I do not return again, were I to touch a cow with my foot, or likewise a Brāhmaṇa or fire. (36)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin which belongs to the man who causes the destruction of wells, groves, and tanks. (37)
May I be tainted by that sin which belongs to the ungrateful and that which belongs to the informer, if I do not return again. 38.
Whatever sin arises for men who are addicted to liquor and meat, by that sin may I be tainted if I do not return again. (39)
Whatever sin arises for men who commit slander against the king, by that sin may I be tainted if I do not return again. (40)
Whatever sin arises for those who sell the Vedas, by that sin may I be tainted, if I do not return again. 41.
If I do not come back again, may I be tainted by that sin of the one of small intellect who prevents the twice-born from what is being given. (42)
May I be tainted by that sin which is proclaimed for those who betray the trusting, if I do not return again.
Whatever sin arises for men who are devoted to hatred of the twice-born, by that sin may I be tainted if I do not return again. 44.
And whatever sin belongs to those who delight in the arguments of others and to those of evil soul—by that sin may I be tainted, if I do not return again. (45)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of those who, being evildoers, eat curd-mixed barley-meal at night.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by the sin of those who eat eggplant, radish, white or red [onions], and garlic.
Pulastya said: Having heard her oaths, his eyes wide with amazement, the tiger then gained confidence and spoke these words. (48)
The tiger said: "Go to Gokula, O blessed lady, and return again; you must not think that this man has been deceived by me. (49)
"O Kapilā, you who are so fond of your offspring, go and see your son; having let him drink from your full breast and having smelled the crown of his head. (50)
Having seen your mother, brother, friends, kinsmen, and relatives, you ought not to act otherwise, but should place truth alone before you.
Pulastya said: Permitted by the king of beasts, that tawny cow, devoted to her calf, set out toward the herd of cows, her face filled with tears and her heart distressed.

Trembling, agitated by fear, and situated in the midst of an ocean of grief, she was like a female elephant seized by a fierce and powerful lion. Then, reaching her own herd, she bellowed again and again.
Then, having heard her voice and recognized his own mother, the calf, filled with great joy, quickly ran toward her with his tail held high. || 54 ||
Seeing her arrival at an improper time and hearing that terrible, tumultuous clamor, the dear child became apprehensive and questioned her.
Vatsa said: I do not perceive any gentleness in you; you appear as if troubled in mind. Tell me, for what reason have you arrived at this unusual hour?
Kapilā said: "Drink from my breast, my son; afterwards, listen also to my reason. I have come out of affection for you; satisfy yourself as much as you desire. (57)
"O son, this is the very last time that a mother's sight will be so difficult to obtain. O son, I must depart today, for I have come here bound by oaths. (58)
"Life must be given by me to the tiger, who can assume any form at will; therefore, O dear son, I have been released from my oaths because of you. (59)
"I must go there today to the presence of the king of beasts; and when, O son, I shall give up my body by means of oaths. (60)
Vatsa said: "I shall go there where you wish to go; for death today with you is surely praiseworthy for me, of this there is no doubt. (61)
Since I must die alone without you, for if a tiger should kill me there while I am with you, [it would be a double loss]. (62)
"Whatever destination belongs to those devoted to their mothers, that shall certainly be mine; therefore, I will surely go with you, there is no doubt. (63)
"Or rather, stay right here; let my oaths be yours. O mother, if you so desire, I shall go to your place."
For one separated from his mother, life is indeed not dear to me; for children who subsist on milk, there is nothing equal to a mother. (65)
There is no protector equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother. Those sons who are devoted to their mothers attain the supreme goal.
Kapila said: "O son, death has been ordained for me alone at this time, not for you. Furthermore, the death of other beings cannot come about through the death of another."
"O son, listen attentively to this final, supreme message from your mother, which will bring you happiness in the end. (68)
"O child, always dwell in the forest and be intent on heedfulness; through heedlessness all beings perish, of this there is no doubt. (69)
One should never, out of greed, cut grass situated on uneven ground; for through greed comes the destruction of living beings both in this world and in the next.
Deluded by greed, people enter the ocean, the forest, and battle; they perform most terrible deeds out of greed and the like, and therefore that greed must indeed be abandoned.
A person is afflicted by three things: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust; therefore, one should not be greedy, nor negligent, nor should one place undue trust.
And one must always protect oneself with great effort, my son, from all beasts of prey, from barbarians, and from thieves and the like. (73)
As you constantly roam in the forest among animals and those of evil birth, you should not feel grief; for death is certain for all.
And hear our reply, which destroys sorrow: for just as a certain traveler seeking shade rests beneath a tree and then departs once he has rested, such is the meeting of living beings. (75)
Pulastya said: Having thus conversed with her calf and smelled its head, she then came to see her mother and her group of friends.
Then, distressed by grief for her son, she spoke these words: "O mothers, listen clearly to my final words. (77)
"You must all protect my little son—he is helpless, weak, and miserable, like a piece of foam, and tormented by grief for his mother. (78)
"This son belongs to those who are yet to be; he must now, and especially so, be bathed, fed, nourished, and protected like one's own son. (79)
"O friends, you must restrain him when he wanders in difficult places, when he wanders among the herds of others' cows, or when he engages in improper acts. (80)
And forgive me, O illustrious ones; I shall go, abiding by the truth, to where that tiger stays by whom I have now been released.
Having heard all her words, they were overcome with grief; falling into a state of extreme despondency, they spoke these words, deeply distressed.
"O Kapilā, you must certainly not go; no fault shall be yours. There is no fault in [taking life] when one's life is at stake, nor in a terrible calamity. (83)
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by sages who proclaim the Dharma: "When a matter of life and death has arisen, there is no sin in taking an oath. (84)
Kapila said: "For the sake of protecting the life of living beings, I may indeed speak an untruth; but for my own sake, I never employ even the slightest falsehood at any time. (85)
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held upon a scale; indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices. (86)
Therefore, I will not make myself a liar out of a desire for life. Noble lady, please give me your command; I shall go where the lord of beasts is.
The friends said: "O Kapilā, you are worthy of homage by all the gods and asuras alike, since you are renouncing your life-breaths—which are so difficult to give up—through supreme truth."
"Death shall certainly not befall you by any means because of my truth; if truth is indeed authoritative, then go, may your path be auspicious. (89)

Pulastya said: Having been addressed thus, Kapilā went to where the lord of beasts was. Then, seeing Kapilā, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke these humble words in a voice faltering with joy: 90. Pulastya said: Having been addressed thus, Kapilā went to where the lord of beasts was. Then, seeing Kapilā, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke these humble words in a voice faltering with joy: 90.
The tiger said: "Welcome to you, O auspicious Kapilā, speaker of truth! Indeed, nothing inauspicious ever befalls those who possess truth. (91)
"You previously spoke with oaths and scriptural citations, O Kapilā; because of that, curiosity has arisen in me as to how she could have gone and returned again. (92)
Therefore, go, released by me, to where that son of yours stays in Gokula, bound up, drinking milk, and deeply distressed. (93)

Pulastya said: At that very time, the king returned to his natural state; freed from the deer-maiden's curse, he assumed a body of divine form. Then, with a joyful soul, he spoke to the truthful Kapilā: || 94 ||
The king said: "By your grace, I am liberated from this most terrible curse. O cow, tell me quickly: what dear service may I do for you today? (95)
Kapila said: "O Indra among kings, I have achieved my purpose since you have been liberated from sin; however, thirst afflicts me greatly, so bring water now. (96)
Know that this which has been spoken by me is not false; it is the truth.
Pulastya said: Then that king, quickly taking a bow in his hand, strung it, took an arrow, and struck the surface of the earth.
Then there arose pure, cool, and auspicious water; having bathed there, that Kapilā became free from thirst. (99)
In the meantime, Dharma himself arrived there and, being delighted, said to Kapilā: "Choose a boon, O beautiful one. (100)
I am pleased by your truthfulness; there is no one like you anywhere. O auspicious one, indeed, there shall be no cow equal to you in all the three worlds.
Kapila said: "By your grace, may I go with the king and the cowherd community to that divine abode, free from old age and death, along with Suprabha. (102)
"May this reservoir of water, which removes all sins and likewise grants all desires for men, become renowned by the name of Manu. (103)
Dharma said: "Those who shall perform their ablutions here in this most meritorious and auspicious water, especially on the fourteenth lunar day, shall attain the supreme goal. (104)

Indeed, by your name this sacred ford shall become most meritorious; a mortal who visits it for the sake of the new moon will obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows. From bathing there, the merit is a hundred-thousandfold, and from giving gifts, it is likewise inexhaustible.
Those high-souled men who, being well-composed, shall perform a śrāddha here, will obtain the fruit of all gifts, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even those insects and moths who, afflicted by thirst, shall immerse themselves in this auspicious water, they too will go to the abode of the dwellers of heaven.
How much more so, then, those men who are endowed with devotion, speakers of truth, high-minded, highly fortunate, full of faith, and wise? || 108 ||
Pulastya said: At that very time, O lord of kings, thousands of celestial chariots arrived there by the power of Kapilā.
Then, having mounted those [vehicles], Kapilā, accompanied by Suprabha and surrounded by cowherds and herds of cows, went to that supreme state.
Therefore, O best of kings, one should perform a bath there with every effort, as well as a śrāddha ceremony and give gifts according to one's capacity.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Kapilātīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: From there, one should go to Agnitīrtha, the supreme purifier for men; it was there that Vahni (the Fire-god) was lost in ancient times and subsequently recovered by the gods.

Yayāti said: "For what reason, O Blessed One, was the fire lost in the past, O best of the twice-born? And how was it recovered right there? This is a matter of great curiosity to me, O great sage. (2)
Pulastya said: In ancient times, there was a cessation of rain for twelve years; the entire world, afflicted by hunger, fell into a state of extreme peril.
For the most part, those remaining on the surface of the earth were dead or nearly dead; the wild animals, domestic livestock, birds, and deer had perished.
When the world of mortals had thus fallen into such distress, O lord of men, Viśvāmitra, the best of sages, fell into a state of great uncertainty.
Due to the absence of food, medicinal herbs, and juices, he was reduced to nothing but bones; on another day, emaciated by hunger, he arrived while wandering through the various directions.
Having reached the dwelling of a Caṇḍāla, he was greatly afflicted by hunger and thirst; there, O best of kings, he saw a dead, dried-up dog.
Having taken it and reached home, he washed it with water; then, emaciated by hunger, he cooked it and offered it into the fire.
O King, O Lord of the Earth, having learned of the consumption of forbidden food, the carrier of oblations (Agni) then directed his great wrath toward Śakra.

In a world where the essence of medicinal herbs has perished, this is indeed appropriate for the present time: whatever kind of oblation is obtained, such is the fire's consumption; it is distinguished by that alone.
"I shall not eat what is forbidden to eat; I will abandon the circle of the earth, by which [abandonment] Indra and the other gods fall into a most miserable state. (11)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the fire-god, filled with anger, abandoned the entire mortal world of moving and non-moving beings and vanished.
When the fire had suddenly vanished, the rites such as the Agniṣṭoma were lost; all the people perished, and especially fell into a state of doubt.
Then all the hosts of gods fell into great doubt; because they were deprived of their sacrificial portions, they then deliberated among themselves.
Once mortals have been abandoned by Fire, men will then go to their destruction; because of the destruction of the remainder, we shall all perish, there is no doubt. (15)
Therefore, let fire be sought out wherever it currently resides; and let a policy be enacted according to how it moves among mortals. (16)
Pulastya said: Having thus made their resolve, all the gods, together with Indra, searched for Agni everywhere across the circle of the earth.
Then, seeing the parrot before them, the weary gods asked with faith: "If Agni has been seen, let it be told."
Śuka said: "This great lineage which was previously consumed by contact with fire has perished; here, O carrier of oblations, I have seen that one of great luster. (19)
Informed by the parrot, the Fire-god, overcome with wrath, cursed him, saying, "Your speech shall become faltering," and having said this, he departed quickly.
He entered the aśvattha tree, the best of trees, which was within a śamī; staying there, he was described by the king of elephants to the gods.
He said to him, "Your tongue shall become perverted. Then, having gone to a body of water on the mountain named Arbuda, [he performed penance]. || 22 ||
The Blessed One entered like fire so that he was not perceived by the gods; there, a frog that had emerged spoke to them regarding the consumer of oblations.
There, that fire remains within a mountain cataract; all aquatic creatures have been burnt by that very water which is intensely heated.
"O gods, I have emerged with great difficulty from that mouth of death. Having heard this, the fire-god (Havyavāhana) applied himself with effort and entered [the cave].
Having cursed that frog, the king became paralyzed.
Then, O King, all the hosts of gods emerged from their watery abode and, having surrounded him, praised him with hymns originating from the Vedas.
The gods said: "O Agni, O Purifier, you move within all living beings; deprived of you, the entire world will quickly go to destruction. (28)

"You are the mouth of all the gods; in you the worlds are established. If the earthly realm is abandoned by you, we all, including Indra, shall surely go to our destruction; therefore, it behooves you to protect us. (29)
You are Brahmā, you are Mahādeva, you are Viṣṇu, and you are the Sun; you are the Moon, you are the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), and you are Marut, the Lord of the Gods.

"O Consumer of Oblations, all the gods, beginning with Indra, are dependent upon you. For what reason, O Blessed One, have you abandoned the mortal world and remained here? For what reason, O Blessed One, do you wish to abandon us who are innocent? (31)
Pulastya said: Surrounded by the gods who were intent on offering praise, the Blessed Lord Vahni (Fire), standing upon the bank of that very waterfall, then spoke these words.
Vahni said: "Śakra desires to employ me in eating what is not to be eaten; for that very reason, this lord of the gods does not send rain upon the mortal world."
Therefore, having abandoned the surface of the earth, I have entered this mountain stream; since human beings have vanished from the world, I do not wish to remain here.
Śakra said: Listen, O Consumer of Oblations (Agni), why I have obstructed the rain. There was one named Devāpi, a knower of dharma and a bringer of glory to the Kṣatriyas. (35)

His son was the virtuous Pratīpa, the best among all those endowed with moral conduct. When Devāpi had gone to heaven, leaving behind his elder brother and predecessor, Śaṃtanu, his younger son, took possession of the kingdom.
For this reason, rain has been withheld from his kingdom; by your command I shall bring it forth, so turn back, O Consumer of Oblations! (37)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, the thousand-eyed Indra swiftly commanded the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds for the purpose of raining upon the surface of the earth.
Then, O lord of the earth, the thundering clouds, commanded by Śakra, emitting deep roars and possessing intense brilliance, filled the entire surface of the world with abundant waters. (39)
Then the blessed carrier of oblations attained supreme satisfaction; for the sake of the gods, he chose to make his dwelling upon the surface of the earth.
The gods said: "O Consumer of Oblations, the rain has been brought about at your command; there is another task [to be done]. Tell us very quickly whatever is pleasing to you. (41)
Agni said: "By your grace, let this meritorious reservoir of water become known upon the surface of the earth as an excellent holy site (tīrtha) bearing my name. (42)
The gods said: "This Agni-tīrtha shall attain great renown in the world; a man who bathes here properly shall go to the world of Agni. (43)
That man who, being well-composed, shall offer sesame seeds at this sacred ford (tīrtha), will obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, all the gods then departed for their respective abodes; and the lordly Fire, O King, resumed his former state.
Whoever, having risen early in the morning, constantly recites this supreme account of the majesty of Agnitīrtha, is liberated from all sins. (46)
Even by merely hearing it, one is liberated from the sin committed during a day and night.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Agnitīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: One should go to the tirtha known as Raktānubandha, renowned throughout the three worlds, where a man who bathes properly is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

In ancient times, there was a lord of the earth named Indrasena, a king. He had a very beloved wife, a beautiful woman named Sunandā, who was devoted to her husband, whose life was her husband, and who always remained intent on what was pleasing to her lord.
Then, after some time, that king, accompanied by his retinue, went to a foreign land to slay a host of invincible enemies.
Having slain him and seized abundant wealth, he set out for home; then, O King, he dispatched a disguised messenger ahead of him.
"Go and tell Sunandā: 'Indrasena has been slain in battle. Then, by my command, her devotion to her husband shall be recognized by her appearance. (5)
If that passionate woman were to reach the certainty of death, then she must be protected with great effort, and my laughter must not be revealed.
Thus addressed, O best of kings, the messenger departed at that very moment and reported to her exactly what had been said by that monarch.
Then, O best of kings, having heard his words, the beautiful-smiling Sunandā, that great chaste woman whose life was her husband, became as if her life-breath had departed.
At the very time when Sunandā, whose ornament was her virtue, died, that king too was seized by her sin.
Then he saw a second shadow upon his body, and likewise his body became heavier and overcome with lassitude. || 10 ||
O best of kings, having heard that it had originated from his wife, the king then returned home to find it devoid of luster, foul-smelling, and discolored.
Afflicted by grief and sorrow, he lamented piteously for his destruction; he realized that he himself was defiled by the sin of killing a woman. (12)
Following the instructions of the Brahmins, he became intent on his journey; having performed her funeral rites with only a few possessions, he first went to Vārāṇasī and there gave away many gifts.
At the Kapālamocana tīrtha, which destroys all sins, the Three-eyed One was indeed formerly liberated from the slaughter of a Brahmin.
O King, his shadow remained there as a second [form] and was not lost; from there he reached Kanakhala, which is highly meritorious and bestows purity upon men. (15)
In that very manner, O King, that best of monarchs reached Puṣkarāraṇya from there, then Amarakaṇṭaka, and after that Kurukṣetra. || 16 ||
Then Prabhāsa and Somatīrtha, and then Kṛmijāṅgala; then Ekahaṃsa, O King, and then Puṇyapāriplava.
Then, O King, he went to Rudrakoṭi, Virūpākṣa, and Pañcanada; wandering through such holy fords and sacred shrines, O protector of the earth, that lord of men became utterly exhausted.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, he arrived at Mount Arbuda; there the lord of men beheld sacred fords and shrines.
He gave various gifts many times at his own will to assemblies of ascetics and to Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas.
He reached the sacred site known as Raktānubandha on that very mountain; having bathed there and emerged, the king looked about.
Until then, the shadow arising from the murder of the second woman was not seen; O Lord of the Earth, lightness has come to all my limbs. (22)
The foul odor vanished and a supreme increase in splendor occurred. Then, with a joyful heart, having given abundant gifts and being praised from the four quarters by bards, he set out for his home.
Then, O King, as Raktānubandha was crossing over the Soma, O Indra among kings, he did so once again in that very same manner.
O best of kings, that shadow is seen upon the body as if it were a second person; O King, that same odor is on the limbs, and there is a loss of luster.
Then, tormented by suffering, he went to that very place at that moment; having reached Raktabandha, he became free from sin once again.

Having understood the supreme majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha), that best of kings, O monarch, gathered wood there, prepared a funeral pyre, gave gifts to the foremost of the twice-born, and then entered the fire.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot and cast off his body, wearing divine garlands and garments, he went to the world of Śiva. || 28 ||

When that best of kings had reached the world of Śiva, the celestial sages then spoke these words out of great wonder: śivalokamanuprāpte tasminpārthivasattame | devarṣayastadā vākyamidamāhuḥ suvismayāt || 29 ||
This is indeed the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the ultimate purifier; for Indrasena was liberated from sin through contact with this sacred ford.
From that time forward, that sacred site became famous on the surface of the earth, because it bestows a connection with blood-red living beings.
Therefore, it is celebrated on earth as "connected with blood" (raktānubandha). O King, he who performs a śrāddha there after having indeed gratified the gods—
In that place, at the transit of the sun, the man who performs his ablutions, endowed with supreme faith, is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The great sages declare that for the man who performs a śrāddha at Gayā, the field of the ancestors, the fruit he obtains is equal to that of a śrāddha performed at Gayā itself.
O best of kings, that man who performs the gift of a cow during an eclipse of the moon or the sun shall deliver seven generations of his lineage.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Raktānubandha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: O best of kings, one should then go to Mahāvināyaka, upon seeing whom the immediate absence of obstacles arises for men.
Yayāti said: O best of the twice-born, how did Vināyaka formerly attain greatness there? At what time did this occur? Tell me everything in detail.
Pulastya said: O King, taking the paste produced from the rubbing of her body, Pārvatī then fashioned a delicate child for the sake of diversion.
O King, having fashioned Skanda as described—devoid of a head due to the absence of clay, yet possessing all other limbs and members—he then spoke these words.
"O Skanda, may you be blessed; bring quickly some ointment for the sake of my head, so that this little son of mine may become your brother, invincible to enemies. (5)
Then, O best of kings, because the ointment could not be obtained despite Gaurī’s command, he saw a rutting, excellent elephant and brought its head.
He applied it to that part of the body where the ointment had arisen, saying: "O son, this head will become very large; why was it brought by you? (7)
And as Pārvatī cried out "No, no! again and again, O lord of men, her body was placed upon his head by the turn of fate.
And from his limbs there arose a preeminent leadership, lovely like a young child and endowed with all auspicious marks.
O Lord of the Earth, it is deep in three places, four cubits long, red in seven parts, elevated in six, long in five, subtle in five, and most beautiful.
O Great King, seeing that [body] was three times as large, Gaurī was greatly amazed; she, whose form is power, restored it to life by means of her own power.
Restored to life by the Goddess, he stood up at that very moment; with his neck bowed in humility, he requested her command.
Seeing him of such wondrous appearance and repeatedly addressing his son, he led him into the presence of Śambhu with a joyful heart.
Then he said to his son: "O God, grant me boons born from the anointing of my own body, by which I may attain greatness. (14)
The Blessed One said: "O daughter of the mountain, since the head is the principal part situated upon the body, this great head has been described by you as having been joined with Skanda."
And because leadership over all beings resides in his body, he shall therefore be known by the name Mahāvināyaka. || 16 ||
O daughter of the mountain, because he shall become the lord of the hosts, sovereignty over all the Gaṇas has been granted to him by me.
In all their undertakings, those mortals who first remember this Lord of the Gaṇas shall certainly experience no failure in their tasks. || 18 ||
Then Skanda gave him a small axe for the sake of play; that very weapon indeed became his constant favorite.
Then Gaurī gave him a food-vessel filled with sweetmeats; having received it out of affection for her son, he then performed a dance in this manner.
By the scent of that food, a mouse emerged from its burrow; through eating it, he became an immortal and was born as his mount.
Pulastya said: O lord of the earth, thus was Mahāvināyaka born there; listen now with a one-pointed mind to the merit that is gained when he is beheld. || 22 ||
O King, whatever sin a man commits in childhood, in old age, or even in youth, he is liberated from that sin.
He who, having fasted on the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, beholds him, becomes eloquent and omniscient. Before him is a very great pool filled with clear water.
O King, that man who bathes there and beholds Vināyaka with devotion—in his lineage, too, all-knowing men shall be born.
O King of kings, he who performs three circumambulations with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā" and beholds that [liṅga] does not behold any evil.
Therefore, one who desires all desires both in this world and in the next should behold that Vināyaka with every effort. (27)
And even a householder who, when a task has arisen, should remember [the Lord] with devotion—all that shall reach successful completion for him without obstacle. (28)
That mortal who, having risen in the morning, remembers the god Vināyaka, indeed finds that all the tasks undertaken on that day reach successful completion. (29)

Whoever remembers Vināyaka with devotion during a marriage, a quarrel, a battle, a journey, agricultural work, or an entrance [into a new home], all that he desires is accomplished through his grace. (30)
He who, being composed in mind, performs this great pacification of Vināyaka, him neither hungry ghosts, nor seizing spirits, nor diseases, nor obstacles shall afflict. (31)
Yayāti said: O best of sages, tell me the Mahāvaināyikī Śānti; what are the mantras and what is the ritual procedure? For my curiosity is great indeed. (32)

Pulastya said: On a bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, under a constellation free from defects, and when the moon possesses excellent strength, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) of Gaṇeśa.
