Having constructed an altar and a pavilion on a level site toward the northeast, one should employ the Gṛhyasūtra for an eight-petaled lotus in the center.
O Lord of the Earth, [one should worship] Indra and the other guardians of the world in all directions, as well as the Mothers, headed by Gaṇeśa, especially.
With offerings of perfumes and flowers, and with the extensive bali-offerings as prescribed, one should place a water-filled jar covered with a pair of white cloths.
In the eastern direction of that very place, there was [a vessel] containing gold and filled with fruit.
O best of kings, one should recite the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā" one thousand and eight times there, as well as the beautiful five-limbed [prayers]. (35)
Having dedicated it to Vināyaka, [one should perform the rite] first in a hand-sized pit (kuṇḍa) that is square, provided with a yoni, and adorned with girdles (mekhalā). || 39 ||
Following the oblations for the planets, one should likewise perform ten thousand oblations with honey, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (akṣata), using the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
O best of kings, the rite must indeed be performed by four clever twice-born men facing the north, O King, who are dressed in yellow garments and anointed with unguents. (41)
And [they were] wearing yellow garments and bearing golden rings; then, O best of kings, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, [he addressed] the sacrificer.
And seated upon a deer-skin, one should bathe him—who is facing east, peaceful, and veiled in white cloth—with these mantras according to the prescribed rite. (43)
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the five rivers at Supuṣkara, [recite] for me the Pāvamāna hymn of Viṣṇu together with the Śrīsūkta and the Vṛṣākapi.
By reciting it correctly, one then attains the destruction of obstacles; the planets become mild, and malevolent spirits perish at that very moment.
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, fierce diseases, and fevers such as those that afflict the wicked—all these, as well as most dreadful portents, shall swiftly perish. (46)
All this that you asked me has been explained: the majesty and greatness of Vināyaka, as well as his power for pacification.
O best of kings, for him who recites this properly on the fourth lunar day with a well-concentrated mind, or he who hears it, there shall always be freedom from obstacles.
Whatever desire one contemplates while performing this sacrifice with a concentrated mind, one certainly attains that very thing through the grace of Gaṇanātha. 49.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vināyaka," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Pārtheśvara, which thus destroys sins; by beholding it properly, a human being is liberated from all transgressions.
O lord of the earth, there was a virtuous and faithful wife named Pārthā, the beloved of Devala; she had previously performed penance at that place.
Formerly, that illustrious wife of a seer was barren; having attained supreme detachment, she then went to Arbuda.
Subsisting on air, taking no food, with a mind equanimous as she sat upon her seat, O Lord of the Earth, at the end of a thousand years, she [worshipped] him with devotion.
Suddenly, having burst through the surface of the earth, the Liṅga rose up; at that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke.
"O highly fortunate lady, worship this most purifying Śiva-liṅga; through your devotion, it has emerged from the surface of the earth as a great bestower of desires."
Whatever desire a person may cherish while worshipping, even another shall obtain that which was intended; there is no doubt in this matter.
"Indeed, this shall become famous in the world by the name 'Pārtheśvara'. Having spoken thus, O lord of the earth, the voice then ceased.
Then, filled with wonder, she worshipped him at that time; consequently, she obtained a hundred divine sons who likewise sustained the lineage.
From that time forward, that Liṅga became famous upon the surface of the earth; there exists pure water there, flowing forth from a mountain cave.
Having bathed there properly and beholding him with devotion, a person shall not experience the suffering arising from the continuity of rebirth within saṃsāra. || 11 ||
He who, fasting, performs a vigil before him on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, certainly obtains a son.
Whoever, being composed in mind, performs the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) there, the ancestors attain the status of his sons through that grace. || 13 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pārtheśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Pulastya said: "Then one should go to Kṛṣṇatīrtha, which is always dear to Kṛṣṇa, where Viṣṇu himself is eternally present, O lord of the earth. Yayāti said: "How did Kṛṣṇatīrtha come to be there, O best of Brāhmaṇas? At what time, O sage? Tell me everything in detail. (2)

Pulastya said: When that terrible single ocean had arisen, and all things mobile and immobile had perished; when the moon, sun, and wind had vanished, and the luminaries had gone to their dissolution.
Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, the lotus-seated one awoke and, being alone, reflected: "How might creation come to be?"
And as the four-faced one was wandering, he saw from afar a four-armed, large-eyed person standing before him.
And the four-faced one said to him: "Who are you, by whom were you created, and for what purpose have you arrived here? Tell me everything in detail."
Then Govinda, smiling, spoke to him with gentle words.
"I am the first person; you too have been created by me. I desire to create once again the fourfold collection of living beings."
Pulastya said: Having heard those words of his, the divine Grandfather became enraged; reproaching him again and again, he spoke these harsh words.
"O fool, you were indeed created by me; I am undoubtedly the first. I shall undoubtedly create thousands more like you. (10)
Thus disputing with one another, O King, those two of great splendor, their eyes copper-red with rivalry and rage, fought each other.
With fists, arms, nails, teeth, and by dragging each other, thus did their battle continue for a thousand years.
Then, O best of kings, at the end of a thousand years, a great, divine, auspicious, and radiant liṅga manifested between those two.
At that very moment, however, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O Brahman, and you, O Viṣṇu, desist from battle at my command."
Whoever shall go to the end of this Liṅga of Maheśvara, he shall be the elder, the all-pervading creator of you both; of this there is no doubt.
"By my command, let one go downward and one go upward. Hearing that, Brahmā quickly took to the path of the sky.
Having split the earth, Kṛṣṇa also went swiftly beneath it; and as he was proceeding downward, having pierced through the seven netherworlds (pātālas), he beheld the Great-Souled One, Kālāgnirudra.
As he exerted his speed, desiring to go further down from there, he was consumed by its flames and turned black.
Then, tormented by fainting and being consumed by that wondrous fire, Viṣṇu suddenly turned back and fell into a state of supreme embarrassment.
Likewise, O Lord of the Earth, having approached the Liṅga, he then performed worship with devotion and offered praise with the supreme, subtle hymns declared in the Vedas. (20)
Brahmā also traveled by way of the sky in his swan-vehicle, yet for a thousand divine years he did not reach its end.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, he saw Ketakī approaching through the path of the sky; she questioned the four-faced one.
"O Brahmin, where are you going on this great path that is without support and empty? Explain the reality of it to me, for my curiosity is indeed great. (23)
Brahmā said: "O beautiful one, a rivalry has arisen between me and Viṣṇu; for whoever among us two shall reach the end of this liṅga... (24)
"He is the superior one, for the other is inferior; this was stated by the wielder of the Pināka bow. I then set out toward the upper path, while Hari went down the lower path."
"Having reached the end of the Liṅga, I shall go across the circle of the earth. Having heard those words of his, that flower spoke to him: ||| 26 ||
"O Lord of the World, your labor is in vain; there is no end to the Linga to be found, O Grandfather, even in ten million cycles of four yugas. (27)
O one of great splendor, the time for my fall from the summit of the Liṅga has arrived; yet, somehow, I have not reached the surface of the earth. (28)
In the same amount of time that the swan travels one yojana, I travel a hundred yojanas.
Therefore, O Lord, it is proper for you to desist at my word; having shown me to Viṣṇu, go now to his presence as his elder brother.
Then, with a joyful mind, the four-faced one took her up and, returning to the surface of the earth at the end of another thousand years, showed her to Viṣṇu; she was upon the top of the Liṅga.
"O Four-Armed One, an auspicious garland was brought by me and found its end; it was found by you. O Puruṣottama, do not speak an untruth to me. (32)
Viṣṇu said: "O Brahmin, I am not able by any means to reach the further shore of the infinite and immeasurable God of gods, the wielder of the trident."
"O Brahmin, if you have somehow reached its end, then the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, has surely become pleased with you. (34)
Nor is its end seen by anyone anywhere in any other way; therefore, you are undoubtedly the elder and the superior, while I am the younger.
Pulastya said: At that very moment, O great king, the Lord whose banner is the bull became enraged toward Brahmā at that instant.
Then, having gone to see him, he said: "Fie, fie upon you, you useless chatterer! What is this rash act you have committed by speaking such falsehoods? (37)
"Since you have falsely claimed to have seen my end, therefore you shall not be worthy of worship by any of the social classes. (38)
And those men who, possessed by delusion, shall worship you, they will encounter supreme hardship and go to their destruction entirely. (39)
And because it was thus spoken by that most wicked Ketakī, "Indeed, by her touch, people shall become outcastes (śvapākas)," [the world became so]. (40)
Having thus pronounced the curse upon them both, the god Maheśvara, being pleased and with a gracious countenance, then spoke to Keśava.
The Blessed One said: "O Vāsudeva, O mighty-armed one, O high-minded one, I am pleased with you simply because of your truthful speech; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. (42)

Śrī Vāsudeva said: "This alone is a praiseworthy boon, O Maheśvara, that you are pleased with me; for you do not attain satisfaction, O Lord, with those who lack merit. If a boon must certainly be granted to me by you, O Lord of Gods—"
"Bring this linga, known as Ananta, to lightness without delay, so that creation may occur in the world and the universe may be pervaded by it."
Pulastya said: Then Maheśvara, having contracted that liṅga and made it small, spoke again to Keśava: "Listen to these words, O Hari. (45)
"O Hari, install my liṅga in this most sacred place; worship it according to the prescribed rite, and you shall attain the supreme good. (46)
"Since he has indeed attained blackness, being burnt by my splendor, he shall therefore attain fame in the world by the name Kṛṣṇa alone."
The person who, having risen in the morning, shall glorify your name "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" with devotion, goes to the supreme goal.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished right there. Vāsudeva, too, taking that liṅga, installed it upon Mount Arbuda in a most meritorious spring of pure water. 49.
Thence arose Kṛṣṇatīrtha on the surface of the earth by name; listen, O tiger among kings, to the fruit obtained by one who has bathed there.
That mortal who, having bathed in the meritorious Kṛṣṇahrada, beholds that Liṅga, obtains all the spiritual welfare arising from every sacred bathing place.
And thus, one who is free from desire shall obtain the fruit of all gifts; even one with desire obtains his desired fruit, though it may be very difficult to attain.
Therefore, one who desires eternal welfare should perform a ritual bath there with every effort; no hesitation should be made in this matter. (53)
O Great King, he who, fasting and with senses subdued, performs a vigil there before the Liṅga with great devotion on the eleventh day— || 54 ||
He who, endowed with faith and knowing the dharma, performs a śrāddha at dawn, shall deliver all his ancestors together with his forefathers.
That mortal who gives black sesame seeds there to the Brāhmaṇas is certainly liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. || 56 ||
O Indra among kings, by the mere sight of Kṛṣṇatīrtha, a human being is liberated from all sins; no deliberation is required in this matter. (57)

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kṛṣṇatīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the sin-destroying holy site known as Māmuhrada on that mountain slope.
A man who bathes there properly, endowed with faith and well-concentrated, is liberated from terrible sins, even those committed in previous births.
O Lord of the Earth, in its western quarter there is a Liṅga that grants all desires to men, established by Mudgala.

That person who, having bathed in the meritorious Lake Mānuhrada on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna, beholds that Liṅga, attains the supreme good which is difficult to obtain at all other sacred fords.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there, taking refuge in the southern image, his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.

In that regard, O King, the great seers praise the offering of wild rice (nīvāra) at a śrāddha for the ancestors; indeed, a śrāddha performed with vegetables, roots, and other such items brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
Yayāti said: "O Lord, how did my name 'Māmuhrada' come to be in ancient times? Tell me everything concerning Mudgala’s hermitage according to the prescribed order. (7)
Pulastya said: O King, in former times, while the high-souled Mudgala was staying there, a messenger of the gods arrived, bringing an excellent celestial chariot.
He said, "O best of sages, I have been sent by the King of the Gods; for your sake, ascend this celestial chariot and go to heaven."
Mudgala said: "O messenger, tell me those merits of heaven and those defects which have been proclaimed; having heard them, I shall indeed do whatever may be appropriate. (10)
"Tell them all that, O messenger; I shall come there from here."
The divine messenger said: "Enough of this pride; let that which was spoken by Śakra be done. O best of the twice-born, you shall return here from there by means of your own merits. (12)
Mudgala said: "I will not go by means of those things you have described; this is my firm resolve in my heart. I shall perform intense austerity and I shall worship Maheśvara. (13)
The messenger said: "One is not able to describe the qualities of heaven even in hundreds of years; I shall speak of them in brief, if you have the firmest resolve."
There are the delightful celestial groves, such as Nandana and others; O best of the twice-born, there are enjoyments unlike any other, and constant satisfaction.

O Lord, there is neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor laziness. There, the foremost Apsarases such as Rambhā and the Gandharvas such as Tumburu delight that man manifold times with songs and dances. (16)
And thus, O ascetic, people dwell there in heaven for as long as their merit lasts; thereafter, they shall experience a fall.
O Sage, there is but one defect that appears to me in the heavenly world: it is this very thing called "falling," which strikes terror into those who dwell in heaven. (18)

O Brahmin, one cannot perform meritorious deeds there in any way whatsoever; O Brahmin, this is known as the land of action (karmabhūmi), while that is remembered as the land of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi).
Whatever virtuous deed is performed here, its fruit is enjoyed there; having seen those residing in celestial chariots, endowed with abundant merit and other virtues, [he reflects thus]. (20)
O best of the twice-born, one who possesses little merit, while staying in heaven, is always distressed by the sorrow born of remorse upon seeing those endowed with great splendor.
"No great merit has been performed by me in any way whatsoever during my mortal existence. (22)
And likewise, seeing others falling by the thousands as well as his own great suffering, that wonder arose. (23)
All this has been related to you, O Brahman, concerning the origin of virtues and faults and the conduct pertaining to heaven; now do whatever you desire.
Mudgala said: "O messenger, I have no need whatsoever for that heaven where there is fear of falling, where merit is diminished, and where there is no increase."
"By my command, you must clearly speak these words to the King of the Gods: 'May my offense be forgiven; I have no longing for heaven.'"
I shall perform that action by which we have no fear of falling; I shall establish those worlds so that they are forever free from the danger of a fall.
Pulastya said: O best of kings, having spoken thus, Mudgala, indifferent to heaven, remained right there, devotedly intent upon meditation on Śiva.
Having heard those words of his in full detail, the messenger also reported them to Śakra; then Śakra spoke to him once more.
Indeed, this celestial chariot of immeasurable size has been fashioned by you; it was never made by anyone before, nor will anyone ever make one like it.
Therefore, go there quickly and bring that sage back by force; bring him here, otherwise I shall undoubtedly cast a curse upon you.
Pulastya said: Having heard the words of Śakra, the messenger, filled with fear, set out quickly for the place where Mudgala was staying.
Mudgala also, seeing him returning again seated in his celestial chariot, then entered the Māmuhrada lake and restrained him.
By the mere word of that excellent sage, he was paralyzed as if painted; by the power of that true muni, he was not able to move at all.
Knowing that the messenger had been gone for a long time, the lord of the thirty-three gods himself went there in anger, mounting the elephant Airāvaṇa.
Then, having seen that the messenger had been paralyzed by Mudgala, he (Indra), intent on killing him, began to whirl his thunderbolt at that time.

At that very time, however, terrible portents occurred there; the deer, beasts, and birds all moved in an inauspicious counter-clockwise direction. Seeing these, Mudgala was filled with wonder and began to reflect.
Then, seeing Hari in the sky with his hand raised to strike with a thunderbolt, Mudgala immediately paralyzed him with a mere glance.
Thereupon, Śakra, his enthusiasm broken, offered praise, O best of kings: "Release me, O most excellent Brāhmaṇa; I shall go to the abode of the thirty gods. (39)
"O twice-born one, stay in heaven or in the mortal world according to your own will; O sage, this effort has indeed been made by me for your benefit."
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—that has always resided in your heart; I shall grant it all to you, even if it be exceedingly difficult to obtain. (41)
Mudgala said: This alone is a praiseworthy boon, O Lord of the Gods, that you have been seen; for a vision of you, O Thousand-eyed One, is very difficult to obtain even in dreams.
O slayer of Vṛtra, if a boon must certainly be granted to me, then by your grace, may my liberation come about very quickly indeed. (43)
"Since I have been addressed by the messenger after arriving at this lake, let it therefore attain fame on the surface of the earth as 'Māmuhrada'."
"O Thousand-eyed One, this is a sacred ford that destroys all sins; having bathed here, may they go to heaven through your grace, O Lord of the Gods. (45)
"Indeed, let the ancestors here receive supreme satisfaction from this offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa)."
Indra said: "O best of the twice-born, by my grace this holy site shall become renowned as Māmuhrada; it will be most excellent, of this there is no doubt. (47)
Those who, being composed in mind, shall again perform their ablutions here on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, they will attain the supreme goal.
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here, they shall obtain a supreme fruit equal to that of Gayā; and the fruit of giving merit here, O best of the twice-born, is beyond all calculation. (49)
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, the wielder of the thunderbolt took the messenger and departed for heaven; Mudgala, for his part, thereafter reflected incessantly upon the Supreme Brahman.
Becoming devoted to pure meditation, he thereafter attained imperishable liberation.
In this regard, O Lord of the Earth, these verses were sung of old by the high-souled Nārada in a great assembly of brahmins on this mountain. (52)
"Having bathed in the Māmu lake and beheld that Mudgaleśvara, a man shall enjoy all desires here and attain liberation at the end; for this reason, O King, it is remembered as the Māmu lake. (53)
That sacred ford is the most excellent of all sacred fords and is renowned throughout the world; therefore, one should perform a ritual bath there with every possible effort.
For one who desires liberation, and especially for one who wishes for the supreme state, having reached the hermitage of Caṇḍikā, why should he suffer any further? (55)

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Māmuhrada," in the first section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
Yayāti said: O best of the twice-born, how did the hermitage of Caṇḍikā come to be there? At what time was it established, and what fruit is obtained by men upon seeing it? (1)
Pulastya said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim a story that destroys sin; by hearing which properly, a human being is completely liberated from all sins.
Long ago, O King, in the age of the gods, there was a Dānava named Mahiṣa, who, arrogant due to a boon from the Grandfather (Brahmā), struck fear into all the gods.
By him, Śakra and the other gods were defeated by the thousands in battle; out of fear of him, they abandoned heaven and fled in every direction.
Having brought the three worlds under his control, he himself indeed became Indra.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Nāsatyas, and the hosts of Maruts—likewise the Daityas were made by him even more powerful, each according to his merit.
Then Vahni, overcome by fear, abandoned the hosts of gods and no longer offered the sacrificial portion to the deities from among the Dānavas.
O best of kings, the sun performs its illumination exactly as it is approved by him, even without a share of the sacrifice, out of fear.
O best of kings, all the world-protectors likewise performed his work like servants, being deprived of their share of the sacrifice.
Then, after some time, all the gods, having assembled together and being full of humility, questioned Bṛhaspati, the best of Brahmins.
"O Blessed One, what shall we do? Where shall we go, being without refuge? Therefore, tell us the means for the destruction of the evil-minded Mahiṣa. (11)
Thus addressed by the gods, O King, the Guru meditated for a long time and then spoke to those deities as if bringing them back to life. (12)

Bṛhaspati said: "O gods, that Daitya has obtained a boon from Brahmā and is established in his manly prowess; he is incapable of being slain by all the gods, with the single exception of one woman. Therefore, go together to Arbuda, the best of mountains."

"Indeed, for the sake of your asceticism, may success be attained by you there without delay—[success] through the supreme Goddess Caṇḍikā, who is the embodiment of power and can assume any form at will. (14)
Worship her in solitude, by whom this entire world is pervaded; she, being pleased, will indeed act for the sake of slaying the evil-minded Mahiṣa.
He will make an effort to bring about his incarnation; by her hand, that evil-minded one shall surely meet his death.
I shall proclaim to you this supreme mantra of Śakti, which, when joined with the ritual of worship, is auspicious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Pulastya said: O King, having been addressed thus, all the gods, filled with great joy, went together with him to Mount Arbuda.
There, O King, Gīṣpati initiated all those who had bathed and purified themselves with supreme mantras that grant immediate success.
There, accompanied by their retinues for three and a half watches of the night, they were honored with offerings of oblations, worship, and gifts, as well as perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
With various mantras and beautiful hymns, they constantly offered prayers with devotion, their minds concentrated upon the light of the lamp.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, they were devoted to their gurus; endowed with the practice of limb-protection (aṅganyāsa), they had attained a state of equanimity. || 22 ||
O best of kings, as they remained thus, seven months passed by, and then the Goddess of the Suras was pleased.
O King, through the entry of the lamp’s light into their bodies, which had been purified by the mantra, their supreme splendor increased.
Within six months, they became as radiant as twelve suns; then, O King, Jīva recognized that they were endowed with such splendor.
He fashioned a mandala that bestows all spiritual accomplishments; then, he seated all the inhabitants of the celestial abodes within it.
O King, by means of those most excellent mantras possessing power, he drew forth the vital energy residing in their bodies and deposited it there within the mandala.
Then a daughter consisting of splendor was born there in her own form; she was the embodiment of power, possessed of a great body, and marked with divine characteristics.
Indra gave her his thunderbolt, and the Lord of Waters gave him his noose; the blessed Agni gave him his spear, and the Lord of Wealth gave him a lion-vehicle.
O best of kings, all the other hosts, being delighted, gave her their own weapons and offered hymns of praise with concentrated minds.

The gods said: "Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods; salutations to you, O you of golden luster! Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; salutations to you, O Mother of the universe! (31)

Salutations to you who possess the universal form, and salutations to you who are praised by the universe; you are the intellect, you are fortitude, you are splendor, you are the nectar of immortality, and you are the night.
You are forbearance, supernatural power, splendor, Svāhā, Sāvitrī, Kamalā, and Satī; you are Gaurī, you are Mahāmāyā, you are Cāmuṇḍā, and you are Sarasvatī.
Bhairavī is of terrifying form, wielding the sword of Caṇḍamuṇḍa; she is beloved by the bhūtas, possesses a massive body, wears a garland of skulls, and is fierce in her valor.
Always fond of wine and meat, and devoted to the protection of those who seek refuge—you pervade this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving. (35)
Pulastya said: Thus praised by all the gods, the Goddess was then greatly delighted; she spoke to them, "O deities, receive a boon from me."
The gods said: "There is a Dānava named Mahiṣa, who, having been granted a boon by the Grandfather (Brahmā), has been made incapable of being slain by any living beings, including the gods. (37)
Therefore, O Goddess, cast down that one woman, excluding her. || 38 ||
The Goddess said: "O all you gods, go to your own abodes, being at peace."
"I shall destroy him when the time has arrived. Having spoken thus, all the gods departed for their own abodes, filled with joy.
The goddess remained right there on the mountain slope, filled with joy; then, after some time, the venerable sage Nārada arrived.
Having beheld the Goddess there, he who was devoted to pilgrimage reached Triviṣṭapa, where Mahiṣa was stationed.
Having seen that the sage had arrived there, Mahiṣāsura, endowed with humility, bowed down and then rose from his seat to greet him.
Then, having known him to be well-rested and comfortably seated, he honored him with offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for the guest (argha), and a seat, and spoke these words.
"O best of sages, from where have you come here, and for what purpose? These sons, as well as the kingdom, wives, and wealth—"
"O best of the twice-born, what need have I for this, since I am already accompanied by my servants? I shall give you everything; tell me what your requirement is. (46)
Nārada said: I rejoice in all this; it is entirely fitting for you, for we are eternally free from desire, having taken refuge in the dharma of sages.
Having arrived here out of curiosity, I have finally attained the sight of you; having come from the mortal world, I shall now depart for the abode of Brahmā.
Mahiṣāsura said: "O Sage, have you ever seen anything wonderful on the surface of the earth—whether divine or human—by which the Dānavas might be overcome, O Lord? (49)

Nārada said: O Lord of the Dānavas, I have seen a great wonder upon the surface of the earth, such as has never been seen before anywhere in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (50)
There is a mountain known as Arbuda upon the surface of the earth.
Adorned with trees in bloom throughout all seasons, it was like heaven itself. || 51 ||
With *bakula*, *campaka*, mango, *aśoka*, and *karṇikāra* trees; with *śāla*, *tāla*, date palms, *vaṭa*, *bhallātaka*, and *dhava* trees. (52)
With *sarala* and *panasa* trees, with *tiṃduka* and *karavīraka*, with *mandāra* and *pārijāta*, and likewise with *malaya* sandalwood trees; || 53 ||
He was surrounded by many varieties of fragrant flowers, as well as all kinds of foods—those to be chewed, licked, and sucked—and the finest fruits.
Neither that tree, nor that creeper, nor that herb exists upon the surface of the earth, O eldest of the Asuras, which was not seen by me there on the mountain.
The birds with sweet songs—the cakoras, peacocks, cātakas, cuckoos, dhārtarāṣṭras, bees, and white-winged ones—[all sang]. || 56 ||
Hearing whose sound even sages who are composed, who know the three periods of time, fall into agitation, tormented by the arrows of Kaṃdarpa.
There were delightful waterfalls and rivers of pure water, along with hundreds of thousands of lakes filled with clusters of lotuses.
The men there have large eyes like lotus petals, are slender-waisted, possess pure smiles, are discerning, and are endowed with scriptural knowledge and vows. (59)

Moreover, what is the use of saying more? Whatever is found there on that mountain—whether known as sweat-born, egg-born, soil-born, or womb-born—all are seen on that most excellent of mountains to be transcendent of the entire world.
Ten yojanas in width and joined by two mountains, that glorious mountain rose five yojanas high; it became a heaven upon earth.
There, filled with curiosity and looking here and there, I beheld a woman who was the beauty of the world, composed of every wonder.
Neither among goddesses, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor among humans, have I ever seen or heard of a woman of such beauty. (63)
Rati, Prīti, Umā, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī—all these women are not equal to even a fraction of that form. (64)
O tiger among Dānavas, having seen a woman of such form, I was afflicted by desire and then fell into a state of extreme agitation. (65)
Then, summoning my fortitude, I thought in my mind: "I shall never engage in conversation with her at any time."
By the mere sight of her, desire has increased within my heart; what more, then, will come of conversing with her? (67)

"Indeed, the asceticism I have practiced for a long time through celibacy will all go to ruin for me, now that I am conquered by the objects of the senses. Therefore, I shall go elsewhere before any further transformation occurs. (68)
A woman was created of old by the Self-born One as an obstacle to asceticism; she is the bolt upon the path to heaven and the staircase to hell. (69)
Courage, austerity, truthfulness, steadfastness, and family shame endure only so long as a woman does not behold [a man] in private, and especially so.
Having reflected upon this in many ways, I then closed my eyes; without speaking to that lady of beautiful hips, I remained right there.
Pulastya said: Having heard the words of Nārada, O Indra among kings, Mahiṣa, tormented by desire, questioned that sage once again even after merely hearing [his reply].
Mahiṣāsura said: "O tiger among Brahmins, who is that beautiful woman of such form, by the mere sight of whom you have become possessed by love? (73)
"O Sage, whether she be a goddess, a human woman, a yakṣiṇī, or a pannagī—whether she be a maiden or accompanied by her husband—tell me everything in full detail."
Nārada said: "I did not ask her anything, nor do I know her lineage; this much remains in my mind—that she is a glorious maiden. (76)
Wearing a rosary and holding a water-pot, that auspicious young woman performed penance on that mountain for some particular reason. (76)
Therefore, O Lord of Daityas, I shall go to the eternal world of Brahmā; I do not venture to engage in conversation with him, being distressed by the fear of his arrows of desire.
Having spoken thus, O King, the sage then departed for the world of Brahmā; Mahiṣa, however, possessed by the god of love, dispatched his messenger to her.
Having gone there quickly and having seen that beautiful woman, [ask]: "For what purpose did she perform penance, and who indeed was her husband? (79)
Then, having gone to Mount Arbuda at the command of Mahiṣa, that messenger saw her, who possessed the luster of the interior of a lotus, and understood all her actions.
Filled with wonder, he reported to Mahiṣa that he had seen a woman, the best among the Daityas, endowed with all auspicious marks.
That maiden of excellent complexion, born from the splendor of the gods, even today continues to perform austerities, having undertaken the vow of perpetual maidenhood for the sake of slaying you.
Thus were all those ascetics questioned there, and they replied: "This is the truth, O illustrious one; now do whatever must follow. (83)
Her form, youth, luster, and complexion cannot be described at all; O Lord, that young girl does not engage in conversation with anyone. (84)
Pulastya said: Having heard those words, Mahiṣa, once again tormented by desire, dispatched a messenger, a discerning Dānava.
"O wise one, go quickly for my sake and bring that ascetic woman here by means of conciliation, sowing dissension, or bribery, and even by force if necessary. (86)
Then that wise one, having prostrated, went quickly to Arbuda, the best of mountains, where that Supreme Goddess resided; and bowing down with humility, he addressed her with these words: || 87 ||
The powerful one known as Mahiṣa, born from the lineage of Danu, was the lord of the three worlds and possessed the ability to assume any form at will. || 88 ||
O auspicious lady, he desires you as his lawful wife according to dharma; therefore, choose him as your husband—he who grants all desires—may prosperity be yours. (89)
If he were your beloved and you likewise his beloved, then the youth of both of you would truly be fulfilled; of this there is no doubt. (90)
Having been addressed thus by him, the goddess then spoke these words, slightly filled with anger and with her lower lip quivering repeatedly.
The Goddess said: "A messenger is everywhere proclaimed to be inviolable in every way; therefore, you were not suddenly reduced to ashes despite your condition."
"Go and speak to the ill-behaved Mahiṣa, that lowest of Dānavas: 'O sinful one, I cannot be obtained by you, nor by anyone else.'"
"I have undertaken all this effort for the purpose of slaying you. Having heard those words of hers, he went back to Mahiṣa.
Overcome by great fear and struck with wonder at her beauty, he reported everything she had done to Mahiṣa—the entire conversation and her state of longing in its entirety. (95)
Having heard that, O King, Mahiṣa, tormented by the arrows of desire, summoned his commander-in-chief and spoke these words. (96)
O Arbuda, marshal on Mount Arbuda an army that is exceedingly difficult to withstand—an awesome force composed of elephants and horses, and teeming with chariots and infantry. (97)
Then he marshaled a fourfold army, variegated with banners and parasols, and adorned with the sound of musical instruments.
Then elephants, equipped with armor and mounted by warriors, were seen running here and there like winged mountains. (99)
And there were also horses, free from speckled markings, possessing the speed of the wind and great luster, equipped with body armor by the hundreds and thousands.
Chariots fashioned in the likeness of celestial palaces were prepared by him, adorned with networks of small bells, large bells, and banners. (101)

And there were foot soldiers of massive stature, great archers, and possessed of great strength; others bore swords and shields, while still others held spears and battle-axes in their hands. || 102 ||
There were one hundred thousand Matanga chariots, three times that number [of others], ten times as many horses, O King, and innumerable foot soldiers. (103)
Then, having reached Arbuda and surrounded it from afar, he rushed toward its vicinity together with his well-matched ministers.
Seeing that goddess established in meditation, he, afflicted by the arrows of Kandarpa, then addressed her with words full of humility. || 105 ||
"O fair-faced one, having heard of such beauty as yours, I have arrived; therefore, choose me quickly through the Gāndharva form of marriage. (106)
"O lady of pure smiles, I have sixty thousand wives; having made me their proud husband, you shall become their mistress. (107)
"O young girl, this asceticism is not for you; enjoy the pleasures as you desire, having become the mistress of the three worlds together with me, day and night. (108)
Although addressed thus by him, she did not utter a reply; thereupon, overcome by passion, he approached her side.
Then, seeing him so greedy, that goddess, filled with wrath, remembered her vehicle, the lion; he arrived, and she mounted him.
He spoke harsh words, saying repeatedly, "Go! Go! [And added: "Otherwise, O lowest of Dānavas, I shall slay you right here in this place."
Then, tormented by the arrows of desire, he surrounded her on all sides together with his ministers in order to seize the goddess.
Then that supreme goddess laughed aloud; from that, thick men emerged together day and night.
Well-armored, bearing weapons, and filled with great rage, the Goddess then said to them, "This man is a sinner; let him be slain!"
Then they all, united together, rushed toward Mahiṣa, shouting "Stay! Stay! while discharging weapons in great abundance.
Then a battle took place between the Gaṇas and the Dānavas; thereafter, all those ministers went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Then that enraged buffalo, having caused his ministers to be struck down, summoned his own army to that mountain slope.
Having mounted his excellent chariot, he addressed the charioteer: "O charioteer, lead me quickly to where she stands established. (118)
"Having slain him today, I shall cross to the further shore of this anger that is so difficult to traverse. Having been addressed thus, O King, the charioteer then urged the horses forward. (119)
By that very path, he drove the chariot to where she stood firm; at that very moment, however, most dreadful portents occurred there.
Many people were on that path by which the king had set out, when a harsh wind, filled with gravel, blew directly against him. || 121 ||
A great meteor fell, striking the solar disc; and the deer moved counter-clockwise along his path, O best of kings. (122)
Seated there, they vomited and passed much urine; then a vulture perched upon the chariot banner let out a cry.
Disregarding all those most terrible and great portents, he, intent on wrath, proceeded directly toward that goddess.
Discharging arrows and uttering cries of "Stay! Stay!", not a single person could be seen among them there, O best of kings. (125)
He who restrains the enraged buffalo in battle, having slain the hosts of the Gaṇas by him, has created a mire of blood.
Then, O King, having approached the goddess, she was addressed with pride: "O timid one, it is certainly not fitting for you to engage in combat with me. (127)
My strength is not that of a fool, nor is it my good fortune or wealth; yet for all that, you do not carry out my word in any way whatsoever.
"Truly, O beautiful woman, I know you by your true nature; you are arrogant. Even now, follow my word and become my dear wife."
Established in my manliness, I do not venture to kill you, a woman; yet Śakra, along with the gods, has been defeated by me in battle more than once.
"O foolish woman, there is no man in the three worlds who is my equal. Having spoken thus, the goddess was then overcome with great anger.
Grasping his bow together with an arrow, he spoke these words: "O wicked one, it is not fitting for you to hold conversation with me."
"Even though you were filled with desire for the maiden, nevertheless hear my words: Śakra was not conquered by you through your own prowess on the field of battle."
O lowest of Dānavas, the gods consider the Grandfather to be the bestower of boons; out of respect for him, you therefore consider yourself superior. (134)
"O sinner, by the Lotus-born One you have been made invulnerable to all living beings on the surface of the earth, with the exception of one woman. (135)
O Dānava, you are the best of grandfathers and are victorious here; if you possess any manliness, then display it quickly! (136)
"I shall lead you to the abode of Yama with these sharp arrows! Having spoken thus, the goddess then released eight shafts.
With four arrows he sent the four horses to the abode of Yama, and with a single shaft he struck off the head of the charioteer from his body.
With one arrow he cut down the banner, and with another he was wounded in the heart; thus, with his body pierced and in great pain, he leaned against the flagpole for support.
O King, accompanied by a fainting spell, he remained with his face cast downward for some time; then, having regained consciousness, he released sharp arrows.
The goddess, accompanied by her companions, struck him in all parts of his body; then, with a razor-edged arrow, she split his bow in two.
Then the Daitya, his bow severed, equipped with shield and sword, suddenly put the Goddess to flight and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (142)
As he was rushing forward, [the other] laughed and quickly severed his sword with two arrows, and his lance with a single half-arrow. (143)
O King, then that lowest of Dānavas was deprived of his weapons and his chariot; thereupon, O ruler of the earth, he remembered his arrows and various other weapons. (144)
Meditating upon the Brahmāstra in his mind, he released a blade of grass at her; however, from that discharged weapon, a trail of smoke was produced.
At that very time, however, Brahmā and those dwellers of heaven were seized by supreme fear upon witnessing his prowess.
Then, O best of kings, the queen meditated for a moment and swiftly struck that weapon with the Brahmā-astra; thereupon, it became useless.
When the Brahmāstra had become fruitless, the best of the Dānavas, filled with rage, discharged the Āgneya weapon; she, however, struck it down with the Vāruṇa weapon.
In this way, the goddess then rendered thousands of those various kinds of missiles discharged by him utterly fruitless.
Thus, having exhausted all his weapons, that exceedingly powerful Dānava created a supreme illusion with divine missiles against the Queen of the Gods.
And he brandished his massive body, which resembled a mountain, possessed long and sharp horns, and was like collyrium in color. (151)
Then that queen mounted him, who had shoulders like those of a lion; with a sharp sword, the queen cut off his head.
The Queen of the Gods pierced him in the region of the back with a trident; then, from that corpse, a great Being emerged.
Bearing a shield and a sword, the fierce one cried out, "Stay! Stay! Seizing him likewise by his mass of hair, the Queen of the Gods [restrained him]. (154)
O best of kings, with his sword he struck the Dānava violently, and he was deprived of life as his side was torn open by the lion. 155.
Then, filled with rage, she struck the Dānavas once again; and those Daityas who remained after being slain emerged, piercing through the surface of the earth.
Terrified by fear and desiring to live, they entered the netherworld; then all the hosts of gods, the Vasus, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins [did likewise]. (157)
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Sādhyas, Rudras, Guhyakas, Kinnaras, and the Ādityas together with Śakra, having assembled before the Supreme Goddess, [spoke]. (158)
From all sides, they scattered divine flowers over that goddess, praising her with various hymns and bowing down with devoted intent.
"Well done, O Great Goddess! Well done, O Beautiful One! That the greatest evildoer has been slain is right; for by this sinner, the entire three worlds have been devastated. (160)

"The kingdom in the triple heaven has been given back to Vāsava by you; therefore, choose a boon that is desired by your mind—blessings be upon you! All the gods are pleased with you and will grant it, of this there is no doubt. (161)
The Goddess said: "If the gods are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, let there be a holy hermitage right here for me, endowed with great renown. (162)
And I, O gods, shall always remain here on this excellent mountain.
O Goddess of the gods, those men who shall behold you here in this highly meritorious hermitage with this form shall attain the supreme goal.
Those men shall become endowed with the knowledge of Brahman. || 165 ||
"Because a fierce deed was performed by you, O slayer of the Dānavas, therefore you shall attain fame in the world by the name Caṇḍikā. (166)
"In your name, this hermitage shall likewise become renowned. || 167 ||
Those who, having performed their ablutions with a concentrated mind, shall offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here on the auspicious fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina; || 168 ||
O Goddess, they shall obtain the fruit of performing the śrāddha at Gayā; likewise, through the sight of you, their liberation from sin shall occur. (169)
Kṛṣṇa said: Those who shall remain here for one night, endowed with faith and devoted to fasting, their sin will go to complete destruction.

Any mortal man who is childless, or a woman likewise composed, who performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and the ritual bath with her mind fixed on Him, shall quickly obtain a virtuous son; of this there is no doubt.
Indra said: "Any king who, having been deprived of his kingdom, performs ablutions and acts of charity here, shall experience the destruction of all his enemies and the recovery of his kingdom. (172)
Agni said: "The man who, having come here, performs a śrāddha with purity according to his own means, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice. (173)
Yama said: "Whoever bathes here and shall give sesame seeds to Brāhmaṇas, for him there will never be any fear of untimely death. (174)
The Rākṣasas said: "O Goddess, those men who shall offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) here in your hermitage, no fear arising from a ghost (preta) shall ever befall them. (175)
Varuṇa said: "He who shall provide water here for the bathing of the foremost of Brahmins will always remain pure in this world and in the next. (176)
Vāyu said: "He who shall give here to the Brahmins bright and especially fragrant ointments will become free from disease. (177)
Dhanada said: "Whoever shall give wealth here to the Brahmins according to their ability, he shall never be destitute of wealth in this world. (178)
Īśvara said: "Whoever, being devoted to this vow, shall dwell here during the four months of the rainy season, for him there will always be happiness both in this world and in the next. (179)
The Vasus said: "That man who shall properly observe a fast for three nights will be liberated from all sins committed from birth until death. (180)
The Sun said: "Those men who, endowed with devotion, give umbrellas and sandals in this meritorious hermitage, for them there are eternal worlds. (181)
The Aśvins said: "Whoever, endowed with faith, shall give sweet food to a Brāhmaṇa here, for him there will be supreme and imperishable delight. (182)
The holy fords said: "From this day forward, there shall be a special residence here in this world-renowned hermitage for all the holy fords. (183)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina, whoever, being devoted to fasting, performs a bath here with devotion, shall indeed obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 4 ||
The Gandharvas said: "Whatever man shall perform songs and instrumental music here, he shall indeed be endowed with beauty for seven future births. (185)
The sages said: "Whoever shall observe a fast for three nights in this hermitage, he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cāndrāyaṇa penances. (186)
Pulastya said: O best of kings, having thus granted all these boons to the Goddess, the gods departed for heaven by her command; the Goddess remained right there.
Then, having seen the Goddess in that hermitage, mortals went to heaven; consequently, Triviṣṭapa became filled with mortals without any effort. || 188 ||
All rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others have perished upon the surface of the earth, as have all other religious acts, with the exception of the worship of the Goddess.
Then, terrified, the thousand-eyed one consulted with his preceptor and swiftly summoned Desire, Anger, Fear, and Pride.
"Go quickly to the mortals who desire to remain in the world of men—both men and women—and dispel the delusion arising from household life, which is accompanied by craving and exhaustion. (191)
By my command, you must indeed resort to the meritorious sanctuary of Caṇḍikā, especially on the final day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina.
Having been addressed thus, O great king, all those beginning with Kāma departed quickly and provided protection everywhere in the mortal world.
Knowing this, O best of kings, go there quickly if you desire the highest welfare in this world and the next. (194)
O King, for him who goes toward Abūrda to behold Caṇḍikā, his ancestors dance and his grandfathers roar with joy. || 195 ||
That son who, having gone here to the hermitage of Caṇḍikā, performs the śrāddha with a concentrated mind, will deliver us all. (196)
O King, by the first [journey] one obtains a kingdom, and by the second, heaven; by the third journey, O Ruler of the Earth, liberation shall be attained. (197)
Therefore, with every effort, one should undertake a pilgrimage there to Arbuda, the best of mountains, auspicious and filled with all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 198 ||
In this regard, a verse was formerly sung by the great seer Nārada, after he had bathed in that holy hermitage during a gathering of many brahmins: (119)
Other holy fords undoubtedly purify one through ritual bathing and charity; however, by the mere sight of Arbuda, one becomes free from sin. (200)
O best of men, he who listens to this sacred narrative endowed with faith attains the desires cherished in his mind. || 201 ||
O King, for him in whose house this written book remains, his desired wishes shall be fulfilled day by day.
O Lord of the Earth, that man who, endowed with faith, recites this, O King, even he, a most excellent person, obtains the fruit of the pilgrimage. (203)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Origin of Caṇḍikā’s Hermitage," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: From there, one should go to the Nāgahrada, a sacred ford that destroys all sins, where the serpents performed austerities on the beautiful slope of the mountain.
Having previously heard the curse of Kadrū, all the nāgas, overcome with fear, bowed their necks and questioned Śeṣa, the king of the nāgas. || 2 ||
"O best of serpents, we are tormented by our mother’s curse; what shall we do, where shall we go, and how might there be release from this curse? (3)
Śeṣa said: In the past, I propitiated my mother for the sake of release from the curse. She said: "Those who are endowed with austerity, righteous-souled, and well-restrained... (4)
For the fire shall not burn them at the sacrifice of the son of Parikṣit; therefore, go to the mountain named Arbuda on the surface of the earth.
"There, you must remain engaged in austerity and well-composed, where that goddess Caṇḍikā herself, who can assume any form at will, resides."
"By the mere recitation of whose name calamities are surely destroyed; worship that Goddess incessantly at my word."

"By her grace, you shall all become free from your feverish distress. O best of Nagas, I see this alone as the means here; whether divine or human, there is no other who can bring about your liberation."
Pulastya said: O King, having been addressed thus by the king of the Nāgas, the serpents then bowed to him and departed toward Mount Arbuda.
Having pierced the surface of the earth and the mountain immediately thereafter, they emerged by way of a tunnel, having made a very wide opening in the chasm.
Then all those of firm vows, devoted to the Goddess and endowed with devotion, dwelt there for the sake of propitiating Caṇḍikā.
They remained there constantly performing fire-sacrifices and the supreme recitation; some took food only once a day, others abstained from food entirely, and still others subsisted on air alone.
Some used their teeth as a mortar, while others were grinders with stones; some practiced the austerity of the five fires, and others likewise washed away their impurities immediately.
Then other gods likewise performed songs and instrumental music before them; seeing those best of serpents endowed with single-minded devotion, [the others did so as well].
Then the goddess, being well-pleased, spoke these words.
The Goddess said: "I am well-pleased with you, my children; for what purpose do you perform this austerity? Choose from me a boon that resides in your hearts."
The Nāgas said: "O Goddess, tormented by our mother’s curse and left without refuge, we have come to you for protection at the command of the King of the Nāgas. (17)

Therefore, protect us from that fear arising from the fire of the curse. Previously, we were cursed by our mother for a certain reason: "In the sacrifice of the son of Parikṣit, the fire shall consume you. (18)
The Goddess said: "As long as his sacrifice shall last, so long do you remain in my presence; stay there without fear and enjoy abundant pleasures. (19)
"And when the sacrifice is completed, you shall go once more to your own abode; for this mountain cave has been divided by you. (20)
That sacred ford on the surface of the earth shall become the Nāgahrada; whoever here, intent on devotion, [performs rites] on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, || 21 ||
The man who performs his bath there shall have no fear of the day of death; furthermore, through the performance of a śrāddha, he will deliver his ancestors.
Whatever enjoyments are renowned on the surface of the earth—whether divine or human—a man shall always obtain them; of this there is no doubt. (23)
Pulastya said: Then, having been freed from that terrible fear, they became joyful; having sought refuge with the Goddess, they remained there on that best of mountains.
Then, after a long time, when the sacrificial session of the son of Parikṣit had concluded, they departed, fully satisfied, for the netherworld (rasātala).
And having been granted permission by the Goddess, O tiger among kings, they prostrated themselves again and again; held firm by her devotion, they departed with great difficulty.
Even today, O King, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, those eager for a vision of the Goddess maintain their presence there.
Therefore, O best of kings, he who desires his own welfare should perform the śrāddha rite there with every effort, as well as the ritual bath. (28)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nāgodbhava Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 37 ||
Pulastya said: O lord of the earth, from there one should go to the pool known as Śivaliṅga, where the river Jāhnavī remains hidden, O best of kings.
A man who bathes there properly obtains the fruit of all sacred fords; he is liberated from every sin committed from birth until the end of life.
Yayāti said: "O Lord, for what reason does that Jāhnavī remain hidden there? At what time did she arrive? For my curiosity is indeed great. (3)
Pulastya said: "O Lord, when the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull was propitiated by the gods, he said: 'O Vibhu, you must remain forever immovable upon this Arbuda.'"
When the Liṅga had been installed there by the Lord Śambhu himself, that very Liṅga which had previously been cast down by the great sages, the Vālakhilyas, [was restored].
Then, due to some other cause involving excessive anger, a vow was made by the God for the sake of all the inhabitants of heaven.
"I must remain right here; of this there is no doubt. Then, as he continued to dwell there for a long period of time, [the following occurred].
The Gaṅgā appeared in the mind of Acaleśvara, wondering, "How shall there be a constant union with her? (8)
Then, O best of kings, as he was reflecting thus many times, the proud Goddess Gaurī, the Supreme Sovereign, perceived his thoughts.
Having reflected upon a very great stratagem arising from contact with the Gaṅgā, all the Gaṇas, led by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, were commanded by him.
"I have a certain intention arising from my vow regarding this reservoir of water; let an excellent sacrificial pit be constructed here on the slope of this mountain."
"There, standing in the midst of the water, I shall remain devoted to the waters. Having heard that, the Gaṇas quickly prepared many sacrificial pits.
It was filled with clear water, possessed excellent landing-stairs, and brought great comfort; then, having taken leave of Gaurī, he became eager for the confluence of the Jāhnavī.
Immediately thereafter, the Lord of Gods entered [the body] under the pretext of a vow; staying there, he meditated upon Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds. (14)
Meditated upon by him, she was united with Śiva at that very moment; thus the Blessed One always enjoys the company of Jāhnavī there.

O Indra among kings, Gaurī did not realize this under the pretext of her vow. Then, after some time had passed, the venerable sage Nārada, endowed with the knowledge of absolute liberation (kaivalya), arrived there while wandering about.
But having seen Mahādeva standing in the water, observing his vow, and possessed of gestures born of desire, he was filled with wonder there.
"What is this distortion of the face and eyes of this observer of vows? Is the sage thus absorbed in meditation while possessed by such desire? (18)
Then, with his vision of meditation, he saw Maheśvara attached to the Gaṅgā; because of Gaurī’s fear, [the Lord] acted with feigned pretense, and at that, [Nārada] was filled with wonder.
Then he related everything regarding the deeds of Hara.
Then the goddess, her eyes copper-red with rage and trembling again and again, went in haste to where Maheśvara was.
Seeing that Maheśvarī had arrived filled with wrath, Jāhnavī, perceiving her through her divine vision, spoke in fear.
"The goddess was announced to us at our meeting by Nārada; she is now approaching in a state of anger. Do what must be done next. (23)

Śrī Mahādeva said: "O Jāhnavī, you must first go before the Daughter of the Mountain to accomplish what is beneficial; for she is exceedingly proud, yet she may be brought under control through conciliation."
At that very moment she becomes virtuous; therefore, be devoted to conciliation. Otherwise, she will undoubtedly cast a curse upon you along with me.
O best of kings, having been addressed thus by Rudra, Jāhnavī then emerged from the pool and proceeded toward him.
Modest and preceded by her hands joined in reverence, she, being well-adorned, bowed her head and then spoke.
"O Goddess, in the past, as I was falling from the sky, I was caught by your husband; this too is known to you for the sake of the king. (28)
Thereupon, the affection of the one named Bhagīratha increased; yet, out of fear of us two, there was no meeting with you anywhere. (29)
"Now, O Goddess of the Suras, by your word I know that I have been summoned by Rudra; or was it of my own free will, O auspicious one? (30)
This one is the lord of the three worlds; having somehow emerged from that [place], he has arrived right here. What I have spoken is the truth. (31)
Pulastya said: Having heard those words of hers, the goddess was then greatly delighted and spoke these sweet words: "What you have spoken is indeed the truth. (32)
Therefore, may you be blessed; choose from me whatever boon you desire, with the single exception of my beloved Maheśvara, who is my husband according to dharma.
Gangā said: "Am I indeed born as the wife of the Wielder of the Trident, though joined with misfortune? Therefore, grant me one day for the sake of sporting with him. (34)
O Goddess of the Suras, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, this shall remain as Śivakuṇḍa for a full day and night, since it has been occupied by me.
And let that pool on the surface of the earth, named Śivagaṅgā, attain fame through your grace, O daughter of the mountain. (36)
Pulastya said: Having said, "So be it," to the great river Gaṅgā, that goddess then dismissed her after embracing her again and again.
Then, when Gaṅgā had departed, she, with her face cast downwards and deeply ashamed, took Rudra by the hand and, wandering about, went toward his home.
Thus did this event occur of old at that pool, O lord of men; therefore, with every effort and composed in mind, one should worship there on the fourteenth day.
O best of kings, one should perform a ritual bath there on the bright lunar day of the month of Caitra, due to the presence of the God of gods and of Gaṅgā.

O best of kings, wherever all that which has been done inauspiciously comes to an end, there a man who gives a bull to a Brāhmaṇa shall certainly dwell in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on its body. (41)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Origin of the Śivagaṅgā Kuṇḍa," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Yayāti said: O Brahmin, as you have previously related, Maheśvara, assuming a stable form, was propitiated by the gods and installed a Liṅga. || 1 ||
Why was that *liṅga* cast down by the high-souled Vālakhilyas? And why did Maheśvara, the God of gods, become immovable there? || 2 ||
You ought to explain all this curiosity of mine exactly as it is; and what merit arises for men when that [place] is beheld? (3)
Pulastya said: O best of kings, listen to the majesty of Maheśvara; herein I shall relate to you another narrative concerning past events.
When Satī, whose prowess was truth, had passed away after being insulted by Dakṣa and not being invited to his sacrifice; || 5 ||
Then Kāma, quickly seizing his flower-bow, approached him; for he had suddenly beheld Kandarpa with an arrow fixed, who is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
Fleeing from his fear, the Destroyer of Tripura vanished; O King, he was then wandering here and there.
Having reached the holy hermitage of the Vālakhilyas, which was adorned with excellent trees, the Blessed One was seen there by them along with their wives, appearing most handsome.

Clad in the directions [as his garment] and speaking very sweet words, he then captivated them with desire; abandoning their sons, homes, and all else, O King, they all followed behind him and spoke incessantly, saying, "Devote yourself to me!"
Some embraced him, others likewise kissed him, and still others touched his linga again and again.
And that Blessed One, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, being free from desire, exists within all living beings by means of his pervasive presence throughout the universe. (11)
And that Blessed Lord Śambhu, wandering there in that hermitage, approached them facing eastward, tormented by desire for their wives.
Then those sages, seeing that transformation resulting from the wife, not knowing it was Mahādeva, became enraged at that Great-souled One.
Deeply distressed on account of their wives, O scorcher of foes, they uttered a curse: "O you most evil-doer, may this linga of yours fall, fall! (14)
"You mock our wife constantly by looking at her; therefore, let the emblem of that enemy of cities fall from you this very instant! (15)
O royal sage, at those words of Brahmā, the earth then trembled; the mountain peaks shattered and the oceans were agitated.
Then, O lord of men, all the hosts of gods were terrified with fear, perceiving that an untimely dissolution had come upon the three worlds. (17)
Then they went to the Grandfather and reported everything to him: "O Supreme Lord, the signs of universal dissolution are being seen. (18)
"O Lord, O best of gods, we do not know what the cause is. Having heard those words of theirs and having meditated for a long time, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) [spoke].
He said: "The Liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow was cast down by the Vālakhilyas; therefore, these terrible portents have arisen, indicating fear. (20)
Therefore, let all the inhabitants of heaven, joined by me, go to where that liṅga is, so that Śiva may install it in its proper place. || 21 ||
"As long as no untimely dissolution arises in the world," having thus deliberated together, they all then went to Arbuda.
At the hermitage of the Vālakhilyas, where that liṅga had fallen, they, filled with humility, praised it with various hymns declared in the Vedas.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who grants fearlessness to your devotees! Salutations to you, the abode of all, and who consists of all sacrifices! (24)
Salutations to the Lord of all, the God, the supreme light; salutations to the Creator who is accessible through most manifest knowledge.
Salutations to the three-eyed one, to the formidable one, who holds the excellent Pināka bow in his hand; in you all this is strung together, like clusters of jewels upon a thread.

O Best of the Wise, O Śaṅkara, in this cycle of existence, there is nothing—neither moving nor unmoving—in these three worlds, however subtle it may be, that is not pervaded by you, O Lord, for the sake of creation and dissolution. (27)
O Lord of the World, the elements such as earth and the rest were created by you according to your will; they shall once again enter into your body. (28)
Be gracious, O Blessed One; therefore, O Lord of the Gods, establish this liṅga in its proper place—may prosperity be yours—so that there shall be no further destruction of progeny.
The Blessed Lord said: "My emblem, belonging to me who am changeless, has been cast down by the Vālakhilyas; how can I take it up again as long as purification has not occurred? (30)
I am capable of easily subduing the Vālakhilyas; however, O best of gods, Brāhmaṇas are to be honored and worshipped by me.
"O Lord, this Liṅga is indeed immovable; it cannot be uprooted. Only one means for this has been prescribed here; no other is remembered. (32)
"O Grandfather, if you had worshipped my Liṅga in the past, then all the hosts of gods, then the Brahmins, and then others [would have done so]. (33)
From that, may the world, both stationary and moving, attain peace for us two.
Pulastya said: O best of kings, having been addressed thus by Śaṅkara, the blessed Brahmā then first worshipped him with great devotion.
After Brahmā came Viṣṇu, then Śakra, and after him the other Brahmins, such as the Vālakhilyas, with the Śatarudriya mantras.
Then those terrible portents were pacified at that very moment; the world became cheerful, and a gentle breeze began to blow.
Then Mahādeva said to all those dwellers of the triple heaven: "Choose from me, all of you, an excellent boon that is desired by your minds."

The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, by the mere touch of your linga, even men who have committed sins shall go to heaven, and their transgressions shall be destroyed. [This shall equal] all vows, all gifts, and ten thousand pilgrimages. (39)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, if you so desire, O Lord, Indra shall cover this supreme liṅga of yours everywhere with his vajra.
The Blessed One said: "O Lotus-born One, this very intention dwells within my heart as well. Let the Lord of the Gods act accordingly for the increase of all dharma."
Pulastya said: Then the lord of the thirty gods covered that linga with his thunderbolt, so that it became invisible to all mortals.
Even today, a person who comes into the presence of that [liṅga] through the touch of the vajra is liberated from sin from birth until death; there is no doubt in this matter. (43)
Since the greatness of that Liṅga was proclaimed by Śaṅkara himself upon the surface of the earth, it was indeed covered with a cloth by Śakra.
From that time forward, the worship of the Liṅga arose in the mortal world; formerly, Śaṅkara was worshipped just as the other dwellers of heaven were.
Thus occurred this event in the past on Arbuda, the best of mountains, concerning the worship of the Liṅga about which you questioned me.
He who offers an oblation of fresh barley to the Lord of Acala on the fourteenth day at the end of the month of Phālguna is not born again in this world.
He who feeds Brāhmaṇas with devotion at that [shrine] using barley, rejoices in heaven for as many ages (yugas) as there are grains of barley.
In that regard, O Great King, the best of sages praise the gift of fresh roasted barley flour, for it was so declared by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) in ancient times. (49)
What is the use of various gifts being given? What is the use of extensive sacrifices? What is the use of various holy places, fire-offerings, or ascetic practices that cause hardship? (50)
On the fourteenth day at the end of Phālguna, in the presence of Sumaheśvara, all these other religious duties do not equal even a sixteenth part [of this]. (51)
Listen, O King, to a most excellent wonder that occurred there in the past: there was a certain man of sinful conduct, a leper with an emaciated body. (52)
Having arrived there for the sake of alms accompanied by other people, he obtained there a *kuḍava* measure of barley meal as his alms, O King.

Then, due to the affliction of disease, he did not take food; tormented by a burning fever, he bathed in that water devoid of devotion and, having placed some barley-meal (saktu) under his pillow, fell asleep at the arrival of night.
Then, while he was overcome by sleep, a hungry dog, joined by other dogs, seized him and devoured him.
Then, O King, out of astonishment he met his death; thereafter, he was born in the house of the lord of Vidarbha as one who remembered his former birth.
Indeed, having recognized that power of the barley-meal on that mountain, [he remembered] Bhīma, the best of kings, who was the father of Damayantī.
Year after year, on the fourteenth day at the end of the month of Phālguna, he would go there, having observed a fast and likewise kept a vigil throughout the night.
Then, in the presence of Acaleśvara, he gave large quantities of barley-meal (saktu), along with gold, to the best of the twice-born, as well as to the beasts, birds, and wild animals.
Then, O King, all those sages, headed by Gālava, filled with curiosity, questioned the king regarding the gift of the barley-meal.
The sages said: "You possess a marvelous power to bestow elephants, horses, and chariots; why then do you wish to give nothing here except for barley meal?"
Pulastya said: Then he related this ancient origin of the greatness of the gift of barley meal (saktu) to the sages of purified souls.
O best of the twice-born, previously, when I was devoid of devotion, my barley meal was indeed taken by a dog; by the power of that act, this attainment has been reached by me.

"I do not know what fruit may come from gifts given out of devotion at this present time; for this reason, I am making this gift of barley-meal (saktu) at this sacred ford, endowed with devotion. By this truth, I touch my own heart. (64)
Pulastya said: Thereupon those sages were delighted and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! And they performed that supreme gift of barley-meal (saktu) according to their own ability.
O royal sage, this power of the gift of barley-meal has been proclaimed; likewise, the majesty of Maheśvara and the truth have also been celebrated. (66)
And whoever listens with devotion to this as it is being told from the mouth of a twice-born man, is liberated from the sins committed during a day and night; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Barley Flour, Preceded by the Description of the Greatness of the Śiva-liṅga Maheśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Kāmeśvara, established there by Kāma; upon seeing whom, a mortal always becomes handsome and radiant.
Yayāti said: "You previously stated that Śambhu, indeed out of fear of the arrows of Kāma, reached the hermitage of the Vālakhilyas, where his *liṅga* fell. (2)
O best of the twice-born, tell me everything regarding how Śambhu was worshipped by him at Kāmeśvara-niveśana; I have a great curiosity.
Pulastya said: Even though the Lord of Devas had cast off his phallus, Smara did not release it; standing behind him, he showed his arrow to him.
Then, out of fear of him, the Destroyer of Tripura reached Vārāṇasī; and there too, he saw the Mind-born (Kāma) holding his bow in that same manner.
Then he reached Prayāga, and after that Kedāra; then Naimiṣa and Bhadrakarṇa, and Tripuṣkara at Jambūmārga.
Gokarṇa, Prabhāsa, the meritorious Kṛmijāṅgala, Gaṅgādvāra, Gayāśīrṣa, Kālābhīṣṭa, and Vaṭeśvara.
What need is there for much speaking? The god went to countless sacred fords and shrines, and likewise beheld Kāma.
O King, wherever Mahādeva goes out of fear of him, there he again beholds Kāma holding his weapon.

Then, after some time had passed, he arrived once more at Arbuda. There, O best of kings, he saw that [being] with his weapon drawn back to his ear as desired, with one foot tucked in, and with a steady gaze.
Then that Blessed One, though peaceful, was filled with grief for his beloved; seeing him standing before him, he became especially enraged.
O King, from the third eye of him who was overcome by anger, a great flame issued forth, by which he was reduced to ashes.
O King, having reached that mountain slope with his bow and arrow, Śaṅkara attained a state of bliss that was bounded by his wrath. || 13 ||

Worshipped by the gods, he went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains. When the Mind-born (Kāma) had been consumed, his devoted wife Rati, wretched and overwhelmed by grief for her husband, lamented piteously.

Then, O lord of men, having gathered wood and prepared a funeral pyre, that woman, distressed by grief for her husband, ascended the blazing pyre; at that moment, the illustrious lady heard a voice coming from the sky.
The voice said: "O daughter, do not act rashly; remain steadfast in austerity, O beautiful one. You shall obtain a husband even more desirable than Kāma, through the grace of the gratified Śambhu."

Having heard those words, that woman of slender waist then rose up; she propitiated the god day and night, unwearied, through vows, gifts, recitations, burnt offerings, fasts, and other such practices.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara was pleased with her and said: "Speak, O auspicious lady, whatever boon resides in your heart. (18)
Rati said: "O Lord, O Blessed One, O Creator of the World, if you are pleased with me, let my beloved Kāma be born again as my husband, with his limbs uninjured. (19)
When these words were spoken by her, he appeared at that very moment; O Great King, he was as joyful as one who has just awakened from sleep, his form being exactly like that.
A most enchanting bow made of sugarcane stalks, equipped with flower-arrows and adorned with a string consisting of rows of bees.
Then, filled with delight, he prostrated before Maheśvara; and being permitted by him, he returned to his own task.
Having seen the greatness of Śiva and having conceived faith, O best of kings, he installed Śiva on the mountain known as Arbuda.
O Great King, whether it be a woman or a man, upon seeing this, one shall not encounter misfortune for seven future births.
Thus have I explained to you, as you asked me, the greatness of Kāmeśvara and the burning away of desire in full detail.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kāmeśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya, where in former times penance was performed by the high-souled Mārkaṇḍa.
In ancient times, there was a brahmin named Mṛkaṇḍa who was firm in his vows; in the latter part of his life, he had a son born to him who was exceedingly handsome.
Complete with all the auspicious marks, peaceful, and possessing a radiance like the sun; then, after some time had passed, O King, he was in that hermitage.
A certain wise Brāhmaṇa, an expert in the science of physiognomy (sāmudra-vid), arrived; meanwhile, that five-year-old boy was playing. || 4 ||
Having gazed for a long time at the tips of his nose and the crest of his topknot, he suddenly laughed; Mṛkaṇḍu indeed perceived him.
Then he said, "O twice-born one, my son has been seen by you for a long time. Thereupon, [the other] laughed again; tell me, what is the reason for this? (6)
When that best of brahmins was questioned repeatedly by Mṛkaṇḍu, he, out of deference to him, reported the matter to him exactly as it was.
O best of the twice-born, by whatever marks are upon the body of this boy, a man shall indeed become undecaying and immortal through them.
"In six months, death will surely come for this child; for this reason, O best of the twice-born, I laughed. Never before have I spoken an untruth, even toward my enemies. (9)
