Pulastya said: Having spoken thus and having stayed there for the night, that wise man, permitted by Mṛkaṇḍu, departed for his desired destination.
O King, Mṛkaṇḍu, having learned that his son’s lifespan was exhausted, though he was only five years old, performed his initiation ceremony with great distress.
"O son, you must always offer salutations to whomever you see before you who is endowed with learning and Vedic study. (12)
Thereupon, the religious student (brahmacārī) carried out his father’s command with particular care.
Whether he saw a child, an old man, or a youth, he would bow with humility before every such person, treating each as a Brahmin.
Then, after some time, the Seven Sages, devoted to pilgrimage, arrived in the vicinity of his hermitage.
Then, O King, having gone quickly to them, the boy, endowed with humility, paid homage to all of them in due order.
"May you live long," said those who were intent on his welfare; and having dismissed the boy, they departed for their desired destination.
Among them was one named Aṅgiras, endowed with divine knowledge; by him, O scorcher of enemies, the boy was observed with subtle vision.
Then, with a touch of wonder, he said to all those sages: "This boy has not been described by you as being long-lived. (19)
"This prince will meet his death on the fifth day; therefore, O best of the twice-born, it is not fitting for our word to become untrue. (20)
"O King, let such a policy be enacted so that he may become long-lived. Then those sages, O monarch, became afraid of their false statement.
Then, taking that child with them, they went to the world of Brahmā; having seen the four-faced one there, the lords of sages paid him homage.
Immediately after them, he was saluted by that boy; and that boy was addressed by Brahmā: "May you be long-lived. (23)
Then, O best of kings, the Seven Sages, joyful in their hearts, spoke to those foremost of munis who were comfortably seated and rested.
Brahmā said: "What is your business? From where have you come here?"
The sages said: While wandering over the surface of the earth in the course of a pilgrimage, we indeed went to the sacred sites on the mountain named Arbuda.
Then, having arrived swiftly from afar, they were saluted by this boy; he was then addressed in many ways: "May you live long! [But] O Lord, on the fifth day his death will also come to pass.
O Four-faced One, O Lord, please do something so that we, along with you, shall not become untruthful on his account. (28)
Then Brahmā, his soul filled with joy upon seeing that young sage, said: "By my grace, this boy shall live for the duration of a kalpa. (29)
Then those sages, being delighted, took him and set out toward their home from the world of Brahmā, after having paid homage to the four-faced one.
Then his father, Mṛkaṇḍa, the best of sages, together with his wife, lamented there, deeply afflicted by grief.
"Alas, my son, my son!"—thus the one who is fond of dharma wept piteously; "Why have you set out upon this long path without even taking leave of me? (32)
"How can one who has fallen under the power of death not perform the duties that ought to be done? O son, being without you, I shall not live by any means. (33)
While he was thus lamenting in many ways, O best of kings, a boy arrived at that place where he had previously been stationed.
Then that boy set forth with a joyful inner soul; and seeing him on the path, O dear one, his father too became exceedingly delighted.

Having placed him on his lap, he asked the reason for his long absence; thereupon, he related everything regarding the conduct of the sage, as well as his vision of the world of Brahmā and the boon from the lotus-born one.
The boy said: "O father, I have been made ageless and immortal by the Self-born One himself; therefore, let this mental fever of yours for my sake truly pass away. (37)
Therefore, having established a beautiful hermitage on Arbuda, the best of mountains, I shall likewise propitiate the four-faced one (Brahmā).
Having heard those words of his son, which flowed like nectar, that twice-born Mṛkaṇḍu, filled with joy, spoke these words to him: || 39 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya also, having gone quickly to the beautiful Mount Arbuda, performed extensive penance while meditating upon the Lord Pitāmaha.

O King, whoever performs the libation for the ancestors specifically on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa at that holy hermitage, shall undoubtedly obtain the entire fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice. || 41 ||
O King, he who gratifies the best of Brahmins there by means of the Ṛṣi-yoga attains a long residence in the world of Brahmā.
Whoever performs a bath there, endowed with perfect faith, for him no fear of untimely death shall ever arise anywhere in his lineage. (43)

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Mārkaṇḍeya’s Hermitage," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 41 ||
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the supreme sin-destroying Liṅga, established by the sage Uddālaka and renowned throughout the world.
When that [liṅga] is touched, or seen, or especially worshipped, a man shall be liberated from all diseases and attain the state of a householder.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 3 ||

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Uddālakeśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to Siddhaliṅga, which bestows perfect success; it is a liṅga established by the Siddhas that destroys all sins.
Therein lies a beautiful pool filled with perfectly pure water; a man who bathes there is completely liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O King, whatever desire a man contemplates while bathing there, he necessarily attains it; and at the end, he reaches the supreme goal.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Siddheśvara," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Gaja-tīrtha, where in former times penance was performed by the elephants of the quarters whose souls were purified.
O King, by supporting the burden of the earth along with others such as Airāvata and his kin, a man who bathes there properly obtains the fruit of gifting an elephant.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Gaja-tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: From there, one should go to Devakhāta, an exceedingly meritorious and supreme tīrtha, whose fame was established by all the gods themselves.

O King, he who performs a śrāddha ceremony there, especially on the new moon day when the sun has entered Virgo, shall attain the supreme state; he truly delivers his ancestors, even those who have fallen into a miserable rebirth.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Śrī Devakhāta," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 45 ||

Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Vyāseśvara, which was indeed established by Vyāsa. By beholding it, a mortal becomes wise, intelligent, and pure for seven future births, according to the word of Vyāsa. (1)

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vyāsatīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the perfectly complete hermitage of Gautama, where in former times penance was performed by the high-souled Gautama.
In ancient times, there was a sage named Gautama who was supremely righteous; he propitiated Maheśvara, the God of gods, with devotion.
O King, as he was propitiating [the Lord] with devotion, a great *liṅga* of the Supreme Maheśvara burst through the surface of the earth and rose up.
At that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke: "Worship this great liṅga which has appeared through your devotion; choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your heart."
Gautama said: "O Lord Śambhu, Master of the Universe, if you are pleased with me, O Prabhū, you should always maintain your presence here in this hermitage."
May he who beholds you with true devotion go to the world of Brahmā.
The voice from the sky said: "O best of brahmins, whoever shall behold me here on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, he shall attain the supreme goal."
Having spoken thus, O Lord of the Earth, the voice then ceased. There is another sacred pool there, filled with water; a man who bathes therein immediately delivers his entire lineage.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there, especially on the day of the new moon, will certainly obtain the entire fruit of a śrāddha performed at Gayā. || 9 ||
In that regard, the preeminent sages praise the gift of sesame seeds; O King, by such a gift one shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are sesame seeds.
During the pilgrimage to Arbuda-Gautamī when Jupiter is situated in Leo, on a Monday coinciding with the new moon day, one obtains twice the fruit of six pilgrimages to the Godāvarī.
Sixty thousand years [of merit] from bathing in the Bhāgīrathī are obtained by a single bath in the Godāvarī when Jupiter is situated in Leo.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gautamāśrama Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eleven thousand verses.
Pulastya said: One should go to that unsurpassed holy site, Kulasaṃtāraṇa, where a man who bathes properly delivers his entire lineage.
O best of kings, a man endowed with faith may, through giving at that place, rescue ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as well. || 2 ||
In former times, there was a king named Aprastuta who was a doer of evil; he possessed neither generosity, nor knowledge, nor meditation, nor virtuous conduct.
While he ruled, there was never any happiness for the people; he was constantly fond of others' wives and devoted to severe punishment.
Whether by just means or unjust means, he who accumulates wealth causes innocent people to suffer; such a man is the worst of evildoers.
Then, having reached old age, he still did not attain tranquility; however, after some time, he was exhorted by his ancestors, who, being deeply distressed, approached him while he was fast asleep.
The ancestors said: "We are of pure conduct, eternally devoted to dharma, characterized by charity, sacrifice, and austerity, and likewise intent upon our own wives."

"O disgrace to your lineage, by your own deeds you have reached heaven as is fitting; yet, having encountered you, a wicked son, we have now arrived at hell. Therefore, perform some auspicious rite and deliver us all."
"O evil-souled one, by your actions these people have resorted to hell; ten others shall go to hell, and you likewise shall become one among them in the future."
Having spoken thus, all those ancestors, being deeply distressed, went once again to hell; and that king also regained his consciousness.
Then, having fallen into distress as he recollected his father’s words, he wept upon rising in the morning; his wife addressed him.
Indumatī said: "For what reason, O tiger among kings, do you weep so loudly? Is all well with your kingdom, your body, or your city? (12)
The king said: "O Goddess, today at the end of my dream, I beheld my father and indeed my grandfather; I saw them, O Goddess, as well as their elder paternal ancestors, all of them distressed. (13)
I have been reproached by all of them for such deeds as these; through our unrighteous and other such actions, we have reached this terrible hell. (14)
Furthermore, ten others will go there, as will those of the future and you yourself; therefore, having performed auspicious deeds, deliver us from this miserable state.
O lady of excellent complexion, having been addressed thus by my ancestors, I awoke; remembering those words in my heart, I fell into a state of great sorrow.
Indumatī said: "O Great King, this which you have been told by your grandfathers is true; I do not recall any virtuous deed performed by you in the past. (17)
O King, just as fathers cross over [to heaven] by obtaining a good son, so too do they go to hell because of a bad son; there is no doubt in this matter. (18)
Therefore, having summoned the best of Brahmins who are experts in the treatises on dharma, consult them and perform that which is for the welfare of your ancestors along with yourself.

Then that king summoned numerous Brahmins who were knowers of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and experts in the Dharmaśāstras; accompanied by his wife, he spoke with humility to those well-wishers.
The King said: O best of the twice-born, by what action do fathers situated in hell go to heaven, being delivered by a virtuous son? Please explain this clearly. (21)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Indra among kings, by performing the Pitṛmedha sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, those dwelling in hell go to heaven, even if they have been great sinners. (22)
The king said: "Let all the twice-born ones initiate me, who have undertaken this vow, for that purpose. Whatever must be done here, let all of that indeed be told. (23)
Thus addressed by the lord of kings, those truthful Brahmins spoke in their entirety to the monarch regarding what was required for the sacrificial rite.
O best of kings, initiation should be received after first performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the sake of purifying the body; only then will it be conducive to spiritual welfare.
O King, since you have been of such sinful conduct from your very childhood, you have committed innumerable transgressions; therefore, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
O best of kings, when you have been consecrated by all the holy fords (tīrthas), you will then become fit for the sacrificial rite through expiation; not otherwise.
There are holy fords on the surface of the earth beginning with Prabhāsa; you must go to all of them and perform your ablutions there with a concentrated mind.

Go with your mind to the difficult places while bestowing unsurpassed gifts; by that, even any inauspiciousness arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin shall perish—O King, that which does not depart for men on earth through bathing at sacred fords and other such means.
Pulastya said: Having heard the words of the brahmins, that king, filled with faith, became intent on a pilgrimage to sacred fords and wandered over the earth.
Restrained and moderate in diet, giving gifts in abundance, he established his son Vasu, whose prowess was truth, upon the throne. (31)
Then, after some time, that king, in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, went indeed to Arbuda, where the water is pure.
There he performed his bath with a mind purified by faith; and as soon as he had bathed in that very body of water, || 33 ||
The fierce ancestors, liberated from hell, were filled with great joy; thereafter, they dwelt in divine celestial chariots, adorned with divine garlands and garments.
They all said to him: "O son, we have now been delivered by you; and by the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha), ten others shall likewise be saved. (35)
And because, O best of kings, your lineage has been rescued by you, my son, through bathing and the libation of water at this sacred ford, therefore [your] self [is purified]. || 36 ||
"This shall become a sacred ford (tīrtha) named Kulasaṃtāraṇa; therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, by the power of this sacred ford, shall go to heaven along with us in this very body. (37)
Pulastya said: Thus addressed, that lord of kings, whose body was then endowed with divine luster, ascended that celestial chariot and went to heaven along with them.
This power of the royal sage, the savior of his lineage, has been fully described by me to you; what more do you wish to ask? (39)
Yayāti said: "What was the power of that king, and how did he, though possessed of such sin, go to heaven in his own body? This is a great curiosity of mine. (40)
Pulastya said: O best of kings, when the full moon coincides with the vyatīpāta yoga, that king who bathes there attains supreme and great merit.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Kulasaṃtāraṇa Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: One should then go to Rāmatīrtha, which is meritorious and frequented by sages; for a mortal who bathes there, the destruction of sin occurs.
And there was supreme satisfaction for the ancestors as long as the dissolution of all beings; formerly there was Rāma Bhārgava, the best among all wielders of weapons. (2)
Having previously performed austerities with the desire for the destruction of his enemies, he was then granted that supreme weapon named Pāśupata.
When three hundred years had passed, Mahādeva, gratified by his asceticism, said, "I am the giver of boons," and he chose the destruction of his enemies as his boon.
Then he gave him that supreme weapon named Pāśupata, by the mere remembrance of which the destruction of enemies is brought about. || 5 ||
And the bull-bannered god, smiling, spoke these words: "O mighty-armed son of Jamadagni, listen to my supreme speech. (6)
"O scion of Bhrigu's line, endowed with this weapon, you shall become invincible to all embodied beings through my grace; of this there is no doubt."
This meritorious reservoir of water shall become famous throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, as "Rāmatīrtha" by my grace.
Those who, being composed in mind, shall perform the Śrāddha ceremony here when the month of Kārttika has arrived, conjoined with the lunar mansion Kṛttikā on the full moon day; || 9 ||
The entire fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice shall belong to them without exception; likewise, O King, there shall be the destruction of their enemies and eternal residence in the heavenly realms.
Pulastya said: Having spoken thus, Mahādeva then vanished from sight; Rāma, too, afflicted by grief for his father, began to slaughter the Kṣatriyas.
There, filled with great joy, he gratified the ancestors twenty-one times; for when Jamadagni had passed away, that high-souled one had made a solemn vow.
O lord of men, seeing the wounds upon his mother’s body caused by the various weapons of the brahmins when their assembly had gathered, [he was overcome with grief] twenty-one times. (13)
"Since my father, a twice-born ascetic, was slain by Kṣatriyas while he was not even fighting, therefore, having performed [the rite] twenty-one times," (14)
"O King, I shall give the earth, devoid of Kṣatriyas, as water for my father's libation; all that came to pass for him through the greatness of the sacred ford."
Therefore, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony there with every effort; especially so for a Kṣatriya who desires the destruction of his enemies. (16)

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rāmatīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: From there, one should go to Koṭitīrtha, which destroys all sins, where, O King, ten million holy sites (tīrthas) were produced effortlessly.
O King, when the terrible Kali age shall prevail upon the earth, all people will become like Mlecchas; through contact with them, there will be a desecration of the sacred fords.
There were three and a half crores of holy sites belonging to those who dwell upon the earth; one crore of them then resided on the mountain known as Arbuda.

O King, there is likewise ten million [sacred sites] at Puṣkara and at Kurukṣetra; at Vārāṇasī, half a crore is praised by the gods together with Indra. O King, all the gods, including Indra, protect these places.
Whenever they are afflicted by fear on all sides from contact with Mlecchas, these sacred fords mentioned [above] quickly take refuge in these very places.
Three crores of holy sites (tīrthas) were produced there upon the surface of the earth, together with half a crore more, and they are the removers of all sins.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath there, especially on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya.
In that place, O King, all acts such as bathing, as well as recitation and fire-offerings, become ten millionfold by his grace; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Koṭitīrtha," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Candrodbheda, a holy site that removes the sins of men and was created by the Lord of the Night.
O King, when Rāhu, who had incurred the enmity of Viṣṇu, had his head severed by Viṣṇu during the eclipse of the moon and the sun, he made a vow.
Then, filled with fear and perceiving the Daitya to be invincible as he was intent on consuming the nectar, Candra went to Arbuda.
There, having split the peak of the mountain and made an excellent opening, he entered into its midst and performed a most difficult penance.
Then, after a long time, Maheśvara was pleased with him and said, "Blessings to you; choose whatever boon resides in your heart."
Candra said: "O best of gods, Rāhu has vowed to seize me. He is powerful, difficult to overcome by nature, and the son of Siṃhikā."
"O best of gods, that nectar has now been consumed by him; moreover, that unassailable Rāhu has seized me in his midst."
While the nectar was being drunk by the gods who had previously been defeated, that Dānava arrived, assuming a divine form.
Rāhu drank the nectar; therefore, his head became immortal and free from death, and that nectar became inexhaustible, while the head remained a source of terror to the gods.
Then the gods offered conciliation, and he was established in the midst of the planets; when the planet was thus assigned to us, fear entered into me. (10)

Out of fear of him, O best of gods, this deep chasm was made by piercing the peak of the mountain for the sake of performing penance, O most excellent of deities; therefore, O destroyer of desire, grant me your grace in this matter.

The Blessed One said: "That one of great strength, Rāhu, who is invincible and cannot be slain by any of the gods, will surely seize you while you are overcome with anger. However, O Lord of the Night, I shall provide a remedy for you."
When the eclipse of you has arrived, people in the world, endowed with perfect well-being, will perform rites such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts. (13)
Because of them, not even the slightest distress shall befall you; for them, their performed deed shall become an inexhaustible merit.

"When your grasping [of me] has occurred through my word, there will be no doubt that because you have split this mountain peak for the sake of penance, it shall become known in the world as the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Candrodbheda. (15)
When the time for your eclipse arrives, whoever performs an ablution here shall not be born again in this world.
Or whoever performs a ritual bath on a Monday and visits that place, O Moon, his residence shall certainly be in your world.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hara vanished from that place; and Candra also, O best of kings, departed for his own abode filled with joy.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Candrodbheda Tīrtha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 51 ||
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the great peak of Īśāna, where Gaurī performed her most meritorious penance, which is renowned throughout the world.
By the mere sight of whom a person is liberated from sin and attains great good fortune for seven future births.
Yayāti said: O Lord of Sages, at what time was this penance performed by the goddess there, and for what purpose? You should explain this great curiosity to me. (3)
Pulastya said: Listen, O King, to this divine and wonderful story renowned throughout the world, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
Long ago, perceiving that [the world] was attached to Gaurī, the gods, including Indra, overcome with fear, gathered in a secluded place and held a consultation.
If the vigor of the Three-eyed One should fall upon the field of Gaurī, our downfall—and indeed that of the entire world—will surely come to pass.
Therefore, let us go for the sake of destroying that continuity.
Having thus consulted together, those gods went to Mount Kailāsa; however, they were all then forbidden by Nandin, as they had not arrived at the appointed time.
Nandin said: "The Lord Rudra is stationed in solitude together with Gaurī; therefore, all you hosts of gods, go to your own abodes."
Then all the hosts of gods, having deceived that group, dispatched Vāyu there and spoke these words secretly: ||| 10 ||
"O Vāyu, go and say to Bhava: 'You must not procreate. O Lord, the hosts of gods, afflicted by fear, entreat you thus. (11)
Then the Wind-god, having gone swiftly, stood where Maheśvara was and loudly proclaimed those words which had been spoken by the inhabitants of the celestial abode.
Then the Blessed Lord Śarva, filled with supreme shame, rose up leaving Gaurī and said, "So be it."
Then Gaurī, afflicted by great sorrow, cursed the inhabitants of the celestial abode.
Gaurī said: "Since I have been rendered childless by the assembled gods, therefore they too shall be deprived of progeny."
"Since you have arrived at this place devoid of people while still possessed of breath, therefore you shall forever be liberated from the body. (16)
Having spoken thus, O King, she who was intent on her husband’s anger then left his side and went to Arbuda, the best of mountains.
For the sake of the meaning of the *Sūtra*, she performed austerities with her speech, body, and mind restrained; then, at the end of a thousand years, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [appeared].
Together with Indra and the other gods, he approached her presence. Then Śakra, with a humble soul, addressed that goddess.
This Lord Śiva has arrived at your side out of his own modesty; he does not come forward further, so let him be propitiated by you—be magnanimous.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the Gods, having been abandoned by my husband in accordance with your word, I shall go to his side after obtaining a son. (21)
Knowing her firm resolve, the Lord himself arrived and, smiling, spoke these words: "Let grace be bestowed."
O Goddess of gods, O fair-faced one, by granting me your sight and by speaking with me, I must perform what is beneficial for the gods in all circumstances, O Pārvatī. (23)

O Goddess of the Suras, you were released by him at an improper time, and he brought his pleasure to an end; for that reason, O Sovereign of the Gods, he undertook this endeavor for the sake of a son.
Therefore, O beloved, by my grace, a son born from your own body will undoubtedly be yours on the fourth day.
O Goddess of the Suras, whatever form you shall assume by taking the impurity from your own body, it shall become exactly like that; of this there is no doubt.
He is the bestower of perfection upon the hosts of gods and especially upon the Daityas, as well as upon all mortals; he assumes many forms.
Thus addressed by the Three-eyed One, the Queen of the Gods was thoroughly satisfied; filled with joy, she engaged in conversation with her husband.

When the fourth day arrived, O King, Śivā bathed; then, taking the ointment produced from the massage paste, she indeed out of curiosity fashioned Vināyaka with four arms, according to the word of Hara.
Then, having regained life by the word of Hara, O great king, that leader was specially established upon the earth; from that time forth, he became renowned among all mortals.
The illustrious Vināyaka became the one to be worshipped by all the inhabitants of the three worlds; indeed, he became the leader (vināyaka) of all the foremost gods. || 31 ||
Then all the hosts of gods, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of the Goddess, granted him divine boons and spoke to the Goddess as well, O King.
The gods said: "O Goddess, this son of yours shall be the leader of us all; when he is worshipped first, only then may worship be accepted by the deities. (33)
O auspicious one, through your service, this beautiful peak of the mountain shall become a remover of all sins for men, even by its mere sight.
Those who shall perform their ablutions here in this most meritorious reservoir of water will go to the supreme abode, which is free from old age and death.
Those who, being composed in mind, observe [this vow] on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, shall remain endowed with happiness for seven future births.
Having spoken thus, all the gods then departed for their own abodes; the Lord also, accompanied by the Goddess, went to Mount Kailāsa.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Peak of Īśāna," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thence one should go to the holy site of Brahmapada, renowned throughout the three worlds, where in former times a footprint was placed by Brahmā, the creator of the world.
In ancient times, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the most pure sages, were concentrated there on the beautiful Arbuda mountain.
O King, during the pilgrimage to Acaleśvara, they were filled with sublime devotion; then all those sages spoke to the god Pitāmaha.
The sages said: "O Grandfather, we are all weary of constant observances, burnt offerings, vows, ritual baths, and fasts."
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, you ought to grant us some true instruction by which we may cross the difficult ocean of saṃsāra.

Tell us how the attainment of heaven is achieved through services performed unasked, through recitations and fire-offerings that are very difficult to perform, as well as through mantras, vows, and gifts.
Having heard those words of theirs, the god, filled with compassion, reflected for a long time and then smiled slightly.
Then, having left his own abode on the delightful mountain slope, Brahmā addressed all the sages with gentle words: ||| 8 ||
Brahmā said: "This Mahāpada is beautiful and the destroyer of all sins; let all the sages touch it, and then you shall go to the state of ultimate bliss."
Without [the need for] bathing, giving, vows, fire-offerings, recitations, and the like—for the benefit of all the worlds—I have established this auspicious state.
When this foot has been placed by me, thousands of worlds shall go [to heaven]; let all the sages and even the gods touch my foot.
In this matter, only one unwavering faith must be cultivated; and he who is endowed with such faith, O lords of sages, shall truly attain this state. (12)
When the full moon day of the month of Kārtika arrives, he shall worship [it] with water, various fruits, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having fed the Brahmins with sweet food according to his ability, he will go to my world, which is very difficult to attain; of this there is no doubt. (14)
Pulastya said: Then all the hosts of sages, endowed with perfect faith, having worshipped that place, departed for the world of Brahmā. || 15 ||
Therefore, O best of men, with every effort you should properly worship the venerable foot of the Grandfather (Brahmā) with faith, for it bestows heaven. (16)
O King, another great curiosity was seen, most wonderful, concerning that footprint, hearing which a great amazement arises. (17)
O King, even when the Kṛta Yuga had arrived with its full extent and breadth, O monarch, the number of those of white complexion could not be calculated by human beings.
Then, when the Tretā Yuga arrived, it was seen to be red in color, clearly manifest, endowed with calculation, and honored by all the worlds.
In the Dvāpara age, that [liṅga] appears as Kapila and of small measure; in the Kali age, it is black and very subtle on the lovely mountain slope.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Origin of Brahmapada," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 53 ||
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to Tripuṣkara, which is dear to the Lotus-born (Brahmā); it was brought by Brahmā to the mountain named Arbuda.
O lord of men, formerly, while Vasiṣṭha’s sacrificial session was underway on that mountain, the supreme gods, beginning with Brahmā, arrived there. || 2 ||

O Great King, a vow was made by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest: "As long as I shall remain in this world of men, so long will I, with a concentrated mind, worship the twilight at Tripuṣkara whenever the time of twilight arrives. (3)
At that very time, as Vasiṣṭha was setting out toward Puṣkara for the sake of the twilight rites, the Lotus-born One spoke to him.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O best of gods, the time for the ritual action has arrived at this sacrifice; O Lord, it will never reach completion without you."

Therefore, O Lotus-born One, bring Tripuṣkara to this very place. Then, O Lord of the Gods, having performed the twilight worship there once more, O Lord of Devas, O Ocean of Compassion, assume the office of Brahmā at this sacrificial session.

Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, meditated and summoned the three Puṣkara lakes—the eldest, the middle, and the youngest—and they arrived at that most meritorious reservoir of water.
From that time forward, Tripuṣkara has been established in this Arbuda mountain.
In that regard, for one who, being composed in mind, performs ritual bathing and gives gifts on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, there are eternal worlds.
And to its north lies the excellent Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa; by performing ablutions, giving gifts, and other rites there, one attains an auspicious state.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Tripuṣkara," in the third section (Arbudakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the auspicious and meritorious Rudrahrada, where a man who bathes with devotion shall attain the status of a lord of the Gaṇas.
Formerly, after slaying the Daitya Andhaka along with his hosts, the bull-bannered Lord bathed there and created a lake; thus it became known as Rudrahada.
O Great King, for that man who performs a ritual bath there on the fourteenth day, his merit shall be equal to that arising from all sacred fords.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudra-hrada," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Guheśvara, the Liṅga situated within a cave that was worshipped by the Siddhas in ancient times.
Whatever desire a person contemplates while performing worship, O King, he obtains that very thing; if free from desire, he shall attain liberation.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Guheśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: O best of kings, one should then go to Aviyuktavana, by seeing which a man shall never at any time be separated from his desires.
There, O King, Śacī first entered, filled with sorrow, after the kingdom of the high-souled Indra had been seized by Nahuṣa. || 2 ||
By its power, O King, Śatakratu was restored even though he had been deprived [of his senses]; then, indeed, a boon was granted to that forest by her.
Whether it be a man or a woman, separated from their loved ones here in this auspicious forest, they shall dwell alone for a single night.
O King, by that [act], he incurs attachment once again just as I did; he dwells with his loved ones for a single night.
The most excellent Brāhmaṇas praise the granting of fruits there, especially for those who are barren, since one may thereby obtain the fruit of a son.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Avi-yukta-kṣetra," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 57 ||
Pulastya said: O King, one should then go to Umāmāheśvara, which bestows great merit and was established in former times by Dhundhumāra, who was filled with devotion.
O lord of men, he who worships the divine couple there with devotion shall not encounter misfortune for seven future births.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Umāmāheśvara Tīrtha," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 58 ||

Pulastya said: Thereafter, O King, one should go to the Tīrtha of great splendor that destroys all sins. Having bathed there, a man is certainly endowed with brilliance; for in ancient times, Śakra fell into extreme dejection due to the fire of Brahman-slaughter.
Deprived of splendor, lacking in luster, and filled with a foul odor, he was abandoned by all the gods and fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Then the Lord of the Gods questioned Bṛhaspati, the best of the twice-born: "O Blessed One, how may my increase of splendor be restored as it was before?"
Bṛhaspati said: "O best of gods, perform a pilgrimage on the surface of the earth; without visiting sacred fords (tīrtha), an increase in your splendor will certainly not occur."

Then, O lord of men, having wandered through many sacred fords (tīrthas), Śakra reached Arbuda in due course; seeing a body of water there, he bathed, and being exhausted, that one of great power lay down to rest. || 5 ||
Freed from the foul odor and surrounded by the gods, he spoke these words with a smile: "Listen, all you deities! (6)

Those who always perform their ablutions here when the festival of Indra’s elevation arrives at the end of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, shall attain the supreme goal and shall always be endowed with great beauty in birth after birth.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Mahaujas Tīrtha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, O best of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Jambū-tīrtha; having bathed there properly, a person shall obtain the desired fruit.
O best of kings, [this concerns] the sacred fords originating in Jambūdvīpa.
In ancient times, there was a Kṣatriya named Nimi, born of the Solar dynasty; in the latter stage of his life, he went to Mount Arbuda.
Having undertaken the vow of fasting unto death, he remained there with a concentrated mind; then, hosts of sages arrived at his side by the thousands.
They delivered meritorious discourses on the great royal sages, the ancient celestial sages, and likewise other high-souled beings.
Then, at the conclusion of the discourse, a certain excellent sage named Lomaśa proclaimed the majesty arising from all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O King, having heard that, Nimi became extremely dejected because he had not previously performed an immersion in a sacred ford.
Then he said to that brahmin: "O best of the twice-born, there is a certain means by which the fruit of all the sacred fords (tīrthas) may be obtained."
Lomaśa said: "O King, compassion has arisen in me upon seeing you so deeply distressed; therefore, for the sake of your pilgrimage, I shall do what is pleasing to you."
And right here, O King of kings, I shall bring forth all the sacred fords originating from Jambūdvīpa by the power of my mantra; of this there is no doubt.
"Perform your ablutions, O Great King, while all these [deities] are united here in this meritorious reservoir; I speak this truth to you. (10)
Having spoken thus, that brahmin-sage, composed in meditation, entered into dhyāna; thereupon, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) arrived there at that very moment.
And for the sake of a sign, O royal sage, a jambu tree appeared there; the king performed his ablutions in that eternal place, which embodies all sacred bathing sites.
And immediately after bathing at that sacred ford (tīrtha), he went to heaven with his physical body; from that time forward, that tīrtha has been remembered as Jambū-tīrtha.
The great sages declare that for the man who performs a śrāddha there when the sun has entered Virgo, his merit is equal to that of Gayāśīrṣa.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Jambū-tīrtha," in the third section (Arbuda-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: O King, one should then go to the highly meritorious Gaṅgādhara, which possesses pure water, where the Gaṅgā was held by him as she was falling from the surface of the sky.
O King, she was summoned with haste by Hara, the god of gods, who had assumed the form of Acaleśvara; that which was previously told to you [concerning her]—[that is what occurred].
Whoever performs a ritual bath there on the eighth day with a concentrated mind shall go to the supreme abode, which is very difficult even for the gods to attain.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gaṅgādhara Tīrtha," in the third Arbuda-khaṇḍa of the seventh Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: Thereafter, one should go to the Kaṭeśvara Liṅga fashioned by Gaurī, as well as the other, Gaṅgeśvara, which was created by Gaṅgā herself. || 1 ||
O king of kings, in ancient times a dispute arose between Umā and Gaṅgā regarding their respective good fortune; thereupon, Gaurī spoke as follows.
She by whom Śambhu has been fully worshipped shall surely soon behold him; she will certainly become possessed of good fortune in both worlds.
Having been addressed thus, Gaṅgā then went quickly to that mountain and searched for the Liṅga; after a long time, she found it.
Then, O Great King, having seen the beautiful mountain ridge in the form of a linga, Gaurī worshipped it at that time.
Then Maheśvara, being pleased because she was endowed with perfect faith, granted her a vision and said, "I am the giver of boons."
Gaurī said: "O Lord, out of jealousy toward my co-wife, this Liṅga was fashioned by me; therefore, its name in the world shall be Kaṭeśvara."

Any woman who has been abandoned by her husband and is distressed by the suffering caused by a co-wife shall, merely by the sight of this [liṅga], become free from fever; she will likewise be endowed with sons and good fortune, and hold her husband as dear as her own life. || 8 ||
O Lord of Men, when Gaṅgā propitiated the God in this very manner, He likewise granted her a boon; therefore, those two Liṅgas should be visited by you.
Especially for women, this [rite] destroys the faults of rival wives; it constantly bestows happiness and good fortune, as well as granting the desires of men. || 10 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaṭeśvara and Gaṅgeśvara," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pulastya said: O great king, I have thus related to you in brief all this concerning the majesty of Arbuda, about which you questioned me.
Even in hundreds of years, their number could not be fully recounted; for here there are countless sacred fords and holy shrines, and at every step dwellings have been constructed by the great seers.
O Lord of the Earth, there is no sacred ford, no spiritual perfection, no tree, no river, and no lord of the gods where his presence does not abide.
O Great King, those who dwell on the most beautiful Arbuda mountain are surely performers of meritorious deeds; they do not dwell in the triple heaven.
O King, what purpose is there in the life of that dull-witted man, what use have his riches or his prayers, if he does not behold Mount Arbuda on all sides?
Even those who are insects, moths, beasts, birds, and wild animals—whether born from sweat, born from eggs, born from sprouts, or born from a womb.
O Great King, those who die there—whether free from desire or even out of desire—attain union with Śiva, which is devoid of old age and death.
O great king, whoever constantly listens to this Purāṇa endowed with faith attains the fruit of the pilgrimage to Arbuda.
Therefore, one who desires success for oneself both in this world and in the next should undertake a pilgrimage there with every effort. (9)

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Hearing of the Fruits of the Greatness of the Arbuda Section," in the third section, the Arbuda-khaṇḍa, of the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, how indeed shall we obtain Madhusūdana in this fierce age known as Kali, which is so crowded with many heretics?
When the three ages had passed away and the terrible Kali Yuga had arrived—a time when people are always devoted to the practice of dharma—[they wondered], "Where is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu? (2)
Sūta said: When the great king Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, had gone to heaven, the surface of the earth was oppressed by the burden of wicked kings.
When Janārdana himself had manifested in the house of Vasudeva for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods and for the removal of the earth's burden.
When the Lord had gone to Nandavraja, having dried up Pūtanā, having slain Tṛṇāvarta, and having overturned the cart; || 5 ||
When the serpent Kāliya had been subdued, Pralamba slain, Mount Govardhana held aloft, and Gokula protected; || 6 ||
When Indra had been consecrated by Surabhi and rendered free from pride, and when the god was intent on his sport with the Rāsa dance after the demon Keśin had been torn asunder; || 7 ||
When Hari had gone to Mathurā at the word of Akrūra, Kuvalayāpīḍa was slain and the king of wrestlers was killed.
While the gods and demons looked on, O King, having struck down the Bhoja monarch, Ugrasena was consecrated as the ruler of men in the city of the Yadus.
When the fierce army of Jarāsaṃdha and the Yavana had been slain on the earth, and when the Caidya had been struck down during that most excellent of sacrifices, the Rājasūya; || 10 ||
When the Bhārata war had ceased and the burden of the earth had been lightened, the Yādava clan was brought to Prabhāsa under the pretext of a pilgrimage.
But when the Yādava clan was ruined by mutual slaughter and extremely violent quarrels arising from their addiction to drinking liquor, [the Lord departed].
When Ananta had cast off his body right there and departed from the surface of the earth, Janārdana took his seat at the foot of an Aśvattha tree.
When his body was pierced by the hunter’s blows and his physical frame had been cast aside, the Lord remained established in His own abode, and Pārtha returned once more.
When the city of Yadu was flooded on all sides by the ocean, he then went to Śakraprastha and had a temple for Hari constructed there.
When the Dvāpara age had passed, mixed with both dharma and adharma, and when the most terrible age known as Kali arrived.

When the true Dharma was waning and unrighteousness was powerful; when the practice of dharma-rites had perished and [the world] was cast outside the teachings of the Vedas; when Dharma stood on only one foot and was devoid of the system of social classes and stages of life—(17)
In this agitated age, all the forest-dwelling sages—Garga, Cyavana, and Bhārgava—having come together, addressed one another.
Asita, Devala, Dhaumya, Kratu, and Uddālaka—these and many others then spoke to one another.
"Behold, O sages, all the quarters of the sky are pervaded by the Kali age; the subjects are being oppressed on all sides by bandits who run about everywhere. (20)
O best of sages, how can that Blessed Viṣṇu be attained by men who are devoted to unrighteousness and have cast aside truth and honesty?

"Who indeed will rescue those of us who have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence? In the Kali age, there is no appearance of that Madhusūdana who manifests in three ages; without that lotus-eyed one, how shall we fare in the Kali yuga? (22)
While those ascetics were thus reflecting in their distress, the sage Uddālaka then spoke these words there.
Uddālaka said: "O best of sages, as long as we are not tainted by the defects of the Kali age, let us go together to the abode of Brahmā, free from sin."
We ask Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world who stands firm in the Kali age: if Viṣṇu were not present in the Kali age along with Rudra and Brahmā, [what would become of us]? (25)
Without that lotus-eyed one, we shall abandon our own bodies; for who in this world will remain during the Kali Yuga without the Blessed Lord? (26)
Having heard those words of his, the sages of rigid vows exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and set out toward the presence of Brahmā.
Discoursing upon the story of Viṣṇu and describing his true nature, all the ascetics, filled with joy, proceeded to the presence of Brahmā.
Then they beheld the God seated upon the supreme throne, surrounded by the Pitāmahas and hosts of beings, both embodied and unembodied.
Having seen the four-faced god, they prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff; then, having bowed to the God of gods, they praised him with a hymn.
The sages said: Salutations to you, O lotus-born one, four-faced, imperishable, and immutable! Salutations to you, the creator of the universe; O Grandfather, let there be salutation to you! (31)
Thus praised by the sages, the lotus-born Brahmā, being well-pleased, honored those preeminent sages with water for the feet and the arghya offering, and questioned them.
Brahmā said: "O dear sons, tell me truly the purpose of your arrival. O highly fortunate ones, is all well with you—your sons, disciples, sacred fires, and kinsmen?"
The sages said: "By your grace, we have obtained the entire fruit of our asceticism, in that we behold you, the Lord and teacher of all the gods. (34)
Listen to this cause, O Śambhu: these have arrived in your presence after the three ages, beginning with Kṛta and ending with Dvāpara, have passed away. (35)
Now that the terrible Kali age has arrived, where on the surface of the earth is Viṣṇu, by seeing whom we shall attain supreme liberation, freed from all bonds? (36)
Brahmā said: "O best of the twice-born, the Lord is known by me through his forms such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others; yet I do not know the supreme form of Viṣṇu."
The sages said: "O dear one, if you do not know the whereabouts of Viṣṇu, we shall go to Prayāga and there cast off our bodies."
Brahmā said: "Do not fall into despair; I shall indeed instruct you for your benefit. Depart from here for Pātāla, where the best of Daityas resides. (39)
"Go to him and question Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas; O twice-born ones, he will know the location of Hari exactly as it is."
Having heard those words of that Brahmā, the Supreme Soul, and having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, those ascetics departed.
With delighted minds, they went along praising the best of the Daityas: "Blessed is this king of the Daityas, who knows Janārdana. (42)
Reflecting thus, those twice-born ones indeed reached Sutala.
Having gone there, they entered his excellent palace; seeing them from afar, Bali, the son of Virocana, then rose up and, together with Prahlāda, paid them due honor.
Having offered the madhuparka, a cow, and likewise the arghya water, he spoke with joined palms and a joyful inner soul.
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! The night has dawned clearly for me, since I behold you; tell me, what may I do for you? (46)
Thus honored by the king of the Daityas, those best of the twice-born then spoke with joyful hearts to the son of the lord of the Dānavas.
The sages said: "O Prahlāda, beloved of Hari, we have arrived here seeking a purpose; therefore, O mighty-armed one, may you be our savior from the ocean of worldly existence. (48)
O Daitya, how indeed shall we fare in this fierce age known as Kali, without Viṣṇu, the bestower of fearlessness upon those who are afraid? (49)
For in this age, eternal Dharma has been conquered by Adharma; Truth has been conquered by Untruth, and Brahmins have been conquered by Śūdras. || 50 ||
The paths of the Vedas have been conquered by the *viṭas*, and men have been conquered by women; even the Brāhmaṇas are being slain by those in the form of Mleccha kings. (51)
In this age when [the world] is mostly in turmoil and the system of castes and stages of life has vanished, yet the path of the Vedas remains undestroyed—where is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu? || 52 ||
Tell us that secret wherein the Blessed One is attained without knowledge, without meditation, and without the restraint of the senses. (53)
"O King of the Daityas, you are our friend and the one who shows us the way; O illustrious one, tell us where Keśava resides. (54)
Thus questioned by the foremost of the twice-born, that best of Daityas, with a joyful mind, bowed with devotion to all the Brāhmaṇas.
Having paid homage to the gods, to Brahmā, and to the Supreme Self, he, being endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, began to speak.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Questioning by the Great Sages Fearing the Kali Age Regarding the Lord’s Presence in the Kali Yuga in the Vicinity of Prahlāda, at the Word of Brahmā," in the Fourth Section on the Greatness of Dvārakā, within the Seventh Book, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 1 ||
Prahlāda said: "Among all beings—whether Daityas, Dānavas, or Rākṣasas—as well as among the gods and others, you are indeed the most worthy of worship."
With your permission and by the grace of Keśava, I shall indeed describe the manifestation of the Blessed One; listen.
It stands situated on the shore of the western ocean; it is the city formerly established by Kuśa, known as Kuśasthalī.
O Brahmins, where the Gomatī flows everywhere into the ocean, that city is celebrated among the Ānartas as Dvāravatī.
In that [city] dwells Hari, the soul of the universe and the granter of all desires, endowed with sixteen kalās and possessed of twelve forms.
That alone is the supreme abode, that alone is the supreme state; and blessed indeed is that Dvārakā where Madhusūdana resides.
Where Kṛṣṇa, four-armed and bearing the conch, discus, and mace resides, men shall attain liberation by going there in the Kali age.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Prahlāda, the best of sages, their minds filled with wonder, spoke to him.
The sages said: When the Yadu lineage had come to its end and the burden of the earth had been removed, Hari, the best of the Yādavas, departed for his own abode at Prabhāsa.
O Daitya, when Dvārāvatī has been submerged on all sides by the ocean, how is that Blessed One proclaimed to be there in the Kali age?
Tell me, O best of gods, how Viṣṇu remains upon the surface of the earth in the region of Ānarta; explain this in detail.
While King Ugrasena was ruling the earth, Kṛṣṇa adorned this city of the Yadus on all sides.
While Hari, the Lord of Ramā, who delights in beautiful women, was sporting, that best of the Yadus once sat in his assembly hall.
While various and manifold stories were being told, Uddhava related the news concerning the joy of the Yadus.
While on his journey, he encountered the sinless Durvāsas, who was staying on the bank of the Gomatī near Cakratīrtha.
Having heard that, the Lord Adhokṣaja, the omnipotent power of the universe, rose up suddenly and went to the house of Rukmiṇī with a joyful mind.
Having arrived, he said to the princess of Vidarbha: "This best of sages has arrived; he is the son of Atri, a man of great asceticism whose sins have been cleansed by penance. (17)
A Brahmin honored with hospitality will bestow great prosperity; for one in whose house there is no wife, the arrival of a worthy recipient is in vain.
"The gods and the ancestors do not accept his water offering; therefore, come, let us go to invite the son of Atri. (19)

Having said, "So be it," that virtuous goddess ascended the chariot. Having mounted the chariot together with Rukmiṇī, Hari, the Lord of Gods, went to the place where Durvāsas, the best of sages, was staying.
Having seen him blazing with ascetic power on the bank of the lord of rivers and streams, well-bathed before the Kāpālika by excellent showers of spray; ||| 21 ||
Having bowed with devotion, the Blessed One then inquired after his well-being; thereafter, Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Vidarbha, prostrated before him.
And Durvāsas, seeing that they had arrived for an audience, greeted them with a welcome and inquired after their welfare.
Durvāsas said: "O Kṛṣṇa, is all well everywhere? Where is your residence now? How many wives, wealth, and offspring do you have? Tell me this in detail. (24)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Brahmin, the ocean granted me a territory of twelve yojanas; while dwelling there, my city is made of gold.
There, by number, are nine hundred thousand palaces made of gold; through your grace, I dwell therein, exceedingly joyful and entirely free from fear.
Having heard those words of his, Durvāsas, his mind filled with wonder, laughed and replied to Madhusūdana.
Tell me, sir, how many of your followers dwell there, as well as the number of your queens, sons, and attendants. (28)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Brāhmaṇa, I have sixteen thousand and eight wives; among them, the daughter of the King of Vidarbha is my most beloved. (29)
O Sage, each one had ten sons and one daughter; thus, my retinue consists of fifty-six crores of Yadus.
"O Brahmin, the remaining classes have no known number. Having heard that, he was struck with wonder and reflected, "What is this? (31)
Oh, behold this infinite activity of the one of boundless power, who remains relying upon his illusory power (māyā) in the state of being the creator of all! (32)
Durvāsas said: Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one! Tell me, what may I do for you? By the very sight of you, my mind has attained great joy.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "If the Blessed One is pleased, then please come to my home; by bearing the water from Your feet upon my head, I shall attain purification."
Durvāsas said: "O Mādhava, why do you lead me away when my entire essence consists of intolerance? Lead me away only if you will carry out my word along with your wife."
Prahlāda said: Having said, "So be it," he indeed departed on his own chariot. Seeing Viṣṇu thus departing, [Hiraṇyakaśipu] laughed and spoke, reviling him.
Durvāsas said: "You do not know Durvāsas; release these excellent horses! Both you and this wife of yours must carry me in my own chariot. (37)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, O Brāhmaṇa, I shall do exactly as you say. O Compassionate One, O Brāhmaṇa, I, along with my kinsmen, have been saved by you.
Prahlāda said: That best of sages addressed those two—the goddess mounted on her own chariot and likewise the lotus-eyed one—saying, "Proceed! Proceed! (39).
Seeing that golden chariot being carried along, all the deities exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke thus to one another.
Oh, behold the supreme devotion of this god who is devoted to Brahman, for he carries the yoke upon his shoulder together with his wife! (41)
Being showered with flowers by the hosts of gods, Janārdana took the chariot and departed for Dvārakā together with his wife.
As that chariot was being driven along, Rukmiṇī became thirsty; the princess of Vidarbha, her eyes agitated by fatigue, spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
"Exhausted and oppressed by the burden, she carries an irritable Brahmin; O beloved, give her water to drink and lead me to your own home. (44)
Having heard those words of hers, the Blessed One brought forth from the surface of the earth by treading upon it with his foot the auspicious Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths.
Having seen that water—spotless, cool, fragrant, and purifying—the thirsty Queen Rukmiṇī drank the water of the Jahnavī.
Seeing that water drunk by her, the best of sages became enraged; blazing like a fire, he cursed the supreme goddess.
Durvāsas said: "Since you, O Rukmiṇī, have drunk water without asking me, therefore you shall always be addicted to drinking; of this there is no doubt. (48)
"Since water was drunk by you without my asking, even though the chariot is inseparable from me, therefore you shall be separated from Kṛṣṇa. (49)
Prahlāda said: Having spoken these words, his eyes bloodshot with anger, the brahmin abandoned the chariot and stood right there upon the ground.
Thus cursed, the goddess then wept most piteously, overwhelmed with distress, and spoke to Kṛṣṇa in a mournful voice: "How shall I remain without you? (51)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Goddess, I shall come to your abode twice every day. Whoever beholds me while I am stationed here beholds you alone."
For that man who, having seen me, does not behold you with devotion, half of the fruit of his pilgrimage shall be lost; of this there is no doubt. (53)
Having thus consoled his beloved, the joy of the Yadus then propitiated the sinless Brāhmaṇa Durvāsas.

Outside, in the midst of the wind, he worshipped him in that manner; having himself washed his own feet with the water used for washing the brahmin’s feet, Hari, the purifier of the world, held it upon his head.
Having offered the water of honor (arghya) and a cow to the brahmin with devotion, he fed that best of the twice-born according to the rules with food of six flavors.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Curse Given to Rukmiṇī by Durvāsas and the Bringing of Durvāsas to Dvārakā," in the fourth section, the *Dvārakāmāhātmya*, of the seventh book, the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: Oh, how great is the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, the deity who is devoted to the Brahmins and possesses immeasurable splendor, in that he did not make the word of the sage false!
Therefore, Janārdana, that guardian of the bridge, felt no anger toward him who bore upon his chest the mark of Bhṛgu’s foot-strike.
But how was that goddess separated from her beloved by him? O Lord of Asuras, tell me how she remained there all alone. (3)
We are exceedingly eager to hear about Dvāravatī with joy; first, we desire to know this in order to dispel the distress of our minds. (4)
Prahlāda said: "Listen, all you sages, as I relate in detail how the beloved of Hari was released from the suffering born of the curse."
Then, having received that piercing curse from Durvāsas, the wife of the lord of the Yādavas suddenly broke into lamentation.
Rukmiṇī said: "Ah, how auspicious this worldly saying is considered to be: 'In both a small well and in the ocean, there is no water exceeding the measure [of its capacity].'"
I am indeed most fortunate, having obtained as my lord the Master of the World; yet, due to the provocation of the gods by Paulastya, I have been left all alone.
Where is the glorious Hari, the abode of auspiciousness and possessor of faultless qualities; and where is this fickle woman of little merit, so full of distress? (9)
Nevertheless, the Creator, skilled in deception, ordained for me this painful affliction of separation as an inauspicious fate.
Otherwise, how could those who are honored for their lineage and have bathed in the path of the triple Veda deign to curse her, who was herself distressed and innocent? (11)

"Has he fashioned this heart of mine out of diamond? For it is indeed exceedingly hard, since it does not shatter into a hundred pieces despite the unbearable separation from the Slayer of Madhu. (12)
It was by virtue of this extremely difficult penance that my first son was obtained by me; yet, though deprived of my child, I have not died here even after five days.
Even having experienced this most terrible suffering, I shall then be saved; for that which truly shakes away my impurity surely approaches me with a hundred-thousandfold increase.

Thus, having lamented excessively, she, distressed in her purpose, grieved impetuously like a female osprey; with her heart reeling from separation and struck down by the curse of the twice-born, she immediately fainted. (15)
Then Rukmiṇī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, having been cursed by Durvāsas, fell into a swoon right there; indeed, the ocean arrived at that very spot.
With a breeze carrying the filaments of lotuses and filled with sprays of nectar, he fanned this goddess Rukmiṇī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
In the meantime, Nārada, lute in hand, arrived there through the path of the sky, singing the virtues of the Blessed One.
Having seen the Mother of the Universe being consoled by the ocean, Nārada, whose fame is well-known, descended and enlightened her.

Nārada said: "O Goddess, O Queen of the Gods, do not grieve for your husband, the Lord of Devas, who has been driven far away by the curse of a Brahmin; O auspicious one, maintain your fortitude. (20)
For you are indeed the Blessed Goddess in person, and Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Person; you have both descended by your own will to remove the burden of the earth.
For he is the divine Supreme Brahman, whose mind is ever free from despondency; you are the power of his illusion (māyā-śakti), who brings about the creation, maintenance, and end of the universe.
Having withdrawn everything, by that power (kalā) he, the self-ruling Lord, lies asleep; even then, the Sovereign, the Lord of the universe, is not separated from you.
The God of gods, the Lord of the universe, is eternally inseparable from you; in all his playful incarnations, you are his companion.
O sinless one, he does not undergo union or separation with you; rather, as the Lord, he imitates the ways of living beings for their benefit. (25)
Those who desire prosperity must constantly propitiate the gods on earth (brahmins); these ascetics, who know the ultimate truth, must never be provoked to anger.
Thus instructing the world, Hari—who was manifest yet concealed as a deceptive human—consented to their separation due to the sage’s curse. (27)
Do you remember, O auspicious lady, that I myself was born in the lineage of Raghu, seeking to favor the world and eager to remove the burden of the earth? (28)
O Rukmiṇī, do you not know that Hari is the Lord of the worlds? For he is indeed that very God who is dearer to him than his own life.
O lady of virtuous vows, this entire universe—both external and internal—is filled by Him; how could there be attachment for the All-pervading One who is unattached? Such is my thought. (30)

"I believe in every way that he has been commissioned by you; therefore, release this excessive anxiety and reflect upon yourself. Be gracious, O Mother, and summon fortitude through your own resolve. (31)
When the celestial sage had spoken thus and concluded, the Lord of Rivers addressed her with words of soft and golden tone.
The Ocean said: "O Goddess, that which the celestial sage has said after bowing to you is indeed the truth; for you are eternally sung of in the Vedas as Viṣṇu’s companion."

The Supreme Person himself, whose physical form has been cast aside, remains hidden as your sovereign; he repeatedly creates the universe and establishes its order by his own radiance, and with you as his companion, he sustains his manifest form.
Therefore, this weariness of yours is not appropriate in the slightest; for you always abide upon the chest of the one who bears the Śrīvatsa mark. (35)
"O Goddess, this divine Bhāgīrathī has arrived at my command; she shall indeed delight you constantly as an embodied being. (36)
Its water shall be soft, sweet, and adorned with lotuses; moreover, this entire region shall become a source of happiness for you. (37)
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with groves, frequented by elephants, and resounded with the sweet humming of bees.
With the grace of fresh sprouts, with auspicious clusters of flowers, with fruits resembling nectar, and likewise with rows of blossoming stalks; (39)
Endowed with the splendor of Nandana and delighting the mind and eyes, this forest here shall indeed become even more beautiful before long.
"O Mother, we are indeed always to be awakened by you; how then can you, whose nature is inaccessible, be awakened by us? (41)
Therefore, grant me leave, be gracious, O Supreme Goddess! Salutations to you, Mother of the Universe; again and again, salutations unto you. || 42 ||
Prahlāda said: Having spoken thus to the Mother of the World, the two of them departed as they had come; and the Goddess Bhāgīrathī herself arrived at that very place.
There a forest came into being, frequented by celestial trees, worthy of being resorted to by all the worlds, and abounding in fruits and flowers.
And by the grace of the beings, the river Gaṅgā, the remover of all sins, that stream which flows from the foot of Viṣṇu, adorned that region.
And by the words of the sage, by the diversion provided by the Gaṅgā, and by the beauty of that region, the king indeed attained some measure of health. (46)
Then, having heard that the goddess Viṣṇupadī was joined with the ocean, those full of faith came from here and there to that river of flowing waters.
And the people dwelling in Dvārakā, their hearts filled with joy at the beauty of the grove, flocked constantly to Rukmiṇī’s forest.
Having heard all of that in its entirety, Durvāsas, who is a portion of Śambhu, became enraged and, smiling, spoke this once more: || 49 ||
Durvāsas said: "Who in the three worlds, even the primordial Grandfather of the worlds among the gods, is able to make my word otherwise? (50)
Does this world not know that when I was stained by the impurity of anger toward Śakra, the three worlds then became bereft of their splendor? || 51 ||
Unaware of my curse, how can that Rukmiṇī take delight there in that forest, which resembles the Nandana grove and is frequented by people? (52)
Therefore, let all these trees have fruits unfit for human consumption; let them be deprived of all their beauty and stripped of their clusters of blossoms. (53)
But this river, scorched by a curse, is the crest-jewel of Hara; its water must be undrinkable, for it cannot remain here.
Prahlāda said: Then everything occurred there exactly as the sage had spoken; for the power of speech was indeed created by Viṣṇu himself for the Brahmins.
But that queen, observing what had thus occurred, was deeply distressed; she considered destiny, which repeatedly brought such calamities, to be insurmountable.
Then, having resolved that death was the remedy for her suffering, she tied something to the outside with her upper garment.
Then, having understood all of that, the storehouse of compassion—who dwells in the secret cave of the hearts of all beings—realized her situation and quickly departed on his vehicle, Suparṇa.
The Lord beheld the goddess in such a state, with a noose around her neck, beneath the branch of a tree, her eyes closed.

The compassionate one perceived her—whose multitude of ornaments had fallen away, whose vine-like body was emaciated, and whose lotus-face had lost its luster—as compassion personified; she who was intent on death, yet was the giver of happiness, possessed of virtues, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before her.

Having heard the cry of the lord of birds, she too opened her lotus-eyes and beheld Kṛṣṇa; with her lotus-eyes turned threefold, she recognized that her beloved friend, the lord of her life, had arrived.

Overwhelmed by horripilation, enveloped in shame, turbid with both anger and affection, and having uttered various lamentations, the Queen—her burden of grief now doubled—alas, became an object of manifold emotions for the eyes. (62)

Removing the noose from her who was trembling and desiring to release it, he took her hand with his beautiful lotus-like hand; then, enlivening her with words like nectar, he spoke these noble words: (63)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O timid one, what is this rash act you wish to perform so thoughtlessly? Pray, O Goddess, tell me; what indeed is the cause of your distress?"
You are knowledge and I am the supreme awakening; you are Māyā and I am the Lord. You are the intellect and I am the individual soul (jīva); how can there be a separation between us?
Those such as Brahmā and Śiva wander about with their minds deluded by you; how then can you be agitated? Do you not recognize your own true nature?
For it is by you that those sages are bound as they move about here through their actions; O woman of excellent complexion, how could a sage possibly curse you?

"O Goddess, this was my endeavor here for the sake of instructing the worlds. A man, possessed by my māyā, acts helplessly; behold how that lord of sages, whose soul was overwhelmed with anger, has now become tranquil. (68)
Prahlāda said: Then that best of sages, Durvāsas, having approached him bowed with devotion; after reflecting upon everything in his mind, he was overcome by remorse. (69)
Saying, "What have I done?", he approached him and fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, rolling about and drenched in tears.
He humbly sought forgiveness from his parents, the gods of the world, and, filled with devotion, he praised them with hymns of praise and secret mantras.
And he said this to the Lord of the World: "If you have favor toward me, then, O God, let my union with the Goddess be restored as it was before. (72)
Then Govinda, smiling, said to that best of sages: "Indeed, your word can never be false."
O twice-born one, how can this bridge established by me be destroyed? This bridge, practiced by the virtuous, is perfected and protects the world.
"O best of sages, I shall come twice every day and, out of desire, I will delight that daughter of the sage in various ways. (75)
I am not pleased by other means of practice, nor even by the recounting of my stories; rather, my delight will arise only when you have worshipped me here in this manner. (76)
And when I have indeed mounted upon Kuṇṭha, O great sage, then my entire splendor shall enter into Trivikrama.
And this Rukmiṇī shall again attain union with my own form; and this Bhāgīrathī as well, equal to the ocean in her qualities, having abandoned all sorrows, shall indeed go to happiness. (78)
Having thus bestowed his grace upon him along with the sage, Keśava entered his own city, having established the muni in close proximity to himself.
That goddess also, having understood his conduct at that time, became free from her fever through the grace of the Blessed One.
And because the goddess, beloved of Hari, was liberated from suffering there, she is therefore called Bhāgīrathī and Duḥkhamocinī (the Deliverer from Suffering).
On the new moon day or the full moon day, that man who bathes at her auspicious confluence is completely liberated from all suffering.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth day, the goddess Rukmiṇī, when beheld, grants all desires to men.
Thus has this been told by the Goddess, O sages: the liberation from suffering and the grace of the God. What more do you wish to hear? (84)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation from Rukmiṇī’s Sorrow," in the Dvārakā-māhātmya, the fourth section of the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, within the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 3 || || 7 ||
Śrī Prahlāda said: Thus honored by Hari, that best of brāhmaṇas, being thoroughly satisfied, spoke to Keśava, saying, "Choose a boon."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, you must remain here; you should never abandon this place."
Durvāsas said: "O Kṛṣṇa, if I remain [here], then you too, O Keśava, must remain with your sixteen parts forever at my word. (3)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O best of the twice-born, what fruit will you grant to those fortunate ones who behold both you and me here with devotion? O Blessed One, please tell us."
Durvāsas said: O Kṛṣṇa, that man who, having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, worships you and me, is liberated from all sins.
Likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, hear another thing: whatever wealth one shall give here after bathing, O Lord of Gods, he shall obtain sixteen times more than what was given to me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "That man who, having worshipped you, shall worship me here—to him I will grant liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to attain."

Prahlāda said: O best of Brahmins, after Kṛṣṇa and Durvāsas had joyfully granted each other boons, they both remained in that place from that time forward. That sacred site is called Varadāna, and it grants all desires. (8)
A man who bathes at Varadāna obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows; it was there that in ancient times the granting of boons occurred between Viṣṇu and Durvāsas.
O best of Brahmins, from that time onwards Hari has remained in Dvārakā; bound by the word of Durvāsas, he never leaves it.
Where the form of the Three-Striding One (Viṣṇu) resides and where the Gomatī flows, men shall attain liberation when they have joined with Cakratīrtha.
When Hari abandoned his body at Prabhāsa, his splendor, together with its constituent parts (kalās), was deposited within that very form.
Therefore, O Brahmins, in the Kali age Hari is not to be found elsewhere; if you have business with Kṛṣṇa, go there without delay.
The sages said: "Excellent, O best of devotees! Excellent, O guide of the path! For that which has been fully realized by you, no one else knows."
What is the fruit of going there, and what is the fruit of seeing Kṛṣṇa? What sacred fords (tīrthas) are located right there, and who are the deities? Tell us that. (15)
In which month, on which lunar day, and at which festival should men go [to the shrine], and what gifts should be given, O bull among the Danujas? (16)
