How much more so, then, for the excellent twice-born and especially the Kṣatriyas, as well as the Śūdras residing there who are engaged in the worship of the three castes? || 18 ||
During the entire month of Kārttika, the twice-born recite the Gītā before Kṛṣṇa, subsisting on a single meal, or eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for.
By means of the *kṛcchra* penance lasting three nights, as well as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, by barley-gruel, the *taptakṛcchra* and other such rites, and by fasting for a fortnight or a month; || 20 ||
And those who observe vows for the month of Kārttika, having bathed in the waters of the Gomatī as well as in the Rukmiṇī-hrada, pass their time there.
Having fasted on the pure Ekādaśī, which is free from contact with the Daśamī, they become dark-complexioned [deities] holding conchs, discs, and maces in their hands.
They perform the śrāddha rite on the twelfth lunar day at the pure Cakratīrtha, having fed the Brāhmaṇas with honey, milk-porridge, and ghee.
Having satisfied them according to the rules with devotion, and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability—namely cows, land, gold, garments, betel-leaf, and fruits.
Sandals, an excellent umbrella, water-filled jars, and white vessels filled with cooked food, accompanied by fruit and monetary gifts. (25)
Thus, for whoever performs [these rites] correctly in the month of Kārttika dedicated to Kṛṣṇa, the ancestors certainly attain a joy equal to that of Mārkaṇḍeya.
And Kṛṣṇa’s satisfaction, together with that of the thirty gods, becomes inexhaustible.
Those most meritorious men who remain for the month of Kārtika engaged in vows and charity, their bodies purified at Rathāṅgatīrtha, go to the holy and imperishable state.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Bathing, Giving Gifts, and Performing Śrāddha at Cakratīrtha in Kārttika," in the fourth section on the Greatness of Dvārakā, within the seventh part, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Prahlāda said: Blessed indeed are those people of the world who have offered water-libations in the Gomatī and who shall worship Kṛṣṇa with ketakī and tulasī leaves. (1)
There is no further rebirth for them here in this terrible thicket of saṃsāra; indeed, there is no death again for them, for they have attained immortality.
Whatever fruit might accrue from [feeding] ten million ascetics elsewhere, even more than that is obtained by feeding a single person in Dvārakā. || 3 ||
Dvārakā, when remembered in the mind, burns away all sins—past, present, and future; of this there is no doubt.
Having realized that in this terrible Kali age all has become senseless with cries of "Alas! Alas!", those best of men who do not abandon Dvārakā have achieved their life's purpose.
Wherein the creatures who have died always abide in Śvetadvīpa.
The Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa—these twenty-one classes of ancestors dwell in Dvārakā.
The sacred fords (tīrthas) such as Puṣkara, the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, the holy fields (kṣetras) such as Kurukṣetra, and the barren lands (ūṣaras) such as Kāśī. || 8 ||
The sacred bathing places for the ancestors such as Gayā, those such as Prabhāsa, whatever other holy sites there are, and the villages where they dwell—indeed, all these.
The cities of Kāśī and others always reside in the abode of Kṛṣṇa during the Kali age—an abode that eternally bestows liberation even upon sinners.

O tiger among Daityas, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, known as Prabodhinī, and on the full moon of Vaiśākha, as well as on the beginnings of the Kalpas and the beginnings of the Yugas—(11).
O leader of the Daityas, there is no doubt that [this applies] during lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginnings of the Manvantaras, during Vyatīpāta, Saṃkrānti, and Vaidhṛti.
Whatever water mixed with sesame seeds is offered at that spot out of devotion to the ancestors, preceded by a bath in the Gomatī, all that is declared to be inexhaustible.
Those who perform a śrāddha ceremony here, preceded by the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas), for them an imperishable satisfaction of the ancestors is produced.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Excellent Fruits of Bathing in the Gomatī, Worshipping Kṛṣṇa, Feeding Ascetics, Giving Gifts, and Performing Śrāddha," in the fourth section, the Dvārakāmāhātmya, of the seventh book, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 41 ||

Prahlāda said: Those who perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) on the full moon day of Vaiśākha or Kārtika, their ancestors, having been freed from the state of being a piśāca, go [to heaven] in Dvārakā. || 1 ||
Having committed such grave sins as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the wife of a preceptor—even those of this kind—2.
O Lord of Daityas, by merely bathing in the Gomatī and beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even those [sins] committed over ten million kalpas go to destruction.
Those men in the Kali age who behold Rukmiṇī with devotion, having circumambulated the city and recited the Thousand Names; || 4 ||
The entire universe has been circumambulated; of this there is no doubt. Whatever fruit is proclaimed elsewhere for great gifts (mahādānas), that is produced when Rukmiṇī is seen in Dvārakā. || 5 ||
When the twelfth day arrives, he who recites this greatness born of Dvārakā in the presence of Viṣṇu—listen, I shall tell you the fruit thereof.
And in all the worlds, he shines, moving at will in a lotus-colored vehicle adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Yoked with divine white horses and moving according to his will, he sports at pleasure with throngs of Apsarases until the dissolution of all beings.

And he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, endowed with ten million kalpas; just as fire is seen in all pieces of wood through friction, so too is Dharma seen in a man through the observance of the twelfth day (dvādaśī).

Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which was proclaimed by the ancestors: "May there be in our lineage a man who, having bathed in the Gomatī with faith and having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, performs the Śrāddha ceremony along with the Sapiṇḍana rite. (10)
"Perhaps there may be one in our family who, having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, beholds Kṛṣṇa for our deliverance. (11)
"Is there perhaps someone in our family who, having heard this greatness of Dvārakā from the mouth of a brāhmaṇa, will worship it with devotion? (12)
"In our family there shall be one who goes to the city of Dvārakā; having reached there on the pure twelfth day (dvādaśī), he who shall perform the vigil (jāgara). (13)
"In our family, there will be born either a son or likewise a daughter who, while offering praise, shall recite the Thousand Names of Kṛṣṇa before Him. (14)
May there be one born in our family who is firm in his vows and who indeed pleases the Vaiṣṇavas by the gift of Gopīcandana. || 15 ||
"Perhaps there may be one in our family who, having conquered his senses, shall recite the greatness of Dvārakā in the presence of the Vaiṣṇavas. (16)
"There will be great glory for our family arising from Dvārakā; having written this, he will keep it in his own home for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa. (17)
The gift of gold, the gift of cows, and likewise the gift of land—these would be as if given for the duration of one's entire life by whoever wears this in the Kali age. (18)
By him who has caused this to be heard in the Kali age, the *taptakṛcchra*, the *mahākṛcchra*, and even the month-long fast have been performed throughout his entire life. (19)
Atonements have been performed for the destruction of sins, and by him the greatness of Dvārakā has been spread throughout the Kali age.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin remain with a person for so long as that creature does not write down this Māhātmya originating from Dvārakā.
What is the use of all those gifts and all those immersions in sacred fords for one who has this greatness of Dvārakā written in his home? (22)
It is the pacifier of all suffering, the accomplisher of all tasks, the eternal bestower of the four aims of life, and the increaser of devotion to Hari. || 23 ||
He certainly incurs no debt, nor does he have any fear of Yama, where he recites the greatness arising from Dvārakā. (24)
In whosever house this remains written, that very place is a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). Now listen with attention to the majesty arising from Dvārakā.

Keśava accepts even a worship that is deficient in ritual rules, mantras, and rites, provided that the greatness [of this text] remains perpetually written in his house; such a person is not tainted by even thousands of committed sins. (26)
Whoever reads or even hears this greatness arising from Dvārakā shall experience neither deficiency of the elements nor deficiency of dharma.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should remember this greatness arising from Dvārakā and what has been said regarding all the twelfth days (dvādaśīs), obtains that fruit.
He who indeed recites this account of the origin of Dvārakā is constantly worshipped by the thirty gods and honored by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas. (29)

Wherever Dvārakā dwells, there is the eternal Viṣṇu; there are all the sacred fords (tīrthas), all the gods including Indra, the sacrifices, the Vedas, the sages, and the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving. || 30 ||
For no human being, my son, is indeed capable of going to Dvārakā; rather, the merit and majesty born from the sight of Kṛṣṇa shall accrue to one who recites this.
Truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, wealth, good character, forgiveness, and straightforwardness—all these are fruitless for him who does not hear of his majesty. (32)
Within six months, a son shall be born and prosperity indeed increases for him who listens with devotion to this greatness arising from Dvārakā. (33)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Performing Rites such as the Release of a Bull in the Field of Dvārakā and Listening to the Greatness of Dvārakā," within the Fourth Section on the Greatness of Dvārakā, in the Seventh Book (Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 42 ||
Prahlāda said: He who worships Sāvitrī, Bhavānī, Durgā, and Sarasvatī with tulasī leaves shall be endowed with the fulfillment of all desires. || 1 ||
Having taken a *tulasī* leaf, one should worship Viṣṇu with devotion; by him, all that exists—including gods, asuras, and humans—is worshipped. (2)
Those who worship Maheśāna on the fourteenth day, Pitāmaha on the full moon day, and Gaṇādhipa with Tulasī on the seventh day; || 3 ||

The water from the conch is superior to the best of sacred fords; the water from the feet is superior to the best of sacred fords. The remains of the food offering are equal to ten million sacrifices; the remains of the floral offerings are equal to vows and gifts.
Whoever eats the remnants of Mukunda’s meal day after day, for every single mouthful, there shall be merit exceeding that of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts. || 5 ||

The man who daily eats the remnants of the food offering mixed with *tulasī*, especially those combined with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, attains the merit of ten million times ten million sacrifices.

He who, with devotion, offers the remnants of Hari’s meal to the ancestors and the deities at the time of the śrāddha—by that very act, through the funeral cakes mixed with the fragrant grasses, his ancestors remain well-satisfied for ten million kalpas.
He who sounds a bell as a musical instrument during the time of the rites of bathing and worship before Vāsudeva shall obtain the merit of giving ten million cows.
The bell, consisting of all musical instruments, is always dear to Keśava; by sounding it, a man obtains merit equal to the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
But in the absence of musical instruments, at the time of worship and always, men should sound a bell, because it embodies the essence of all musical instruments.
Whoever offers sandalwood produced from Tulasī wood to Hari shall burn away every sin accumulated over hundreds of previous births.
If one offers Tulasī wood and sandalwood upon the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the ancestors, the ancestors attain satisfaction just as they would from a śrāddha performed at Gayā.
In the Kali age, sandalwood from the wood of the tulasī plant is always beloved by all the gods, and especially by Hari and the ancestors.
Those who, though being devotees of Hari, do not always offer sandalwood paste from tulasī wood to Viṣṇu, are not true devotees in the Kali age.
He whose body is cremated by the fire of *tulasī* wood goes to the world of Viṣṇu, even if he is being led away by Yama.

If even a single piece of Tulasī wood should be placed in the midst of the wood [of a funeral pyre], then at the time of cremation, one is liberated from tens of millions and thousands of crores of sins.
Seeing a man being consumed by the fire of *tulasī* wood, Janārdana is gratified by him for thousands of millions of births.
As the man is being consumed by the fire of Tulasī wood, all the hosts of gods stationed in their celestial chariots scatter handfuls of flowers upon him.
There, O Lord of Daityas, where the fire of Tulasī wood blazes, the delighted Apsaras dance and sing songs in melodious tones.
Viṣṇu, together with Śambhu, being well-pleased, cast his gaze upon him.
Taking that man by the hand himself, Śauri wiped away his sins before the very eyes of the inhabitants of heaven, having first performed a great festival preceded by shouts of "Victory! (21).
Sūta said: Having heard the majesty of Dvārakā as proclaimed by Prahlāda, all the sages as well as Bali, the lord of the Daityas, were greatly delighted.
Then, having all congratulated Prahlāda, the bull among the Daityas, they set out for Dvārakā to behold the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa.
Then those sages of rigid vows, having arrived at Dvārakā together with Balarāma, bathed in the Gomatī according to the prescribed rites.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa, having worshipped him, and having performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites, they gave many gifts and thereby became fulfilled.
They went to their own abodes; Bali went to Pātāla, and having quickly prostrated before Prahlāda, he considered his purpose fulfilled.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Pilgrimage to Dvārakā Performed by the Brāhmaṇa with Bālin," following the conclusion of the Dialogue between Prahlāda and the Brāhmaṇa, which included the description of the fruits of hearing the *Dvārakāmāhātmya* and the subsequent description of the greatness of the *Tulasī* leaf and wood, within the *Dvārakāmāhātmya*, the fourth section of the seventh book (*Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: This entire Purāṇa was formerly spoken by Skanda to Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā; from him, Aṅgiras likewise received it.
From him Cyavana received it, and from him the sage Ṛcīka; thus it was transmitted in succession throughout all the worlds.
This Skanda Purāṇa was formerly extracted by Kumāra; the man who hears it in the midst of the virtuous is liberated from sin.
This Purāṇa, which bestows long life and grants happiness to the four castes, was composed here by the great-souled Ṣaṇmukha with constancy.
Thus has this narrative been fully declared; may prosperity be unto you.
If a person should listen to the Skanda Purāṇa, which is adorned with seven sections, no one would be able to calculate the extent of his merit.
He who bestows this greatness of the Dharma upon a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the heavenly world for as long as the number of its syllables.
Just as the drops of rain when it rains, or as the stars in the sky, or as the sands in the Ganges—likewise, their number is not known.
Whatever man listens with devotion for even a few days, he shall become successful in all his aims; so too the man who recites this.
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring wealth obtains wealth; and a maiden desiring a husband obtains a charming husband.
Relatives who are abroad obtain reunion with one another; indeed, by hearing the Skanda Purāṇa, a man attains his heart's desire.
It bestows all desires upon men who hear it and read it. || 12 ||
Having heard this ancient Purāṇa, one indeed attains long life; a king conquers the earth and also overcomes his enemies. (13)
A Brahmin learned in the Vedas shall become free from fear; a Kṣatriya shall obtain a kingdom; likewise, a Vaiśya shall obtain wealth and grain, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness.
Whoever should hear even one chapter, or a verse, or even half a verse, or should hear a single quarter-verse of it, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, whoever honors the reciter after hearing this Purāṇa, by him Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra themselves have been fully honored. (16)
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no object on earth by giving which he could truly become free from debt. (17)
Therefore, Vyāsa, the instructor of the scriptures, must be fully honored with cows, land, gold, garments, and other such gifts, as well as with foods that provide for all desires.
He who, endowed with such devotion, having heard this unsurpassed scripture, honors the instructor, shall attain the state of Śiva. || 19 ||
Merely by hearing the Purāṇas, the sin accumulated over many births is pacified, and one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 20 ||
May he who protects you—though all the gods die from the nectar residing within his belly, yet he himself lives despite the poison situated in his throat—protect you! 21.
Vyāsa said: When the Sūta had ceased after speaking thus, the great ṛṣis, Śaunaka and the others, having honored the Sūta according to the rules and praised him, then greeted him with joy.
The sages said: "The primary creation has been described by you, as well as the secondary creation, the history of the dynasties and their branches, and the sequence of the Purāṇas. (23)
The duration of a Manvantara, the expansion of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), and the true nature of the celestial sphere have been described exactly as they are. (24)
"We are blessed, we have accomplished our purpose, having heard the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa from your lotus-like mouth, O Sūta; we are exceedingly delighted. (25)
We, the great sages and brahmins, bestow upon you our blessings today: O highly wise disciple of Vyāsa, live long and be happy! (26)
Having thus bestowed blessings upon him and given him garments and ornaments, they dismissed the charioteer Lomaśa and then proceeded with the sacrificial rites.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion Marking the Completion of the Entire Skanda Mahāpurāṇa Text and the Account of the Honoring of Sūta," following the description of the greatness of listening to, reciting, and gifting the book of the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, as well as the worship of the Paurāṇika and Vyāsa, within the Dvārakāmāhātmya, the fourth section of the seventh Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 44 ||
